title: I DSD And So Can You
text:
Although folks will mainly try to choose their DAC on reports of the sound, my experience has been that all DACs for the last 8 years or so sound great. Tonal differences are (almost?) all down to taste, I think, with these tastes largely breaking down between DACs that are highly-detailed and with upper-mid/high emphasis (supposedly most Sabre-based DACs and Schiit, for example) versus those (like this one, Nad, AudioEngine D3) that people describe as "not the last word in detail" and "musical/non-fatiguing." I've had several over the past 14 years, and they all sounded awesome at the time. So, beyond the basic tonal divide, selecting based on features makes more sense to me, particularly within a given price bracket: the IDSD Nano is friggen huge compared to things like the Microstreamer or Dragonfly, for example; Microstreamer and IDSD are the ones that work with an IPhone without adding a powered hub; LH Geek Out is the one that drives any headphones to ear-bleeding levels without further amping; IDSD and Geek Out have DSD playback (for all two of the free DSD tracks you can legally obtain...); and the IDSD runs on a
battery (like another more expensive unit called the Glacier), eliminating drain on your mobile host device.

Comparisons, based on 2 months ownership [now 6 months], all listening through Senheizer HD-600s...
* HRT Microstreamer: The Microstreamer remains a real contender. It has a "fatter" tone. Instruments are less well-defined than on the Nano and the MS has more emphasis in the upper midrange. When feeding a dedicated amp, the MS is more fun and makes the Nano by comparison sound "polite." The Nano is more accurate, however, offering better definition and soundstage depth, and I prefer it slightly over the MS sans additional amp. By comparison, its mids are slightly leaner and has a spotlit quality to the highs (again, this is relative to the MS). I find the difference unimportant, though, next to feature choices.
* TEAC UD-501: This unit packs in lots of audiophile voodoo for 4x the price of the IDSD Nano. I would predict that the IDSD Micro would be somewhat similar, save for the addition of the IFI warmer "house" sound, since it's a similar dual-DAC-chip design. The UD-501 is noticeably more open than the other two units, with more resolved depiction of instruments (they can sound somewhat toy-like on the portables in a side-by-side comparison, but not in real-world listening), and there is more extension both on top and in the bass. I credit the increased channel separation of the two-chip design. Also a more neutral sound, which in fact is a bit boring to me on rock music in these comparisons. Long-term, though, "boring" = neutral = transparent, and so the TEAC is what I stay plugged into long term (and why colorful equipment by contrast always eventually ends up as a FOTM). The TEAC's sonic superiority is in the "noticeable" range, not a gasp or anything that I would cross the room for.
On speakers, however, the difference becomes very important . I have a very good and "neutral" setup with Dynaudio Excite X-12s and the TEAC AX-501. Playing both DACs through the same generic RCA cable, USB cable, and amp, the IDSD Nano just loses out to the UD-501 to a small but obvious degree on all counts, sounding just "lighter," bass not as extended and vocals and other instruments less etched than the UD-501 (Microstreamer, same limitations but moreso). Still good against this quality of DAC, but--as its designer has said--the IDSD Nano was designed around headphones, with the fact that it makes a "passable" preamp being a "not insignificant side effect." I swapped these out a couple of times to at least reduce the chances of self-delusion, and really it's pretty plain on speakers, whereas the IDSD sounded just slightly more "lush" on headphones because of the same qualities.
All of the DACs noted above use the Bur-Brown 1793 (MS, Nano) or 1795 (UD) chips, where the latter is just the 32-bit, sonically-the-same version of the former.

Note six months after purchase: I just purchased a pair of IEMs and these reveal a hiss from the IDSD Nano, plus I can hear clicks (stepping) from the volume knob. The clicks are barely audible, but the hiss is definitely "there" until the music starts, and so that higher noise floor will have an effect on perception, though not a particularly important one. IEMs do generally reveal hiss in these portable DACs. Might be worth trying a 75-Ohm in-line adaptor to increase the impedance. There are cheap after-market knock-offs of the Etymotic ER4P-to-ER4S adaptors that would work.
More importantly, my IEMs (Fidue A83) are forward/warm in the midrange and sound harsh through the iDSD Nano, revealing that both the IDSD Nano and the Microstreamer (again, both of which have the same 1793 chip) lift the midrange as well. What this means is that I'd be weary of buying the Nano if your headphones/earphones have a very warm or forward midrange. The IDSD might make them sound harsh. (For frequencies much higher than 8kHz, my own hearing is not good enough to make recommendations)

I've been surprised by two things: First, the IDSD drives the Senheizer HD-600s pretty well. Only a couple of times have I felt the need for very slightly more power, although peak volume should be "only" 105dB with 91dB or so averages for highly-dynamic recordings, according to the math (IDSD seems to put out 1.6V by inferring from the 80w @32ohms spec, although the designer stated 1.8V for the rca jacks). Results are similar for the HE-400s: it's plenty for most of us, almost all the time, with both of these headphones. For me the break point thus far seems to be a dynamic range of 15 or lower, which means quite literally 99.9% of my extensive collection. I do have an ICan Micro (not nano) here as well, but it doesn`t add anything to my experience of the Nano other than volume. "Stacking" the IFI units is not automatically recommended: try it on its own first, like I SHOULD have done. The Schiit Magni would be well worth considering, if you do need more power. Use volume to make that determination, though, not metaphorical claims about "grabbing it with more authority" or the like. That's because, like most of these devices, it will not distort even at full volume, since a computer source normally won't go above 0dbfs and the output voltage is fixed to deliver that level cleanly. The knob controls an analog (not digital) signal attenuator to scale BACK the output voltage to the desired level. So, all that's left is whether or not it gets loud enough for ya. I'm not an engineer, but that's what engineers I've read/talked to have said. The IDSD, like the Microstreamer, implements volume strictly in the analog domain, not risking the loss of resolution (1 bit for each -6dB) that is the result of digital volume attenuation, like the Geek Out (so, all those folks grabbing the Geek Out 1000 for their IEMs and then turning it way down are getting low-res audio, in effect. You can have excessive gain).

The second surprise was DSD. Once I got it working in Foobar (geeks only: otherwise, don't try this at home), I was pretty surprised. Given DSD material that is actually good, there's an immediate sense of sharper attacks on toms, snares, and high-hats; noticeably better instrument separation; and just overall a sense of more clarity and space--in short, what we were promised with 24-bit PCM, but for real this time. It's not "huge," but it is immediately apparent. I've never heard anything like it, but my long-dormant teenage memories of LPs stir.
I do not, however, notice any benefits at all transcoding PCM to DSD for playback, as some have claimed (nor do I hear any negative effects of just leaving the Foobar DSD output component active all the time for PCM material). Also, mediocre SACDs that don't improve much or at all on the Redbook version (which seems to be a whole lot of them) remain not worth it as SACD rips, of course, if you're going that route. DSD isn't at all likely IMO to ever become widespread, since blue-ray seems to be faring better than SACD did as a medium, and virtually all studio masters today are PCM to start with and so PCM downloads make more sense. However, I've included my DSD listening notes at the end of the review FWIW.
Like many of the DSD-capable DACs, this one uses DoP (DSD over PCM), which is a protocol that transmits the DSD data in a PCM "wrapper." This is not a damaging conversion to PCM, but just the addition of header bits. It is indistinguishable to me from the "native DSD" mode the UD-501 is capable of. Finally, the filter switch on this unit, while seeming to have no effect in PCM mode, definitely makes music sound "harder" and brighter in the down position, implying that there's less filtering of high frequencies there than in the default "up" position, despite the confusing labels on the switch.

A unique feature of the IDSD (Nano as well as the upcoming IDSD Micro) is that it runs on batteries, even when it is charging the battery through the USB connection. This is an electrical noise solution as well as a big benefit for I-device/Android users (extra cables required), since there should be no "too much power" error messages and it won't drain the phone/tablet's battery while in use. Plugging the iPhone 5 into the camera connector>IDSD was flawless. I would note that, by the same token, I'm not interested in the IDSD Micro, judging from the specs pre-release, because these devices both have lithium-polymer batteries that, like all batteries, only have so many hundreds of charges in them before requiring replacement at the factory. I'm reluctantly ok with that in an Apple device, but not my stereo equipment. I'm also ok with it for the Nano's price, but not higher. One annoyance I've already experienced is that, when I forget to turn the IDSD off and it's unplugged, I can't get it to be recognized by the computer next time, even in USB-powered mode, until I let the battery charge up. This has happened a couple of times now.

The reviewer who noted that Windows is required for the firmware upgrade is regrettably correct, though you only need to knock on your buddy's door or go to the office once to do it. The firmware update (which of course is already installed for new units) does fix the problem they were having with my MBA's USB 3 ports (I run Windows 8.1 via bootcamp, btw).
One other note on firmware/drivers: People often mistakenly talk about 24/192-capable DACs as being newer or more advanced than those that top out at 96kHz, not understanding that this is about USB class-1 vs. class-2, which is not the same thing as the USB spec version (1.1, 2.0, 3.0). I had an asynchronous 24/192 DAC back in 2006 with the AKM 4396 chip (that was the E-MU 0404 USB: today, the AudioEngine D3 and Schiit Modi use this chip), long before there was any 24-bit commercial music available. Class-1 devices rely on adaptive rather than isochronous/asynchronous mode and top out at 96kHz (AudioEngine D3, Microstreamer, Dragonfly) because the manufacturer didn't want to require users to install a driver under Windows. ...Well, that fact, and the fact that hi-res music is more about marketing than big sound quality gains. Unlike OS X, IOS, Android, and Linux, Windows does not build in native support for class-2, for no other reason than Microsoft's lack of interest. Hence, class-2 devices (including all 192-capable DACs, like Merridian Explorer, IDSD, Geek Out) require a driver under Windows. Some of us have had bad experiences with manufacturers ceasing to update drivers at a certain point, leaving us with a brick or else an outdated Windows version. For the IDSD, good news is that the driver from AMR/IFI seems stable, and the control panel applet provides reference information.

Let's see, what else?
* rca-type digital pass-through in case you want to, um, bypass the DAC...? Actually, I can think of two uses for this: 1) I used it to compare this to another DAC by switching between them without unplugging the IDSD from the computer. 2) you can use it to connect an IPhone to your DAC, which could be cool.
* LED light changes color for every--EVERY--variation of bitrate you can play. "What's your favorite color, Baby?"
* Inserting anything into the headphone jack mutes the rca outputs.
* The Windows volume control has no effect on the unit's analog volume control, so it's all with the knob.
* It comes with a generic (no ferride beads) USB cable, a little over 1 ft. in length. Also, a typical thin anti-scratch draw-string bag, which has a cut-out for the USB cable to come out. Also included are little silicon stick-on feet and an odd little plasticky pad, which I guess you can use as an alternative (it's not adhesive, though). Finally, a couple of useless rubber bands for strapping it to your phone.
* The Amazon Basics portable hard drive hard shell case (or the CaseLogic version) makes an ideal protective travel case for the Nano, though you need to wrap the cable around the unit for it to fit. Really nice fit, though, and protects the knob and switch.
* Upon reading some of designer Thorsten Loesch's comments about designing the DAC, I came away thinking that its approach to both PCM and DSD was unique and innovative. However, upon further research, it seems to be just the way the BB 1793 and 1795 chips do things: top 6 bits through multibit and the rest as delta-sigma. Same as the UD-01/301/501. Look it up, if you must:) IFI is as bad as its competitors these days at using the engineers as promoters deploying advanced techno-snow. Which doesn't make the products "bad," though.
* Another annoyance I've had is that the device is only recognized on the USB port where it was connected when I installed the driver. It could be a port issue, but my hunch is that the driver is device-identifier specific and tied to the original port.
* Oh, and I think the little slants on the case top and faceplate accents at the corners are homely.

End of product review. But... DSD listening tests, my two cents: Since we now have DSD playback for under $200, I'll include some commonplace notes on my experiences with DSD--mainly from the past couple of weeks with the IDSD, but I've also had an SACD player for a few years and a few SACDs. As a perspective that runs counter to the DSD enthusiasts (e.g., Andreas Koch), there's some good skeptical (Mark Waldrop) and open-minded (Archimago) info out there about DSD versus PCM. I got a friend to make SACD rips of some SACDs that either I or he owned, so that I could make some comparisons with CDs and commercial hi-res purchased downloads of the same albums. Results below.
1) Redbook layer vs. DSD layer of the same discs: When sourced from an analog tape master, most DSD layers exhibited the benefits I noted above. Not particularly subtle, disc after disc. Highly addictive. On the other hand, when the master was known to be 16-bit PCM (starting around 1983, and almost all recordings from late 80s until PCM 24-bit recording became common around 2000), I could hear little if any difference on headphones. At the moment, my take on this is that any PCM stage in the mastering process kills the DSD advantages. Maybe it's about the PCM filtering, or maybe it's about DSD's different approach. So, it's good so far for me with analog tape masters dumped directly to DSD without a lot of PCM DAW tinkering.
2) 24/96 vs. DSD: First comparison was between two contemporaneous excellent dynamic masterings of the same analog tapes, one analog>DSD and the other analog>24/96. The only difference seems to be mastering choices, with the DSD somewhat more dynamic (1-2 dB), warmer, rolled-off at the top; 24/96 a bit louder, more power, a "dry" sound, but so slight as not to be noticeable except in close comparison. This was also true for a couple of SACDs vs. my commercial 24/44 versions of the same albums. However, when I compared my HDTracks 24/96 flat transfer of an album to the equivalent DSD (different and nastily-EQ-goosed mastering), there was the DSD magic again by comparison. Maybe the differences, such as they are, are more noticeable on certain kinds of music. Wish I had more material to test with.
3) Found several CDs I prefer to the SACDs, usually because of the SACD using a later generation of master tape or being too compressed. CDs are dead, long live CDs.
4) Put a bullet next to this one, because it's the take-away. HDTracks 24/88.1 (the downsample they sell of an SACD) versus the same mastering in original DSD: HDTracks badly washed out and weak by comparison! I'm attempting to account for the -6dB gain that happens when downsampling in Foobar, also. This is also what I experience with downsampling my own DSD test tracks. Maybe less so with 176kHz PCM, but still the "magic" goes out of the recording. I now regret all the 24/88kHz albums I've bought, since I believe all of these to have been downsamples of SACDs.
Why does DSD seem to have sharper attack and a slightly more life-like presentation, particularly if the source is directly from analog masters to DSD? Theory 1: DSD was designed to allow high-quality reproduction with simpler circuitry, according to a very old Stereophile article--just 1-bit quantization, like 90s CD players, at super high sampling rate with a low-pass filter. So, maybe even in these little DACs, DSD just has more punch because of constraints on the PCM side of the "budget" DAC implementation. There's something to this, since virtually all DAC chips today use delta-sigma anyway for PCM, with the old Bur-Brown PCM 1704 being the only true multi-bit chip still in production that I know of. 1795/1793 use a hybrid approach. Theory #2: it's a psycho-acoustic phenomenon. Humans actually don't like high fidelity in certain ways. Our brains are hard-wired to filter out background noise, and things like tape hiss or other forms of noise get naturally filtered out, making the result sound immediate and exciting. This is ONE reason for the LP and analog devotion. DSD does apparently carry a lot of ultrasonic noise in the signal (quantization errors), with the dance being to filter out just enough but not too much. The noise-shaping algorithms could even be "thinning out" the sound, imparting a slight holographic-seeming cast to it. Also, the real world has a lot of ambient high-frequency content--many blind people rely on this fact as a navigational aid, calling it "echolocation." It's random in a DSD recording, but maybe it delivers a heightened sense of being in a 3D space. In short: shrug. Theory 3: maybe 1-bit quantization just rocks, or there's something fundamentally flawed with PCM that we haven't measured yet.
While it seems to be the case that the format does sound SLIGHTLY different from PCM, I doubt it's greater fidelity to the source signal, strictly speaking. But some material seems to take advantage of whatever difference exists, because those particular discs/files sound truly amazing.

title: Darth Vader's Bass Amp
text:
Ok, I know: Darth would go for one of SVS's giant cylindrical subwoofer monsters, but let's move on.

I only want to answer one question here, which is the one question I couldn't find any answer to when I was thinking about buying this sub: if I already have a moderately good sub that goes down to 32Hz, will the sound of a "better" sub really sound better, and will the extra extension down to 24Hz or 27Hz matter? This is on a music-only system.

Answer: yes.

I had a Klipsch RW-8 8" front-ported sub that, when it first came out in 2003, cost close to the same as the SB-1000 and got much better reviews than the other Klipsch subs in its vicinity, and good reviews all around. I bought it as B-stock and had it for 9 years before wanting to go to a "Class D" amplifier in a sub to keep the power consumption down. The "auto-off" function of Class-D subs is supposed to be much more reliable than traditional Class-AB active subs, which apparently keep running the amp even when in standby but only disconnect the voice coil (or whatever).

To answer my question about bass extension, I disconnected the LR speakers and listened ONLY to the sub, turning its cut-off frequency all the way down to 40Hz. I was stunned at how much content still came through the sub. And if that were the case, lower extension would yield a much more resolved set of notes down there.

It sure did. I took advantage of SVS's generous return policy to give it a shot, and I heard notes I'd never suspected existed on albums featuring synthesized bass. Pink Floyd's "Welcome to the Machine" became a different experience. Erykah Badu's "Rim Shot" filled in gaps I already suspected were probably gaps. Brian Eno's _Another Day On Earth_ made me briefly think I was having a heart attack, because something very dark and heavy I'd never heard/felt before on this familiar album was trying to break out of my chest from behind! ...ok, I turned the sub down a bit at that point. I've read in several places that low-E on a bass guitar is supposedly 40Hz, but electric bass lines on, say, the Staples Singers' _Be Altitude_ are much more well-defined than on the older sub as well.

Keeping the sub "blended" at low gain and only a few clicks up from the lowest cut-off frequency was ultimately the right setup for my system for a "natural" integration. Even here, the blackness of the notes is just strikingly juicier than what I was getting before. So yep, it was worth it for me.

It also fits nicely underneath the little shelf unit i use for my other mini-components (see my other recent reviews), so that it in effect occupies 0 space.

Finally, another great bit of design is that the knobs (which are "fake" knobs in that they just change digital processor parameters) are stepped. They "click" into position, in other words, and so won't ever slip from where you set them.

The veneer is very thin vinyl and unimpressive.

Only other complaint is that the speaker-level binding posts are too shallow for the banana plugs that I have--two different kinds, in fact. So, I have to use bare wire. [update: I think one is supposed to just open the terminals all the way, since they tighten in that position as well and the banana plugs sit inside the binding post this way. I have an amp that does the same thing]

Finally, the class D amp seems to put out a lot of RFI, because I have a tuner that fuzzes out whenever the sub powers up and then goes back to normal when it goes into standby. Older class D modules were pretty famous for this. I didn't ever notice this behavior when I had a better tuner (Sony XRF-HD1) in the system, however.

title: Initially didn't think it was a dog, but it is at least a small dog
text:
Promised update: Yep, 5 GHz performance issues, as so many other people report. And USB transfer speeds aren't great (average of less than 300mbps, at least in Windows). So, I do not recommend this router. Particularly since every brand new computer I'm looking at buying to carry me through the lifespan of the router has only 2x2 antennas. Still, its direct Netgear and Linksys competitors don't have some of the software features on the stock firmware.
I tried file transfer tests after maybe a week to 10 days uptime, and indeed read speeds from my usb 3.0 drive connected to the router dropped to 14.1 MB/s for a 1.8Gb iso file. Write speeds were only slightly slower than measured previously, at 28-41 MB/s. I turned off all "AI Protection" features, but impact was negligible. I rebooted the router and read speeds immediately went back up to 35-41MB/s and same for write speeds. I have also noticed several times that, when I open the lid of my laptop, the system tray icon indicates that I am/was on the 2.4 GHz band, suggesting that it had disconnected/reconnected to the 5GHz band at some point. So, I enabled the reboot schedule again.

---original review---
Wow, this has to be the most-maligned router I've seen, after looking at all the Small NetBuilder threads. Review comes after more than a week for me, and I am obsessive about updating my reviews; so, what you read below does hold on the date you're reading it, unless I'm dead or the like.

I picked up a refurb unit from "the vendor formerly known as Egghead" on the chance that (a) "refurbished" meant factory-refurbished in case the 5GHz drop-out problems were hardware rather than firmware (I have no idea if my unit was factory refurb or just customer return) and (b) I'd luck out otherwise. So far, I have. I'm on fw 9460 and never a dropped connection on 5G, despite having 100% Apple devices (the two biggest gripes about this router).

My only let-down was range, which isn't much different than the NetGear WNDR3700 v1 it replaces. Throughput at a given range is greater, though: up to double for 2.4GHz 11n and about triple for 11AC (over the prior 5 GHz 11n.

My router is at the back of a 1700sqft 1-story house. Speed is extremely limited 50ft away in the front bedroom, still. But I can connect on the front porch with AC, whereas I couldn't with 5 GHz n before.

Clients:
I am reserving 5 GHz for 11ac clients, so just a mid-2013 MBA (mainly running Windows under Bootcamp) and ATV4.
2.4Ghz: ATV2, 2011 MBP, Ipad Mini, crappy Lenovo mini PC, Iphone 5S and 5C.
ethnernet wired: printer, MyBookLive first-gen.
USB: 4 Tb Mybook

2.4 GHz environment is extremely crowded, thanks to an apartment building 20 feet away from my house. So, no such thing as >144mbps (20 Hz channels). Under these conditions, I can get 100mbps "connection rate" according to Windows in the acursed front bedroom on the MBA, but varies from 4-20 mbps on an iphone (note: "connection rate" is what Network Settings reports, not throughput).
ATV4 gets my full 52mbps downlink service according to Speedtest, 50 feet away on 11ac.

I am using universal beamforming on the 2.4GHz band and explicit beamforming for the two 11ac clients. Not sure if the explicit beamforming is doing anything, but it seemed like my reported connection rate at my desk was consistently 586mbps before turning it on, and 708 after. The universal beam forming (which I think of as "the Eye of Sauron") seems to take awhile to "see" the client, but throughput will go way up at long range after the first speedtest run, so I suspect, without having really run back and forth to test it, that the beamforming is helping at long range. I haven't seen obvious disconnects on Apple devices due to beamforming, as reported anecdotally by others.

With a 708mbps "connection rate," I can get up to 48MB/sec upload rates to a USB 3.0 hard drive connected to the router (same room, some obstructions, 11ac). That's about 380mbps upload on wi-fi, so I'm not unhappy. More typical write speed is 34MB/s average sustained when copying a 1.8Gb iso file, and about the same for read speed. This is with an NTFS drive and copying in Windows Exploder. I've read that ftp would be significantly faster, and so protocols may be the bottleneck (e.g., maybe a Linksys WRT1900 wouldn't do much better in this scenario). Plugging the drive directly into the computer yields 138MB/s write and a read speed too fast for me to even read when copying the file.

On the 2.4 GHz band, meanwhile, the USB 3.0 drive does degrade the signal, though not enough to nix an internet link. I consider it a minor problem. Asus put the USB 3.0 jack on the front to help with this, since the AC68U really had it bad in this regard, apparently (the Linksys ESATA option looks very attractive, consequently). But hey, I'm on 5GHz, so I got mine, jack; and the GF hasn't complained yet.

Turning on anti-virus and the like on the router impacts performance somewhat, but not dramatically.

I keep looking at reviews of routers like the Nighthawk x4 and Linksys WRT1900AC with "buyer's remorse" since, after all, I'm supposed to hate this router like everyone else, right? But my MBA has been connected for more than a day on 5 GHz without a drop, and I've never seen a dropped connection. I was telling the router to reboot nightly, but realized that wasn't a fair reliability test and so turned that off yesterday.

I've used the torrent app, Telnetted in to disable stp, turned on adaptive QOS and all the other whistles, and never a hitch. I also really like the AICloud iphone app, since I can actually read/download from all the shares on my entire network, such as Windows computers or my MyBookLive. Streams music well, too.

Only complaints, really, are the fact that it looks like a game console and the ridiculously poor deployments of my mother tongue throughout all Asus interfaces and documentation (U.S. to Taiwan: "your file is download already," to a native speaker, is saying that the file was downloaded prior to executing the command and so sounds like an error message...). The router is the largest computer in my house at this point, come to think of it.

title: Can You Hear Me Now?
text:
Perhaps the best $20 I've spent in a long while. I replaced one of the stock antennae on an AC68p that was incapable of reliably getting a 2.4GHz signal from the back of the house 50 ft. through two external walls and 1-2 interior ones onto the front porch. Pre-dawn (lower heat in the back room and/or fewer neighbors using their networks in the apartment building 30 feet away), I could previously get 11mbps downstream on my IPhone (2.4GHz 11n) in this location, according to SpeedTest. During daylight, at least in warmer months, throughput disappeared--still connected on 2.4GHz, but no usable data transmission. I had adjusted the control channel and took similar usual optimization measures. My AP wasn't even the strongest signal on the porch, thanks to one neighbor (damn you, Babaganoush!). Meanwhile, my 11AC laptop on 5GHz was still able to get 27mbps link rate (according to Windows, not throughput) when my phone lost connectivity: under ideal conditions (pre-dawn, cool temps), this could go up to 117mbps.
Unscrew, screw in new antenna, point. Although the phone still registers only 2 of 3 bars most of the time, it oscillates with 3 bars, SpeedTest consistently gives me 24mbps+ in the afternoon. My laptop link rate on 11ac is not significantly better, however.

I wasn't expecting more. In fact, this is better than I'd expected on 2.4GHz. All of my devices are either 1x1 I-devices or 2x2 laptops. So, I still have the two omnidirectional antennas in place, plus this directional one pointed straight down the length of my house. I was a good candidate for a directional antenna like this to work well for the specific problem location.

I'll also note that purchasing this came after an entire day spent trying to get an old DD-WRT router set up as a repeater. The crowded network environment and lack of clear channels really didn't let me do this at all. Not to mention, I upgraded my router in the first place so that I wouldn't have to have multiple routers plugged in. And, the repeater would have needed a separate SSID for stability, it seems. So, the antenna was a much more elegant solution.

title: The Dell specs are obviously better, being newer
text:
I wanted to provide the tidbit of info that I was unable to find on the Internet when I was shopping for this, which is how it compares in specific terms to a Macbook Air 11-inch, which I also own (mid-2013), and on which I run Windows 10 in Bootcamp. The Dell specs are obviously better, being newer, but I wanted to note a few things about the ergonomics.

Keyboard: I prefer typing on the Dell. Even though the keys are plastic, they're quieter and somehow more comfortable to use and touch. I also find myself preferring the rubberized paint-on-carbon fiber to the bare aluminum of the MBA. For some unfathomable reason, too, I make fewer touch typing errors on the Dell. The Dell keys MIGHT be smaller and spaced more, which could be what helps. My large hands tend to get lost on the Mac keyboard more (touch typing = not looking at my hands). The two keyboards are outwardly extremely similar, but the experinece is better on the Dell. Key travel is effectively the same, although technically the MBA has a tad more based on the specs.
Strictly from a Windows-on-MBA standpoint, I basically can't move from one machine to the other for word processing, because the Fn key and Control key are transposed between the two. Also, the dedicated delete key is hard to swap back and forth from reaching for Fn+Backspace in Bootcamp. I'm talking about muscle memory for a fast touch typist. Meanwhile, the two keyboards are also similar in needing FN+arrow key combinations for home, end, PgUp, and PgDwn (I find these to be intuitive key combinations and I don't really miss the dedicated keys).

Heft: The Dell sort of feels like a more serious MBA--halfway between an Air and a Pro in size/weight. Although the Dell is only insignificantly wider/deeper, it's almost twice as thick, much of this in the screen (I have the basic screen, non-touch). The Dell is obviously heavier. Still, it's a wonderfully ergonomic one-handed carry laptop--in fact, I have no problem carrying both laptops simultaneously in one hand by their edge. The XPS13 feels solid and authoritative. Every bit as sleek as Apple IMO. The long rubberized feet on the bottom are also much more effective than the MBA's metallic round nubs.

Heat/noise: the Dell gets warm on the bottom near the exhaust vents and the fan runs quite a bit. The fan noise is noticeable, but only barely. I find both heat and noise a non-issue. It's a much more powerful processor, after all. The fan on my I7 MBA almost never turns on.

Plug: The AC adaptor sticks straight out. This means that a fall off the desk on that side could mash in the power port. Why on Earth they didn't make a right-angle plug is beyond me. Probably a non-issue, but still a "potential" one.

Track pad: I have big meaty hands, and I have big issues with accidental clicks and movement, even with settings enabled that are supposed to avoid this. On the Dell, I haven't had a single issue. Not even sure why: better software?

Sound: The Dell is crap. On the bright side, it's as loud at 50% as the MBA is at 100% under Bootcamp (OSX is much louder: this is a Bootcamp issue). The sound equalization is just way better and more natural on the MBA. The Dell is tinny and congested. It's perfectly functional for business use, though, even in moderately loud environments. So, it's an aesthetic rather than a functional issue.

In terms of laptops, I bought one Dell 15 years ago as a consumer and have been forced to use 3 more Dell Lattitudes for my work. I've also owned and loved an IBM PS/2 (1992-97), a Lenovo X60 (2006-2010), and an NEC Windows 98 machine in between. I have to say, I'm amazed to find myself concluding that this time, Dell actually made a really good machine.

title: Getting there, but perhaps not there yet
text:
I grabbed this on impulse when I happened to see it listed the day before it was released. It's a pricepoint I can "play with" for my first gizmo of this sort. I doubt we'll ever pay less than $50 for a wi-fi doodad. So, it's a nifty toy. It has limitations, though. The speaker is better than I expected. Maybe equivalent to an IPhone 7 or an ipad. That's the plus. Now for the longer list of minuses.

1) Surely, they're working on a skill for the echo to control the Fire TV products...right?

2) The speaker setup is a limitation: I think they really want you to buy the Tap or Echo when it comes to streaming. Plugging in a cable to the 3.5mm jack mutes the onboard audio entirely, and it actually takes several seconds to come back after unplugging a cable. So, one has to have a speaker plugged in and always on, whether that's bluetooth or hardwired. Any speaker that draws so little power that I'd leave it on 24/7 isn't going to offer much improvement over the tablet-like speaker built in. Why isn't there a skill like "Alexa, play through speakers" so I can talk to/listen to Alexa with my stereo (or whatever) off, then choose to listen to music more immersively without having to shuffle cables? Bluetooth seems to be the way to go to combine "casual conversation" with Alexa with listening to radio stations, etc.
There should be an option to always play Alexa herself through the built-in speaker.

3) On bluetooth, I presume there's no support for APTX, since they'd mention it if it had it, so no CD-quality. Also no pairing with a speaker that requires a pin. On wi-fi, there's no support for 802.11ac.

4) I'm deducting a star because the Alexa app doesn't work well with Voiceover on an iphone. App development on Apple products makes accessibility for blind people the default, largely, but Amazon has managed to create a really clunky app in this regard. Taps just stop having an effect, as if the screen contents Voiceover is reporting aren't what's on the screen, perhaps. Kind of a nightmare to manage the device using this app, and it's required. I often have to close the app and restart to regain the ability to navigate the menu.

5) "Skills" are buggy. Once you're using the app, you get to see how poorly rated many skills like home automation skills are. Currently, IDevices just doesn't work. I'm sure that's more a matter of IDevices than Amazon, but it's probably shared responsibility.

6) I have to speak very loudly for the microphones to hear me over anything at all playing from the builtin speaker, such as news. Plan to hit the Action button to talk to her while things are playing if you don't want to holler.

I bought it with the idea of controlling my IDevices switch and socket, plus playing Pandora and radio. Between buggy home automation and the limitations of playing through speakers, I won't be doing either, at least not yet. So, what I have is a talking clock at the moment. Other folks will find it more useful, obviously, and I'm sure the automation will get worked out eventually. Personally, I'm betting that the 5th gen Apple TV will sport a "Hey Siri" microphone array, and then there's Google Home. But at the price, it's hard to say the doodad (do-Dot) won't be worth it. Or, maybe it'll join the ranks of doodads in my drawer that all seemed like good ideas at the time, but which ended up just over-complicating things when they promised to simplify them. We shall see.

title: Rather Good
text:
Ordered from the manufacturer. It's definitely a rather high quality gain control, but I don't believe it is transparent. I don't have a way to do a rapid a/b comparison, but pulled wires back and forth several times to compare with the unit in and out of a system comprising Dynaudio X-12 speakers ($1200), Parasound Zamp v3 ($350 but awesome), and TEAC UD-501 ($899 when new). Result: I *think* I can hear the added component. Which, after all, is far from surprising. The good news is that a lot of the delicate detail is retained. What I think I noticed was a slight harshness in treble combined with narrower sound stage; however, this is in the questionable range. The music certainly continued to sound "good" with the unit in the system. Therefore, overall, it's a good component if you are forced to add something like this to the signal chain.
The remote is indeed flimsy, and the slide-out coin-battery compartment fell open the first time the remote hit the floor. MCM says that additional IR hex codes are available to control other devices, btw. Housing is metal on the unit itself. I wish the sensor was wider and convex to allow better off-axis reception. I also REALLY wish it had volume up/down buttons on the unit itself (it only has mute and power lights flanking the IR sensor).

I don't register "for the price" mentally when I'm thinking about sound: either it sounds good or I wouldn't turn it on, so it would be worthless. But this certainly would be considered a value, since a hobbyist would spend at least $10 and a few hours building an equivalent.

Definitely glad to have this in my toolkit, since the Zamp v3 only has dual gain controls on the back of the unit, and I additionally have some amps without IR control. I'm glad not to need it for my main music rig, though. For a more typical consumer big box system of any kind, or any system I was putting together for under $800 total, this would not be a bottle neck at all.

title: A more in-depth review...
text:
Since I didn't purchase it here, this review won't appear as a verified review unless it's one of the most helpful. But I'm frustrated by how unsubstantial most of the reviews here are, particularly among the crowd who were given the unit for free.

Sound: In terms of sheer output, it's probably as good as can be expected for a driver that's less than 3" in diameter and is portable. There's some compression going on here to produce more bass, and that's not at all a bad thing in a speaker this size. It boosts the lowest frequencies that it can muster to give the impression of more bass than a speaker this size can actually produce. It does the same with the highs, which most big-box-store brands do because many people like the music to sound sharply detailed. I don't like either end being boosted, but, hey, it's a tiny speaker for casual listening. Anyone who wants something more than that either hasn't ever really heard a stereo system (and I suspect many young people actually haven't) or else needs to go larger (AudioEngine HD3, Marshall Stanmore, PeachTree Deep Blue 2, Aiwa Exos-9, or an actual wired system with bluetooth adaptor plugged in). What's hard to pull off is a small speaker that actually doesn't sound tinny. I have two excellent table radios, both of which happen to likewise have 3" diameter full-range drivers: a Sangean WR2 and Tivoli Model 1. The Revolve made me appreciate those all over again, because their mids and highs are so, so much more open and natural than the Revolve's. But they're vastly larger with more wattage. The only reasons to consider the Revolve over a *good* table radio would be size and portability.
The vertical orientation of the Revolve allows it to have a deeper cone and greater excursion (more movement of the driver) than the Bose Mini 2, so it likely plays louder with less disdortion than that unit. I'm not amazed in any way, but it's good. If you want to be overwhelmed with boomy bass, look elsewhere. But the Revolve is definitely to be compared more with a good-quality table radio, not a stereo microsystem. Although the revolve can certainly hit and exceed 80dB volumes without appreciable distortion, the boosted treble is going to make this increasingly unpleasant. it's a speaker for detailed low and medium volume, not blasting.

So long as the physical law by which frequency is the inverse of wavelength holds true in our universe, no amount of technologizing can make a little driver genuinely play lower. The only things to do to compensate are (a) boost the crap out of low frequencies that are otherwise rolled off, (b) play with reflections off of nearby surfaces to boost those rolled-off frequencies, (c) apply DSP compression, and (d) put more watts through the speaker. Oh, and add passive radiators (a woofer diaphragm with no driver behind it, basically) to transform some of the air motion into usable low-end frequency output. The Revolve does all the above except, of course, pump lots of power. The result in the bass was really obnoxious at first, but it calmed down after a few hours of playtime as the driver limbered up (this much of the hype over "break in," at least, is real). On internet radio stations where the signal is itself extremely compressed, there remains a one-note rumble from the boosted low-end frequencies, and it's really distracting. One-note bass indeed. But for my actual music collection, it sounds rather good and the bass is fairly well-balanced within an overall "smily" EQ, if you know what that is. I'd say that "real" bass output rolls off significantly around 120Hz, but that's just a guess. It starts boosting below that. On bass-heavy recordings like Eryka Baddu's Badduizm or Brian Ino's Another Day On Earth, there's a good chunk of notes that just ain't there at all. I wouldn't expect them to be at this size.
[update: my comments about rumble and high-frequency tizz reflect my experience of near-field listening to the speaker while it was sitting on my desk. I end the review remarking that Bose does better often from a greater distance. After I hit submit, I decided I should put that claim to the test. I moved the Bose to the corner of the room 10 feet away from me, where corner reflections would play a role. Lowe and behold, it sounded pretty good. Corner reflections boost the lower mid-range, offsetting Bose's boosted highs, and the bass became well-defined and surprising, if not over-accentuated. So, it's just not a speaker for near-field listening. It sounds a bit "bigger" and warmer placed in a corner, and becomes just fine for ambient listening in a vacation house, for instance. If you're too close to the speaker for bass frequencies to resolve, though, bass is just a low-pitched vibration with no relationship to the music other than keeping good time. Cellos aren't a friend to the Revolve under these circumstances, though upright bass fares a bit better]

Design: Like a typical subwoofer, it's a single downward-firing driver flanked with passive radiators. That's a really good idea, since one decent-sized driver will always play lower and more clearly than two drivers half the size. The ability to leverage sound reflections off the surface it's sitting on results in more volume with less power draw, just like in downward-firing versus front-firing subwoofers (at the expense of some definition). Bose has done the subwoofer idea one better, though, by designing a reflector inside the unit's base, rather than just pointing the driver at the table the unit sits on. It's an elegant solution. The result isn't amazing, but see above on the laws of physics.
Other aspects of design also point to quality. The aluminum isn't all that impressive, because it has a slightly rough texture and, when tapped, sounds thin. The unit has plenty of heft, though, and feels solid. The top and base are both rubberized. The soft-touch buttons are easy to press. Handling it is a joy, actually, and exudes class. It has a tripod mount on the bottom. Do you have a tripod? Me neither. Moving on...

Features: Nowhere has anyone mentioned yet that this unit actually can act as a USB audio device. Plug it directly into your PC as a secondary sound device without the hassle of bluetooth. Also, the USB Audio/Auxiliary button gives you complete control over selecting which channel is active. press the bluetooth button to return to bluetooth. So, you can have multiple devices connected simultaneously, which is something I'm prone to do: computer, phone, and maybe something else if I'm on a week-long trip. This is a habit from the days when bluetooth sucked, to the extent that it sucks less now. However, pressing the Aux button disconnects all bluetooth devices. Pressing bluetooth re-initiates connection with the last two devices connected, and this happens within a very few seconds. So, there will be some fiddling to do when switching modes. Many other units will default back to aux when bluetooth disconnects, which would be better in cases where you want this sitting across the room. When powering up, the unit remembers which input source was active when the power was turned off. Note that the USB audio device stays attached to the computer regardless of what mode the Revolve is in (even when the Revolve is powered off, in fact), and that the multifunction button does not operate the USB audio device. Also note that, because the speaker sounds so much better when placed across the room, the utility of connecting a USB device goes down sharply, since my PC is in front of me.
Multipoint bluetooth is problematic. Yes, it connects to the last two devices on power-up or when switching back to bluetooth. But, the moment one of these disconnects, such as the phone going to sleep, it won't reconnect automatically and one has to press the bluetooth button until the name of the device is spoken (e.g., initiating a connection from the speaker), or else the connection is restored using the phone's bluetooth settings. In either case, it's now just connected to that one device. Another thing I've encountered is that my Echo Dot monopolizes playback, not letting my phone or PC use the speaker even if the Dot is paused. So, it's kind of a trick to get two devices connected at once in a usable way.
But it's great having the voice menu speak the names of paired bt devices. Just scroll through the list and the speaker will initiate connections on its own. It connects in about 3 seconds.
Audio interface: this is an eyes-free device. Battery level is announced on startup and whenever the power button is held down for several seconds. Plugging in the usb cable gives an ascending tone, and unplugging it gives a descending tone. Bluetooth connection/disconnection status is announced. Etc., etc. The only thing that isn't played/spoken is power off, which, since that's instantaneous at present, would slow things down. Obviously, you can turn these voice prompts off with the app or an arcane button combo.

Multifunction button: aside from the dedicated buttons (bluetooth, power, aux/usb audio toggle, and the two volume buttons), the multifunction button performs the same functions as on other Bose units. Pressing once is play/pause (or mute for aux devices), twice goes to the next track, three times goes to previous. The manual also lists speaker phone functions of the multifunction button, but I haven't tried this. Holding it down activates voice assistants like Siri if an IOS device is connected, and this works fairly well--although, the volume is very low.

It supports "party mode," in which one Revolve pairs directly with a second Revolve/Revolve+/Color2 (and, I think, mini 2). This means that the streaming device needs to remain within 30 feet of the first device, but not the second: the second device needs to remain within 30 feet of the first Revolve. In stereo mode, the same probably applies, but obviously you want the units equidistant from your ears. I can't see stereo mode being worth too much: the limited bass extension will be very apparent, and for $400, you can buy a goodish 2.1 powered speaker system. Two revolves, however, is the same price as the roughly-equivalent AudioEngine HD3, for instance. If Bose makes a subwoofer to throw into the mix, maybe it would be of interest to some small population who are allergic to wires.

Note that Bose doesn't provide any technical specifications--not even frequency response or power. No word on whether this supports the APTX codec. For a speaker this size, however, lossy compression isn't really going to be noticed due to the limitations of the speaker stemming from its size. I'll say that bluetooth itself is at a much lower volume than aux/usb, and that it has a distinctly different sonic signature than the other channels: bt is more familiar smily-faced in the EQ, with pulled back mids and sparkle at the top frequencies. Both analog and USB, by contrast, don't have that sparkle and seem more jacked in the upper mids, lending tizz to S sounds and high hats in a way that I'm not fond of. Maybe it's just the fact that it's a small speaker shoved into a fancy aluminum can with holes poked in it.

I'm not a fan of Bose normally. They got onto most of our radars with the Bose Wave Radio how ever many years ago, and they've been overcharging for their products ever since without delivering any more sound quality than several other brands. But I do trust their engineering for overall quality. The Revolve ticks all my boxes for usability without loading the unit down with weird features. The revolve is not waterproof: it is "splash resistant." But I hate the beach and don't like sitting in the rain, so I was happy to buy it for the classy design, expectation of reliability, and better-than-decent sound quality. However, I am not wild about the Bose sound signature, if this is what that is. I can enjoy listening to my music on the Revolve, as far as high-quality mono radio speakers in the corner go, but very compressed internet radio streams (including my NPR station, regrettably) suffer from the most sibilance and the most low-frequency rumble, both of which are pronounced--they're at least somewhat noticeable on any speaker, so it's not strictly the Revolve's fault. The Amazon Tap isn't nearly as good a speaker by any stretch, but by the same token doesn't show off the problems with over-compressed radio streams. It's been my experience, ever since spending a lot of time with my GF's Bose Wave Radio of ten years ago, that the "Bose sound" is best enjoyed uncritically and at a distance. I don't mean that to sound snide, but just in the sense that it produces a nicely airy, room-filling ambiance. I've never found their stuff to reward careful listening, but it's good for bouncing sound off walls and makes any room feel a little classier. That's what's on offer here, IMO, and the 360 degree design supports it.
There are unfortunate downsides, though. The size and buttons would make this ideal for sitting on a desk while I'm working, but it sounds rather poor there. Placed 10 feet away, I won't be connecting my PC via USB and all those nice buttons are out of reach. Finally, although it boasts 360-degree listening, it needs to be by a wall, and two walls are even better: in the middle of a room or table, it's at its worst, though it's still clear, loud enough, lets you know the bass notes are there, and has a small footprint. I'm keeping the Bose for travel, but ended up buying a completely over-the-top Marshall Woburn for the bedroom, which *is* the sound of a small stereo (without the stereo ness).

Epilogue: The identically-priced Riva Turbo X is now sitting in the same corner, and I'm still not overwhelmed. Still a good table radio. Even with Turbo and surround modes turned on, it has slightly less and slightly-less-defined bass than the Revolve. Both play beyond 82 dB, but not by much: I've made the Riva crackle and warble at what I found reasonable volumes a couple of times for an instant, unlike the Bose. It's definitely a more "honest" presentation, since its drivers actually end at 16kHz and so high-frequency tizz is impossible. As a decidedly mid-range focused speaker, it's warmer and very nicely detailed in the mids. Perhaps too much so in some frequencies: although vocals stand out, certain notes on a piano as well as snares stick out too much and make the speaker sound a bit small at times. I actually went back and forth on the same tracks from an Alvin Batiste album a few times between the Riva and Bose in the same position. In some ways, going back to the Riva after acclimating to the syrup Bose pours all over everything in an attempt to not sound like a small speaker was like recovering from a skin disease. The mid-range cleared up amazingly. If that wasn't plain enough, the Riva is a better-sounding speaker, though the Sangean WR2 is far better still, except for bass. But it's funny: you can get used to sound very quickly, and I can enjoy listening to any of them. IMO, the Riva and Bose are in the same class, just with opposite sound signatures. Younger people--including me when I was 18--will prefer the Bose sound hands down, and more experienced listeners will be just as confident about preferring the Riva, at least with surround and the stupidly-named turbo engaged, both of which lean in the direction of the Bose without overdoing it. I also really hate interacting with the Riva, because the buttons aren't real buttons--they're just proximity sensors--and I tap them by mistake, or else they don't fire at all, I have to worry about whether "Turbo" and "Trillium" are turned on, and in fact if the battery is engaged. Then there's the Riva's laptop-style power brick. The Aux jack on my unit dumps tons of rf interference through the speaker anyway, so it's on the way back to Amazon. .

Hopefully final final update: I suspect that the Revolve does not support APTX. My supposition is based on several tests. The AAC codec seems to be responsible for sculpting the bluetooth sound signature to accentuate lows and highs, even more than the Bose already does. From my iPhone (non-APTX), I can hear this effect on both the Bose and the Riva. But playing from my APTX-enabled Windows PC, I get the same effect on the Bose, while the Riva via bluetooth then sounds identical to the Riva via Aux. As noted above, by contrast, the Bose sounds very different on Aux versus Bluetooth with the same track playing from an APTX-enabled PC. I actually like the AAC codec sound, at least initially, but long-term listening, as always, starts to favor the more natural sound, which is the APTX codec.
[4-week update: the bluetooth died. No longer announces devices and doesn't automatically reconnect on powering up. It's on its way back for an exchange. So much for my belief in Bose quality...]

title: Woburn and Deep Blue 2: 21st Century Jam Boxes
text:
First, some correctives regarding older so-called pro reviews. The remote is plastic, not metal, and might actually be the remote from some other kind of unit, repainted. It has power; a typical circular “D-pad” with volume (noon and 6:00), bass (9:00 and 3:00) and mute (center);
And buttons for the three input sources. There’s no app, and no special mode to compensate for wall placement, as some reviews claimed. Perhaps these were changes made when they dropped the price at the beginning of 2017. I’m also not overly impressed with the sound quality, as described below.

In 1989, I headed off to college with IMO the best jam box ever made. It was a JVC with detachable speakers, a 5-band equalizer, and something called “hyper bass that involved a long rectangular port that really moved air. The Marshall Woburn and PeachTree Deep Blue 2 are the 21st Century equivalents: no less and, essentially, no more, easily outclassing all of the portable units, which generally fall a bit short of table radio performance, while not measuring up to any $400+ component 2.1 system. I purchased both and set them both up in the identical position, playing the same range of tracks (Beethoven, Nirvana, and most things in between). I stuck to the optical input as my source, using Airplay to an Apple TV2 (APTX from my PC adds a non-problematic level of buzz on both units, and APTX is still limited to less than 400kbps as opposed to full 16-bit, 44.1kHz Airplay). Here are my thoughts.

The Woburn is a far superior speaker for sound quality. It just delivers more power, regardless of volume level, by which I mean that there’s better attack, more air displacement, or… I don’t really know how to say it without metaphors. It’s punchier. It’s also much more "analog"-sounding. Although you know there are chips and switching-mode amplifiers inside the Woburn, it’s not letting on that it’s anything but the old-school piece of rock’n-roll gear its exterior advertises. It sounds like a fairly good non-adulterated large bookshelf speaker, only with way more bass than any other speaker I know of for its size (other than the Sjofn Clue). I’m talking about volume knob at 2ish, too (60-85 dB in a small room). Things just get better from there. You can read my full review of the Woburn for more details.
The moment I hit play with the Deep Blue 2, I knew I wasn’t going to like it that much, being used to the Woburn by now. It IS that jam box from 1989, only with better bass. It sounds like the plastic enclosure that it is. Certain frequencies in the lower mid-range strain at the box, sounding a touch hollow. It’s still good, but it absolutely sounds like something one would buy at the big box electronics stores. Volume DSP doesn’t help. At lower volumes, treble sounds slightly brittle and unnatural, while mids are 2-dimensional. Typical mediocre-quality digital sound reminiscent of the 90s.
At higher volumes, the treble recedes back into normality but the mid-range sounds more hollow, almost vibrating the plastic enclosure. Again: quintessential jam box behavior. For all that, it is still just fine for the price. It delivers the full spectrum without anything being lost or muffled, with relatively good detail, though nothing like my bookshelf speakers. An advantage it has over the Woburn is that, thanks to its mid-range and tweeter drivers being angled a few degrees outward, it doesn’t sound as boxy as the Woburn can on dense mixes. In other words, the DB2 isn’t quite a mono speaker the way the Woburn is.
Did they remove some damping material or bracing when they "cheapened" the product? Did they wait until all the rave reviews were posted before doing so, knowing that most consumers would get their impressions from those early reviews, rather than hearing it in a store? At $350, it's still a solid performer for the price. It may have actually been a better bargain, though, when it cost more.

I think bass between the two units is about what you’d expect, given the woofer dimensions. The Woburn has MORE bass, and really thrusts out with, say, 45-80 Hz. The DB2 seems to dig deeper--definitely down into the mid-30Hzs--and does not have a mid-bass hump at all. For awhile, I was wondering if the DB2’s woofer was working, or if I didn’t have the bass high enough; but, when I switched from Billie Holiday to Raising Sand, the bass flooded in. That’s a good sign. On the Woburn, bass is a constant companion, never quite booming but you never ever need to wonder what the bassist is doing, so long as the bass knob is at least on 4, which is where I keep it.

Hiss is prodigious
from the Deep Blue 2, regardless of any cables being plugged into it, regardless of volume, regardless of source. In a quiet room, I can hear hiss from 10 feet away. It's probably more than any other device I have, give or take a little from my tube gear. Either the amplifiers are very noisy, or else it's extremely sensitive to AC line noise. On the Woburn, hiss is average and is audible from only about a foot away. I'm frankly not minding the hiss on the DB2, though, since it's not a high-resolution system on which the background noise, which is in any case inaudible during music playback, would ever smear the sound presentation.

Ergonomically, the IR remote on the DB2 is a big plus, but it works poorly. The controller has to be pointed right at the speaker to turn it on, and even then sometimes takes two or three tries and several seconds for the speaker to respond. After that, it works ok. The carry handle is great—have I mentioned jam box in this review? I’d have no problems plopping this in a suitcase or laundry basket to take on a car trip. It’s quite a solid unit. The “buttons” are just round places on the cabinet top—not real buttons, but capacitive ones, which I loathe. They don't work for me half the time. Honestly, the DB2 reminds me a lot of the Riva Turbo X in its styling . The capacitive buttons and grill material are literally identical, so that I'd be very surprised if the two weren't made in the same factory. The Riva didn’t over-process the audio, though, so sounds frankly better at low volumes. It won’t go as loud as the DB2, and doesn’t go as low.
The Woburn is a beautiful ergonomic nightmare. Heavy to move and desperately needing a handle. The fact that it lacks a remote makes it quite awkward for what I suspect is the most common use scenario for units like this: a bedroom. It does at least have an auto-power-off mode, which the DB2 conspicuously lacks. And I think that my own use scenario (playing from an Apple TV2) might be the only one in which you wouldn’t be able to adjust volume from your source after setting the Woburn’s volume at a decently high max level of 3 or 4. It goes without saying that the Woburn’s brass-plated buttons, knobs, and switch are things of beauty.

I happen to really dislike “digital-sounding” audio and plastic-sounding speakers. If the DB2 didn’t give me such a vivid flashback to jam boxes or things like the Bose Wave Radio, I wouldn’t have any complaints. I enjoy listening to it at night without reservation, regardless. The Woburn is sort of on another level, but obviously has its drawbacks as well.

title: I may actually look forward to somebody stealing these cameras...
text:
First time I've ever felt actively deceived here. As always I looked over the various "styles" to see which pack of cameras offered the best deal. The 4-pack was clearly it. "The other store" offers it for the same price, so I think A was price-matching it. But the "other store" sells a pack unique to that retailer, and includes the security metal mount. I assumed Amazon did, too. But the fine print (ok, not so fine) indicated it was a 3-pack plus add-on camera. Cool, I said: this way I get an extra power adaptor (regardless of kit size, Netgear only includes one adaptor!). But the package I received did not have the security mount ($20). So, I made a mistake purchasing here. Went to the review page for that package to warn others, and A had locked down the ability to write reviews of it! So, I'm reviewing the 3-pack, which is what I in fact own...plus the add-on camera... Sold as a "4-pack," but not the official 4r-pack.

One of the cameras I received has to go back, because the rubber gasket around the lens was not firmly inside the camera housing--it was coming out.
The plastic base station couldn't be cheaper if it tried. I guess it'll do the job, but it ain't an Apple Airport, for example.
The base station has to be plugged into the router, since the base station has its own proprietary wi-fi signal to the cameras. The router will interfere with it if it's too close. So, it has to be by the router but not by the router. Awkward. Having it too close is probably part of the problem people have had with connectivity, since NetGear is one of the best for wi-fi signals, generally.

The IP65 water rating isn't really enough to be waterproof: that would be '66. The rubber cover for the micro USB port has a tendancy to fall open. It's rather cheap. And, the battery compartment (the whole back of the unit, including the mounting screw, secured to the rest of the camera only by a flexible hinge) doesn't look like it would really keep out water.

The mounting screw hole is so close to the magnetic dedent that there's no way to use a screw in the hole while using the supplied half-moon mounts (I'd had the idea of using a chain and a bolt with washer to add a sort of anti-theft chain for outdoor use while using the supplied mounts, but it isn't going to work). The half-moon mount only hangs on the wall with one of those keyhole-style screw notches. So, in addition to being able to steal the camera, they can just lift the mount off the hanging screw, if jostling doesn't do it. So, a different mount or jury-rig is necessary for outdoor use.
Netgear hasn't seemingly embraced the idea of plugging these in. They don't yet sell a waterproof cable of their own, don't include the outdoor mounts, only include one power adaptor per kit, etc.

But whatcha gonna do? The list of wi-fi outdoor cameras with batteries is really small, and this is one of the least-expensive systems. Unless you want a camera so cheap that you can easily measure the network traffic heading from your house to Chinese and Russian servers (I don't care if Russian hackers or the North Koreans watch my driveway so much as I worry about the pimple-faced college hacker next door, but any access to my network can lead them to financial info on my computers, for instance). For that reason alone, I'd stick with name brands. At least they don't INTEND to be hacked...
I tried to do my research on "NVR" systems (network video recorders), but couldn't really find anything overall better: I wanted sound, local backup, 7-day free cloud storage, the ability to plug in as well as use battery, and wi-fi. Oh, and for it to not require constant tinkering and techie head-scratching like a DIY system. I'm through with that at my age.
So, for close to this price point, I don't think I could have done better at this point. Sorry I purchased here, though.

title: Lightweight
text:
The minute I picked up the shipping box, I knew it wasn't going to work: it was practically weightless.

The unit functions fine. The base is large enough to keep it from toppling over, unless the cord is tangled around the shaft. But the thin aluminum shaft wabbles like a bobblehead under the weight of even light headphones, and the "cradle" is just a bit narrow for the HD800 headband, though it works ok and would even work ok for the Audeze LCDs if the dip in the middle isn't a problem.

I have this one in the bedroom, but immediately ordered the Woo Audio double stand to sit by my main system, and it's one heavy hunk of metal by comparison. Although it's overpriced, it's actually not overpriced by much. No regrets about that one, and I guess I do need two stands. My banana hanger hook is too narrow for either the HD800s or the Focal Clears, though I could hang LCD-Xs on it by using one of the steel strips in the suspension headband. The banana hanger or this one worked equally well for the HD600s. Of all options, the all-metal banana hanger is my favorite for cost effectiveness, but the hook is too narrow for headbands spanning more than an inch at the most.

title: great features, cheap build and noisy preamps
text:
Really, 3.5 stars...
I purchased the LS-P4 elsewhere simply because on that particular day the price was better, though it's come down here now.

Build:
Very light weight plastic. Any Web site review that claims it's metal was written by someone who has never held the device. It's just a metallic paint job. Switches feel flimsy, and the USB dongle risks breaking under the weight of the device. The manual warns never to use any USB extender other than Olympus' own, but we'll just see how that goes. The speaker is tinny/tiny but adequate. The build isn't awful: it's just typical semi-disposable consumer grade. By contrast, the DM series claims to be made of an unspecified metal, but no reviews of the DM-720 mention this as a stand-out. Looking up the page, this one does claim a "metal body," but if it's not just a metallic paint, it's some sort of plastic-metal composite.

In the box, there's a telephone book-sized manual, the recorder, AAA NIMH battery, and a screw adapter for standard tripods. You'll need one of those, because the plastic casing transmits more handling noise than any device I've ever used. There's no way one could hold the recorder and make a usable recording. No way at all.

I would happily paid $100 more for a solid metal body with metal buttons/switches and enough padding in the case to dramatically reduce handling noise. Plus a case and table mount.

Performance:
The microphone array is quite sensitive. In terms of full-spectrum frequency pickup and ramping up the gain to pick up distant sounds, it blows away my Iphone and is on paar with professional audio interface/Audiotechnica microphones that I have. When I say "on paar," I mean that in a general way: diaphragm size and price always matter here. But it definitely sounds more like any of my pro gear than any of my smartphones or old pocket recorders (Zoom H2 or Ederol not included). Zoom and Tascam are the go-tos for field recorders around this same price point. Those have far more options and quieter preamps. The Olympus recorders are obviously intended for "pocket" applications like dictation or meetings, though it could do a gig fine, too, for casual use. I recorded a conference room meeting among 12 or so people and the result was sharp and glorious. I could hear the most distant quiet-talking woman better on the recording than in the meeting. While I usually downsample recordings to mono to create smaller downloads when I create voice-only files for distribution, doing that to this recording really made it sound about like an Iphone recording, though the Olympus mics pick up better. There's a lot to be said for the realism of stereo recording, even when there's no need for it. The three-mic system here is a good arrangement: an XY stereo plus omni. This means the stereo image is subtler than either turning the omnidirectional mic off or from a stereo mic that places the capsules further apart. But it does a good job focusing the center while additionally capturing things behind the recorder (not much rejection going on).

Unfortunately, Olympus' mic preamps keep getting noisier, it seems. I can clearly hear self-noise when recording with medium or high sensitivity and auto gain when recording sources of roughly 65dB--conversation, radio in background, etc. it will be usable, but it is far more noticeable than on my Iphone or other recorders. I suspect that, if I could ramp up the Iphone or my BookPort Plus to the same gain levels, it might be similar. My Samson UB-1 USB boundary mic was noisy to me when I first got it, but it's quieter than the Olympus. The LG V30 mics are also quieter and just as sensitive, but the V30 is unusable for me because its DSP, juggles the mic array and seems to add noise cancellation that can't be turned off, all of which create the usual "underwater" artifacts and audible cutting in and out of background noise: the Olympus is better. I also have an IRig HD Pre, and it's virtually silent. That's getting into "prosumer" territory, though. On order, I have a Blue Nano in hopes it will exhibit less self-noise; however, I'm tugged by the stereo microphone on the Olympus, as noted above.

I've owned a slew of Olympus pocket recorders over the past 18 years or so. My favorite remains the first one of these, the DM4: thick metal body, simple enough not to require a display, and the box contained earbuds and a suade carrying case. I've also had the DS2, one of the WS models, and the LS-7, which died when the battery leaked (this seems to have been a common issue with recent Olympus recorders, so here's hoping the curse is lifted). The DS-2 had a leather in-use case and the LS-7 came with a wind sock and cloth pouch. None of that for the LS-P4. So, Olympus keeps cheapening their offerings year over year.
The LS-P4 is the same size as the DM4 and LS-7 (thinner than the LS-7). Although the build is far worse than the DM4 and somewhat worse than the metal LS-7, the menu options keep improving.

I need to record and distribute class lectures and discussions on a regular basis for courses I teach. I'll never use the recorder for music-recording. For my purposes, the key options are these:
* FLAC format recording, though this disables many of the editing functions
* Low-cut filter for reducing noise from humming equipment, though I keep this off generally because it does impact SQ
* Zoom mic for the widest possible pickup pattern, but this is DSP-controlled and, again, I generally keep it off.
* automatic gain control. Just like on the old models, I set sensitivity to high and let it control gain. This picks up an entire classroom easily. A manual mode is also available, and a full automatic mode.
* Voice guidance, because I'm blind. I was able to turn the device on right out of the box and use it, because speech was enabled by default and it speaks virtually all of the menu options and recorder functions (like hold/unhold, folder lists, etc.). Power on and off even have distinct sound effects, and record-pause, record, and stop each have different beep patterns. Good usability. However, the bluetooth menus do not speak, and Voice Guide does not work on either the attached bluetooth speaker or the device itself when connected. Likewise, few of the options in the File menu speak, such as moving files or file properties. The Voice Guide is not "real" text-to-speech, but is instead a set of recorded voice announcements, explaining the limitations.

The lS-P4 will also connect as a USB audio interface when choosing "composite device" in the USB Class menu option. Selecting "Variable" from the USB connection mode menu item causes the recorder to prompt the user each time the recorder is plugged into a PC whether to connect in charging mode or as a flash drive.

I have many other microphones and in fact the IPhone works fine for most voice applications. But nothing whatsoever beats the convenience of one of these pocket recorders for decent if noisy stereo recording, including far-field recording.

title: Turns out a headset didn't fit the bill
text:
I should have done my homework on this, since there are plenty of mic tests on YouTube. The mic is as good as anything else in this pricepoint, but the only people who should buy something like this are dwellers in a loud office. Noise cancellation is good, but the mic has a very narrow pick-up frequency range. It sounds as good as other headset mics, but you'll sound worse than everyone else on your call who is sitting in front of their laptop.

The headphone quality is very good within its limits. There are no lows or highs: I'd say freq response goes from maybe 150 Hz to 8 kHz. But the mids are sparkling. I enjoy listening to YouTube. The somewhat narrow range isn't noticeable until you listen to music. On the other hand, activating the mic (e.g., on a call or during any audio recording), quality goes down just a tad. I suspect the USB 2 bandwidth limitations are the cause. I have the USB C version, but that of course only refers to the connector type. I guess USB 3.0 is more expensive to implement.

I have absolutely no use case for this, as it turns out. I have a Blue Yedi on my desk, and decided to plug in some ancient Apple Earpods to it for an infinitely better "headset." The Macbook Air mic is better, so I don't think I would use it traveling with that computer, or even my PC laptop. Zoom does just about as good a job at noise cancelling as a headset mic, so that isn't a draw, either. If I had my laptop in my lap and needed to be on a call, this would do the trick.

The input gain does not respond to the Windows setting for microphone gain at all, and the gain level is ridiculously low. Zoom pulls it up, but that in turn leads to a less-natural sound because of its noise cancelling. On a Mac, plugging it in sometimes makes input gain responsive, and other times not; in both cases, gain does nothing above 50%, and it is likewise very low. On my Macbook Air, plugging into the headphone jack (accessed by pulling the cable out of the USB dongle) works just as well as the USB connection, and makes the mic responsive to the input gain control. My ultraportable headset jack absolutely sucks, so that isn't an option for me there.

I guess I'll keep it for the headphones, and then the mic will be just in case I am in a really loud environment on a call.

The Poly Headphone Hub app, BTW, allows for customizing the beeps for volume/mute and voice announcements.

A con is its integrated USB cable. Another is the cheap plastic of the housing and buttons (the grill is better). I'd pay more for an aluminum housing with clicky buttons and detachable cord.
