title: Good system but you may have to do some work to get it to stop sqeaking.
text:
I was looking for a way to get my surround sound speakers working without having to climb into the attic to run speaker cable down the wall. Came across this Amphony system and didn't have much luck finding anything similar to compare against them so I decided to give 'em a shot.

It's wireless and works on the 5 Ghz range which would be nice if it weren't for so many other things using the 5 Ghz range: our cell phones, DVD player, Wireless Router. Not sure why everything else wreaks havoc with the Amphony system but seem to work just fine themselves.

Plugging them in for the first time had them popping and farting constantly. Tried shutting down the 5 Ghz band on the wireless router, shutting off WiFi on the phones, etc. Shutting down the router had no effect. Shutting off WiFi on the phones seemed to do well but still hiccuped often. Had to shut off BlueTooth on the Mrs phone. No idea why it was on but that seemed to make a difference as well.

Currently, we both use the 2 Ghz band on our phones for the Wireless Router and it seems to be working properly without hardly any squawking.

title: Absolutely fantastic
text:
This is a review of a few antennas and why I finally settled on the Terk HDTVa. I only tested them with ATSC signals, so I can't comment on any analog reception.

I just ordered this from Amazon.com and I can say without a doubt that it's the best antenna I've ever used. I'm about 25 miles away from most TV transmitters, and it picks up all of them. I was extremely surprised and very happy to see that it also picked up NBC and FOX, both VHF channels here, at full strength, something I was never able to do with my other two antennas.
I ran a longer coax cable and put the antenna on a window sill, I never have to fiddle with the rabbit ears or move it around to get a clear picture. This is on the window sill of a first floor (3 floor building) apartment that is surrounded by other apartment buildings. Also, the UHF element can be mounted with the blades oriented horizontally or vertically, perfect for putting it on the window sill and still being able to close the blinds.
The only con I can think of is that the VHF elements aren't as freely moved as they are on a lot of other antennas, like on an old pair of bunny ears. Basically, if you want to aim them horizontally, they have to be pointing in the OPPOSITE direction of the UHF element, or straight up, or tilted slightly forward. Aiming them horizontally in the same direction as the UHF element is impossible. This is only a minor issue, since the reception is so damn good I could aim the VHF elements however I wanted to and still get a clear picture; this isn't even enough of a nuisance to take one star off for. DEFINITELY get this; it's the best indoor antenna you'll ever use.
This is also the only antenna I've ever used that didn't lose signal on every single channel, both UHF and VHF, when someone was using a cell phone. Definitely a good perk.

[[ASIN:B000W8XQJC GE 24775 Quantum Indoor HDTV Antenna]]
Mediocre, at best. This is one of the only antennas I've seen with ONE VHF element, which isn't exactly a problem in this market since most of our DTV stations are UHF, but don't count on being able to receive more than one VHF station with this setup. You'll find yourself moving the lone bunny ear around a lot if you've got 3-4 VHF stations you want to watch, even when the transmitters for these stations are on the same tower!
The UHF panel design is a gimmick at best, it does help if one station is in a different direction and you only want to aim one panel at it, but the reception for some reason is not consistent. The FIXED LENGTH power and coax cables are the nails in the coffin.
This antenna would be great at $10, maybe $15, not the $30 GE is trying to sell it at. For some reason, this antenna is also very limited in how many ways you can aim the VHF element; I'd prefer being able to aim the VHF element in whatever direction I want and have limited range on the UHF element since receiving those signals is much easier.
It did seem to like being placed in as high a location as possible; I'm on the first floor so it's not easy to get it very high up. When held to the ceiling reception did improve greatly, and as soon as I figure out how to staple it to my ceiling I'll find a use for it. Right now it's chugging along fine in the living room.
This antenna is definitely a good choice if you're in a tall building or out in the boonies away from any other buildings. WiFi, microwaves, and cell phones only bother it on certain VHF stations, but it can barely pull those in anyways.

[[ASIN:B000ES8EG0 Philips High Performance Amplified Indoor Uhf/Vhf/Fm/HDTV Antenna]]
I used this antenna for the longest time, all while being mildly annoyed by it. First off, it pulls in UHF signals like nobody's business, regardless of how it's oriented or where it is placed. It doesn't seem to mind multipath interference at all. VHF stations are a completely different story; it takes hours and hours of messing with these rabbit ears to get any picture, unlike the other two antennas reviewed. And then when you DO finally have the picture, heaven forbid you start to move around the room or even move on the couch, the picture will drop out.
I had this antenna at my old 3rd floor apartment, and tried it in two locations in my new 1st floor apartment. In the living room, I really couldn't pick up anything useful with it, so I moved it to the bedroom and tried with a Pinnacle ATSC tuner. When I finally had the rabbit ears set up right, for some reason I could no longer tune the strongest UHF signal in the area, go figure.
On the third floor, the only thing I had to worry about was the fact that it was VERY susceptible to RF interference. Is anyone in a nearby apartment using a microwave or making a cell phone call? Signal drops out. Get a text message? No TV. On the first floor, you can only sit in certain spots while watching TV or you've got no picture. This was especially annoying since it was being used to record shows while I was away, the signal would get weaker without someone in the room.
It just might have been my unit that was poorly shielded, but the more I turned down the amplification, the less susceptible it was to RF interference
item_title: Terk 60 Mile Range High Performance Amplified Indoor HDTV Antenna - Supports UHF, VHF 1080 HDTV Broadcasts for Free

title: This is a dream GPS and Bluetooth is a must
text:
Hello, I am writing to let those buyers that are still deciding whether they should get a 350 or 360 with bluetooth. GET THE 360 with bluetooth. The GPS part is a dream and we all know it, based on tons of feedbacks here so I am not going attempt to bore you. This is the best GPS there is on the planet. Now, back to the bluetooth side. This is by far the most convenient feature that I find myself using, even more than using the GPS itself around my home town.

After you paired your phone with the 360, every time you get into the car you automatically have the best speaker phone to use safely while driving. The speaker is very loud and crystal clear. The wonderful thing is my callers don't know that I am using a speaker phone. They think I am talking to them normally which is great. They hear me super clear and clean.

When some one calls me, I get a caller ID displays on the Garmin, allowing me to ignore or take the call. My phone address books is accessible via the Garmin and I can dial any one or any POI. Essentially, you have a walking city phone book in the palm of your hand.

Say you find a restaurant you want to call, just one click on the Garmin 360 and it will dial the number straight and route the call through. Well, you may think that you can certainly get my phone out and dial the number yourself; well, you can do that but if you're driving and trying to do all that is just dangerous and so not needed with bluetooth technology. Why make things so hard on yourself? Another thing is when you're in your car, most conversations will be short so it is perfect (I actually talked on the speaker for almost 1/2 hour with great pleasure). If you want to have a more private conversation, just route the conversation back to the phone via the Garmin interface.

For those that already has the Garmin 350 with no bluetooth, you have the best GPS there, but I would strongly recommend selling it or donating it to charity :) and get the bluetooth version of this already AWESOME unit. Please I was one of those who was trying to taught me out of buying the 360 and how I don't need bluetooth. Trust me! this will make you use your GPS much much more. Isn't that the point of buying anything? is to actually put it to good use. I hope this helps and remember this is only my humble opinion. Thank you for reading.

title: AMAZING. Mount directly inside my couch
text:
Got this and quickly set it up, using the "couch leg method" and I was OK with it. Movies with it was good but not fantastic. Watching concerts got annoying after awhile UNTIL...

I then asked couple friends over this weekend and we installed the transducer directly into my couch and the result is 1000% better. The vibration seems more evenly distributed to the whole couch and much more dynamic.

Why it was annoying with watching concerts with couch leg mount method:
When you hear a kick drum, the transducer vibrates the couch leg and you feel the sound but then you immediately feel the muted sound in your body simply because the mount is directly on the floor and it quickly cuts off because of my tile floor. So after a short while, watching a concert gets a bit tired and annoying. With movies it was better but could be much much better.

After installed directly into the couch:
WOW, what a HUGE HUGE impact it made. The kick drum is more alive and dynamic and travels through the couch and your body in a much much much smoother way. You actually feel the different levels of sustain and volume with the low end sounds, even with the kick drum. The kick drum no longer cut off by the tile floor and works 1000% better with your sub.

How did we install directly into the couch?:
Simple really. We went to local hardware store and got some longer nuts and bolts, a piece of red wood board (the strongest wood) and some metal brackets. We drilled holes to mount the transducer onto the wood board and mounted this board to the frame of the sofa, using the metal brackets. And no, there are no rattling with these brackets. We used the tough long screws and screwed them into the sofa wood frames (plenty of room in there). VERY IMPORTANT: DO NOT mount the transducer side way. You want it vertically mounted, just like it was with the couch leg method.

General why buttKicker good:
The vibration from this is very dynamic from soft to loud and everything in between. For example, an earthquake sound will produce strong vibration at first and then softer and softer as the sound goes away. So your couch does not just shake, it shakes in unison with the audio dynamically. In other words, the vibration has volume and it is awesome.

Wife/girlfriend test:
Generally, women don't care about these things like us boys do, but my lovely wife loves it after a few tries. She even mentioned that I should install another one on our other love seat. Wow, that brought tears to my eyes :)

Advice: Do it RIGHT the first time, or don't do it at all. Get this and try it with the couch leg method (you may love it and leave it). But roll up your sleeves and install it inside your couch and you will come back and rank this review to be the "Most Helpful". Good luck.

title: A pretty good player ... unless you like audiobooks.
text:
I bought this player because it was the first one I found with several features that are very important to me:

1. Solid-state flash memory instead of a micro hard drive. The base unit is equipped with 1 GB, and you can add up to 2 additional GB via a Secure Digital card. (Currently a 2GB SD card will run you about $150 on eBay, but this is certain to become much cheaper.)

2. Works on a single, REPLACEABLE type AAA battery, said to be good for 15+ hours depending on various usage factors. The original battery which came with my unit ran for about 9 hours; but all of my .mp3 files are 320 kbps, and the larger file sizes apparently drain power faster. Installing brand-new alkaline instead of the cheap original would probably help, too. And you can always use rechargeables.

3. Simple drag-and-drop file management, with no lame-brained "jukebox" applications to fumble with. The unit simply appears as a new disk drive on my Windows desktop. (You can use this unit as a portable flash drive for any type of file storage if you like.)

4. Large LCD display screen with full .mp3 ID support and easy navigation. ("Shuffle." Yeah, right, Apple.)

5. FM stereo radio.

I generally like this unit. The volume is adequate, and sound quality is very, very good. A better pair of earphones would probably make it sound even better, but the supplied pair is quite acceptable. There is absolutely none of the annoying background noise or electronic whine you often hear with CD-based players. The audio background is dead quiet. Don't bother with the SRS WOW "feature"; to my ears, it simply makes the sound louder and adds mid-bass. It also eats up extra battery power.

Navigation and UI are easy and reasonably intuitive. I only glanced at the user manaul once for a few clarifications. The unit is very tiny and lightweight.

Now for the disappointments:

1. Do NOT purchase this unit if you listen to a lot of audiobooks. If you put the player on PAUSE to interrupt a book reading, the player will remember where you left off, BUT ONLY IF YOU LEAVE THE POWER TURNED ON. If you turn the power off, or if you let the automatic power-off feature turn it off for you (which it will do after a few minutes), you will LOSE YOUR PLACE in the audiobook! DUH! Did the people at Audible who cut the cross-marketing deal with Sandisk know about this stupid design oversight? With flash memory, it would have been trivial to implement some kind of bookmark system.

2. The USB port and SD card slot are covered with a tiny pieces of pressure-fitted white plastic, which must be removed to access the openings. These cover pieces are NOT attached to the player, and they are very, very easy to misplace. Bad engineers. No doughnut.

3. The supplied USB cable (with its proprietary connector for the player -- GROWL) is only about 5 inches long. This is a big problem if you only have USB ports on the back of your computer! I ended up having to purchase a 6-foot USB extension cord (for twenty bucks extra -- GROWL) so I could attach the unit conveniently.

This unit is worth considering if you want a flash-based music player with good sound and a potentially large storage capacity. It is a BAD choice if you listen to audiobooks, or classical music with long movements ... like me. I like the unit too much to return it, but next time I'm going to check out audiobook compatibility very, very carefully before I buy.

###

MORE ON THE LACK OF A BOOKMARK FEATURE

The reviewer Audible_Alex (see above) is apparently confusing the PAUSE feature of this player (which does work, and IS documented in the manual) with the NON-EXISTENT bookmark feature.

It is true that you can PAUSE playback by pressing the PLAY/PAUSE button once, and resume playback at the same point by pressing the PLAY/PAUSE button again ... AS LONG AS YOU DON'T TURN OFF THE PLAYER. If you power down the player while it is paused, or let the automatic power-down feature do it for you, the player WILL remember what track you were playing, but it WILL NOT remember WHERE YOU WERE in that track. When you hit the PLAY button after power-down, the player ALWAYS begins AT THE BEGINNING of the last track played. In other words, THERE IS NO BOOKMARK FEATURE.

This sort of design is okay for pop music; who cares if you have to start a 3 minute song over again? But it's not very useful for audiobooks, classical music, or any other sound files that have long tracks, because you're forced to listen to the ENTIRE track every time you restart ... unless, of course, you're willing to disable the auto power-off feature (which you can do) and leave the player turned on all the time so it doesn't lose its place. This has unpleasant implications for battery life. :)

I stand by my original review. This otherwise fine mp3 player is simply not suitable for audiobooks. Maybe Sansa can offer customers a firmware upgrade to correct the problem. If they do, I'll be happy to give the player 4 or 5 stars instead of just 3.

###

Another reviewer mentioned that the player DOES bookmark audiobooks from Audible. It seemed incredible to me that Sandisk would implement bookmarks for only one type of audio file -- and a closed, proprietary format, at that -- but, in the spirit of experimentation, I installed Audible Manager 4.0 (which you MUST use to upload and play Audible files -- GROWL) and loaded part of an Audible book, using the free one-month subscription that comes with the player. And you know what? Bookmarks really DO work with Audible files! AARGH! This makes the TOTAL LACK of bookmarks on regular .mp3 files all the more senseless and infuriating! WHAT WERE THE ENGINEERS OF THIS THING THINKING?

I got a certain grim satisfaction by cancelling my new Audible account. :)

The good news: If bookmarks are POSSIBLE with Audible files on this unit, they may be POSSIBLE with any other type of audio file via a firmware upgrade. I don't know if this player allows user firmware upgrades or not, but if it does, I hope Sandisk is hard at work preparing a new version.

title: A little gem! Why isn't anyone else doing this?
text:
I recently moved to a home outside Boston, located on the wrong side of a hill. My FM radio reception is lousy. I can't get a decent signal from either of the two radio stations that still play classical music.

What I needed was a device that could play my classical .mp3s without having to deal with Apple, overpriced docks, chargers and lots of wires and bother.

This little Timex is EXACTLY what I was looking for. It's basically a clock radio with a USB jack and an SD card slot. Just fill a USB flash drive or SD card with .mp3s and this thing will play them, in sequence or randomly. No extra wires, no docks or chargers, no Apple, no fuss.

I took my library of 320 Kbps, 44.1 kHz stereo .mp3s and converted them to 56 Kbps, 22 kHz mono. At this bitrate, I can fit over 75 HOURS of classical music on a single 2 GB SD card that costs $15. The resulting sound quality is like a super-high-quality FM broadcast ... without any commercials or pledge drives. It's a personal radio station on a chip!

The radio has a single 3" driver, ported out the back. The quality is pretty respectable for an $70 unit. It's not as good as one of the high-end table radios from Bose, Tivoli or Boston Acoustics, but it's noticeably better than a typical cheap clock radio, and more than adequate for casual listening.

I now enjoy my Sunday mornings listening to ONLY the music I like, without interruptions. Way to go, Timex!

title: Simple, effective replacement for cheap sound cards
text:
My PC at work has the usual OEM motherboard audio, and sounds mediocre when played through an external amp and decent speakers. So I jumped at the chance to replace it with something better.

This Creative unit is small and very attractive. Installation could not be simpler. You simply plug it into a USB port. It configures itself, and stereo audio immediately becomes available at the outputs. However, the large volume control knob on the top will NOT work unless you install the optional drivers and software on the included CD. The apps are snazzy and offer lots of tweaks like a graphic equalizer and various THX-branded enhancements, but I turned all that stuff off. A nice feature: When you turn the knob, an onscreen graphic appears that shows the current setting as it changes, vanishing as soon as you release the knob. So you don't have to be able to see the knob, and can tuck the unit out of sight behind your monitor if you want.

There are lots of I/O options, including 6-channel analog and Dolby Digital via an optical connector. I only use the stereo outs.

The sound quality on this PC is now noticeably improved, smoother and clearer, with less harshness. The faint but persistent background noise I was hearing before is completely gone.

If you listen to a lot of music or movies, and use high-quality speakers/headphones, do yourself a favor and get one of these. Easily worth the modest price.

title: Impressive sound, storage capability and value
text:
I listen primarily to classical music. All of my files are 320 kbps .mp3. These sound very good on decent equipment, but take a lot of storage space, so memory capacity and audio quality are my primary concerns.

The 8 gig Clip Zip delivers on both. Listening with Sennheiser 595 or Bose QC2 headphones is a delight. The audio is clean and transparent, with inaudible distortion and noise, and plenty of volume when needed. I can easily hear "through" the player and distinguish the inherent qualities of the actual recordings. Remarkable performance for the money. A separate headphone amp seems unnecessary.

For around thirty bucks, I added a 32 gig microSD chip, giving me a high-quality music player with 40 gigs of storage for less than $100 total, including a $5 silicone case.

The user interface is a bit wanky, but after ten minutes I figured it out. Documentation is perfunctory.

I tried the FM radio. Reception on local stations is acceptable.

Transferring files to the player is stupid easy, as it simply appears as a disk drive on my PC when I plug it in. No need for special bloatware.

Be sure to get the latest firmware upgrade from the Sandisk web site.

If this thing holds together, it will be one of the neatest gadgets I've bought in years.

title: Take your time installing, and it comes out great
text:
My 12-year-old was handed an iPad by his school. After only a week, I noticed a few small scratches and nicks on the screen. Nothing serious, but nine more months of such treatment would leave the screen looking as if it had been scrubbed with steel wool.

So I sprang for this screen protector. It's just a clear plastic film that clings to the glass and (hopefully) absorbs some of the inevitable abuse.

Installation seems tricky, but it's not actually not that difficult. Watch the company's YouTube instructional video and read the printed directions carefully. Be sure to wash your hands and keep your fingers very wet (using the included liquid spray) to avoid fingerprints.

I was worried about whether I would be able to position the film accurately. Luckily, it's not like applying a piece of duct tape. Once the film is thoroughly sprayed on both sides, it's fairly easy to slide it around the glass until it fits perfectly. Don't be afraid to get the glass nice and wet before sliding the film into place!

After I used the included squeegee to flatten the film, and dried it with the cloth, I was dismayed to see lots of residual smudges, bubbles and streaks under the film. But I put the iPad out of sight for 24 hours, as recommended. Sure enough, the dried film was completely free of defects, and practically invisible. Looks like a factory job. The iPad behaves exactly as before, and feels pretty much the same.

I can't imagine spending $500+ on an iPad and not applying this film on day one.

Four stars are for the ease of installation and great initial appearance. If it lasts more than a few months, I'll up it to five.

title: Fast and compact, better suited for fixed installations
text:
This was my first USB 3.0 flash drive.

Curious to see how it stacked up, I quick-formatted it along with a 32GB USB 2.0 drive (NTFS under Windows 7), and copied a folder containing 48 .flac audio files (942 MB total) onto both. (Glenn Gould's performances of Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier, Books I and II, if you care.)

The USB 2.0 drive took 5 minutes and 46 seconds to write the files. The new Lexar took 93 seconds.

After restarting the PC to clear its cache, I read the folder backs to my hard drive. The 2.0 drive completed in 64 seconds. The Lexar took just 30 seconds.

So, yeah. It's faster than 2.0.

Physically, the drive has a nifty design that folds up when you rotate it, so it's quite compact. There's a tie point for attaching a lanyard, and an LED that blinks when the device is active.

The USB plug is made of plastic. Not sure how durable this would be if it was plugged in and out a lot. But for situations in which the drive isn't moved around often, it probably wouldn't be a problem.

title: Perfect bathroom companion
text:

So, be ready. There are voice announcements for major functions.

The SuperStar isn't very big, but it's capable of playing at volume levels much higher than I would ever need. There's no deep bass, but the midbass is tweaked to produce a satisfyingly "full" effect. Corner placement enhances the lows. Bluetooth connection is stupid-easy. I had my Android tablet playing through it in no time. Once linked, the speaker can be taken anywhere in my house without losing signal. It's fun to experiment with various room placements. High shelves often sound good.

I'm not about to throw this thing in the bathtub -- it's rated "splash resistant," not waterproof. But shower steam doesn't seem to faze it at all. So now my baths are accompanied by Internet "easy listening" radio. Ah, decadence.

Never could understand why anyone would want a wireless speaker. But I'm finding ways to use this one all the time.

title: High power, respectable sound, nice audiophile features, but control app is MIA
text:
This portable speaker has quite a lot going for it.

It's small, inobtrusive and classy-looking. Even the packaging is impressive.

The controls are fairly intuitive. I didn't need to read anything to figure out basic operation.

Bluetooth pairing is easy and fast. It locked onto my Android tablet and phone in seconds with no issues. There's a very occasional "hiccup" in the signal, but this has happened with every Bluetooth audio device I have ever tested, regardless of range.

It's a powerful device, capable of filling a large room with ample volume at low distortion.

Audio quality is nearly as good as the Bose Soundtouch systems. That is a compliment. There's no really deep bass, but you shouldn't expect any from a device this small. Like most portable speakers, the mid-bass is somewhat exaggerated, but placing the unit a few feet away from a corner or wall helps to compensate. The rest of the spectrum is reasonably smooth and well-balanced. Not what I would call high fidelity, but pleasant for casual listening.

There's a button labeled Surround. If you engage this and place yourself directly in front of the unit at a distance of 2-4 feet, you will notice a slight increase in the width of the soundstage, accompanied by a reduction in focus and midbass. If you stand anywhere else, the effect is unnoticeable. I keep it turned off.

The unit can be powered by its built-in rechargeable battery, and can also run on AC power using the included wall wart. This is a very welcome feature. The unit runs on any common voltage, and adapters for various countries are provided in the package. Another nice touch: You can use the speaker's battery to charge USB devices, using a jack provided on the back.

There's an auxiliary 1/8" stereo input that lets you to directly connect the speaker to any audio device. This means you can avoid Bluetooth compression and enjoy lossless audio quality. I hooked up my HD audio player and easily heard the difference. Cables for both 1/8" stereo and twin-RCA audio devices are provided in the package.

Audiophile alert! Most portable speakers (including this one) employ a peak limiter. This helps to avoid overloads, but also squashes the dynamic range of the music. Happily, the Riva S has a Phono mode that disables the limiter and increases the gain. Terrific option.

My only complaint about the Riva S is the remote control. There isn't one. Both the package and the Riva web site claim that there's an app available on iTunes and Google Play that will allow you to control this device from your phone/tablet. I could not find one. There IS an app for the Riva Turbo speaker, but this app does NOT seem to work with the Riva S. Hopefully Riva will get its act together and publish a compatible app.

Great gift for a quality-conscious music lover.

title: Too tight, marginal sound, mic only works on single-jack hardware
text:
I really need a decent headphone/mic combo for Skype and voice chat. So I was delighted when I got a chance to try this.

No luck. There is only one input plug that provides both the stereo headphone output and the microphone input. Not one of my PCs or laptops (including a high-end Alienware gaming rig) supports this arrangement. They all require separate jacks for input and output.

Also, the microphone appears to be located on the cord, about a foot away from the earpiece. Hard to imagine getting decent sound from a dangling position like that, but I couldn't test it to find out.

The headphones themselves look as inexpensive as they are. Many of the reviewers here praise their comfort. Not me. Guess I have a big skull, because even when the foldable headband is opened to maximum width, they feel REALLY tight. The sealed earcups provide some isolation from background sounds, but also cause rapid heat build-up around my ears. Can't imagine wearing these for more than 10-20 minutes.

Sound quality is tubby and a bit dull, but I don't expect an audiophile experience at this price. They seem efficient, though, and play much louder than my high-end phones at the same volume setting.

Build quality does not inspire confidence. The detachable cord (which can be plugged into EITHER side; a nice touch!) is insubstantial, and likely to incur damage with regular use. Easily-broken cords is the reason I stopped buying cheap headphones for my kid.

Okay for a backup pair, but there are better choices at or around this price range.
item_title: Altec Lansing MZX656-BLUE Over Ear Foldable Headphones with Mic, Blue

title: Great curb appeal, but ... but ...
text:
I've owned a few Bang & Olufsen hi-fi products over the years. They were exquisitely built and beautiful to look at, but their audio performance never particularly impressed me, despite the enthusiastic pricing.

These headphones are no exception. Everything about them exudes high-class luxury. The construction and finish are flawless. Even the packaging is gorgeous. Only the detachable cord disappointed me with its relative flimsiness.

The earcups are closed and fully cover your ears. There's plenty of adjustment range, but the best-sounding fit is fairly tight. This helps reduce interference from outside noise, but the pressure gets fatiguing after a half hour or so. You won't easily forget that you're wearing these.

I got a nasty surprise when I plugged the H6 into my home music system for the first time. Couldn't hear a thing! The cord included in my package was apparently designed specifically for use with iPhones and iPads; the extra conductors on the plug are incompatible with many standard headphone jacks. This important detail isn't mentioned anywhere on the Amazon product page, as far as I can tell.

I had no choice but to order one of the U9000-1 replacement cords recommended by several other reviewers. Swapping out the stock cord with the new one did the trick.

For listening purposes, I used Neil Young's superb 24-bit 192 kHz remasterings of "After the Gold Rush" and "Harvest," two albums I've heard literally hundreds of times, reproduced through a decent DAC and headphone amp.

The sound isn't bad at modest volume levels. The bass is deep, natural and well-articulated, with a smooth, extended high end. (The tape hiss from the 70s-era recordings was clearly audible.) Spectrally, the left and right drivers are closely matched; vocal and instrumental staging is rock solid. When Neil's voice is panned center, he is focused RIGHT THERE.

But there's something going on in the mid-to-upper midrange I don't like. There's a distinct bump in there that makes everything sound too close. It's tolerable at low listening levels, but turning up the volume made me wince. Too "present" for my taste.

I really wanted to like these stunning headphones. I'd probably wear them if I wanted to impress a first-class flight attendant with my wealth and taste. But for this price you can find a pair of far more comfortable Sennheisers that sound significantly better. And you won't have to buy a new cord, either.

UPDATE 8/27/16

Been using these for a few more weeks. Some additional notes:

When correctly fitted, the outside sound rejection of these phones is REALLY good, among the best I've encountered without active noise cancellation (which always degrades the audio quality somewhat). This makes them especially well suited for use in noisy environments like planes, trains and busy offices.

The midrange bump is certainly there, and I still don't care for it. But considering that these phones are explicitly intended for use with mobile devices, it makes sense from a design perspective. A certain amount of "presence" boost helps vocals cut through distracting background sounds. I prefer using an equalizer to make such compensations, but casual users may be better served by B&O's approach.

Remember that "quality" is relative to purpose. I'm not changing my 3-star rating, because I can't recommend these phones for critical, long-period listening in quiet rooms. But an on-the-go iPhone or iPad user with deep pockets might be very well served by them.

And they really ARE handsome.

title: Good choice for "family" computing
text:
This is the first all-in-one PC I've ever set up or used. I'm impressed.

It all comes in a single, cleverly-designed carton the size of a monitor. System consists of a 23" 1920x1080 screen with integrated PC, a wireless keyboard and a wireless mouse.

Setup took less than ten minutes, without a glance at the instructions. The mouse and keyboard both require a pair of AA batteries. Four genuine Duracell alkalines are provided. The wireless connection for the keyboard and mouse is provided by a small USB dongle, which must be installed in one of the four USB ports on the monitor. (Odd that a separate dongle is necessary. Why isn't the radio built-in? Or why not use the available Bluetooth?)

Attach the AC power cord to the back of the monitor, make sure the power switches on the keyboard and mouse are turned on (they already were on my sample), and turn the unit on. You'll immediately enter the standard Windows 10 setup process. This REQUIRES a live connection to the Internet, which can be provided either by a hardwired Ethernet connection (via a jack on the back of the monitor), or via WiFi.

The unit discovered my 5 GHz home WiFi instantly. Windows initialization proceeded with no issues at all, and took less than 10 minutes, including updates. This is about as easy as it gets nowadays.

The unit itself employs an Intel Core i3-6100U processor clocked at 2.3 GHz, supported by 8 gigs of RAM, vanilla motherboard graphics and a 500 GB rotary hard drive. The actual amount of free drive space available on my newly-initialized system was 426 GB.

There are four USB ports: A pair of USB 2.0 ports on the back, and a pair of USB 3.0 ports on the left side. The USB dongle uses up a port; I sacrificed one of the 2.0 ports on the back. The left side also has a media-card reader and a stereo headphone jack. There is no separate microphone input, but there is a front-facing microphone above the screen beside the lens of the video camera.

Beside the USB 2.0 and Ethernet ports on the back, there is an audio output jack (line-level, I assume) and ... this was a surprise! ... an HDMI video port. It is described in the instruction sheet as an INPUT port, but other reviewers report that it's actually an OUTPUT port, suitable for extending the desktop with a second monitor.

The right side of the unit has a DVD RW drive (too bad it can't play Blu-rays), video controls and the main power switch.

This thing is REALLY quiet. The only sound is the faint whir of the hard drive.

McAfee virus protection comes pre-installed, probably with a subscription that needs to be renewed. You also get all the standard Windows 10 bloatware, much of which (but not all) can be disabled or uninstalled if it annoys you.

This is NOT a high-performance system suitable for hardcore 3D gaming or HD video production. But it's more than adequate for Web surfing, music/video streaming, home and small-office productivity apps and other everyday uses.

Bottom line: A basic, useful computer in a convenient form factor, easy to set up and use.

title: Lush, authoritative sound;  Alexa optional.
text:
This is one of the most impressive Bluetooth speakers I've had the pleasure of auditioning.

It combines the retro-tweed look and rugged build quality of a Marshall guitar amp with a clear, pleasantly-balanced and seriously powerful audio system. My Bose SoundTouch 30 (which costs significantly more, sports fewer features, and isn't nearly as cool-looking) now faces a deadly rival.

Most amplified home speakers need to be cranked to sound their best. This Marshall accomplishes the rare feat of sounding good at both high and low volume levels. It seems to do this without increasing its bass output at quieter setttings, unlike the SoundTouch, which applies this old trick shamelessly. Its tonal balance is warmer than the Bose, with a gently rolled-off high end. I suspect it is deliberately voiced to suggest the richness and bloom of tube-based audio systems, which makes perfect sense considering its pedigree.

At medium and high volume levels, the Bose presentation is slicker, more modern and probably more accurate. But the Marshall sounds like cream and honey at any level, especially at low volume, where the Bose becomes distinctly tubby.

Such a tactile pleasure to have actual KNOBS (tastefully accented with tiny LED level indicators) for controlling volume, bass and treble! A pushbutton is used to select one of four input sources: WiFi, Bluetooth, a pair of rear-panel RCA phono jacks and a conveniently top-mounted 1/8" jack.

The instruction book urged me to download an app to control the unit. You'll probably need to do that if you want to use Wifi, Alexa or multi-speaker setups. But all I care about are the direct inputs and Bluetooth. Happily, you do NOT need to use an app, or enable WiFi, to access these modes. Switch the input selector to Bluetooth, hold down the button and the unit goes into pairing mode. It found my Android phone in a few seconds, and maintains a perfect connection from anywhere in my 2-story house.

One glaring oversight: No power switch. The unit stays on all the time, unless you unplug it. This needlessly wastes both energy and money, and also poses a annoyance if you leave the input selector on Bluetooth and move any paired devices out of range. This situation (which happens whenever I leave the house with my phone) causes the speaker's polite female voice to complain (loudly, continuously and at eerily-random intervals) about the lack of connectivity. Tedious solution: Set the input selector to one of the hardwired sources.

Perhaps the Marshall Voice app provides a power switch. But I don't want another app, thank you very much, and I shouldn't need one to turn off an electrical appliance.

Frankly, I hesitated to evaluate this unit (and other recent speaker and headphone products) because of privacy concerns about Alexa. There's a switch on the Marshall that purports to turn off the microphone array. Nevertheless, I prefer leaving the unit disconnected from the Internet, and have preserved the modesty of the microphone ports by covering them with discreet squares of foam tape.

Call me paranoid. I don't care. My music sounds really great. And, KNOBS.

title: Significant speed boost when deployed as a USB 3 external drive
text:
My aging PC doesn't have the M.2 slot required to fully exploit the speed potential of this NVMe SSD. Its USB 3.0 ports could use an upgrade, too.

Nevertheless, I decided to configure the Sabrent as an external USB 3 SSD, using one of Sabrent's USB 3.1 aluminum EC-NVME enclosures (which I recommend, despite the rather high price).

As an informal test, I copied a 1 GB HD audio file from an external USB 3.1 HDD (Western Digital) to my PC's internal SATA drive. Because my Windows 10 PC has lots of RAM (12 GB), this operation also copied most or all of the file into Windows's RAM file cache.

When I copied the same file back to the external HDD, the average write speed was around 210 megabytes per second.

Then I copied the file to the external Sabrent SSD. Average write speed jumped to about 280 megabytes per second.

I also ran an ATTO benchmark on the two external drives. The HDD reported an average write/read speed of about 220 MB/sec. The Sabrent averaged 430 MB/sec; almost twice as fast, but well below USB 3.0's maximum data rate of 625 MB/sec.

My poor old USB 3.0 ports are obviously incapable of taking full advantage of ANY USB 3.1 device, be it a hard drive or an SSD. Even full 3.1 speed falls short of what NVMe can deliver when installed on an M.2 motherboard. But this portable SSD is still substantially faster than any of my numerous portable HHDs. It's also less than half the size.

title: Turns my smartphone into a multimedia center
text:
I've been using a standard Android 7 phone with a micro-USB OTG (On-The-Go) connector to send FLAC audio files to an external DAC for playback on my stereo equipment.

The setup works, and sounds great, but there's a nagging problem: Both the phone and the DAC had to be powered from the phone's battery, because OTG does not support simultaneous peripheral use and charging. A few hours of listening depleted the battery. Bummer.

Recently, I got my hands on a Sony Xperia 10 Plus, an ultra-widescreen Android 9 phone that uses a USB C connector for charging and peripherals. Combined with this DesertWest USB C hub, the Sony has become the centerpiece of a complete home entertainment system that also happens to be a really powerful smartphone.

The DesertWest hub is a sturdy, attractive aluminum box less than half the size of the phone. A six-inch cable (permanently attached) terminates in a USB C male plug, which connects to my phone. Connectors around the sides provide support for three USB 3.0 devices (including storage, audio DACs, a keyboard and/or mouse, etc), a Gigabit Ethernet port, an HDMI output capable of 4K/30p, readers for both standard and micro SD/SDXC cards, a dedicated USB C Power Delivery port, and a USB C passthrough port that also works for charging.

That passthrough port is important. This hub requires power, so it needs to be connected to a charger to do anything. But that charger will simulataneously supply power the to hub's host device (my phone) AND any devices connected to the hub's USB 3.0 outlets! So I can now play music through my USB DAC without draining the phone's battery. The phone doesn't charge as quickly as it does without any peripherals attached, but at least it isn't dying.

I'm betting that a USB C Power Delivery charger (connected to the dedicated port) would deliver more than enough current to charge my phone at full speed while effortlessly supporting any USB peripherals as well.

Still haven't tried feeding an .mp4 file or Netflix stream through the HDMI port. You need an HDMI 2.0 cable to take full advantage of 4K/30p resolution.

The packaging of the DesertWest hub is notably classy. Looks more like an expensive watch case than a computer peripheral.

If you or someone you know has recently aquired a device with USB C connectivity, this handsome Swiss Army hub would indeed make an excellent gift.

title: Impressive volume, visceral tactile effect
text:
My only previous experience with a neckband speaker was a $130 JVC model. I thought it was fairly good ... until I slipped on this Avantree.

Night and day. No contest.

The midrange and high-end response of both units is respectable at modest volume levels, especially with a bit of careful EQ. But the JVC sounds obviously distorted at high volume, and offers no significant bass at any level.

The Avantree delivers MUCH higher volume without breaking up. And although it has no more ACTUAL deep bass than the JVC, it cleverly simulates the EFFECT of deep bass through bone conduction.

When worn against the skin, or over light clothing, the Avantree transduces low-frequency information in the music to a physical vibration. Even at modest volume levels, you can FEEL the kick drum and tom-toms pounding away on your shoulders. Sustained bass notes make your collar bone tremble. At high volume, the sensation is literally thrilling! Put on some power pop, crank up the volume and drape this neckband on a friend. Watch their mouth drop open.

It's not REAL bass, though. Once you get over the initial surprise, and settle down for extended listening, the vibration assumes a somewhat artificial quality. All drums produce a similar "thump;" deep bass pitches are distinguishable mainly by their overtones. I found myself reducing the overall bass level to minimize the distraction. But I suspect a majority of listeners care more about impact than accuracy, and will find the tactile effect thoroughly satisfying.

One place this neckband really shines is in a car. Plenty of volume, a perfect stereo image, and nothing covering your ears. I'd use these instead of typical car speakers anytime.

Bluetooth operation is quite acceptable. No issues pairing with my phone. Range is typical; at least 25 feet line of sight, less around corners. The controls for power, volume and track skipping work as expected. I haven't used it for phone calls.

One odd (and odd-looking) feature: A pair of standard wired earbuds is built-in, one bud peering incongruously from each side of the neckband. A switch lets you choose where the sound goes. (The vibration effect only works with the neckband.) Sliders retract the earbud wires when not needed. I tried the buds once. Nothing special.

Battery life seems more than ample. I've played them for hours at decent volume, but the power-on status voice has yet to report anything but "full" or "high" battery level.

Note that this is NOT a "private" listening device. Anyone in the same room or vehicle with you will CLEARLY hear whatever you're enjoying, even at modest volume levels.

If audiophile sound quality is important to you, look elsewhere. But for casual listening in private environments, this Aventune neckband is well worth auditioning. I crank them whenever I drive alone.

title: Perfectly suited to my application
text:
My deskstop includes a pair of Windows PCs shared by three enormous monitors, so switching to my lone-screen laptop for remote work is kind of painful. I've always wanted to get a second monitor for the laptop, but even the smallest I could find weren't portable enough.

This Huyouming monitor fits the bill pretty well. It's lightweight and extremely thin, even when enclosed by its protective folder/stand, and takes up very little space in my laptop case.

Hooking it up as a second Windows monitor is stupid-easy. It's powered by a USB cable (supplied) that fits any standard USB-B or C socket. The monitor powers up immediately when connected; unfortunately, there's no dedicated power switch.

Video is supplied by a separate HDMI cable. I'm using the one supplied with the monitor, with a standard HDMI plug on one end (for my laptop/PC) and a mini-HDMI plug on the other to feed the monitor. The monitor immediately sensed the presence of input, and my laptop's HD screen is mirrored perfectly. I can use Windows utilities to assign the second monitor's position and orientation relative to the laptop's monitor. Everything works without issues.

The monitor also accepts an HDMI signal via USB-C from laptops, phones and tablets that support it. None of my current Android devices can perform this trick, so I can't report on how well it works.

The quality of the 1920 x 1080 IPS display is more than adequate for my purposes.

The monitor's faux-leather folder can configured as a support easel with the aid of a plastic accessory stand. It works, but looks and feels a bit flimsy. However, the back of the monitor is equipped with a set of four VESA holes (matching screws included) which allows it to be mounted onto any VESA-compatible support device. I ordered a desktop-clamping support with a swiveling arm that will let me position the unit freely.

I didn't need to consult the instruction manual. This is a good thing, because the printing is barely legible without a magnifying glass. The teeny diagram showing the location of the connectors and controls is inaccurate. It shows only one mini-HDMI input and one speaker hole. The unit actually has two of each. Both of the speaker holes are located on the left side of the monitor, an odd arrangement not conducive to watching movies with stereo sound. Luckily, there's also a 1/8" stereo headphone jack.

I'm looking forward to experimenting with this monitor. Its compact size and VESA mountability should make for some interesting placement options.

title: If you're into ChromeOS, here's a Rolls Royce
text:
My old Windows laptops are nearing the end of their lifecycles. I didn't think a Chromebook would meet my needs, since most of them seem relatively underpowered. But I figured I'd give this high-end model a shot.

This is easily the most portable laptop I've ever owned. It's the size and thickness of a paper notebook,
and nearly as lightweight. Despite this, the keyboard (which is backlit!) is essentially full-sized, and
feels great under the fingers.

The 13" screen offers full HD (1920 x 1080) native resolution, which is both a blessing (when watching movies and/or using multiple apps) and a curse (when trying to read text, which can be a challenge at this size/scale). Luckily, the virtual dimensions of the display are easily upscaled, and the quality of the upscaled image is outstanding, unlike many Windows devices, which become noticeably pixelated. The touchscreen works as expected, though I almost always use a mouse.

Aside from a 1/8" stereo headphone jack, there are only three ports: a pair of USC-C 3.2 Gen 1s which
both support charging/power delivery and/or DisplayPort output, and a single USB-A 3.2 Gen 1 port. This arrangement may be adequate for many users, but if you use multiple peripherals like I do, you'll probably want to obtain a USB-C hub, preferably one that supports power delivery. The DesertWest
hub I use gives me three USB-A ports, an HDMI output, an Ethernet jack and slots for several different types of memory cards. All of the ports work flawlessly with the Chromebook, including the HDMI, which
lets me connect the laptop to almost any external monitor or HDTV.

Added bonus: You can connect a SIM card and run the laptop off 4G cellphone towers. Very handy for frequent travelers.

I typically use a laptop as the control center for HD music listening. My library resides on an external
4TB HDD, and my playback rig is a Schiit Modi 3 DAC driving a Magni 2 headphone amp. I'm happy to report that this Chromebook drives my setup with no issues at all when I plug the Modi directly into the USB-A port. (It would probably work through a USB-C hub as well, though I haven't tried it.) Both of my preferred audio apps (Neutron and Foobar2000) are available on the Chrome store and operate as expected.

Hard to fault the performance. This Acer powers up in seconds, connects to every wireless device I've tried effortlessly, and runs off a fully-charged battery for the better part of a day. Web browsing with Chrome is as brisk as my most powerful desktops. Web-based apps like Zoom, Slack and VS Code are also highly responsive, and so are the handful of apps I've downloaded from the Chrome store.

The 128GB onboard memory is skimpy by Windows standards. There's no built-in memory card slot (an odd and annoying omission that cost my review 1 star), but it's easily and cheaply expandable via the slots available on most USB-C hubs. A 128 GB MicroSD card will double this laptop's capacity for less than $20.

The biggest issue with this unit is its price. At nearly $800, it's competing with a number of Windows 10/11 laptops with similar specifications/feature sets. But if you're accustomed to the ChromeOS ecosystem, or just want a zippy laptop/tablet that's ultra-portable and stupid-easy to use, this high-end Acer is worth serious consideration.

title: Versatile alternative to cans and hoses
text:
I've been drilling holes in granite lately, a task that produces a great deal of powdery dust. The stuff needs to be clean away frequently because it blocks your view, slows the bit and is dangerous to breathe.

I've tried plastic blowing tubes (awkward) and cans of compressed air (expensive, don't last long). There are electric blowers available, but they require AC power, which is not always available outdoors. When I saw this handheld battery-powered Koonie unit, I decided to give it a try.

The two-speed unit can function either as a vacuum or a blower. Two brush extensions are provided for the vaccum mode, and one for the blower. Build quality seems pretty solid (better than I expected, actually).

It's powered by a rather hefty battery that claims to provide up to 90 minutes of service with a full charge. I've only used it on and off for about 30 minutes so far, so I can't estimate the actual capacity, but so far it hasn't slowed down perceptibly.

The battery is charged with a standard USB cable. A charger that delivers a full 2A is recommended (most USB ports only supply 1A.) Even with a 2A source, expect a charging time of several hours when fully drained. The battery can also serve as a high-capacity charger for USB-powered devices, a nice touch.

The power switch is VERY sensitive. A slight touch is enough to start the motor. I detach the battery when storing the unit to avoid accidental start-ups.

The blower isn't super-powerful, but more than adequate to keep my drill holes clear of dust. I just turn the unit on at full power and place it on its side with the nozzle aimed at the drill bit, a few inches away. Occasionally I pause to blow dust out of the hole (and let the tool cool down). Works like a charm for my application.

I only tried the vaccuum once, on some dust bunnies under a chair. Not a good day for the bunnies.

Definitely worth considering if you need a portable air mover.

I have had tons of micro sd cards. Most of them have been Sandisk but switched to Samsung when Sandisk had a bad run of Ultras(class 10s) that were failing in Android phones.

I've used class 10 or higher since using sdswap on phones (starting around 6 years ago). Back then most phones had 8 to 16gb of internal storage and wasn't enough room to handle what I needed.

Sdswap made the phone think the external storage was the internal (essentially giving me 32 to 64gb of internal memory) and the internal the external. Because of this I always needed high speed memory or the read/write of the card would significantly slow down my phone.

Sandisk had always been the most reliable card that was also fast and cost effective until about 3 years ago. During that time, whether it was due to a bad batch of cards or due to the way a new version of how a new version of Android's OS accessed them, they began to fail. Obviously losing data is a nightmare so I switch to the more costly Samsung class 10+ cards.

*I know Sandisk addressed the problem, because they fixed the issue and released a new upgraded batch. They even "tried" to replace my cards by publicly tweeting me a link to do so, in apology for the cards failures (in response to a comment I made on Twitter that asked other Android devs/testers if their Sandisk cards were failing them).

But unfortunately in the end neither of my cards were replaced. One of the cards I had already thrown away and the other I found a few days later. Unfortunately, after multiple attempts, I wasn't able to receive a response from the company after their initial response (which told me they needed the bad cards serial #s etc...) essentially they dissappeared once I was able to find the info and send it to them. So I took that as a HR saving face moment on Twitter and moved on.

Obviously I didn't think much of the company after that and stayed away from them for a couple years.

I finally started buying cards from them again for my devices that held less critical data. Over the last year or so (mid 2014) I haven't had any issues. I am glad Sandisk has become reliable once again.

title: If you're coming from another remote in the Harmony family this is a no brainier
text:
This is my 4th Harmony remote. I originally had a Harmony 880, then stepped up to the 900 when it was released. At the time the 900 was perfect (The only Bluetooth (BT) remote back then was for the PS3 and Logitech released a RF to BT add on to make it compatible). So I used the 900 for many years. I only retired it when I, unfortunately, broke the screen.

At the time, dropping another $200 - $300 on a remote just didn't seem worth it. So I ended up just getting a 650. I'm glad I did because only a little while later everything started switching to Bluetooth and this is where the Smart control really makes sense.

With Cable, Amazon Fire, Gaming Systems, etc... remotes being Bluetooth the 650 and all other non BT Harmony systems became obsolete. So if you are like me and want to make sure the new Hub style system will work (before dropping $300 on the Ultimate) this is a great way to go for $70.

If you are coming from an old Harmony remote you can just transfer everything from it directly to this Hub (through the Computer Software). If this is your first Harmony remote you're going to have a rough go at first. The setup of these systems is pretty intense and they also have a sharp learning curve.

Pros
*Easy to transfer old Harmony data to
*Works with almost everything now
*Can teach it how to control cheap Chinese items like HDMI switches (by using the remote those devices originally came with)
*Macros are available and every button is customizable for short and long press
*Bluetooth Compatibility
*IR repeaters and blasters work with it
*Price

Cons
*No way to integrate Xfinity or Amazon Voice Control (the voice controls that are native to those remotes)
*Can only control full Activities via the remote. IE You can't change the remote to just control single "device" like what is possible with previous Harmony remotes (and current models with screens)
*Remote doesn't have IR (only the Hub does)
*Hard to program at first
*Not the most intuitive programming for Activities, even once you understand the system
*No backlight
*Remote's buttons are almost flush so feeling out what to push is tough.
*Can't add a new device to an activity that is already programed (Afaik) so you have to re run them if you get a new HDMI switch etc.
*Still has issues with TVs that have odd input switching

Even with all those cons I strongly recommend this remote. Once you put in the time to understand it, and get the programming down, it is a life changer. I use one hub in my bedroom and another In the family room, where everything is stored in the closet of the room behind the wall where the TV is mounted. It works great for both situations except for the remote only using RF and not having IR. But an IR blaster is simple enough to add.

title: Need to be a bit tech savy
text:
Update: 12-19-19 The EAP225 V3 is still going strong. But I've added another Access Point (AP) to extend the range of my separate "Smart Things" network. This time I bought the N300, which is the EAP115. There are some major differences between the two and I listed them below.

EAP115 (N300) -
- This AP is Wireless N (n,b,g) only, so no 5GHz, it only has the 2.4GHz channel. For Smart Devices (IOT) it's perfect.
-The LAN port going in is 100Mbps instead of the 1,000Mbps (Gigabit) port on the 225
- It does NOT come with the PoE injector. This device will work with PoE (Power over Ethernet) but you'd need your own injector or PoE switch - the 225 comes with said injector.

Original Review of EAP 225 (AC1350)
I use this AP mainly as my "Smart Things" Access Point but also to extend my 5ghz wifi for my phones etc.

If you are somewhat tech savvy this is a no brainer. If you aren't, then just read and watch some videos before purchasing and everything should still go smoothly.

I struggle when it gets around the time I feel I need to buy and/or replace/upgrade my router. With new high end routers going for $400 - $600 I always end up going down the rabbit hole and stress about buying something at the wrong time, or worry about getting stuck with a new piece of tech that has a crap chip in it, or bad software.

So I decided to just grab this AP during black Friday (for $45) and use it to hold me over. I was definitely not disappointed. You can install these anywhere you want, and even install them like a smoke detector (since it can run without an outlet, when using PoE). That is what I did at first and it worked great. It comes with an injector for PoE, so even if you don't have a PoE switch you are safe and won't have to spend any more money.

For those that don't know PoE is simply Power over Ethernet. It is something that allows devices, like this and other things, to get their power directly from the Ethernet cable. This means you don't need to run a separate power cord as well as an Ethernet cable to it to use it. It also doesn't take a special Ethernet cable to do so either. But it does take an injector (that has an Ethernet input from your router or switch, and outputs a powered Ethernet line) or a PoE switch.

I originally installed this in my garage (as pictured) and used it to boost both my 2.4 and 5 signals. Setting it up with the same SSIDs and passwords. Working out how to get the handover to my main router took only a little while. I used the web based interface and was able to set the strength (power level of the antennas) of the signals to the right point for each one so that my main router would take over once I was halfway through the house.

That worked remarkably well, until I finally decided on a new router. By the time I bought the new router I had also purchased a bunch of smart wifi devices. So I now use this as the access point for them (on the 2.4 GHz) and only use the 5 GHz to extend the range for my other devices. This device is able to setup multiple SSIDs and I am using a different SSID for the 2.4 (and am keeping it isolated to protect my home devices) but I am using the same for the 5 GHz and only allow the phones and tablets (devices that aren't in a fixed place) to connect to it.

I'm a fairly trust worthy person, but would rather play it safe with my WiFi IoT stuff. So this is a wonderful solution for that problem.

Update: 8 months later and it's still going strong. 3 2.4 SSID's setup and over 20 wifi smart things connected. With load balancing, QOS and rate limiting I've been able to control all of it. I added a second pic with my speeds on 5GHz wifi (limited by my phone's antenna) and it's as good as my router.

The ability to balance the rear speakers relative volume (to the front) has been extremely helpful but the lack of R/L balance on them still bothers me a bit. Overall though I'm a happy customer and am changing my review from a 4 to a 5.

Original:
Update: a month later, This thing has been a game changer. It has made a very mediocre soundbar sound so much better. Just go ahead and pull the trigger on it. I added pictures and a video to show the size of items and how the display on the soundbar changes to add new options.

Unlike some of the others (reviewers) I didn't have any issues connecting this to my HW-R60C. Simply shut it off and then pressed the mute (annoyingly it says volume, which is technically correct, but the function is mute) for 5 seconds, it paired instantly and worked.

The menu will now actually change on your soundbar. After Treble, Bass and Audio Delay there are two additional Rear selections now. The first is to simply turn the rears off and on and the second is their volumes (-6/+6).

Pros:
*Cheap way to upgrade a 3.1 system to 5.1.
*Ease of pairing
*Wireless connection from soundbar to Rear Box

Cons:
*Not wireless to the actual speakers
*Lack of L/R Balance
*Mounting system is a keyhole... Lack of threads means you need a clamping mount 👎

So the audio sounds great and I'm happy with it but the lack of a Left/Right balance option really sucks. This is the only reason I'm knocking a star off. I was able to work around it, but it forced me to have to install the speakers in sub optimal locations (aesthetically).

title: Works well, buttons a little too responsive, loses wireless connection
text:
I've had this Elecom wireless trackball for about a week and a half. Connected via Bluetooth initially and it worked poorly. Slow response, stuttering, and skipping at both 'Low' and 'High' settings were noted from 3 feet away from my PC. Pairing was also a bit difficult, as I had to hold it right next to the PC before it was recognized. Switched over to the wireless dongle and worked fine until just yesterday.

The past 2 days have certainly been troublesome. When powering on my PC the dongle is no longer recognized and the wireless mouse does not connect. Yesterday I was able to remove and replace the dongle in the same USB port and it started working. Today I had to move it to a different port for it to be recognized. When it is actually connected the mouse works well, it is very responsive and quick, although the buttons are prone to accidental pushes at even the lightest of touches.

On the subject of the buttons two of them are in awkward positions which makes them hard to activate when timing is of the essence. Additionally not all the buttons are programmable, and even then they are subject to specific commands allowed by the software. So no macros, or even modified key + button press can be set e.g. Control + Button 3 .

It is a decent wireless trackball overall, but just middle of the road.

title: For advanced users, this is incredible- Line in and out
text:
This thing is amazing. With all the basic iPhone users out there, the selection of bluetooth audio receivers is pretty bad. Most are basic cig lighter plug-ins that only broadcast on FM which completely ruins the audio quality. This receiver has both line in and line out as well as optional USB charging port.

The line out allows you to connect the audio directly into your AUX (or often incorrectly labeled iPhone) port on your radio if so equipped. My car has a line in (AUX) mounted down near the console. I spliced the line out from this bluetooth adapter directly to the wiring of the AUX port and then spliced the AUX port itself to the line in on the bluetooth receiver. What that equates to, is not having an ugly plug hanging out of the AUX port as the wiring is all concealed and no wires are exposed. It also means that the AUX port built into my car is still usable should a friend with an ipod, mp3 player, guitar, drum machine, hell, even a cassette Walkman can still plug into my car's AUX as if nothing was modified. There is no other device like this that I have seen on the market other than the same unit sold under different brand names. (Note to any custom installers, if you try this, don't forget about the ground short to switch the inputs on with no plug sitting in the jack)

Oh yeah, and this thing also will output over FM as well if you like and it allows any frequency, unlike most of these devices which offer only a few to choose from. There is no better bluetooth receiver on the market.

CON:
I found the Livio app absolutely worthless, I didn't take stars off for that though, as I didn't even know about Livio or it's app when I purchased this device, I bought it solely for it's Bluetooth/Line in/Line out capabilities only.

Should work with any standard EDR Bluetooth device, (Android, Blackberry, WinMo, Android Tabs, iPhone/pad, etc.)

title: Great case, quality build and good functional design.
text:
I have been using this case for a few weeks now and I am glad I bought it. It seems a bit expensive to me, but no other viable case options for surface book cost any less, so it is what it is.
The case has a very nice feel to it and compliments the surface book very well. It also hides the fact that it is a laptop from a distance and looks like a simple note portfolio when you are walking around in public with it, which is an added security bonus.
It has a pen holder loop on the lower side, but I find that clipping the pen on the screen part if the case more convenient, especially when using just the tablet portion. I use an aftermarket surface pen which had a traditional metal pocket clip like a regular writing pen has and I clip that piece onto the case itself where there are openings along the side if the screen.

Pros:
Looks great
Quality build
Very functional
Adds a little more traction to the body so it does not want to slip out of your hands and lap as easily.
2 piece design so you can easily separate the screen from the dock without fussing with the case.
Strong magnets keep the screen and base parts of the case connected and when the screen is separated, the lower flap wraps around the bottom of the screen automatically created a nice enclosed tablet.

Cons:
The pen loop is in a bad spot, first if you use it for the pen, than when in tablet mode, the pen is attached to the base, not the screen where you need it. Also it make access to the power port a little more challenging, not a big problem, but could some refinement.
Price!
I feel this is the best case out there right now as options are pretty limited for surface book cases.

Another note, when using a case on your surface, any case, monitor your device temps when doing anything resource intensive such as gaming, rendering or video encoding as all case reduce heat dissipation. You may want to remove the case when doing these types if tasks.

Very cute. Im not knocking off stars because it I don't blame them for using the buzz word, but while this probably is a pwm fan it is very obviously being controlled by having a 3 or 6 ohm resistor switched in line for medium and low speeds respectively (no resistance for high, open circuit for off)

The sticker under the pretty silver circle says .28A 5V, 1.4W. That should mean as far as the circuit is concerned the motor is a 17.8 ohm resistor. When operating the fan at its lowest speed you add 6 ohms, making the current 210mA and meaning you waste an entire 345 milliwatts on the resistor in the controller! How utterly inconsequential!

All of that to say... This fan does not utilize the tachometer or pulse width modulation for control, because it absolutely doesn't need to. There's no point, nothing is monitoring this fan's speed. All this means is they are controlling a high quality fan motor by the simplest means possible which is just fine for me because I'm actually going to modify this fan to use the PWM function. Hopefully.

Anyways. I got a good laugh and a few minutes entertainment doing the math on the power requirements on this fan. Hats off to the designer for keeping it simple.

title: Frustrating, but finally got to be useful.  ( PLEASE READ HOW I DID IT)
text: This is an update to the review I left two hours ago.  This is what I've discovered using my Spyder X Elite.  Basically, you need to figure out your ideal White Point on your computer's built-in display color controls (it's the "Display" function inside the Mac's System Preferences), and have your computer's screen brightness be at the max, as it is in your computer's default color setting.  Then, when doing a calibration in Spyder X, you leave the White Point and Brightness controls set to "Do Not Adjust", then do the color calibration.  THAT is the ONLY way I can get this thing to actually work.  If I have Spyder X change the White Point or Brightness of my monitor during the calibration, what it does is so unbelievably stupid looking.  It makes my monitor look broken.  Anyways, at least after trying this out for 5 hours I was finally able to have it work for me.  I hope this review is helpful to some people.

title: Finicky, prevents Windows 10 from booting, run-around for RMA
text:
Recently purchased a PCIe USB card from Amazon. This card prevents windows from booting. I removed the card and now my computer boots properly. I do not have the original packaging, so I cannot return to Amazon, and I would like RMA consideration. Below is the card I purchased.
Sonnet Allegro Pro USB 3.2 Type A PCIe Card (Four SuperSpeed 10Gbps USB Connectors)

--

Regarding the issue: this may be that the USB devices are pulling more than 2A of power per device. The Allegro cards include resettable fuses built into these cards’ ports that will trip when a connected device pulls more than 2A of power. Have you tried connecting one device to port 1, and another to port 4?
See our tech note here for more details, and how to reset these fuses for testing.

Your PC computer, or the USB peripheral, may require additional setup for best connection usage. Have you also tried updating the BIOS of the computer, as well as the USB and motherboard chipset drivers? Does the USB peripheral have (or require) a firmware update for optimized usage? Is there additional USB software required or recommended for use of these?
We have seen that some complex USB devices require firmware/software updates for use, otherwise, errors (like no connection, or, a BSOD) can occur when using more complicated devices connected to the same domain. You can also enter BIOS/EFI and look for advanced options like ‘PCI > ‘Auto’ or similar and set this to ‘Gen2’ then test again.

Regrettably, Microsoft lags in supporting new, faster controller chips. You can try downloading the latest driver here. You may also find additional downloads from Microsoft directly. See here for additional, albeit older, downloads.

Your OEM may also have other drivers available directly from their website. Look for the drivers for the ASM3142 chip. These are the chips used in the Allegro Pro cards. Similar drivers (ASM1142, ASM2142) may also help. See the Device Manager for more information.

text: The case is nice for what I was looking to do.  I had everything installed and when I went to power on, nothing.  I pulled everything out and started inspecting and testing that I could, power supply was good, ram was good, but I did not have another amd chip or board as this is my first amd build.  I bought another board and the apu was fine so I thought the other board I initially bought was bad.  I stuck an old xp machine into the case and tried powering one and no go.  I ended up taking it apart to only find that one of the leads to the power button had detached.  The soldering job for the other connection was poor.  After re-soldering, re-installing, it works.  This will by my 10th pc build, first amd build and this is the first time I ever had a problem with a case.  Would I recommend this to any one else looking to build a micro atx setup?  Sure as the price is cheap but just take the front panel off remove the housing for the buttons and usb and inspect the connections prior to installing.  The case itself I would give a 5/5 price per value. Now I can get back to completing my HTPC/server.

title: I have had mine for 34 years, and it still works perfectly
text:
My k1000 will be 30 years old this Christmas, and it has been the most reliable camera I have ever owned. My lenses are still nice and sharp. My light meter and flash shoe still work. I have probably changed the battery 3 times. There are no light leaks. Everything works just like the day I got it.

This is a great first camera for any person who wants to learn about photography: exposure, composition, etc. With digital point and shoots, it's really easy to just be a documentarian and rely on photoshop or filters to fix things up a bit later, but there's no real incentive to get things right in the first instance. Film - real film - requires patience and discipline and a critical eye. Which is why I am teaching my 11 year old son to use this.

A tip on loading the film (I was dead broke for a lot of the first decade I owned this and could not afford to waste a bit): Before you try to load the film, bend just the last little bit down, so that it makes a little l-shaped piece that will catch in the slot. Put the tag into the slot and carefully pull out just enough to fit the film snugly into the camera. BY HAND, turn the spool on the left side about half a turn to set the film on the spool and make sure the holes are caught on the teeth. When you turn the left spool, the film should come easily out of the canister. Only do a little bit, and if it seems to be working (i.e. pulling the film out of the canister), close the back of the camera. Cock the camera - WATCH the film counter to make sure the film is advancing. If it's not, don't rewind unless you are sure you can do so without losing your leading edge into the film canister. Just open the back and re-set the edge onto the spool and try again. If it is - and you should be able to feel the resistance in the mechanism - shoot a picture. The first one won't come out. The second one may, and by loading carefully, you should be able to get an extra couple of shots on every roll of film.

Digital point and shoot is a much different animal from old film photography, but I still want an excellent lens, because without one, I feel like I might as well just stick with my iPhone or Bloggie and not have an actual camera at all.

I bought the Lumix for the Leica lens, and I was a little disappointed that it does not render accurately close up. In the automatic setting, there's a noticeable amount of fisheye distortion that is clearly visible in any close up photo involving lines that should be straight or in portraits, which end up looking like funhouse shots. It took some experimenting, but it turns out that the portrait setting completely corrects this (and you can use it for still life shots, too). Once I gave up my notion of how I thought things ought to be and started to work with the camera to get the results I wanted, I sort of fell a little in love with the thing.

It's got a very large LCD. I have lupus and am losing my eyesight. Tiny lcds just don't work for me. Setting navigation is easy and very very intuitive. The buttons aren't too tiny. I did not install the included software or read the instructions, and I am having a very easy time finding my way around and loading up the pictures. Once you figure out what setting you need to depict accurately the person, place, or thing you are trying to photograph, you get sharp, accurate pictures, even in low light or under other difficult shooting conditions.
