title: HBO is on the Way!  Good for Not-Too-Tech-Savvy Seniors - Easy Set Up - Fast Smooth Streaming - Few Nitpicks
text:
I have some cognitive impairment and mobility challenges from lupus, and I was able to set up Fire TV really easily. The batteries go in the remote; the hdmi cable goes where it goes, and the power plugs in where it plugs in. The interface is simple and intuitive, and you can get everywhere with the home button, the directionals, back, and select. The only painful part for me/my hands was logging into my wireless network via the onscreen qwerty keyboard.

The screens are responsive with virtually no latency, thanks to the quad core processor and 2 gb ram. And video streaming is also very smooth. I have only been using this a day, but I haven't had it pause to buffer yet. I have a Chromecast in my son's room, a recent model Mac Mini in the living room, an older C2D Mac Mini in my room with Boxee on it, and a Raspberry Pi, and they all buffer at some point during just about every movie. I stayed in a vacation home with a Roku 2 last summer, and it was great, but it also had to buffer a lot. We also have three game consoles that have streaming video apps, and they buffer, too. I think the Fire's secret may be its wifi card. I am sure that, at some point, my ISP will find a way to slow it down.

So, yeah, I am giving the Fire TV four stars for doing exactly what I need it to do. I had come to Amazon to get another Chromecast, but I saw this and thought it would probably be better suited to what I need in my bedroom (I need my husband to be able to watch a tv show without my help - he is completely tech-challenged and cannot work the Dish remote - too many buttons).

The reason it doesn't get five stars is that there aren't yet enough content apps. There is a manga channel, a documentary channel, an art house channel, along with Crackle and Flixter and Plex (Plex is a for pay service that lets you stream your home content). There is plenty to watch if you are a Prime member (I am - and I appreciated having that already set up on my Fire TV - Thank you, Amazon!) I am also a Dish subscriber, with HBO and a Hopper. I have apps for those directly on some of my devices. I can get them on the internet on the tbs I have hooked up to computers. I can even blast them over to my Chromecast from my tablets. But they aren't on Fire TV, and none of my tablets will screencast to Fire TV. Soon as they are, this is a five star device for me.

I read in Entertainment Weekly that HBO and Amazon Prime have come to an understanding that will make lots and lots of HBO shows available through prime, which will also make them available through Fire TV. For the ones that are not, HBOGO will have an app for this. Between that news and my son's enjoyment of an eight dollar (as opposed to 40 to 60 dollars) platformed on this thing, I am adding a star.

title: Not an easy set up on a Mac running Mavericks
text:
Compared to a similar camera made by Belkin, setting up the D-Link was kind of a pain. Not as much of a pain as setting up a Foscam F18918W - where you get directed to a third party domain name provider and get to learn the joys of port forwarding - but a relative hassle.

For the Belkin, I opened the box, plugged into my router, ran a set up program that took less than five minutes, downloaded an app, and I was up and running. While this is a very similar product in both look and function, it took over an hour - and two ethernet cables - to set it up. There is no Mac software on the installation cd. The box states that a Windows pc is required, but the website has a Mac download available. You have to scroll through the product photos, which aren't in alphanumeric order. Just keep looking until you find the DCS-930L - AFTER the 931L and the 932L and the 934L. Have faith. Keep going. It's there.

Once you get the program installed, it takes very little time to *find* the camera and teach it to log into your wireless network. And then you are back to the website to set up your account and view your camera. Except you are on a Mac, and the viewer requires you to install the Java Runtime Environment. JRE is a big old security vulnerability on Macs. So much so that Apple advises against using it. Mavericks lets you turn it on case by case - and, by default, it will ask you every time before running it. If you are on an OS below Mavericks, check the googles for setting your preferences so that you're not running JRE all the time.

Okay, so now you've got JRE going, and the first thing the program tells you is that you have to update your firmware AND you need to have the camera AND your computer ethernet-jacked right into your router. LOLWUT? I'm lucky. I am on a laptop, and I have an extra ethernet cable and an empty port. So, I did that, and there I was, up and running, about an hour, hour and a half, thereabouts, after I started.

Image quality is pretty good - not great. Audio is okay. The settings are very customizable. But the wifi receiver is very weak, and that limits the usefulness of this product.

title: This is My All-time Favorite Logitech Remote
text:
This is exactly what I wanted. I have set up two different activity-based logitech-type remotes. Neither really did everything I needed them to do, and even though both had lighted buttons, they were of limited use to me with my bedroom set up, because I still needed my glasses to do anything with them.

Why I like this (and who will most likely feel the same way): I have reasonably new components in a reasonably common configuration in a smallish bedroom. When I started this particular set up, my dish joey remote did everything I needed it to do: turn on the tv and joey, turn off same, adjust channel from the cable guide, set dvr, control volume on the tv, *MOST IMPORTANT* fit on my bedside table. As time went on, I acquired a sound bar and a FireTV, neither of which was controlled by the dish remote. The dish remote also would not change the input on my tv, so I had to have that out as well if I wanted to use the FireTV. I have experience and patience with the logitech set up process. My husband and I both have smartphones (and mine is already on my bedside table at night). Set up took a bit of time and patience, but resulted in a universal remote AND smartphone app that control everything I need them to control (and I can use accessibility features on my smartphone so that I don't usually need my glasses to find the buttons). That's a lot of problems for one device to solve, and this one did it.

Also, if you have wanted an activity-based universal remote and haven't wanted to pay hundreds of dollars for a product from this manufacturer, this is an awesome choice.

Who may NOT like this: People with devices that are not 100% controlled with the logitech app/program. People who don't have/don't like smartphones. Senior citizens who are uncomfortable with technology (although I would not be above putting the app on a big bright tablet for a parent or grandparent who is open to the idea, especially since many tablets can be made to play a sound that will let you find where you set them down). People who are fine with having/using a few different remotes or who really don't use more than one or two remotes. I mean, this thing is really cool, and I love it, but if you're not having any problems with what you're doing, you may not want to spend money to solve a problem you don't have.

title: So easy to set up
text:
Arlo is not perfect, but it is wicked close.

What's Great: You can put it anywhere within range of the link/router. The alerts are reliable, if a little slow on the uptake. The picture is good. Set up was simple and worked the first time. A reasonable amount of cloud storage is free, and it's easy to download whatever you want to save. The cameras are easy to move around to wherever you need them, and you don't have to set them up again.

What's Okay: A person who walks fast can get through a room almost faster than Arlo can start recording. Now, it's still much faster than an old Belkin Netcam HD, which sends pictures of where the motion WAS. Before the picture. And the D-Link 930L, which is a fine monitor cam, but has never been able to send a snap or a clip, no matter how many times it has been set up to do that. However, both of those cameras have audio and stream reasonably good images via their apps (the Belkin video resolution is way better than the Dlink). That makes them okay monitors next to smart security sensors - if the sensor alerts, you can look to see what tripped it and listen to see what's going on. Arlo will - most of the time - catch whatever set it off and let you know within seconds. And it's free, not an extra $$$ feature.

What Could Be Better: The link thing is enormous. It could be a little less expensive. And it would be WONDERFUL if it integrated with Z-Wave or Smart Things. The plan here is to station the Arlo cams near other devices that send push notifications - Nest Alarms, Smanos smart sensors, etc.

How It Compares: Beats the Canary I couldn't get to activate. Way better than the other netcams in the house. Love it. Just added another camera.

title: Good Compromise Machine
text:
This is a tablet running a real operating system (Windows 10) hooked up to a small keyboard with a trackpad. And it's all right.

It's thicker and heavier but smaller than my 11 inch MacBook Air, which makes it more convenient in some respects and less convenient in others. The MacBook Air is a used 2012 model with a Core i5 and 4gb ram. It's snappy, but it didn't come with an SD slot, and used it cost about a hundred more than this. The quad core atom processor on the transformer book is pretty fast for a tablet, but it is definitely a lightweight compared to a core i5. Or even an i3.

My iPad Air runs iOS. Way less versatile than Windows 10 in terms of doing work-a-day things, having a browser respond the way you're used to having it respond, etc., but it's still pretty good. However, the keyboard experience is something of a pain, especially since there's no trackpad and you have to touch the tablet face to do the mouse-like things. And using the mail program is harder on the iPad than it is on a mac laptop or on the transformer book.

The transformer book is noticeably slower than either of the other devices, but I was able to do everything I set out to do on it. The Office apps are good and integrate seamlessly with the other Office installations on my other stuff. The screen is as nice as or nicer than my iPad Air. I had a MeMo for a year, and I loved the screen on that. This is very similar - excellent resolution, nice and bright, a bit wider aspect than what the iPad Air has.

The sound is about as good as one would expect. Which is to say, meh. But that's what headphones are for.

Cortano makes it easy to get set up. I asked it to find the apps I wanted. When I want something from the control panel, I ask for that. Since this is my first time with Windows 10, having the assistant helps a lot.

There do seem to be some battery issues. Charging takes a long time. There was an issue with the MeMos, as well, that I sort of resolved by fully cycling the battery a couple of times.

All things considered, I like this tablet/transformer book quite a bit. My only significant issue with it is weight. For my purposes, the ultralight notebook or the regular tablet will meet my needs on any given day. However, if you like your PC desktop and need, essentially, a shuttle craft, though. this is a pretty good compromise machine. It's a decent enough tablet. You can do business stuff, check email, surf the web, and watch movies. You won't be transcoding video or playing resource intense games, but this ultimately is a nice tablet with a keyboard. Not a desktop substitute. Maybe not even a laptop substitute, depending on your needs. But definitely a nice tablet.

UPDATE WITH USAGE ISSUES:

I was getting really annoyed with battery life/charging issues. My iPad Air will stand by for a couple of weeks, no problem, whereas this thing dies if I leave it off the charger a couple of days. It also needs its OEM charger if you intend to charge it within a few hours time, as opposed to overnight and then some. I was able to solve some of this by running task manager and disabling some of the high impact background apps (Microsoft OneDrive is a big offender). And, similar to my other Asus tablet, the battery charging problem seems to improve with conditioning. On the positive side, the more I use this, the better I like it.

text:

I was having issues with holiday season package thieves and a non-working wireless doorbell. Ring is the only video doorbell I could find that will work wirelessly. The first one had battery issues. Replaced no problem. The second one had sound issues. Replaced no problem. The third on works FLAWLESSLY. I absolutely love it.

The smart motion sensor works well. I see everyone who comes onto my porch, but not my neighbors' porches (three doors lined up on one big house). Two way sound is mostly good -> if it's really windy, it's hard to hear sometimes. The video is way better than I thought it would be. I can see well enough on my phone, but if I download and watch on my computer, it is very impressive.

I signed up for the cloud recording - it's the least expensive pay service of any of my security cameras, and it has been reliable over the few weeks I have been using it. The doorbell is also conspicuous enough to act as a deterrent. I've had a couple of alerts where people looked like they were going to come up the steps and then changed their minds. Both my postal carrier and my UPS driver said that a lot of their stops have these, and they really like them.

Bottom line: It took a couple of tries, but I am one hundred percent happy with this doorbell. If you have an issue, use the warranty. It's a real thing.

title: Meh
text:
UPDATE: After over a year of using these, I have to say that the bad outweighs the good, especially for how expensive they are.

It is true. There is nothing easier to set up. But it's next to useless when you actually need it. They trigger way too slowly. And the batteries are not set up to charge or even work very well when it's really cold out, so even though they are close enough to an outlet for me to charge them without taking them down, I have to bring them inside to charge them when it is cold. But it's the slow trigger that really makes this system not worth the expense.

For example: New Year's Eve, someone wrote Happy New Year in the snow on my windshield. One of my Arlo cameras is pointed right at my car. I have a clip from before it happened. I have a clip from after it happened. If I did not also have wired cameras that record continuously, I would not know whom to thank (our sweet next door neighbors - they are so lovely!).

The cameras make decent deterrents. And they are handy to have when I need a live view of something. But if you want to catch somebody doing something, there are better options.

_____________
Original Review Follows
_____________

I'm going to give you the bad, then the just okay, and then the good. Short version of all that is that I wish these triggered a bit faster and weren't so expensive, but they are a substantial improvement over my older Arlo system. Skip to the end if you want to know how to set up the siren.

Bottom line: This system is not quite perfect, and it is quite expensive, but it is wireless, weatherproof, super easy to set up, and backwards compatible. I would recommend this to a family member or anyone else who needs a wireless outdoor install.

Okay, so the bad (and it isn't really that bad) is that the Arlo Pro cameras have some trigger lag. Depending on how fast the trigger is moving, you may catch them just as they leave the frame, or you might miss them altogether. If it's a person walking, no problem. A person walking briskly? Might be a little problem. Basically, these are better for a zombie apocalypse than for a werewolf invasion. I have a hardwired CCTV DVR system that is always "recording," so when it gets a motion alert, it "starts" the clip five seconds in the past.

The just okay part is that, for this kind of money, I wish the cameras had more configurability. I would like to be able to set the exact parameters of the field I want to monitor (currently, you can pan and zoom but that's not really what I am looking to do), and I would like to be able to set the sensitivity in a meaningful way (I live in a city on a fairly busy street and get hundreds of alerts/clips no matter how I try to minimize them). Additionally, the over-sensitivity is a drain on battery life, which is an indirect functional limitation on where I install the cameras. With batteries needing to be changed/charged within a matter of days, I need to be able to get to these easily.

Now for the good stuff:

I like Arlo a lot. I have three of the old ones, and even with the lag, they are great for outdoor applications. The Arlo Pro cameras are better. The video quality is better. While there is lag, it is not as bad as it is on the older models. These are also BY FAR the easiest cameras to set up and keep running. I have wifi range extenders throughout my weird old condo, and my Arlo cameras never drop their signals.

The Arlo Pro base station will work with your old Arlo cameras. I kept my old base station running, though, so that I can run different cameras on different schedules. It also works with IFTTT and with the Smart Things App.

The Siren was not intuitive to set up, but it is a cool feature. The default is OFF for all cameras, so don't worry about setting it off while you are setting your system up. You activate it in the settings of each camera - camera by camera. You can also trigger it from the smart phone app, so in the event that someone breaks in while you are home, you can turn on the alarm (better for a werewolf invasion than for the zombie apocalypse).

From the Arlo website:
To create a rule that includes a siren trigger:
Launch the Arlo app or log in to your Arlo account at arlo.netgear.com.
Tap or click Mode to access the mode tab.
Tap or click the Arlo Pro base station for which you would like to add a siren trigger.
Tap the pencil icon or click > next to the mode that you would like to edit.
Under Rules, tap the pencil icon or click Edit next to the device that you want to trigger the siren.
Select the Turn Siren ON check box.
Tap the pencil icon or click > next to Turn Siren ON.
Set the sliders for Siren Duration and Siren Loudness.
Tap < Edit Rule or click Back.
Tap Done or click Save.
Note: This rule is not active until you activate the mode to which you added the siren trigger.

title: Buggy But Fast
text:
UPDATE: After a few months, I'm still fairly okay with the performance of the Orbi when it is working. However, there are a few things I wish I'd known ahead of time. For one, you won't get all the features if you have FIOS. You have to run the Orbi in bridge mode, which means no Circle. For another, the router does a poor-to-mediocre job of saving the names it lets you give your devices. I spent a day running down which MAC address went to which device. Next day, poof. Gone. A third issue is that the router needs to be reset every so often when it inexplicably slows down to dial-up speeds. Wouldn't be such a big deal if - IF - everything would just connect back up, but the Orbi doesn't play well with some devices. It HATES my Ecobee thermostat, which I have to assign a new static IP to with each reset, because the Orbi refuses to let it on dynamically and always gives the old static IP to another device. I wasn't looking for something so high maintenance when I forked over the money to buy these things.

Basically, this is a fast wifi network system that really does cover my whole house and is working well with a nighthawk EX7500 as an extender. It has some bugs and some limitations. It comes into a mostly Apple ecosystem and works fine with the computers and airport express extenders as well (but not airport extreme routers, because they will only bridge another airport extreme). The bugs are bad enough to knock it to three stars, but I like the speed so much that if the network stays up a week in a row, I will add a star.

I do not hate this at all. I bought the system because I was spending too much time on the phone with my ISP over an end-of-life router situation. There is no brand replacement coming for that router, at least not anytime soon, which is a bummer. I scoured the internet and settled on this.

I have set it up a couple of times now. The first time, it took all day to convince it to stay connected to its own satellite, worked a couple of days, and then would not connect to the internet. I called my ISP and got them to look at it through my modem (I don't know what it is they do or how they are able to "see" what router is connected to my modem). It went back up at screaming speed. This time it worked for about 24 hours before booting half of my smart devices. So, I set them up again, which took a while, since I now needed static IP addresses for some of them in order for Orbi to let them online. I do not know why.

I also tried to add a NetGear Nighthawk EX7000 extender so that I could have a remote disk via USB. So much nope. Even though it was in bridge mode, with no reason to exist except to make an external hard drive accessible on my network, the extender and Orbi were doubling IP addresses, so every so often people would get the "another computer is using your IP address" message. Pulled the extender and no more issues since then. It has only been about three days without an incident.

The good is great. I get coverage everywhere in my condo in an Edwardian building that has been added onto in strange and wonderful ways that make good wifi impossible upstairs. It works with an EX7500 extender (which is boss). I get well over 200Mpbs near the main router, and the lowest I get is 175 anywhere else. I am only paying for 200. As noted above, it also works with my Apple Airport Expresses, so I can have remote USB disks and printers.

I enabled Circle to stop my teenager from going on the internet in the middle of school nights without having to keep my husband, who works nights, from being able to check his email when he gets home. So far, that is rudimentary but okay. I am trying to figure out where QOS settings are. I think I found them on one of the router login places (there's the Orbi app, the Netgear Genie, the Orbi login page, and I think one other). So far, I think the only thing that works with Alexa are some very basic commands like pause the internet and when is my bedtime. I need to be able to tell it to pause the kid's internet. EDIT TO ADD: I can pause the kid's internet through IFTTT.

Bottom line: I'm okay with this, but I expected a smoother set up process for the money. If I'd known what it was going to entail, I probably would have waited to buy.

title: Excruciating Set Up - Infuriating Restrictions
text:
This is an updated version of a mesh system router and satellite I already have. The technology is great when it's working, but, for whatever reason, my system has needed to be reset once a week or more, and the coverage is nowhere near as good as it claims it should be.

My hope was that the newer version would be faster and have better coverage. It isn't. It doesn't. And, like the earlier version, it has to be in AP mode to work with my FIOS modem (FIOS has a version of this available with its own firmware, but you have to buy a new one, and it won't work with any other ISP). Those hopes dashed, my next hope was that I could at least use the router as a satellite on my existing system, which, of course not.

So, you would think I could at LEAST use the satellite from the new one with the old system or the old satellite with the new one? They are the same model, after all. And that, too, would be a nope.

What I finally did, after hours on the internet (and other hours just trying to set up the new one by itself - it was the same with the old one - it for some reason despises custom settings and will not save them the first many times. It will also lose them after firmware upgrades, I expect, like its predecessor), was set it up alongside the old one with its own network name. Now I have one network serving one side of the house and the other serving the other. Speeds are good. So far, no routing issues, and I don't really expect any. The two network solution seems to have worked well for others.

But really.

If you are looking to expand your Orbi network, check out the nighthawk mesh expanders. I have the 7500, and it's excellent. Also, don't take my lukewarm review for a no-rec. The Orbi is, as far as I can tell from personal experience, buggy and locked down, but, again from personal experience, it beats the Velop (its nearest competitor) by a mile for coverage.

title: The Spy Who Loves Me
text:
I'm not paranoid (famous last words). No, really, I welcome my personal assistant overlords. My family is pretty vanilla. So it only creeps me out a little when my husband and I have "test" discussions about things we don't talk about, don't search the internet for, and would never actually buy in a million years only to see such items pushed to us in advertising feeds. Is one of our assistants listening when it is supposed to be asleep? If so, which one? All three of the majors are in our house. Both of the cats have turned Siri on by walking across my laptop. And Alexa hears her name sometimes inexplicably. Maybe it's my husband's Long Island accent?

Or maybe it is just randomness and the assistants are functioning as advertised. Either way, I won't be getting rid of them anytime soon. The Echo Plus recognized all but two of my smart bulbs and found all of my switches and everything else that still works (old WeMo stuff went offline over a year ago when Belkin pushed a firmware upgrade and killed their wifi connections). It has controlled them flawlessly so far, and this has allowed me to free up the ethernet ports I'd dedicated to several different hubs.

My Echo devices are the ones we use most around here, both because the house runs on Amazon Prime and Subscribe and Save (I have lupus and cannot easily shop in the real world) AND because the Echos allow me to reach my teenager and tell him things whether he wants to hear them or not. He can ignore my texts and refuse to answer the phone, but Alexa lets me yell at him from anywhere in the world. (And the app lets me see his history of ridiculous teenaged boy questions - unlike Siri, Alexa is not a potty mouth and does not like it when you are.)

On the downside, Alexa won't give you suggestions if she doesn't know something. She just gives you an Elizabeth Jennings (The Americans) type, "Hmmm," and a disappointed note.

The Echo Plus also seems to "hear" better and have fewer false activations. And the sound is better for music - by a surprising amount. So, if Alexa has a place in your home, the Echo Plus is a good way to get her. Four stars. I'd give five if the wake word were more customizable.

title: Installed in 2010 Mac Mini - Don't Be Afraid to Upgrade
text:
Revving up old Macs is like one of my favorite things. I don't do much of it anymore, because (a) arthritis in my hands has made the turning of tiny screws much more of a chore, and (b) I was running out of old Macs.

The last one I had was a 2010 mini that was the first computer I'd bought new since probably 1993 (also a Mac). It had the last of the Core2Duo processors and a spin up hard drive and a couple of gigs of ram that I upgraded pretty much right away. It served as a DVR for a while, then a minecraft server, media streamer, then got put away. I resurrected it to bounce DATS to .WAV to mp3 when I learned that it had digital audio input and output. I had been researching all these expensive things to make that happen, and it turned out that my little friend was able to save me hundreds of dollars with something that had been built in all along.

But it was slow because of the HDD. And upgrading looked really daunting. I'd done one of the earlier minis, and it had been an exercise in anxiety.

But the other day, I decided to give it a try. Two bits of advice: if you can get through this without disconnecting the wifi connector (you can if you are really careful), do so, and (2) if you accidentally disconnect the wifi connector (I did), don't panic. Watch videos of people putting iPhones back together (the older, the better). These connectors are fussy. Do not force them. If they are seated correctly, a light press will connect them. You'll feel the click. But it's almost like threading a needle to get it seated correctly. And if you push too hard, you'll break it. Same with the fan. Just be careful. If you are pushing and it's not connecting right away, it's not lined up right.

Okay, so deciding to do the drive replacement took awhile because the above two steps seemed very daunting. And the project took me several hours, because I had to stop and rest a few times (if your hands work and you keep your screws organized, it should take about 45 minutes). But it was worth every minute.

This is an excellent drive. The form factor lines up exactly with the HDD I pulled from the mini (some of the drives I have used in old white MacBooks and older MacBook Pros have not). Not a millimeter off. The OS install flew. This drive is stellar in this context. If you need a 2.5" SSD, I highly recommend this one.

title: Sometimes Old Tech Is the Best Tech
text:
In music production, one stupid mistake can cost you a hundred hours of irreplaceable files. You may think you have a foolproof system, but how do you know it's foolproof if you're the fool who came up with it?

Say you're a fool in an Apple ecosystem who hates Time Machine and won't use paid software smart backup and has a friend who says just buy two identical drives, record to one, and clone to the other -> let's just say you're THAT fool.

It all goes well for a few years. Every six months or so, you buy new drives, and you use an adorable naming convention that makes perfect sense to you, and you faithfully copy over one with the other - when you can remember to do it. And then one day, you go looking for something recent on your recording drive, and it's not there.

You realize that you accidentally cloned in the wrong direction.

Now what?

You go to your wife, who suggested smart backups, redundant backups, and a mechanical failsafe solution - all of which you rejected - and ask her what your options are. Data recovery is not an affordable option considering that the files you lost were just your own stuff and you overwrote the whole drive.

If you'd lost client files, you'd be looking at a much more serious situation, so thank goodness.

But here you are, back at the original suggestion she gave you: cloning drive toaster with two different sized drives so that you can never clone in the wrong direction.

TA Da!

text:
My son has ASD with sensory issues. Earbuds are his number one coping mechanism. He's musical, and his hearing is hyper acute, so at first, I bought him the best-sounding ones we could afford.

But his number two coping mechanism is fidgeting his earbud cable. He swims by twirling it and picking at it, We tried models with replaceable cables - spent a ton of money - and finally gave up. I started buying the cheapest multipacks of basic earbuds that I could find.

And the thing is: most sound almost as good as many of the expensive ones and some sound better than a few of the popular *cough* overpriced *cough* brand names. So that's what we've been doing for a couple of years now.

This 21-pack looked like a winner (we go through them at a rate of one or two a month). And these will do in a pinch. For the price, there is no way I can be sorry I got them or not recommend them.

If your person regularly breaks these this, this pack is good to have on hand. However, if audio quality is an issue, you might want to choose a different inexpensive brand. These are about as good as the very first buds that shipped with the original iPhone. Sound is muffled and lacks discernible highs and lows.

It will block outside noise and let someone cope for a bit. Recommend with caveat.

title: Very pleased & happy to be an early adopter
text:
As others have stated, it is important to understand what you are getting and not getting with the Chromebook. For me, this is a supplementary, portable computing device. I still have my primary laptop and my home computer and those aren't going away.

What is great about the Chromebook is what it is being advertised for: everything in the cloud and instantly accessible. If you are not currently using gmail and Google apps, this may be more of an adjustment than you are ready for right now. It is also not 100% "ready for prime time". Agreed that Skype would be nice, however Google chat with video is there, instant and seamless.

I did weigh this against a tablet or iPad but really wanted the keyboard (and aside from the missing "delete" key, it's a very nice keyboard)

I also weighed this against a Win7 netbook with a Chrome OS partition. What sold me on the Chromebook was the 3G capability with the "pay as you go plan". Other Vzn 3G netbooks require the full Vzn data plan ($50/month). The free 100mb/month is pretty laughable (I'll have used that up within the week) but I do like that I have month to month capability with the data plan so I'm only paying for 3G when I'm using it.

I was a little anxious about buying this -- the reviews are mixed but not about the device -- it's really a stylish, well designed device -- but about the whole Chrome, in the cloud, web only philosophy. If you're not buying in to that concept, this probably isn't the device for you just yet but I'm willing to take the bet on it.

title: Good quality wi-fi; mixed support experience
text:
We installed the Orbi Pro in an L shaped building with two goals in mind.
1. Increase the range so that both legs of the L could be part of a mesh network or
2. Failing that, increase the range so that only one wireless access point would serve one entire leg of the building.

The Orbi accomplished the second goal. The two legs of the L are separated by a fire door that severely restricts wireless signals, so the Orbi signal was not strong enough to overcome the fire door problem. (This issue is not unique to the Orbi, but we hoped the Orbi could overcome it.)

Installation as a wireless access point is relatively straightforward. It was not necessary to disable the wireless access point in the DSL router that handles DHCP assignments. Presumably, this would have been necessary if we were using the Orbi as a router and a DHCP host. For some reason, I was only able to get through the installation by using a combination of a smartphone and a computer that was directly connected to the Orbi. Some aspects only worked on the phone, and some aspects only worked on the computer, but by using both, it was possible to get through the setup without issues.

The Orbi can be set up to have 3 networks: an internal network, and “employee” network, and a guest network. Since the employee network does not allow access to networked printers, it is impractical and essentially useless.

We ran into an issue with the guest network. The way the Orbi firmware works, a guest who logs into the guest network is redirected to a Terms and Conditions screen, which they must accept and then they are connected to the internet. To accomplish this, the Orbi sends the user to routerlogin.net. When we tried this, some devices received an authentication error and others did not. On the devices that received the authentication error, upon actually entering routerlogin.net as the destination URL, the screen came up and from there everything proceeded normally.

To resolve this issue, I contacted Netgear Technical Support. At this point, it became clear that all the comments trashing Netgear Technical Support are true, with regard to Level 1 support. The Asia-based phone support people behave as if their primary goal is to get you off the phone so that they can take more calls. The first technician absolutely refused to provide support because, as it turns out, the serial number printed on the box is not identical to the real serial number. There is no place in the Administrator screens that shows the unit serial number. The only way for me to get that number was to go up to the ceiling mounted Orbi and de-install it since the serial number label is covered by the mounting bracketry. There is no justification for NetGear to refuse support. They made the device and their support people would be of no use to someone with a non-Netgear device. They made the unit; they should support it, at least with regard to installation and setup questions.

Eventually, I was able to make my way to Level 2 support. For as bad as Level 1 support is, the Ireland-based Level 2 support people are excellent. They took ownership of the issue, spent a long time working with me on troubleshooting, and followed up regularly. Eventually, the issue was escalated to Level 3 (engineering). Communication with this level was indirect. All communication with Level 3 went through Level 2. Ultimately, they decided that the guest network authentication issue only affected users with older browsers. Some phone applications are not updated for older phones, and those users cannot update their apps. Since one cannot control the software on the devices carried by guests, the Netgear guest network is less than ideal. However, over time, older devices will disappear, and most guest users should have no issue with the Orbi guest network.

title: Fast Downloads! But know your Carrier APN value-name.
text:
Know your carrier APN in order for the router to know what carrier the SIM card is associated with in order to search out the Cell Tower.

Make sure you get a 4G SIM card because 5G won't work. Some carriers, like T-Mobile just sell the cards and don't ask why and for what purpose you'll be using it. Initially I bought a T-Mobile 5G SIM and it didn't work. So I switched to a Verizon 4G it worked like a charm. Like I previously said, very important, you must know the carriers APN value or name. Because you have to properly enter it when setting it up. It is the way the router can apply the SIM to the proper carrier it has to connect to. Each carrier has a unique APN name or value. You can Google the carrier APN. ie: Verizon APN. AT&T APN etc.

In terms of T-Mobile, they wasted my time on the phone for a total of 4.5 hours trying to troubleshoot why I could not get Cell service. They had no clue. The technicians just read a computer algorithm list of issues. The T-mobile salesman was just that and had no experience or knowledge of what he was doing.

Once I set it up with Verizon it worked like a charm. I recommend you take the router with you to the Carrier of your choice and make sure it is working prior to leaving.

title: Does the job for me, best price could find too!
text:
So, I read many reviews on similar units and took my chances on this one....

Heres my current setup and reason for purchasing this product - I have/use the following in my Home Entertainment environment at this time;

1. Toshiba 52" TV (3-HDMIs inputs, 1 went bad 15mo's post purchase - now down to 2inputs avail)
2. A self built custom HTPC 3yrs ago, HDMI output
3. XBox 360 Elite, HDMI output
4. PS3 primarily for BluRay but not bad for games too =), HDMI ouput
5. Wii, no-HDMI

My attempt at following objectives;
1.) planning for 2nd HDMI input to fail on Toshiba TV, making only 1 available
2.) stop changing the TV to 3 different inputs each time manually and
3.) split/extend the PS3 BluRay HDMI to another TV in a different room....

First, this unit does NOT come with a Power Supply...but works just fine in lieu of that.

Also, it has a bright blue LED active HDMI port indicator light that I've found compliments my Entertainment Center, which is a pleasant secondary effect.

Finally, I wanted something to "inexpensively" combine my HTPC, XBox and BluRay into a single HDMI output.
Hence my search for weeks ending in the purchase of this item.

While in use LESS THAN 1 MONTH so far...Its worked perfectly to date, no complaints - yet!

HTPC is HDMI 1 - on at all times, which keeps the HDMI input active at all times - perfect for my situation
PS3 is HDMI 2 - when powering the PS3 on, this product auto switches to that as its input, displaying BluRay to output
XBox is HDMI 3 - once more, when powered on, auto switches to this as input, displaying Xbox to output

When PS3 and XBox are off, the unit auto switches to the HTPC default perfectly

While certainly not a super user/enthusiast who demands excellence of Audio and Video systems, I cannot see any degradation of picture quality nor hearing its sound vs. direct connections without this unit in the middle.

I also EXTEND HDMI over CAT5e converters to another TV 80ft away....this units auto switching and output has been working very well to date, no problems seeing/hearing any of the 3 (HTPC, PS3/BluRay, XBox) on either ends, the local TV or the one 80ft away.

The only thing I cannot comment on nor guarantee, is that it will remain working in 6, 12 or 18 months...but, for the price of $13.80/ea, I bought 2 and have one on standby in the event the active one in use eventually fails.

Also a side benefit, if the TVs 2nd of 3 HDMIs goes bad, this unit will definitely be required providing a tremendous savings vs. buying a new TV.

Here's hoping it lasts long! =)

title: Now have total of 3 of these units (update-qty 5 as of December 2013)
text:
UPDATE December 6, 2013

Last feedback was March 2013 - at that time, we had 3 units (dual and quad drive models of Synology NAS systems) - As of this update in December, we now have 5 today (3 dual, 2 quad storage models).

With the Holidays around the corner, we've felt it worth updating this purchase/review.

Now in production are nearly 25TB of storage...for the most part, we believe these systems have operated flawlessly to date...while there have been some "streaming" problems, we cannot say with certainty that these issues were specific to these units.

We're backing up approx 80-100 hrs of shows (dups and trips) each week. This includes daytime shows, soaps, talk shows and evening programs of essentially all major US broadcast stations, ABC, CBS, CW, FOX, NBC and PBS - usually between 8pm and 11pm. Then during the night, they're offloaded to the NAS drives and in coming days, are played back on Windows Media Center around the house.

Most NICs in the systems are 10/100mb and a few are 1000mb. Our Switching systems are Enterprise level/grade equipment too.

All in all, these have performed as hoped and expected - aside from the initial lengthy setup processes involved - to date these have performed extremely well and we are very satisfied!

Still our recommended solution to family and friends.

Good luck!

==============

Presently using (2) 2-Bay and (1) 4-Bay units. We have a total of 5 NAS solutions,

1 USRobotics (from 2006)
1 Buffalo Storage (from 2007), and
3 Synology DiskStatons from 2011-2012.

Aside from initial system setup of the Hard Drives (system and integrity checking, which took 1-2 days for completion), these Synology products are pretty cool. Using the DSM Software is rather intuitive once its up/running, for those who are familiar with Storage features and abilities. We dont use RAID, as our needs are about storing multiple copies of the same thing (music, tv shows, movies, etc.).

Presently, we're storing over 500gb of music, 10tb of movies, 8-10tb of tv shows, along with several pc images, and of course, data (docs, pics, etc.) backups and much more - spanning several units for multiple copies/backups in case of computer problems.

4 Windows Media Center PVR systems offload nightly recordings (approx. 50hrs week) of multiple/duplicate shows onto our NAS solutions. You know Windows, sometimes it works, sometimes not...sometimes perfect recordings, sometimes system doesnt record, errors out, freezes, etc...therefore, our Storage solutions are meant for duplicates and/or triplicates of our media needs.

The Synology devices are quite, compact, functional and thus far, problem free from our experiences with them. Although a bit pricey, we feel to date that we're getting our monies worth from these products. Hopefully they will continue to perform and perhaps outlive their internal hard drive counterparts for years to come...but so far, we're very happy with these Synology NAS solutions - so much so, that a few of our friends and family have also bought them based on our recommendations.

And should you buy one, good luck to you too =)

We have another, mounted about 5ft off the floor, on the wall, looking horizontal across the rooms door entrance. Upon entering the laundry room, it suppose to activate and turn on the light. While inside, doing laundry, moving around, etc...expectations are that it remains on/active, until it detects that we've exited. In the same year, just a few feet away from the switch, this unit (and we've tried one other), dont seem to work correctly, every single time...possibly about 70-80% of the time, it functions as expected.

3. Maintenance Room

4. Garage Door

2 have needed to be returned, failing right out of the box upon arrival. 2-3 others have needed to be returned, after failing to sync/connect up with other devices, for whatever reason.

For our deployments, the short distances, and its purpose for development, sale and installation - we'd expect better.

We're discouraged from buying more....

Had they worked better, we'd own another 15-20 units, especially for our space reserved for guests/in-laws, as the technology is ideal for such a space affording lighting control as necessary to save money (they forget to turn lights off, specially daytime).

other things worth mentioning...

2. upon power outages, we've found that most units require "resynching" with their respective light switches, possibly due to the light switches since they are hard wired, and the sensor is not...nonetheless, going around every few months re-establishing connectivity with these motion sensor units post power failures is becoming problematic. title: These particular models (compared to our originals) did not work for us...
text:
We have 4 original HDHR tuners (larger, off-white/grayish colored units) purchased 5+ years ago. They are all on the same cable system providers internet network to our residence. They all originally/recently tuned correctly, even as late as Q4 of 2012. However, we wanted additional recording redundancy, so we bought these units.

Mind you, all internal to our house, all on same cable system network, all seeing/tuning/using the same exact signals.

After approx. 1 full month of "trying" to get them to work correctly, like our original standard systems - and after contacting their product support for help, we returned 2/both of these units bought.

Our problem was:
We PVR/DVR all the major local broadcast channels such as; ABC, CBS, FOX, CW, NBC.
After installing, tuning, scanning with the manufacturer software systems, everything seemed to be ok.
Channels aligned as expected (4.1, 7.1, 13.1, etc.) where the vendor software was concerned.
Using VLC player inside the vendor software, each of the channels were viewable (video), but for some reason, no audio.

However, the ultimate problem, when we then tried to get Microsoft Windows Media Center to recognize them as TV tuners.

This is where larger problems were encountered.
When playing low end channels, the units/media center worked fine.

However, when trying to playback/record channels 11.1 FOX and 13.1 CW - Windows Media Center kept citing them as encrypted and unable to play (which in itself is strange, because our original tuners are working solidly - no errors, no statements of cannot record due to encryption or the likes - they just work).

But with these units, Media Center (2 systems, not just one) could not play/show the channels content, aside from text/metadata such as show title, duration, synopsis, etc. But the actual video and audio, nothing.

Another issue arose different than the originals implemented, rather than the proper channel of 7.1 like all other systems in our house, Media Center shows this particular, single channel of 7.1 as 66.6 (and yes, ironically thats 666 in our book too).

Anyhow, when Media Center was returned to the OLDER/ORIGINAL tuners at its tv source (again, 2 systems not just one) for playback/recording, those particular units played fine.

NO encryption errors, audio and video displayed perfectly and such...

But, when redirecting back to these new tuners, it failed. Oddly, aside no audio, the vendors own software functioned fine (showed proper channel numbers, played content ok too, except for sound) - in turn, limiting our problems to these specific new tuners.

Lost hours upon hours, uninstalling, reinstalling softwares, Media Center, rebooting, etc. Nothing corrected these issues.

So, back they went....

Wish we could buy more of the "original" tuners, to test further and see if its specific to these newer ones, but finding them new and reasonable prices has proven difficult, we've tried. Aside from used models, where we risk them rendered unusable at any time without protection (warranty/etc.), we're limited in what we can do at this point in time.

Make no mistake, our original units are and have been working well for nearly 5 years, and we're very happy with those - its these new ones that became difficult - unfortunately.

title: WARNING: Product/Unit received from Seller actually does NOT support MicroSD slot on the Tablet!!!
text:
***IMPORTANT TO NOTE: I contacted the Seller (March 2022), who responded right away and ultimately issued me a full refund as a direct result of this manufacturing defect. But, I think it's necessary to post my findings from the experience, as I felt mislead by the advertising and disappointed in the product because of this mistake.***

Though I am giving "high" ratings on most STARS, because aside this important, actual fact below, all else seemed to work, function and operate as I would have expected.

However, as can be seen in the attached pictures...my newly purchased Samsung Galaxy Tab A8 w/ 10.5 screen, Model: SMX200 / SM-X200 was attempted to be covered by this Product/Case. While inserting the Tablet, I discovered that the MicroSD slot on the Tablet, did NOT HAVE the related opening/slot/cutout in the Case.

In the "About this item" section, under the generic specs, pictures, pricing, description above...it clearly claims as follows:

***Presice Cutouts: Easy access to all the controls and features without removing the case, Perfect cutouts for speakers, camera and other ports.***

Further, in the QnA Section, I found a direct, specific question that was also misleading, which is as follows:

***Question: Are the hole positions accurate? Will it affect the camera and buttons?
Answer: Yes all button creases and holes are accurate and well designed to align with all buttons and key output outlets.
By George A. on February 9, 2022***

From the Unit/Product I received by the Seller for this item, these comments are INCORRECT and UNTRUE. You can see for yourself, from the pictures I am attaching, that there is no Case opening for the Tablets MicroSD Card Slot. Therefore, I would have to REMOVE/INSERT the Tablet each time I wanted to utilize the MicroSD Card. For me, this would be a huge inconvenience - thus the complaint to the Seller, the request for a refund, and this review.

My experience, should not be individual/unique, others who have bought this product and used it for the intended device Samsung Galaxy Tab A8, 10.5 screen, Model SMX200/SM-X200, apparently have not caught this issue for whatever reason(s) - that I don't quite understand.

Nonetheless, if the MicroSD Card use and respective Case opening/slot/cutout is not of importance to buyers - than this is a decent product and should meet their needs.

Hope this review and discovery of a Case defect of missing MicroSD opening/slot/cutout helps future buyers, until the Seller/Manufacturer resolves this, such information may help buyers like me realize if they need constant, frequent, regular access to the MicroSD Card - this case would be worthy of avoiding at this time, or until such time the Seller/Manufacturer corrects the problem.

title: Very good headphones but not perfect
text:
After a few days of use I must admit that I have started to notice things that I would like to be better, but know there likely are no better headphones on the market that combine all of the things I wanted these to do. The noise cancelling is not what I expected it to be, but they are my first pair and I likely expected the technology to be somewhere more advanced than it is. Higher frequencies and non-periodic noise make it through much more than periodic noise and lower frequencies. The fact that it handles periodic noise so well makes me wonder if it is running an FFT to efficiently find frequencies to intelligently cancel, or that I just happen to be around periodic noises that are effectively cancelled by these headphones. Anyway, stuff like music at Starbucks makes its way through, but with significant attenuation, to the point I can't hear Starbucks-level music over my own music, but I can between songs (though it isn't annoying).

They are light and pretty comfortable for someone with pretty big ears, but I find myself taking them off a few times per hour to give my ears some air to cool down. When I am looking down at a book or something, they like to slide down unless they are tighter, which I accept because these cause a serious case of headphone hair if you have them on tight enough to prevent this (which isn't desirable when you are in public). But, they are pretty comfortable. I expected worse for closed back headphones.

The sound is quite nice and I deal with the extra bass to make sure the audio is coming in at high quality when I am listening to my FLAC files. When streaming, I would recommend just change the EQ to your liking because your music will NOT be anywhere near audiophile quality unless you pay specifically for it to be. Comparing them to my open back headphones, the difference is very clear. Not necessarily in quality, but in how it sounds. I personally prefer the sound of the open back, but they are awful to use in public and these are likely the best option to go for when you need to be in your own space in public, yet not bug people with your music (which is a really annoying issue these days, for some reason...).

I work in a physics lab and this is where I really appreciated these headphones. I have a bunch of fans on electronics running and vacuum pumps, large AC units, etc and the noise is annoying as can be. I put these on an even without music I entered a whole new world. I can't see myself working without these anymore. The lack of cable is why I got them for my lab (the ANC was for public), but the ANC became a really great aspect of these for my lab life. I was hesitant for a while about paying $350 for these, but being in the lab with them made up my mind-worth it (but now I don't hear my boss come in which can be awkward).

The case is amazing... though the storage pouch on the outside is on the bottom.... WHY? You made the interior separators so that you can't move them and then put the mesh pouch on the bottom... such a weird design choice. Otherwise, the case is amazing, despite the pathetically short USB-c cable that came with it. That was a really dumb way to save a few cents that did not go unnoticed. But, the entire package is worth it.

The primary perks are not having to rest your hands awkwardly on your macbook, rather comfortably on the table, and extremely easily switching devices. title: Good dock for the Steam Deck
text:
This dock from Park Sung fits the bill if you're looking for a capable dock for the Steam Deck. The deck fits comfortably in the dock and is easily connected via the supplied 1ft usb-c cable. I tested the dock with 2 different decks and it had no issues recognizing the dock. A mouse connected via usb was instantly usable; HDMI plugin was recognized and display easily configurable; worked at 4K 60hz. The ethernet port was able to fully utilize my fiber connection getting over 900mbps either direction and would be great for big game downloads over the built-in wifi. I did my testing with all 3 modes (SteamOS/Steam Desktop/WIndows 10) and it performed flawlessly.

The dock functions fine without being supplied with power; display out and ethernet worked well. I would of course recommend doing so to avoid power interruptions.

The dock has 4 non-slip pads on the bottom which are fairly grippy and 2 in the trough where the deck goes though it's somewhat easy to move the deck side to side but they do help. The trough has some free space so I imagine the deck will fit with most deck cases. There is a cutout for airflow on the right side in the trough. There are power lights on the back at the power-in usb port when usb power is being supplied and an activity light on the ethernet port.

My only 'meh' about this is the usb cable provided isn't right-angled but that's easily remedied with a replacement if you so choose. Other than that I am quite satisfied with its performance and utility. I think other devices similar size to the deck would work well in here except for ones that have the usb port on the bottom (Nintendo Switch).

This dock turned my deck into the brains for a mini gaming station and I recommend this product if that is your intention.

title: Neat bag, but...
text:
[[VIDEOID:28a20d0e078404d3139615dfdb08865b]] So the bag itself is pretty cool - but there's not a lot of customization options as the app is pretty lacking. There's some cute preloaded options however! My 11 month old loves watching it.

The app does work well with my phone (Z Fold 3), and I never had issues with connecting.

The screen itself is pretty clear, and feels very durable. I like that it's rechargable and doesn't require a powerbank at all times. However the battery life isn't super long - after running some errands for a few hours it was pretty much dead. I'll just turn it off periodically to conserve battery moving forward.

The on/off/charging port is easy to access outside of the bag which I like. I can just quickly reach around and mess with it as needed.

The magnetic buckle is pretty cool - I like to secure my bags to shopping carts when I go out and that makes it super easy. I wish more bags had that option!

The bag itself does feel quite durable and should last with my normal wear and tear, it doesn't feel "cheap" by any means.

What I don't like? I really don't like the top flap that folds down. The magnet isn't super strong and if you have something in the bag that's just a hair too tall, it won't stay down and it looks goofy. I'd honestly prefer a zipper over that.

I also don't like the strap being so short. Maybe that's just a me thing - but I have a larger chest and prefer to have a bit of a longer bag. I adjusted it at max length - it's acceptable but meh for me.

The bag itself is large enough to hold my essentials like phone, wallet, and other small odds and ends. I'm able to organize everything neatly with the pockets. So I can definitely use this as my every day bag.

Overall, its cool bag/purse/sling - whatever you want to call it, but it is limited. Maybe if the app gets more features I could rate it higher (or use a different app entirely?) but I don't think it's worth the $80 price (maybe $45).

title: Solid controller, but “Turbo” function doesn’t work
text:
UPDATE: After seeing my review the company reached out to me right away to help with the remote. They let me know that I mis-read the instructions and that it wasn’t the turbo button that needed held down but it was the assigned button. After setting turbo to a button you can then hold that button and it will rapidly press it for you. Upon testing this worked great, and thus I have updated my rating. The customer service provided as well was excellent and I highly recommend this remote.

——

ORIGINAL REVIEW:
My son has really wanted to get a Nintendo Switch remote that had a turbo button so that he could quickly place blocks in Minecraft. When I had the opportunity to try this remote I jumped on it as it. The huge negative I have with the remote is that the turbo button, while functional to adjust settings such as vibration speed, does not work to assign a turbo key as stated in the instructions. You should be able to hold turbo and then press the key to assign and let go, then next time you hold turbo it will rapid fire that key. It would not, even when trying this in multiple different games. It is not an issue with a specific game, but seems to be an issue with the remote.

Outside of the issue with the turbo key the remote is very solid and appears well made. I like that you can change the joy stick grips to the colored ones included, this is a nice touch. The remote is only slightly smaller than the Nintendo switch pro controller, so I wouldn’t necessarily call it “Mini”. The included plastic case is a nice touch, though I don’t know how often I’ll feel like storing it in here between play sessions. When traveling though it could be nice for putting it in a bag to avoid buttons and joy sticks being pressed and moved.

Overall if you don’t care about having a turbo function this is an excellent remote well worth the price. If you want to have the turbo function available I would look elsewhere, as this didn’t pan out. *See updates, now I have no reservation of recommending this remote as the turbo works excellent*

title: Can I give it 6 stars?!?
text:
This thing is AMAZING! I can’t say enough good things about it, and I’m in love. I have an older truck (2016, so not too old) that was just before they started adding in nice displays and Car Play. For other reasons I haven’t wanted to remove the factory stereo but have missed having Car Play and a big GPS screen for long trips. This is a huge display, and I love how wide it is for navigation (no picture of that, just for location sharing reasons) but the turn by turn takes up the majority of the screen.

Connecting to the device was very easy. Upon powering on clicking on “Car Play” gave on screen instructions, basically just open Bluetooth, select the device, and say to use wireless Car Play. That’s it, it then automatically updates the date/time based on the connected device and everything just works. No settings to configure, no confusing prompts, just 100% functionality. If you want to use your car speakers you turn to the FM Transmitter option and then set the station you want to broadcast with. Then set your car radio to the same station and the audio comes through your car instead of the device. This does provide better audio clarity, though the device has decent volume for its size.

The only thing I wish was different is the time on the device itself. This is set to a 24 hour clock, aka military time, and I cannot find any option to change that. I’ve been through all the settings (clock even pictured) and there is no option otherwise. It’s not a huge issue, especially since it normally has the devices time as well as the Car Play time on the screen at the same time, and the Car Play option is in the preferred format. One other thing to note, this only has an adapter for 12v, not USB. It has a USB C connection on the device but the cord included only connects to 12v. I powered this with USB-C to a high power device and it worked fine, but with a lower powered connection, like the built in USB in the car, it doesn’t provide enough power. That is not an issue as I don’t use my 12v for anything else, but if you do keep this in mind.

Overall I can’t stress enough how much I really do like this device. It has added a great visual screen to my older vehicle and made it feel like a HUGE upgrade. Having the option to take it out and move it if I want to is another big plus, while keeping my vehicle with OEM equipment. If I could give more than 5 stars I definitely would, and I’ve never said this about other products before.

The Lorax app allows you to still view everything remotely when not at home, but avoids any monthly subscriptions. I’ve always had ring devices but hated having to not only pay for storing recordings but also being limited to not record 24/7, as 3 minute clips is not always enough. One thing I didn’t care for is that the cameras feel light weight and a bit cheaper, being made of plastic. When installed they do not look bad, but I’m afraid that the sun is going to be very hard on the plastic on the south side of my house and I fear for the longevity of them over multiple years. If they were made from metal it would easily get 5 stars, but the plastic made it feel a lot cheaper.

So far I have 2 of these cameras up and running, and I’m waiting on the other 2 as the included wire is not long enough. It only has 60’ wires and each need ran to the base individually. I was able to install the two front cameras using the 60’ wire, but the back of my house needs to have at least double, if not triple this distance. I’m working to order some of those to get all 4 cameras installed, but those will be a bit more difficult to run the wires where I need them. Be prepared to know you can get wires to where you want everything, as there is no wireless option. Another important consideration is that if you need to go more than 60’ you need to purchase additional wiring, and if you have to go more than 300’ you will need to have power at the camera as the power cannot travel more than 300’ according to the instructions.

title: Larger than your average backpack
text:
This is a really nice, well made backpack. The very first thing I noticed though is that it is considerably larger than your average backpack, and I have a large laptop backpack I've used for years. This is taller, wider, and deeper. I got this for traveling as my family cram all their stuff into my backpack for the plane, and I have been tired of carrying it all the time. I really wanted to be able to wheel it around instead, but have the convenience of a backpack still. This works great for that, and the extra size in this situation is awesome.

I won't post additional pictures as a lot of others already have, but there are great pockets for keeping your two main items in, and then two smaller pockets on the front for additional items. It is nice still having a small front pocket for smaller, easy to grab items like eye drops, keys, wallet, etc that you might not always be able to keep in your pocket (thanks TSA!). There are additional straps on each side to help keep the bag from coming open too wide when unzipped, which is helpful when wheeling it around.

The only downside I have to this is that unless the bag has a good amount of items in it then it likes to tip as the weight is not kept stable enough in one area. If you just have a laptop and tablet inside then it likes to fall backwards. Also, there are 4 wheels on the bottom which helps for keeping the bag off the ground, but using all 4 wheels hasn't worked well for me. Rolling on just two works great, but rolling upright can be a challenge depending on how you have packed the backpack.

Overall for traveling and keeping a lot of stuff easily accessible this is a great pack, and I much prefer this to a standard carry on suitcase for that reason. I wouldn't pack more than a day or two of clothes in it though, as it would become a wrinkled mess, so your standard carry on still has its use but this works well for everything you might want while onboard the plane, right under your seat!

Most of the comments I read here at Amazon, where people complain about these batteries not holding the same charge, indicate a lot of folks just don't have an understanding of lithium-ion batteries.  The first rechargeable batteries were nickel cadmium, and you really needed to fully discharge them to avoid the memory effect (batteries failing to fully charge).  Lithium-ion batteries are exactly the opposite.  Allowing them to fully discharge shortens the life of the battery, and prevents them from holding a full charge.  At this price you can afford to get two or three and change them out when your camera indicates half of the power has been depleted.  Regardless of what you may read, OEM doesn't necessarily mean you are getting a better product.  These batteries are great and, yes, you can use them in your Canon charger.

title: CAUTION! Must be washed before using this cloth.
text: Rarely do I write reviews and usually do so for products that are either outstanding or don't measure up to promises made in the listings. These cloths actually fall into both categories and you will see why I deducted one star from the overall rating, even though all three features earned five stars. I have used these cloths for several years and, in the past, have just thrown them away when they became soiled. Well, that was just too wasteful and I finally decided to start washing them for reuse. When I did I was shocked to see the large amount of black dye that came out. Since I use these on my glasses and camera lens, all of which have coatings that must be taken into consideration when cleaning, I finally understood why my glasses became dull as time went by. Nothing strange was used to clean them. I used pure Castile soap and reverse osmosis water; no detergent was involved in cleaning. To illustrate what I found, I took a brand new cloth, washed it, and collected the rinse in a test tube. You can see for yourself, in the picture, what came out. I'm not saying these aren't great cleaning cloths; they are, and I highly recommend them. I just encourage everyone to wash them before the first use to remove the dye, since it has the potential to damage the coatings of glasses and lens. This was never addressed in the advertisement, and that is the reason I deducted one star from the overall rating. I hope this information helps you out.

I had some reservations after reading the reviews, but bought the item to see for myself. None of the posted concerns came to fruition for me. The device was not at all difficult to install. I have not experienced any loss of vision to the edges of the viewfinder. I have been conscious of this lately as I have been having a problem with my alignment in getting the image level due to rushing the shot. In order to correct this, I have been more deliberate in my composition and loss of part of the image would be noticed. Regarding twisting the unit in order to shoot portrait (vertical), the movement is rather stiff. For those who make that adjustment, it may improve over time. I shoot a lot of vertical, often shooting both and deciding in post which I prefer. I have found that even though the fit to face is not as precise, I can still get an accurate shot by leaving the device in horizontal position. That may not work for everyone and I can assure you if it did not work for me I would be complaining about that feature as when I am on a shoot I do not have time to keep twisting the eyepiece between shots. Things are just happening too fast. I will offer a couple of caveats. First, it has been reported and is true that the Hoodeye prevents using the factory plastic cover that protects the LCD screen on the D7000. For anyone who has kept that plate on, you will have to remove it. I highly recommend some protection, whether using the Hoodeye or not. The best I have found is the GGS II. This is a great product, but the caveat is, install it BEFORE you install the Hoodeye. A screen protector can be installed after the Hoodeye, but it can be a hassle. That leads to my only other reservation. Though I found it easy to install, I gave up after a while trying to remove it (in order to install the screen protector). title: What Internet Wireless Should Have Been From The Start
text: I have lived with this system long enough to pass my judgement. I have a house with open floor plan and three finished levels. The prior system was a traditional wireless router located in the front corner of the bottom level due to where the internet utility was available. That proved ineffective from the start so I added an extender of the same manufacture almost immediately. Wireless coverage was spotty in about 30 % of the house and weak in another 50% leaving only 20 % with what I consider strong coverage. I ran my heavy lifting desktop computers on hard wired Ethernet and did all my streaming from a single home theater location that was also hard wired out of necessity. There had to be a better way. I also had plans to extend streaming capabilities to the other two levels of the house. I heard about Eero and began reading reviews. The concept sounded like the answer for me so I ordered one with two beacons. I placed the main unit in a central location on the lower level, up high near the ceiling in order to allow the signal to reach the floor above. I located a beacon in the living room on the second level and one in the hallway on the third level, split between my wife's upstairs office and the master bedroom where I wanted to add a Roku. In order to continue the hard wire option I added a high speed Ethernet switch because the Eero has only one output jack. That led to both my only real negative issue and the positive opinion that this system is ideal for my needs. None of the Ethernet connections are working and my IT guy tells me it is a static IP address issue that is above my pay grade but he assures me it will be an easy fix. So until he can get me on his schedule I am running everything wireless. The really good news is this system is carrying the water for the entire house with one qualification. My home theater rack is located in an isolated concrete enclosure with cables hidden and installed through the walls before the dry wall went up. Hence the hard wired steaming device. The location of the rack was such that the signal from the lower level Eero could not provide enough signal through those walls to stream the HD video. My solution was to order an additional beacon that I placed in the room with the equipment rack. Now I have very strong wireless throughout the house with no weak spots. HD streaming is a breeze on all three levels through the Roku devices. The setup was amazingly simple and straight forward. Adding the additional beacon was too easy. The system monitoring through my iPhone app is flawless. Obviously, since the static IP issue is beyond me, I am no tech head. I do not fully understand how a mesh system differs from traditional wireless nor do I need to. I am an end user who just wants solid wireless internet that works. Eero fills the bill for me.

CONs: the user's guide sucks, the included chassis fan is very noise even at low setting.

I was able to install an ASRock X58 Extreme motherboard, an Intel i7 920 CPU, and a Scythe Mugen 2 CPU fan, along with 3 DDR3 just fine in this case. The noise of the included rear chassis fan is agonizing. The fan has 3 settings, and even as I used the lowest setting, it was still so noisy that it made me wonder why Antec would include such a noisy fan in a "quiet" case. I ended up replacing the Antec fan with a Scythe Gentle Typhoon 1150rpm and installed a second Scythe fan behind the front panel. The volume of air moved by the original Antec fan is much higher than the Scythe fan, but I compensated for the loss with having 2 Scythe fans and ended up with a whisper-quiet PC.

I actually got greedy and overclocked the CPU from 2.6MHz to 3.4MHz. The CPU temperature would jump from a 42C-idle to 49C in moderate use, on a 80-F day.

It would have been nicer if Antec added some sound insulation foam inside the case to make it even more quiet. I ended up putting 2 sound-proof panels, one at 12" behind the rear, the other next to the side of the case (on the outside) to absorb some noise and that helps even more.

Beside that, I'm happy enough with this case.

The cable is on one side so the headphone easier to put on and take off. I was about to buy a second one for my laptop (as I do editing of music), but then realized I could just unplug the headphone from its cable and take the headphone with me to my laptop (with a 3.5mm cable waiting). So I saved money while being able to keep my work area tidy with using just 1 headphone instead of two.

I used to have Audio Technica ATH-M40fs and Sony MDRV55. Both have vinyl/plastic lining on the ear cups, and the lining both got peeled off after 3-5 years which force me to throw them away (as they left a big mess on my ears and keyboard). title: New Trent NT31B
text: Received the package. It was well packed in an attractive retail packaging. Installation was easy enough. It appears to be well made. I like the size of the keys and the separation of them make them easy for me to type. The only thing I notice that is not just right is that the screen protector doesn't seem to stick down without having bubbles. It takes some work, but I was able to get most of them smoothed out, to the point that you only notice them when you are looking at a full white screen. Like I said before the keyboard has large keys, I also like the function keys. They make the ipad "feel" more like a laptop. Allowing you to do tasks such as adjusting sound and brightness is a nice perk. The outside of the case is well made. I like the telescoping hinge. It allows me to adjust the angle of the screen when using it in my lap. The closure strap is a little tricky. I can't seem to get it to lock into the hole provided. The charging port is easy enough to get to, although I think I would have preferred that the charging port be made the same as the apple, so that I could use one charger, starting by charging the ipad and then just move it to the keyboard. All in all I would recommend this device. The price point is good, it performs well, and the keyboard battery life is longer than I expected. All the external controls work and don't require any extra effort to operate. So if you are looking to make you ipad mini more useful pick it up.
