title: Great concept, a bit weak in the implementation
text:
Amazon's price and super-saver shipping were unbeatable for this product, especially at the deeply discounted price I paid.

I've had my HDHR a little over a month now...took most of that time learning how to get it happy in a Linux environment but once past the learning curve, it and Mythtv are working well. The Linux support from SiliconDust is weak and Mythtv's elaborate menus can be intimidating. That said, it is really great to be able to record two HD programs in one time slot.

One major flaw is the quality of the atsc tuners: plenty of sensitivity but really weak multipath rejection. I have a small hill behind my house that is about 60 degrees off the axis of my line of sight to the transmitters and on ch 11, the local PBS affiliate, I have to turn the antenna so that its backside is to the hill to kill a reflected signal. This position is useable with some signal loss for most of the other stations but I really need a rotator. The tuners in my cheap Tivax DTV converters and in my Sony Bravia HDTV have no problem with the multipath. It's nearly impossible to predict the multipath situation for a given location in advance and none of the systems or TVs specify this characteristic. I would have preferred to spend a bit more to get better tuners in the HDHR.

I would recommend that HDHR owners who are using their desktop computer to run the HDHR get a separate hard drive for the output of the HDHR, as it really works the drive with virtually constant access while recording or during playback. If not, a really scrupulous program of backup is essential to protect your other data. I predict a high rate of drive failure with such heavy drive thrashing. Also, careful selection of your video card is required to be able to feed both sound and video to a separate TV...full HDMI support can't be assumed in the video cards just because they have an HDMI connector so some will require a separate audio feed. Both of the above caveats apply to any "home theatre" computer system, not just the HDHR.

title: First impressions RT-N 66U
text:
Pros:

Attractive router that was easy to set up in linux even with the total lack of help from the manual or online. I'm looking forward to learning its very rich feature set. This unit was ordered 05/22/2013, has S/N D31A08001771 and was shipped with 3.0.0.4.260 firmware.

Cons:

Amazing firmware for factory but badly misses boat in a few areas: most glaring is inability to save bandwidth data. Why bother to monitor if you can't save the evidence? All the eye candy makes for a bloated firmware package.
Stupid (although attractive) mechanical design placing frequently used USB ports close to power switch which seems to get turned off every time I remove a USB key. I'll probably learn in time but it's a real pain now.

More later as I get to know this little computer.:

Firmware support is very good as of mid 2013. Asus has kept a steady stream of firmware upgrades going since introduction, many necessitated by early bugs. Unit shipped had the newer CFE bootloader which accesses the full 64K of nvram. Open source firmware is available from RMerlin and Shibby which extends functionality and improves performance. Firmware upgrades were made easier on these newer devices with the 1.0.1.3 CFE. Recovery from a bad upgrade seems to be pretty well worked out.

The top exit for the cables is awkward and top heavy using the included upright stand but the unit seems to cool better upright than laying flat which is mechanically more stable. The designers obviously don't have to use the routers themselves or they would know better. Also, the close spacing of connectors and control buttons on the back panel is awkward for adult human hands. Again, actual users would know better.

I have yet to figure out how to use the USB ports on this box. The manual and online instructions are worthless and getting the printer working has also eluded me.

Edit August 2016: The RT-N66U is a rock. Absolutely no problems with it but one of the early things I did was to ditch the factory firmware for TomatoUSB/Shibby which is much more versatile and has vastly superior bandwidth monitoring. I am up to the 138 version now. It is easy to flash and easy to use with too many features to recount. It has all the speed I can use with my ISP. My wifi HP printer is on the network and working well with the router. I expect to run this until it, or I, die, whichever comes first; but no sign of aging on the RT-N66U

I bought this for a new 43" Samsung and it weighs as much as the set. It is fab'd from heavy duty steel and is extremely rigid. The instructions, as far as they go, are comprehensive but hard to follow because all the various languages are on the same page and the print is quite small, requiring a magnifier even with my reading glasses Because of the wide range of sizes this mount will accommodate, the instructions are of absolutely no help in locating the mounting level for the back mount and this requires extreme attention if the height of the set is important. You have to install the TV side mounting and then measure the set and wall mounting to get it right.

It looks pretty massive and black on our white wall and because it needs the studs for security, the lateral location may be offset a bit from where you might like it. The arm allows adjusting the set's position but of course the wall mount is fixed by the stud location. It seems a bit stiff but this is only a 43" set on a mount that will handle much larger and heavier, and it is still new.

Bought this to replace a 17 year old receiver. It is just what I was looking for. The amp is smooth, clean and powerful. The built in phono input is a perfect match for my Music Hall MMF 2.2 turntable. The biggest surprise has been the sound quality of the tuner. Not a HD tuner but you would never know it. Lots of detail and dynamic range. And quiet reception for even weak stations as it has a mono button on the remote to quiet weak stations. The hookups are clear and straightforward, and easy to hook up. The sleep timer is a real nice touch for those who fall asleep to music.

Only four stars as the ergonomics are a disaster. Huge cabinet, tiny non-lighted source buttons are a pain. The remote is huge but the buttons tiny and virtually unreadable lettering.

title: Fine sounding CDP-A bargain considering the build quality
text:
Bought this from another vendor to use up some bonus points. I paid $200 less my 98 bonus dollars. So I have $102 in this very nice CDP.

First off it is built like a brick house. Best made component I have used since the early 80's. Be sure to use a good set of interconnects, it does make a difference. Mine were $30 from BlueJeans Cables.

The first thing you notice is the total absence of background noise of any sort. No hiss, hum, static, transformer noise. NONE Totally black. This alone lets the music come across with more detail and clarity.

With my old disc player, if you had the LP and the CD, the LP 98% of the time would sound better. Now the CD most times, sounds just as nice as the LP. I really like getting off my rear end, half as often to change albums.

The remote works great from any angle.

Smartest purchase I have made for my audio system.

title: Impressed, glad I didn't have to pay for unwanted features
text:
Bought this a month or so ago. I paid $55. I also own a FireTV 2 which is hard wired to my AT&T U-Verse router and viewed on a Philips 55" 4K TV. So far I have no issues with the latest FireTV. It setup perfectly the first time and provides s stunning 4K HDR experience on my LG TV. 1080p picture quality is also VVG as this is available from the DirecTV Now app.

This is used for streaming my Amazon Prime content, DirecTV Now, YouTube, and MLB.at bat apps in my bedroom. The Amazon 4K content looks great. Been watching the mid 2000's Battlestar Galactica episodes and they look much better in 1080p than when they were originally broadcast. Can't use a ethernet hookup as it is already used and glad I did not have to pay for that feature. It is nearly as fast as the wired box so no complaints there. The dongle doesn't hang out the side and is not visible from my viewing position.

I understand those who wanted all the features, but really you should not have expected those at a lower price. You get what you pay for.

Update: Two + months since my purchase and still happy with my selection. Glad I got this over ordering another basic FireTV Stick. Nothing wrong with the Stick but for a few bucks more IT IS a step up IMO. No surprises here, In two months I have only had to restart the device once. That was after some apps got updated for my MLB.tv

Order with confidence

title: If You Have A Mac
text:
I mostly bought the SanDisk MicroMate to use on the road with other people's computers. When I did use it with my Mac at home, it locked up my entire system and forced manual reboot. Didn't matter what type of card, how many gigs, etc. I read online that a lot of other Mac users are experiencing the same problem. I called SanDisk and here's what I found out ...

According to SanDisk, Mac users must insert the card into the reader BEFORE inserting the reader into the computer. That makes sense now that I think about it ... I was inserting the reader first into the computer, then inserting the card.

So, this is a fine product! Don't let internet reviews detailing mac crashing problems scare you away from buying. Try putting card into reader, then into computer, and you should be fine. Worked for me!

title: Fantastic! You won't be disappointed!
text:
OMG, we LOVE this projector! I probably researched more than 20 different projectors old and new, all different makes and models in the $600 or less price range with similar specifications for our outdoor movie setup. We even bought a top-rated 720p Optoma trying to save some money but hated it and returned it within a couple days (great upscaling, but horrible color and bad rainbow effect). Then we stumbled across this older projector from Epson ...

This was a really helpful review for our research and ultimately helped us decide to buy: http://www.projectorcentral.com/epson_home_cinema_2030_projector_review.htm. We also found the color setting recommendations in this article to be perfect for us.

Other expert reviews we read claimed this projector was one of the best 3D projectors made at the time (at any price point). We haven't tried the 3D yet so I can't say ... Also, reviews we read said "fast" mode is adequate for gaming. We're big gamers but we haven't tried yet; we really bought this for movies.

Note, we bought this through Amazon from Epson refurbished for $599 in June 2015 and saved a couple hundred bucks over the new price. But even the full price for the new product is a STEAL for this type of quality ...

The true 1080p and color are simply amazing (and I know a thing or two about color; I work in graphic design and do a lot of professional photo editing and preparing files for press and online). It's definitely comparable to, maybe even better than our Samsung LCD TVs or our Samsung plasma. And it's bright enough to use during the day, no problem (and we use outdoors!). At night, it's not so bright that it's hard on the eyes (the 3200 lumens on the Optoma even ratcheted down was still painful!). And absolutely NO rainbow.

Also, the features/controls are great and easy to use. The built in lens cover and horizontal and vertical keystone correction is really nice, too. The projector doesn't have lens shift, but we didn't need it. It's light. And it looks cool; we like the white curved design.

It's rated a bit louder than some other projectors when it's not in eco mode (37dB versus 32dB or less with other makes/models), but this thing's sitting a few inches above our heads (mounted from ceiling) in the gazebo and it doesn't bother us at all. And we don't notice the sound of the auto iris, either.

We have ours hooked up through a new Roku 3 and are loving it for Netflix and Amazon streaming. Seriously, the picture is sooooo good. I can't speak for the sound; we have our sound running through Yamaha receiver off of HDMI for surround.

Seriously gang, you can't do better than this if you're on a budget. Expert reviewers say it rivals much more expensive models. Truly, it's fantastic. You won't be disappointed.

title: Better than my Sennheiser
text:
I have been using a Sennheiser TR130 for well over a year without much satisfaction. It crackles. It pops. It fades in and out. And that's just sitting 10' away from the transmitter with all the controls at supposedly the optimum settings.

My new Panasonic BackBeat 906 Stereo Bluetooth headset outperforms the Sennheiser in every way!

My primary use for the headset is to watch TV late at night without disturbing my wife while she's asleep. The dongle plugs into the phone jack output of the amplifier. The behind-the-ear headphone is comfortable even when resting on the headrest of the recliner. Using the universal remote for the entertainment center controls the volume with ease.

I do have to pair the headset with the dongle each time I want to use the headset. But that's a minor inconvenience compared to the problems I've had with the Sennheiser. The automatic power off on the dongle prevents wasting battery power, but at the same time also loses pairing with the headset. Never mind that last part, because I power off both the headset and the dongle after each use.

I love the pure sound with the BackBeat 906. I can roam anywhere around the house (up to about 40' away with several walls in between) and never miss a note.

And the other beauty is that this headset pairs up with my iPod Touch 4G without the dongle! Talk about having your cake and eat it too!

title: Great video/photo light!
text:
It's not the brightest light in the room, but when I need just the right additional light, this will do it. And since I don't have to mount it my camera (any of them, including my iPhone and iPad), it's the best bargain for the buck I've found anywhere.

When I aimed this at my wife, she exclaimed, "Don't shine that at me! It's blinding me!" I was 10 feet away. It wasn't even turned up full. And the diffuser was installed.

I ran a test in a dimly lit room with and without the light, with and without HDR both times. The subject was a plant 15' away near an open window with daylight coming through on a cloudy day, and a colorful couch 10' away in the same field of view. The extra light obviously won, and the HDR wasn't really needed with the light. Some levels adjustment was used to lighten the shadows just a little for the image using the light for both the HDR and non-HDR image. The result was exceptionally pleasing. Of course, hardly anything could be done to save the image with no light nor even the one with no HDR and no light.

Hey! This will even work to remove shadows or enhance images in an outdoor shoot in full sunlight!

It's a little heavy, so I hope you do your exercises before a long shoot. Or put it on a stand.

title: Glad I did.
text:
This is my first foray into case lighting since I modded my nzxt phantom to add a window. I must say I am thoroughly impressed with what came in the box.

BUILD QUALITY
It's quite obvious they aren't the cheap led rolls everyone and their mother sells on Amazon. The strips are solid, the included remote is neat and there is a battery barrier like another reviewer suggested to ensure it doesn't come with a depleted battery so, I guess customer support listened.

INSTALLATION
It took me 5 mins to install.....no joke. The strips both have a rubber covered magnet on each end so it just sticks to any part of the pc case and there is a 4 pin extension cord included so you can place strips on opposite sides of case for max coverage.
PLEASE NOTE 4 pin connector has neg and positive so if you plug it in and it doesn't light up, just unplug and flip it, it happened to me.
After that you just need to plug into a free molex plug and ur good to go.
SOMETHING TO KEEP IN MIND, put the it receiver within line of sight of where you plan to point remote for ease of use.

I must say I am totally stoked to get these lights and really have no qualms whatsoever, I looked for days for a viable lighting solution and this one won out.

In the immortal words of Adam Sessler I give these LEDs a 5 out of 5.

text: Excellent replacement screen for my iPad2. It is complete with pre-placed adhesive in the correct places. The fit of everything and the cabling is exactly like the original. I have been using it successfully now for a couple of weeks on a daily basis and it works just like the original. Be sure to test everything before closing it up, then remove the adhesive strips and then, finally, remove the protective plastic from the inside surface. That way you will avoid finger marks on the glass. You should also use clamps and a heat gun or hair dryer to help the edge adhesive set well to be sure you have a good edge seal. If you are patient, have the proper tools and a good place to work with good lighting, save a bundle on screen repair by using this screen instead of paying Apple $155 plus shipping to do the work. There are many videos online showing tips on how to do the repair. The trickiest part is avoiding the wifi and (if you have them on your model) 3G antennae--follow the videos carefully to avoid damaging those. Use good tools also, get some if you need to and you will save yourself time and do a neater repair. Mine works and looks like new again now.

I have only two RJ45s connected to it: one that comes from my DSL modem (I think it is marked on the device with "WAN"), and only one of the 4-ports that I connecto my my internal network. That only port is connected to another switch in my intranet. I wanted to connect a computer directly to one of this guy's 4-ports, but it dropped the connection (or reset itself) so frequently, I got fed up with it and just treat it as if it is part of my DSL modem.

So, if you have the idea that you could use this as your internal swotch, I urge you to reconsider that aspect. Use it as a firewall, as a wireless router, a DHCP server, etc., but not as a general purpose switch togeher with the rest.

title: Great price, silent, perfect fit for home server, great packaging
text:
I've been watching 1TB Seagate and WD for a few months; needless to say, I was in no hurry. But my home server's 640GB RAID-1 was reaching its 5 year range, and that makes me nervous with electro-mechanical devices that run 24x7. I was running out of space anyhow; so an upgrade was in order. I bought Intel DG41TY MoBo, Intel E1400 CPU, and 2GB GSkill SDRAM for the MoBo. Since my old drives were ATA and I have no intention of throwing them away, I slapped in an IDE/ATA PCI card, too.

I purchased two WD10EADS over Seagate's 1TB due to the reduced number of platters (EADS has one fewer plate than EACS) and the BIOS complaints I read about Seagate. Feedback on another retailer's packaging indicated less than desired protection for HDs, and I am very satisfied with Amazon's packaging. There were lots of bubbly cushioning in the carton that contains two individual boxes for each drive with additional cushioning in each HD box; as opposed to two bare OEM disks wrapped in bubblies and thrown in a cardboard box one might see elsewhere. Timing was right on mark, too. Good service Amazon!

Overall, these HDs are part of a Fedora Core 10 x64 installation running on a single OS drive. The HW has one IDE/ATA RAID-1 off of the PCI card, and another RAID-1 with these two SATA 1TBs connected to the MoBo. I can't hear these additional two 1TB drives: the noise from the older two IDE/ATA drives totally masks the new two SATAs noise. Eventually, when the IDEs die, I'm sure I'll have a much calmer server.

As for speed, I access these guys over my 1GB network from several clients spread across the house. I haven't run a speed test, but no one in the household has any complaints. I have quite a bit of additional space.

title: Perfect for swappable backup media
text:
I read a lot of reviews and a lot about other similar products, and decided to give this a shot given its low price for quality. I was not mistaken; this thing is perfect for what I need. What do I need? OK, read on.

I can't yet speak to its long-term reliability; I may update this once I used it long enough. The construction looks sturdy enough. My only suspicion is the connections of those grommet-like rubber suspenders to reduce noise and absorb vibration. If you don't jiggle them a lot, and there is no reason to since you do that only at unit installation time, they should last a long time.

I have a rather complicated home network topology that challenges a small business network with multiple failover, backup, and mirroring facilities. I need to swap two 1-2TB backup disks, leaving one of then active while storing the other one in a remote location for geo-location safety. You can use multiple USB devices, but it is ugly. First, you have to have USB cables, power adapters sitting outside your computer case, and your automated backup software should be intelligent enough to pick the USB device with the disk attached. It can be done, and I've done it, but the complexity is always bad. So, instead, get this hot-swappable tray that requires no external cables, no extra power adapters, and simply plugs to a molex plug and into your MoBo's SATA port. Bonus: SATA is way faster than USB; not that everyone cares where backup runs in the middle of the night. But, hey, I'll take it.

You don't have to connect that extra cable to get the front-leds to blink. If you don't care about watching the entertainment LEDs, just skip that connection anyways. The hot-swap works; I tried with a 1TB WD disk on 64-bit Win7. Also, the disk I out in there is BitLocker protected, not that it matters since it is done entirely in software (but, hot-swap didn't destroy the encryption state, either; so it is kind of important. Wouldn't you say?). But, what does matter is that I moved this disk from a USB frame into this tray, and BitLocker didn't hick-up a bit.

title: After lots of investigation and comparison
text:
My D-Link DI-624 started giving trouble; more trouble that is. It always had the problem of rebooting when more than one RJ-45 LAN ports were connected and active. So, I had another switch connected to only one of its LAN ports, and DI-624 was my wireless AP and internet gateway/switch without affecting my internal network. That was all fine when I had only one WiFi device active at once. Things have changed, and I have multiple WiFi devices active simultaneously, and DI-624 started crapping out: reboots, infinite delays and just dropping one or more of the WiFi connections. It was time to get a better Firewall/WirelessAP.

I gave up on D-Link with my rather extensive home network (several switches, multiple floors, heteregoneous devices, wired/wireless of all sorts, media streaming, etc.), and started looking at "better" ones. I don't want to pay a real Cisco router I use at work, so dumb it down and look at LinkSys or NetGear. Well, it was a tought decision, actually. NetGear won at the end not only because I had a number of Netgear switches already and they work without a glitch for many years. It won because its detailed specs; also, this device sits somewhere in the back of something else where no one looks at other than me peeking at it every now and then - not that it malfunctions. Cisco/LinkSys one appear too shiny with less advanced features.

This is not perfect. I don't care about the USB NAS drive; I have real stuff for that - so I am not going to comment on it. Otherwise, this thing just works in my environment. No problem NetFlix/YouTube/etc. streaming at all. WiFi (I only tested 2.4GHz so far) works with multiple devices active at the same time: I tested with 5 simultaneous devices so far spread across the guest and internal network (yes, that separation is a must for me, and it works, AFAICT).

What is missing? DNS setting is very primitive. I want to specify an internal DNS server with scoping, and then want to say "for all others, relay to DNS you received from WAM DHCP". This is pretty common with private DNS servers (think NAT). NetGear, I like your products, but do you hear this? It is not a big deal, add that on, please.

title: Simple Solution - Better Instructions Would Help!
text:
What's not to like. Every StarTech product I've purchase has lived up to my performance expectations. I expect nothing less than an easy install letting Windows 7. load any needed drivers. Purchase this my new computer motherboard didn't come with a port for our HP 895Csi.

May 25, 2014 Update. Always had good luck with StarTech products and given them 5 star ratings. NOT THIS ONE!!! Installation was easy. However, it Went downhill from there. On restart, the computer saw the card but did not know what to do with it. Loaded the CD that came with the card. It is a JOKE! There are more files with a bunch of information but no, I repeat, no installation files. Went to the Startech web site. Downloaded a.zip file that was suppose to have the drivers needed. Extracted the files. Again, no setup/installation files. If your like me, it is very frustrating going through folder after folder looking for installation files that are not there. If there are setup/installation files, StarTech has them nicely hidden. Don't purchase this card and install it in a computer with Windows 7/64 bit OS unless you want alot of frustration.

May 31 Update. Received and email from StarTech. They suggested doing the following:

Below are the steps that need to be taken to install the drivers from our website on a Windows 7 64bit machine:

Please download the drivers for your product using this link: [...]

When you download files, Windows usually saves them in the Downloads folder which is located under your user name in the users folder on the drive where Windows is installed (for example C:\users\your name\downloads).

After the download is complete, extract all of the files.

1. Right click the "PLX_PCI.zip" or the "PLX_PCIe.zip" file.
2. Select Extract All.
3. Take note of location that files will be extracted to.
4. Select "Extract".
5. When complete, extracted files will automatically open.

To open Device Manager:
o Press Windows Key + R
o Type - devmgmt.msc
o Click OK.

Driver Installation
1. Right click the device, which will be indicated with a "!" next to it and select Update Driver.
2. Select "Browse my computer for driver software."
3. Select "Let me pick from a list of device drivers on my computer."
4. If a list of hardware types appears leave it set to show all and click Next.
5. Click the Have Disk button and browse to the extracted folder, open the Windows folder and the 32-bit or 64-bit folder based on what system type your computer is and select the file named "OxMf" or "OxPCIeMf." Click OK and then Next to install it.
6. Repeat steps 1-5 for each serial port that appears after the OxMf or OxPCIeMf driver is installed, this time choosing "OxPCIeSer."

Note: To check your System Type, click Start > right-click Computer > Properties

Since I already downloaded the .zip file I knew where to look for the drivers. Following the installation I was able to upload the drivers. However, I still could not print a test page. Doing a little checking of the Printer Properties I noticed the drivers I downloaded set-up the printer on LPT1. My computer was looking for the printer on LPT3. Once I changed it over everything worked fine.

Sent an email back to StarTech Tech Support suggestion they get the installation instructions updated and make mention of checking Port connection. Changed my rating to reflect my feelings.

title: Quiet and handsome but optical door cover unreliable
text:
What a great case. This looks elegant in my stereo rack, and completes the quietest computer I've ever owned. As others noted one quirk is that you will need a smaller heatsink/fan than full size cases. I researched heatsinks quite a bit and decided on the Big Shuriken, which works great with my Core i7 860 processor.

It seems to move a decent amount of air quietly with just the three included 120mm fans, and my video card fan is louder than the case fans. But because I have it in a somewhat claustrophobic rack, I just ordered a couple of ENERMAX UC-8EB 80mm low rpm Case Fans for the back. Five slow fans are much better than the one noisy fan you find on most cases. The fan cable included with the case does not support PWM speed control; it just powers all three 120mm fans at constant 1200rpm (slow) from an IDE power connector. But that's not a problem since the fans are so quiet at full speed.

It is a bit cramped inside, but the airflow is well designed so that the limited airspace is used effectively to draw air across critical components.

The only downside for my use is the lack of IR or SD cardreader, but those are easily added externally with USB. A front eSATA connector would have also been nice but I can't be too picky. Do make sure to check dimensions carefully if you are going to try installing anything unusual; I found that there was no way to fit a corsair water cooler that I was lusting after. I'm using a full height dual-slot video card and there's not much if any room for cables between the top of the video card and the case lid, so I'm glad I don't have too many cables going from the PS/HD side to the Mobo side otherwise they might not all fit.

I also wish the power button (and unnecessarily large unlabelled system reset button) were protected or deemphasized more; I worry about guests pressing the power or reset button thinking they are turning off the stereo, since this thing looks so much like a stereo component and those are the only buttons on it.

UPDATE after using this case for a year:
----------------------------------------

I'm still a huge fan. But the optical door cover clearance is way too tight for comfort. Over time the alignment caused problems opening the door, and then later the drive mechanism failed to open even with the door cover removed. I think the door cover did in my optical drive; it only opens with a paperclip and pliers now. I'm leaving the door cover off from now on. I've heard that the GD05 case doesn't have this door cover issue, so that might be worth investigating.

I recently removed the useless front panel reset switch and installed my USB IR receiver inside the case behind where that button was. It required some drilling to mount an L bracket for the receiver and get the cable out to the back usb port, but I am happy not to have that external IR receiver which I was forever having to reposition as it got knocked around.

I just realized I've got eight fans in this little box: heatsink, gpu, 2 rear, 1 bottom psu, 1 left, 2 right. Perhaps counterintuitively all these fans make it quieter because they move air through more area and more evenly.

One annoyance is that the fan dust screens are on the inside where some disassembly is needed to vacuum the dust buildup off the screens. It's not practical to clean them every 3 months as the instructions recommend, but do plan on disassembling this thing once a year to clean the screens.

title: The Ford Escort of power supplies.
text:
I'm starting to get back into electronics hacking after a long hiatus, and this is a good tool for that purpose.

It arrived with the feet punched through the single wall cardboard box, and sawdust or dirt or something on the feet and bottom inside the plastic bag. It's clear they cut every corner they could to keep costs down, but if you know that going into it, I think this is a good deal.

I tested it out by hooking up a couple of 500 watt lights, and it delivered 18.8V and 3.1A, so it meets the specs. I heard only one relay click at about 9V, which means that it uses only two taps from the transformer... Other power supplies click a few times or more; more taps would make it waste less power throughout the range and run cooler, but if you use it infrequently wasting a bit of AC is not a big deal.

The meters seems decently accurate; my fluke 189 said 18.64V when it said 18.8V. The fluke said 3.077A when the mastech said 3.11A.

I'm not sure about the ripple though. I put the probe of my new Instek 1062a digital storage oscilloscope onto the banana clip outputs, and it measured approx 2mVpp ripple (varied from about 1.6mVpp to 2.4mVpp, mostly staying above 2mVpp). This is higher than the rated 0.5mV But when I tried switching between the 1x and 10x settings of the probe the measured ripple didn't change nor did waveform ripple that I saw on the screen, so there's something weird about my measuring setup; the 2V test signal on the oscilloscope at 1X did change to a 200mV signal with the 10X setting. I'm a beginner at using my DSO so take this with a grain of salt and if anyone can explain how to get a more reliable ripple measurement please tell me.

I did try powering a cheap old radio shack amplifier (277-1008c) with it, and didn't hear any more noise or hum than when powering it from 9V battery, so the ripple so far isn't an issue for me.

The binding posts are extremely cheesy; there's no hole in the posts so you have to wrap a long section of wire around the post, and there's only a very small contact area on the post base, making bare-wire connections not very practical. I think using banana plugs or perhaps spade connectors is the way to go with this. Probably not a bad idea to use a banana to binding post converter for bare wire connections, which you can easily unplug during power on to avoid any spikes from frying your circuits.

I agree with other posters that the coarse adjustment dials are sufficient, and I found it easy to adjust the voltage or current to within practical tolerances. I did find that the Voltage dial tends to cover up the "Voltage" label when this is on a tabletop, so I got confused and thought the Current label above it applied to the Voltage dial. Newbie mistake; I'll probably attach my own labels to make sure I don't get them confused. It would be nice to have backlights for the LCDs but they are readable enough in normal room light.

Overall, this seems like the Ford Escort of power supplies: Good enough to get the job done, but without any luxury or frills.

title: Quieter but not as powerful as the Lepai
text:
I prefer this amp to the Lepai LP-2020A+ 20W amplifier from parts express because the build quality is better and it doesn't hum or make static sound when adjusting the controls, even though it puts out less power than the Lepai.

I brought both onto my test bench where I fed them sine wave signals and looked at the output with an oscilloscope while they were driving a conventional advent speaker. They clip in very different ways; the lepai shows a nice smooth sine wave until you get within 10-20% of clipping, whereas the Lepai starts to distort the waveform at around 50% of clipping level. This may be the advantage of the tripath chip on the Lepai. With a 1kHz tone I got clipped waveforms at around 15Vpp output on the Pyle, but 21Vpp from the Lepai. So the Lepai has about twice the clean power of the Pyle, and about 30% more distorted clipped power.

But the build quality of the Lepai amplifier is just not quite good enough for me. It comes with a switching wall-wart transformer that does not have any indication that it was designed for audio. There were some comments on the partsexpress reviews about how partsexpress replaced the transformers because the old ones were problematic, so that explains why the box that I received the Lepai in was ripped and clearly not fresh. The Pyle arrived in a nice sealed box.

The Lepai circuit board has a lot more small surface mount components which may be part of the quality problem reported on the partsexpress board. The Pyle on the other hand comes with a real old fashioned copper transformer inside the box, making it much heavier than the Lepai. The Pyle circuit board is older technology, single sided through-hole versus the double sided Lepai. The Pyle has much fewer but larger components, which makes me trust them a bit more.

Personally I like the streamlined no frills nature of the Pyle without extra LEDs or tone controls, even though it doesn't put out quite as much power. The deciding factor for me was that the Pyle doesn't exhibit any hum, whereas the Lepai would hum audibly about 60Hz whenever I touched the case or any controls, and turning the controls would cause a scratching noise with the Lepai.

title: Nothing else like it, great for single sided deafness
text:
I have single sided deafness, and when I'm doing audio mixing work I need headphones that combine both channels into my good ear; otherwise I won't be able to adjust the levels of the sound going into my nonfunctional ear.

These headphones are totally perfect for this use: The 1/4" right angle plug somehow stays plugged in to the field mixer extremely well even when I jostle things around. The coiled cord is the perfect length for devices worn on or near the body. And the headphones are decently comfortable, decently rugged.

The one issue is the tonal quality. These are not audiophile grade by any means and the sound is noticeably thin and distorted (compared to top end headphones). So I cannot judge tonal qualities of what I'm mixing, which is becoming an issue the deeper I get into mixing. For that reason I'm looking for other single sided options with higher quality. If anyone knows of any please let me know. I'm going to try the One Good Earbud/ScanSound ones, but what I'd really like is a headphone cable with a passive crossfeed network built in, which I could solder onto some known-good MDR-V6 headphones or similar.

I'm sort of an electrical geek so I opened these up to see how they mix the two channels together. It turns out they do it in a way that's a bit "iffy": They simply short the tip and ring of the connector together. Anyway, the point is that the different sound quality this produces on different devices may come down to how well the amplifer topology handles the kind of abuse these headphones dish out. As most people know, you shouldn't use a Y connector to sum two signals together, and these headphones effectively have a Y connector built in.

One surprise was what looks like a pair of back to back diodes across the driver. I think the purpose of these is to limit the signal level so that people don't damage their hearing, or to protect the driver from strong signals.

title: Quality control marginal but great sound. Wired beats wireless.
text:
The first one I got from amazon seller smsl died in about two hours of use. No problems returning it for a full refund including shipping. I ordered a second one from Shenzhen amazon seller and it has been working great for weeks.

I use this with my Samsung tv for night listening to avoid waking up the house. I originally tried the Roku remote with headphone jack but got frequent dropouts probably due to the wifi transmission. I tried Bluetooth headphones but didn’t like recharging often. Both these wireless solutions had passable but not great sound quality and were weak in low frequencies.

This DAC has sound quality that just sounds effortless and pure through my koss porta pro headphones. And it has plenty of signal to drive these high efficiency headphones louder than I would ever need.

What was disconcerting was the differences between the two units I got from the different sellers/lots. The LEDs were different brightness and patterns, and whereas the smsl unit had non locking buttons the Shenzhen unit had locking buttons that mechanically had in and out positions. This tells me that they have very loose specs around parts and just use whatever is cheapest and or available.

But this strategy works: I got a unit for very cheap price that has sound quality in the same class as my old Denon $2000 receiver with burr brown DACs. It was worth the hassle of dealing with a defective unit.

It is definitely worth taking the time to run a toslink cable around the baseboards from tv to the couch to avoid the hassles of wireless. And this works just fine with a 25 foot Toslink and 25 foot headphone extension.

One annoyance is that there is a mechanical relay inside which clicks every time the audio signal comes or goes. This means you hear the clicking every time a tv program starts, and it clicks when pressing pause or switching sources. The signal doesn’t have any clicks (once I made sure I wasn’t feeding it 5.1 formats; set your source to pcm) but the sound comes from the box itself. Not an issue once used to it but it seems strange to use a mechanical relay in this day and age. I don’t remember the relay clicks from the first unit so again this may be a part difference. Or maybe I didn’t have a chance to notice it on the first unit before it died.

Unlike other reviews I found the toslink connector to be perfectly tight with the bluerigger cable sold on amazon.

Enjoy!

title: Get an external fan to keep this cool.  Runs hot.  Great sound quality.
text:
This replaced my old Denon 3808ci, which had the best sound quality I had owned. Multeq XT32 took the sound quality to another level; the bass with my 2 subwoofers is frankly the best I have heard; the old 3808ci would sometimes let through an unnatural rumbling sound, but the 4500 just sounds effortlessly powerful and balanced. This (along with the older 4400 and 4300) is the lowest costing Denon receiver that has all the discrete circuitry, DACs, and processing to sound in league with the top end receivers.

But these do run hot. My old Denon 3808ci, which was for the day an equivalent predecessor of the 4500, failed was sent to Denon service three times and all times they said the issues were from overheating. Each time I moved it to locations with more airflow and finally got it stable. Placing the 4500 in the same position that had been stable for the 3808ci, it failed after a few months with overheating issues. These overheating issues seem to damage the computers; I got more and more random features not working; the onscreen display started showing only every other scan line, then some inputs started not working, and finally all hdmi inputs didn't work.

When I got it back from service the last time (always seems to take 2-3 months turnaround), I invested in an ACInfinity T9 fan with top exhaust. Since then it has been stable for a long while, and most importantly it is never hot to the touch, whereas it often was very hot to the touch before the fan. Since I keep my house at 80 degrees in the summer with air conditioning, I set the smart fan to 95 degrees.

I use an external amp for the front channels and subs, so I am able to get a full Atmos 11.2 setup with this receiver. Frankly I'm not too excited about the height channels; they don't seem to add much to the 7.2 setup so when I move I may not bother installing height channels. Only a very small amount of Atmos source material is available via streaming, and a lot of what exists doesn't seem to use the height channels much if at all. You have to have a streaming device that supports Atmos, an app on that device that supports Atmos, and a program that has Atmos. Getting all three aligned often requires me to use streaming devices I wouldn't otherwise like my Panny UDP802 disc player which is the only device I have found that supports atmos apps for both netflix and amazon. The Roku ultra, LG C8 tv, and Xbox X all don't support atmos on at least some of the streaming apps. tldr: don't bother with height channels unless you are really dedicated to being on the cutting edge.

Ironically this is opposite of what they say they support; wyze is supposed to only support 32 while the eufy is documented to accept 128.

title: Great all around monitor.  The 32" size is much more useful for 4k than 27".  VESA mount.
text:
Needed a big monitor for my 15" MacBook Pro mid 2015 and old Windows PC. I originally tried the Dell U2720Q monitor which is highly rated. I didn't like the way the 27" screen makes the pixels so small that you don't really get any more usable real estate than with a laptop monitor. I would rather use my pixels to get more desktop space than to approach retina resolution. So when I accidentally cracked the U2720Q, I decided to go with a 32" replacement.

The concern then is that the bigger the screen, the more the colors will look off angle at the edges of the screen. You can spend a whole lot of money on a fancy IPS screen with amazing viewing angles, or just get a curved screen like this. If you are positioned at the focal point of the screen, it doesn't even look curved.

Out of the box, the color seemed a little wonky and I was starting to worry about whether this would be useful for color correcting photos. But after spending an hour calibrating it by eye using test patterns at full 4k resolution, the color seemed very usable.

Don't get me wrong, this doesn't have the color uniformity and accuracy that one would expect from an apple laptop monitor. But it's close, and the contrast ratio is better due to the VA panel.
There was a calibration data sheet included which said that this monitor was calibrated to 0.49 delta E, and that all AOC monitors are calibrated to delta E < 2. I wish they would advertise this more; this level of calibration is impressive.

I think it's good enough for doing media production.

I will also share that getting 4k 60hz output was a challenge with my older hardware. In my 6 year old MacBook Pro and Windows computer, the HDMI used an older standard that only supported 30Hz at 4k. So I had to use the displayport connectors on both computers instead of HDMI. And there were non-obvious steps involved to set the computers to 60Hz. Newer computers that support 4k 60Hz from HDMI are just starting to become common. Anyway, because there is only one displayport input on this monitor, I had to use an external displayport switcher box to switch between the mac and PC. The switcher box and extra cable add another $40 to the cost of using this monitor.

This was the only curved 32" 4k monitor I found that worked for me. The dell model has known incompatibility issues with M1 Macs which I will likely upgrade to, and the other curved 32" 4k monitors didn't properly accept vesa mounts for external stands. This works great mounted to the ESA mount.

The surprising bonus is that the curved shape actually is better than flat at rejecting light from the windows opposite the monitor. The flat Dell had reflected them across the whole screen, but with the curved screen I can adjust focal point to get most of the reflections at the edge of the screen.

I would have preferred a glossy screen, but since they are not available in this size this seems to be the next best.

Maybe someday we will have perfect monitors with perfect off angle response, but for now curved is perhaps the only way to get great color across a big screen without paying several times as much.

title: I'm glad this exists but the four short segments are hard to install, and have a stripe on one side.
text:

This worked well for me to hide the switch and cord of a reading light above a bed. But it is much more difficult to work with than it should be. The adhesive doesn't seem strong enough to keep it in place where people might brush up against it, and makes it hard to align the 4 segments in a straight line since you can't reposition it.

What worked for me was to buy furniture pushpins from Lowes, and use those to mount it to the wall, through holes I drilled in the plastic, one at the top and bottom of each segment. That let me position it next to a straight edge to get it just right before pushing the pin to fix it to the wall.

You should be aware that this is a "clamshell" shape where one side is fixed, and bending that side to open it causes the grey plastic of mine to turn white, so there was basically a white stripe on one side.

The other issue is that this is not self-aligning like other channels; there is nothing about the product that will hold segments together or aligned, so it is completely up to the installer to get the segments aligned on the wall. Other product with detachable covers can self-align by offsetting the cover so the gaps are not at the same place as the base channel. But not this.

title: I can now use my iPad on the other side of my house!
text:
My story is that we have a ranch style house with the DSL modem/router on one end, and my office is on the other end. My iPad can't pick up the signal, and I had been wanting to get a WiFi extender but didn't want to pay a lot for it. I just happened to stumble across the Edimax.

Installing it took all of 10 minutes. I flipped the switch on the bottom, plugged it in, and pointed my iPhone to the setup website. It immediately found all the wifi networks in the area, and asked which was mine. I selected my router's name, and entered the password. The Edimax web setup initially hiccuped and stated that I need to make my own static IP address. I had no idea where to go from there, so I decided to try it once more. Second time was the charm, no static IP address needed. The Edimax picked the name for its signal, and kept the same password as the original router. That's it, setup is done!

I guess I should also point out that placement is key. If you put it right on the edge of where your wifi ends, it probably won't work as well, and I'm guessing that might be why some folks are reporting that the Edimax loses signal. I placed mine about 2/3s of the way between my dead zone and the router. The iPad gives me 2/3 bars in the once dead-zone; note that the signal is going through 3 walls!

I should lastly comment that web surfing is just as fast. I don't really notice any speed differences between the Edimax signal in my office versus the signal next to the router. I haven't tried downloading or any speed tests, however. I don't think I would even try downloading anything from the Edimax; it just makes sense to me that if you are going to be moving lots of data, it would be best to be as close to the source (i.e. original router) as you can get (or just hook up an ethernet cable!).

Needless to say, I really like this extender, and highly recommend it!

title: -I'll start off by saying that like many others
text:
I plan on updating this review as time goes along.
-I'll start off by saying that like many others, my ipad in it's case didn't seem to want to fit in the slot on the keyboard. Every time I would try to open the clamshell up, the ipad would pop out. Here's my solution...the slot is made of metal. Just try to pry the metal open a little bit. It's incredibly strong, and you won't be blue to bend it by much, but even a little bit helps. My ipad/case now fit into the slot very well. I'd also recommend working the hinge a little bit to loosen it up. I'm dropping a star for now because I feel like I shouldn't have had to "fix" the Slimbook to make it work properly.
-the other point I want to make is that I've read where people are comparing this to the keyboard on a MacBook. No way in haites this is anything as good as a Macbook keyboard. The keys feel rubbery, and there's more travel. You have to hit the keys harder or else you'll miss characters. It takes a while for your brain and fingers to get used to that if you've been using a Mac keyboard. The Slimbook does have a decent keyboard, but let's not fool ourselves here.
-For now, I do like this setup a lot. I theoretically like being able to pop my iPad out and use it, but to be honest I don't see myself doing it that much, it's just so much more functional in its "laptop" mode. It will definitely make your iPad more useful.

title: Weird key positions...
text:
Surprisingly high number of good reviews for a product with too many flaws...
Dislikes:
-General typing experience - the keys are cramped because it’s a small keyboard, I understand that. But some of the punctuation keys (especially the apostrophe) require an unusual key combination that is unlike any other keyboard I’ve used. Really slows down typing to have to hit a different key combo to get a frequently used punctuation symbol. Others reviews recommend using autocorrect, but that feature is inconsistent. The small keyboard and weird punctuation keys lead to numerous typing errors, which are compounded by the fact that the delete key is too far down on the keyboard—and as such, I keep missing it. After spending several hours typing on the keyboard, I just can’t adapt my years of typing experience to make it work for me.
-iPad holder is slightly turned when open - this is more of a “nit-pick” but when I open the keyboard, the hinge at the bottom (which rotates the iPad) locks the tablet into place with the screen facing slightly towards my right. It’s like having someone turn your computer monitor to the side; you can still type and work on your computer, but you just want to turn the screen back to the way it should be, facing straight in front of you. Unfortunately, you can’t adjust the rotation as it just snaps back into the odd position.
-Weight - I don’t see how anyone could want to use it in “tablet” position (with screen folded back on the keyboard) as it is just too heavy.
Likes:
-One thing I liked was that I could rotate the screen around (keyboard in the back), drop the screen down to an acute angle, and use the Apple Pencil with the Mini 5 for drawing and highlighting documents. You can prop it up to nearly any angle you want, and it will stay.
-Backlighting works great, multiple colors and levels of brightness.
Overall, I just can’t adapt to the typing experience, and as such I’m going to send it back. If you’re willing to deal with trying to retrain your hands to find certain keys, then this keyboard might work for you. For the rest of us out there, skip it!

title: Awesome lightweight iPad mini keyboard, but with compromises
text:
The Hou keyboard is my third iPad mini 6 keyboard I've reviewed. The other two are the Greenlaw keyboard and the Magic Keyboard Case, both found on Amazon. I've finally come to grips with the notion that keyboards in this size are just too small, and can't come without one of two compromises: either 1) you get a keyboard with keys that are of a decent size, but extra characters like punctuation require unusual key combinations or 2) you get a keyboard with punctuation keys in the usual spots, but all the keys are tiny and difficult to type on with even small hands. This keyboard falls in category 1. I can find the keys just fine with my regular adult sized fingers, but I have to use the option key to get simple punctuation like the apostrophe. Fortunately, Apple's built-in spell check picks up most of the errors and can correct the punctuation, but if you do a lot of touch-typing, it is hard to let your brain relax and forget about the additional characters. Also, the keys do require a slightly firmer strike than I like for them to register. So, with these limitations, I would only use this keyboard for short texts, typing URLs into a web browser, making reminders, and other lightweight tasks. I thought about writing this review with the keyboard, realized what a headache it would be, then grabbed my MacBook to type it instead. Two last negatives include the lack of a backlight and trackpad (not deal-breakers in my opinion).

Now that I've gotten those issues out of the way, I'll say I do like how versatile the keyboard is--you can flip it back and hold the device in portrait mode like a book, or you can keep the back open with the keyboard flipped backward to prop-up the iPad for drawing. And it's super easy to remove the iPad to use it without the keyboard. It's also an extremely lightweight keyboard...absolutely the lightest available. The outer texture is a material very similar to what Apple is using on their iPad keyboards, a rubbery-type material. I also wanted to mention that I actually CAN use this keyboard on my lap. It works great if I've got my legs propped up on, say, the couch, and the keyboard and iPad in its stand are in a great position for typing. Just be very careful on an unstable surface, as I don't entirely trust the magnets when the back is flipped down (less surface area with magnets attached as opposed to when the entire back is stuck to the iPad).

So in the end, would I recommend this iPad? My best use scenario would be a leisurely carry into a coffee shop where I'm just hanging out and enjoying a drink, not doing any sort of detailed work. The keyboard and iPad combo are so lightweight and slim that I would say it's the most portable duo on the market. You just have to be willing to accept the sacrifices that come with such a tiny keyboard!

title: A good mouse on a budget
text:

Pros:

-only one Bluetooth device connection possible. I have multiple devices, always nice when a mouse can connect to two or more devices with easy switching.

I will definitely use this mouse in a pinch, but the clicky buttons make it a less attractive option for me. I’d recommend it if you’re on a tight budget and only need to connect to a single device if using Bluetooth.

title: It works, but one big issue…
text:
-I purchased the JOCONU wireless HDMI display, mirroring receiver to use with my iPhone 13 Pro Max and big screen TV made by Samsung.

What I like:
–Easy connection. The device uses your home Wi-Fi network to send a signal wirelessly from your phone to the TV via an HDMI cable. you simply scan a QR code on the screen, enter your Wi-Fi network, password, and start screen sharing on the phone. Took me less than five minutes to set up.
-Landscape screen resolution is very good.

What I dislike:
-There’s a small, but significant screen lag between the phone and what’s displayed on the TV. Unfortunately, there is no lag on the audio, so what you see on the TV doesn’t match up with the audio. For example, when someone is talking on the show, their words come out just slightly before their mouths move. It can be distracting.
-The delay between the audio and video worsens with video resolution. It’s not as bad with low resolution videos, but high resolution videos are very laggy.
-The single button on the device locks the picture into landscape. It’s kind of useless, because when the phone is in portrait with landscape locked, the resolution is terrible.
-Not a big deal, but the device itself needs to be plugged into a USB outlet, so make sure you have one nearby.

Final verdict:
-The JUCONU is usable, but the delay between audio and video is pretty annoying. I have a lot of videos in low resolution format, and as stated above, the delay is less noticeable, and thus more tolerable.
-I think the JUCONU could be used for presentations and slideshows. Might be nice to flip through photos on a big screen.

title: Decent keyboard, but overall bulky
text:
I use the Wireless Keyboard with my iPad Pro 11” 2018. I’m typing this review on it!

What I like:
-Keyboard is actually pretty good. It’s plastic-feeling, and the keys rattle when you type, but the key travel is good, I don’t have to mash hard on the keys to get them to respond, and I’m not making any more mistakes than I do with other keyboards. Feels like an inexpensive keyboard, but it works just fine.
-The top row of function keys have all the extra keys you need, including volume and screen brightness controls, and I don’t need to hit an extra key to get them to function.
-The keyboard isn’t permanently attached (uses magnets), so you can adjust the screen to whatever angle you need.
-The case is bulky and actually seems protective.
-Flap covers the camera when closed.
-Apple Pencil can charge at the top, and there’s a protective slot at the bottom of the case.
-The keys are in all the right places for a touch-typist; I don’t find myself hitting the wrong keys or having to use a function key to get to standard punctuation characters.
-The material of the case feels nice, smooth and slightly rubbery.

What I don’t like:
-Baby blue color is meh.
-The case is bulky, heavy, and makes me not want to carry around the whole unit.
-Comes with a protective rubber keyboard cover that degrades the typing experience. Fortunately it is removable.
-The keyboard actually ends up resting on the iPad screen when the whole unit is closed. I’d rather not have undue pressure on my iPad’s screen.
-The keyboard/case combo is not easy to use on a lap. The bottom part to which the keyboard magnetically attaches tends to bend downward, so it makes the setup feel unstable on my lap. Works perfectly fine though on a desk.
-I can’t really place the iPad screen at a good angle for drawing with the keyboard removed. There are three notches in the bottom part of the case to keep the iPad from slipping, but they keep the iPad too upright for drawing.
-The footprint is rather large; I think it’s about twice the size of an airplane tray, so this wouldn’t be the case I’d use for doing work in-flight!

Final verdict:
-It’s a good (but not amazing!) typing experience. I think it would be useful for travel as it is certainly bulky/protective, but I don’t like how the keyboard rests on my iPad screen when the unit is closed. It’s an above-average keyboard/case combo in a very crowded market of iPad cases and keyboards.

title: It's a decent system
text:
The TDK 3 Speaker Boombox stands out from other music players in its category. It should! The TDK 3 Speaker Boombox costs a great deal more than every other unit you'd logically compare it to.

This stylish piece of hardware manages to pull off a modern yet retro appearance. Fittingly named, the 3 Speaker Boombox is profiled with three large uncovered speakers, two woofers and one sub-woofer. Completing the 3-speaker look, TDK designed/built two tweeters over-top the two woofers. The forty pound Boombox is well-crafted and solid, apparently built with high quality material.

Some of the unit's highlights include, but are not limited to the following.
bass and treble EQ with dynamic graphic analyzer
touch capacitive input selector
on-board mixer allowing users to simultaneously set volume levels of two blended audio sources
limited playback distortion at relatively high/room filling volume levels
an LCD track name display for MP3 title selection and playback
AC and DC power options
relatively portable
decent bass response for many songs
an array of audio inputs (mic, component line-in, electronic instruments/gear, apple devices like iPod, USB drives)

Disappointing aspects of this unit include, but are not limited to the following.
no remote control
no place to secure or dock the user's audio source player (negates the portability of the unit)
no SD card slot/option
no Bluetooth compatibility
awkward AM/FM antenna setup (negates the portability of the unit)
no dedicated mid-range mid-level EQ adjustment options
average overall tonal/sound quality (considering the price)
no enhancement of the sound quality of sub-par MP3/audio files

Techies and music enthusiasts will appreciate TDK's 3 Speaker Boombox as a fine piece of audio gear. However, the unit's price is far from wallet-friendly, as it lacks a few features and its overall performance could be a little better. When considering portable audio equipment of this nature, know that TDK's 3 Speaker Boombox breaks away from the pack. At this time, its only true competitor is Monster's Beats by Dre' Boombox. At $500.00, it's doubtful that the average Joe will be purchasing TDK's 3 Speaker Boombox until after the price goes down.

title: Close But No Cigar
text:
The wifi connection with the doorbell and other products is weak. The motion detection is far from reliable. The doorbell's camera/video shows people leaving the door after they have walked onto the property, up the steps, and have done whatever they came to do. I see the mailman, delivery guys, and others walking away. I don't even get to see their faces. The bell doesn't always chime my phone or the additional chime I purchased from Ring. This product is a great idea. The execution of this product leaves a lot to be desired. Did they consult with a tech manufacturer before putting this product to market? It's so close to being a good product though. But, no cigar.

The Ring help pages tend to point to the other items connected to the product as being the problem. No. It's the doorbell that's the problem. When you experience problems, they suggest things like moving the placement of the Ring doorbell. That's laughable. They should be ashamed of themselves for suggesting something like that. The doorbell is placed where a doorbell would go. No one is going to move their doorbell. We can't move the entrance to our homes. Then they suggest moving the placement of the router. This is less offensive than the prior suggestion. But, it still not satisfactory. They don't know how many other things are connected to a person's home routers. Moving it just for the Ring might not be a feasible option. In most cases, it is not. But, I think whoever came up with that so-called solution is very aware of that fact. My cell phones and tablets get great wifi reception in the location where the ring is. To me, this points to the Ring has having sub-par internal wifi connection. I think they can do better.

title: Sadly my Linksys 54G cannot handle the higher speeds that ...
text:
Sadly my Linksys 54G cannot handle the higher speeds that my internet now offers (100mbit fiber connection) and I had to upgrade. I tried some other similar products first, even ones that you could root and install dd-wrt, but those inevitably had stability issues and had to be rebooted multiple times with or without dd-wrt.

Now steps in Buffalo, this has run solidly for 6 months without a reboot needed.

Update:
Now into 9 months of ownership I wanted to add a USB drive for media storage. One issue the Buffalo AirStation has is it cannot mount NTFS partitions, the standard for Windows since the days of XP. The choice is FAT32 for up to 32Gb, then XFS (a linux file system) for drives larger than 32Gb.

My solution was to switch from the Buffalo AirStation firmware to DD-WRT instead, Buffalo informed me that doing this would void the warranty on the device, but since it has ran solid for 8 months I'm not worried. So far two weeks and no trouble, works great with my NTFS partition. The DD-WRT interface can be a little intimidating to people who aren't used to setting up networking equipment, but if you are coming from a Linksys 54G with DD-WRT you should feel right at home.

Another feature that appears to be missing on the Buffalo firmware is SSH access to the device, this greatly decreases it's usefulness for those that like to tinker and roll our own solutions. Again with DD-WRT firmware loaded you now have SSH access to the device.

With both these features you can then create custom scripts to run upon plugging in a device, e.g. starting up Transmission BitTorrent when the device gets mounted, and making sure it mounts to the correct partition, have it read the torrent directory, and start up. Useful if you don't want to run your external drive all the time but want it for the occasional new linux distribution release.

title: They miss the mark on too many levels
text:
The Sennheiser PXC 550 are almost, almost there. I so wanted to love these. It was painful to come to the decision that despite their flawless cord to BT switching, and multiple device pairing, and call handling, that there were two areas that just didn't cut it.

1) Comfort, they focused on travel size and shrunk the size of the phones to no longer be over ear but on ear. This and the head band was stiffer and had less padding. I could wear these for 15 minutes and be happy when I took them off. As many others described it, their ears felt hot wearing them, a common sign of fatigue in wearing headphones.

2) The audio quality, even with their special app, was just not up to par. Even using the USB cable connected to the laptop where it does this amazing job of allowing for much better audio through the USB cable, but still could not match the pair of Sennheiser HD 598's I got.

Ultimately it was a combination of both that really pushed me to return them. I picked up the HD 598 for $120, compared to these for around $300. For that price I was expecting the same performance and comfort that is what Sennheiser stands for.

The noise cancelling was decent, not as good as Bose, but enough that my wife would get mad as she was leaving for work as I could not hear anything she said if I had a little music playing. That's sort of the key to their noise cancelling, it works fantastically with other noise going through them, but only mediocre as a system by themselves. Add to it that they get uncomfortable for extended periods of time and I couldn't see making the 14hr trans-pacific flights with these on.

The touch interface left me wanting. Solid buttons still have their place, and it would have been great to have a single button I could press and hold, or press again, to allow pass through for conversation, but alas it is stuck in their touch menu somewhere with a two taps to turn on, two to turn off, but don't confuse it with tap to pause, or volume, or something else. Most functions I would have welcomed a solid button to press as many have reported the touch on the side can accidentally get pressed when trying to watch a movie in bed, or even simply adjust the uncomfortable headset. This wasn't the deal breaker, I could learn to deal with it, but it is an annoyance.

I will be waiting for the next generation to come out that fixes these issues, for now I'll be going with the HD 598 for an affordable over the ear headset.

title: Developers favorite keyboard
text:
I am a software developer. My hands are on a keyboard all day, everyday. Over the years I have used every conceivable kind of keyboard on desktops and laptops. Throughout the day I often have to type on a variety of generic keyboards in front of various workstations. When it comes time to sit at my own machine, this keyboard helps relax my hands and arms so I can concentrate on my code.

Why do I like this keyboard?

1. Using an ergonomic keyboard is a very personal decision. And yes, it can make it more difficult to switch between non-ergonomic keyboards and your own during the day. One of my coworkers reminds me of that every time he sits at my machine. Personally, I have learned to go back and forth with little fuss.

2. Compared to other ergo keyboards I have used, only this one provides a (almost) traditional (read IBM PC/AT) layout. What does that mean? It means F5 and F11 are where I need them to be. If you write code or work in SQL, you understand why I care. The arrows and Insert-PgDn cluster are in the traditional location. I have a Microsoft Comfort 5000 keyboard that I tried using for work, but it has found a home hooked up to my home TV PC. The 5000 has a very entertainment-centric layout. The function keys (F1 - F12) are minimized, small and not at the top of the keyboard. The main row of top keys are audio / visual related: play, pause, volume up and down, etc. I constantly struggled to find the F5 key on the 5000.

3. The key feel on the Natural Elite is moderately firm with full key travel and positive finish to each key strike. No, this is not a clickity-clacky, spring loaded feel like the old model M's. But it has a nice, full feel through each keystroke.

The only variation from the IBM layout, and my single dislike about the Elite Natural keyboard, is that the Insert/Delete/Home/End/PgUp/Pgdn cluster is vertically oriented rather than horizontally oriented. Those 6 keys are laid out 2 wide by 3 high, rather than 3 wide by 2 high.

I bought my first Microsoft Natural Elite several years ago. It still works perfectly today. The only trouble was it had so much mileage on it, the original white color had turned to a sad, dirty beige. My solution: buy a black one!

This vendor is great. Keyboards (I bought 2) arrived fast and in proper packaging.

title: Almost great
text:
I was truly excited about this camera. Everything about the X10 from ergonomics to specs sounded like someone had finally made a camera just for me. Taking it out of the box I was immediately impressed with the heft and solid feel. Then I turn it on and things went down hill from there.

What the X10 is not: a rangefinder. The X10 is purely a point and shoot operation. I hoped for more manual control. The X10 is just not designed that way. Manual focus mode on the X10 is insultingly useless. Shooting in aperture priority mode should be easy but the LCD screen is useless in bright sun and that is the only way to access the aperture and shutter settings.

ISO: specs sound great. "ISO 100- 12800" But the highest sensitivities are only available when shooting small JPEGs. No raw above ISO 3200.

Mechanics: the zoom / power control ring on the lens sounded like a good idea. But reality is mine had a very sticky spot at the 50mm mark and the actual "on" position is ambiguous. No weather sealing on a $600 point and shoot? 80% humidity limit! I would have happily paid $700 if it was weather sealed.

Lens: optics are great. But the front element is very exposed without the impossible to obtain hood / filter adapter. While compact in the off position, with the lens extended the front will get hit on something eventually.

Viewfinder: optical viewfinder is an absolute necessity for me. That was 90% of why I bought the X10. But it is too quickly blocked by the extending lens and of too limited coverage. Having only LED indicators on the outside next to the viewfinder makes the viewfinder itself really only useful as a sighting tool in daylight (which is good as the LCD is unreadable in sun). Just having basic exposure and focus confirmation in the viewfinder would have made this 10X more useful.

I returned the X10. Perhaps a version or two in the future Fuji will have refined this design into what I need. But this is not it. For now i wil continue relying on my DSLRs for "real" camera functions and a trusty Canon A590 point-n-shoot for a pocket camera. The A590 does everything the X10 does and it cost me $100.

title: functional despite initial probelms
text:
Keep in mind that this entire product category has fallen to a $30 price range. So I do not view this as a bargain basement item. Especially since this is a name brand Samsung item versus a generic enclosure.

The enclosure is light weight glossy plastic on top and sturdier textured plastic underneath. Light weight is probably good if you want to carry this around. On the other hand, I have a tiny laptop without a DVD drive so I don't have to carry around a DVD drive built in to the computer or otherwise. I expect this thing to never leave my house and only be used for occasional software installs or re-imaging.

NEGATIVES:

When I first connected the device it did not power up. I examined the plugs and decided the micro USB connection on the device itself did not look like it was fully inserted even though I firmly pushed in the cable. I gave the USB plug a very, very hard push (harder than I would have been willing to do on a laptop or camera for example). It slid further into the connector and the device powered up.

Then I push the open button on the CD tray and I get a grinding noise. I try a few more times and the tray will not open but sounds like the open/close motor is just grinding like something is holding the tray in place. I get a paper clip and start poking at the emergency release hole next to the release button. The tray still won't pop open even using the "manual" release method. I decide to try the electronic button again and suddenly the tray pops open.

The dual USB power connection method is a good idea but poorly executed here. The included dual connection cable is too short to reach any pair of USB ports that are not directly over/under. I only see those on old laptops and desktops. I deal with numerous laptops at home and work and all have USB ports spread around at least several inches away from each other even if they are on the same side of the computer. Only because I have lots of random PC cables did I happen to have a USB extension that allowed me to connect this at all. Be aware that you will likely need a USB extension cable at least 3 to 6 inches long to reach 2 ports on a typical laptop unless you have a pair of directly over/under ports.

POSITIVE:

I put the unit through it paces by burning a 4 DVD recovery media set from a new laptop and then writing back those discs onto a new SSD. All discs were created and read without error.

I suspect that I probably put more effort into getting it to work out of the box then some other user may be inclined to (hence some of the other negative reviews). Quality control seems a bit lacking for a Samsung product. I would happily pay another ten bucks for a more substantial enclosure and a better USB cable in the box. I think Samsung really cut a few corners trying to get to this price point.

Bottom line is this works.

title: High quality sound is overshadowed by poor interface and controls
text:
Cowon has been and still appears to be the absolute best sound you can get in a portable device. Their user interface was never great. But the controls on the iaudio 9 are terrible. The diagonal touch slider is overly sensitive even when adjusted to lowest sensitivity. Even after downloading the PDF version of the user guide from the cowon website there are still confusions.

Sound quality is phenomenal. Only comparable sound I have heard is from my Yamaha receiver through headphones. I have an old Creative Zen and it is a close second for overall fidelity. No other brands I have used even come close to the sound quality.

Volume is very inconsistent. I tried both my in-ear Sonys and over-the-ear Sennheisers headphones. The radio was comfortable around volume level 6. But when playing MP3 or WMA audio files I had to go up to 15+. Then switching back to radio I would blast my eardrums forgetting that the volume was so high.

The interface is utterly frustrating. I am willing to put up with a few idiosyncrasies. But the iaudio controls seem either backwards or purposely confusing at times. I personally prefer the solid click of a button when using a player. The controls here are just too sensitive. I almost felt like a stylus would have been useful as my fingers were constantly missing the intended targets.

The radio receptions was disappointing. For comparison I had my old Zen player with me and switched headphones between the two devices while on a moving bus listening to the radio. The Zen was solid and clear. on all stations I normally listen to. Switching to the Cowon I got periodic clicking and static. As I was switching the headphones which are the antenna between the players I know the problem was purely with the Cowon's radio.

The Cowon player feels rather weak physically. Yes it is slim and light weight. But my Zen just feels more solid in the hand. The plastic on the cowon feels very soft and I expect this would quickly show wear and scratches.

Shooting outdoors at f/8 this lens excels. Indoors or at night the super high ISO performance of the K-5 helps support this lens at smaller apertures. For simple product photography this is my go to lens because it provides a comfortable working distance appropriate for most table top work and it has great IQ close in at f/11.
