I dislike tablet covers as bulky and cumbersome. The screen protector keeps the Kindle safe without restricting access of decreasing portability. As the screen is recessed it is already protected from much surface contact when placed against another flat hard surface as a table top or in a bag against a laptop. title: Fuji, once again, almost got it right
text:
What do it want a camera to do: exactly what I tell it to do.

I don't want a point and shoot. Today's ever escalating arms race of shoving more and more bandaid technologies into tiny cameras allowing the user to do nothing more than push a button is really frustrating. I know how to take photographs and I just want a camera that will not get between me and the image I want to capture.

In film days I always used small fully manual SLR's. That is what I was comfortable with. Digital SLR's have always been frustratingly big and over saturated with automation features for my taste. I have heard arguments that SLR have to be the size they are due to the mirror. Nonsense. The Pentax K1000 (one of my all time favorite cameras) measures just 94mm H x 143mm W x 50mm D. Compare that to most DSLR bodies today that are at least 75mm deep. A mirror does not require a 75mm deep body. Rangefinders always appealed to me for the optical clarify of the viewfinder and their small sized lenses. But Leica body and lens prices were always prohibitive.

The Fuji X100s had looked to be exactly what I had always wanted. Compact size. Superb optical rangefinder style viewfinder.

There are very, very few gadgets that I would ever even consider "pre-ordering". The X100s was one. I anted up and placed an order for one long before it was expected to ship earlier this year and was apparently one of the first to actually get one.

The "hybrid" viewfinder is superb. It is a real step forward in the evolution of photographic equipment and I hope other manufacturer will follow Fuji's lead here. The X100s is truly pocketable unlike any SDLR and unlike many so called point and shoots.

Initial impressions of the build quality were disappointing. While the top and body feel solid, it is a bit of a façade. The small USB port door on the side is flimsy and the battery / memory card slot on the bottom is pathetic plastic. The X100s should have been weather sealed. I believe Fuji could have done this for a modest increase in final price. I would gladly have paid another 10 or even 20% for a weather sealed body. This is supposed to be a go anywhere street shooters camera. It has too many entry points for moisture to be safely carried in even moderate precipitation.

In use, the camera continues to frustrate. Even after thoroughly reading the owners manual many functions and features are hidden in obtuse menus. Many things just seemed backwards to me. The so-called shortcut for ISO changing is done by pushing the Fn button and then scrolling left and right using the top right command dial. Trouble is my brain always says smaller numbers should be to the left. Yet rolling the dial left gets you bigger ISO numbers. There are many places where I found the Fuji menus and selections just backwards from what my intuition and previous camera experience led me to expect.

I avoided the original X100 because one thing I have learned is that I have to have absolutely instantaneous power up and no shutter lag. This has kept me using DSLR's as those are the only digital options with real instant on capability. The X100s was touted as having much faster performance. Yes, sort of. Power up is slow but can be sped up by playing with custom power saving menu options. The shutter lag is low but only when the camera is prefocused.

Manual focusing should cure the prefocus shutter lag issue but here again the X100x is crippled by it half manual half auto hybrid design. The focus by wire system means when you turn the focus ring on the lens you are not actually changing anything mechanically in the lens elements. You are sending electronic signals to the camera asking it to change the lens focus. This may be better than the X100 but it is not good enough for real manual focusing. At least not good enough for me.

I spent too much time looking for settings in menus and struggling with focus lag causing shutter lag.

Image quality is great, when you can get a shot. But what good is it if the camera is so difficult to use that it prevents getting those in the moment shots. Or if it is so delicate that I am afraid to carry it outside.

What would make me happy?

1. Remove about 90% of the electronic menu functions from this camera. I do not want to edit my photos on the back of my camera.
2. Give it real mechanical manual focusing.
3. Weather seal it. Come on, a $1000 plus camera without even basic seals on the battery door? That is embarrassing
4. Remove the built in flash.

title: Pentax really got it right
text:
The first thing that strikes my each time I pick up the K-5 is how solid it feels. Yet, it is small and lighter weight than all other DSLR's I have owned. Knowing the body (and some lenses) are weather sealed makes it easy to carry in any weather without giving a second thought to sheltering it from the elements. This is how a camera should be built.

Shooting is fluid and the K-5 is instantly on and ready with either the power switch from fully off or with the shutter button from its power saving sleep state. Shutter lag is zero to my perception and the camera is clearly faster than me.

Having shake reduction built into the body rather than the system's lenses was a great selling point for me. It means I can put on a twenty year old manual focus Pentax-M lens and it has the same vibration reduction as a brand new lens. I have mounted the K-5 to a telescope and also made great use of the "SR" (shake reduction) feature.

Image quality is relative to the quality of the lens you mount on any camera. Coupled with good lenses the sensor in the K-5 renders colors accurately and the wide dynamic range provides alot of detail to work with in post processing. I always shoot RAW and find the results consistent and pleasing even straight from the camera.

I primarily went to the Pentax system because I liked their small prime DA Limited series lenses. Coupled with the K-5 the 21mm makes a super small package for easy carrying under arm. The 18-55mm kit lens is amazing and my normal choice for carrying while hiking.

There are more custom menu and in camera editing features than I would prefer. Some of the Pentax menus are not full intuitive. I think Nikon still wins in that category. So in some ways this may be a Mac vs PC kind of comparison. I guess I am a PC guy. I prefer making exposure and setup decisions myself and am willing to live with some mild idiosyncrasies of menus and button placement.

Battery life has exceeded my expectations and while I carry a spare I have never run out of juice and needed to swap while carrying the K-5.

I can activate the remote while standing behind the camera. Most IR remotes only work when in front of the camera unless you can bounce the signal off a wall or mirror.

The only issue I can find with this remote is that the button action is a bit vague. If using this remote for constant exposure checking or auto-focusing where the pre-release stage of the shutter was needed it might be frustrating.

Overall a very good value.

title: DSLR image quality in a compact body with some caveats
text:
Why did I buy the Fuji X-E2? I was tired of carrying my DSLR around. Even the smallest DSLR is twice the depth and weight of the Fuji body. The APC Fuji sensor is fantastic and provides the same effective field of view and depth of field at a given focal length as any comparable DSLR.

You can read about specs and peek at pixels all day. The bottom line is the best camera is the one you have with you when you need to take a photo. An 8x10 large format camera with an 800 megapixel scanning back will give you better image quality than this or any so-called "full-frame" DSLR. Good luck walking around with either that 8x10 camera or that bulky DSLR all day.

Fuji has hit the sweet spot of brilliant image quality in a body + lens package that is light and small enough to carry all day without a second thought.

The only detractors for this body are its lack of weather sealing and an optical view finder. Weather sealing (especially at this price point) should have been provided. Because the whole point of a carry everywhere camera is that you can carry it everywhere regardless of weather. As far as the EVF (electronic view finder) versus OVF (optical view finder) argument goes, you have to decide for your self. I owned the Fuji X-Pro1 that has an OVF but found the camera body too big and the EVF was horribly slow and grainy. The EVF on the X-E2 is worlds beyond the X-Pro1 or any other EVF I have ever used. The EVF is smooth and bright. But it is not an optical finder. There is still some lag in the display and in extreme bright daylight the EVF is near impossible to see until I have cupped my hand over my viewing eye and let my eye adjust to the light differential for several seconds. Big deal? Well, it can be. Those few seconds are the difference between getting the shot and not in many candid situations.

The EVF is better than an optical non-TTL view finder because for macro work you HAVE TO USE THE EVF! I like macro shooting and even the X-Pro1 switches to its EVF when in macro mode. The EVF also can give an amazing real time display of exposure which is a revelation coming from a purely optical SLR system.

** Update after a few months of use **

The more a got to know this camera the less I liked it. The novelty wore off. I shoot outdoors. And at least where I live we have "weather" outdoors. Without fail every time I take this camera with me it either snows or rains. Lacking any weather sealing I have to shelter it under my jacket of shove it in a bag where it is a useful as a rock.

The EVF had a real "wow" factor at first but as I carried this camera daily I found it lacking in many typical situations. Bright daylight and snow: the EVF is simply not nearly as bright as daylight. When my eyes are looking at the real world in full sunlight they are adjusted to very bright light. When I move my eye to the EVF the image is so much dimmer that it takes my eye several seconds to adjust and open up so I can see the EVF image at all. Then moving my eye back to daylight I am blinded for several seconds before I can see again in daylight. I do not walk around with the camera glued to my eye. I only put the camera to my eye when I want to get a shot. The lag time of human eye adjustment between the brightness level is just too long and introduces too much delay into the photo process.

Using an optical viewfinder (SLR or rangefinder) equalizes the brightness level much more closely between the real world and your view through the camera. An optical viewfinder is simply faster to use in brightly lit environments.

Ironically, the EVF suffers from being too bright when in a low light environment. I often found myself blinded by the EVF when indoors shooting in dark rooms or outdoors at night.

I have given up on the X system and returned to using DSLR's full time. Yes they are heavier and bigger. But the SLR optical viewfinder simply does not get in my way when shooting. The EVF is simply not good enough for me in daily use.

title: Optically great if you can deal with the Fuji X system shortcomings
text:
My view of the entire Fuji "X" system is a mixed bag. Having tried many of the bodies and lenses I can only say the same thing over and over again in my reviews: "Fuji almost did it, but not quite."

Optics: Outstanding clarity and color rendition. But if you pay the full retail price on this lens it should be outstanding.

Build: OK. Why, oh why, did Fuji not make it's first or second generations of X bodies and lenses weather sealed. Only now are big, heavy zooms being announced with weather sealing to mate with the X-T1.

Handling: Less than OK. I have tried and given up on Fuji's fly-by-wire manual focusing. I like mechanically coupled focusing. I do not like the ambiguity and inconsistency of the electronically coupled "manual" focusing on all the Fuji lenses.

Focal length: 35mm is sort of normal. 35mm is a great focal length on 35mm film or a 24mm x 36mm "full frame" sensor. But on the APC sensor of the X system this gives a slightly longer than "normal" perspective like a 53mm lens on film. Trouble is that a really great "normal" 50mm lens costs half of what a comparable 35mm lens does.

Feels to me like Fuji went with the fastest way to market with these first three X lenses (18mm, 35mm, 60mm macro). Instead of designing a truly original lens they just took old tried and true optical designs and stuck an X mount on them. Is that entirely bad? No. The optics are great. But, it feels just like buying my first DSLR back in 2001. Cool new technology in the camera body with only the old film design lenses to attach to it. Then we spent 10 years watching (and still watching) the big manufacturers experiment with big versus small sensors and eventually going both directions while finally providing "digital specific" lenses designed with focal lengths appropriate for the APC sensor size.

title: Saves space but not as convenient as jewel cases for easy access
text:
I started using these sleeves almost 20 years ago. They are well made and definitely worth the price over generic sleeves that may harm your valuable discs during storage or removal. However, be aware of what you are committing to before moving your collection to this type of storage.

Going from jewel cases to sleeves is really a one way conversion in storage. To move a CD from jewel case to sleeve along with the original case backing labels and inserts you must tear apart the original case backer. The soft sleeves have narrow slots at the top into which you can fit the edge labels from a jewel case. Every one I have transferred was perforated and relatively easy to tear off from the 5x5 inch jewel case backing label. You then gingerly slide the tiny label into the sleeve window. My cases once came with a special plastic "pusher" tool do help with this but I don't know if that is still standard equipment. It does make the job easier but not easy. Now you can flip through your labelled sleeves and read the info along the top edges sort of like thumb tabs in a dictionary.

After many years of storing in sleeves I am regretting not keeping my jewel cases and most importantly the jewel cases backers intact. It is much easier to find a disc when your can read the edge label on a jewel case versus flipping through the sleeves. If you frequently get discs in and out of your library this becomes a real pain.

I kept the separated 5x5 backer sheets from all my discs but I have tried putting the separate narrow edge labels back into jewel cases and it does not work. The edge labels have to be attached to the 5x5 backer to hold them in place along the edge of the jewel case. I wish I had never torn apart my case backer sheets.

Yes, sleeves reduce storage space by about a 3:1 ratio over standard jewel cases but you are giving up alot of convenience in seeing edge labels. Also, soft sleeves are not a good choice for taking disc with you unless you have a dedicated transport case to carry them in. A jewel case can just be thrown into a pocket or bag with no worry about the safety of the disc. Sleeves do not protect the disc unless they are inside of some type of carrier case.

title: Good build quality but does not perform up to claimed specifications
text:
Induro tripods and monopods have been my faithful companions for years. All perform flawlessly. I thought an Induro head would be a good investment. But my overall impression is not that great.

Build quality is good and on par with similarly priced heads of both domestic and foreign manufacture. Movements are smooth.

The highly textured finish is not a great idea on a head. Clearly it was done to match the aesthetics of the brand's tripod. But the rough texture attracts and holds dirt. It is not easily cleaned off in the field. Collecting dust and grit on the knobs and outer shell makes it likely that grime will find its way into the inner ball area. That would cause an ongoing maintenance headache.

Functionally the head works smoothly and locks quickly. However, the head claims a support capacity of 20kg. I put a 1kg camera and lens on it and found the head settling out of position after locking. Adjustment to the drag made no difference once the ball was locked.

I have found that heads and tripods rated several times above my maximum expected load are the most stable for me. While the BHL-1 is the smallest of the Induro heads it is still rated 20 times above the load I applied. I was in no way pushing the limits according to the specifications. Yet the head sagged under load as if I was near its maximum load. I do not believe the 20kg rating is accurate.

The BHL heads are a "split shell" design. The outer shell of the head has a vertical slot cut into it. Tightening the locking knob compresses the shell horizontally around the ball. I find ball heads that use a "lifter" design where the shell is solid and the locking knob lifts the ball into the reduced neck of the shell provide a more positive lock.

Weight savings of this head compared to others offering substantially better support is negligible. I have not used the larger Induro heads so I cannot compare to those directly. I do own other brand ball heads that are only slightly heavier than the BHL-1 which offer considerably better support. My Sunway XB-44 weighs 460g compared to the Induro at 430g. Yet the XB-44 holds a 2kg load with zero sag on the same Induro tripod.

title: Absolutely delighted with size, performance and image quality
text:
I replaced a Canon 5D Mark III and 70-200mm f/2.8L IS II system with Olympus OM-D E-M1 Mark II and it is awesome! I shoot a lot of action sports and was initially concerned about AF performance and depth of field differences. On both counts the Olympus system has exceeded all my expectations.

First the Olympus is much easier to hand hold. The E-M1 is 1334 g. Canon 2440 g. That's over a kilogram or 2 1/2 pounds lighter! I typically carry 2 bodies and 2 - 4 lenses. That becomes a total weight savings of 5+ pounds! Plus I can use a smaller and lighter tripod with the lighter camera. That's another couple pounds off.

The AF options and adjustability of the OM-D is mind boggling. Using the EVF is far, far superior to the optical viewfinder of the Canon 5D. First, it's WYSIWYG. You can see the exposure changes in real time before taking the shot. The entire frame is available to the AF system, not just a smaller central portion like on the Canon.

Yes, DOF is increased at comparable FOV and aperture when using the smaller format system due to using 1/2 focal length. Is it enough to bother me? No. Not in the least. Look at real numbers comparing equivalent lens focal length giving the same field of view and with the same aperture the maintain the same exposure.

This example is with subject distance of 30 meters (mid soccer field from side line) to get one or two players fully in frame:

Canon 5D "full frame" 200mm @ f/2.8 => Vertical FOV 3.6 m, DOF = 3.6 m, DOF behind subject = 1.9 m
Olympus E-M1 II m43 100mm @ f/2.8 => Vertical FOV 3.9 m, DOF = 7.1 m, DOF behind subject = 4.0 m

So yes, you do get more depth of field when using a shorter focal length lens at the same aperture at the same distance. Is the difference of ~2 meters increased background sharpness at a distance of 30 meters enough to effect my shots? No, it is not. If anything it is an advantage as I often shot at f/4 on the Canon lens just to increase my DOF and improve sharpness. The Olympus lens is razor sharp wide open.

The E-M1 images are silky smooth from base ISO 200 up to 1600. Noise is noticeable from 1600 to 3200. At 6400 the images have noticeable "grain" when viewed at full print size. This is roughly one stop less than the Canon achieved. Again, does this negatively impact me? No. I typically shoot in the ISO 400 to 1600 range and the Olympus performance is excellent throughout the range.

Build quality of the E-M1 is stellar. Period.

Would I give up my Olympus micro four thirds and go back to "full frame" Canon? No way.

Run the available "Synology Assistant" app on your PC and all your NAS units are shown on the network. Click to connect via browser. Go through simple guided setup process and you are in business.

For absolute simple default settings you need little tech knowledge beyond assembly and plugging it in. For more advanced tasks you may need to visit the synology website. While there is tons of info, much of it is out of date. I found discrepancies on every knowledge base document I looked at as they were apparently written for previous versions of the DSM operating system and have not been updated. You can generally figure out what you need even if exact terms no longer match up with the current DSM version.

I've used other storage systems and Synology is the best for simple, nearly plug-and-play use. I suggest learning some of the more advanced features and taking advantage of the various "packages" (apps) available to install on the NAS. This can be whatever you need it to be. Simple, zero effort storage and backup system or full blown mail and media hosting server.

title: Yes, it is an excellent lens.  No, it is not the same as a 600mm f/4.
text:
Olympus needs to stop claiming this 300mm lens is "comparable" to a DSLR 600mm f/4. Olympus uses that word repeatedly in their marketing. I have used micro four thirds cameras from both Olympus and Lumix with this lens. The OIS and resolution are impressive. But do not put this lens on your m43 camera and expect to get results even remotely similar to a 600mm f/4 lens on a 24x36mm sensor camera.

If you are invested in m43 and want the best long lens you can get, then buy this lens. Performance is especially good if you use Olympus. The stabilization is not as impressive on a Lumix body as it cannot combine the IBIS with lens OIS. You only get the full potential when used on Olympus bodies.

Do not buy into the m43 system just to get this lens believing that it is a 1-for-1 substitute for a Canon/Nikon/Sony camera with matching 600mm f/4. The results from the Olympus 300mm f/4 are comparable to putting a 300mm f/4 on a full frame body and cropping half the image. With a larger sensor camera you also get 2 stops better noise and ISO performance plus the option to not crop down the final image.

To make a m43 lens "comparable" with a full frame lens you must convert the focal length AND the aperture. A 600mm f/4 full frame lens would be equivalent to a 300mm f/2.0 m43 lens! Nikon made a few. They were manual focus and weighed 16 pounds. A modern 600mm f/4 has auto focus and only weighs 8 pounds.

I am not a Canikony fan boy just trying to rain on the m43 parade. I use m43 and I enjoy in specific circumstances. I also use APS-C Fuji cameras and full frame cameras. My experience with the m43 system in general and this lens specifically led me to decide that m43 is ideal for ultra light weight, compact equipment used for bright daylight shooting. It is not ideal for low light or long focal lengths. You can get "comparable" (there's that word again) results using a APS-C or full frame sensor camera with a equivalent focal length and aperture. A 600mm f/8 lens yields similar background separation for the same subject distance. For roughly the same price, the Canon 7D II and EF 100-400mm f4.5-5.6L II lens yields nearly identical results to the Oly E-M1 II and this 300mm f/4 while being a far more all-around useful combination. For even less money, the Nikon D500 and 300mm f/4 PF lens is actually smaller and lighter. If you are starting from scratch or already own a Canon or Nikon body, go that route instead.

This is a 300mm f/4 lens. It does not magically become a "600mm" when attached to a small sensor camera. A 300mm lens is always 300mm. Period. Compare it to other 300mm f/4 lenses, all of which cost less than half of what this lens does.

Inserting and removing the big NP-FZ100 batteries is easy. The smaller NP-BX1 batteries are a bit difficult to remove with my fat fingers.

Be sure to get a good quality 18W QC compatible USB-A power block to use with this device as it only comes with a cable. This is a positive to me as I already have multiple power adapters and would not want to pay for another one I didn't need.

Overall an impressive device that I'd recommend to anyone who uses different Sony cameras requiring these battery types. For travel you can find smaller chargers such as the Nitecore. But the ISDT has the advantage of doing double or triple duty potentially replacing multiple chargers. So it may actually be more efficient to only travel with one of these devices rather than 2 or 3 separate smaller chargers.

When charging is complete, the display dims to the lowest brightness level. I wish the display would completely turn off. The display dims enough that it does not bother me and I have not felt the need to cover it with a dimming sticker.

title: Avoid this stuff like the Plague
text:
I used to swear by this stuff and I thought it was the greatest thing since sliced cheese. It's a little bit difficult to apply but I got low temps with this stuff. This was way back in 2011-2012 when I was big into watercooling.

This paste pitted the hell out of the IHS on my 3930k. They aren't huge pits like the in the pictures on TPU. These are smaller pits that are the size of a grain of sand. There were several of these smaller pits. I left the waterblock on the CPU for 4 years though. However, I assume it was a collection of diamonds that pitted the IHS on my CPU, not really the time I had left it on.

I wasn't too alarmed by this because I had recently done research on TIM because it's been years since I have bought any. I wanted to see if a better product had come out to the market. So I knew about this problem before I pulled the waterblock off my CPU. However to my defense, because I know the Innovative Cooling company will almost troll to defend their product, I have pulled the heatsink/waterblock of my CPU and graphics cards a couple dozen times. I have used AS5, MX-2, and Shin-Etsu in the past and I never had anything pit or damage the IHS of any of my processors.

Back in 2011 I jumped on the IC Diamond bandwagon because of the awesome benchmark results I've seen on other sites. As far as performance goes it beats the best version of Shin-Etsu by a degree or two depending on how successful you apply the paste. Personally I saw a 3c-4c difference between the IC Diamond 7 compound and the MX-2. Not all Thermal compounds are the same and when you're overclocking to the moon it's important to keep the temps as low as possible because a 3c difference can be make it or break it. I had a Core i7-2600k that could do 4.8ghz and it stayed at 72c on Prime95 with an old Corsair H70. This stuff knocked the temps down to 70c.

I replaced this stuff with that expensive Thermal Grizzly Kryonaut paste and they seem to perform the same. I saw not difference in temps whatsoever. Core i7-3930k at stock speeds, 57c at the highest core, Prime95. After figuring out how to apply the Kryonaut, I managed to get the temps down 3c from the IC Diamond 7. The key is to warm up the Kryonaut and spread it thin.

The I tried Cool Laboratory Liquid Ultra and got my temps down even further over the Kryonaut. But considering the pains of the metal stuff I'd suggest sticking to the Kryonaut or GC Extreme.

title: 28 PCI-E lanes
text:
If you want to see why fanboyism is a mental disorder then read the comments to my review. Some people really should just stick to consoles and smartphones. The chipset Nhazi fails to realize the PCI-E lanes from the x99 chipset mirror what the h110 chipset has, which is very slow and weak PCI-E 2.0 lanes, and you only get x8 lanes. With this 6800k you're getting 24 lanes which would be enough for two GPU's at x8 and a couple PCI-E x4 devices. Using the chipset lanes also adds a little bit of latency so your speeds will be within 95% of what the CPU based lanes can get you.

The 6800k isn't a bad deal if you're only going to connect 1 card, 1 NVMe drive, and 1 add on card.

I managed to overclock this thing to 4.3ghz but I decided to roll it back to 4ghz. Since I have a 1440p 144hz monitor paired with a GTX 1080, in many games I was getting between 90fps to 120fps, with the fps averaging around 100fps but with constant drops to 90fps. With the 8700k that I clocked up to 4.7ghz my framerate spread went to 100-125fps with the average fps sitting at around 115fps. However there were far less FPS drops. At least this CPU runs stable with my 3200mhz CL 14 memory. This system also get used for creating videos.

If you really go and read benchmarks,you will be hard pressed to find situations where the 6800k was a better alternative to the 6700k or even the 7700k. Since the processors on the x99 platform really didn't clock up too high, it's only really worth looking at this platform if you needed at least 8 cores or you need a CPU that has 40 PCI-E lanes. This platform is now worthless, and you can find these x99 motherboards and processors for a relatively low price on the used market.

Once I upgraded my 6800k system to the 8700k, I gave the 6800k to my brother who was still rocking a 2500k along with a GTX 1070 he had just bought to replace his GTX 660ti. The 6800k is a good setup for him since all he does is plays games on a 1080p 60hz monitor.

title: Please STOP buying this stuff!
text:
Check the date of these reviews. Anyone who recommends this stuff is out of touch and probably still recommends a 32-bit OS, or they have no idea how to apply thermal compound.

The rants are raves people gave this stuff were from the Core 2 and Athlon 64 days. Processors have advanced and so has thermal paste.

What are the drawbacks of AS5?

-conductive.
If you get any on you motherboard then it's game over. I'm sure that ruined the day for someone who paid a mint for their q6600 and x38 board in 2007.

-200 hour break in cycle
Again an issue back in the Conroe era.

-poor performance compared to newer pastes. Gelid Extreme or Thermal Grizzly Kryonaut will outperform this paste. Even a cheaper paste like MX4 is better than AS5.

This was the first paste I ever purchased. But then I tried Shin Etsu and got better temps. Then tried IC Diamond 7 (dont buy) and my temps got even better. Tried Kryonaut and my temps dropped some more.

The coolers I run are either large AIO cooler like the H100i or open loop cooling with EK Evo waterblocks. I have tried a dozen different compounds from this stuff to the Liquid Ultra metal compounds, MX2, MX4, ICD7, GC Extreme, Shin Etsu x23-7783d, Kryonaut, Noctua NT-H1, etc. I have remounted coolers to the point it's subconscious. I overclock and use Prime95. I know pastes and this stuff is just average and it falls below the pastes I listed.

Do a websearch for Thermal Paste benchmarks. AS5 falls in the middle. It's neither good or bad. However the recommendations are far off.

If I was going to recommend a paste to a newbie I would recommend Gelid GC Extreme. Even after the break-in, the GC-E is going to shave off 5c under stress using Prime95. Kryonaut is the best but it's tricky to apply.

The Corsair AIO coolers have a paste that's better than AS5. However the application of the pre applied Shin Etsu is thicker than what it should be.

If the paste is thinner like MX4 then the dot method will work the best. If you're working with a thicker paste then spreading it to cover the IHS with a thin coat works the best. However leave room around the edge of the IHS.

If the paste responds well to being warmed up then the dot method will work just as long as the paste is hot when you seat the Cooler over the CPU.

The trick is to just use enough paste to provide coverage between the cooler and the CPU. If you don't use enough you want get coverage. This is why the dot method generally works the best.

title: Great but tricky.
text:
Five stars for performance. I would deduct stars because of the price but I bought this through the Amazon Free same day shipping option.

If you like it then buy it in bulk.

I had used IC Diamond 7 which gave me great temps over other pastes like Dinosaur Silver 5, wait I mean Arctic Silver.

The first application yielded the same temperature, I tried the B.B. sized dot in the middle. The deal with Kryonaut is... it's thick and doesn't spread easily. Then I tried a super thin layer over the IHS of my CPU and it dropped my temps by 3c.

Then next time I apply this stuff I'll warm it up with a Hot Hands body warmer. It's very pasty and hard to spread. You know the drill, if you get just enough to make contact, without air pockets then you're golden.

Keep in mind that was my best application method for IC Diamond 7. Which the ICD7 put a couple pit marks on the IHS of my CPU.

I also put this on an old GTX 670 and it not only dropped the temps by a solid 6c but it would cool the card quicker than the other card. Had 2 EVGA FTW cards in SLI.

Nevertheless, the extra hoop of the application is worth it if you want the best temps.

text:
I bought the EVGA P2 1200w. I wish amazon would limit the reviews to the specific product because a defect can be limited to one specific product but not another one.

EDIT 10/20/2018
This power supply has been running for 25 months with no problems whatsoever. The system has been upgraded throughout the year and now it has 2x EVGA GTX 1080ti cards in SLI along with upgrading to a Core i7-7820x with the Rampage VI Apex. The system also has a custom loop that's cooling the CPU.

One of the biggest selling points I can think of is this P2 power supply appears on the Tom's Hardware Teir 1 list, but the G2 series is also on the teir 1 list. After doing a bit more research I found the P2 models have better caps than the G2 versions. One selling point I found impressive is this P2 power supply holds up very well at 50c. You're also getting nearly 1200w on the +12v rail alone, not counting the +5v and the +3.3v rails. There is no guesswork when it comes to this power supply.

Just make sure you register this within 30 days. Once you do then you'll get EVGA's legendary warranty service and the 10 year warranty on this power supply. Although, I've had to RMA power supplies back to both Corsair and Seasonic and those warranty processes were very easy with no hassle. Also with those 2 brands I wasn't required to register the product.

Once you register the product with EVGA, you can upload the invoice just in case. If you do require an RMA then you will already have this step taken care of. You can also pay for an advanced RMA at any time. I did this with a GTX 590 I bought when EVGA had lifetime warranties on their products. 5 years later the card went out and half the RMA process was already taken care of.

It's certainly one of the nicest looking power supplies I've ever bought. The powder coating is tough so I don't have to worry about it flaking off or getting scratched.

The setup I'm running has a Core i7-4930k overclocked with a custom loop on a Rampage Extreme IV motherboard. I had a GTX 670 SLI setup going before getting a good price on a couple 8gb RX 480 cards. I bought a 3rd 8gb RX 480 card for my brothers PC, but I couldn't resist the urge to run the 480's in 3-way crossfire just to see what would happen. The results weren't impressive but at least the power supply held up fine.

The reason I've always bought such large power supplies is I used to know people who built test systems for a well known gaming company. They would turn around and sell the graphics cards at cost or sometimes below cost. They got out of the business and my gravy train ended but it was fun to pay next to nothing for these high end cards, benchmark them, test them in games, then turn around and sell them while taking no loss at all.

text:
*Changed to one star because the temps on my 12900k and couple graphics cards went down the toilet not long after I applied this stuff. I have the contract frame on my 12900k, so it isn't that. After doing some research I found that Kryonaut pumps out once temps exceed +80c.

The temps on the 3930k never exceeded 75c, and my overclocked Xeon E5-1680 v2 temps never exceeded 68c. Kryonaut is fine for old parts like this that were never blistering hot to begin with.

Roman or whoever designs this paste needs to go back to the drawing board and come out with a new paste that doesn't pump out. At least Arctic takes responsibility and pulls their dysfunctional paste off the shelf, then comes out with a new version.

This is the best paste out there, bar none. When it's applied correctly it beats out ICD7 by 3c at load. In the past I've tried nearly every paste out there and I only recommend this or GC-Extreme. This still beats out GC-E by a degree or 2 but I don't recommend it for the casual builder or newbie who's using this on a non-overclocking CPU.

This is the larger tube though. This is a good choice if you have a lot of work to do.

If you're going to delid, do yourself a favor and use Thermal Grizzly Conductonaut. While the Kryonaut beats the pants off the Intel stock paste. The Conductonaut will get you results that rival the Indium solder. Conductonaut is also easier to work than that messy Liquid Ultra.

title: Best Gaming CPU out there
text:
Preordered mine elsewhere after being wishy-washy because my overclocked 4930x at 4.5ghz still does a good job. I'm not disappointed. I overclock and it was too hard to pass on a Hexacore CPU that can hit 5ghz. This is probably the most attractive overclocking CPU Ive seen since the 2600k and 3930k.

Initially I left the MCE on and the FPS in CS:GO went from 250fps to 350 at 2160p.

Tested with MCE enabled using a custom W/C loop and the CPU hit 71c package temps, Prime95 Blend. The need to delid this thing and using Conductonaut is undeniable.

I dont endorse or recommend using MCE without adjusting the voltages. Initially with the MCE on the 8700k was using 1.345v while running a stress test. I manually clocked the cores to 47x ×100.00 and threw in a .10 voltage offset, no LCC. That helped drop my temp 10c. I'll tweak my settings more to see if I got a good chip or not. At least my CPU power consumption remained below 100w while testing and it held steady at 4.7ghz.

I'm using the Asus Maximus 10 Apex board.

********Overclocking results 11/26/2017**********
Not De-Lidded

5.0ghz
XMP enabled Corsair Dominator 3200mhz CL 16 2x8gb
Manual VCore in BIOS 1.3v, 1.34v according to CPU-Z
LLC Level 6
VCCIO 1.1v
VCCSA 1.15v
No AVX offset

Top temp while stress testing 94c using a custom loop with a EK Supremacy EVO copper block, Kryonaut paste, 360mm HW Labs Black Ice GTX radiator(Purchased in 2012), 3x Noctua NF-F12 fans. I'm pretty sure I could reach 5.1ghz stable if it's delidded. I find it very sad that a delidded 8700k with a top of the line AIO cooler can beat my non-delidded CPU with a custom loop. That goes to show the insulation effect this 3M TIM has.

EDIT 2/25/2018

Originally I used this to upgrade the overclocked 4930k system which was running a GTX 1080ti on a 60hz 4k monitor. There is no noticeable difference in this situation because the monitor is capped at 60fps and at 4k the workload is shifted to my GTX 1080ti.

I moved the core components to my daughter's system that has a 1440p 144hz monitor and had a Core i7-6800k with a Strix GTX 1080. She plays games like Black Desert online. The Core i7-6800k was overclocked to 4.0ghz

Her framerates would bounce between 90fps-120fps, the fluctuations were quite massive but for the most part they would stay at 100fps.

With the Core i7-8700k manually clocked to 4.7ghz her framerates stayed between 100fps-120fps. The fps stayed around 110fps and they were far more stable at 110fps. There were less drops to 100fps with the 8700k, than the 90fps drops with the 6800k.

I highly recommend this CPU if you're gaming on a 144hz display, you plan to buy one in the future, or you are benchmarking. If youre gaming on a monitor that's capped at 60fps then you wouldn't see much of a difference if you had a Core i7-4790k or even a 4770k for that matter. The only thing the 8700k would do is mitigate the FPS drops a little bit. In which case a Ryzen 5 1600x does an incredible job of mitigating those FPS drops. Upgrading to this CPU depends entirely on your situation and goals.

Also, I highly recommend this over the Core i7-7700k and the rest of the z270 1151 v1 platform. The 8700k and the z370 lineup is futureproof. Some people hate the idea of futureproofing but I have always built my systems with that in mind and it's never failed me. Right now the 8700k is $50 than a 7700k and that seems like a good buy to me considering that an 8700k is going to outlast a 7700k by a couple years.

title: The CLC 280 is beating my 360mm AIO cooler to a pulp, Still the best PERFORMER on the Market.
text:
****Revised 01/12/19****

The CLC 280 is beating my H150i Pro by 8c on a Core i7-2600k that I have a stable overclock of 5.0ghz at 1.48v while running Prime95 Blend. With my 9900k the CLC 280 hits 91c @ 4.8ghz, 1.312v, Prime95 Small FFT, while the 9900k throttles with the H150i. It's pretty sad that a smaller cooler is beating a bigger one that's made by the No.1 company in AIO cooling.

The only 2 drawbacks with the CLC 280 is the software is buggy and the fans are loud at 100%. I don't mind the loud fans because I favor performance but people who favor quiet over performance will. IMHO, someone who is seeking silence should look at a larger heatsink or a 240mm AIO cooler, and they should probably run their gear at or near stock settings.

If you're looking for the best AIO cooler on the market in terms of performance, then get the CLC 280. Just look at the independent benchmarks......... it beats everything.

*****Original Review********

Too many Pros to list. The fans that are used on the clc280 have decent Static pressure and this propels the clc280 over the older h115i and the x62 but these are very slight gains that aren't worth considering when push comes to shove.

-One of the best AIO coolers you can get. If you don't give 2 cents about abundant RGB lighting then get this.... I did. This one only has the bare minimum. Go check reviews of 280mm AIO coolers and you will see the EVGA clc280 tops all the charts, but like I said it's by a degree or 2 over the other 280mm radiators.

- I also have the older H115i that came with the SP series fans and the EVGA clc280 is much quieter when the fans are cranked to 100%.

-These 360mm AIO coolers really don't have much more cooling power than a good 280mm AIO cooler. What you have to look at is square mm or inches here. The 360mm x 120mm radiators only give you 10% more square area, but they only cool a degree or 2 better on an overclocked processor.

-The reason I go with an AIO cooler over a large heatsink is because it's easier to manage. Large heatsinks obstruct parts like the RAM, fan headers and sometimes they are too close to the 8-Pin CPU connector. These chunky heatsinks have become so bad that you need to go to their site to look up a compatibility list to see if they will work with your motherboard. The only pluses I can give a large heatsink is they cool better than a 120mm x 120mm AIO cooler, they won't leak, and the don't have a pump.

-EVGA! What a wonderful company to do business with. Best customer support in the hardware industry. My registered products list is a mile long because I know I'm getting a Top notch product with EVGA. When my GTX 590 died, the RMA was approved within 2 emails....... and I got a much better card in the end. One time I couldn't get a 790i motherboard to boot correctly which happened on a Sunday. Their support rep walked me through the steps and I got that board running in No Time. EVGA is a pleasure to do business with. I had no problems dropping $750 on a GTX 1080ti with these guys.

3 weeks ago I had a 10 email exchange with Corsair over a k95 keyboard.

-When I unboxed this cooler, it came with the 140mm fans installed and what was in the box seemed a little bit better organized than Corsair's offerings. I added this after I unboxed an H150i pro and all of this dawned on me after I spent 10+ minutes on organizing everything and installing the 3x 120mm fans on the H150i.

Cons:
These big AIO coolers do have more cooling power than a large heatsink like the D15 but it's not that much more when you think about it. You are going to get more bang for your buck with a Scythe Mugen 5 or the Fuma. If you have plans to do any real overclocking then get the EVGA clc280. If you want something that works well then get the Mugen 5.

-The link software/Flow Control doesn't run that great with AMD processors. If you're looking for an AIO cooler to run with a Ryzen CPU then get the Corsair. I loathe having to use the Link cable which I hate for many reasons. The cable is messy and it hinders cable management. Corsair and NZXT uses this able too. I had a problem with the H115i I bought a couple years ago for a Core i7-6800k, and I could not get it resolved until I found an unrelated thread that said to turn off all Windows power saving features to the USB 2.0 ports in Device Manager.

-No matter what you get, it's an Asetek cooler. The only difference between one or the other is the fans that are used, and which generation Asetek pump it has. These are generally all the same so if you're going to buy one then you might as well buy an EVGA since it cools a degree or 2 better than the H115i or the x62 and you get EVGA's unrivaled customer support. The EVGA clc280 used the Asetek Gen 5 pump but the newer H150i Pro and the newer H115i Pro used the 6th Gen Asetek pump.

-You have to run the fans at max, which is quite loud, for it to get the performance that buries larger heat sinks.

-There is always a chance it will leak. Although I have owned many Corsair AIO coolers and not one of them has ever leaked. The older coolers from 2011-2013 had a higher chance of leaking because AIO coolers from 5 years ago aren't as well refined as today's AIO coolers. You have a much higher chance of the pump dying. I've studied anxiety and CBT and even if there is a 1 in 10k chance of something happening, people will still freak out about it. EVGA, Corsair, and NZXT will pay for the parts that are damaged by a leak just as long as you correctly installed the cooler and you didn't modify it.

-The Flow software is buggy. EVGA seems to have software issues with many of their products so no surprise here. If I select to have the Flow software run on startup, it will fail.

title: Beats my 8700k but not by as much as I expected. Needs to be delidded
text:
After seeing a pcpp build list with the 8086k and a Gigabyte Aorus Gaming 5 by a first time builder, and seeing other first time builders eyeball or insist on this CPU, i felt I had to add the following. There is no point in spending the extra $$$£££€€€ unless you intend to overclock the 8086k as high as possible. If you're going to spend extra on this for OCing, then you might as well spend extra on the motherboard by getting something along the lines of an ASRock Taichi or Professional, Maximus X, or the Gigabyte Gaming 7. The effect the extra 300mhz has on gaming is very minimal and you'd barely notice the difference even if you're trying to push a 144hz monitor. You can actually shore the difference up between the 8700k and this 8086k by using 3200mhz CL14 memory. This CPU is for the people who are willing to Mod or spend the extra dough on trying to get their numbers as high as they can get.

You're welcome to buy one of these if you want to because it's your money but be warned.....this CPU will not do too much to help you. Making cuts elsewhere in your build to accommodate the price of this CPU isn't worthwhile.

According to CPU-Z/HWMonitor I was able to get this thing stable at 1.32v at 5ghz with no AVX offset but my 8700k can do 5ghz no AVX offset at 1.35v. I guess I got a pretty solid 8700k, that would be able to do 5.2ghz full-time (AVX offset -2 if I delidded it).

The only real thing I can say is this runs a lot cooler than my 8700k. The 8086k was able to find stability with an EVGA clc280 and the temps stopped at 98c. When I tested my 8700k I hit 96c while using my system that has a custom loop w/ a 60mm thick 360mm radiator and the EK Supremacy EVO waterblock. The only way I would be able to find out how much voltage I need to get 5.3ghz stable with AVX offset -2 is by delidding.

I might have more tweaking to do but it wasn't stable at around 1.31v at 5ghz. Keep in mind this is testing with the newest version of Prime95 that runs the FMA3/AVX2 instruction sets that put the screws to anything Haswell or later. Even while using AVX offsets, I can do hours or Realbench Stress and Benchmark but I can only do a few minutes of Prime95.

For full time use, I was able to strike a middle ground by setting the AVX offset to -2 at 5.1ghz the 8086k at 1.28v and my temps never went above 90c, and when running Prime95 v26.6 the temps never went above 89c at 5.1ghz. I kept my 8700k at 4.9ghz (AVX offset -2) and the temps were still hot so I'm happy this does as well as it does.

The results I got fell a little bit short of what I was hoping for because I was hoping to do 5ghz with less than 1.3v while running the FPU/AVX stress tests with no AVX offsets. I'm using the Maximus X Apex board but I might retry both processors with a Gigabyte Gaming 7 board and after I delid at least the 8700k. The 8086k at least did a lot better than my 8700k at 4.8ghz-4.9ghz. One thing is for sure, you're going to have to delid and use Conductonaut if you want to find the voltage headwall but I knew that before I bought it.

Yes, I would buy this again, and again, and again. I've been toying with a Core i5-8600k recently and it doesn't even come close to overclocking as well as this CPU.

The most my 8600k can do 5ghz with AVX offset at -2 with 1.376V.

title: Know your power!
text:
I actually bought this 550w power supply to reduce the weight of a rig that had an older Antec 900w power supply. This is a rig that I gave to my dad which has a Xeon x5690,an EVGA x58 FTW3 motherboard, 12gb of RAM with an EVGA GTX 660ti. I found a smaller Antec case and I used the 212 as the CPU cooler which works decently for an older 32nm CPU. I really wanted to get a 1050ti for this rig but I'm not going to pay +$50 over MSRP for an entry level card.

It was worth it to pay a little bit more for the G3 version because it should be more reliable than a Bronze unit and more efficient. This isn't a run of the mill unit that's questionable and the power output is going to be as advertised. If you're on the fence and you have a little bit of extra money to pare then you can't go wrong with the G3 line.

550w is enough to power a basic gaming rig. 450w is fine for a basic rig with a GTX 1050ti but I avoid recommending a 450w power supply just in case the user upgrades the GPU to a higher tier card that needs at least a 550w power supply.

Parts like the RAM, SSD, HDD, and a few fans won't burn up a lot of power. The Graphics card is the main culprit when it comes to burning up a lot of power, unless you go with a low power card like a GTX 1050ti which doesn't use a lot of juice. This 550w unit is good enough for a card like the GTX 1070 or 1080. If you're going to step up to the GTX 1080ti, if you an R9 390x/290x, or if you're going to go with a Vega 64 or 56 then you will need a 650w power supply at the least.

HEDT platforms like Intel x299 and AMD x399 need a power supply that's in the 750w-850w and above range. It's not that these platforms chew though a lot of power so much as it's the motherboards need dual CPU connectors that are only on bigger power supplies.

Yes, I have the Crosshair VII Hero Wifi board but I got mine somewhere else. Yes, this board does not work correctly and it's not usable. I build systems for people so this is no sweat off my back but I can't imagine being some college kid or someone on a tight budget who had to scrimp an save for an Asus board, then Asus lets them down by playing the RMA game with them.

The lesson here is to test the motherboard and the system as much as you possibly can as soon as it arrives. The person I bought this board for decided to go with Intel and I just let this board sit for about a month. When I got to it a month later everything worked fine at first. I was able to load the drivers. The 2nd time around I went to tinker with the system but all hell broke loose. The reason I know it's the system and not the software is when I removed the SSD, or tried a different SSD, the system was still slow, would freeze up, or take 20 minutes to boot.

I've already sent this in for an RMA and they said they couldn't find a problem with my board. At this point I'd rather have a refund.

The problem here is the board will slow to a crawl until I reset the BIOS. According to POST codes such as b4, the error is likely the chipset. Even if I remove the SSD, or use another SSD, the board will slow down, POST times take 20 minutes, and sometimes the board will freeze in the BIOS. Like I sais Asus can't wrap their head around this problem.
The problem is when you initially RMA a board back to Asus/Pegatron, the have their low level technicians look at the board. They don't want to put any real effort into fixing your board until the 2nd or 3rd time it's been sent into them.

Within the last 2 years I've bought an Asus z170, two z370, and an x299 board from Asus. The z170 board doesn't work right but Asus can't find a problem with it. The x299 board is the Rampage VI Apex. The first one I bought didn't work so I exchanged it and the 2nd one works well. The two z370 boards are the Maximus X Apex and the Z370-A which both work very well. So in that span of time I've acquired 6 different Asus boards and only 3 of them have worked correctly. title: Well I like it
text:
8 cores, Hyperthreading with reasonable temps at stock speeds. When I first tested mine I had Asus Multi-core Enhancement enabled and it clocked all cores to 4.7ghz at 1.375v with temps reaching as high as 82c for a brief moment. The reason I bought this is because of the higher Turbo speeds, and I don’t like keeping processors overclocked for long periods of time.

I had a 4930k that was running at 4.5ghz for a couple of years at 1.4v, and my old 2600k was clocked to 4.8ghz at 1.35v for 1 full year then 4.4ghz 1.23v for 3 more years and those processors still pass stress tests with no signs of degradation. Overclocking is great but the 9900k fills my need for high clock speeds and stability.

It couldn’t do 5.1ghz, AVX offset -2, at 1.305v, LLC6. It would fail when the CPU hit around 190w.

5.0ghz on all cores passed at 1.29v, AVX offset -2, LLC6, 4.2ghz cache, XMP enabled. 86c Highest temp.
When I first tested the 9900k I set the core voltage to 1.30v at 5.0ghz but it passed everything, so I tried for 5.1ghz.

It doesn’t overclock nearly as well as my 8700k which can do 5.2ghz and or my 8086k which can do 5.3ghz, both with AVX offset -2. It sounds like 5.0ghz is a average number for the chip.

I stress test with Prime95 v26.6 and 29.4, LinpackXtreme, and Aida64. Realbench seems to pass with bad settings so I don’t use that anymore.

Asus Maximus X Apex
32gb G.Skill 2x16gb DDR4-3200 cl16
Strix A8G GTX 1080 (Upgraded to an EVGA GTX 1080ti)
Seasonic X-1250
EVGA 280clc
Dell 1440p 144hz S2716DGR

I know people are concerned with value and that’s great. Vote with your wallet. The thing is Not everyone is building a PC for the cost valuebecause Everyone has a different reason to build a PC. The value may not be that good but it’s not super terrible either. The 9900k is a Jack of All Trades but a Master of None.

Now if Zen2 wipes the floor with the 9900k then I’ll regret buying it.

After reading a few reviews, I'd like to point the out reasoning behind the AVX offsets and how it can help you. The AVX2 (AVX-512 2066 processors) instruction set/s consume an incredible about of power and generate an incredible amount of heat. But I'll cut straight to the point, Whatever your CPU can do (while remaining stable) at 5.0ghz while running these hardcore AVX instruction sets, with non-AVX instructions the CPU will be able to run at 5.2ghz. So far I've overclocked a 6800k with a board that has an AVX offset feature, a 7700k, 8600k, 8700k, 8086k, 7820x w/EVGA Dark, and finally the 9900k in the picture. If the CPU can pass non-AVX stress tests such as Prime95 26.6 at a speed like 5.1ghz, the CPU will pass Prime95 29.8 or LinpackXtreme at a speed like 4.9ghz. So as you can hopefully see, the AVX offset feature can be leveraged to your advantage.

title: Not worth more than $180
text:
This is the 4th z370 motherboard I've purchased so I'm able to compare the z370 Classified K board with the Asus Maximus X Apex, Asus Prime Z370-A, and the Gigabyte Aorus z370 Gaming 7.

So far the board has been functional and stable. The 8086k I'm using with it is working, the 32gb 4x8gb DDR4-3200 cl16 Dominator memory is working with the XMP profile enabled, all stress tests pass. I could try my G.Skill RAM with the Samsung B-Dies but I don't see much point. When I stress test the CPU I noticed the CPU temps were 5c higher with XMP enabled. Otherwise the temps are good, at stock speeds the CPU isn't being overvolted, you know.... like what I'd see on an Asus board with MCE Disabled.

Obviously this EVGA board isn't going to be in the same league as the Apex but it's not really even comparable to the Gigabyte z370 Gaming 7 board either. Since the normal pricetag of this board is the same as the Gigabyte Aorus z370 Gaming 7, you think it would be. The biggest bonus you're getting with this board is EVGA's customer service which you hopefully will never need to use. For the normal price, I think EVGA could offer a lot more.

The Classified K is on par, or slightly above the Prime Z370-A/Strix at best but the EVGA board comes with a couple bonus features like dual LAN and the handy LED debug reader. You also get a dual BIOS. The VRM's on the EVGA board are a little bit better than what you'd see in the Strix and the Prime Z370-A, and they are on par with the Fatil1ty K6/Extreme4, but they are not even close to being in the same league as the Gigabyte Gaming 7 board. The look and feel of the Classified K is similar to what you'd see and feel on the Prime Z370-A. The VRM cooling blocks aren't a whole lot better. The BIOS/UEFI has less options that what I'd see on my Prime Z370-A motherboard.

Don't get me wrong though, I'd pick this EVGA board over the Strix-E or the Prime Z370-A if I had to but it's really not much better than those boards. At least for the price EVGA is charging it should come with 3x full sized M.2 slots, RGB, Top Tier VRM's and a beefier heatsink.

I was looking at buying an MSI z390 or a Gigabyte z390 motherboard, since the Maximus XI line cheaped out on the VRM's, but the $100 pricetag on Cyber Monday was too good to pass up. I have the 8086k that I'm giving to my brother for Christmas so he can run run his 144hz display EVGA's legendary customer service is the reason I pulled the trigger here. If I would have paid $220 for this then I would have felt cheated. However for $99 this board is a steal.

EVGA needs to go back to making boards like the x79 Dark, x299 Dark, X58 3-Way SLI, or any of those old Sandy Bridge- Nehalem quality boards.

text:
This review is for the 360mm ML360R version.

This cooler lacked the Socket 2066/2011-v3/2011 mounts, but it came with 2 sets/2 pairs of AMD hardware.

I ended up having to return this AIO cooler because my h150i beats it by 5c, on top of lacking the Intel HEDT hardware. I bought this based off the Tomshardware review but I'm not sure why their review is different from my own tests. It seems like the review that's on Techpowerup might be more accurate.

Core i7-2600k @ 5.0ghz (4997mhz), 1.485v, Z77 Sabertooth, Corsair Vengeance 8gb (2x4gb) DDR3-1600 cl9 at 1333mhz 9-9-9-24.

The temps go into the 90's when I run Small FFT after 10 minutes. With the clc280 the temps don't exceed 79c. With Prime95 Blend, the estimated CPU wattage is 125w, and it's 135w running Small FFT's.

I reseated the block while reapplying the paste. I made sure the fan and pump speeds were at 100%. Mounting pressure was as tight as I could get it, and the TIM spread evenly both times. I used Kryonaut as the paste on all these coolers.

Aside from that, there were a few slightly indented spots on the radiator fins, and the fins aren't as even as they are on my H150i. It comes with a gob of cables. However, I was able to find the right combination to make the RGB and lighting work with an older z77 motherboard. This might be more simple on a modern board with RGB Headers.

If you're looking for overall performance, nothing seems to be able to beat the clc280. These 360mm AIO coolers seem to have too many issues and maybe the Gen 5 or 6 Asetek pump can't handle a 360mm radiator at 2300rpm.

This card is better suited for professional use and Crypto mining. I've tested this with mining and it does really well, depending on the currency you're mining. I haven't toyed with it much but with a few tweaks with ETHash's Claymore miner this card gets 90mh/s at 227w while staying at 85c.

However, your experience will vary depending on if you win the Silicon lottery.

The first Radeon VII I ordered was horrible! Hot Spot temps would quickly reach 113c unless I pushed the voltage down to the bare minimum while running the fan at 80%. The Hot Spot temps were still too high after all this work. Overclocking the first card I got was Abysmal, as it couldn't even hold 1900mhz with the stock 1104mv while running Super Position. With mining I couldn't get the card to consistently mine Eth at 90mh/s. This card needed around 1000mv (1.0v) to stay stable at stock speeds.

The 2nd card fares a lot better. With Eth I can mine at 90mh/s stable with the fans at 65%, the core voltage at 975mv, Hot Spot temps at 85c, while pulling 227w on the card. At stock voltage of around 1104mv I can pass Super Position at 2000mhz while the Hot Spot Temps are 98c, but it does scale back to 1987mhz to 1997mhz. At stock speeds I can crank the voltage down to right around 970mv.

For me, my eyes popped when I saw Lisa Su introduce it because of how much and how fast the HMB2 memory is. All I could see is how fast this would make scene rendering. Then I thought of how these Cryptocurrency miners would have fought over this card if it was available during the mining craze. I didn't think about gaming with it at all.

This card would end up being a crash course in overclocking for a newbie. If the user/buyer got a card that is a Silicon Lottery winner then the user wouldn't have much tweaking to to. If the user/buyer got a card that was like my 1st card then they would be frustrated with the thermal throttling, FPS drops, and possibly not knowing what to do. I recommend MSI Afterburner but I've been using Afterburner for years.

title: More Asus Q.C. Problems
text:
***Note*** you can run a Ryzen 3000 series CPU if you can figure out how to work the BIOS Flashback feature.

***Final Update ***
I returned the CH6H because it was having issues with recognizing the Video Card while booting up. I tried an RX 570, 4gb RX 580, and a GTX 1070 and all these cards had random boot issues of some kind or another. 4 times out of 5 the system would boot but the boot cycle was delayed. The problems were massive screen discoloration (not the infamous AMD Green screen but something worse) or the One Long, Three Short Beep error.

Despite the first thing on google saying One Long Three short is a RAM error, it isn’t with Asus boards with the American Megatrends BIOS. I have another old Asus P67 board that has a fried PCIE x16 slot and it gives me the One Long Three Short beep error if I place a card in that slot.

In the last 2.5 years I’ve bought 6 Asus Motherboards and only 2 of those boards were functional without any issues. Way to keep up on the quality Control Asus. All The other brands all have their quirks and issues so you’re jumping from one problem to another by choosing another brand.

I'm running this with the 3rd Gen Ryzen 7 3800x but I had to do the BIOS Flashback on the board. Damn, I just finished installing Windows 10 1909 on the new machine. I'll add more later as I test this board out.

The board I got came with BIOS version 6101 (Printed on the board). This will work with a 2nd Generation chip out of the Box but not a 3rd Gen chip. I flashed the board to version 7601.

There are plenty of guides on how to do a BIOS Flashback, but here are some tips.

-Download the BRenamer program. This will rename the BIOS file to C6H.CAP

-With the USB Drive, make sure there are no additional partitions on the ThumbDrive. The only partition will need to be smaller than 32gb , because you will have to format the drive to a "Fat32" format. The CAP file will be a little bit over 16mb so you don't need a large Thumbdrive.

-Make sure the C6H.CAP file is in the root directory of the Thumb Drive.

-If the flash is successful, the Flashback Button will flash for a few minutes then the light will turn off. If the flash fails, the light will flash a few times then remain on. My first few attempts didn’t work because the thumbdrive had a recovery partition that I wasn’t able to remove in Windows.

Update 12-11-2019
So far the C6H is working fine with the Ryzen 7 3800x. VRM temps hit the low 40’s while running Prime95 but they stay in the 30’s for everything else. I was able to clock my G.Skill memory up to 3600mhz 16-15-15-35. Best Cinebench r15 score I have got so far is 2203. System hasn’t crashed yet. No problem.

Clock speeds boost up to 4.54ghz single core with the right cooler. At first I tried older H100i v2 but that cooler didn’t do so well with the 3800x. The Floe Riing 360 did well. Then I tried a D15 with a 2500rpm 140mm fan and that also did well. I got slightly better all core boost clock speeds with the D15 as opposed to the Floe Riing.

The only other suggestion I can make is to test whatever motherboard you buy as soon as it arrives. Last year I bought a C7H Wifi board with a 2700x but I didn’t get around to testing the system for a month. The board was bad and I messed with Asus for 7 weeks before they replaced the motherboard.

text:
I might not be a verified buyer but I’ve owned this board since June of 2018.

The VRM’s are of high quality and they would normally have no trouble with the likes of the mighty 9900k except that Gigabyte borked the Thermal pads between the VRM heatsink and VRM’s. With my 8700k at a nominal 4.7ghz at 1.23v the VRM heat up to 100c in 5 minutes while running Prime95. The VRM’s will throttle at 125c.

Thankfully I’ve been running my 8700k at stock speeds this whole time so I have no worries.

The fix is to either buy a more efficient 1.5mm thermal pad or ditch the washers behind the VRM block holddown screws to get a tighter fit. If losing the washers doesn’t work then replacing the Thermal Pads will.

Other than that, the board has been a dream and my system has been super stable for the most part. The system boots in seconds, and the BIOS has a good amount of overclocking options. If you’re coming from Asus boards then the BIOS on the Gaming 7 will take a bit of time to figure out. The board feels like it’s made with quality so I have little doubt that it will last for years.

The only other problem Ive had is with the Killer LAN drivers causing BSOD’s but that’s easily fixed by using the Intel LAN instead.

This motherboard has some sort of issue with Nvidia's 10-Series Pascal cards. The problem is monitor detection is slow, and sometimes the screen will never kick on. The system will boot, I'll get the normal beep, then a One long, three short beep, and then after a minute the monitor will usually kick on... depending on which monitor I use.
There is no way to get into the BIOS with these Pascal cards. So far I've tried a 1080ti Founders edition, 1080ti SC2, a 1070ti, and finally a GTX 1070. This motherboard sometimes has detection issues with a Radeon VII as well (Yep, I still have one that works).

Works fine with a 3070, 3080, 3080ti, RX 6800xt, RX 5700xt. The board also works fine with old cards like the GT 240, HD 5870, and GTX 670.... but old cards like this will re-enable CSM.

The sound quality and volume is terrible. I had to swap boards with someone for a Taichi Razer Edition and despite the x570 TRE board having problems with the sound cutting out, the sound quality and volume is 2x better than the Crosshair VIII Hero.

When I did the swap, I replaced my 5950x with a 5900x. Despite resetting the BIOS and pulling the battery, the board did not want to boot with the 5900x. Once I reswapped the CPU, then swapped again, the 5900x worked with the CH8H board. Kinda surprising considering I had the 5900x in with the CH8H at one time.

Originally I bought a 3800x to run with this board but I upgraded to the 3900x, then the 5900x, and finally a 5950x after 8 months of trying to find one at MSRP.

Otherwise overclocking with this board is good. After tuning some dual-ranked, B-Die, DDR4-4000 memory to 3800MT/s with a 1900mhz FCLK, I'm scoring over 5000 in Cinebench r15 and over 13k in the CPU-Z benchmark. My 12900k scores around 11.5k in the CPU-Z benchmark. I haven't tried overclocking the CPU core yet.

Come to think of it, I've built four AMD Ryzen systems so far and I've had problems with three of them. My last Ryzen build was around a B550 Tomahawk board and a 5700x....Zero problems with that build. My first one was around a 2700x and a Crosshair 7 Hero Wifi board which had a faulty chipset. Fought Asus tooth and nail for 3 months to get them to replace the board. Then there was this system which works alright with anything but 10-series cards. Then around a 5600x and the Razer Taichi board which has problems with the sound and Ethernet. These motherboard manufacturers really need to get their act together with AMD boards.

title: The Legendary cooler
text:
This is a good cooler for quad-core and some hexacore processors but I wouldn't dare pair this thing with processors like the 8700k(overclocked), 10600k(stock), and higher. Back in the day the 212 was a great cooler to pair up with legendary processors like the 2600k, 4690k, etc. However, I tried to pair a stock i9-9900k up with a Mugen 5 and while running the CPU at 100% load the temps would climb up in the 90's until the TB function stopped.... the the CPU would run at 3.6ghz and the power consumption for the CPU would fall to around 95w. Funny how that work. The 9900k fared far better with my EVGA 280clc with the fans cranked up and at least it would hold at 4.5ghz to 4.7ghz because the 280clc was able to keep up.

I know there are some people in some forums who claim the 212 is more than enough for the 9900k because the 9900k has a 95w TDP and the 212 more than exceeds 95w of cooling power, but the 9900k is very much guilty of having insane power consumption that more than exceeds what the 212 is capable of.

Now the Mugen 5 and 280clc are superior to the 212, so the 212 is NOT going to fare well with a power eating processor like the 9900k.

Right now I have the 212 paired up with the practically unknown Core i7-5775c in another rig and it holds up just fine. I can effortlessly overclock the 5775c to 4.0ghz without having to give any voltage bumps and the 212 is holding up just fine and dandy.

At one time the 212 was a great cooler for the money and it was impossible to beat for the price. I remember recommending it to people back when the Core i5-2500k was the King CPU for a gaming PC. However once these processors started to consume more than 150w while overclocked, the 212 lost it's luster. Now some these processors are pushing 250w when all cores are pushed at stock speeds. The 212 will go down in history as being the go to cooler for the quad-core era. If I was to build a 2010's decade time capsule PC I would combine a z77 or z68 Sabertooth, a 2600k, possibly a GTX 970 or maybe a 670, and a Cooler Master 212.

title: Tune the RAM, it will help a lot.
text:
With the old G.Skill DDR4-4000 cl18 Memory (Single Rank, 2x8gb) I have, I was able to clock the RAM to 4000mhz, manually adjust the timings, and set the F-Clock to 2000mhz. In Cinebench r15 I'm able to get a score of close to 4700. Here soon I'm going to try with a different kit of dual rank 4000mhz memory with better timings.

The I upgraded to a set of G.Skill Royal 2x16gb DDR4-4000, Dual Rank, CL16 RAM. I was able to run the RAM a little bit past 3800mhz, but it posted the best benchmark scores with the RAM at 3800mhz and the Fabric Clock at 1900mhz. It did take some time to dial in the sub timings. I posted better benchmark scores running Dual Rank RAM at a slower speed in comparison to Single Rank RAM at a higher speed. So far, I can get a scores of 11600 in Cinebench R20 and 4950 in Cinebench R15. The key here is to get good RAM and tweak the subtimings..... which might take a while.

I also have PBO enabled and I downloaded the PBO program. Although I didn't touch the PBO program. Having ti running seems to help benchmark scores. If you're having trouble getting the PBO program to install then Restore the BIOS to Default settings.

When I got my RTX 3080ti I tested it in a system with an overclocked 8700k (actually an 8086k) at 5.3ghz with an AVX offset of -2, and I have a kit of RAM running at 3600mhz, cl16 with XMP enabled. Running the FFXV benchmark, 1080p Standard Quality, it scored 17500. With the 5950x (RAM tuned at 3800mhz, 1900mhz FCLK, subtiming tightened) the score was 22100. That's a pretty big bump. However, at 4k with the settings turned up you may not notice a difference.

The board I'm using is the Crosshair VIII Hero wifi and I'm using the Arctic Liquid Freezer II 420. I was using the 360mm version of the Arctic cooler, but I'm getting slightly higher clock speeds with the 420mm version.

The main Con I have is it took way too long to get this CPU. I've been trying since day 1 and it took several months to get this processor. The other con I have is by the end of 2021 AMD is going to release a version of this CPU that had more cache. Look up AMD V-Cache. I found this out after getting this CPU. Even with all that said, I feel fortunate to have this CPU and I'm very happy with it. I compress a lot of files and this CPU make doing this a breeze.

text:
With my 5950x, I noticed the clock speeds are a little bit higher than what they were with my Liquid Freezer II 360. My benchmark scores have gone up a little bit but nothing major. I went ahead and used the offset mount with my 5950x. The board is the Crosshair VIII Hero Wifi and I had no mounting issues. I liked it a little bit better because I was able to use the Thumbscrews, and not screws like I had to use with my LFII 360.

When I first got this I slapped it on an old p67 board and I overclocked a 2700k to 5.0ghz. Most of these large coolers on the market can't hold up to my 2700k running at 5.0ghz while running a stress test. The only problem I had is I had to mount the block sideways on my p67 board.... which is the P8P67 WS Revolution. The temps got a little bit high but they held up.... but the temps still weren't as good as my custom loop.

The mounting system is okay but it's a little bit more difficult to use in comparison to the Corsair and EVGA AIO coolers that I have. The thumbscrews are a little bit too small and the threads are a little bit too tight. I pretty much have to use my screwdriver on everything. I also don't like the little stickers that are used between the standoffs and the motherboard, and I would rather see plastic washers used here instead. The stickers really don't work for me because I swap coolers like underwear.

The fans can be a bit noisy when the temps ramp up.... but I don't mind the noise and I have the CPU fan settings turned up all the way.

The biggest plus I can think of is this cooler only has 1 cable that connects to the motherboard. I really, really loathe the fistful of cables that come with these Corsair and other Asetek coolers. I can and I would rather control the fan settings through my motherboard anyway. That way I don't have to mess with unreliable bloatware that doesn't work 100% of the time. The only complaint I have about the cable is where it comes off of the block.

I have this mounted in a Corsair Obsidian 900D.

title: It's a 9900k, what more do you want?
text:
I would 100% recommend this to anyone that already has a lga1151 300-series board or an older board with a modded BIOS. If you're building a new system then I'd recommend going with the 10700k because it has a better clock profile, it's usually cheaper, and it has a slightly better upgrade path.

The one I got seems to be able to hit 5.1ghz with a -2 AVX, 49x (4.9ghz) cache, 1.35v offset and it has no problems running a 32gb kit of Samsung-B die memory at 3600mhz cl16-16-16-36. I made some tweaks to the System Agent voltage to get the RAM to run. Although I haven't tested it enough to see if it's really stable. This is the 3rd 9900k I bought. The 2nd one went into my brother's system and the 1st one went into my daughter's system. I bought the 1st one right after the 9900k came out and it clocks to 5.0ghz at 1.31v. The first one seemed like it could hit 5.1ghz but it was getting too hot when I tested it. This newer 9900k is certainly better than the 1st SRELS model I got.

I am able to run games with the new 9900k at 5.2ghz, -2 AVX but more stressful tasks seem to make it Bluescreen and it needs more than 1.4v to work. Also, since it gets too hot, I really don't see the benefit in the benchmarks. From what I've seen in the benchmarks scores... It seems better to clock the 9900k up to the point that the temps are manageable while running the cache and RAM as high as possible.

After some tweaking and tuning it can get close to a tweaked and tuned 5950x. If a person is just gaming then I don't really see the point of trading in an lga1151 300-series system for Ryzen. The framerates you can get with Zen 3 might be higher but they don't crush Zen 3. I tested tuned 9900k with an RTX 3080ti and I was able to score as high as 21000 in the FFXV Benchmark at 1920x1080 Standard.... which is almost as good as my 5950x system with the same 3080ti installed.... which scores 22000.

I'm running the 9900k with an Aorus z390 Master board, 4x8gb (32gb) of G.Skill 3600 cl16 RAM, EVGA T2 power supply, Arctic Liquid Freezer II 360, and the RTX 3080ti.
