title: Great, not as good as the 932, but better than Today's ARGB boxes
text:
A little over 10 years ago I built a PC for my Dad using the 922. I went with the i5-2500k, Gigabyte z68 UD5 motherboard, a GTX 560ti, an Antec 850w power supply, two 1tb Samsung Spinpoint 3.5 drives in RAID 0, and a 64gb boot drive.

The only real problem I has was the Antec Truepower 850w power supply didn't have long cables so the cable management wasn't good. This case is spacious so the cables have to stretch quite far. The cutout behind the motherboard tray was made for lga775, so it took some trickery whenever I wanted to swap coolers. The CPU cooler I used was the Corsair Hydro H70 which was the best AIO cooler at that time..... the H100 hadn't been released yet. Eventually I upgraded the cooler the the Scythe Fuma. I added my own door fans to help maximize airflow.

Some later versions of the case had the correct cutout for cooler mounting. The one I had was an earlier version which had a solid door that only had a screen for two 120mm fans, and the interior of the case was painted a light grey.

I'm dinging a star off because the metal that's used in this case is not the same quality or thickness that's used for the 932. Also, It look like Cooler Master could have redesigned the door and used a 200mm fan, like they did with the 932. Through a tiny bit of modding, I might be able to mount a 240mm AIO cooler to the top, but I wouldn't be able to do so using the current mounting holes because there isn't enough clearance between the top of the motherboard and the top of the case.

Mounting a 280mm AIO cooler is probably not possible but a 360mm AIO cooler is out of the question.

The other problem I had was with mounting a larger heatsink like the D15 while having a fan installed on the upper part of the door.

The fans that came with the case lasted about 5-6 years.

text:
The thing I like the most about this cooler is it's build quality. The Gammax feels and looks more solid compared to the legendary 212. The RGB lights are also a nice addition.
I put the Gammax it in a spare parts build with an i5-8600k, an Asus Prime b365-a, 16gb of G.Skill DDR4-3200 Grey, WD SN750 500gb, ancient case, and an Antec EarthWatts 650w PSU. I ended up giving it to some kid for Christmas who has an old AMD FX-8320 build that wasn't quite working right.

The temps were fine for a CPU like m7 8600k. The Gammax would also work fine on something like a stock Core i7-8700k or a Core i5-10400. It's fine for a Ryzen 5 CPU as well. In another PC, I have a Scythe Fuma paired with a 9900k, and the Fuma is just enough to handle the 9900k at stock speeds. So I wouldn't recommend this for an Intel 8-core CPU like the 11700k, 10700k, or 9900k. These CPU's might have a 125w or 95w TDP but if you know the way PL1 and PL2 work, then you wouldn't want to pair these Intel CPU with a cooler that's only suited to handle the CPU in PL1. PL2 consumes far more than 125w.

Long story short, look at the PL2 power consumption figures when looking for a cooler to pair with an Intel CPU.

title: The 1600W Titanium PSU rules
text:
I'll betcha more and more people will look at these things when Ada Lovelace and the 4090 arrives. They were kinda forgotten about for years because people stopped buying a 2nd card for SLI.

I own two of these 1600w T2 units and I have the Super Flower version. These T2 units are made by Super Flower and they have the EVGA label slapped on them. Great power supply units, nonetheless. If you go look up reviews for these PSUs, you'll see they earn really high scores.

Right now I have one of the T2 units in a rig with a 3090 and an overclocked 7960x, and the SF unit and the other T2 units are being used in mining rigs. I've had one of these T2 units in a mining rig for years and I've never had a problem with it. Miners prefer these because they have more PCI-E connectors than what other companies offer with their 1500w and 1600w PSU.

I know some miners and Gamers think they're saving money with these offbrand PSU, but if things go south and something catches on fire, those miners will wish they had bought one of these. Think of a good power supply as insurance.

I wouldn't recommend a 1600w unit to anyone though, because you have to think of the efficiency curve. In my experience of tracking PSU energy usage, about 50% usage is usually the peak of the efficiency curve. Some people think it's okay to push a PSU to 80% because a high-quality PSU will hold up well at 80% and even 90% usage, but at that usage the Caps are being pushed and they're aging faster than they should be. So if your system power draw is at 800w to 1000w while gaming then the 1600w T2 is a decent one to consider. If you're gaming with a 5800x and an RTX 3070 then this thing is too much.

title: Beware…. It’s Big!
text:
This is the longest card I’ve ever seen… it’s a bit less than 14”. Thankfully I’m still using the Corsair Obsidian 900d case. The only problem with the 900d and it’s obsolete design is it’s difficult to screw down these 4.5” wide cards. A magnetic flex bit holder is highly recommend for this task. Due to the design of this card, it was almost impossible to screw the card down, whereas I didn’t have a whole lot of trouble screwing down an EVGA FTW3 card.

The 6800xt was the card I wanted all along, but I ended up getting a 3070 because that’s what I was able to find in early 2021. I wasn’t willing to pay the post tariff prices for the 6800xt. Then I used the Step-up program to get a 3080.

At lower a res like 1080p, the 6800xt crushes it. It does well at 4k which is what I use. R/T still has a long way to go so I don’t use that and the 6800xt is too powerful for needing DLSS or FSR. The 6800xt is a much, much better buy than a comparable priced 3070ti.

The only strange observation I have to report is my Ryzen system boots quicker with this card. I don’t know why… no idea. The POST time is what has been reduced. Now it takes 10 to 12 seconds to get into the O.S.

Since 2019, I’ve had a RX 580, RX 5700xt, Radeon VII, 1070ti, 1080ti, 3070, and a 3080 in my Ryzen system with a Crosshair VIII Hero board. It would take about 30 seconds to get into the O.S. with these cards. The Pascal cards took the longest.

Fan speeds will stay at around 25% to 40% if you don’t set a fan curve. Hot spot temps could be better at stock settings. The card is loud once the fan speeds go above 65%, but it’s not annoying like other cards. GPU wattage is a bit over 250w. It would pay dividends to undervolt this card, but pretty much every CPU & GPU should be undervolted. With every GPU, I recommend undervolting and setting a fan curve that will keep hotspot temps at or below 80c.

2. The sound can get very loud - I set it off to the side, about 4-6ft away from the party and have to keep the volume on the low side because its loud.

Things that make this upgrade worth it:
-VERY fast GPS signal location
-Provides time for fastest mile, even if that was between miles, i.e. mile 1.3-2.3
-Stays connected to phone, uploads data automatically and quickly
-Lots of great, FREE watch faces to choose from
-Very long battery life (lasts a week, even with about 4 runs logged)

The only cons I've had:

-Some of the watch faces mess the device up - I started with one that had tons of data on the main screen and, after the watch completely froze to the point of being unusable (can't restart, no buttons work, etc), I narrowed the culprit down to being the watch face. -I don't like wearing it to bed, so I turn it off at the end of the day. This seems to throw off the BT connection and sometimes I have to re-add the device. I'd say this is typical for BT devices, however.

As usual, Garmin packs a ton of high-quality, low-maintenance functionality into a great product once again. To me, they are the gold standard for fitness devices.

title: Quality running headphones that don't fall out and stand up to long runs
text:
EDIT #2: After reaching out to the company, they sent a replacement with their apologies. I'll be honest, I had my doubts they would hold up after the battery issue, so I waited and used these for several months. No issues. I guess the pair I initially received were really just a fluke. Another positive of this experience: not once did the company hound me to change my review. It seems every time I leave a critical review the company may replace it, but then wants me to change to a 5 star review because they replaced or refunded. I was never asked to change my review once, which really says to me that these guys have confidence in their product and believe it truly will last.

EDIT: These were the *perfect* headphones for a few months. The night before my first marathon with these, I topped off the charge with some extra juice. Standing at the starting line I turned them on to get amped for the race - totally dead!!! Won't turn on at all!! So disappointed! Will contact seller to see if a replacement will fix this issue, but it's going to take me a long time to trust these, if ever, again.

When I first came across these, I was on the exact journey that Phaiser describes in their description - I've been a regular runner for about 5 years and have struggled hard to find headphones that don't suck. Up until these, I had almost only tried wired headphones to avoid having to manage yet another battery-powered device.

I've bought special "made for runners" headphones off Amazon, some bulky ones that hook around the ears from Radioshack or Target, and always have the same issues:
-Falling out or moving out enough to create a sound imbalance
-Shorting out with sweat, despite being "water resistant"
-Cord getting in the way or moving
-Poor sound quality
-Moving in ears while running

I knew there HAD to be something that worked, and I definitely wasn't going to spend $100+ on "deluxe" headphones because a) that's ridiculous and b) people shouldn't have to pay that much money for quality sound and simple comfort.

I have been VERY impressed with these headphones overall and have only found minimal features to complain about.

Testing: I run a lot and used these several times a week. Sometimes I wore a hat and hood and/or sunglasses, which took some adjustment, but was doable without sound loss. I ran in freezing weather as well as steady rain. My runs ranged from 4 miles to 16; 30mins to over 2 hours.

Pros:
-They ACTUALLY STAY IN YOUR EARS. While it's impossible to have headphones not move at all while you're running, these come pretty damn close. Even when running in the rain, they just need minor adjustments now and again. This was with the regular plastic inserts too, not the fancy foam ones.
-Sound quality is great, though the slight noise cancellation features take some getting used to (can't hear myself or anything around me almost at all)
-Comfortable for long runs (2+ hours)
-Battery life is very long - 8hrs is a good estimate, but might be low. After about 3 weeks of running with them several times a week, they only got down to 30%
-No cord and nothing to get in the way, connecting plastic arm doesn't bounce on your neck or get annoying

Cons:
-Button Design: Phaiser - WHY did you make the buttons so small and WHY is it so hard to skip songs????? I almost took a star off for the buttons alone, they're all very small and the skip function is double-tapping the volume-up button. It's hard and annoying! Why can't it be the play/pause twice? Who's using these to make phone calls??

I get questions all the time about the equipment I use while running and I've always been very negative about headphones. For over a year at a time I would simply give up listening to music while running because I couldn't stand having to deal with obnoxious, ill-fitting headphones the whole time. Phaiser actually did it - they've created a quality product that I'm proud to wear and tell EVERYONE about.

title: Great for outdoor and indoor rides on the trainer
text:
I compete in triathlons and purchased this to help me train accurately on a trainer during the winter months. I haven't used every single feature and, frankly, don't see the purpose or use of some of the navigation features (return home just seems to point an arrow directly back as the crow flies, I was expecting turn-by turn), but I didn't really get it for those features anyway.

I have found this computer to be accurate and very customizable. I was initially frustrated with the data screens available, until I did more exploring and realized how easy it is to make different riding modes with different data screens - and there are screens for everything. Even so, when I'm riding outside and in I don't find it difficult to reach over and press the arrow buttons to change screens and view different data. Make sure you download and use the Garmin Connect app to get access to even more data screens.

I found all of the sensors accurate and easy to install. I have ridden the bike in light rain and not had any issues with them falling off, getting jostled, or breaking. They don't seem to be the most accurate for indoor use, but I think this would be tough to do anyway - when I'm pedaling in high gear to really push myself, the sensors just see a slower speed, as I don't currently have any power sensors installed. I guess that will be the next investment...

The screen size is nice and easy to see while outside. The included attaching kit works well and provides lots of options - even though I have come to expect the best from Garmin, I was still impressed with the amount of different attachment options they offered. After adding aero bars, I ended up having to switch to a different attachment set up, which I wouldn't have been able to do if Garmin hadn't provided a variety of options.

My only complaint is small but frustrating all the same - most of the time, after I've completed a workout, it won't automatically upload to the Garmin app on my phone until I turn the computer off and on. It only takes a couple minutes to resolve, but it honestly happens more often than it doesn't and it's annoying. I mentioned the issue to a fellow 520 user and she said she has never had a problem with it. Mine probably needs an update, but I haven't been able to figure out how to do that quite yet.

Overall, I am satisfied. I recently purchased a Garmin 935 and was planning on selling my 520, but it's honestly still so useful I'm just going to hang on to it. The screen size and battery life is great, and it's nice to have something ready to go for indoor training.

title: Etymotic ER4XR vs Etymotic hf3 vs Shure SE535
text:
I felt compelled to write a review of these IEMs having obsessed about them for months now.
They are all very good!
They should be for the price! Haha.

So where do I begin?
Most important, above all is sound quality.
They are all good with certain signature differences.

I have been using Etymotics for years.
Using the Etymotic hf3.
Excellent overall. Very accurate. Just not a lot of punch or presence to the bass.
It's there but doesn’t hit you over the head.

I tried other brands of phones and found them to sound inaccurate or sloppy.
I had some older Shure IEMs and I wanted to see if their newer models sounded better.
I tried the Shure SE315. and the Shure SE425.
Didn’t sound as good as my old model. Back they went.
Decided I would need triple drivers to get a significantly better sound.
Bought the Shure SE535. Lots of money!
And wow! Very impressive!
Having come from the Etymotics, the sound is very different.
Its warmer and slicker sounding. The voice range is a little less forward, which may be simply because the bass presence and detail is huge compared to the Etymotics.
The Shure SE535s are very entertaining to listen to.
More so than the Etymotics.
With the Shures, you feel more like you are being washed with music.
With the Etymotics, it just feels more like you are analyzing the sound.
There is way more punch and space to the sound in the Shure SE535s. Almost too much punch on certain tracks. 😳

Let me go back to the Etymotics.
I tried out the Etymotic ER4XR and the Etymotic ER4SR.
Very little discernible difference. Maybe slightly more bass presence with the XR.
I have been using the Etymotic hf3 for many years.
In my opinion, the hf3 sounds as good if not better than the ER4XR.
The reason is that the ER4XR has a higher impedance than the hf3.
On an iPhone, you have to turn up the volume essentially all the way to get the full sound out of the ER4XR.
This is not the case with the hf3s. They are good at 3/4 volume.
Makes a significant difference!
Other than that, there is maybe a slightly discernible improvement in separation on the ER4XR. But I mean slight.
Overall the hf3 sounds better. And they cost way less!

And there is another point.
Comfort.
This is a tricky issue when it comes to IEMs.
After trying to use the triple flange cone tips, I gave up do to discomfort and the scariness of sticking a little plastic Christmas tree up your ear canal.
I found that using the cylindrical foam tips created just as good a sealed fit and bass response as the "tree" did. So that is what I use.
The Soft Flex Sleeves are also an excellent alternative. Really good isolation and amazing bass response!
That brings me to the difference between the Etymotics and the Shures.
The Etymotics are simply more comfortable.
The drivers are smaller and weigh less than the Shures. Less of a pull on your ear structure.
Shures design is supposed to route the wire over and behind your ear.
I find this distracting and annoying in addition to being uncomfortable.
My solution is to let the wires remain in front of my ears, hanging down in front of me.
Much more comfortable. (See photos)
This however, necessitates using a shirt clip to cancel out the weight of the cord pulling on your ears. I bought some from Amazon. Works well to make the phones as weightless as possible.
With the Etymotics, this is less of an issue because the earpieces weigh so much less and the foam goes straight into your ear canal.
The Shures have to kind of sit on your ear structure. Not so comfortable.
I'm hoping over time that I will be bothered less and less by this slight pressure.
It is worth it to get the sonic results that the 535s deliver.

Back to the Shures.
I payed a very large amount for the 535s. For me they are worth it for the spectacular performance they deliver. I can only imagine how nice the Shure SE846s sound.
I just couldn't bring myself to spend one thousand dollars on IEMs. I do after all have a family to support! 😛

So I am happy I have both.
I will probably usually use my 535s for my daily commute to Manhattan.
But it's nice to switch out to the Etymotics for a lighter more Spartan sound signature.

Hope this review helps some of you out there.

With streaming music, it's like being a kid in a candy store every day.
And with these headphones, You can hear the candy really really well! 😊

title: Etymotic hf3 vs Etymotic ER4XR vs Shure SE535
text:
I felt compelled to write a review of these IEMs having obsessed about them for months now.
They are all very good!
They should be for the price! Haha.

So where do I begin?
Most important, above all is sound quality.
They are all good with certain signature differences.

I have been using Etymotics for years.
Using the Etymotic hf3.
Excellent overall. Very accurate. Just not a lot of punch or presence to the bass.
It's there but doesn’t hit you over the head.

I tried other brands of phones and found them to sound inaccurate or sloppy.
I had some older Shure IEMs and I wanted to see if their newer models sounded better.
I tried the Shure SE315. and the Shure SE425.
Didn’t sound as good as my old model. Back they went.
Decided I would need triple drivers to get a significantly better sound.
Bought the Shure SE535. Lots of money!
And wow! Very impressive!
Having come from the Etymotics, the sound is very different.
Its warmer and slicker sounding. The voice range is a little less forward, which may be simply because the bass presence and detail is huge compared to the Etymotics.
The Shure SE535s are very entertaining to listen to.
More so than the Etymotics.
With the Shures, you feel more like you are being washed with music.
With the Etymotics, it just feels more like you are analyzing the sound.
There is way more punch and space to the sound in the Shure SE535s. Almost too much punch on certain tracks. 😳

Let me go back to the Etymotics.
I tried out the Etymotic ER4XR and the Etymotic ER4SR.
Very little discernible difference. Maybe slightly more bass presence with the XR.
I have been using the Etymotic hf3 for many years.
In my opinion, the hf3 sounds as good if not better than the ER4XR.
The reason is that the ER4XR has a higher impedance than the hf3.
On an iPhone, you have to turn up the volume essentially all the way to get the full sound out of the ER4XR.
This is not the case with the hf3s. They are good at 3/4 volume.
Makes a significant difference!
Other than that, there is maybe a slightly discernible improvement in separation on the ER4XR. But I mean slight.
Overall the hf3 sounds better. And they cost way less!

And there is another point.
Comfort.
This is a tricky issue when it comes to IEMs.
After trying to use the triple flange cone tips, I gave up do to discomfort and the scariness of sticking a little plastic Christmas tree up your ear canal.
I found that using the cylindrical foam tips created just as good a sealed fit and bass response as the "tree" did. So that is what I use.
The Soft Flex Sleeves are also an excellent alternative. Really good isolation and amazing bass response!
That brings me to the difference between the Etymotics and the Shures.
The Etymotics are simply more comfortable.
The drivers are smaller and weigh less than the Shures. Less of a pull on your ear structure.
Shures design is supposed to route the wire over and behind your ear.
I find this distracting and annoying in addition to being uncomfortable.
My solution is to let the wires remain in front of my ears, hanging down in front of me.
Much more comfortable. (See photos)
This however, necessitates using a shirt clip to cancel out the weight of the cord pulling on your ears. I bought some from Amazon. Works well to make the phones as weightless as possible.
With the Etymotics, this is less of an issue because the earpieces weigh so much less and the foam goes straight into your ear canal.
The Shures have to kind of sit on your ear structure. Not so comfortable.
I'm hoping over time that I will be bothered less and less by this slight pressure.
It is worth it to get the sonic results that the 535s deliver.

Back to the Shures.
I payed a very large amount for the 535s. For me they are worth it for the spectacular performance they deliver. I can only imagine how nice the Shure SE846s sound.
I just couldn't bring myself to spend one thousand dollars on IEMs. I do after all have a family to support! 😛

So I am happy I have both.
I will probably usually use my 535s for my daily commute to Manhattan.
But it's nice to switch out to the Etymotics for a lighter more Spartan sound signature.

Hope this review helps some of you out there.

With streaming music, it's like being a kid in a candy store every day.
And with these headphones, You can hear the candy really really well! 😊

title: Excellent Choice! (And reasonably priced)
text:
I recently decided to replace the stock cables that came with my SE 535s. I bought all three available cables from Shure to compare them. These simple cables are well made and sound fantastic.
I tried:
Shure RMCE-BT2 High-Resolution Bluetooth 5.0 Communication Cable
$149
Shure RMCE-UNI Universal Communication Cable for Detachable SE Sound Isolating Earphones.
$29
Shure EAC46BKS 46-Inch Black Detachable Earphone Cable
$35

The EAC 46BKS cable does not have an inline mic/volume control. and it doesn’t sound any better than the RMCE.
The RMCE is cheaper, sounds just as good and is more functional. The clear winner.

The RMCE BT2 is wireless which is great. But the sound is not quite the same. The sound personality or signature is similar to the wired option but as you might expect, the high end and low end of the dynamic range is less present. The overall sound is pleasing and balanced but the upper transients and the lower thump of the bass is quieted. Also the sensitivity of the drivers is decreased, At maximum volume, the sound level for loud critical listening is achieved. With the wired connection, you cant turn it up beyond 3/4 without it becoming painful. When walking around with the wireless set up the playback volume is more than sufficient. There is a nice clean presentation of the sound overall.

Having both options is great, depending on the circumstance. The wireless option is excellent if I don’t want a cord in the way. But when you want maximum playback dynamics you can choose the wired solution.
Yes, it’s luxurious to own both, but so is owning the se535s. :)
Im extremely happy with the two options. I highly recommend them both.

title: If you can handle the discomfort, these are The Best!
text:
Ok, so Im a maniac about my Shure SE 535s. I love the incredible sound these IEMs are capable of.
For years I have been using Shures Yellow Foam tips. The seal is great, they are comfortable, and the sound is excellent.
But when I bought Shures wireless Bluetooth Cable, I was inspired to try the Triple Flanges again.
Once I was able to get them seated correctly, I gave a very close listen and did a thorough comparison.
The Triple Flanges are better.
The only problem is, the Flanges are inherently uncomfortable.
I tried every combination of trimming them down:
I cut the top flange off. (Kills the dynamic range they are capable of. Like turning a great studio monitor into a mediocre 2 way bookshelf speaker)
I tried cutting the bottom flange off. (Really killed the isolation and bass response)
The only thing that improved the comfort without killing the sound was to cut 4mm of the stem off at the base of the flanges. Makes the cone shorter so the monitor can sit in your ear more easily. The sound is maintained.

And concerning the sound, this is why they are worth the discomfort:
The sound is amazingly accurate, detailed, fast articulation, incredibly balanced, deep full bass with an amazing dynamic range and quality. There is an uncanny resonance you can here in the sound. The foam tips just dont present that. They may sound pretty good, but not this good.

Hopefully, over time I will become accustomed to the weird feeling they create inside my ear canals.
I will hold out hope. It is worth the sacrifice.

title: Beautiful, Accurate, Warm, Comfortable Sound
text:
Before buying these KEFs, I like many others obsessionally belabored the choice. I read a zillion reviews. Watched a zillion YouTube reviews. I considered all the current bookshelf speakers that are being talked about in the current year. I bought and auditioned the Triangle Bro 3, the Klipsch RP 600M, Elac Unifi 2.0 and this KEF Q350. All of these speakers are highly regarded. The Q350 was not released recently but the KEF sound with the Uni-Q drivers has been praised for many years. (The new KEF LS50 Meta is their current media darling. Would have loved to buy it but it costs literally twice as much. And these are already pretty pricey for my budget. 😊)
After much critical listening I decided to keep these.
Their precision and detail are simply better and more exact than the others. Their imaging is remarkable. And aside from that, they simply sound more beautiful. Like the difference between a really nice Yamaha piano and a Steinway. The sound is richer. The notes resonate better.
My second favorite was the Elac Unfi 2.0. Really great also. But didnt quite have as good separation as the Q350s. The KEFS also have a comforting sound. That’s why I use the term “warm”. It’s not that it is colored. It just sounds more real. (Like the difference a tube amp makes. Just more realness.)
As many reviews have mentioned, these speakers will sound pretty different depending on how you position them in the room. I intend to try many more configurations as time goes on to see where they work the best in my given space. These speakers have a very strong centering of the vocals. I wouldn’t mind diffusing that a little bit if I can. Ive already heard that I can alter that a bit by placement changes.
I’m running these with an Elac 10” subwoofer which fills out the sound nicely at the bottom. I may try another woofer to get a faster tighter bass hit in the future.
I use Qobuz and stream high bit rate files whenever available. Definitely ups the game well beyond typical streaming (Spotify)
I will report back on this review after Ive “broken them in” (Some people claim this opens the sound stage over time. It may simply be a placebo effect or my own hearing re-learning what to expect from the given sound source. We shall see...)
At close range with a bit of toe-in, these speakers are like listening to giant studio-grade headphones. The exactness is thrilling. Like headphones without anything clamping your head. 😁
Oh, and looks wise, they are very elegant. Unique.
So far I’m digging these KEFs 👍🏻

4 stars because of a significant problem with power management. OMG I love this thing. Every time I use it I'm again surprised by how well designed it is. Forgive me but Microsoft is not known for elegant thoughtful design in its products. This thing is so Apple-like in so many ways. Clearly the designers were given tremendous authority (as Jonny Ives is famous for over at Apple) over the engineering of this product. Someone thought about that and made it so. I am so impressed with this thing. It is powerful enough to run Lightroom and Photoshop. I love the OneDrive in the cloud. I love the docking station with all of its ports. I love the magnetic power connection (I know, Apple did that a long time ago). I love the light yet very firm and waterproof keyboard. I love the infinite-position kickstand. I love the face-recognition log in. I LOVE the touchscreen, that I find myself using all the time as I tap on menus rather than use the keyboard or pen - it's just easier and more intuitive.

Best tech purchase for me in the last 24 months.

title: Worth every penny
text:
When I saw how expensive the OEM hoods were, I was more then willing to try a generic after market brand.
I got three different sizes, one for a 18-55mm, one for a 55-250, and one for a 50mm.

Every one fits perfect, and works.

One of the common complaints is that they don't fit correctly, either too tight or too loose. I will say that even if you have more then one lens with the same cap size (all of mine are 58mm), these hoods are NOT interchangeable. Only the one designed specifically for the lens you have will fit properly.

Go to you camera brand's website and search for your exact lens.
When you find your exact lens, look for the 'Suggested Accessories" link.
Find the OEM model number on their lens hood.
Make sure the after market hood is designed as a direct replacement for the specific OEM model your lens requires.

IMHO, this would fix the majority of complaints about the hoods not fitting properly. So far I'm 3 for 3. If I acquire another lens, I'll order another one in a heart beat.

I'm very pleased and would recommend.

title: Better then expected.
text:
This is my first set of macro tubes, so I didn't want to spend too much.

These are made of metal, and are very solid with a nice finish.

They work as advertised.

No lens just space, so they do change the parameters of the lens. At some focal lengths you have to get very close but that's expected.

This set does NOT have electric contacts, so you can not change the lens aperture, and no auto focus, but that's expected.

There are a few complaints about the lens mount sticking to the lens, but there is a small release button that disengages a pin that locks the lens to the mount. I've had no issue releasing the lens.

The threads felt a little rough so I applied silicon grease and worked them in a bit, then wiped away the grease to avoid contaminating a lens and (or) the camera body.

I'm surprised at some of the complaints that compare these to a dedicated Macro lens. I've achieved impressive results with these but like anything, the best results do require some work.

All and all, I'm very satisfied, and recommend these.

title: EXTREMELY difficult to assemble.
text:
The fabric is way too tight and the rods are overkill since there are eight of them, they could have been much lighter.
I actually permanently bent a few of the rods a few degrees during assembly, and bruised my thumb in the process (YES I followed the instructions).
There is NO WAY one could use this out side of the studio, or on location, unless you arrived 1/2 early to wrestle before your client arrived.
If you're a female (no offense), or if you don't have very strong hands, forget it, you're NOT getting this thing together.

The flash bracket is supposed to be locked and released by a single thumb screw, but it's only one of 4 secure points and the bracket does NOT fit behind the other 3 points, so to correctly mount, you have to remove at least one of the other screws (with a screw driver) and replace that screw after mounting the bracket, or the bracket will NOT be secure and the soft box will fall.

Trying to dissemble is actually worse than assembly.

I'm baffled that engineers over at Fotodiox who designed this thing failed so horribly on the most elementary aspects of this item.

Since I bent a few of the rods, I may have to return this unit, if I do end up returning it, I'm asking for a refund, not an exchange.

What a way to ruin a day. Instead of shooting photos, I'm dealing with with this...

Update:
Since I finally got this thing together, I shot a few test shots, and despite the impressively flawed design, the light wasn't too bad. The outer 4-5 inches of the box is brighter than the center, but not the worst I've seen. A speedlite defuser (fong) would most likely eliminate this small difference.

Also, there is only ONE screw/bolt holding the inner speedlite mount to the base. That means that only ONE screw/bolt is holding the entire softbox in place. It has a tendency to want to pivot on that screw, so don't allow your speedlite head to rest inside the ring, but keep it just outside of the box to avoid contact and possible damage should the box pivot on it's single bolt.

* Replace all four ring mounting screws with thumb screws.
* Added a second bolt to attach the base.
* use much lighter rods (as they do on other softboxes).

This softbox would have been a win.

title: Way more complicated then it needs to be for an intervolmeter. Keep a cheat sheet handy.
text:
I've used to several times on my Canon 7D.
The back light is much brighter than the intervalometer I use for my t3i.
Does all the functions as advertised.
Unlike some of these units, this one has a power button to power off, and a removable cable.

Amended:
After using the unit a few times I ran into some complications and after some research this is what I learned.
Setting the intervolmeter is WAY more complicated than it really should be. It appears that they wanted to add a useless feature, so they messed up the most useful function.

This unit makes it possible to take a defined group if timed photos, than take a duplicate group after a defined delay (ex. 100 timed shutters, waits 30 minutes, then takes another 100 timed shutters, repeat).

On a simple Intervalometer:
• Set Interval
• Number of shot ("--" for infinity).
• DONE, walk away.

On the NW-880:
• Set interval time.
• Number if shots (N1, no infinity)
• Set cycle repeat ("RE") number.
• Set Cycle delay (make sure it matches the interval time or it will skip the interval and mess up the time lapse flow)
• Wait for the first cycle to run through to make sure it repeats correctly.
• If you made a mistake, start over.

This includes setting "N1", "RE", and "N2". for EVERY time lapse.
Here's a good video I found that explains it.
[...]
Imagine working on a cold, dark mountain, trying to set up your camera, or cameras, and having to deal with this process.

Because I believe that most people are buying this for it's intervolmeter capabilities, I have to drop my rating from 5 stars to 2 stars.

Amended #2:
Even though I wrote the above instructions, I attempted to take a time lapse of tonight's sunset, and I couldn't remember how to program this piece of junk. It kept firing 2 shots one right after the other and I couldn't figure out why? The last time lapse I did, It did the same thing so I had to delete half of all the images I took to make the time lapse.
The result tonight is that I missed the sunset entirely trying to figure out why I couldn't get it to work correctly.
Any gear that causes you to miss the shot should be DESTROYED IMMEDIATELY!
It's not worth the frustration, don't even know if it's defective because of all of the setting involved.

title: These are great, but there is no reason you should ever buy them...
text: These speakers will out-perform any other brand, generally, of the same size for under $100. I cannot recommend anyone to ever buy these, though. I'll tell you why. Infinity sells a set of Infinity Kappa 6.5 on this very site for only $20 more. The improvements are very substantial. The Kappas have Infinity's special glass-fiber woofer cone. I did a side-by-side comparison to eliminate the change for the placebo-effect to taint my judgment, and the Kappa's mid-range just seemed a little sweeter and had more fidelity. The bass that the Kappa's produces also seemed more musically accurate. Some speakers produce bass in a more punchy way. Some people prefer this type. The Kappa's have a richer tonality and a smoother, more accurate bass reproduction. The Kappa's also have a different tweeter. The tweeter is vastly superior to the Reference tweeter sound-wise, but isn't just because of the tweeter itself. The Kappa has a computer-controlled cross-over that blurs the line between coaxial and component speakers in terms of sound quality. The Reference just have the typical capacitor wired in. Capacitors work just fine, and they're what you have to expect for this price-point, but for $20 more, the computer-controlled cross-over is a no-brainer. A huge advantage about the more advanced cross-over is the low-pass on the woofers. All the higher frequencies on the Reference speakers come through the woofer and can come across distorted at higher volumes. Again, this is not a problem with the Kappas.  I'd like to add that both speakers had a more than reasonably break-in--I've actually had the Kappas longer. I realize this isn't a review for this particular product, but the Kappas are everything these are and more. I'd highly suggest spending the extra $20 and reaping all the benefits.

title: Phenomenal.
text: I'm just going to give review readers a few words of advice to help decipher some of the reviews on this site. If you noticed, all the positive reviews are made by those with highly implied credentials--implied not only by their noted experience, but proven by their grammar. The negative reviews aren't backed by any substantial relativity to the product at hand. These speakers are an absolute steal for the price. They offer the whole package--high quality drivers, high quality amplification and top-notch signal processing--so no room for error. Although the performance of these is relatively seamless, you won't get good results without high-quality music--FLAC, WAV, or professionally recorded CDs. These are far beyond MP3s lossy compression, and if you try to use MP3s, you'll pay the price. Now, I'm going to address the most reoccurring negatives in the reviews. As for the apparent "lack of bass due to the lack of subwoofer," there is no lack of bass--speaking relatively. These obviously aren't designed to shake windows or move mass amounts or air; they're designed to accurately reproduce bass the way it was recorded, which it does almost flawlessly. It would seem obvious that these speakers aren't designed for SPL or subsonic exaggeration, but by some of the negative reviews, that fact isn't obvious enough. Also worth noting, these speakers should only be used via USB connection. The internal DAC isn't the only reason for this. There is an integrated equalization process that manipulates the frequency response to particularly suit these speakers exactly--another important part of the aforementioned "whole package." Another "flaw" these speakers apparently have is most typically refereed to as "moving out of the sweet spot." Upon further investigation, you'll notice that non of the positive reviews(written by those with the powerful credentials)mention this as a problem. I'll tell you why. These speakers are designed to be listened to while directly focused at your ears. This may seem obvious, but let me expand on this further. The professionals don't mention this as a flaw because they know that the waveguide on these speakers isn't designed for acoustical seperation across a room, but for concentration to a relatively single point--hence the exceptional clarity. The fidelity that these speakers offer simply could not be focused at every point in a room--it's not possible. If they were designed for room-filling sound, the sound waves would bounce off the hard surfaces in your environment and reach your ears at different times, cause perceived distortion. Headphones don't suffer the same fate as speakers since the sound is directed straight at your ears and nowhere else--somewhat similar to the design these speakers have! Essentially, the design's main concern is fidelity and realism, not room-filling party speakers. I don't have any issues with these speakers, and the only people that do are either using them for the wrong purposes, or have them setup incorrectly. Thanks! Spidy out.

title: Good TV, but not much better than a midrange LED
text:
For starters, I will say I calibrated the TV using the recommendations from RTINGS.com. I also viewed a series of test image patterns on Bluray disc to finely-tune the image.

After hearing more and more talk about how these quantum dot TVs are supposed to outperform OLED TVs, I decided to buy one to replace my 2016 LG OLED B6 panel. Unfortunately, I can't say I am impressed. I noticed a lot of blooming around bright objects in darkly-lit scenes when the local dimming kicks in. Additionally, the panel motion is not great (not talking about using the motion smoother features). I was very impressed with the way brightly-lit scenes appeared (The Cat Returns, Studio Ghibli, for instance) but anything dark resulted in a lot of gray as the panel attempted to display the highlights and dark areas at the same time. I also ran into issues trying to watch HDR content through my Xbox One X. The TV would not pickup the HDR signal (thanks Samsung for not having an HDR promt appear on-screen when HDR content is detected like every other manufacturer I've seen). I enabled the HDMI ports to accept "full signal" in the TV's menus but no luck. The HDR content I was able to view on YouTube did well when very bright highlights appeared, but the poor black performance resulted in worse contrast than I'd like.

I honestly can't say this TV does all that much better than my Sharp 50in TV I picked up from Best Buy in 2018 (re-branded Hinsense). The HDR performance is very similar and the XBox One X even works with my Sharp TV. Sad thing is, the Sharp was a $400 TV.

I hate to be another voice in the crowd, but I'd say "get an OLED" because these backlit panels just can't compete at the end of the day. I returned this TV and got a Sony A9G and there's no comparison. I don't think you'd be disappointed with the Samsung, but given the cost, it's just not worth it when a $500 TV can perform at the same level. Spending $1800? Just get an OLED at that point. Much obliged.

title: Top tier motherboard brand with their reasonably priced model
text: I like the tuf models because they offer a middle ground between value and quality. Their strix models are much more expensive, but the tuf models for example have heatsinks on their vrm and pch that can help your performance. The one thing that doesn't make sense is the pcie slots near the x16 pcie slot. A gaming targeted motherboard should not have pcie slots next to the x16 pcie slot in the next 2 slots. Not only are there 2, but one of them is a x4 slot. If they put 2 x4 slots at the bottom and put the m.2 slots under the x16 slot, you have better placement to use the pcie slots. But almost never will you use the top x4 pcie slot since either your gpu will be in the way or you will block the fans of the gpu if it was only a 2 slot gpu.

title: If you need LiPO and LiFePO4 this is great, otherwise its just good...
text: So its good, not great. Its slow... 750ma if you charge just one cell... otherwise its 350ma... So why still 4 stars, well it does charge cells full and wont damage your cells. Big deal right, most do just fine. title: You don't get what you don't pay for
text:
I tried this filter (not bought via Amazon) and threw it away. I could see my reflection in the "Glass" (looked like plastic to me).

A good UV filter should make you wonder if there is anything there at all. It should never create reflections from the anti-glare coating on the lens.

You know those Claritin commericials where they peel away a haze to see clearly? Photos taken with this filter seemed to always have the haze. I might not even have noticed, except that I took a shot without the filter (I had taken it off to clean it and then something came up so I made some unfiltered shots.) The difference was amazing, so I did a test, on a tripod, of a bunch of tulips getting good light through a window. One with the filter, one without. There should have been no difference, but the one without the filter showed more color saturation and was sharper (tho both were in focus.)

I replaced it with a B+H filter (again, not sold here) and can't tell the difference between filter on or off for most shots, but a recent trip to Tibet (photos at 14,000 feet on a bright day) demonstrated real UV filtering power. Without the filter, they had a slight blue cast.

Recommendation: Get a good UV filter to protect your much more expensive lens from stray scratches. Don't let your lens' high quality optics suffer from putting cheap glass (or plastic) in front of it.

Now, I've tried this newer model and they've addressed all the minor shortcomings. There's a quick release. The legs bend a bit more easily. The ball joints are a little smaller, which improves the grip (when I saw it, I mistakenly assumed the opposite). Then even added a bubble level in the small head.

I've even used it for things other than its intended purpose. I bent the legs into an insect shape (two legs bent at the "knees" and one sticking back as a tail. Then I rested my iPhone on the "seat" up against the ball head and had a nifty stand for a movie and then later, for overnight (I use the phone as my alarm clock). I'm pretty sure it would handle an iPad, tho that would be the maximum size. A Kindle Fire would be fine.

However, the main use I get from it is to hold my remote flash. I'm a big fan of off camera flash and so I use the gorilla pod to hold the flash someplace off to the side and then fire away, getting nice sidelight and the shadows I want.

This is a great item for a very reasonable price. I've even given two away as holiday presents in recent years.

title: WOW, WOW, WOW
text:
I just got my card and replaced the 8GB card I had in the camera. I've had that one since 8GB was considered a large card.

I use a Canon 60D, and shoot in RAW. On the old 8GB card, I could shoot 8 images and the buffer would fill, it would take 4 seconds before I could get another shot and 40 seconds to clear the buffer entirely. There is room on the card for more than 999 images.

On this card, I can get 18 shots, take another in 3 seconds (actually 2 more in 5) and clear the entire buffer in 45 seconds (that's 2x images in just a bit more time).

Copying from the card via my Lexar UDMA reader and USB 2.0 port is also cut nearly in half. This test was done by copying my 2GB outlook PST file to the card and back to another directory.

I should note that when I use my laptop's built-in SD card reader, the read time is unchanged. Clearly, the limit is imposed by the laptop's circuitry.

Different cameras and different PCs will have different test results. According to the Canon specs, my 60D can use these cards but not take full advantage of them.

For me, SDXC Class 10 is a winner.

title: Perfect for my needs. Loving it!
text:
I'm not a fan of buying something because it is new. I am a fan of buying things that solve problems. The problem I'm having is that I'm getting older and my heavy DSLR and long Canon "L" lenses were getting too heavy to cart around all day. So I made a list of Must have and Nice to have items.

Must have: small, lightweight, interchangeable lenses (and a variety to choose from), fully articulated LCD, near zero shutter lag, raw processing, 8 shot buffer minimum, high ISO, viewfinder (with visible histogram), hot shoe.

Nice to have: wireless remote, iOS app, GPS.

This camera has all the items on both lists. (The GPS requires connection to a phone, and that drains the battery on both, so I probably won't use it much)

Then there are some unexpected bonuses. One is that Canon introduced a new raw format called CR3. It is highly compressed and lossless, so it will save considerable disk space. This is getting important with >20Mpixels on modern sensors (24 here, IIRC). The camera came out March 26. Adobe updated its software April 3 to handle it.

You'll get a lot of opinion on what make a camera a professional's camera. Non-photographers judge by bulk, and that's just stereotype. To me, a professional camera has better weather sealing, multiple memory cards and a large buffer (transfers image to the card). It would also have a bigger offset between the tripod screw and the battery cover. (So the battery could be changed easily without removing the tripod or plate.

As for full frame, it doesn't matter. Imagine an 8x12 picture, perhaps from a magazine. Then put a mat on it where the sides are 1 inch thick. The part of the picture you see now is 6x10. That's what a 1.6 crop sensor does (in round numbers). The part of the image you see is completely unchanged. If the lens manufacturers just changed the numbers on the lens itself, no one would ever know. A lens marked 10mm becomes 16mm, but all else is the same. If you like the fisheye look, then you have to go full frame, but for pretty much anything else it doesn't matter.

As for video, that's a matter of the buffer. Shooting at 30 frames a second means filling the buffer fast (just hold the shutter button down on the camera you have now and see how fast it fills). To make continuous images for video, any camera has to crop the image before even sending it to the buffer and then the card. So video means a tighter crop. Again, a pro might want a more video capable camera .

The only glitch I ran into was with a third party lens from Tokina. The new software in the camera didn't talk to the software in the lens, and so it generated an error message about the connectors not being clean. After returning the first lens and getting a second with the same problem I called Tokina and they told me about the mismatch. They said that they're working on a firmware ujpgrade that will require me sending in the lens, but they had no due date on the fix. (I sent it back). If you're considering a lens from them or any 3rd party, I suggest giving them a call first. When they fix it I'll buy the lens again and update this review.

EDITED TO ADD:

1. Thing I miss the most: Port for wired remote shutter release. Yes, the smartphone app does the job but it burns the battery. Also, no way to take time lapse, which uses an intervalometer (and that feature isn't in the app, even if battery wasn't a problem)

2. This Arca-Swiss compatible plate fits the camera and still leaves room to access the battery compartment. https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00XK2790Y/ref=oh_aui_detailpage_o06_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1

title: Tried it, went back to my old one. Read on for details.
text:
Disclaimer: this was an free-to-me product for review. I agreed to try this product because I wanted to be able to expand my range via their “Velop” nodes. My current router misses out on the gazebo in the back yard and the garage. I never got that far in my experiments. But let’s take this from the beginning.

1. Installation
Easy, perhaps too easy. I downloaded the Linksys app to my phone, unboxed the router and moved all the plugs and cables from the old one over. The app connected fast, then took me through several screens.
First was to create an account with Linksys (not thrilled with that, but it is a trade of privacy for promised firmware updates and there was no opting out).

Then it asked me to create “WIFI Name” (SSID for those who know the term, although they didn’t mention that) and a password. I kept the same SSID and password I was using before (but see note further down) and that made it seamless for the other devices using that SSID.

By then Linksys had sent me an email to verify the account I created and I had to respond to that. Fortunately, the router was passing data already.

2. Configuration
The app asked me to choose a name picked from a list. It offered “Custom” but I could not figure out how to create my own so I chose “office” from the list.

Next was to allow auto update and crash reports and I said OK

Then it asked me to go to the “dashboard” to connect devices, but since I had not gotten any Velop nodes I skipped that step. By then, I was finding that working the app was getting a bit cumbersome so I connected via my desktop browser.

4. Note
This is a good place for me to go into some detail on that note I mentioned. My old router, a Linksys EA4500, let me create several separate SSIDs and I made one for 802.11G service, one for 802.11N, and one for guest (802.11b, good for email and FB, but not streaming). I had my Tivo and Roku set to 11N, my desktop and my wife’s laptop plus my iPad set to 11G. I put her Kindle reader on guest since the only thing she did with online was download a new book from time to time. With that configuration, I never got the dreaded “Buffering” beachball while watching Netflix on the Tivo or Prime video on the Roku.

4. Desktop browser software
On logging in, it asked me for the pin code for the router. That was the first time I saw one even mentioned. Fortunately, there was a link to login via the account information I set up early in the installation. The main page came up with several tiles to choose from.

My first stop was to configure the device priority list. I wanted to emulate what I had setup on the old router and described in the note, but my only option was to set some devices to “high priority.” Although the router boasts “Tri-Band” I had no options other than that.

I then went to set up guest access and wanted to use the same SSID as before, but it kept pushing me back to a default that was based on the router model plus the word guest. Given that several people already had my guest account programmed into their phones, that was an annoyance.

I found, quite by accident, a tile on the main page called “Wifi Settings”. On that page is the pin that logging in asked for. 8 digits.

5. End game

Later that night I tried to watch a movie and got the buffering message. Maybe I could have played around with the settings, but I shouldn’t have to and didn’t.

I figured out how to solve all of these problems. I took out the old router, moved the plugs back to where they were and started it up again. This one is now in its box on a shelf. If I had paid for it, I would have returned it. My community runs an electronics recycling day in August. That’s where it is headed.

title: Minor design improvement to a mature product
text:
It is really hard to stand out when dealing with a product that has very stringent design limitations and a technology that is already mature. This Sony product moves the needle forward a tiny bit.

The most obvious change is that there is no write-protect switch. I've had several SD cards from a wide variety of manufacturers and the only time I ever noticed one was when it broke off in the locked position and I had to buy a new card while on vacation in order to keep shooting on the last two days. I think that removing it was a long overdue decision

The other small change is that the read speed is 277mb/s, which is about 10% higher than most other cards on the market. However, the degree of benefit from that is limited by the read speed of your computer's SD card interface. The data will transfer at whichever end, the card or the computer, has the lower data rate.

I'll be using this in the mix with my other cards, but the improvement isn't enough to make me want to go out and replace the ones I have.

I can't really comment on price. SD cards often go on sale at various vendors, sometimes at steep discount. Prices today have this Sony a bit higher than the Lexars I use, but not by much.

title: You must purchase memory card separately
text:
This is a cool little camera for the price. So far in using it, I've noticed some pros and cons:
Pros:
-very small and light weight--easily fits in the palm of one's hand.
-an inexpensive choice
-comes with two batteries already charged, so you can use it right away and have a spare battery
Cons:
-additional purchase is required. You need to buy an SD card to use the camera. I guess that is not any different than buying a still camera.
-no optical zoom, only digital zoom, but the with 24 MP, you have room to zoom.
-directions were hard to understand--maybe that is because I'm so ignorant of video cameras--it might be intuitive for others.

Over all I would say this is a great starter camera--might be a good choice for an older child who wants to experiment with making plays or movies. And it is a good camera for me to learn on. Having two batteries is a plus--one to use and the other to recharge. The batteries came charged, so if you purchase an SD card in advance, you will be ready to go with this camera.

Don't expect a lot of special features here for this price point. There's no slo-mo feature and no optical zoom, though you can use digital zoom. Still there is a lot of cool things to to with this camera.

If you have ever wanted to try out a digital camera, this is a good one to start with and then you can upgrade if you find you want more features.

title: A little low on memory, but well worth the price
text:
This computer has as a 2.3 GHz AMD Ryzen 7 3700U Processor with Radeon Vega Mobile Graphics with 8 GB of RAM, although only about 6 are usable. The HD touchscreen has a little more friction than a phone’s touchscreen does, and should probably be used with a stylus or electronic pen, which was not included. I did have a problem once with the touchscreen not working, although it was easily fixed by the proverbial restart.

This computer can be used in a lot of modes. Tent mode is nice for watching videos; if you don’t like the attached keyboard you can flip the laptop into tent mode and attach your own keyboard and mouse. The screen feels sturdy when being moved and in tent mode, although when in tablet mode it feels like it may be bending too far, even though it isn’t. Tablet mode is just an enlarged version of the start menu. You can do everything you normally would, but you have to use the touchscreen. An onscreen keyboard appears when you need to type something, although due to the size of the screen it is too big to be used efficiently. The privacy shutter works, and is a nice touch.

The fingerprint sensor started out precise and quick, with me only needing to barely tap the sensor. However, after a few days if I didn’t clean the sensor, it would take me multiple tries to scan my finger. Login is quick, and it takes at most 15 seconds from powering on to logging in.

Re: the battery, a single charge never lasted me close to 8 hours, but that’s probably because I was using CPU and GPU intensive programs and games. That being said, I can easily see it lasting 8 hours with only using low CPU intensive programs.

I would have liked more USB ports, but 2 USB-A and 1 USB-C usually fit my needs. The camera is about the same quality as a mid-end phone.

With 237 GB of memory, it can certainly use more. I haven’t had a problem with the low RAM yet.

It can run 3D AAA from 2013 or so on high settings. CSGO runs smoothly on high settings. I have had a scaling issue with a few programs, but the problem was easily solved.

Bottom line: Overall a great laptop, although it could do better memory wise, it is certainly worth the money.

title: Nice little camera, but not as waterproof as I’d hoped
text:
This is a nice little palm-sized action camera you use with your smart phone. Before you turn it on I recommend doing two things. Download the app onto your phone and go online and read the instruction manual. Then you will be ready to use the camera with greater ease and without doing something to damage the camera.

I’m not in a position to compare this camera to a GoPro as this is my first camera of this sort. So I will try to share some other things that may be helpful as you consider whether or not to buy this camera.

First, be aware that many of these are being offered by third party sellers, so if you have a problem with it, you may not get the help you expect. But Amazon is good with returns so that may not trouble you. Second, I recommend getting the camera in a package that includes an extra battery and a memory card. You are going to want those items anyway and getting them separately is going to cost you more than getting the camera with those things and a whole lot of other “bells and whistles,” too. You’ll save money in the long run.

Finally, and this is the one that caused me to give this 4 stars rather than 5, be aware that you cannot use this in the water with active water sports. If you are careful to check all the seals, you can use it with shallow water snorkeling, but don’t think you are going to wear it on your head to catch the next big wave! You can’t jump (or fall) in the water with this. That creates too much force and would damage the camera. So it’s under water use is very limited.

Hope this helps you make an intelligent buying decision.

title: Astounding sound and picture quality, but do you have enough internet?
text:
Wow! We are upgrading from a bottom of the line 40 inch "unintelligent" TV to this spectacular 55" smart TV. The picture quality is incredible--I knew Keith Morrison had wrinkles, but now I can practically feel the creases in his face. (Remind me not to go on television!) And the sound is like being at a movie theatre. No burned out pixels as some viewers have complained of. Just excellent picture quality that makes you feel like you could reach out and touch the people and things on the screen. Love it! Love it!

Here's the problem, though. We did not consider that we need more internet speed and capacity. Come to find out we need at 15-25 mbps for 4K AND we will be using tons more data. An hour of 4K streaming uses about 14GB. So before we can fully appreciate this TV we are going to have to make a tough decision about changing internet providers and/or upping our current subscription. So count the cost before ordering. The TV isn't cheap, but is fabulous. But to fully utilize it, you may have significant additional expense to expand your internet capabilities.

In summary this is a fabulous entertainment product. But consider the cost of getting it up to speed in your home, if this is your first smart TV.

title: OK - BACK UP TO FIVE STARS FROM ONE STAR
text:
I opted to try this French Press for K-Cups instead of buying the more expensive Single Serve K-Cup brewers. The main complaint of the less expensive brewers was that after a while the pumps stopped working. We received the Cafejo unit about a week ago, and it worked great when we first tried it. We had company tonight, and after brewing about 3 cups, the water was NOT flowing through the press. Turns out the small sharp blade at the bottom of.the K-Cup basket had broken. Thus the bottom of the K-Cup wasn't being punctured and no water could flow through it. I was able to pre-puncture the bottom of each K-Cup, and get it to work for the remainder of the guests. The rest of the press seems to be fine. I am very thankful that the blade tip was badly bent, instead of actually breaking off and possibly winding up in one of my guests cups. Prior to tonight's use and failure, I had tried it four times, and then on the third time tonight, it failed. That's seven times it was used, NOT a very good indicator. I have since contacted Cafejo and advised them of this problem and IF I hear from them, I will update this review. Other reviewers have come across this same problem, but I thought it may have been a fluke. I thought wrong....

05/03/13 UPDATE: I have not heard a thing from Cafejo. I guess they could care less whether or not their products are reliable or if their customers are satisfied with the purchased product. I am lowering the 2 stars down to a 1 star.

06/07/13 UPDATE: ONE VERY WEAK POINT - BUT ABLE TO BE FIXED - Since I never heard from Cafejo, I decided to try and fix the broken blade. I was able to make it work by using a stainless steel sheet metal screw, with a thread depth of exactly one inch. It can actually be a bit longer, but then the screw would interfere with those plastic re-usable K-Cup pods. When threaded thru the original hole of the K-Cup basket from the bottom, this screw acts as a very strong "punch". It will NOT seal the hole it punches, because it is going in straight without "screwing" thru the hole it makes. The threads kind of act as a channel for the coffee to flow thru. There are also 3 additional holes in the bottom of the basket, and it seems to work just fine (with absolutely NO THANKS to Cafejo). JUST BE SURE TO USE A STAINLESS STEEL SCREW.

08/16/13 - It seems Cafejo read my review and commented on it, and asked me to call them. I left a message on the number they gave me and apparently the owner of the company, named Pat, returned my call. He apologised for the problems and said that they had addressed the issues and took my info to send me new parts. I received the parts today and it does look like they now have a heavier duty blade. I was also sent a spare "top punch" that is at the bottom of the water cylinder.

PLEASE NOTE - per my 6/7 update, I HAVE BEEN USING THIS PRESS. I was simply disappointed that Cafejo did not contact me from the message I left via their website. Except for the blade breaking, the sytem is fantastic. Using K-Cups, it makes a wonderful cup of coffee. I encourage you to give this system a try, and if you have any problems, contact them (but I don't suggest you use the "contact" function on their website).

title: WAS A GREAT IMPROVEMENT OVER OUR ANTENNA'S ORIGINAL AMPLIFIER - UPDATE 07/27/18
text:
A little background, several months ago I purchased a 70 mile HD indoor antenna. I needed it to get over the air broadcasts as I was planning on "cutting the cord". Most of the channels I wanted came in and were pretty good in clear sunny weather. Add some rain or clouds and the 2 main channels I needed would cut out and get pixelly. I was using a Magnavox DVR to do over the air recordings and fairly often,, we couldn't watch what was recorded due to constant breakup. That 70 mile antenna came with an amplifier, but didn't seem to help. I read some antenna reviews trying to find a better one and some reviewer referred to this Winegard amplifier as one of the better ones. So I ordered it and it came today and the weather happened to be rainy. The 2 channels I needed were pixelly and as soon as I replaced the original antenna amp with the Winegard the 2 channels instantly cleared up, even in the rain. The TV and antenna were in the center of the house, NOT near any window or outside wall. What a joy to behold. I tested the 2 channels on and off all day and only got an occasional pixel blip that did NOT affect the viewing. One minor thing, the included AC adapter was NOT as pictured, but was a straight design, not the 90 degree adapter shown. NOT A PROBLEM -- Just an FYI.

An additional note - I was going to buy another one for our upstairs TV that had the same problem with those 2 channels. (That TV had an amplified 50 mile antenna mounted on an outside wall). Instead I decided I would try adding the downstairs replaced amplifier in line with the existing one a little further down the line just before the coax went into the back of that DVR. So I had the antenna, its amplifier, 3 feet of coax, then the now extra antenna amp, then into the back of the DVR. VOILA ... none of the channels exhibited any pixelling, they all cleared up. All opinions were that you could not do this, You can't put 2 amps in line, but if it works, it works. Go figure.

UPDATE 07/27/18 - It was working great, but then some of the shows we taped showed lots of breakup. Viewing the channel live that we really wanted, (and was working great with this amplifier) , we could see the pixelating even in good weather. Not sure what happened, But this amplifier ultimately did not achieve the permanent improvement it first displayed. We are back to square one. Removed 2 stars.

Now we have excellent reception, but only for that room. BUT ... the Recast DVR links to ALL the Fire TV sticks in the house. WE NOW HAVE A "WHOLE HOUSE" DVR. We can use any TV to view and record all the received channels. There is even a guide for the channels (but for now it seems to go only a few days ahead). You can high light a show in the guide to record, with options to adjust start and end times, choose the single episode or record the series (with the option for just new or all episodes), and also select the recording quality (lower quality, less space needed on the storage volume). We chose the 1 TB 4 channel recording model, so I doubt if we'll run low on capacity. At this time we opted NOT to link up the voice commands thru Alexa, so I can't say much about that feature. All we use are the present Fire Stick remotes, and they do just fine. We are SO happy with this Amazon Recast DVR. It solved ALL of our OTA viewing and recording problems. AND NO MONTHLY FEE !!!!

text:
I have been waiting years for the newest version that has replaceable batteries in the garage door transmitter. Just received and installed it, real easy. The garage door unit needs to be installed so the transmitter sits vertically (when door is closed). The transmitter comes with velcro (one piece on the transmitter and one piece for the door). This makes removing the transmitter for battery replacement much easier. As the door is opened, the vertical panel will go horizontal, bringing the transmitter with it. I am assuming some kind of "tilt" switch activates the transmitter and the signal will activate the receiver. The receiver comes with a small AC adapter and the receiver sits vertically. Very visible red LED's will flash with a beeping when activated. If you are like me, I sometimes work for periods with the garage door open, so the beeping can be annoying in the house. There is an option to disable the beep. We have the receiver in a prominent location, so just the very noticeable LEDs are enough to remind us the garage door is open. I am very happy with this newest version. If I find any long term problems I will update.

02/17/22 UPDATE - The system has been working very well. It stopped working after about 10 months after install. The problem was the batteries died. So I guess for my usage, the batteries will last about10 months. I installed the garage door sensing unit with Velcro, so popping it off was easy. The battery door is held in place with a very tiny phillips screw. So a mini screw driver would be handy. I bought extra batteries when I bought the unit, so I had them on hand, and it took me all of 10 minutes to do the deed. STILL VERY HAPPY WITH THE SYSTEM.

title: An indispensible tool for runners!
text:
UPDATE APRIL 2017: I had given this 5 stars, but that's changed now that Garmin Connect no longer recognizes the 305, which makes the data far less useful. After reading entries on various sites it appears that's why I can no longer upload data from the 305 to Garmin Connect. My computer sees the 305 but Garmin Connect won't find it. Several months ago I used e___ (the big auction website) to find someone to replace the battery for cheap, but now wish I hadn't. What does it say about a company when the try to force former customers to buy new equipment before it should be necessary!

I've been using the 305 for several years now, pretty much since it was first released, and I love it. I had an older and cheaper model previously, which was okay, but the 305 is a major leap forward.

I run 5 times per week, from a few miles to 12 or 15 each run. Using the Garmin over time I've been able to establish a consistency I didn't think I was capable of. That means that if I'm on an easy, mindless run my per-mile time is always within a few seconds of my norm. On days I want to push harder I can take a quick glance at my wrist to check my pace and confirm that I'm running within my limits. One of the things I really like is that if I'm running well and trying for a PR I can check my time and pace and make the needed adjustments.

Normally the 305 finds the needed satellites quickly, although once in a while it takes a bit longer. That means it's helpful to remember to turn it on a couple of minutes before you want to start just in case it's one of those days when the satellites are hiding.

The transfer of data to the website and your PC is fast and easy, as is charging. You can even watch your run afterwards by means of a marker that moves along your route on a map, coupled with speed and other data. Pretty cool.

So far as I can tell the heart-rate monitor is accurate. I've got a heart-rate app on my phone (it uses the camera against your skin to measure your pulse) and the two have been in agreement when I've compared them. (Of course, the app doesn't link to the other running data.)

Bottom line, the 305 is a great tool to help improve your running, and it's very easy to learn and to use. Well worth the price.

title: A user friendly microscope that captures great images!

That took 3 or 4 minutes, assembly 20 seconds, and I was taking photos of what I was seeing within a few minutes. There's not much of a learning curve, impressive for something that provides such powerful images.

To view items you use one knob for the general view you want, then make fine focus adjustments with another. You can elevate the eyepiece for a broad view or bring it all the way down for the tightest view possible. By means of a USB cable you instantly see on your computer screen whatever the microscope is seeing, meaning you don't use an eyepiece but instead can see the real-time image as large as you wish on your screen. There's a variable light adjustment in-line on the cable, as well as a trigger/shutter control for the camera. The shutter control being on the cable means there's no jostling of the image as you take photos. You use the software to organize photo directories, etc.., on the same screen that you use to view images.

In a period of about 15 minutes I examined a penny, a piece of a dried flower, a piece of glass jewelry, a postage stamp, and some grains of pepper. (Things I had immediately at hand.) I'm posting a photo of each of those things in the same order.

I'll be playing around with this more over the days to come and will update my review if I think of things to add. Meanwhile, I highly recommend this microscope for school kids of any age or anyone with an inquisitive mind!

title: Great image quality, tons of games, good functionality
text:
This player has a lot going for it, but also some things to be aware of. The picture quality is very good, as is the sound. As other reviewers have said, the TV function is all but non-existent for US residents since the mandated switch from analog. I think TV is still possible, but I believe it would require extra equipment. My recommendation therefore is to consider purchasing this item based on everything but the TV application.

The detailed user’s manual is in English that sometimes requires a bit of interpretation. It’s not bad, just off enough that there are some passages that require a bit of thought. For example, under the explanation of the double arrow button on the remote control it says, “Under DVD playback, backward quickly, looking for specific objectives broadcast.” Given the context I haven’t found anything that couldn’t be fairly readily figured out, just be aware it’s not written in perfect English. Some of it is actually a bit entertaining!

I’m not really a video game player so I can’t say much about the games, but I can tell you there are 300 games on the provided disk! Random selections: Tetris, Majong, Iron Fighter, 9142, Mario, Circus, Battle City, and obviously too many more to list. They’ve got the expected (fairly basic) graphics, and all the sounds you’ve heard in arcades. (Thankfully, there’s a headphone jack.)

The user’s manual does have lots of information, but I had to find my way through the system with some experimentation. In fact, it’s the issues with the manual, that for me at least meant some frustration, that are my only real concern with this player. Frustration isn’t the ideal introduction to a new piece of equipment, but ultimately it doesn’t get in the way of its operation. The functions all seem to work just fine, and there’s no set-up required, although you can adjust various audio and visual settings, inputs, etc. I’ve got no criticisms whatsoever of the DVD player. It’s intuitive, works well, and looks and sounds great. The swivel function works very well. It moves easily yet also stays as you positioned it. The remote control has extensive functionality with 34 keys, but it’s not complicated. In addition to the controls on the top of the base, there are is also the game port, a USB port, the DC power input, an SD card slot, HDMI port, headphone port, AV out and AV in, and the regular TV port.

I can’t address every aspect of this player in a single review, so I recommend reading various other reviews as well as the answered questions. There’s a lot of good information there, e.g., using the player as a second monitor for a laptop; something I never would have realized.

I’m used to the heft of a laptop, and this player is very different and much lighter, yet I don’t see anything that appears fragile. I’ve been using the player for a six days now, so although I can’t speak to its longevity, so far everything works well. It’s hard to take photos of screen images that do a screen justice, but I’ll upload some photos that will hopefully convey the screen’s clarity. Please keep in mind that the Amazon system further reduces image quality.

The player was provided to me in exchange for my honest review, and I’ve tried hard to present a balanced perspective, good and bad, and the 4 stars I’ve awarded were earned, with the caveats as noted above.
