update: 1.5 years of working and now every time someone uses the doorbell it goes offline. Ring said the doorbell itself is not functioning correctly and offered me $100 credit. They will not replace it, and they want me to spend another $150 to replace a product that only lasted 1.5 years!

NO!

DO NOT GET IT, THEY DO NOT STAND BEHIND THEIR PRODUCTS!

________
it took nothing to install but a bit to get it working consistently and quickly on my network. i was not impressed with ring support they suggested a repeater (I could see from my router the connection was more than adequate - and the live video was good once it connected.)

the issue i had was connection time. luckily someone here mentioned putting it on it's own named network, and ring mentioned not to name the repeater the same thing as your wifi networks - i reconfigured my wifi so the 2.4 and 5.0 networks had different names put all the computers on the 5.0 and it is fast as heck now (no repeaters needed). they obviously don't have network people on their support lines i tried to explain i did networking and had already checked connectivity but they follow a script period.

as for working well YES IT'S GREAT.

i love being able to adjust the motion area - as my wind chimes were setting it off and i just went around them. the night vision is great too.

there is a bit of a delay for video and it could be more "active" farther out but i'm probably the only one who wants 100+ feet away to be in my motion area (i have a really long driveway). i love seeing who is in the driveway and it makes me more secure (plus i know if the bear goes accross my driveway i'll know)

the physical install was not hard at all (and i don't do electrical) finding the right circuit breaker took forever (basement was the key -- apparently there is a "box" down there for your doorbell so the breaker is based on that box not your chime) ... if you can use a screwdriver you can do this it is that easy.

The signals going through these cables are digital. There will be no improved picture or audio quality going with a name brand. Digital signaling like this works, or does not work. Do yourself a favor and buy the AmazonBasics cables and don't waste your money on cables from Best Buy, or Monster, or whoever.

title: Just about perfect
text:
My notebook's built-in ethernet port never really worked right. I was using an Ethernet PC Card to plug in and gain a working Ethernet connection, but I managed to mangle the pins inside the slot and it stopped working as well.

But wireless has always worked fine, so as long as I am at a hotel with in-room free wireless, no worries. Unfortunately, many hotels have only wired ehternet in their rooms.

So I picked up on of these TRENDnets on a lark. I figured it would be complicated to set up; not so. Instead of plugging the ethernet cable into my laptop, I instead plug the cable into the TRENDnet. The TRENDnet requires electricity, which can be provided by an AC adapter or - great idea - a provided special USB cable (although using the USB cable obviously ties down my laptop to whatever hotel desk the ethernet cable happens to be at - but that's not a limitation, it's an option).

The fantasic news is that once you do this, the TRENDnet appears as an ordinary WiFi hotspot on my notebook's wireless network setup. Since I am using this on somebody else's wired network, I have no need for setting special security levels or passwords; it simply works. I will defer to other reviewers for using the TRENDnet to set up a wireless access point at home or business where security might be a concern. For my purposes, it is almost perfect. My only gripe deals with power: the AC adapter should have the now-commonplace swapout plug pins for U.S. and common European outlets (it has fixed flat plugs for U.S./Japan only); and the power jack on the TRENDnet itself should use the virtually universal mini-USB, so even if you forget or lose your special cable, any mini-USB cable would work.

I also want to clarify a statement from a prior poster concerning compatibility with Apple products. As I said, the TrendNET works straight out of the box; there is no setup, configuration, or installation to get it to work. It therefore will work with any computer, whether PC, Apple, Linux, whatever; if your computer can access wireless networks, it will work with the TrendNET. So it is not entirely true that it "won't work with an Apple." However, if you want to do anything beyond simply connecting - setting up security settings, or firewalls, or changing Wireless names or IDs, ec., this will have to be done through your computer, in which case other reviewers who have actually tried setting it up would be more authorative.

title: Close to perfect for the price
text:
Will it illuminate a bridge a hundred yards away? Nope.

Will it rotate in any direction so you can bounce flash off the ceiling when you are doing "fashion" angled pictures? Nah-uh.

Can you shoot continuous shots with the flash keeping up as fast as your memory card? No way.

It's not a $900 professional flash. But the performance it gives for the price is extraordinary. Really, the only things I would add are the ability to use rechargeables that would charge in-unit (i.e. charge the cameras, charge the flash); the ability to run off the camera's power if the battery is dead (but that might be a limitation of the camera that precludes such a feature); and the ability to at least rotate 90 degrees so you could bounce when taking a picture in the portrait position (you can of course bounce off a wall, but the results are, well, unpredictable). Results out to 15 feet are outstanding, out to 30 feet not bad, and its integration with Nikon DSLR's logic is incredible. I remember the Canon AE-1 (dating myself here), the world's first "automatic" camera with TTL metering, and how exciting it was when "automatic" flashes appeared as accessories. Well, "semi-automatic," as they still required dialing in numbers. I don't know how, but between the Nikon and this flash, they figure everything out together. You set your desired brightness as if you were dialing in an index number (assuming you want to even bother doing that much), the duo figure out how far away the target is, and adjusts everything accordingly. The instructions warn that they don't promise consistent results when bouncing - and you will bounce, that's the whole point of such a flash (no more red-eye, ever!) - but to be honest we've had nothing but excellent results even bouncing off high ceilings. The unit even powers down when you turn off the camera so you don't waste batteries. You won't do continuous shooting but you'll get a shot every five seconds or better with fresh batteries.

One thing I was concerned about was lens shadow - we have the zoom autostabilizing lens and it causes a shadow when using the the pop-up flash at all but one zoom level. Not a problem at all. If you use the autostabilizer or one of the longer focal length zooms with a lens hood then you might have issues. Of course, if you're bouncing, then by definition the problem goes away.

One last beef, which is not a limitation of the flash but rather then D40 camera, is that the camera's software does not check if an external flash is attached when you hit the popup button, so it is possible to deploy the popup which then smacks into the external. I'm not sure what happens if you were to try to take a picture with both flashes up and on - it would be great if they actually all synched together, but since the D40 pop-up is not able to fully deploy with this flash sitting on top, I seriously doubt it.

title: Works. Period.
text:
YMMV if you are running anything other than Windows 7 with Media center. But if you are and you have cable TV: plug it in. Start Media Center and let Media Center do through its normal TV tuner wizard (Tasks, Settings, TV, TV Signal if you've previously set up Media Center). Whenever Media Center asks you to make a decision, stick with the default Windows suggestion.

This device is recognized instantly by Windows 7, no CDs or drivers or downloads. Do you understand the difference between analog cable, digital cable, 720p, 1080i, and ClearQAM? Yes? No? Good news: the AVerTV does all of them and Media Center will activate everything for you. Even as a tech-savvy user, I found it refreshing to see a device that simply worked without me having to know all sorts of techical details. And I will tell you that very few USB tuners will do both analog and digital, and fewer still (none to my knowledge other than this one) will do them both and automatically set both of them up.

Oh, and they (I liked it so much I bought a second one as a present) arrived nicely boxed in two days on free Super Saver. Why not five stars? It is sufficient bulky that on many laptops it will block nearby connectors. On the other hand, a short USB extender cable was including to address just this issue (I would have given the product 4-1/2 stars but that wasn't an Amazon option).

One "downside" to having a tuner that automatically does both analog and digital: this of course depends on your cable provider, but you will probably wind up with duplicate channels (analog crappy pictures, digital better pictures, digital HD amazing pictures). Spend a few minutes going through Media Center guide and killing the lower-resolution duplicates (right-click on the channel name and select "disable channel"). Pearl of wisdom: don't kill a channel just because ther Guide shows a higher-resolution version, actually open that channel up and make sure it plays. The reason is that the HD channel may be encrypted and, while Media Center has correctly identified it as a channel transmitting a signal, you may not be able to actually watch it (in which case it's the HD channel you want to disable).

The Windows 7 idea is probably more versatile, but I won't ever need the ability to run different things on each monitor - just my recorded TV.

It works, but once in a while Vista will get confused and reset itself to 800x600. Oddly, it seems to work exactly the same way with and without the external power supply - I had a terrible picture on the downstairs monitor and figured I was losing signal through the long run so I reconnected the power supply to no avail. It turned out to be the monitor's fault, unable to recognize that it was a PC signal, and when I connected the splitter to the computer's DVI output through a DVI-HDMI adapter the problem was instantly fixed regardless of whether or not the splitter was plugged into power. On the other hand, my living room monitor always had an intermittent problem "waking up" when the PC resumed and that issue appears to have gone away, as the splitter seems to "wake up" the monitor when the monitor is turned on - you can see the splitter's LEDs blinking as it tries to lock onto the monitor.

title: Odd quirks - but amazing value
text:
Received this as a Xmas present. It has several quirks ranging from puzzling to frustrating, but for the price it simply cannot be beat. If you are okay with these quirks then don't hesitate!

Obviously if you want things like Bluetooth or live traffic, you'll need a more capable machine.

1. It does not accept SD cards, but instead has more than enough memory to handle all your maps. Here's why this might be important: when you get a map of say Europe, it can come on a DVD or on a read-only SD card. The DVD gets registered to your GPS and ONLY that GPS; you cannot move it to another GPS, ever, if you buy an additional GPS or your current one breaks and Garmin sends you a replacement. The SD cards can be freely moved from one GPS to another.

2. Fr some bizarre reason, your Favorites (stored locations) are contained within a tree of selections based on how you programmed them. For example, if you taught the GPS a location by entering its address, that's under one folder. If you taught the GPS a location by tapping on the screen and selecting "remember this location," that's a different folder. So when you want to navigate somewhere you've programmed, you cannot simply click "Go to" and click on the location, you have to continue to click through a series of folders (there is an "all" selection but even then, it's an extra click). Why on Earth did Garmin do this? Did they receive a flood of letters from customers complaining that they needed to segregate their locations based on how they programmed them into the unit? Is there a single customer who actually finds a benefit to this "feature"?

3. Like virtually all new GPS units, this receives power through mini USB and, like many (but not all) recent Garmin units, this GPS gets easily confused. Better units (and older Garmins) look to see if the USB data lines are actually connected before switching to "programming" mode, but this unit and most current Garmins simply examine the line voltage; if it's anything other than what's expected, it assumes it's connected to a computer and enters programming mode. In other words: plug in the GPS using the SUPPLIED lighter cord and it works, but use a different lighter cord and it enters data mode and cannot operate as a GPS. My Ford Escape's lighter jack is always on so using the stock adapter, the Garmin would never switch off (it can be manually turned off by holding down a recessed button). So I used a USB cable to connect to the Ford Synch's USB jack: data mode. I cut open the cable and physically snipped the two data wires, leaving ONLY the electrical line: data mode. I wound up solving the problem by using a Garmin electrical adapter and plugging it into the Escape's 110V dash outlet, which does switch off with the car.

4. This is a complaint not specific to this unit, but is true of modern Garmins in general: if you zoom in while navigating, the moment you stop zooming the unit will decide that you shouldn't be looking at that level of detail and will instantly zoom back out. That is indeed very frustrating, I basically have to keep tapping the zoom icon to see the next street coming up (and, I should add, WHILE DRIVING). Older Garmins know that when the user zooms in, the user should get the last word.

5. The daytime map uses black to outline major roads and light gray to outline side streets. Most of the map is white, and the side streets are white. So a white street on a white background bordered by light gray. The net result of this is that side streets are effectively invisible (certainly not clearly visible during a quick glance). Older Garmins allowed the user to choose colors, and other current Garmins use contrasting colors (my Zumo uses red streets on a yellow background, now that's really visible). This effect is less when using the 3D map (since streets near you are wider than those in the distance) but makes the map almost unusable in 2D mode. This would have been a showstopper for me, but I have come to live with having the unit always in nighttime mode which has no such contrast issue.

6. Terrible battery life; maybe 30 minutes of continuous operation tops. But you didn't buy it to go hiking with anyway, right?

Gee, sounds like I hate it, doesn't it? And if it was $300 that'd be true. But it has a VERY large screen, it's quite accurate (only one major mistake with the map in three months), pretty fast rerouting (and without that pointless and annoying "recalculated" announcement - thank you Garmin!), weighs next to nothing, and the silly split-screen showing an almost photo-realistic image of the next lane turns out to be pretty damned useful once you try it.

For not much more than a hundred bucks, I can most definitely live with its quirks.

title: WARNING!!!
text:
This review is not for Linux experts, so please do not respond "yes you can do that" followed by a highly technical explanation. This review is targeted towards the typical home user, like me. Not explained in the product description is that this unit installs the operating system into a Linux partition and formats the remainder of the drive in Linux. Why does that matter? Because when the unit fails (not "if," because all hardware fails eventually) you cannot simply pop the drive out and read its contents from a Windows or Mac computer. I tried doing exactly that and while with a lot of figuring was eventually able to "mount" the drive under Windows XP, I could not actually read anything off of it dispite trying several freeware Linux readers. Not some complicated RAID-5 striped setup, mind you, but just a single simple drive.

I am particularly sensitive to this issue having gone through a nightmare three years ago with a Netgear SC101; that also formatted its drive with a non-Windows (and in that case, completely non-standard) operating system, and when it failed I had to buy another SC101 just to get my data back. I am sure experienced owners here will respond that the Synology is more reliable (but ALL hardware fails eventually) and that this does use a "standard" format and can be read by someone technically proficient; but that's why I'm giving it three stars and not one. The unit will format an external drive in FAT or NTFS (i.e. standard Windows/Mac stuff) but only via USB 2.0, which is way behind the times (now everything is USB 3 or eSATA, many times faster).

Also somewhat disappointing was that I had to install software on my PC to get the Synology to work. I was really hesitant about that because the Netgear required special (and very buggy) software to be installed on every PC that accessed it. Fortunately in this case, the software is only used to load the provided Linux system onto the Synology's hard drive and from that point forward you access it from any computer via web browser. Still kind of disconcerting that I have to actually install software on my computer, I'd be more comfortable if the program simply ran without installing.

Before returning it, I did check out the extensive features supported and they are impressive. So in conclusion for someone technically comfortable with messing around with Unix Roots and such, perhaps a great bargain - but someone looking for simple, rock-solid and foolproof storage should probably look for something that allows storage to a format natively recognized by Windows for when disaster strikes.

title: Almost completely "wow"
text:

"Supposedly" allows sharing of tuners (and recorded TV?) across networks with other Windows 7 computers...but I haven't tried that.

Cons: Continuous "No Tuner" errors. Fixed by updating firmware, which was very easy once you know how (Start, all programs, Centon, Update) but oddly the update tab within Media Center, where you'd expect this, has the ability to see the installed version and the latest version on Ceton's web site but frustratingly no ability to do anything about it. I suspect that many if not all of the negative reviews did not have the latest firmware...since this is critical to its ability to function properly, it is mysterious why Ceton would not have made it easy and obvious to update from within Media Center, which is where by definition a Ceton user will be. I suspect it's just an oversight, but a damned odd one considering how refined and well thought out every other aspect of the hardware and software is. Would have been five stars if not for this.

Other Thoughts: Long time owner of an ATI TV Wonder (e.g. <http://www.amazon.com/Wonder-Digital-Cable-Tuner-Ntsc/dp/B000VOG04A/ref=sr_1_1?ie=UTF8&qid=1339517514&sr=8-1&keywords=ati+tv+wonder+cablecard>), both internal and then (after I fried it) USB. The ATI is extremely cable company friendly and user hostile (and of course only one channel). Everything about the ATI was secretive and difficult requiring special knowledge ATI won't part with to troubleshoot. The Ceton takes the opposite approach with easy, no fuss installation and boatloads of information screens. Most importantly, the ATI was designed for Vista and its oppressively draconian Digital Rights Management rules (anything whatsoever not exactly as expected = no you're not going to record that show) whereas the Ceton works with the more liberal Windows 7 - meaning few (if any) shows missed because a signal was weak or you turned off the monitor at the wrong time and the tuner decided you're trying to illegally copy "Mad Men." And of course, unlike the ATI the Ceton does not require support built into the BIOS of your PC, meaning it can be installed on any halfway decent computer running Windows 7 rather than having to be installed only by the computer manufacturer.

10/29/15 update: I replaced this with a Silicon Dust HomeRun because it keeps freezing and losing track that it exists - without a CableCard. I cancelled cable and just kept Internet, handing my CableCard back in. It turned out that a) any cable at all (including Internet) still comes with local channels and b) the Ceton is REALLY BAD at receiving them - I doubt they even tested the tuner without a CableCard installed. Two-thirds of shows not recorded due to Tuner Not Found errors. Quitting Media Center, re-running the Ceton setup, then going back to Media Center and re-running TV setup fixes the problem for N shows, where N = some random number from 1 to at most 4. Not lowering my star rating because it really is very good when a CableCard is installed; but don't be fooled by the marketing hype that it works with ClearQAM - this is not the tuner you're looking for.

title: Maps of Ancient Rome
text:
I won't repeat the many other posts about the nuvi's performance in any detail; it is indeed compact, bright (not bright enough for motorcycle really...but that's true of all the "motorcycle" GPS units as well and it's as bright or brighter than any of the dedicated motorcycle units on the market), easy to use, and quick on the draw. The mounting absolutely sucks for a motorcycle (not positively secured like a Rider or Zumo) but, unless you are a serious offroader you won't care - while the excellent long-life battery adds some heft, the days of GPS units being so heavy that they need to be chained down are happily a thing of the past and the car-style clip-on mount works fine. You'll need to come up with your own means of mounting (I got a $3 RAM ball - make sure it's nuvi-sized - and mounted it right under the bug screen; and the "Arkon GN032," sold here on Amazon, worked great on my bicycle).

But one star off for the extraordinary soft screen - I mean soft like wax paper. It almost immediately got major gouges in the surface from being tossed in a bag with my keys. No apparent ill effect but so deep and large that I can plainly see it when operating.

And a big star off for maps that - well, "outdated" doesn't quite suffice. Constantly wrong when it comes to Points of Interest. My local Home Depot isn't listed and it's been there for eight years. Restaurants that moved six years ago are still listed in the old location. Not paying for the latest information might be a cost-cutting decision that the GPS developers made - but not paying for the previous version of the previous version of the previous version is ludicrous.

One final note: the high-capacity battery in this unit pulls a fair amount of power. As I learned the hard way, if you operate it with a cell phone charger it will operate fine but not charge the battery; use the provided car charger cable and if you use an AC adapter make sure it is specifically for a GPS, not a cell phone.

title: New and improved
text:
This is now the third Powerline set I have bought over the past dozen years. The first one was literally the size of a brick and supposed to run at 1mbps, but two out of three times they wouldn't even find each other. Which was disappointing, considering I paid one hundred dollars for each brick.

The next set was the size of a large travel adapter and rated at 54mbps. I could regularly get 16mbps but it would still constantly disconnect. Those quickly went into the trash as improving wireless router technology almost immediately eliminated the need for them.

So when I purchased a new Blu-Ray player that not only does updates via web but also has a built-in Netflix player, it was with considerable trepidation that I bought one of the new TP-Links. They are tiny; they come boxed with a complete set, including patch cords in case you don't already have a box full; and they work. You don't even need to be connected to anything to pair them up, just plug them in and press the Pair button, and watch the green LEDs confirm they have found one another. Don't know the exact speed they're running at, since I don't have them connected to a computer whose tools I could use to measure speed; but they certainly have no problem keeping up with hi-definition TV bandwidth.

While they'll of course never be as fast or as cheap or as reliable than a plain old wire, and for most situations wireless has exceeded what these can do, I am in awe of how much they have improved in every way (faster, smaller, more reliable, easier to pair, and much MUCH cheaper); and when an Ethernet cable is the only option and you can't or won't run one...this is the way to go. Recommendable, at last.

title: The good, the bad, and the neutral
text:
The good: extremely light, good picture. Touch works very well. Love the fold-out stand, which worked perfectly for me - I wanted this to serve as a temporary second monitor when I play Flight Simulator (so I can display my virtual aircraft's control panel next to me and actually change my instruments and switches by physically touching them - works terrific, and although I have to set my monitors up so that Windows thinks my secondary monitor is the primary each time, that's a Microsoft thing and not in any way this monitor's fault) but when I'm not playing, I fold in the stand and return the monitor to my VESA-compatible wall mount that I use to broadcast Netflix to through my Netgear Push2TV. One of the smallest monitors out there that's true 1080P.

The bad: A touch small for the wall application, but that's a matter of taste. You've also read other reviews about how tinny the speakers are (true) and at least one reviewer recommending that you plug an external set of speakers into the monitor. That reviewer should have actually tried that before making that recommendation, because unfortunately it is quite impossible: the 1/8" audio jack on the back of the monitor is a stereo INPUT not an OUTPUT. There is no way to hook a set of speakers up to this monitor, and it needs it pretty badly. Audio in is far less important since it already receives audio through the HDMI connection (which also carries audio) and fewer and fewer users are going to need a separate audio in, but the poor speakers demand an audio out for any serious multimedia application. Lacks scaling options, which are a standard feature on just about every other HDMI monitor, but which is becoming less important as "underscanning/overscaling" becomes a forgotten technology so probably not a concern.

The neutral: glossy screen sure to show fingerprints, but that's true of all touchscreens. Powered by a small power brick instead of a cord directly in; I prefer the simplicity of a single cord but I took a couple of sticky tabs and just glued the little brick to the back of the monitor, so for all practical purposes it's the same as having a cord plugging directly in.

title: Perfect solution (but a bit too bright)
text:
Lots of gizmos that allow different sources to be connected to a single monitor, a capability that is rapidly becoming moot as more and more monitors are shipping with multiple HDMI inputs. Not so many gizmos that do the opposite, allowing a single source to switch between different monitors. This particular gizmo does both, and does it well.

To be extremely, exceedingly, absolutely clear: you will not be able to watch video on two monitors at the same time with this. While it is theoretically possible, most of the video in the world that is flowing through an HDMI cable happens to be copyrighted and therefore copy protected (HDCP). There are schemes to allow HDCP video on two monitors at the same time (my Kindle Fire in combination with my Netgear Push2TV does it) but a) only under certain circumstances and b) only in the way the copyright owner wants it, not the way you want it. (For example, I can see video on my Kindle and on one and only one monitor - the Push2TV still doesn't allow the signal to go to more than one monitor.) So if you want to display an HDMI signal on two monitors at once, this device won't do it, and you may have to lower your expectations because of the technological limitations mandated by copyright laws.

For me, I usually have my HTPC connected to both my living room TV and a monitor down in the gym. No, I still can't watch both at once, but Windows 7 makes it easy to instantly switch between them. But I sometimes play Flight Simulator and use a little touchscreen monitor to display the instruments. It's a hassle to have to dig behind the HTPC to switch cables, so the Portta with a little 1-foot cable is just the ticket. I use the Windows-P key combination to toggle to "extend desktop," push the button on the front of the Portta, and now I have a live HDMI jack I can plug into. When I'm finished playing, I just reverse the procedure and I can still watch Mad Men in the living room or P90X in the gym.

Using the Portta to do the opposite - to allow one monitor to switch between two different HDMI sources, say a cable box and a BluRay player - is just as easy. Be aware, however, that the Portta does not "automatically" switch between sources (so for example if you turn the power on to the BluRay player, the Portta does not recognize that you want to watch BluRay and switch over to that source). There are other switches that do that, some sold here on Amazon. As I said, this particular functionality is rapidly becoming moot: even my little 20" touchscreen came with two HDMI inputs.

One minus, but not enough to deduct a whole star: Portta has unfortunately followed the fashionable trend of having a really, really bright blue LED shining into your eyes. As in, bright enough to read by. I will probably get around to putting a piece of electrical tape over it.

title: Lower noise, maybe, but not low noise
text:
Compared to the stock external fans that came with my wine cooler (yes, they use these things for stuff other than tower PCs), it was indeed a little quieter. But when the wine cooler is first cooling down and the fan is kicked into high gear, it was many times louder than the other fan I purchased (http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B005ZF65E0/ref=oh_aui_detailpage_o01_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1) for the other zone. My internal fans I used 80mm units from here on Amazon that had their own mini-speed controller, but I couldn't find a completely adjustable 92mm. In any event, even when doing the initial cooldown the other fan was quieter, and upon reaching temperature setpoint the other fan really was silent while the Artic F9 was audible, although certainly quiet.

12/13/14 update: sigh, there is no perfect solution. Now that's it's colder, the fans in my wine cooler work a lot less hard and often come to a complete stop. The "other" fan emits a whiny buzz when stopped while the Artic is dead silent. So pick your poison, one is quieter when turning, and the Artic is quieter when not turning. If your fan may be going so slowly as to stop completely, get the Artic and save some money.

That does not earn the Artic any additional stars, but it did cost its competitor a star. It did, however, earn the Artic an extra sale: I bought another one to replace the buzzy red "silent" fan, which went into the trash. Sigh...

title: Great value for the price and good value at any price
text:
It is indeed very sturdy, well-designed, and well manufactured. Bravo for an excellent piece of kit. But there are a couple of caveats a buyer needs to know.

1. This is NOT, absolutely no way, a stand that does any acrobatics. You will not be grabbing one monitor and pushing it up and grabbing the other monitor and swinging it left and down and then raising them both the same amount off the desk, that sort of thing. This is intended to be set-and-forget. The monitors do swivel and rotate and that should satisfy 95% of users; but if you want to be moving monitors around all the time, this stand is not for you. For that matter, probably any stand under $200 is not for you.

2. Not easily discernable in the picture, but the desk mount actually is two pieces. You wind up tightening down the big eye screws to secure the stand, but first you screw the two halves of the mount together. The mount has three sets of two screw holes, so you will screw those pieces together in the narrowest combination that will still clear the tabletop. This is very clever, you basically get three different mounts to accommodate anything from a thin glass desktop to a monster oak desk with a steel beam running below it.

3. The only genuinely tough part about installation is tightening the (hidden) bolt that sets the vertical angle of the monitor. It takes a LOT of force to keep the monitor from "drooping," and the included wrench is quite short. But it does work, and you might happen to have a real wrench the same size.

4. I think this would be just borderline do-able with 27" monitors. With two 24" screens, there's more than enough width, with extra left over to have them tilted in towards one another, a space between them, way forward in your face, whatever you like. A larger monitor might be limited to just side-by-side and further back from you. But it would definitely still work.

5. The manufacturer includes extra screws, extra joint covers, extra everything.

6. The only thing the manufacturer didn't include was longer VGA, HDMI, and USB cables - having so much flexibility means I ran out of cable and had to buy extensions!

title: Function depends on what you plug into it
text:
I am giving this three stars "by default" because I could not verify that it does or does not work. Learn from my lesson: if you have something that needs to plug into a DB9 connector and which requires its own driver, you are stepping way outside the realm of "plug and play" and expecting that device with its peculiar drivers and the USB-to-serial converter with its drivers to all work together is overoptimistic. In my case I have an old Wacom tablet that needs Wacom-specific software that expects a Wacom tablet to be connected directly to a serial port. I incorrectly assumed that at the hardware level the Wacom software would see the TRENDnet as simply an ordinary serial port but while the TRENDnet appeared in Device Manager as operational, the Wacom refused to recognize that a tablet was plugged in.

I have numerous TRENDnet products and always have had very good experiences with them, I suspect that I just had unrealistic expectations about different hardware and drivers from different manufacturers to all work together. If all you need is a serial port and there's nothing complicated about what you are plugging into it, this still seems like a good bet.

EDIT: Beware the one-star reviews on this product. Looking through them, many unwittingly admit right in their posts that they're using it incorrectly. This needs to go in the middle of your run - putting it at the start of the run may fail to accomplish anything since your cable can only handle a certain maximum signal, while putting it at the end will boost only whatever is left of the signal and also boost the noise. If you have a 50 foot cable that isn't working and you put this at the end of the cable, this is not going to re-create the digital information that has already been lost...giving a product one star because it failed to perform magic is unreasonable. A 25 foot on either side, or a 20 foot on one side and a 30 foot on the other side, and it would probably have had much better results.

title: Great screen, minor quibbles
text:
I was extremely nervous about this for two reasons.

1. Excessively, incredibly large number of pixels equals excessively, incredibly high likelihood of dead or stuck pixels. I hate 'em. It's...lessee...width times height...carry the one...just shy of FIVE MILLION pixels. Well, your mileage may vary, but mine had no pixel problems whatsoever. I have to stress that: not a single bad pixel out of five million. Wow.

2. Excessively, incredibly large number of pixels equals excessively, incredibly high burden on graphics adapter. Now I will admit that I had not bought a computer in a long time but my brand-new Ultrabox (formerly known as Hush PC) is a completely silent model, meaning no fans; so while it is the "newest generation" it is also not running at nearly whatever speed the latest and greatest are capable of. Didn't matter; hooked up through DisplayPort and alongside (I realize how disgusting this must sound) a partner 1920x1080P touchscreen on DVI (yes I really do use both, more on that in a moment), I'm still able to pump out full 3440x1440x60Hz and play full-screen 1080 videos without a hitch.

Having said that, there are some issues. The first is with the DisplayPort itself: I have sound piped through the Envy by default, but about one out of six times the sound instead directs through the sister monitor. Control Panel insists that the Envy is disconnected. Not disabled; disconnected. Unplugging the DisplayPort cable and plugging back in instantly solves the problem. I don't think there is going to be a retroactive fix for that, hopefully they will at least find and fix the bug causing this going forward. By the way, you could simply use HDMI but at this resolution and this version of HDMI (1.2 I believe) it will only manage 30Hz at full resolution*. For some that may be okay but kind of defeats the purpose of such a high resolution monitor. Before you ask, yes I tried running just the Envy by itself, but still about one in six times it had no audio connection. EDIT: I've now tried two different DisplayPort cables with the same issue, so it does look like this is a bug inside the Envy (if it was the video card or its drivers, that wouldn't explain why the sound still works on HDMI). UPDATE: I found a possible obscure solution on the Internet. Right-click desktop, Personalize, Screen Saver, Change Power Settings, Change plan settings (for whatever is your current setup), Change advanced power settings (look, I said it was obscure), USB settings, USB selective suspend setting, and change the setting (active > disabled or disabled > active). From what I have read, this setting that supposedly is associated with selectively sending power only to certain USB ports has its fingers in all sorts of other Windows functions, including the DisplayPort driver. The theory is that part of this routine's job is to either remember your multi-monitor arrangement or to not remember it and figure it out each time you boot. Since the Envy sends sound over DisplayPort, there's my culprit. I changed it to enabled and my problem has gone from one in six boots to one out of, oh, probably fifty times. Your mileage may vary, and if you don't use the Envy alongside other monitors or you don't use the Envy for audio, this problem may never happen to you in the first place.

*Thanks for "JMT" for inquiring about this: he explained that he was interested in connecting an XBox to an Envy. Looking at the attached screenshots, you'll see that I start out with the Envy (by itself, so nobody might get confused thinking this is because a second monitor was connected) set to full 3440x1440 resolution. Connected via DisplayPort, I go into Advanced Settings | Monitor and you see that it is set to 60Hz refresh (that's good). Next, you'll see that when connected via HDMI, 30Hz (and ONLY 30Hz) appears an a refresh option (that's bad). Finally, and in answer to JMT's question, while still connected to HDMI I changed the resolution to 1920x1080, and the refresh is back to 60Hz. So the Envy is capable of 60Hz at full resolution and capable of 60Hz on HDMI, just not both - for that, you need DisplayPort. Supposedly you can get 60Hz at full resolution over HDMI 2.0, but your O/S, cable, video card, and drivers would all have to be 2.0 (and even then, I'll believe it when I see it). By the way within the Envy's menus you can select what version of DisplayPort to use, but there is no corresponding menu item for HDMI.

My video adapter cannot put out 4K (for example if you try playing House of Cards in the new 4K format) so I can't speak to how the Envy deals with such ultrahigh resolutions, but 3440x1440 is just a tad shy of 4K anyway.

Color is generally excellent, but you get a LOT of light bleed along the bottom. Only noticeable when the entire screen is very dark; refer to attached photo and note how the light bleeds in from the bottom but only on the dark portions on either side of the color gradient graphic; this is the only situation where I see it (that photo is deliberately overexposed to emphasize the bleed). Oddly, I get a bad gamma problem when Windows is booting up (screen picture way too bright and way too little contrast) but a few seconds after displaying the desktop it fixes itself - usually. This is of course a Windows thing but it no doubt comes from Windows and the Envy handshaking and once in a great while (about 1 in 100 boots) it never does fix itself. Again, unplugging and re-plugging the DisplayPort cable does the trick.

The curve is actually really good. I thought I wanted a seriously curved monitor to get a wraparound effect. I now realize that the monitor does not appear curved at all - it looks like it is perfectly flat and straight, which of course means the curve is doing exactly what it should.

Sound is excellent, but the volume control is really annoying. It's a physical rotating wheel under the left bezel, and you have to turn it to raise the volume. And turn. And turn some more. It should be literally ten times more sensitive than it is. I just keep it cranked (no buzzing or hissing) and use Windows to control the volume.

Okay, I know you're wondering why on Earth I need a second monitor with something as huge as the Envy, so I'll explain: I play Flight Simulator, turn virtual cockpit off, and drag the instrument panel over to the other monitor and resize it to fit. Now I have an completely uninterrupted (and HUGE) view of my surroundings in front of me, and my instrument panel is on the smaller monitor - which is a touchscreen, so I can actually click buttons and spin wheels with my fingers. I use Megascenary's photorealistic (actual photographs) scenery and get good refresh rates; I have read that if I was using the autogenerated scenery that comes with Flight Simulator then I would need a much more powerful computer with a screen as big as the Envy.

Like pretty much every modern monitor, you can plug this into a USB port and use it as a USB hub/extender. But the extension USB ports are in a terrible location, about dead center of the back, requiring you to crawl around to get to them. Why not near or even along the side like other monitors?

It can be set to kill the power if the screen goes blank, so you can use your power-off screensaver or a third-party program (I use the excellent little "Wizmo" and tie it to a hotkey) and the monitor will power itself off after a few seconds. You might think all monitors do this, but it's hit and miss with some brands so I thought I'd mention it.

Running Windows 7 or 8 you can really take advantage of the "drag windows to the side and watch Windows resize window to exactly fill half the screen" feature. Looks great running two applications side-by-side and the Windows 7/8 snap-to-side feature makes it, well, a snap. One unusual use of this is if you have older programs that simply will not run in Win7 and have to run in the "Virtual XP" mode. You can drag your Windows XP Mode window over to the right side of the Envy and Windows will resize it to fill the right side of the screen - and because the Envy has so much real estate, it's like you have a complete Windows XP system sitting side-by-side with Windows 7.

EDIT: Because it's not a problem for me, I did not mention these items earlier, but in answering other Amazon customer's questions I realized that this is worth bringing up. First, be aware that the Envy comes with a fixed-height stand with only about 10 degrees of angle adjustment. It also lacks the VESA screw holes on the back to put it on a universal stand (the manual references what sounds like a kludgy adapter plate that is included "with select models" but my Envy didn't come with one so I guess it's not a select model). The height of the stand and the height of my desk worked out perfectly for me, but potentially not for you. I don't know if the Envy's competitors are adjustable or can be screwed to a separate stand; but if that's a concern for you, you might want to look into other brands. Secondly, the Envy lacks a digital audio out. (EDIT: Thanks to "Leaddog99" for pointing out to me that the 1/8" audio jack in the back of the 34C is an analog audio IN - that is truly non-obvious and, since there is no analog video - is anybody in the solar system actually going to connect a 3440x1440 monitor to a VGA/DVI adapter? - as far as I can figure, utterly useless. So for all intents and purposes, no audio in at all.) This could present a (minor) problem if you have a surround sound or other audio processor. As of this writing, it appears that nobody makes a DisplayPort adapter that will divert the audio to a separate processor. Those adapters are common (and cheap) for HDMI, but as I said you only get 30Hz refresh running HDMI and at least with my ATI video card, I cannot run both DisplayPort (for the Envy) and HDMI (for sound) at the same time - my workaround for the touchscreen was to connect the second monitor through a DVI-to-HDMI adapter, but DVI doesn't pass the sound through.*** You could of course just run audio out of your computer (if you don't have a digital audio output, there's lots of internal and external solutions out there) but that would mean an extra wire or optical cable. Not a showstopper for anyone, but if you need this capability and you are torn between the Envy and another monitor that has an audio out, possibly a reason to go with the other one.

***EDIT: Duh, of course it does, I already said that sometimes sound gets routed to the touchscreen through HDMI and that *is* via DVI on my setup. But I don't know if Windows will recognize a sound diverter as a valid HDMI output and allow you to clone displays and send sound over the DVI (if I unplug the HDMI cable from my second monitor it disappears from control panel). There's probably some obscure Windows setting to work around this; but if you need an audio out, why not just buy a monitor that already has one?

Finally, I get some horizontal tearing playing large or full-screen videos. I have not yet determined if that's the Envy or a video adapter or driver issue. It's not a showstopper in any event, only noticeable on occasion.

At this price, unless you have an older computer coupled to an older graphics adapter, you really don't have an excuse not to buy one.

I did NOT write this review in exchange for receiving this product for free. I paid for it just like anybody else. title: Works - but misleading
text:
Fairly simple setup, and works. Situation: recently "cut the cord" by canceling Cablevision and turning in the CableCard to my Ceton 4-tuner USB box. The thing is, I discovered entirely by accident that even though I no longer paid for cable TV, I actually still received the local channels - they must be included with the internet service, but Cablevision doesn't exactly go out of their way to advertise that (they would have gladly had me pay $12.95 a month for channels I already get). But even though technically I could get them, the Ceton was just terrible at receiving them; it would get confused (especially when trying to record two things at once) and required a laborious reset and rescan process. Don't get me wrong, the Ceton is a fabulous five-star device when running off CableCard, I suspect they never thought anybody would ever use it for ClearQAM cable signals and so while it technically lists QAM as one of its capabilities, it doesn't look like they put much effort into it (and yes I have all the latest drivers and firmware). I found a Microsoft Windows 7 patch whose description indicated it was what I needed, but I kept getting the helpful message "This update is not applicable."

So I replaced it with the HDHomeRun, but not without some trepidation: according to the product description, I had no reason to think it would work at all! For starters, according to the product comparison table it is SD not HD: yes, but only when you are using it wirelessly; a PC or laptop that is hardwired to the network receives glorious HD just fine. And more importantly, according to the Amazon product description it MUST be connected to an antenna. It's even repeated right on the box: Antenna >required<. Except that it's not: "antenna or television cable carrying QAM signal required" would be more accurate.

The instructions tell you to log onto SiliconDust's web site to download the drivers and set things up, so hopefully they will stay in business (I filed away the driver for a rainy day). And getting ClearQAM to work was a bit of an [undocumented] hassle: first set up the channels ON THE WEB SITE (EDIT: or, as I accidentally discovered, the Home Run program that the setup will install on your desktop), and then and only then go into Media Center and run TV signal setup, otherwise you get a Tuner Not Found error. All in all it took about an hour to set up, although most of that time consisted of the Web Site and then Media Center scanning for channels and I didn't have to be in front of the PC during that time. And worth the effort: unlike the Ceton, the HomeRun instantly switches from channel to channel and it has thus far faithfully recorded my local shows. (EDIT: once in a great while it pops up a "cannot record" or "tuner busy" message even though only one other thing was being recorded or watched. I have Media Center set to start recording several minutes in advance and while the message is a bit disconcerting, so far I don't think it has actually failed to record a show, I think it just keeps trying until whatever the error is clears itself.) title: Two years and dead
text:
Two years of moderate use, database access perhaps an hour a day, in a desktop (no moving/jarring), and dead. So dead, unrecognized in Administrative Tools | Computer Management, connecting it via a USB adapter gives a never-ending installing driver, shows up during boot in the SATA adapter's display but Windows 7 just hangs. Sometimes on USB it will be "recognized" and provides a drive name consisting of a long string of random characters (but still does not appear in Computer Management or Explorer).

I've read FAQs from Micron (the maker of Crucial drives), updated its firmware (which had to be done in DOS, using an ISO image burned to CD to create a bootable CD since Windows won't recognize the drive), downloaded the "Crucial Executive" software (which also failed to see the drive), repeatedly cycled the power on for two hours and off for five minutes to reactivate the firmware (apparently a common problem with Crucial drives - as I feared, my older M500 also subsequently died and this power cycling revived it, at least long enough to copy everything off of it), and the best I could do was to occasionally have Windows pop up a drive found message followed by a could not format error (and still not appearing in Device Manager or Disk Management). Since the drive is recognized by the BIOS during bootup, on a hunch I tried booting from an Acronis Backup CD and sure enough, the files appeared; as I type this I am attempting to have Acronis "back up" (with the intention to immediately "restore") the files. How frustrating is that? The files aren't gone, but neither Windows nor the software from the SSD manufacturer can find them.

EDIT: Upgrading from two to three stars, as I now strongly suspect that the drive(s) did not fail on their own. A few weeks later, the entire computer stopped turning on, which turned out to be a bad power supply. The clue was the Micron FAQ about the power cycling, which is described by the FAQ as a way to sometimes bring a Crucial drive back after it has been exposed to inconsistent power.

But three stars is the most they'll get - my much older STEC drive (my swap drive - heavy use!) and main Kingston (O/S partition) were on the same power supply and neither one even hiccuped while both Crucials died.

title: Good value and coverage, but awkward setup and buggy reliability
text:
Setup is not for the faint of heart, and (perhaps this is true of all extenders but I don't see why, from a technical perspective, it must be so) it does not allow you to mix different security measures. I use MAC address screening (with my >Netgear< wireless router), which is essentially unhackable without sophisticated snooping equipment and a lot of expertise, but a pain to implement because every device allowed on the network has to be manually added (i.e. not what you'd want for a hotel but fine for a private house with two users and four devices). Well, the MAC address that was printed on the back of the N300 did not match the MAC address that the Netgear router said was connected, and neither of them worked anyway - the moment I turned MAC screening on in the router, the N300 vanished. Then I tried using the much-touted WPS, where you press a button on the router and press a button on the extender and they automatically see each other and pair, like a bluetooth device. Well, that worked but doing so caused every device enrolled in the router by MAC address to stop working (regardless of whether they were connected to the N300 or directly to the Netgear router) - you cannot combine the two types of security. So I've had to abandon the hardware-based security I've used for fifteen years and go to using WPA passwords. One star off.

Second star off is reliability. Everybody connected got booted, and although I could manually connect from a laptop I could not get into the N300's settings (which in typical Netgear fashion is done from a dummy webpage, although they have had the decency to give it an alias www.-type name instead of a long numeric URL - yes, I know what it means and why they do it, but it's simply easier to type in a name than a string of numbers. Except in this case, it wouldn't connect. Looked at the unit and red light. Why? Manual says no device is connected but I am connected, so what's up? Power off/power on and all devices re-connected, but not pleased with the unexplained failure. (No power outage, and besides that's hardly an excuse).

Update: every couple of weeks the N300 device connection light turns amber ("fair" signal) even though multiple connected devices are only a few feet away, and the connection disappears. Going back into any tablet's WiFi setup instantly reestablishes the connection (light turns green) and then no problems for several more weeks. Looks like an annoying, although by no means crippling, bug - when not in use, the tablets only transmit wirelessly occasionally to save power and it appears that the N300 decides to enter some sort of sleep mode. Keeping the review at three stars.

title: Great hardware but terrible software - WITH WORKAROUNDS
text:
Hardware is outstanding, five stars. Software is a huge letdown by comparison. No real editing, only the ability to trim the start and end - not that matters, because it crashes every single time in Windows 7 on two different computers whenever video is edited or even when it is converting from its proprietary format to standard format. The format used also crashes Windows Movie Maker, so I had to figure out a workaround: record the video, stop recording (or allow the pre-set recording time to run out), open Movie Maker WITHOUT continuing (which crashes) or closing (which deletes the just-recorded files) Elgato, load the recorded video, let Movie Maker produce a new file (.mp4, 640 x 480 x 1283kbps [that's what the elgato software produces from an NTSC video signal] and highest audio bitrate Movie Maker allows). Then and only then quit the Elgato software (which automatically deletes the original recording!), remove the clip from Movie Maker (or quit Movie Maker and don't save), and then finally bring your newly-created .mp4 back into Movie Maker. From that point on, everything works fine.

Also, note that you have to install both the driver software and the application from the Elgato web site - that's not obvious or explained. If you have other editing software that allows direct video capture (I used to use VideoStudio but it's no longer compatible with newer versions of Windows), first try just installing the driver by itself and see if you fare better with your own software.

On the other hand, the software does at least let you assign a destination drive (although you have to tell it again every time you run it - it always defaults back to whatever Windows is using for My Documents), which is good since these files can get pretty big; and you can set a predetermined amount of time for it to record so you don't have to sit next to your computer waiting for that VCR tape to end the whole time.

It seems like it was designed as a Mac product and Apple users may fare better. For the price (~$70) I expected way more and I perhaps should have gone with one of the units here on Amazon for more like half this price.

(People love flat screen TVs with the smallest bezel possible, which unfortunately leaves room for speakers no larger than the last joint of your thumb.) The 6000 basically takes a feed from the audio-out of your TV and you use your TV's Setup Menu to turn off the TV's speakers. My Toshiba TV only allows you to do that if it senses that you are using a Regza Link sound system, which the SurroundBar 6000 is NOT. So be sure you can really turn off your TV's speakers before you buy this system. Also, as other have noted the wireless connection to the subwoofer can be quirky. That can be especially frustrating because in this system, using a wireless connection is rather silly. Because of the small size of the speakers in the soundbar (so that it can fit under the TV), the sub has to produce sound at higher frequencies than true home theater system subs have to. This means that you will actually be able to detect the location of the sub so you want it to be close to the TV and soundbar. So why not use a wired connection and eliminate the issues and expense of a wireless connection?

The Yamaha YSP-2000 soundbar system can be found for $600 from reputable sellers on the well-known auction site, which isn't that much more expensive than this Polk. It is a Regza Link system, includes HDMI switching for three devices, has a wired connection to the subwoofer, and does produce surround sound. The Yamaha's surround sound really only gets to the sides of the listener not the rear, but it's pretty good and a better home theater experience than the Polk. After I read Sound & Vision Magazine's review of the Yamaha YSP-2000 I bought it and sold the Polk. I'm happy I did.

title: Excellent for a soundbar
text:
First of all, be aware that if you want true 5.1 or 7.1 surround sound you really do need a home theater speaker system that has the rear speakers. Soundbars are intended for folks who for various reasons can't or don't want to run wires to the rear of the room. Soundbars are also intended for smaller rooms, not large ones. Within those limitations the YST-2200 is an excellent system. It produces surround sound to the sides of, but not much behind the listener. That said, the sound is rich and does envelop the listener for video sources (TV and movies). It has a frequency response "hole" between around 500hz where the soundbar drops off, and around 150hz where the subwoofer kicks in. This isn't noticeable for movies or TV program surround but does mean it's not as good as a true 5.1 system for music.

Setup is easy and the HDMI 3-source switching is very convenient. It's a Regza Link system which means it works with my Toshiba TV which won't let you turn off its speakers unless it detects that you're using a Regza Link home theater audio system. One caveat is that for some reason the YST-2200 doesn't like the HDMI output of my old but much beloved Toshiba RD-SX52 hard drive DVD Recorder - to get everything stable I finally had to abandon the HDMI from the RD-SX52 and run its video to the TV with colorstream component video cables and audio to the YST-2200 with a TosLink fiber cable. This means that to use the RD-SX52 I have to switch both the TV and soundbar inputs which is less convenient but at least with the RD-SX52 I can still play DVDs and see their Closed Caption output. (Blu Ray players do not convey DVD Closed Caption output, only Subtitles which are unlikely to be present on a DVD.)

The bass output from the sub is surprisingly good (in a small-ish room). In fact I had a spare powered subwoofer from a previous installation that I added to the YST-2200. After tweaking its crossover and volume with the tones on the Avia Guide to Home Theater DVD I could hear the difference with the additional powered sub but surprisingly it wasn't very much of a difference. I don't know why a few reviewers here said the sound isn't good on this system. I can tell you though, that when they said it wasn't as good as you'd expect for an $800 system that's because they didn't shop around. You can get easily the YST-2200 from reputable dealers on the famous auction site for $600 (as of this writing). And the YST-2200 is easily worth $165 more than the Polk Surroundbar 6000 (see my review of that system). Take a look at the Sound & Vision Magazine review of the YST-2200 for a professional reviewer's opinion.

title: Great screen but way more complex than necessary when you're driving
text:
I've used a Nuvi 1450 for a few years but wanted to have a larger (6") screen, and the Nuvi 67LM does have a great screen. And getting a Garmin with "LM" (i.e. Lifetime Maps) is a good idea since otherwise a map update download is a significant cost relative to buying a new GPS.

However, in my view the Nuvi 67LM adds a LOT more capabilities which adds a lot more complexity, which is fine if the capabilities are what you want. For example it provides a lot of "location categories" which provide a lot more info about what's available around you at your location. It also allows you to browse into social media databases like your Foursquare or Basecamp accounts to find a location. BUT, raise your hand if you think a social media driver doing all that while driving, is a good idea.

The other issue is that Garmin has put a lot of new restrictions, both real and imaginary, around your use of the device:
1. You cannot use other voices unless they are the few that Garmin allows you to download from the Garmin Express app. Forget using all the other "Garmin compatible" voices available on the Internet - this new GPS blocks them.
2. If you use a non-OEM power supply (like the coiled cord one available on Amazon that provides a way cleaner automobile car dashboard look than the way-way-too-long OEM Garmin power cord), the 67LM constantly whines that the non-Garmin power supply won't charge the GPS. Which you will quickly find is total BS - it charges the GPS just fine.
3. You can download other vehicles from websites to your computer, but you can't install them with the Garmin Express app. You have to connect the GPS with the USB mini cable (which is no longer used by anyone except Garmin) and hope that your computer will perceive it as another storage drive at the OS level. Sometimes it does, sometimes not. When it does, you can transfer the vehicle's srf file (a file format unique to Garmin) to the Garmin and then start the Garmin to change the displayed vehicle.

So basically I'm happy with it now, but unhappy with how much time it too to set it up the way I was happy with the Nuvi 1450.

Processor is too slow todo any on the fly transcoding so their apps like video station only support formats containing h264... And then eat 80% processor remixing ac3 audio to AAC. Multiple apps needed to serve multiple formats without crushing the system. New plex does the same at 45-50%. Transcoding divx to chromecast, ipad, web...99% processor

Photo station needs a lot of work and is inconsistent with a bad app. The album creation limitations and inconsistent upload can't replace iCloud

Cloud station is a disaster with large numbers of files ... Like a Lightroom folder structure. Unfortunate

Dsm could use more options like flattening folders and multiple select with checkboxes and other features..using dsm on a tablet isn't great and the mobile site is limited

The good.

Business function is top notch with ample apps and many options. Security is easy, most mobile apps are good. Many backup options in addition to hot swap, glacier, NAS to NAS, NAS to external. Windows 8 file versions work perfectly.

Multiple VPN options for server client tunnel
Easy security
Decent web services and firewall/rules
Easy Ddns
Runs dir server and client well with open directory. Does support roaming profiles on Mac and PC
Easy windows file versioning
Time machine support for OS X
And a lot more great features

This can easily run a small workgroup and serve a website while providing easy management and expandability.

Dsm 5 is coming soon and looks very good,

If you want a central file backup solution and easy management along with some web serving and more, get it...

If you are looking for a center to your entertainment digitally, it has big limitations.

title: Overpriced and doesn't work half the time
text:
I cannot recommend this FitBit. It is not worth the $300 they are charging for it. I would have returned it if I hadn't been reimbursed for it through my health insurance. I had a FitBit Charge a few years ago and none of the software issues have been resolved since then.

When I first got this, it refused to update or connect to my Google Pixel 3a XL. I had to use a work iPad to get it to update. It will not connect to my phone DAILY and none of the resolution steps fix it. I turn bluetooth on and off, I turn the Fitbit on and off, I turn my phone on and off. I should not have to do this daily to get it to sync to my phone. It sporadically connects with no rhyme or reason as to why it's finally connecting. I don't have time to fiddle with and troubleshoot it daily.

The band it comes with is awful. I have sensitive skin and it constantly irritates the skin on my wrist to the point I have to take it off to let the skin heal, which defeats the purpose of having it. It also starts to smell disgusting if you don't wash it. I understand you're sweating and dead skin, but I had a $30 tracker from China that never had this issue which makes me think it's something to do with the material of the strap.

The battery was dying within 2 days of charging when I had alerts setup reminding me to drink and relax. I had to turn them off to extend battery life, again defeating the purpose of wearing it.

I'm hopeful that with Google buying Fitbit they'll fix the issues with the software. I don't know how a company in 5 years hasn't fixed glaring issues with their software functionality.

title: Surprisingly sturdy monitor riser with some smart features
text:
[[VIDEOID:de8398704754f98c8a265ecae5390b1]] I ordered this monitor riser on Amazon Vine because I needed one for my work from home desk which is also my personal gaming desk when I am not working.

-This monitor riser arrived in nice packaging with one of the better instruction booklets I've received with a product that's from overseas (sometimes the translations take some deciphering to understand.)

-I was pleasantly surprised with the build quality of this item. It's a very sturdy plastic and the legs on this riser have heavy big springs that allow it to be reconfigured with the legs folded up under if you need more space or even one leg folded with the other open. There's also a neat textured design on the top of this stand that I didn't notice in the item listing. See the photo attached to this review. My monitor is not tippy or wobbly on it either.

-I love the pen slots, drawer, and phone stand and that you can close the drawer and phone stand when not in use. One thing to note with the phone stand, I have a PopSocket on my phone case and this causes the phone to sit a bit forward at a weird angle when in the stand horizontally, which it has to be if I want to charge the phone while it sits there. It's not as bad when the phone is in vertical mode but just something to note if you use a Popsocket.

-The RGB works great and has a variety of settings that you can toggle through using the front button. I tried to capture this on video but the lights get washed out on my cell phone camera. You can toggle between solid red, green, blue, sky blue, or purple as well as some rainbow blinking options.

-The four USB slots on the front are working great so far with my mouse dongle, my phone, and mechanical keyboard plugged in and working (my phone will not charge because it doesn't put out enough power :( ) Because I got this as a review unit, I was unable to pick the 3.0 USB version and if I were buying this I would spend the extra five bucks for the 3.0 slots. (at time of this review the 2.0 version is $35, the 3.0 is $40.)

I have two minor nitpicks with this stand.
1.) I wish the USB ports were on the back or there were ports on both the front and back. It looks kind of messy with cable management having the ports on the front but you could run your wires up under the riser for a cleaner look.
2.) There are really cheesy, cheap looking stickers on each side that say "Monitor Stand Riser". See the photo I've included with this review. These really takeaway from the look of the riser. They can be pulled off, though I will need some Goo Gone or rubbing alcohol to get the adhesive off. My advice to the manufacturer is to get rid of these stickers. They're redundant and takeaway from the overall aesthetic of this riser, in my opinion.

Overall, I would spend $30-40 on this stand. I hope the RGB lasts but even if it doesn't, I'd still use it.
item_title: KeiBn Monitor Stand Riser with 4 USB 2.0 Hub, RGB Lights Computer Monitor Stand with Phone Holder and Storage Drawer,Desk Organizer Monitor Shelf for PC,Laptop,iMac

These radios work great for two vehicles traveling on busy roads. They are quite easy to handle "one handed", which makes them usable by drivers. Just make sure all the vehicles are close together. Remember that communications on these radios aren't private.

title: great with DD-WRT 5ghz bridge and as DLNA NAS
text:
I upgraded to Comcast internet from DSL and bought this router to replace my DSL router. It works great as a router and much more.

A couple of weeks afterward, I purchased a refurbished Netgear WNDR3400 V1 dual frequency router for $37.00 to attach as a 5 GHz wireless bridge. I loaded DD-WRT on the WNDR3400 using instructions I found online and DD-WRT fired up with no problems. Next I found instructions on how to configure the WNDR3400 as a wireless bridge. No changes were required on the RT-N56U. Again, it worked perfectly. I have a couple of media devices wired into the WNDR3400. The WNDR3400 talks to the RT-N56U at 5 GHz quite well and very fast. Later I turned on the 2.4GHz radio on the WNDR3400, configured the 2.4 GHz band as an AP, and entered a unique SSID and password into the 2.4 GHz band on the WNDR3400. To my pleasant surprise, the WNDR3400 responded at 2.4 GHZ. Thus, the WNDR3400 now also functions as a repeater at 2.4 GHz while the only communication between it and the RT-N56U is at 5 GHz. DD-WRT supports guest networks while the RT-N56U does not. Thus the 2.4GHZ band on the WNDR3400 has a useful purpose while the 5GHz band provides fast media access.

Later I digitized my music CDs into 110 GB of MP3 music and tried to use the RT-N56U as a DLNA media server (using the 5 GHz wireless bridge). I loaded the music on a 128 GB LEXAR flash drive and plugged it into the RT-N56U. This turned out to be a little tricky, but I think I finally figured out how to make the RT-N56U work reliably as a DLNA server via USB. The files were encoded as 320k VBR highest quality using iTunes. 10,000 files were involved. They play through my DLNA supported dvd player into my home theater via the 5 GHz wireless bridge mentioned above.

Basically, the RT-N56U worked well with 16GB of music and no issues were encountered. Ditto with about 50 GB. By the time I finished, the media server has issues with 110GB. The DLNA server was down and apparently overpowered, at first. Through trial and error I think I solved the problem. The 128 GB drive was initially loaded with FAT32 formatting. This worked well with only a few files but apparently gave the RT-N56U problems at high capacity. I reformatted the 128 GB LEXAR flash drive with exFAT and the RT-N56U couldn't read it. Then I put NTFS on it and no problems (at least so far). Response is very fast.

Also, I used a USB extension cord so the flash drive is not directly attached to the RT-N56U. Heat buildup may have caused a problem. I have had no issues when using the USB extension.

Finally, I noticed that you should unplug the RT-N56U for about 30 seconds after every firmware upgrade. Firmware changes also adversely affected the DLNA server. Unplugging the router seemed to fix those problems.

If you're a consumer looking for a useful router, look elsewhere.

The GUI is fair for home router purposes and probably less friendly than just about everyone else's.This is even after you run the wizard that creates a probably useful configuration (v1.6). OpenVPN is not supported unless you go into the CLI and, hopefully, find documentation somewhere that supports your objective. no-ip is not a DDNS selection, although you can use the CLI for a workaround. Their forum is reputed to be good, but I found it less than friendly if you asked questions that didn't meet the image they saw themselves as being a part of.

If you're a rugged individualist, a hobbyist, someone who likes researching hard to find documentation, have objections to using common technology, or highly skilled with commercial routers then this is a good choice. Otherwise, save the $100.

title: Easy once I figured it out.
text:
I like them. It took about 10 cables for me to figure out my technique. Now I make reliable patch cables quickly.

I watched several videos and got the basics from them. The nuances I had to figure out myself.

My technique:

1) Strip at least 1 1/2 inches of insulation. Unwind the strands. Trim the insulation cleanly. Cut out the center spacer.
2) Straighten each strand individually.Use the thumb and forefinger. One at a time is better than all at once.
3) Fan out the strands widely. Place them in the correct order. Work them together until they are tightly together a little from the top. The top will always be messy. Don't worry about it.
4) Trim the strands where they are together tightly, holding them snugly with your thumb. Cut an even straight line all the way across.
5) Slide the load bar over the wires. More times than not it should go on easily. Inspect.
6) Push the load bar as far down as it will go. Hold it snug. Trim the excess wires cleanly.
7) Put the connector on, Push it down as far as it can go. Crimp.
8) Use your tester when done with both ends.

The videos I watched told me to push the load bar towards the connector with a small screwdriver. It often didn't work and the cable looked bad even when I made a good one. Everything works best if you push the connector towards a snug load bar.

If it lives, it will become a spare main router and a wireless bridge for another room.

My first Asus router was an RT-N56U. It was given to a family member who uses it as an access point in a large home. It's still a good router. Reliable x 10.

I had originally ordered a Netgear R6700. I returned it unopened after discovering how fluid Netgear is in replacing perfectly good V1 models with V2 models without specifying it in the sales description. I read that the R6700 is now a R6700V2 and may be less reliable than the original model. I was very happy with my Netgear R6400v1 but the higher valued R6700 is on sale and at a lower cost at this time.

Asus went to great pains to note this is a RT-AC66U-B1 at Amazon. The reviews gave a good impression. Subsequent research makes it look like it is upgraded from the original model and close to an AC1750 version of an AC-RT68U model, an AC1900 router, but at a much lower price. Very nice. Who cares about wireless-n at 450 vs 600? Not me.

Update a couple of days later: The conversion of the TM-AC1900 into a full RT-N68U succeeded. I took it from the 'newest' 3181 firmware to the current Asus firmware. There's a lot of steps but it's a reasonably forgiving process, too. The wireless on the Netgear R6400v1 seems a little stronger at a distance so it remained the access point attached to my wired pfSense router (note, it's a v1. Netgear v2/v3/v4 updates are all different routers and not necessarily comparable even if they have the same main router model number).The Asus routers will be media bridges for now. The ASUS AIProtection on both routers looks interesting. It has the potential to adequately replace my pfSense router (uses SNORT and pfBlockerNG), if needed.

title: Good buy...
text:
I have had one - now for 3 years. Have given 2 as gifts.

Sound quality is fine for a tiny speaker. The volume up/down toggle does seem to become less effect over a long period of time.

Battery life is great but don't leave it on in ALERT mode unless you are under severe weather - it drains the batteries - also the alarm tones might spook you!

I do not recommend leaving any battery powered radio in a car - if you live in cold weather country. Ultra cold is a battery killer.

Have had better Sangean and Oregon Scientific NOAA models - but neither lasted.

Formerly was in TV news. Several times of the year - I would be at VA Tech in SW Virginia. Storms build fast there.
Used to carry a lightning detector beeper (didn't last..) when doing outdoor events and also had this radio.
This radio was the better deal and it lived in my camera bag or hung on a press creds lanyard from my rear view mirror.

The only time that it didn't work - was last Summer in rural Arkansas by the Caddo River flood disaster. Why - the NOAA transmitter there had not been replaced since Hurricane Ike....when near Little Rock and Fort Smith - no problem.

It's a good little radio - buy one and keep alkaline batteries in it!
