I was uncertain - this was my first touchscreen still camera - have an older Sony touchscreen low-end broadcast video camera...I find that I LIKE the touchscreen on the N!
I bought my closeout N for street photography - it is not intimidating because it is so small.
I also wanted that wide end of the zoom and f 3 aperture.
Definitely use wifi to transfer files, getting the micro SDHC card in/out is very difficult. I still need to get my iPad to talk to my N. The new Canon software app should be used with the N.
The zoom lens/shutter release thing is fine in daylight - however at night - hard to feel and see.
The touchscreen is more responsive.
(Update 12-27-2016 - when in flash mode - it under-exposes about 75% of the time.
Movie mode is wonderful. Bought a DotLine mini metal grip to help steady my shooting - I suggest it as an accessory. Also bought a charger and 2 more batteries. When out in 40 degree weather or lower - the batteries go fast...).
The six wacky simul photo mode is soooo Japanese. I found all of the choices are crappy.
I like shooting with the in-camera B&W mode, especially with the zoom at its widest. The miniature mode is disappointing. Faux fisheye mode looks better in daylight.
Do use the neck strap - the camera feels unbalanced with just the wrist strap.
Do buy extra batteries and a separate charge rather than charge a battery through the camera.
I seem to be very happy with my new older model N!

title: There must be better cameras
text:
I've owned this camera for 3-months and waited until now to write a review because it was a gift and I really wanted to like this camera. But the more I've used it the less I like it. To be fair, it can take a descent picture under optimal conditions if you are careful, but so can a 1968 Kodak Brownie in the right hands. I really expected more from Nikon and modern electronic technology.

Let me give you a little more background... I'm 63 years old and I've been taking pictures since I was 8 years old. Last winter I suffered a stroke which affected the coordination in my left hand and I found it difficuly to operate my Nikon D50 SLR. My wife, trying to be nice to me bought an S6100 for my birthday because she assumed that a point-and-shoot would be easier and less frustrating for me to use than my D50 SLR. I was excited to get it and try it out. The Nikon S6100 was smaller, lighter and easier to carry. As far as being easier to use,
it is NOT! A person would expect an automatic point-and-shoot camera to be just that, point it, press the shutter release and get a fair picture most of the time. That's something this camera can't do with any regularity. A pox on Nikons house for the damn touch screen controls! Why have a touch screen shutter release function that duplicates the function of the shutter release button? While you try to hold the camera with your right hand you are almost forced to touch the screen while trying to frame the image and push the "real button". This more often than not activates the shutter resulting in a picture of the ground, your pant leg, or shoe. Then while you wait for the exceedingly slow electronics to store that image on the memory card, you miss several oportunities to try for a good shot. Would that this was the only problem with the touch screen. Nikon designed this cameras controls so the ONLY way to control various camera functions is through a menu system controlled using the touch screen. If that were not bad enough the screen itself is not sensitive enough to respond well to a finger touch unless you use a long finger nail or the little stylus hung on the wrist strap. This almost insures that you can't make any sort of quick option changes while you try to shoot. You may wonder if that screen does anything else. Yes, it shows a fairly bright image to use as a viewfinder or to review pictures of your shoes taken by mistake. Of course it is constantly smugged and dirty because you have to be touching it all the time.
How about the overall function? The S6100 is as functional as most of it's competitors in the crowded point-and-shoot field. It's a snapshot camera at best loaded with difficult to control features and totally unecessary post shooting editing functions that are much better done on your computer after you download the pictures. I expected better from Nikon and I certainly thought that a 16 megapixel sensor would capture better quality shots. Again I was disappointed. My 6 megapixel D50 captures better images and it's over 5-years old. In anything other than optimal light, the automatic functions of the S6100 bump up the ISO a few clicks and once that's happened the image quickly gets grainy without gaining good exposure. Again I sure expected better from the newer class of sensors and software. The S6100 can also take Quicktime movies with a single press of the movie button on the back. This would be a nice function if the movie button were not small placed directly below the right side thumb grip, almost ensuring that you will take some short movies you didn't want, again usually of the ground, your shoe, or the sky.
Oh, and then there is battery life. Not too good. I can get maybe 200 shots and a short movie before the "battery exhausted" message pops up on the screen, and then you are done since the only way to recharge it is to plug the whole camera into the charger or a computer USB port, you will be out of luck in the field unless you invest in a second battery, keep it charged and in your pocket while you'r out shooting.

Do you think I've been be too negative about the S6100?
Here are the good things about it:
1. It's small, light, and fits easily in a shirt pocket or purse
2. The zoom lens is Nikon, and they do make the best optics and the wide to full zoom is all you will probably ever need.
3. When you manage to get a snap shot it's usually of adequate quality, at least for your family album.

MY RECOMMEDATIONS:
If you want a point-and shoot Nikon, check out the S8100 or S9100, both much better cameras at only a slightly higher price.
If you want great pictures and care about control of your camera functions get a Digital SLR and learn how to use it.

If you want a touch screen get a smart phone. Most of those will take pictures and movies too, and might be easier to use than this camera, plus when you get frustrated with the smugged up touch screen, at least you can use it to call someone who cares.
item_title: Nikon COOLPIX S6100 16 MP Digital Camera with 7x NIKKOR Wide-Angle Optical Zoom Lens and 3-Inch Touch-Panel LCD (Black)

title: This is the hands free speaker I needed all along
text:
Here in my State it's now illegal to hold a phone while driving. It's OK to hold a cup of coffee, shave, apply makeup, read a book, talk to others in the car with your hands while driving, but to hold a phone is now a misdemeanor. WHATEVER! OK, end of political statement... I continue now with the review.

I've tried several different hands free options for my cell phone since the law was passed. First I tried using the speaker-phone option on the cell phone itself along with the phones voice dialing cabpability and a belt clip to hold it on the visor. This kind of worked, but the phones volume was insufficient and I had to yell at it to make myself heard over road noise at the other end. Next I tried a bluetooth ear piece I picked up from Verizon. It worked OK if I remembered to charge it and take it with me when I went somewhere. Often I'd forget though. I wear glasses and I kept knocking the ear piece out with them. The ear piece was always falling out, or was in the way, and after a couple of hours waring it, it became uncomfortable in my ear. So I started leaving it home most of the time. Then, my wife bought a new car with built-in bluetooth that worked so well I fell in love with it. But it was her car and my truck didn't have these new modern niceties. Last, I tried buying a bluetooth speaker device from Amazon made my Motorola. The Motorola speaker was to put it nicely, a piece of junk. It would only pair to my Motorola cell phone when it wanted to not when I needed it to, it would not allow access to the phone's voice dialing features, and went back to Amazon within days.

I'd almost given up when one of the Amazon suggestions came up with this Jabra DRIVE as a suggestion for something I might be interested in. I thought, "what the heck, I'll try one more device before I give up"! I'm SO glad that I did. This speaker is the bluetooth device I was looking for. It's priced lower than some of the others I've seen, that's a plus. It paired to my old Motorola KRAZR phone on the first try. And best of all it just works. It accesses all of the phone features with no muss or fuss. It's loud enough to be heard in the truck. It's mic. cancels road noise like it should and I'm easily understood on the other end. Battery life is long enough to last all day, at least so far. Controls are very simple. An on-off switch on the side,a large volume rocker avove the speaker grill, and a hidden call/answer push button behind the grill are the extent of it. There are no difficult to find controls, you don't have to search all over the device while driving to make or anser a call. Just turn on the Jabra when you get in and provided you phone has its bluetooth powered on, Jabra says "conected" and you are ready to go. When you get a call Jabra DRIVE answers automatically fo you with nothing to push. Just talk. To make a call, press the phone icon on the speaker and you are connected to your phones voice functions. Assuming you already know how to use the features of voice commands on your phone there is nothing else to do or learn. To hang up, press that phone icon again and you're done.

I LOVE THIS SPEAKER PHONE!

I only have one suggestion for Jabra. The 12v USB charger for the car is great, but it would be nice if you included a 110v house charger as well. It was no big deal for me since the charger for my now retired ear piece worked nicely, it was a Jabra too. But others might like a home charger. Like me they may want to charge it in the house at night since some vehicles power off the 12v port when the key is turned off.

title: OK for a couple of months, later not so much
text:
Bought this cheap laptop for my 12-year old grandson as a Christmas present. Although it comes with Windows 8.1 I figured it was a good value. Before I gave it to him I spent a few hours upgrading it to Windows 10. Microsoft just keeps bugging you if you don't upgrade and I didn't want him to have to deal with that B.S. The upgrade went flawlessly and this laptop ran great under Windows 10. I didn't remove the Asus bloat-ware but I should have. My grandson used his laptop until February and loved it until he managed to install enough "so-called games" that he had it totally infected with virus' and malware. It became unusable at that point because of constant pop-ups and other virus symptoms. In retrospect I never should have trusted Microsoft Defender as the anti-virus program. OK, lesson well learned, I'll never use that useless piece of software again.
From here on things worse by the hour. I took his laptop home to restore it back to the factory configuration. Asus says this is easy, just press F9 with the power button and the process will start. NOPE! It just kept booting the infected Windows 10 OS. Then I created a bootable flash drive with the Sophos antivirus program to clean it up. Just hold down F2 and power to enter the BIOS and reset the boot device to USB. Three times I tried to boot from the flash drive. I wouldn't work. A day and a half into my "easy cleanup" I was still spinning my wheels because this laptop would not perform the easy tasks that the Asus documentation and a dozen YouTube videos said would work. In utter frustration on day #2 I kept at it, trying every BIOS setting variant that I thought might get the darn laptop to boot from flash drive, when without warning it actually started the ASUS recovery utility that failed to load with F9. So here I sit, 21% into restoring this thing back to Windows 8.1 without any of the user files created since Christmas. I'll have a very disappointed grandson, but it's his own fault for downloading whatever it was that infected this laptop in the first place. OK, enough of my horror story. Let me get on with why I only give this laptop 2-stars:

PRO: T
The hardware is solid and well built. It stood up to a 12-year old boys abuse for two months so far. He hasn't been able to break anything, and believe me he can break stuff, his phone, ear buds, glasses, door handle in my pickup. So ASUS gets 3 stars for hardware quality only.
CON: Here's where I deduct stars...
NO CD or DVD Drive. Why? Without an optical disk of some sort obtaining necessary software like antivirus, Office, etc. while not impossible becomes quite difficult. I'll never ever buy another computer without an optical drive. I consider it a necessity.
Support; there is none. The ASUS web site is next to useless, forcing you online to YouTube, user forums or so-called expert web sites to search for your own solutions to problems.
Junk software, this laptop comes full of it. Most of it useless at best.
Virtually non-functioning system restore option. You need to create a system restore disk the very first thing yourself, but without an optical drive how can you do that? I'll be working on that question myself later today but I'm not holding my breath right now.

SUMMARY: I still give this laptop 2-stars because it's fairly fast, well built and cheap. Would I buy this model again? "NO", not unless it cam with a DVD, recovery disks and a real manual in the box.

title: Know what bands your stations broadcast on
text:
Even before you start shopping for over the air antenna option to cut the cable cord you need to know several things:
First, what bands do your stations transmit on. Channels 2 thru 6 use UHF frequencies. Channels 7 thru 13 still use high band VHF. Most of these plastic antennas like this one will do OK with close by UHF. Most will also often fail to pull in VHF stations in they are over about 15-20 miles away.
Second, I've found that amplified antennas don't seem to do any better than non-amplified ones.
Third, you will have to buy and try lots of different antennas before you will find one that might work in your location. And location is important! One may work in your family room and fail miserably in your bedroom or den.
So back to this specific antenna... Of the 4 different ones I've tried, this one was the worst, picking up a few of us UHF stations in my den but no VHF stations at all. A cheap flat plastic antenna did better, a little better. The best results I got were with a cheap old RCA set of rabbit ears with a UHF loop in the middle.
I don't recommend this antenna at all.
Good luck with your cord cutting experiment. At least Amazon will let you return the ones you try that don't meet your needs.

text:
This review is being wrote on the first day that I've owned this TV and so far I have to say that I'm 100% satisfied with my new TV. This Samsung flat 32-inch replaced a 30 year old Zenith standard definition TV in my bedroom which just simply refused to die but because I was switching my DirecTV service to a new Geini with Geni wireless minis for the secondary TV's it seemed like a good time to retire my old Zenith work horse.

3. Yup, the sound is a little lower and not as crisp as a surround sound TV. I knew that going in. I didn't want tp blast the sheets off the bed with mega woofers. Just want to hear a program adequately in a quiet bedroom. This TV does that just fine.
OK, with that out of the way I'll continue:

Unpacking and setup was a breeze. About all you need to do is attach the two stand legs with the four supplied Philips screws. You do own a #2 Philips screw driver don't you. Then set the TV where you want it, plug it in, install the two AAA batteries (supplied) in the remote, attach the video source of you choosing and that's about it. This Samsung has 2 HDMI ports on the side, Composite and/or component video ports. There's also standard audio input for those using Component or composite video input. And of course there's an antenna hookup too if you're a cord cutter. Oh I forgot to mention, there's also an optical audio out port for use by those who may want to add a sound bar and gain blasting sound.

If you've ever owned another Samsung TV you'll find the on-screen setup menu and remote controls familiar. You won't have to setup much except let the TV scan for local channels and it starts playing TV shows right off the bat. There are other optional setup options for color, sound, whatever, but those are just for folks who like to fiddle around with sort of thing. You can consult the adequate manual for all that stuff.

Closing comments:
This nice little TV has wonderful color, adequate sound for smaller rooms, and it's easy to use. I couldn't be happier. If you need or want smart functions, Wi-Fi, blasting sound this is probably not the TV for you, look at other more expensive models. But if you want a good TV to go with a cable or satellite box in a smaller room I doubt if you can beat this Samsung TV.

title: Best Choice for my needs
text:
First let me tell you that I have had 3 different tablets in the past. Here's what I have used:

1) First generation Kindle Fire, which I've owned for years. I still have it and it still works just fine for a book reader although the screen is beginning to dim, the case is worn out and the USB port is loose but it still charges. I prefer the old Fire as a Kindle reader over the newer Kindle devices for various reasons and I may still use it sometimes to read E-books because it's just so easy to use for that one purpose.

2) iPad; i was forced to use an iPad by my work because there was one app that they required me to use that was only available for the iPad. And I hated that iPad for so many reasons I won't even go into here. Suffice it to say that being locked into the Apple universe was simply a maddening experience for me. My phone is an Android and I much prefer the open environment of Android.

Now, this Samsung tablet might not have been my first choice if I'd simply chosen it based on specifications and newness. But price was a huge factor for me and at $149, nothing out there seemed to come close. I wanted enough memory and 32GB was adequate especially because I also bought a 128GB micro SD card for my tablet. That's probably more total memory than I'll ever come close to using. But you just can't have too much memory.
My phone is a Samsung S8 so the learning curve was very small and setting up my tablet only took 20 minutes or so including downloading a few apps that I knew I wanted, including all of the Amazon ones I'll use like Kindle, Prime video, shopping, etc. The primary use for this tablet will be to replace my first gen Kindle Fire. But there's so much more I can do with this beyond what my old Kindle could do. Having Microsoft Office apps preinstalled was a nice surprise. Of course it looks like I'll need a blue tooth keyboard to make good use of them but that's no big deal. I get to buy another toy.
Like others have said, not having the bottom function keys back lit is disappointing but not a real big deal for me personally since I don't work in the dark and I know where those buttons are from using other Android devices.
The screen resolution is amazing. I'm impressed for the price. I bought a case with the same order and I'd recommend anyone to do the same. It looks like it would be way too easy for me to drop and crack the screen without protection. Especially because my left hand is disabled and clumsy.
I can't comment on battery life yet because I haven't used it long enough to get a good feel for how long the battery will go in day-to-day use.

The bottom line; I'm 100% pleased with this tablet and I'd buy it again.

title: Yongnuo receiver and transmitter
text:
These work flawlessly with my Pentax k5/k20d cameras and af540fgz flashes. I use two flashes for wedding and field work and could never rely on the built in wireless capability of the Pentax system outdoors. This is due to the fact that it is an optical light(exposure calculation uses communication flashes) slave system that is affected by ambient light. I have another wireless system that only works with studio flashes due to these pre-flash communications of the Pentax eTTL wireless remote system. With the old wireless system the hot shoe flashes gave black pictures due to the exposure communication pre-flashes happening before the shutter fires.
The Yougnuo 2.4ghz units work flawlessly on both my Pentax flashes(manual mode) and my AlienBees B1600 and JTL studio strobes. I bought the extra receiver so i could control 2 hot shoe or studio strobes.

A significant feature is the low profile hot shoe mounting(~1 inch) that provides more stability for light stand mounting(1/4 screw thread),desktop hot shoe stands, or mounting in my soft box adapter rings. Some of the other units I looked at had 2 or 3 inches of vertical height that made for a very unstable platform and didn't fit my soft box adapters.

Another perk is the included camera remote connection cable that lets me use the transmitter/receiver units to wake-up, pre-focus, and fire the shutter on my Pentax K5 and K20D backup camera(same as Canon Rebel series(2.5mm mini-phone plug) but not 7D). I already had a wireless shutter remote but this enables less gear to carry in my kit. They have a really solid build quality also.

I also love the use of cheaper AAA batteries in the receivers and firm on/off switches. No more expensive lithium batteries that get depleted because the switch was bumped inadvertently.

These seem to be a lot of good reasons (IMHO) to buy this system. These units are a really good deal at any price but the Amazon price was very sweet!

title: Good Quality Mini Amp
text: This is the smallest stereo hi fi amp I have ever used that had good sound quality. I am using this to power two Bose speakers and a Phillips sub from my phone, laptop and tablet via Phillips Bluetooth. I hear no white noise or hum when no music is playing. The sub vol. is a nice and it controls that vol. separate from the main vol. Since there was no English manual I am guessing that a blue led by the sub crossover control is some type if vol. clipping warning. It flashes with very little vol. given to the sub. By the way the sub crossover control does not seem to do anything. There are two paired connections - yoked together - for sub speakers. This uses 12v. power so it can easily be used in a vehicle or at home with the included power supply. It comes with a separate "brick" power supply, thus keeping the heat from the power supply away from the amp. At a reasonable vol. neither the amp or the power supply even get warm. I am not sure why the 68 watt sub output unless you were using massive sub speakers. With the setup I am using I barely have the vol. up for the 8" sub. It has an aux input on the front for a 1/8" stereo jack and RCA jacks on the back for input also. Also on the back us a USB power outlet, but don't expect to play your flash drive Mp3's through it. It is not that sophisticated! The only con with this unit is the fact that it has no English manual. Lepai's web site is minimal with no downloadable English manual.

title: Fantastic Bluetooth Receiver
text: It often seems that when a company gets it right, they discontinue that product, as Phillips has done with this Bluetooth receiver. Anyway, if you find one to buy, buy it.  It is one of the best rated on the market and at the right price. It is strictly plug and play. When you power it up a blue led flashed on the top indicating it is ready to pair with your device. You set your device to search, it finds the Phillips and pairs with it.  That is it. I paired three devices in less than five minutes and had music playing through it to a Lepai amp in seconds.There is a pair of RCA and a 1/8" phone output jack on the unit. There is also a power input jack. There is no off on switch. If you want to clear its memory of the up to 7 devices you hold down the blue button on the top for 2 seconds. Walked all over the house without loosing connection.  I hope whatever they have replacing this is as good.  And I hope it lasts. In the past many of the Phillips device I have had fail after about a year. We will see.

title: Perfect casual-use surge protector for me
text:
CyberPower seems to have a knack for offering products that are just different enough to get my attention. There are an untold number of power strips out there that look about the same as this one, but CyberPower gave it a little twist by including 900 Joule surge protection. Perhaps not robust enough for the most expensive equipment, but about average for surge protectors in this price range - AND it's a proper power strip as well.

The outlets look like standard duplex outlets, which means they are spaced somewhat wider than most surge protectors, and that leaves more room for power bricks (the bane of modern man). I would say that the outlets also have the preferred orientation, or at least, it seems to me that most power bricks seem to be moving in the direction of what one might call a horizontal orientation, such that two could be plugged in right next to each other in a standard duplex outlet...which again, is the kind of outlets that this power strip has.

The case is a silver-gray finished steel, and there are keyhole mounting point on the back (bottom?) of the strip, making it great for surface mounting The power cord is pretty nice...more flexible than most. There is not light in the switch, and I suppose that one can take that as a benefit or not, but personally, I like it. Those neon-lit power switches always die a flickery death anyway.

I like the sturdy build quality, I like the color, and I like the outlet orientation and spacing. I know it's from China, but an old-school American sentiment is there, nonetheless. Nice job CyberPower.
item_title: CyberPower CSB806 Essential Surge Protector, 1800J/125V, 8 Outlets, 6ft Power Cord

title: Nice features, good value, superior battery maintenance/life.
text:
Ah CyberPower. The Chinese manufacturer that I seem to keep coming back to. They introduced this LCD series when APC was still using LEDs. The LCD display conveys a lot of useful information, and just generally looks cooler than a row of LEDs.

But more importantly than that, in this model, CyberPower seems to have done what others have failed to do for many years. Namely, to respect the batteries. Every other brand of UPS that I have ever used just ate batteries for lunch. We have a bunch of them here, and we were typically getting significant;y less than two years out of a battery pack. Since switching to CyberPower, we have yet to wear out a battery pack. That's over five years without any battery failures. So way to go on that CyberPower.

With that said, I bought this unit to replace a failed one. So no failed batteries (yay!) but one dead UPS. And interestingly CyberPower does not offer any parts or service beyond the warranty period. Not that APC does either...we just retired another APC UPS for the lack of a 50 cent proprietary battery power connector.

Anyway, I think the batteries were costing us more than the UPS units themselves, so if we lose a UPS every five years, we're probably still ahead. And it has just been glorious to not have the batteries failing all over the place. And that is to say nothing of the time and trouble that has been saved.

And, for what it's worth, these units use less power in everyday standby mode than the other brands that we have used, so if you have environmental tendencies like I do, it's another selling point. And if you have a great many UPSes, you may actually be able to justify the brand in terms of energy cost reduction. I know it's just another product made in China, but I think it's a cut above the pack, both in terms of features and value, and in terms of performance.

title: this seems to be a great choice. Personally
text:
Bang for the buck, this seems to be a great choice. Personally, I think the styling is better than anything I have seen under $2k. It is sculptural and clean while also being sturdy.

With that said, there are some aspects of the design that I'm not thrilled about. First, the picture that is shown for this model must have been taken with the largest possible TV attached to it, because my 42" looks much smaller...or to put it another way, the stand looks much larger. I would argue that it's bigger than it needs to be. The front of the base is just about the same width as the TV. I think it would almost look silly with a 37" monitor on it. Although it certainly would be stout-looking!

The finish looks like powder coat. It's not smooth. I kind of like it, but I would say that it does not look like a fine finish. It's more of an industrial look. The styling is sculptural enough that it might otherwise be at home even in an elegant setting, but the finish kind of kills it. I don't know...personal preference I suppose. The packaging seems thoughtful, but that didn't save the finish from getting marred in transit. The box and the styorofoam packing material inside was partially crushed, which allowed the pieces to rub together, hence the damage. I was tempted to send it back, but it's a small spot, mostly hidden by the TV, so I didn't.

The height is very difficult to adjust once the TV has been mounted, even with two people. It's quite easy to adjust before mounting the bracket to the two verticals, so it certainly can be adjusted, but it seems like more of a one-time adjustment. There is a small amount of slop in the telescoping verticals, so for example, if one hold the base, one can twist the top horizontal part of the mount to some extent. It wouldn't do this if it had bolts in it, but that's not the design characteristic. It is as if they wanted it to be adjustable (or appear to be adjustable) while the TV is installed, even though it's not really practical to do so. So in my mind, it would have been better to just lock it down and call it permanent. But in fairness, this is not going to be a problem for me in actual use. The mount is still quite sturdy, even if it could have been even more so.

Once I saw it all put together, my first impression was that the base was higher off of the ground than I would have preferred. And yet, the casters seem smaller than I would have preferred. They are nice-quality casters, but just seem small compared to the mount. They have a threaded-stud mount, so I'm sure it would be easy enough to find replacements, but then that would make the base seem even taller...unless one could find casters with both bigger wheels and a lower profile. I'm not even sure that's possible. And again, it's not really a big issue anyway. I'm just saying, I think it would look better if the base was lower slung. And the casters would work better it they had bigger wheels. Perhaps mutually exclusive, but just sharing my thoughts here.

Speaking of the wheels, I noticed that it is somewhat challenging to move on carpet, first because the wheels don't just roll without any resistance on carpet, but more than that, because there is nothing handy to grab onto other than the TV. And I don't think it's a good idea to put that much torque on the TV. This would be less of a problem on a hard floor because the smallish wheels roll effortlessly, but it still might be kind of unhandy to have nothing to grab. Kanto could solve this problem by including telescoping handles on the horizontal mounting bar so that one could basically just reach around the edge of the TV and grab the handle instead of the TV's bezel. In my case, I will be mounting some electronics on the back of the TV, so I'll just attach an aluminum plate to expand the surface area of the horizontal piece, and that same plate can double as a place to grab.

The shelf is plastic. I knew it was plastic before I bought it, so no surprise, but I just wish it was metal. The camera mount is metal, so why not the shelf? Mine is in a home office setting, so I'd like it better if it was a bit more elegant. I am thinking about replacing it with a piece of nicely-finished hardwood. The bracket design will make that idea somewhat difficult though. The shelf mounting system also a bit of a disappointment in that it just clamps onto to the verticals, meaning that if one thought it would be handy to be able to adjust the height of the TV on the fly, this is yet another reason why that wouldn't work very well. But then, if they never intended to for the height to be adjusted after the fact, then it's not really a problem. Just seems slightly misleading. Much of which is a direct result of the fact that there is very little written information about this product. There is an assembly video, but the rest of the manufacturer's website looks like it was designed for very casual viewing on a tablet. None of the images can be enlarged. There is essentially no written information in the manual - just pictures. I found it easy enough to assemble, but nothing that I could find online was very informative. I would have paid money to see a dimensional drawing before buying it, but finally just had to take a chance. The minimum installed TV height is a little taller than I was hoping for, but more on that later.

The wire management system looks pretty handy in the video, but it's worth noticing that it won't work with the verticals set in their lowest position because the holes are telescoped inside of the larger verticals. The thing is rather tall. Probably intended to accompany a standing presenter in a conference room. But I will be using mine while seated, and I would like the center of the screen to be near eye level, which means that even the lowest setting is a little higher than I would prefer. I can make it lower buy attaching the mounting rails up higher on the TV's VESA mounting holes, but then the brackets will be taller than the TV, meaning that I would have to cut them off. I can certainly do that, but at that point, I will be moving out of the realm of what many people would be willing to do. All I'm saying is, just be aware of the height. If you want it tall, then nothing in the paragraph will bother you. If you want it as short as I do, it can certainly be accomplished, but some modifications will be required.

The base has some large oval holes, fitted with white plastic grommets. I have no idea what Kanto thought would be passing through those holes, but the cable management system ends in the back of the verticals, and above the base, so no wires will need to exit from the base. I have no idea, so I took mine out. I think it looks a lot better without them and I can't see any down side. Just seems odd, that's all.

As a side note, I had planned to use an Atlantic 63607104 Universal Adjustable Sound bar mount, but it didn't work will with the Kanto stand because the back of the TV is actually rather close to the vertical supports. The way the Atlantic mount is made, it hits the verticals long before the speaker is far enough back to be flush with the TV in the front. My TV has a 200mm mounting pattern, so as it turns out, that is just slightly wider than the center-lines of Kanto's vertical supports, so the adjustable brackets on the Atlantic mount hit the verticals. It just didn't work out for me, although I'm sure it would be fine with a TV that has a wider mounting pattern.

I knocked off one star for the lack of pre-sale information, the base height, smallish wheels, plastic shelf and finish quality. But with all of that said, I do rather like it anyway, and after searching extensively, both locally and on the internet, I still think this is the best sanely-priced option available.

title: It works fine, to a point
text:
It works fine, to a point. First, SiliconDust seems to me to be kind of an odd company. The product works, but with some notable problems, and the company doesn't really seem to take ownership of long-known problems. I think that a lot of people might buy this gadget imaging that they could watch TV on an iPhone or iPad, but that is not true, at least, not without some supporting hardware and software.

It works fine on my wired gigabit network, but it uses a lot of bandwidth, so Wi-Fi is not dependable. It works fine with SageTV, which is my main interest in the product, but the bundled Windows client doesn't seem to do any de-interlacing, so it's not worth much in my mind. Of course it does work fine with Windows Media Center, but Microsoft seems to be trying to distance themselves from their own product, so it's certainly not what it might otherwise be.

With all of that said, the tuner in this gadget is better than the one in my Hauppauge WinTV-HVR-2250 tuner card, so it can reliably receive at least one network channel that the Hauppauge card cannot. I am not speaking of raw sensitivity, as both turners are sensitive almost to a fault. I'm talking about the ability to avoid drop-outs when trees move in the antenna's path. I found that it helped to insert attenuators into the line before this tuner. Naturally, signal strength was reduced, but the signal quality numbers improved dramatically in my particular case. I am within 16 miles of the transmitter, and I have a large outdoor antenna up about 20 feet, but I am in a forested area - it is the trees that cause the most trouble here.

So, it works well for what it does, but I knocked off a star for the manufacturer's lack of ownership of known issues, the weak software bundle, and the lack of attention to iDevices. For example, it wouldn't kill them to provide a credible administrative app for the purpose of antenna positioning and tuning. A third-party app does exist, but it's not great and its not free.

title: Elegant and Best-In-Class, even if it isn’t perfect…
text:
EDIT: I just wanted to add that the key caps started to wear off after just four months, allowing the back-light to show though I attached a picture that shows the what has happened to the"A" and "S" keys. And all of the rubber pads have already come un-glued from the bottom. I think its pretty tacky for such an expensive keyboard. If they were $20 each, I'd just buy some spares and resign myself to the fact that they don't last very long. But they aren't $20, are they? Anyway, I don't like it, so I;m knocking off some stars. My original review follows:

I will start by saying that I haven't been able to find anything better in a wired keyboard, so please take the rest of this review with that in mind!.

With that said, this keyboard seems to be artificially expensive. There are other keyboards that are better in certain ways, including some form Logitech, that are less expensive. But I want a wired keyboard. I see absolutely no reason to put up with a wireless keyboard when it is sitting two feet away from a perfectly good USB port. A simple wired connection eliminates the need for batteries and charging, and all things being equal, a wired connection will always be faster and more reliable than a wireless connection.

Sadly, Logitech's wire is not ideal...it has a bit of a memory, so it never lays completely straight and flat, even after months of use. It's not really a problem, but I'm just saying that at this price point, it wouldn't kill them to use better materials. The back-light itself is even and pleasing. It is bright enough for the most part, although I wouldn't mind if it had a bit more brightness at the top end of the adjustment range. The flat style is sleek and attractive, but not ideal for touch typists. For example, it's hard to find the home keys without looking. The keyboard has little flip-down feet intended to raise the back, but it's not really enough to be ergonomic. And the feet are tiny, with oh-so-tiny little pads on them. There are also less-tiny little rubber pads at the front of the keyboard. These pads start falling off after a few months. After a year or so, they're all gone. I know this because I've had half a dozen of these keyboards, and the same thing happened to all of them. It still works without the pads, but it kind of slides around on the desk. Perhaps it would be more forgivable on a $12 keyboard, but at this price point, one hopes for better. To my great surprise, I have not yet seen any of the flip-down feet actually break off. It certainly looks like they would, though, so I try to treat them gently.

The key travel is a bit short, but far from the worst, and the keys have nice tactile feedback. I'm not nearly as fast on this keyboard as I was on something like the old keytronic, with it's long key travel and firm feedback. But on the other hand, the back-light really does help offset the glare from my low-mounted dual monitors. Technically, being a touch typist, I shouldn't need to see the keys anyway, but for some reason, I find it crippling when I cannot. Hard to explain unless you've experienced it yourself. But then I suppose what if everyone was a touch typist who didn't need to see the keys, that there would be no reason for a back-lit keyboard, right? So I think we have to assume that there is some valid reason for eh back-lighting, if only the fact that it looks cool.

The arrangement of the keys is what I would consider to be "standard", which I very much appreciate, although I would comment that the function keys are only about two-thirds of full size. I'd like it better if they were full size. And Logitech could easily do that without increasing the footprint of the keyboard simply by getting rid of the clear plastic lip on the edge. I mean, I guess it looks nice, but I'd be happy to trade it for full-size keys. And on that note, the clear lip on the edges increases the size of the keyboard just enough so that it barely fits the keyboard drawer on one of our smaller desks. Maybe I would love the lip more if it too was back-lit...(?)

I think I've read that there are some gaming key combinations that the keyboard does not do. I'm not a hard-core gamer, but for what its worth, it works fine with the games that I do play.

I'm not really sure if this is a fault, but I think it's worth commenting that it is basically impossible to take this model apart for cleaning. It is built kind of like a notebook computer, with about a gazillion tiny screws, all very similar, but not exactly the same, so they cannot be interchanged. My last one died because it got enough debris under the keys that it started missing certain letters. I did manage to take it apart, but it's not easy to clean, even when it's apart. I managed to get it working again, but it took the better part of an hour and some compressed air to get it done, so it's not for the faint of heart...or for anyone who's time is worth more than cost of a replacement keyboard.

So, as you can see, I gave it four stars just because I can't find anything better. That makes it a class-leading product, even if it does have some draw-backs, not the least of which is the ransom that one must pay to get one. I just had to knock off a star for that, if nothing else.
item_title: Logitech Illuminated Ultrathin Keyboard K740 with Laser-Etched Backlit Keyboard and Soft-Touch Palm Rest - Black

title: Resonable compromise between size, performance and cost
text:
[[ASIN:B0024R4B5C RCA Compact Outdoor Yagi HDTV Antenna with 70 Mile Range]]
No secret sauce here, but it works fine for UHF channels, and to a lesser extent, high VHF channels. The only "secret" is that outdoor antennas work a lot better than indoor antennas, and this design represents a reasonable compromise between compact dimensions and performance. It is relatively inexpensive compared to amplified esoteric luxury designs, and out-performs all of the compact antennas (that I have tried), simply because physics dictate that a physically larger beam antenna will do a better job of rejecting off-axis signals, all else being equal.

In my particular case, the TV could receive four channels fairly reliably with an indoor antenna on top of the TV and that expanded to around 35 channels with this antenna mounted about ten feet higher, right outside the window. 70 mile claim seems pretty optimistic, but if it could be mounted high enough to have line of sight with the transmitter antenna, it would probably work fine. Thing is, almost nobody will be able to mount it that high.

title: Obsolete / arcane firmware and software, No good at night!
text:
This camera looks pretty good by day, but at night, it has no hope without the IR LEDs. And you might think that would be okay, since the specs would lead you to believe that the IR range is 196 feet. Sounds good, but in actual practice, it is not. I wound up setting the IRCUT Mode to manual, and that let me manually select "Day Mode", but obviously that is less than ideal because it leaves the IR filter in place, making the already marginal sensitivity just that much worse. Still, it looks better than the totally washed out IR-lit mode, so that was the best I could do with it. I called up GW and was told that I could disconnect the IR LEDs by opening up the camera. I tried that, but it seemed to cause new problems with the already buggy software, so I gave up on that idea pretty fast. Obviously it would be better to be able to control monochrome/color, IR filter and the LED lights all individually. But even then, it would still have serious problems at night.

An added irritation is that the light metering and the auto white balance are not center-weighted, so both of those things always seem to be inaccurate in mixed lighting situations.

The included software is arcane, at best, so it took me a while to get anywhere at all. When I finally did get it going, I was then disappointed that the software was so very bad. For example, the included "UC" software for Windows immediately filled my second monitor with a camera grid - and there was no way to get rid of it, making it all but useless on my dual monitor setup.

The SearchTools software can be used to monitor video, but it’s pretty rude because there is no way to close or minimize the SearchTools window without also losing the video window. And it will go full screen only on the primary monitor.

A browser interface is advertised, but it only works in Internet Explorer, and even then, there is very little control of the window size. The options are a small window in the middle of the browser window, or full screen. Nothing in between.. And again, it can only be maximized onto the primary monitor. Practically speaking, there is no way to casually monitor the camera while working on other tasks on a Windows machine.

All of the software interfaces have zoom controls, but none of them actually works with this camera. The camera is capable of 2592x1920 resolution, but since there is no way to do a digital zoom using ANY of the included software, the extra pixels are pretty much useless, unless one has a 4k computer monitor. I don’t have one, so I don’t know if that would help or not. My guess is that it would not, because all of the software was designed long before 4K was a thing.

Many of the settings in the included "SearchTools" Windows software either don't work or have no effect on the camera. For example, WDR doesn't work at all. Changing the frame rate does not affect the shutter speed of the camera, only the video encoding. I discovered this as I was trying to figure out how to squeeze a little better low light performance out of the camera by reducing the framerate. Again, It looks pretty good in daylight, as long as there aren't any harsh shadows or challenging backlight situations, but as night falls, it switches to IR mode. And when that happens, all quality is lost. It gets wicked reflections and washout when mounted under an eve, and even when it's not under anything, it still gets all kinds of artifacts from the lens and/or glass front. It is all but unusable. It's pretty hard to see anything, but from what I can tell, the useful IR range is more like 100 feet. That might not be too bad if the lens angle was set wide, but then the lighting pattern is not as wide as the lens, so you just see a spotlight in the center. If you could actually see anything, that is.

I downloaded a trial of Blue Iris and found that software to be considerable more intuitive and useful than the bundled "UC" software, but it’s not “included”, making a camera that might otherwise seem like a "deal", no deal at all.

Most people are going to be interested in mobile apps, and the one included with this camera is called “Danale”. It is more modern that the PC software, but it also seems quite Chinese. Both in terms of assuming that everything (including your friends) have QR codes, and also in the terminology, syntax and wording. I actually had to call Danale in order to get it working. Once working, it seems okay, except that it cannot access the full resolution of the camera. It can only access the “Sub Stream”, and the maximum resolution option for that stream is 720x480 – that would be like 480p, or “standard-def.” in TV speak. You can pinch to zoom in, but the resolution remains low, so mostly it just makes for bigger blurry video. Viewed casually on a small phone, it’s okay as long as you don’t look too hard. There is also an iPad app, but that one is almost a beta. And in any case, the iPad app can’t access the main stream either, so given the bigger screen, the low resolution is even more limiting.

[EDIT: I upgraded the camera firmware, hoping that might help, but all I can tell that it did was to make it so that the Danale app doesn't work right anymore, including the zoom feature.]

Just to touch on network security, this camera comes per-configured for a DNS server in China. Even after changing that, the camera still opened 41 outbound ports. Most of the remaining IP addresses show as being in the US, but none of this is explained in the documentation. The documentation seems pretty much useless to me.

I have called GW Security multiple times, and I’ve talked to some good people, but apparently these problems are inherent, both in the hardware and the software. I am told that there are some newer models that have better software, but it’s not clear how many problems that would solve. And in any case, they were not willing to allow me to upgrade, because the chipset in the camera that I bought is now considered to be obsolete. No kidding. So is the software. If they had offered me an upgrade path to a better camera, I might have considered it, but since they did not, I might as well try my luck with a different brand. My experience with GW Security has not been good, so I certainly don’t want to make the same mistake twice.

title: Works with Apple headset and Zomm H6 recorder
text:
I bought this so that I could use my Apple headset with a Zoom H6 audio recorder. And it works with a few caveats. I noticed that some of the reviews indicated that it doesn't work with one headset or another, but I'm wondering if those people are aware that condenser microphones require power, be it from a battery compartment that is part of the microphone, or via phantom power or plug in power from the connected device.

In the case of the Apple headset, power normally comes from an iDevice via plug in power. In my case, the Zoom H6 can provide plug-in power. This would be a requirement with any cable or adapter. In any case, it works - I can hear sound from the Zoom via the headset and I can also hear my own voice from the headset mic.

It may be worth mentioning that this particular cable is a little bit shorter than ideal for the Zoom H6, since the headphone jack is near the bottom of the left side and the mic input is at the upper right, on the X/Y capsule. It reaches, but one has to either run the cable under the recorder, or over the top of it. I attached a photo so you can see what I mean. That's not really a knock against this adapter, unless one intends to use it for exactly the same purpose, and even then, it is workable.

As for quality, when the headset is the only thing connected to the H6, that audio quality is quite good. Much better than one might expect after hearing the same headset used with for a phone call from an iPhone. It is as good as some dedicated lav/lapel mics that I have. There is no audible hum, although Apple's mic does have some self-noise, again, similar to some sub $100 lavaliere mics. I believe that one could reasonably use a similar setup for any number of applications and that 99 percent of listeners would think it sounded great.

With that said, there is some cross-talk/bleed between the headset and the microphone. If I max out both the mic gain and the headphone volume on the Zoom H6, it actually causes feedback. Keeping in mind that there is a lot of gain going on when I do that. I can hear my own breath quite loudly, so the levels are way beyond anything "normal".

Other reviewers have stated that this adapter causes bleed-through with their headset, but I'm not sure that it's fair to blame the adapter because I have used this same headset with the Rode Rec app on my iPhone (and thus, no adapters), and it is possible to cause feedback with that setup as well. So I would conclude that most, if not all of the cross-talk/bleed-though/feedback with this particular headset happens within the headset itself. I would expect differing results with other headsets.

And then the shielding issue that some have mentioned. If I connect my digital piano to the H6 at the same time as the headset, I then hear some hum. It's not a lot of hum, but it's there. If I handle the TRRS jack on the adapter cable, it then hums much louder. It's not clear to me exactly what is taking place, but I can only assume that the piano connection exposes the recorder to the AC lines in some way, although, to be clear, there is zero hum when the adapter/headset combination is not connected. For example, if I connect the piano and my iPhone at the same time, that does not cause any hum at all. And other self-powered microphones plugged directly into the H6 also cause no hum.

I have a working theory that it has something to do with the CTIA standard itself, because contrary to good engineering practice, that standard puts the mic line on the shell of the connector, which by all logic, is where the shield should be. The only way that one could effectively shield a CTIA connectors would be to use a secondary shield around the entire connector body, which is something that I have not yet seen done. Interestingly, the competing OMTP standard does, in fact, make the shell ground, but Apple has traditionally gone out of their way to buck any and all industry standards, so it's not too surprising that they didn't adopt OMTP. One can only wonder why others followed.

If I'm right, then all CTIA-based microphones are going to be prone to hum, which would be no fault of this adapter. One could argue that MillSO could have come up with a way to provide shielding, but at the same time, it's not hard to imagine that they would just go with the standard, even though it may have a tragic flaw. Apple has since abandoned their own standard in favor of Lightning, yet another proprietary standard, and most recently, now that the world has purchased untold millions of dollar worth of Lightning adapters, they appear to be moving toward USB-C, which is bound to be the first time that Apple has ever adopted an existing industry standard. One might applaud if it were not for the investment in Lightning.

None of that speaks to the needs of any serious audio production work, but it certainly will muddy the waters for headphone and headset makers. And I have not offered a complete answer as to the quality of this adapter. All I can offer at this time is that I plan to try building my own. We have a cable shop here, so I am wondering if we can do a better job with using off-the-shelf components, but my initial searches for shielded TRRS jacks did not turn anything up. FWIW, I intend to use this adapter for a while and see if the hum is a problem in a real-world recording. I think it may be okay, and beyond that, I’m not sure that any other adapter would be any better. Most of the sellers on Amazon aren’t even willing to commit to the CTIA standard, let alone reveal any technical details like shielding, so while this adapter may be imperfect, it may also be as good as one can easily get.

title: Powerful and fast, but it is not small
text:
It's bigger than I imagined. This A7000 dwarfs the A6200. It's quite large. I have a 17" Samsung UltraBook (which is a big laptop for an UltraBook, and this adapter only clear the table by about 1/8" when plugged directly into a USB port. It also blocks the adjacent USB. port. The good thing about it almost touch the table is that it allows ths table to support it in case something pushes down on it.

Of course it does come with an external stand, so that offers some additional flexibility. But the cable that is permanently attached to the stand is also quite large and not particularly flexible. And it's worth mentioning that the stand has a warning label about "strong magnet". Lost on me, since I seldom use my laptop on a metal surface, which just means that the big stiff cable has a tendency to tip the whole giant thing over.

This model continues Netgear's unintuitive installation, where the software must be installed (from CD no less) before plugging the adapter in. Fortunately, my laptop happens to have an optical drive, but then I actually laughed out loud when the installation routine then prompted me to install an updated version from the internet. So the assumption is that whoever is using this adapter already has in internet connection? Hmmm. Well, as it turns out, my laptop has has built-in WI-Fi, so I was able to make it through the install routine, but wow, what a lot of silly assumptions.

I have installed any number of USB Wi-Fi adapters that "just worked" without any external software Seems like Netgear could do similar, if only so that folks could get connected to the internet well enough to then download their full-boat software. Because the reality is that many laptops have no optical drive. And of those that do, how many will be connected to the internet before the USB adapter can be used?

Once installed, the software works okay...although it looks about like it has for a long time and it seems rather slow and unresponsive. For example, it reported that it failed to connect to my access point three times before I realized that it had actually connected just fine. And then only after all of that did it finally show to be connected. The software doesn't appear to provide access to any diagnostic tools, such as signal strength (in dBm) or signal-to-noise ratio/signal quality. I saw no way to see or control which band is connected, nor any way to control output power. "Meh" at best.

With all of that having been said, it does certain things very well. It has great receivers, in that I can see dozens of access points that my built-in wireless never sees. Some that I happen to know about are on the next street and/or five houses down the block. It is also powerful, because I can connect to multiple open Xfininty access points that my built-in Wi-Fi can just barely detect, let alone connect to. I was quite impressed to see 60Mpbs download speeds on the same AP that my native Wi-FI can't connect to at all. The A7000 connects to things that even the old champion A6200 could not. I didn't get a good read on the maximum throughput under ideal conditions, but its fair to say that it was faster than anything else I have ever tried in that particular spot.

text:
I guess I'm going to have to give up on UGREEN cables. I got one that I thought was good, but now I've gotten three in a row that are terrible. This particular cable is so stiff that it flips my iPhone over if I try to make the cable lie flat on my desk. It also tends to spin the phone around so that I can't read it. It's just a very bulky, stiff, and unhandy cable.

The outside diameter is hard to measure because the cable is kind of lumpy, meaning that the OD varies depending on the exact point of measurement, but it's about 4.4 mm ( 0.173"). For comparison, the Apple cable that came with my iPhone is 2.9 mm (0.114") and a 1m Apple USB-C / Lightning cable is 3.4 mm (0.134"). This cable is a lot bulkier and the difference in flexibility is not insignificant.

For anyone who associates thickness with goodness, maybe this cable will seem good, but in my mind, the lack of flexibility serves only to impose excessive strain on the connectors, both on the cable and also in the connected devices. There's more to durability and build quality than sheer size. Personally, I don't think this cable will prove to be all that durable, but even if it did, if it destroyed my chargers and my connected devices, it would be a lousy trade-off.

Dump truck tires are bigger and more durable than grand touring tires, but which would be better for a road trip in a nice car? Speaking for myself, I'm going to return this cable and go for Apple's "GT"-like offering.

title: Great little antenna from great name
text:
The Channel Master brand has been around since the late forties. It has changed hands a few times, but if this little antenna is any indication, they have managed to hold onto the finest traditions of the brand.

This particular design seems to be focused upon UHF channels, as evidenced by the corner reflector design that comprises the majority of the elements. That's where most terrestrial channels now reside, so it makes sense, but with that said, the antenna also has a few longer elements behind the corner reflector, which seems to do a decent job with high VHF channels too. For Example, we have local channels 8 and 11, and both are coming in well with this antenna just a few feet above the edge of the roof and looking into 60-foot-tall trees less than 50 feet away.

For anyone with VHF channels below channel 8, this antenna probably won't be a strong performer, but keep in mind that the real RF channels are not the same as the virtual channel numbers - for example our local "Channel 2" is actually on UHF RF channel 35.

In any case, because of the small size and light weight, this antenna is about as easy to install as any outdoor antenna could be. The classic offers a low wind profile as compared to some of the goofy plastic-laden "modern":designs that typically make such exorbitant claims. It is, after all, an antenna, so it makes perfect sense to me that it should look like an antenna...function over form.

title: Anker cables keep getting bulkier and stiffer
text:
I bought this cable because some people commented that it was flexible. I suppose it's a relative concept, because I have some others that are even worse than this one, but in my mind, this is not a "flexible" cable. Looking at the drawing on the item page, it looks like it has a solid aluminum shield. 'Not sure why that would ever be a good idea for anything other than RF in the gigahertz range. The torsional flexibility is just awful. If it's not obvious to Anker, for flexibility, the shield needs to be serve or braided, not solid. There should be no solid conductors in a cable that is subject to constant handling, or where flexibility is desirable. And it's big and bulky too.

Genuine Apple USB-C to Lightning cables have an OD of around 3.4mm. I have an Anker Powerline III cable that also measures ~3.4mm, although it is less flexible than the genuine Apple cables. And just to be clear, even the Apple cables are a lot thicker and less flexible than they used to be - I have some with USB-2 plugs on them that measure a svelte 2.9 mm. Those were pretty good cables. Perhaps more fragile, but I still have some that are fine after a decade, and they are a lot easier and more pleasing to use.. They lay flat on a surface, they don't flip my Airpods over. They put less stress on the connectors. This is one case where bigger is not better.

title: Not as quiet as the price suggests
text:
People say these fans are utterly silent. Inaudible. But unfortunately, that simply isn't true. At full speed, Noctua's own spec is 22.6 dB(A), but they don't reveal the test conditions or the distance. Me thinks they must have used a rather large anechoic test chamber to come up with that number. In my own informal testing, in free air, resting on a table, at at distance of 1 meter from the intake side of the fan, I measured 38.7 dB(A). At 30 centimeters, I measured 46.3 dB(A).

Practically speaking, I think most people are about a meter away from their computers while using them, so there really isn't much use in quoting specs at greater distances. In my suburban home, the noise floor during the day is about 28 dB(A). If the NF-A12x25 PWM actually was 22.6 dB at 1m, that truly would be approaching inaudible, even in a very quiet environment. But FWIW, even with my noise floor of 28 dB(A), I can still hear this fan at 6 meters, which seems to suggest that it's still over 28 dB at that distance. Would Noctua have used a distance as great as 10 meters?

But again, it's almost 39 dB(A) at 1m, and at that distance, the noise from NF-A12x25 PWM is significant. The noise signature makes it more noticeable because it's not just the white noise associated with rushing air. Instead, it has a prominent whine that my spectrum analyzer app shows to be 323Hz. To my ear, it sounds about the same as G4 on a keyboard, which would be 392Hz. In any case, there is a whine somewhere in that range that is at least 6dB louder than the white noise. And for my ears, it is an annoying frequency.

I suppose that most people will use PWM to slow it down, but then almost all fans are pretty quiet below 1000 RPM, so then what is the point of a supposedly quiet fan? IDK...I just feel like its a whiny fan. I think I like the noise signature of the old Noctua blade design better. This one may put up better numbers on a meter, but the numbers fail to reflect the real-world human experience.

On the plus side, it seems to move a fairly broad stream of air, which might make it desirable as an intake fan. I can't speak for cooler applications. I had intended to use these as case exhaust fans, but I'll have to see how the thermals compare to the "lesser" fans they will replace. If they turn out to be louder for the same thermal performance, I will be even more disappointed than I already am.
item_title: Noctua NF-A12x25 PWM, Premium Quiet Fan, 4-Pin (120mm, Brown)

title: Unimaginable time spent chasing problems caused by these risers!
text:
Some work, some don't. The ones that don't work look just like the ones that do work. Endless swapping of cables, adapters and riser boards. No way to tell which parts are good, if any. Multiple combinations that cause immediate crashes. And then one package that seems to work just fine. Until it doesn't - in at least in one case simply moving the cable caused the rig to crash. It is as if they are right on the edge of not working, so any little disturbance causes failure. In one case, moving a rig that was somehow working with these risers an inch closer to a PDU caused the rig to crash every few minutes. It was very hard to believe that moving the rig a few inches could make that much difference. Perhaps the shielding is poor.

There may be a clue may in the lack of any logos on the connectors, but it also appears that there might be something unique about the included cables, because swapping to a known good cable that came with a different brand of riser does not work. When I test the cables with a Trendnet cable USB tester, the quick test sometimes shows good, but then switching to a different brand of cable shows bad, which suggests that while they pass the quick test, they are wired differently than other brands.

Some components on the board are not even soldered down. The leads are not trimmed which causes the rubber pads to fall off. The socket locks are unhandy. But all of that is trivial compared to the maddening inconsistency and never-ending random failures. More trouble from this batch of risers that from all of others combined. One can almost accept the occasional bad riser board or cable, but to swap it out for another one and then find that one to be bad too? And then a second and a third? It's just unacceptable.

I've been chasing these never-ending issues for weeks - to the point that they are no longer eligible for return, so not only have they cost me an untold amount of time and frustration, but now I'm stuck with them. I think I have to throw them away in hopes of salvaging my sanity.

title: Engenius failed to include a way to mount this model on a surface!
text:
It's not clear from the photos...it looks like a nice, clean access point. On the Engenius website, it is shown very neatly flush-mounted on a drywall ceiling. And most of the photos show it in residential settings, but it's not actually possible to mount it in a home with typical drywall construction, using what comes in the box.
One might be able to hack up the included T-Rail bracket so that it could mount flat on a surface, but then it wouldn't be anything like a flush mount and it wouldn’t be pretty. None of the photos even show the unfinished side of the AP. I have attached a photo that shows what you will see, except that it will be a full inch off of the ceiling (and crooked if one uses the unmodified included T-rail clip). You’ll have your cable coming out in full view and then presumably going up through an fully-visible hole in your ceiling. Unless you terminate the cable in place, the hole will have to be big enough to accommodate the RJ-45 plug, so it will be extra ugly. And the access point will hang down so far that you might even be able to see the cable from the far side.

When did it become acceptable for the Ethernet and power connectors to be fully exposed? That's not okay for a home or for a business. IMHO, it's just stupid. It is almost as if there should be a mounting plate with a plastic cover for the ports, but apparently it doesn't exist. This is someone's bright idea of how to build an access point. Very disappointing from a company that has made so very many perfectly acceptable access points over the years. FWIW, the EAP1300 mounts just like one would expect an access point to mount. Maybe this is some other brand of access point that Engenius just slapped their brand name on, although I can’t imagine why.

Oh, and it runs pretty hot too. The specs say that up to 104F ambient is acceptable, but this thing might actually melt if the ambient temperature was that high. I’m not sure what’s it’s good for. Perhaps a very cold unfinished space with a suspended ceiling…(?)

title: Trick to get it to work properly with the iPhone
text:
I spent a couple of frustrating days trying to keep a connection long enough to transfer a photo and was about to give up and send it back when I happened upon an idea I should have thought of myself. Credit goes to a user who posted on the Nikon site.

You don't need to mess with all the network settings in the app - you can if you like, but it is not necessary. The trick to get a reliable connection is to put your iPhone into airplane mode (thereby eliminating all forms of potential network interference) and then enable ONLY the wifi connection to the camera. Do this and everything will work just fine. When you are done, simply disable airplane mode and all your original settings will be in place again and you can go on your merry way.

As for all the other network settings in the app:

Renaming the network is probably smart if you don't want to advertise that you have an expensive Nikon in the vicinity. Password protecting the network may be overkill, but it can't hurt. You really don't need to touch anything else.

title: A really good value for a heavy-duty set up.  It should last a long time and serve well.
text:
This is, indeed, a heavy-duty stand. The air-cushioning in the stands allows for adjusting the height without worry about anything collapsing in the process. Well done. The sections of the cross-beam are also impressive. They connect easily and remain secure. With all 5 sections (15 feet), you will see sagging, but you have to expect it at that width. I can't imagine even needing all 15' of width.

The packaging suffered a bit during shipment, but the contents were mostly OK. There was one dent in a leg of one of the stand, but nothing sufficient to compel a return. Also noticed some nicks in the paint on the cross beam sections as if someone has grasped them with pliers. Again, nothing I couldn't correct with a little clear nail polish to seal the metal again. In the long run, powder-coated metal will always get nicked up, so I'm not terribly concerned. I was, however, a bit concerned about a tightening screw for the spigot on one stand. The thread in the stand was not completely machined through, so the screw wouldn't tighten on the spigot. Again, nothing I couldn't correct, but I shouldn't have needed to. The other stand was perfect. Perhaps a little quality control issue in the factory? Otherwise, everything is fine.

The included case is most welcomed as it accommodates all the bits and pieces nicely. An zippered, internal pocket would be a nice addition to hold the spigots (with washers and nuts) and the clamps – perhaps an enhancement for future designs? However, I still have to chide Ravelli for the rough aluminum zipper. After going to the trouble to design an otherwise nice case, a brass zipper should have been the automatic choice. This zipper is only slightly better than the completely unusable zipper on the case that came with my medium-duty Ravelli stand.

title: A great little package
text:
I waited a few months before writing a review so I could back it up with fact and experience.

I purchased this for myself and find it to be an invaluable tool. I travel on average 42 weeks per year all over the US for work. I take it along to help me find my way from Airport to work site to hotel and lots of POI's in between. It has not let me down, rather it has dummied me down more than anything else. No need to look for street signs or wondering when my next turn would happen. No more fumbling through printed out direction from Yahoo or Map Quest. I feel safer knowing my Nuvi will tell me when and where to turn. The maps are not perfect, as is evident in my own town and a few familiar places, but they have always gotten me to where I've wanted to go, and most importantly, back to my hotel after a day being out and about.

The turn by turn voice directions are great. Since this is my first GPS, I don't know what it would be like if they didn't read street names or POI's name. I prefer the UK male voice because he's oh so proper. He's no better or worse than the US male voice. They both get it wrong some times. Both will read BR, which in some areas means Business Route, but translate it to Bridge. Dr is sometimes read as Doctor not Drive. They do make me think about what I just heard, but I just laugh it off.

I say, if you're looking for a GPS, I would recommend the NUVI 350. Not only will it get you where you want to go, it will get you there safely and in style. The small size fits great in my briefcase as well as my shirt pocket.

title: Please avoid this one.
text:
My first negative review for any product bought at Amazon. I read all prior reviews regarding this FM transmitter and was interested in this one since it played double duty, FM transmitter and power supply for my Zune. I don't always believe everything I read in reviews, but I should have where this product is concerned. Let me start by saying I have an iRiver FM transmitter that worked great, but wanted one that would also power my device, enter the Zune transmitter.
Following the instruction that came with the Zune transmitter and reading suggestions from others (the reviews here at Amazon) I bought this one. Right from the start the Zune transmitter couldn't find an open frequency. After a few attempts I just manually set it to one I personally discovered was one of the best for my area. The Zune transmitter broadcasted on this frequency, but it sounded like a static AM Radio. Words with an "S" in them were slurred, along with frequent bouts of static being transmitted. I tried moving the Zune around the interior of the car since the cord was the sending antenna, but there was no difference. After moving the car to a new location, I again attempted to lock onto a FM frequency (yes my car radio was turned off). Again the Zune transmitter couldn't find one. My personal experience with the slurring S's was due to playing the devise was set at a too high output volume. Turning down the volume on the device and up on the car radio always resulted in a clear and clean sound with my iRiver MP3 player and FM transmitter. With the Zune and the Zune FM transmitter, you can't make changes to the output volume. I'm certain that if I could change the volume the transmitter might work better.
After plugging my iRiver FM transmitter back on my Zune, I'm enjoying my Zune tunes in my car. My recommendation, don't buy this Zune transmitter, buy the iRiver FM transmitter. Sorry Zune.
