I've waited a while before deciding to write a review. I wanted to give it some time, so that what I write would be after months of experience with it. To sum up my kindle, now known as the kindle with keyboard, it's GREAT! It's convenient and has been a pleasure to own. I've never held such a light weight book in my hand, or shall I say books. I usually keep about 4 books on board, and a few magazines that I subscribed to. When I'm done reading a book I just remove it from the device, and it's waiting for me in the Cloud the next time I want to read it. Click the Archive link, and in seconds it's back on the device.

The kindle I bought was the one with "Special Offers". A few other reviews hated it, but I'm here to tell you, other than displaying the offers, or advertisements, on the screen saver screen, and a little, very obscure banner, at the bottom of the index page, I hardly see it's there. I do like the offers I've received from them, you can't beat $1.00 book offers, or other discounts on Amazon purchases. I suggest to everyone, get the model with the special offers. You'll enjoy the savings now, and continue to enjoy the savings in the future.

As for the "Experimental" features, I loaded some music on it, and play it softly on the device in the background. It just adds a bit of background music to block out the background noises. The "Text to Speech" feature is okay, but I'm not an audio book fan, so it's not an important feature to me. The "Browser", if you need to use the browser, it has one, but it's really not worth the time or effort to fire it up. Using the browser is rather clunky.

Shortly after I purchased my kindle, Amazon announced the new Kindle Fire. I only had buyers remorse for about 5 seconds. The screen size is a bit bigger, and yes it's a color display with many advanced features, but after reading on my sisters Nook one day, I'd rather read books on the eInk display. It's much easier on the eyes, and I was able to take it my kindle to the beaches of Lake Michigan and read it just like a paper book. Sister carted a paper back from her library wishing she could have had her e-reader instead. If you're thinking about the Nook, don't. Barnes and Noble does not have the great customer service Amazon has, nor does their web site offer much in self help support either. What a lame excuse for a device, let alone a company.

Bottom line; I love my kindle and the simplicity of owning an e-reader. If you've been thinking it over, stop thinking and just push the buy button now, you'll be happy you did. Oh yeah, bite the bullet and get the lighted leather case. Sure it's slightly expensive, but an accessory you shouldn't go with out. title: An observers review.
text:
This review is geared to those people that are whining about the Kindle Fire, and their perception of what it's lacking. Let me say this; First and foremost, it's an "AMAZON" e-reader with multimedia capabilities, linking to Amazon's content. That said, if you're looking for something more, pay more and get a full featured tablet.

1. This device is linked to the largest book store on the Internet. You're not reading every book you ever bought, so storing read books in the cloud is a great resource should you want to re-read the book again. If you want free books to read, they have a lending library, and they gave you the ability to link it to your local library. Only thing you need is a library card.

2. Amazon built this device so you can access their video library while within range of wifi, yours at home or a wifi hotspot. There are apps available to Netflix, Hulu and others, so you have choices. If you expected to watch their free movies on a train, plane or automobile, you should have bought a tablet from Sprint, Verizon, AT&T, and subscribed to their 3g, 4g or lte to stream them to your device when ever, where ever. If you had expectations for Xfinity, Comcast is not in the tablet business.

3. Amazon will sell you music in the mp3 format. They'll store that music for you on the cloud, for free no less, and allow you access to it any time you want while in wifi range. Want to add music from your personal library of cd's and mp3, you can do that too. Want to listen to your tunes on your cell phone or desktop, you'll have access on those devices as well.

4. Amazon has a wonderful App store where you can download a plethora of Android apps. This is a reading/multimedia device. If you wanted access to the Android Market, you should have spent the money on a full featured tablet. Give Amazon some time; I'm sure they're adding new apps nearly every day.

5. Text to Voice is gone. Agreed. It's a book reader. If you want to have your books read to you, Audible dot com has a solution for you. You can download audible books to the device, and store them for future listening in the Amazon cloud.

6. The silk browser is there as a convenience. If surfing the internet is your main reason for buying this device, and your disappointed, what do you expect for $199.00 and a 7" screen? Really people.

7. You'll have to give Amazon your credit card information. Once done, you'll never have to pull it out of your wallet or purse again. How much more convenient can that be? It's your reading device. Amazon is trying to make it easy for you so you won't have to enter that data again. And yes, you can password protect your purchases.

8. I can't access my e-mail. Really? They included an app that will link to the most popular e-mail providers. Enter you e-mail information and they're there. Feel a need to post to facebook, there's an app for that too... Yup, I want to read your post, "I'm sitting down to read a book". Priceless.

9. If you're expecting the AMAZON Fire (e-reader/multimedia device) to give you access to your office's network and all its resources, why? It's a 7" personal e-reader/multimedia device, not a replacement of your laptop or desktop. The same complaints here are written in the reviews on the full featured tablets.
10. If you feel a need to compare the Amazon Fire to an iPad, don't. You're comparing an orange to a banana. Reviews that say they're going to buy a Nook, you'll have the same whine and complaints there that you'll have here, plus some more.

In general, read the description Amazon has regarding their device. Nowhere does it say it's a replacement of a full featured tablet, laptop or desktop computer. It's an e-reader/multimedia device linking directly to Amazon's content and then some.

For those who post about the lack of Google Play, then they should have bought a stock Android tablet. It's that simple! I have both an Asus tablet and HTC phone that can access Play, and yes there are more apps available there, but what are you looking for that you can't get at Amazon or can't live without? I found that several apps at Play are only available for phones and can't be put on an Android tablet. Not a deal breaker.

The only thing, if a bridge happens to be out and the detour signs are in your path, follow the detour so you don't end up in a river or driving off the side of a mountain.

title: It's just okay.
text:
After a several frustrating hours I finally have my TV and Home Entertainment system setup and working correctly, and let me say this, no thanks to Samsung. What a worthless customer service department Samsung has.
First off, my Home Entertainment setup consists of the now Samsung 48” LED TV, Onkyo Receiver, Motorola (Xfinity) set top box, Roku 2, Panasonic Blue Ray, Emerson VCR, that are all controlled by a Logitec Harmony all-in-one remote control. Every source HDMI or Composite output is connected to the Onkyo Receiver that then sends the audio and video signal out through an HDMI cable to the a single input on the TV with audio flowing back from the TV to the Onkyo for playback controlled by the Onkyo receiver through the attached 5.1 speakers. Confusing I know, but after setting this up years ago, it all began making sense as it does now.
Here was the problem I experienced. When I press the button on the remote to watch TV, the sequence is ; Turn on the set top box, then the receiver setting the source to Cable/Sat, and lastly the TV. As everything turns on/boots up I begin to see the picture and hear the audio. As the Samsung continued its boot sequence flashing input coming in on HDMI 1, it would change the Source Input on the receiver to TV/CD and go to a Blue Screen (reminiscent of Microsoft’s Windows blue screen of death). Only resolve would be to manually change the receivers source back to Cable/Sat. Frustrating as I just couldn’t understand why this kept happening. I checked, double checked, triple check the programming on the Logitec remote, nothing there was amiss, nothing was setup to change the source input from Cable/Sat to TV/CD.
Time to call Samsung. That was a ping pong match at best, where I was sent from one tech to another. The sad part was, not 1 tech had ever heard of Motorola, Onkyo or Logitec. They couldn’t even begin to understand how this system worked. If what I owned didn’t have Samsung written on it, they were clueless. Their only suggestion was to throw out everything I owned and just watch TV on the Samsung and be happy with that or connect all devices to the available HDMI inputs and live with crappy sound from the TV and have a dozen remotes sitting around the living room. I did Google the issue and found others that were experiencing the same problem I was, and after digging around for a while settled on the solution. Turn off the Anynet + on the Samsung. The down side of that, and one I can live with, you lose the ability to successfully use their SmartTV services. Sure I can still pull it up, but the audio out fails. Lucky me, I’ve got my Roku, which is 100 times better than anything Samsung could dream up.
As for the performance of the TV, it’s okay. I miss my Panasonic 42” Plasma, which died after just 3 year, as the picture quality was far superior. I would have gotten another Plasma TV, but I don’t have the wall space for one, as they’re only available on 55” + screen sizes. Colors on the screen are good, rather bright and vibrant. The only thing I don’t like, the whites are a bit too bright. I’ll try turning down the backlighting. I also find the picture quality to be a bit grain’ish. That’s typical of an LED/LCD TV, especially on larger screen sizes. This is not Samsung’s fault, it the nature of the breast.
Would I recommend this set, maybe… but I wouldn’t recommend a call to Samsungs customer service center. You’re talking to someone in a foreign country that’s reading/replying from prompts on a computer monitor. This way Samsung doesn’t have to hire someone with knowledge, they only need an employee that can type and read English. It’s sad we’re still enduring poor customer service in the year 2015. Samsung has not learned what other quality companies have, bring CS back to the States.

The operating system, Windows 10 is pretty solid and works smoothly on the Surface, but I still have some reservations with it, as features/apps I use to enjoy on Win 7 were missing on 10 but available through the app store. Just not sure why so few selections and/or why most include obnoxious ads thrown in your face. Read them carefully before installing, the ones without the ads are there, but you have to dig deep to find them or pay big dollars for the ones without the ads. I did download Chrome on here and it's working flawlessly, just like on my desktop and Chrome book. All of the bloatware apps that came on windows 10 were removed. The one I bought was the 128/4 gig ram version, where experience over the past years taught me that storage and ram are important. I have a 64 gig micro ssd card installed, but in time I'm sure I'll get the 128 gig one. So far everything I've thrown at the Surface 3 is working smoothly.

Update: 11/25/2015
I've read several reviews prior to and more after I bought the Surface referencing charging issues. After sleuthing the web I happened up a workaround solution a Surface blog. It doesn't require anything special, just reversing what we've been doing all these years.
1. Make sure the charger is unplugged from the electrical outlet.
2. Plug the Micro USB into the Surface
3. Plug the USB into the charger
4. Plug the charger into the electrical outlet.
Yup, Bass Ackwards from what we've been doing, but no more charging concerns.

title: A fun and promising gadget.
text:
So far so good. First thing after opening the package was charge the watch. It fired right up when connected to the charger and it started setup process. I had already downloaded Android Wear Manager, so when it told me to download the app to my phone I just opened the app, answered a few questions and the watch was connected to my HTC M8 - Marshmallow. The watch then started downloading updates. Be prepared, mine went through about 3 updates over the first hour on the charger. Please note this was not written anywhere, the watch connected/showed connection, but to get true 2 way connection between the phone and watch, I restarted my phone. After that Android Wear and Asus Manager were talking properly with the watch.

My learning curve was quick. Follow the few on-screen demo's and you'll be swiping like a pro in no time. "Ok Google" works great. After reading some comments that Pandora didn't play nice with Android Wwe, wrong. I said Ok Google, play Pandora. The app fired up on my phone and music started streaming. All the player controls showed up on the screen, a few swipes later and and I've thumbed up/down songs, skipped forwards, stopped and restarted right from the watch screen. Notifications are cool, you can read the whole incoming e-mails and texts. Say Ok Google, Text (insert persons name), leaving now, see you at the restaurant shortly. Confirm and you're message is off and running. You should also be able to control most apps on the phone by just talking to your wrist.

So why did I buy the Asus first generation Smartwatch and not the second generation? First I've been considering getting a smartwatch for a while and when the price of this Asus dropped to $99 here at Amazon, I thought why not. Only difference is gen. 2 is wifi. I was also considering waiting for the new HTC 10 and possible announcement of HTC's Smartwatch, but at this price if I didn't like it I hadn't lost much money. I think I'll like it, I'm a gadget junky. I'm also a frequent traveler and the apps I use for airlines and travel information all connect with Smartwatches and they should deliver flight information straight to my wrist. We'll see come Monday morning when I head off to far off places.

As for how it looks on my wrist, I'm pleased. I do have a small wrist for a guy, and it is a bit bigger than what I would have liked, but not to big to stand out like a sore thumb. I thought I would have to adjust the band to a smaller setting, but this wasn't the case. I feel all grown up now.

So in summary from my short term experience, I think it's going to be a fun gadget/enhancement to my phone. Should I have any negative experiences I'll come back and add them to this post.

title: Another successful purchase
text:
This is my second Harmony remote, the first being the 550, so I had a basic understanding of the programming process before jumping in. The Harmony Smart Control was no different. There are important prep-steps you need do before you even start programming your new Harmony Smart Control. Run around the room and get the manufacturer's name and exact model numbers of each device you plan to add into the mix. Guessing will be more frustrating as you’ll still be turning around the TV, flipping over the Blueray player, pulling out the receiver and cable box….. Now that you have all the information in hand you’re ready to tackle the task. If you have a desktop or laptop computer, use it as your 5” cell phone screen and keyboard are just a bit to small for adult hands. Also, grab your reading glasses and take your time to read your screen. All told, I downloaded the software and configured 6 devices/activities in under 30 minutes.

Now that I’ve completed the above task, I like this Harmony Smart Control. A few things I would have liked better on the hand held control are more buttons for action/activities. Now it’s a short button press or using the same button a long press to to perform an activity. The musical note button was programmed to watch the Blueray, long press on the video means watch the VCR (yup I still have old school)... Another thing, the number pad buttons could be a bit larger. They’re too narrow in height for the average finger. I know these are minor concerns, but there are many of us that would rather grab a remote then fire up an app on a cell phone.

Going Alexa with the Harmony??? After you download the skill and log it into your Harmony account, you need to know this one little tip. I learned this on my own as it wasn’t written anywhere I looked. If you say “Alexa change channel to 1003” and she comes back and says she can’t find that skill, backup one huge step. Using your remote turn off the TV (activity) and set it back on the coffee table. Now say “Alexa, turn on TV”. All your devices will fire up and now Alexa will be happy to control your entertainment world with simple commands. Don’t forget when you’re done to say “Alex, turn of TV” Same rule applies to watching your Roku, Blueray player and VCR. If you’re watching TV and you wish to switch to your Roku, say “Alexa, turn on Roku”, she doesn’t understand the words “Watch or Switch".

As for other AI Smart Home device programming on the Harmony, I can’t speak for that. My home automation is via Iris by Lowes and I have the skill configured within Alexa. I’m just an Alexa command away from turning on/off/dimming lights, changing the thermostat etc...

title: A rather easy transition
text:
I got word that Iris, my previous home automation system, was shutting down at the end of March 2019, so I immediately ordered a Smartthings hub as my replacement. It didn't hurt that this was one of Lowe's recommendation and that the vast majority of my devices would transition. The setup and transition was fairly painless. I removed one by one each of my transferable devices and immediately paired it with Smartthings. I had an issue with one device, which required some Smartthings phone support to get paired, turned out to be simple after Daniel got on the phone. My biggest concern was my thermostat This one was an Iris 1st generation device. Everything I read said it would pair, as it turned out we need to download and install the previous version of the Smartthings app and install it from there and it showed up on the new app. I have 3 devices yet to transition over, I just wasn't in the mood to crawl under the house or move my car in the garage for 2 of them. I'll do that this coming week as they're not mission critical today.

Programming Scenes, scheduling tasks and assigning button functions was no more difficult than Iris was, actually it may have been a bit easier, or Iris gave me some good experiences. Programming options are about the same, just wish there was a history event log. From Iris I could see at a very quick glance if she preformed the tasks and/or when the last time the garage door either went up or down. The Geo Tracking function in theory looks promising, however it seems very slow to recognize when I return home and run the assigned scene. In time I'll add my Iris fob and assign scenes to run with the press of a button from the car rather then rely on the Geo Tracking function if doesn't speed up.

I'm not a home automation power programmer as some I've seen out on the internet, but for my simple needs I'm hoping to have as good a relationship with Smartthings as I had with Iris. Rest in peace Iris, it was a fun ride.

One more thing: Smartthings, find Daniel in customer service, give the guy a hefty raise!!! He understood my needs and came to the rescue in a cool, calm, and very knowledgeable way. Guys like him are hard to find and easily lost.

After deleting old partitions and a quick format, it has worked flawlessly on every device I've plugged it into. title: Huge improvement for my build!
text:
For the longest time, I've been using an Asus P8H61-I R2.0, paired with an Intel i5-3470 and 16Gb of Kingston DDR3-10600. I started with some HDDs and a very crappy Geforce GTS450. Eventually, I upgraded to SSDs and an a GTX-1060. While it still performed everything I asked of it quite nicely, the new generation of hardware was too much of a temptation and decided to upgrade. The main reason I chose this board was the built-in Thunderbolt connectivity and the form factor. The RGB is a nice bonus too...

After setting everything up, I haven't experienced any issues. Installing my Ryzen 7 3700x was a breeze. Space to "maneuver" is scarce, but that's a given with any mITX board. I went with a Noctua NH-L9i chromax.Black, which is one of the recommended coolers for this board and it fits in quite nicely. Make sure to install the CPU and cooler first! I was able to load the correct XMP profiles for the pair of HyperX Predator DDR4 3200MHz, plug my old SATA SSDs (which now work considerably faster, given that they are now plugged to SATA 3 ports rather than SATA 2 ports) and my GTX-1060. Even Windows 10 loaded without too much hassle, just a few bangs in device manager due lack of drivers and it complaining about "activation". Installed updated drivers, the latest BIOS, fixed Windows' activation nag and have been a happy camper since.

Of course, nothing is perfect, I do have a complaint about the included manual. The one I got didn't have a board layout schematic, so it was difficult to ID the headers. To top it off, the case header is next to a USB 2.0 header which is almost identical. The board is all black and there's no text on itself to ID the headers. I downloaded one of the manuals from Asrock's website which did have the board layout schematic. Armed with that, I was reminded how much I hate plugging individual pins to a header. That's not a fault of the board, but a fault of the case. I wish Silverstone would have fitted the RVZ-02 with one of those "unified" case plugs...

I read a few reviews of users complaining about the angled SATA ports, which I thought could give me a bit of trouble, but it really hasn't. I think that would depend on the case and cables, I guess.

I still need to get a Thunderbolt dock, an NVMe drive, a better monitor, a different case and some water cooling to finish how I want to set everything up, but as it is right now, it's working fantastically. Everything is super snappy and I haven't even played with the overclocking yet. This board was certified by Intel for it's Thunderbolt, I doubt it'll be an issue. I've used Asrock boards in the past and have been very happy with their reliability and their longevity. I expect this to continue with this one.

title: PITA and I'm not talking what you put falafel in
text:
I needed a 10Gb capable switch. While my case is sorta unique. I need a mix of SFP+ and RJ45 10Gb ports and I needed cheap. This look to fit the bill for about 280 or so out the door.

I have a ubiquiti USG, 48 port PoE with 2 SFP+ ports and a few APs, what i'm looking to build out is a repurpose of some old and some newer hardware, refreshed, to handle all my media, containers, and lab work. Im looking to build a 10Gb back end storage solution for most of these nodes and this switch I was hoping would fit in.

I spent about 8 hours using this switch and I really only need it to function as a dumb switch. Plug one end into my SFP+ on the ubiquiti and set the whole thing to a storage lan. Well this didn't work out very well. The 2M DAC I ordered here didn't work with my switch and this switch so had to stack the Mikro on top and use a 12" cable. That worked fine. The 2M cable worked fine in a synology with an SFP+ card and plugged to the other SFP+ port. Worked, just fine. No in and out issues at all.

Booting up the Mikro only 6 of the ports would init which I found odd. Their RouterOS to be set to "SwoS" simply doesn't work well, or isn't documented clearly but really I tried everything but the console and I couldn't set it to SwitchOS. Not only that but when I would make some changes the switch would run fine, when I would reboot it to make sure the changes persisted, the switch was not accessible.

If you read around and check the forums there is a whole history of issues and stability problems, with people's switches suddenly not being accessible and that sort of thing, and to me it's just not worth it, for when a ubiquiti XG that has 12 SFP+ AND 4 RJ45 is about 280 more. So what's a headache worth? What's a MUCH better UI worth? What's stability worth? What's a smiley face to your wife and kids worth while working on your network/tech projects? What's ease of use and better dashboard worth? It's worth much more than 280 bucks that's for sure. The only reason I don't give this 1 star is that it seems this works out for some people, but really I'd stay away from it.

title: Big punch, small price
text: I got this because I hadn't had a waterproof speaker in awhile since my JBL speaker died. So, when I saw this, I figured it was worth a shot to try it since something this inexpensive would probably just be middling at best. Well, boy oh boy, was I wrong about that. This is far and away BETTER than my JBL ever was, and then some. The speaker was simple to pair with my phone and on first test, was EXTREMELY loud at max volume. Loud enough that i had it set on my desk and the loudness (and the insane bass) had the speaker jumping on the desk and moving around. I never had my JBL do that at max volume. The button set up is a bit odd unless you are just pairing to a phone or whatnot. I do love the option for a sd card if I want to use it. The lights dancing to music is pretty good and the clock is nice since it seems to sync with the phone/device thats pairing to it. Definitely recommend this to someone wanting a speaker in a damp place like a bathroom while showering.

title: Big cooler, little noise
text:
I was going to buy a Noctua cooler for my new Ryzen 7 3700X, having dealt with them before and been impressed by them, but for reasons that escape me Noctua continues to use that awful brown color on their fans. After looking around for alternatives I arrived at this cooler, and I'm glad I did. It performs every bit as well as any other Noctua cooler I've used including the NH-D15 and it's just as quiet, while also being much more attractive. It isn't any cheaper, unfortunately, but as they say, you get what you pay for.

Ryzen 3000 series parts are known to run hot, and this cooler allows my 3700X to boost to its maximum frequency all the time while never passing 75C, even though my MSI motherboard is pushing higher voltage than I think is strictly necessary, hovering at 1.4-1.45V. It does this without even a whisper. It's even quieter than the stock Wraith Spire that I was using with my Ryzen 7 1700 before, and that cooler was praised by reviewers when Zen first released because it was so quiet, compared to the stock coolers Intel ships.

Installation was simple enough, Noctua gets plenty of praise for their mounting system but this system is actually better in my opinion, because with this cooler two of the caps in the top come out and they line up exactly with the mounting brackets, so you don't have to try to hard to hit the screws the first time. They also thoughtfully provide a 4 pin PWM fan Y-cable so you can connect both of the fans to one fan header, if you want them both to run off the same PWM signal or if you only have one CPU fan header.

Overall, I'm impressed. I expected to have to make a compromise to get something that wasn't ugly as sin to cool my new CPU, but this is every bit as good as a Noctua cooler, if not slightly better in terms of installation, and it looks way better. I would definitely recommend this for anyone looking for a high end air cooler.

title: Seems Like a Quality Tripod
text:

With that said, I already know that a solid tripod is invaluable. I had a $20 cheapy model that I'd had for years for my video camera. It wobbles. It's cheaply put together. It's hard to adjust. I knew I needed something better and quick.

Well, the problem with the "good" ones is that they cost a lot (IMO). That's where this AmazonBasics tripod comes in. The price is right and it will handle a decent amount of weight. Too good to be true?

I'm happy to say (again, IMO) that it isn't. This thing is very solid. No wobble at all. All parts seem to be of good quality. Very little plastic bits (mainly the clamps). The trigger head is also very nice. It is made of metal and seems solid and holds its position. If it gets loose, there's an adjustment screw (wrenches provided). Can move around in most any angle one might need (even straight down or straight up).

Now, I haven't had much time with it yet so the real test will be how it holds up. It seems solid enough and well built I suspect it will do well. I'll update my review if and when it breaks on me.

Oh, this thing is heavy at 8.2 lbs, so know what you are getting into. While it does come with a bag, it might be a chore to carry long distances or long periods of time. I personally bought it partly because of this though, as the heavier the more stable.

I would recommend this tripod.

title: Nice Cameras for the Price
text:
[[VIDEOID:536c92ad8394e600238696433d81c8cc]] I have had three of these setup for a few days now and been running them through some tests. So far, for the money spent, I’m pretty happy. I installed these on our RV to monitor while we are away from it (we boondock a lot in remote areas).

WiFi seems strong but we don’t have much ground to cover in a 30 foot RV.

Sync module has lost WiFi connection several times but did recover itself within 10 minutes or so. Wasn’t really happy about the time it took to re-login but I think some of it has to do with our internet connection. We use a hotspot since we are camping. It has plenty of bandwidth but I think sometimes the cell tower itself gets bogged down which may be our issue. More time will tell.

Overall video quality is good, not great, but good. I’ve tried all the quality settings and settled on ‘best’ or 720p due to our internet connection. The ‘enhanced’ or 1080p setting really didn’t seem that much better and increases the file sizes.

Night vision is acceptable but is a bit lacking IMO. Quality of the clips goes down and is obviously more noisy.

Motion sensing is pretty good. We’ve gotten clips from the early morning hours as small critters roam around our campsite. You can tell what they are so not too bad. However, there have been times while testing the system when it failed to see me open our door and exit the RV. Also the ten second delay between clips is a bit much but I think I understand why they do it (time for the camera to upload the clip to the sync module is my guess).

Based on other reviews I purchased other wall mounts and was very glad that I did after seeing the mounts they come with. They don’t swivel much.

Overall though, I’m happy with the purchase. Very easy to setup and works pretty well even for our remote usage.

We had cameras on our home for many years and I like these better. YMMV.

title: Bought it for VPN
text:
Yes this router has VPN server built into it.
It means:
You can mask your IP address or destination (lets say while being connected to wifi at work) with the IP address that is assigned to this router by your modem.

You have to understand that in order for VPN to work for external connections such as from work etc, you have to have our modem to be in a PASS THROUGH mode.
It means MODEM WILL NOT give router local IP address such as 10.0.0.05 for example, but rather give it your external, your real IP address.

This external IP address is then used to connect to your VPN from outside.

It may sound confusing but hear me out. There are lots of tutorials on youtube and on the web telling you how to setup and connect to your VPN server in this router, but no one mentions that your modem has to pass external IP address to the router in order for VPN to be accessible from the internet. Caz you know, VPN is on the router, not on the modem

Or buy your self VPN modem. Will be easier and less hoops to jump. Not sure of such exist but who knows.

title: IT WILL KILL YOUR MOTHERBOARD
text:
Here is a problem with this switch.
Its connecting two power lines parallel so you always have voltage on either active or not cable.
When that happens, motherboard will likely to fail to shutdown in some cases and corrupt bios or something else.
I had 2 motherboards that refused to boot after normal shutdown while connected to this device.
One of the fans was attempting to spin even when motherboard was turned off because power was back feeding from the HDMI port through video card into PCIE slot etc.

This made motherboard to stop booting at all. I dont know how i managed to make it work again but i did.

for that reason, these also cause problems with back feeding power so you cant use two separate inputs depending on how the device handles it.
Some DSRL will not like to be in a pair with other devices.

Be careful. It can not only kill your motherboard, it can kill ANY device attached to it because power lines are paralleled.

Also about the capacity, for the battery that comes with HF100, there is no significant benefit buying one 16GB Vs 2 of 8GB cards (right now, 2 8GB cards go for $10 less than a 16GB). title: great lens...
text:
I am not going to list down all the performance characteristics of this lens here: much better and smarter photographers have done that already at too many places(If you haven't seen one yet, try photozone.de). I am just going to list down what "I" felt with my my first L lens :)

I am not a pro, and I am not a complete novice either. I dont use a mag glass and pixel peep, but I can easily make out what went wrong with pictures I take. I bought my first DSLR (Canon Digital Rebel) in 2004. I still use the same body, but bought two lenses on the way: Canon 50mm f/1.4 and Sigma 70-300 APO Macro. I use the 50mm almost always. I use the Sigma when I am traveling to some parks or visiting botanical gardens (for its macro capability as well). The problem with Sigma was that I could rarely get sharp pictures "hand held" beyond probably 150mm. Many of my photos suffered from camera shake. Even when there is no shake, that lens is quite a beginner lens in terms of IQ - after shooting with it for 2-3 years, I now see something bad with every picture out of that lens :) That's when I hit the market to get a new lens. I decided that I will buy only those lenses that I would keep for a long time (if not forever).

I started off looking for a lens that goes all the way to 300 with a budget of under $600. My requirements were great IQ, easy handling (I have a small build), and that I shouldn't grow out of its capabilities in the next few years. The Canon 70-300 IS was the first I looked at. Though it is a great lens, I figured from online reviews that I will end up with another upgrade when I upgrade my body later this year (mostly to 50d). I also found that there is no other good 300mm zooms at that price point or even $1000. So I started looking 200mm zooms. I started with a Canon 70-200 f/4L. It is rated high at just about every review online and it fit the budget too. But from my Sigma 70-300 experience, I knew it was difficult to hand hold a lens at 200 and beyond unless it is bright outdoors. For the next set of candidates, I realized my $600 budget isnt going to cut it. So I made it ~$1200. That brought in 3 candidates: Sigma 70-200 f2.8 EX, Canon 70-200 f/4 IS and Canon 70-200 F/2.8. This decision was tough from a performance stand point. They all are VERY good. The Sigma didnt have OS, but it was F/2.8 and $400 cheaper. The Canon F/2.8 IS didnt make the list because it was way over my budget. There were many reviews online that mentioned that f/4 IS is probably the best optically among all 4 Canon 70-200 lenses. However, F/2.8 was tempting on the sigma and the canon. After a long while, I finally made my choice: Canon 70-200 L IS. Why? At 3 pounds, I cant carry the Sigma and the Canon 2.8 for long. At half that weight, I can carry the F/4 IS much longer. I lose an f-stop, but I can compensate with the better IS that F/4 has (which is 4 - making it effectively F/1.4 when there is no subject motion), and possibly higher isos (which is not as bad with the new bodies as it used to be in the past).

I received the lens about a month ago. First thing I realized is how good/balanced it feels. When I read reviews about the build quality of L-lenses, I could never comprehend it. How good could it be, was always my thought. Now I know :) I have shot hundreds of shots now, and I can confirm that there is a big difference in the results compared to my Sigma. Of course, it is expected because the Sigma is a $200 lens, but the point is "I" could take better pictures with this lens with a 6MP Digital Rebel. I am very happy with the purchase, and I am convinced I am now prepared for a 50D :)

A point of caution for first time users of IS: you need to wait a second (or fraction of second) with shutter half-depressed for IS to compensate for motion. If you dont, it is as if there was no IS itself. I didnt know this initially and I was disappointed with the results. Once I figured that out, the results have been spectacular - I have had hand-held shots at less that 1/10th of a second.

title: nice card, speedy enough for most people
text:
30MB/sec is good enough for anyone who does not shoot RAW bursts of 20+ frames continuously, provided they use modern cameras (i.e. made in the last 2-3 years). These cameras have enough in-camera buffer to sustain its max frame rate for 2-3 seconds, so the speed of the card does not matter much at all there. For a Canon 50D, for e.g. you can buy the slowest CF card there is, and still shoot at 6fps RAW for 2+ seconds before you have to slow down (i.e. 12-15 shots). You can get faster rated 16GB cards from other brands at the same price, but I would rather have this slower Sandisk, as those are known to be more reliable (not to say they just dont fail).

30MB/sec is much faster than what is required to shoot HD videos on any DSLR. Canon HD videos need only 6MB/sec at 1080p. Don't get fooled into buying faster cards. If you are into videos, buy larger cards, *not* faster - 16GB can store only less than an hour of HD video at highest resolution).

UPDATE (4/20/2011):
After 7 months of use on a Canon 50D, mostly shooting RAW or RAW+jpg, the card is going strong. Never slowed me down, but then I don't ever shoot more than 4-5 frame bursts.

UPDATE (6/8/2011):
Still no problems with the card.

Another point about the speed, for those who care :) If you fill in this card (i.e 16GB worth of images/video), it can take a few minutes to transfer that whole data over to your computer. The exact time it takes depends on your card reader and computer, but a good estimate would be 10 minutes. If you had the really fast 90MB/sec UDMA cards with a USB3.0 UDMA reader, you would probably finish this in half the time (you wont see a 3x improvement practically, because now your hard drive and the transfer link would start becoming the bottlenecks). But if you are like me, you would empty the card every 50-100 shots, and that should finish in seconds.

Update 8/30/2015:
I upgraded my camera to Canon 70D about a year ago. I still have the camera and this card, and the card is still flawless. I just don't use it as much as I used to.

title: Great TV in general, with some minor (?) annoyances
text:
I was looking for a second HD TV (the other being a 57" Mitsubishi DLP), with online streaming capability. Given its placement in my home, I needed IQ over a wide viewing angle. This delivers on that count. The picture quality is excellent from all angles.

One thing that I missed even after extensive research was lack of DLNA (a technology that lets you stream media on your PC or Network attached storage to your TVs, PS3s, etc) on this model. Just about every other TV that does Netflix streaming can do DLNA as well, but this one cant. I didnt realize it until after I placed the order. I had the opportunity to cancel the order after I realized it, but at 750$ it wasn't worth fretting about. Besides, it could show up in one of the future firmware updates (I am not really counting on it though - I already have a computer connected to the TV on HDMI to stream just about anything I want).

The sound is not great, but I didnt expect it (or need it) to be. For those planning to connect this to your own receiver, be aware that the TV has just an optical out. No headset jacks or red/white analog out.

The Viera Media player is pretty good, but very picky about video. It plays the AVCHD files out of new HD Camcorders/cameras, but doesn't play any other MP4/wmv/mpg etc. The jpgs display fine (from both USB disks and SD cards).The Viera Cast has only about 10 apps, but everything I needed (Netflix, Youtube, Picasa, Pandora) were there. Checkout Viera Cast page at Panasonic to see if they have what you are looking for.

For network connectivity, I used a repeater ([[ASIN:B002SQ9ZX2 ASUS RT-N12 Wireless-N Router, Access Point, and Repeater]]) instead of Panasonic's wireless adapter. The TV is connected to this repeater using wired connection. I suggest going in that route, because it lets you connect other wired-only devices (like blue-ray player) to your existing wireless network. It costs much less as well. Once connected it updated the firmware automatically.

Despite all the annoyances, I still rate this 5 stars, mainly because it has everything I care about (picture quality, online streaming). 3D was a nice bonus, and I will get to it someday :)

title: Stylish watch,  bad fitness tracker,  flawed bands
text:
I bought a Gear S2 ( not the classic version) as a more stylish replacement for my Fitbit Charge HR. l considered many android wear watches and even tried a Moto360 first generation. But they had two deal breakers ffor me- battery life, and accuracy of the fitness tracking features,especially the heart rate measurement while exercising. Based on early reviews, this looked like Gear S2 would be the perfect solution for me. But unfortunately it didnt work out that way.

Best thing about Gear S2 is the style. It looks like a normal watch. It is perfect size for my thin wrist. The display has high resolution that makes all kinds of watch faces like its the real deal. These are lots of watch faces available from Samsung & third parties. There is an always-on mode for display, but it only shows the clock handles if you have an analog watch face. If its digital, it just shows the time(not other info)- of course, when you raise the hand to look at the face, it turns on the whole watch face. I guess they do this to avoid burn-in of AMOLED display. But, overall its not bad. Fitbit is way behind in this department. Moto360, I would say is somewhat close-but Gear S2 is a clear winner here.

About battery life, 3-day estimate is highly optimistic. l don't have very many notifications, I dont use it for media play back and such, I dont have always-on mode, I had wifi turned off ( connecting to my Nexus6 using bluetooth)- and with that if I take it off the charger one morning, l can comfortably take it to the next night. It wont last that second night.It is much better than Moto 360, but quite worse than Fitbit which lasts 3-4days easily. In other words, you don't need to carry a charger for an overnight trip, which is the minimum I needed - so, still not a deal breaker.

Fitness tracking is where Gear S2 starts becoming a problem, especially compared with fitbit. Great s2 can't detect any activity or sleep by itself. You have to manually start the activity or enter the data manually. It does measure steps by itself, of course, but it is not very accurate. How wrong it is, depends. See, every once in a while the pedometer stops recording. I am not sure what causes it to stop, but it does and after a few minutes it will start again byitself. If you walked a lot when pedometer took that break you lose all that steps, but if you didn't walk at that time the tracker pretty accurate :) I measured this by walking in circles in my home with fitbit also on the same hand. Each circle was about 30 steps, as I counted myself. First 10 cycles resulted in both trackers counting about 300 steps. After the next 5, fit bit counted another 150, while gear s2 counted 0! The next 5 cycles ended up as 100 for s2 and another 150 for fitbit. I and my wife went for a trek last weekend. End of it her fitbit showed about 8000 steps, and my s2 showed 6000 :( I have now withdrawn from daily steps competition with her. I don't stand a chance! Fit bit on the other hand does all activity tackling automatically. It knows when you go to sleep, when you walk, run, play sports, etc. It clearly shows all this on the app. Fitbit is the absolute winner here.

Heart rate measurement is also quite random. It has trouble sometimes measuring idle heart rate when I am resting. But once I start an activity on the watch manually, it continually displays heart rate. But given its struggles at rest, I am not certain about is accuracy.

Now the biggest flaw, and the reason why I am returning the watch, is the band. Gear s2 has a special type of band that makes it easy to remove. Problem is, it is way too easy to remove. Any slight pressure on it would make it come undone! I nearly dropped the watch twice when the band's came off. This I think is a serious flaw, unless I got a bad lemon. I doubt it though, because both bands that came with it had the same problem.

I am back on market for something else. If it wasn't for the looks, I would have gone with fitbit again.

title: SO EASY- Anyone can install this drive!
text:
I was a bit fearful of attempting to install a new hard drive on my Macbook Pro but when I saw OWC's site and the instructional video, it looked very simple so decided to give it a shot. I called Best Buy's Geek Squad because I wanted to see what they would charge to install the drive just in case. They quoted me $95 plus tax to install the drive and then another $95 plus tax to transfer all of my data and apps over. I must admit, this was the part that scared me the most- transferring all of my apps to the new drive. I decided to go ahead and try it myself, and if I needed to, I could always take it in to Best Buy.

Let me tell you, if I could give OWC 10 stars I would! Their videos on their website and step-by-step instructions are SO easy to follow, ANYONE can do this! It took me literally 10 minutes to remove and install the hard drive. Thanks Geek Squad- I saved myself $100 in this step! This product comes with a case for the old hard drive and the MUST have special screw drivers, do yourself a favor and purchase these items with the new drive! The time consuming part was reinstalling the Mojave OS- I have slow internet and that took about an hour. No problem, go do something while the installation is proceeding. Once OS was re-installed, I had the old hard drive already connected to the Mac and just followed the directions to transfer the files and apps to the new drive. Took about 25 minutes and DONE! Saved myself ANOTHER $100 Geek Squad...

You can erase the old hard drive and use it as another USB/external hard drive, but I plan to keep it as is in case I ever need to reinstall the data for some reason. What I really love about OWC is that they have all of the videos and instructions you need to do this yourself and a hotline for help if you need it, but that was not necessary for me.

title: NOT WORTH IT. PLZ DO YOUR RESEARCH
text:
This is a Great device for what it promises.
It did come with a variety or ports. And looks very nice etc . However there are a few things your really should know.

If want to use this item to attach additional monitors and your Laptop's power adapter isnt USB-C , you wont be able to plug into the hub's USB-C Power Delivery port. (because thats the only option) And the additional monitors will not work. Also buying an additional 75W- 72W (min recommended power supply) power adapter is a bit pricey.

The VGA port did not work on the item I received. (Yes i did try multiple cables and monitors)

The Micro SD card slot also did not work. However the (larger) slot for the micro sd card adapter did work.

All the Other USB ports did work just fine. Quick and easy. Plug and play.

However, This little device got very hot to the touch. So hot that I was very concerned about having it on my desk. It remained very hot , even when I removed all other devices and had only 1 USB dongle plugged in for my wireless mouse and keyboard. Which was very much alarming.

The description does have a partial list of compatible laptops. But the comments did say that any laptop will work.

For the cost Avg amazon cost of $70USD. To have the unfortunate experience of this item not being something that works for you , may just be as easy as returning it etc. But if you are ordering from another country (like myself), It may end up costing you more than what you spent on the item, just to return it.

I had such high hopes for this item, mainly because of all the good reviews. And having to work from home now due to covid-19 restrictions. You try to make the work space a bit easier . Unfortunately , I did not have the best experience for this product. And I would have to not recommend this product.

spend your money elsewhere.

title: Gets worse with time!
text:
3/6/2011 UPDATE: I've had this thing for over 3 months now, and I'm getting more and more unhappy with it. The battery still doesn't hold a charge for that long - I even sent the remote back and got a new one, and it still doesn't last a week before it needs to be recharged. I don't leave it in the cradle or charge it before it gets fully drained, so the battery life should have been optimal.

The worst problem with the remote by far is that it is getting more and more unreliable - the 'hiccups' are getting more and more frequent when I choose an activity. For example, when I hit 'watch a dvd' sometimes it doesn't turn on the dvd player, or doesn't set the correct input for the amplifier, or something else - so then I have to hit 'devices', choose the specific device, go into that menu and hit power or input settings, then go back to current activity. The one-touch operation is one of the biggest selling points for this remote, so the fact that it is routinely messing up is really disappointing. I wouldn't buy this remote again.

I've had an old Sony commander remote for 6+ years - it was a great universal touch-screen remote, but was basically the size of an ipad so when I got a new tv I talked myself into upgrading.

Pros: the Logitech harmony one is pretty, feels like a regular remote (fantastic design, not cumbersome or awkward), and controls pretty much everything. I'm still discovering the different ways to use it, but the customizable layouts and touch screens are pretty awesome.

title: Protecting The Family Joules, a very objective look at surge protectors.
text:
I've been involved with electronics all of my life and I make a living at it.
So, here's my take on this Surge Protector; this is actually a tutorial on surge protection for those serious enough to read through it!

First of all, some facts: To be considered a "good" surge protector, three things are required:.
1. Appropriate clamping voltage: 330 is excellent and 400 is OK, anything higher is questionable.
2. Sufficient amount of energy absorption (rated in Joules) 2,500 Joules or more to be considered good now days.
3. Good quality, tight gripping outlet sockets. Hard to measure unless you have an outlet "grip" tester.

No electronic device with solid state devices or built in CPUs or Logic controllers should be hooked to any outlet without a good surge protector being used. This includes modern refrigerators, freezers, washing machines, dryers, microwave ovens, digital toaster ovens and other digital appliances, as well as your computer, home theater and other home audio equipment..

Line surges and spikes are devious and silent killers. Every time any reactive device is turned on and off, a voltage spike is generated. Motors are the most serious offenders. So, your furnace motor, AC compressor, vacuum cleaner, freezer, and refrigerator motors all create spikes inside your own home and these spikes travel down the power lines exposing the other electrical equipment to these excess voltage levels. Normally, unless the spike is huge, it does not take out appliances on the first shot. However, repetitive spikes cause little pin holes and carbon tracks to develop in transformer windings and capacitors, as well as stressing solid state devices (transistors, diodes and I.C.s) eventually leading to premature failure.

Not only should the surge suppressor be protecting your appliances, but it should also be protecting itself by being large enough, joule-wise, to be able to withstand large surges. Remember, surge protectors will clamp off the over-voltage, or die trying. Most surge protectors die quietly and you don't even realize that you are no longer protected. So, be sure to get one rated high enough, in joules, so that it will withstand all but the most catastrophic surges. This is double insurance and better than an extended maintenance agreement. IMHO

Also, the joule rating is misleading, as it is the sum of protection given across all 3 electrical leg-pairs. So, in reality, if equally distributed, only 1/3 of the total rating is what is afforded across the hot to neutral, or the hot to ground legs.

So, how does the ISOBAR4 ULTRA measure up?

First it has a clamping voltage of 330 volts which is excellent.
Second, it has a joule rating of 3300 joules which is also excellent.
Third, the outlets appear to be of high quality construction.
Fourth, the design has built-in EMI/RFI suppression to also reduce the RF hash that sneaks in on your power lines.
Fifth, it is all contained inside a fire resistant metal box, in case something flames up.

Overall, for $40. this unit is a real bargain and built to last. Highly recommended!

title: Know the Facts!
text:
With any surge protector, most of the ads are just hype, marketing & sales.
What you really need to know is just 3 things:

1. Surge rating (in joules), how much energy the device can absorb for a given period of time, once the clamping voltage is exceeded. The higher the number, the better. Remember this value is the sum of all 3 legs, so any leg to leg value is 1/3 the stated value (if evenly distributed). I suggest an over-all value of 3,000 joules or more. Remember, that's only 1,000 joules per leg.

2. Clamping voltage rating (in volts), which is the voltage value at which the device starts to limit any further increase in voltage. Generally, the lower, the better. 330 volts is the "best" clamping or let-through value, 400 is fair, and 500 is poor. Remember that a voltage spike is usually quite brief, micro or nanoseconds, but it can be huge! So, the earlier the clamping starts, the safer your equipment will be.

3. The surge protection device not only protects your equipment plugged into it, it also protects itself. Therefore, the high joule, low clamping voltage rating should be 3,000 joules minimum & 330 volts, respectively. Investing in a good protector is a good investment and you won't have to replace it prematurely.

text:
As a life long electronics technician, and electronics instructor (Technical College Level)

There are two parameters that define the worthiness of an electrical surge protector:
1. Clamping Voltage: The lower, the better. 330=Good 400=Fair 500=Poor
(this unit is rated at 400v from hot to neutral & 500 volts for the other two leg to ground pairing. 500 volts, is
a bit high, but the 400 volt rating on the main pair is okay.

2. Joule Rating: The higher the better. I advise at least 3,000 joules as this also protect the unit itself.
This is the amount of excess energy that the unit can withstand once the voltage rating has been exceeded.
This unit is rated at 4320 joules, which is good.

However, it might be a million joules, and not do any good if the clamping voltage is too high and the it doesn't start clipping off the excess voltage soon enough! Also a metal enclosure is better than plastic in case of fire. This is a plastic casel.

title: It;s time to make the jump to digital
text:
I've been looking at digital cameras for over a year now and I have been holding off. When this camera came out it got my attention. I finally bought one three weeks ago when I was on a trip and I forgot my film point and shoot.
Had I known what this camera could do I would have bought it three months ago when I could have. The camera functions great in fully automatic mode. The automatic "creative" settings and the "manual" modes also work very well. The only thing you have to watch for are the focus points which will vary so keeping clicking half way until they are on the important points. The camera with the stock lens is plenty sharp - and this is coming from a long time Nikkor lens guy shooting on F2's and F3's.
Get a 1gig flash card and you will not believe how many large files you can get on a card. Battery life is good for around 350 large photos with alot of flash shots, but you need a spare battery. The 512 battery is less expensive and works as well if not better than the 511. Do not bother to get a card reader - you do not need it.
It took this camera to get a dedicated 35mm shooter to make the jump. The only problem is that now I have a whole different series of lens to buy. I got a great deal on the 75-300 USM III lens and I have been happy with it. You can and will shoot more photos than you ever did with a 35mm - and I generally shoot with a motor drive - and you will be amazed with the results. Do not rely on the LCD to decide if you want to keep the shot - wait unitl you get home. You get a video out cord to show the photos on a television. My only question about the camera is its long term durability as it is not heavily built - but then again I'm used to shooting with a camera that is known to be a real tank. I looked at the Sony 828 but it is not a SLR and the feature set is harder to access - aside from the numerous problems that we have heard about that camera.
Did I say that I was very happy with this camera?

title: Good piece of equipment but some issues
text:
Before I got the 305 I had used a Polar RS200sd and the Nike+ system. I liked the Polar system most of the time but hated it when it would turn on and off by itself. However the distance information from the footpod was inaccurate and the footpod itself was too large and heavy. The Nike* system has the same problem with distance accuracy and it does not measure heart rate. The voice is very nice and if you're going to use a Nano anyway it is a great deal.

The 305 does a good job with distance and heart rate. The menu system is pretty easy to navigate and easier than the Polar. Instaneous pace is a bit of a guess but you're in the ball park. My unit only gets fair reception even in a clear area but rarely do I lose the signal even under tree cover. The calorie count is way off. When you down load the information you sometimes get different information from what is showing on the unit. Yesterday I ran 20 miles but the MotionBased software said I ran 21.45 miles. The date is also off. The MotionBased software requires some work to get it set up and you need to pay money to get all of the features that you are going to want to have.

The bottom line is that the 305 does what I need it to do for pace and distance and is, in my view, far superior to any of the pod based systems. Hopefully some of the other issues are being resolved through software upgrades.

title: Superb with a few faults
text:
Just came back from two weeks in Thailand, Cambodia and Laos with the S95 as my only camera. I was breaking the SLR habit as I needed to travel light and it is genuinely liberating not to have a SLR around your neck. You can carry the S95 and two extra batteries in a single pocket.

A quick review of the 2400 plus photos I came back with in Picassa on the iMac 27 shows great color rendition, excellent contrast and great sharpness. I'm not at all regretting the decision to bring only the S95. I was also looking at the LX-5 as the 24mm Leica lens was very attractive to me. However the additional size would be an issue and there seems to be some concern about the JPEG color rendition. I have no interest in a great deal of post processing so JPEG rendition is very important to me. This is the fourth small Canon I've had. I've only had a problem with one, a is870 that developed a gray spot on the LCD. I bought and would recommend a screen protector for the LCD in an abundance of caution even though I'm not generally a screen saver kind of guy.

Some random thoughts: The camera is pretty sturdy (at times it reminded me of my old Nikon F3 for reasons not entirely clear to me) and the black finish is tough and plenty grippy, LCD screen is excellent and is visible even in bright light. Full auto mode is hard to beat. Other modes are useful for specific situations. The other mode I used most often is low light. However you should set up the buttons so that with one push you can set WB to the scene as the auto mode in low light is not always accurate. The problem with the low light mode is that it jacks the ISO up quite a bit. However it can capture photos in extremely low light conditions that even my SLR could not take. There are sometimes focus issues in low light mode but it easily goes into manual focus. The pixilation at ISO's up to 800 is not bad.

You can set up different modes to access immediately key settings. For example you can set up Tv to shoot vivid or slide film color mode and then use auto or another mode to shoot normal color. You can also shoot in different aspect ratios. There are many different modes, some of which are useful. The external ring is best used to set focal length in my experience. The rotating ring on the back is most often used for exposure variation unless you are shooting in full manual mode.

The battery life is not impressive although I admit that I have no idea of how many photos per battery I was getting. However having three batteries was mandatory for a full days' shooting - although you'll have to recharge more before you go out at night. The size of the camera is a blessing and a curse. The small size makes panning smoothly in video mode difficult and getting photos level even with the grid in place sometimes difficult.

I have to say that while there are minor nits they are far outweighed by the enormous capabilities of this camera. If you're looking for a solid camera with a wide range of capabilities and a solid auto mode when you just want to look for targets the S95 would be difficult to beat.

title: Glad I got it
text:
At the last minute I decided that I needed a GPS for my 10 day trip to Colorado. I had to get a unit overnight and I got busy so I saw something on the 1350MT and decided to go for it. Had I had more time I might have been tempted to get a 5" unit but I'm glad I didn't. I'm happy with this unit and it is an excellent value for the price. I'm not happy I bought a "beanbag" mount as I really prefer the windshield mount where I can mount the unit next to my rear view mirror and route the power cord over the mirror and down to the power outlet. A 5" model would block more of my view and the 4.3" screen gives you plenty of legible information.

As noted by one of the other reviewers the unit does a couple of weird things. First, it seems to avoid freeways even though I have it set on fastest travel time. Going to DIA from Aurora in Denver it sent me down a regular four lane road which ended up being the quickest option at 0500 since there was no traffic and the lights were timed but its' hard to believe the unit is that smart. Second, on one occasion it sent me in the wrong direction on a regular street. Third it sent me the wrong way on a freeway only to tell me at the last minute I was going the wrong way. Unlike the one reviewer, this only happened to me one time so far.

My only point of comparison is my built in Mercedes unit which occassionally will try to send me in the wrong lane on a freeway. With all of the concern about the ads, I have not yet invoked the traffic but I understand that if you pay a fee of $8.00 that somehow you can make the ads go away. This is what I've heard but I don't know how to accomplish this. Traffic is a significant addtional expense on the Mercedes system and map upgrades are almost $300 so the Nuvi really is a bargain from a functionality perspective.

Anyway I'm very happy I got the Nuvi 1350MT and would recommend it.

title: Pretty good computer
text:
This is a pretty good computer for the money.

Pros: Starts up fast, operates quickly tech specs nothwithstanding, looks great, is light, has a great back lit keyboard, can be cleaned up of stickers and most unnecessary software reasonably easily and is I think a good deal for the money.

Cons: Battery life is not what I hoped. The display is overly glossly, its resolution merely average and its color rendition and depth is not great on anything less than full brightness - which is not all that bright. It's wi-fi connectivity is okay but not proactive. The outside of mine is a fingerprint magnet. HP Tech Support was not great when I called to try to find out how to minimize fan use for noise and battery usage issues. No native email client. I bought mine at Best Buy which sells the same computer with the identical specs for $679 but with the sales tax the cost is roughly the same.

This computer brought me back to a place where I realize that I cannot do it all on an iPad Logitech keyboard or not (I wrote and had published an article that an iPad could be a laptop replacement) and that I needed a real laptop. Having gotten to that point I now recognized that as good as the Envy is for the money that its shortcomings - and here I'm talking really about battery life and the display - were not ideal for me.

I used the 30 day trade in option at Best Buy to get a MacBook Air 13" at essentially double the cost. The Air has a plainly superior but slightly smaller (1" smaller on the horizontal) screen and battery life is better but since the Ar has a solid state (and half the size) hard drive this is not surprising. And I had to buy the Mac version of the Office programs and got no credit for the PC version. Apple tech support, while friendlier, really was of no greater assistance than the HP tech support.

You could question whether the the MacBook is worth double of what the Envy costs. Having now what is generally considered to be one of if not the best ultrabooks I have to say that the Envy is a very good computer for the money.

title: Great bang for the buck
text:
I got a pair of these while I was waiting for Airpods2. I've been very happy with them They fit my ear pretty well and they come with a set of tips so they should fit anyone. The sound is good but not great. Unless I really cram the tip into my ear there is not much bass. They pair up instantly. Calls were okay but sometimes you can sound muffled. What's cool is that they pair up separately as you can see on the list of bluetooth devices on your phone so you can operate off one which is what I often did. The case has a button and series of lights so you can see its state of charge. The pods show a red light when they need charging but it is hard to tell the state of their charge until its too late.

I finally got my AirPods. First off I like the fact that they do not need tips and they still stay in my ear well. They feel better to me. I think they sound significantly better. Phone calls are also significantly better. Their minimalistic controls help as you can invoke Siri to do most things. I think the AirPods have a longer range and better battery life on the pods. The SoundPeats battery case definitely has better battery life although it is significantly larger, heavier and rectangular which makes it a paint to carry. With either you always want to have the case with you so as not to lose the pods and to keep them charged.

Certainly the SoundPeats are a great product and they have a great bang for the buck. I'm very happy with them unless I'm on a phone call or am listening critically. I highly recommend them and mine are definitely not for sale. Are they really competition for AirPods? Not really. They are not as easy to carry around, they do not sound as good, they do not work as well for phone calls and they don't have Siri or pause/play controls. Are AirPods worth the additional $125 or so? They are for me but your mileage may very.

The bottom line is that the SoundPeats are an excellent product. If you are someone who easily loses things get these (although Find my iPhone will find your AirPods) just in case. If you are likely to lose a pod these are the way to go. They are perfect for teenagers as all is not lost if a pod is. If you don't want to spend any more money than you need to these are the way to go. Good luck!

title: Not perfect but a good bike computer
text:
I washed my beloved Garmin 500 accidentally and needed a new computer. I looked at all options and decided that the 830 was the best choice. Having had this computer for 6 months that remains my opinion.

Pros: Great display, accurate, great mapping and generally reliable.
Cons: Fairly constant lockups at the end of the ride and fairly complex

Get used to the computer not saving the ride at the end. Not a big deal. Turn it off completely and when you turn it back on, preferably in range of your wi-fi, your ride will be saved and sent to Garmin Connect. That is the only continuing problem I've had. Take some time to learn about the computer and you will be rewarded. Being able to switch through screens including navigation is great. I've had no connection issues - end of ride issue aside - and my iPhone connects well with the unit. You can read messages sent to you which is nice.

I understand some of the other reviewers opinions. Before I really got to know the unit I shared their opinions. But in this case familiarity breeds confidence. Some hints: Make sure that the unit is turned all the way off after you use it. Try to avoid getting too low on the battery life (>25%) as the unit voltage decreases and sometimes other issues result. Check the battery charge regularly. If you set the display to auto adjust you will save yourself some battery life. But it looks so good when you set it at 76%.

I'm hoping that someday soon Garmin will issue a firm update to solve some of the issues. But in the meantime this is a very useful unit that works well once you become familiar with it and its operation. BTW almost all units out there have some problem with them. There is nothing that is perfect. At least the 830 at the end of the day is reliable, accurate and reliable.

title: Great turntable with real tech support!
text:
My RT-85 and we were very much looking forward to enjoying an afternoon bathed in the wonderful sounds of a Ortofon Blue cartridge.

The turntable assembled easily. I balanced the tonearm and then set it tracking to 1.8g using an external electronic gauge. I checked cartridge alignment by using a Hudson HiFi alignment disc. I set tracking using the gauge on the tonearm to 1.8. The turntable was perfectly leveled.

We put on Bill Evans live at the Village Vanguard to enjoy our Sunday dalliance with him. This is a remarkably well recorded album. Song one on the A side was pretty remarkable considering the cartridge had zero playtime. But as the tonearm approached the middle of the album there was distortion and then skipping. We had played this album previously on my Thorens so we knew this was not a record defect.

I double checked skating first, then the alignment and reset the tracking force as well. As a check I broke out in old but clean copy of Welcome by Santana which is an album I know note by note. I also know that it worked fine on turntables that are not a match for the RT 85. Unfortunately the first track played fine but as the tone arm moved towards the center of the album once again there was distortion and then skipping.

Update: I contacted Fluance's tech support. I was impressed how quickly I could actually speak to a knowledgeable person by the name of Brent. Real and accessible tech support is always a very pleasant surprise. I doubt that some of the other turntable manufacturers have anything close to this level of tech support because few distribute directly to consumers. They made a couple of suggestions and when they did not solve the problem they told me to exchange the turntable. Amazon made this process easy and quick.

So I now have my new RT-85 and it is everything that I could have hoped for and then some. I'm very happy!

title: Great bluetooth headphones
text:
Since I mostly work from home and listen to music when I'm not on the phone I use several bluetooth ear pods including AirPod Pros.

The Max version has always intrigued me but I have quite a few over ear headphones so until they went on sale there was nothing compelling me to purchase them.

I've had them long enough to break in the drivers to some degree. Yes like most dynamic headphones these need to be broken in for 20 to 50 hours before they can be judged for sound quality.

1. I'm a headphone guy so sound quality is my first priority. This is an excellent headphone. They blow away my bluetooth Sennheisers on sound quality. They even compete with some wired headphones. They may not reach the level of my Grado 325's but they are much more comfortable. My Focal Clears, which incidentally match well with the output voltage of my iPhone, are superior but are much more expensive. And wired. BTW you can't get Lossless audio through Bluetooth so a wired headphone has that advantage. And you can't talk through the Clears. My wired Sennheisers don't really have the output levels to match an iPhone so they are not in the consideration. These have a wide range sonically and reproduce all kinds of music well. And unlike some Beats models they are not bass heavy. I think they work best with Spatial Audio off. iMy only complaint is that the midlevel sound stage is a bit compressed regardless of volume. Apple did their home work in designing these headphones. I'd go so far to say that you will not find another headphone wired or not that has as good as sound for the money.

2. Comfort/Fit. One goes with the other. The head band is comfortable for my large head and does not squeeze my ears. The ear pad material is not what I'd like but it is surprisingly comfortable. Typical of any headphones they are best used without glasses for maximum comfortable. If you use glasses put the pads on your ears with the glasses on for maximum comfort. I do not notice any weight - these are much lighter than most wired headphones. The ear space fits my large ears although ideally a couple of extra mm's would be better.

3. They connect easily once you go through the initial connection procedure. Most importantly they have excellent battery life. They have double or more battery life than Pros. Put them in the case when you are through with them for the day as it is the only way they turn off. You will otherwise lose battery life as they are otherwise constantly scanning for possible bluetooth targets. The case is not great but it works well for being put into a bag or backpack. Generally they do a good job of picking up your voice in telephone or FaceTime mode.

4. They are an excellent value. Usually a substantial discount means that there is a newer model is coming out. My research suggests that is not the case. There is likely to be a newer model of the Pros coming out which explains their greater discount.

I am very pleased with these headphones and I think that you will be equally as pleased.

title: Amazing monitor - highly recommend
text:
I spent months agonizing about which monitor to purchase. Finally, I decided I definitely wanted to go 4k and decided to try the curved 21:9. It was down to this or the LG 34UC97.

Based on a Tom's hardware review and the Dell being a few hundred cheaper, I decided to give it a go.

Impressions:
- This monitor is huge. I saw a 29" ultrawide in a store and this thing is much bigger. I can display a 4 page Word document in Print Layout mode and each page is bigger than an 8.5 x 11. Great for choosing page breaks, etc.
- The video quality is amazing. I've been watching some 4k stuff on YouTube and it looks amazing.
- Great packaging. Lots of cables included.
- Easy to set up. Literally less than 5 minutes. No settings to mess around with. Just connected my laptop up with an HDMI cable and turned it on.
- Controls are very intuitive. It has a user guide on CD (no paper one) but I haven't really needed it.

One really cool thing about this monitor is the uplink USB ports. I'm not an expert on monitors so maybe other ones have this too. Basically, I plugged my Corsair keyboard (dual cable) and Corsair mouse into 3 USB ports on the monitor and then plugged two outgoing USB cables into my work and personal laptops. With a little fiddling around in the menus, now I can flip back and forth between the two machines and the keyboard and mouse control both. Very cool. The monitor only comes with one of the uplink cables so make sure you'll need an extra if you want to hook up a second machine. You can use any USB to USB-B cable (the one with the funky end on it)

My work laptop had a mini HDMI connector so I had to pick up a separate cable. If you buy this monitor, I'd recommended making sure you get that cable if you need it.

One last thing. It has one HDMI and one MHL port. Without getting in to the details of MHL... You can also use it for an HDMI port. so basically the monitor has 2 HDMI ports if you want them.

title: Great polarizer, Made for a great birthday party surprise!
text:
Very clean polarizer.

Caution: If you learn about polarizers, you will discover that it is not a true filter, but changes the light rather than filtering. This can be altered by a nearby substrate like the protective sheet. So the polarizer effect is the strongest once you remove the protective coating. I was worried that it was not a good polarizer until the sheet was removed which allowed it to block more polarized light.

Made for a great Spiderwick Chronicles birthday surprise. My daughter wanted this theme for her birthday and if you have seen the movie, there is an element where he looks through a circular stone and suddenly he can see the magical world around him. After brainstorming on how I could achieve the effect, I found that an LCD monitor shows blank white if you remove the polarizing film. So I did that and inserted a piece of this polarizer into a fake circular stone for each kid. Then the magic was that they could search through the house and find the Magic Window (lcd screen) and they could see the picture only by looking through their stone. They loved it
