title: Amateur photographer friendly!
text:
This was an upgrade from a Nikon P100 model. That camera was a step up from a digital because of it's manual capabilities. When the Sony came around I still wasn't confident enough even though it isn't a true DSLR. With the Sony NEX-5N there are even more capabilities available to the amateur; at times rather daunting. I have taken a very long time to write a review and I suspect that even now I will not be able to fully express all that this camera can accomplish under the proper hand. This review will be very simplistic/basic in its terms because I am an amateur. I love taking photos of the kiddies/family throughout the year. As well as nature and my Summer terrace garden. If you are going from a straight point and shoot or even a model like the Nikon P100 then you will find my review helpful. Professionals may not, because they want the technical, which I am still trying to learn/master myself.

The camera body itself is so light it is rather funny. In your hands it feels like a small point and shoot. The heft increases as you add the lens and a viewfinder if necessary. Even with the 18-55mm lens it doesn't feel bad. It is something to get used to though because you can no longer just stick it in your pocket or small purse. With the 200mm lens it becomes a bit front-end heavy and collapses on its face. The one thing that I absolutely adore is the 10fps. My Nikon did not have that ability and it is such a picture saver when it comes to action scenes or the kids not sitting still. Sony threw in the 55-210mm lens (grateful!), and it has saved me at the school plays and a Memorial Day NY Mets game. I still find it rather difficult and cumbersome having to figure out which lens I am going to need for the day. With my Nikon P100 I had 26X optical zoom with wide angle lens. I would be able to sit on my terrace and zoom in across the street at the neighbors pear tree and actual pears. I do see that these lenses are far better and truly stabilize on even the furthest zoom, where the aforementioned would have shake in the image.

The camera is 95 percent menu driven and accessed by the touchscreen. This becomes annoying at times. It can take 5 steps or more to reach the desired location or certain function. There is a selection wheel where your thumb grips the camera. This wheel delves deeper into the menu option for specific functions. With that being said, the touchscreen menu is rather fool/idiot-proof because there are instructions on each menu and even helpful tips on how that function would be useful. The touchscreen is large and all the info can be easily displayed if desired. What I don't like is since the menus are only accessible via the touchscreen, it is a fingerprint, sweat and dirt magnet. There are always stubborn streaks on the screen. When we took the camera to the baseball game in field box seats on a 98 degree day, I couldn't see the screen no matter which angle. I was pretty much shooting blind; luckily my images came out without any glaring issues. There is not a viewfinder included; one can be purchased separately right here on Amazon for 274 dollars. This should be equated into the total cost of ownership if a viewfinder is important to the consumer.

The battery life seems good for now. Before I venture out, the pack is fully charged and after a 45 minute school function I will be left with about 78 percent. That is with recording for about 9 minutes and using 10fps option. If travelling or needing to use the camera for extended periods, then I suggest purchasing a back-up battery pack. I LOVE that you can see what percentage of battery you have remaining. No more guessing and losing the perfect shot (happened so many times!) because 1/4 remaining battery equates to 2 percent!

This is the first time that the auto modes actually work for me. I have been able to take low light shots, indoor, sunny outdoor, nighttime etc. without any issues. The panoramic 3D works but I seem to have some issues with some of the baseball players missing limbs from the frame. I suspect that it is indeed user error rather than the camera's fault. I will upload the pics to Amazon's site as a reference. Onto colors: It has been a joy shooting images where the colors pop out of the screen! Depending on the shooting mode and style, you can have it that all the blues, yellow, greens or red pop and the rest of the image is black and white. There are many different styles but I have never had that function and it has proven to be not only fun but useful. I will attach those images as well. We have not attached the flash so I cannot review its effectiveness. There is no lag whatsoever from when the shutter is pressed and released! What more could I want?! I am finally able to capture images as they are seen by my naked eye.

Shooting Full HD 1080P: Shooting HD video is as simple as pressing the red button and you are there. I have not experienced the loud sound or rattling that other users have. We have recorded at noisy school functions and in our quiet bedroom. Hopefully, we have an updated model and won't experience that issue. There is no jittering, freezing or sync issues as I've experienced with the Nikon model. I used a SDHC Class 10 16GB card and have had wonderful results.

Highly recommend to any individual that wants to slowly step up to a DSLR. If your point and shoot isn't doing it for you any longer, you want macros and if your budget allows then this would be a wonderful camera to practice on. The image quality would not disappoint even the professional. I can only imagine what a professional could accomplish. IT is too expensive for not being a DSLR and every thing that is standard on other digital cameras needs to be purchased separately; down to the viewfinder. A few months ago it was very difficult to find a case that fit this model perfectly. I am hoping that it will be different now. Finally, it's clunky... not like a true DSLR but something to get used to from your little cute point and shoot. At the end of the day it will all be forgotten as you are awed by the images taken with your hands. Thanks Sony, you make me look like a better photographer than I am!

Bob's Burgers looked as if they were playing straight from our LCD. The kids surely got a big kick out of it. For cartoons the brightness is best... not for those who want a dark movie theater experience. Watching "Watch What Happens Live" wasn't as pleasing of an experience. After careful study I found that it was reproducing the image perfectly. With a steady hand we zoomed the lens and slid to a larger size where we could see Andy Cohen's corner mouth spittle with the same amount of disgust on our faces.

White pages can be viewed beautifully and with such clarity. I wish that they had these machines back when I was in school. It is a compact machine the size of a small DVR box that comes with a nifty carry bag for transport. The lumens and color brightness are both rated at 3000. I have learned that the 3000 number for brightness coupled with the lumens makes a difference when compared to competitor brands with the same amount of lumens but lower brightness. Those images from the competitors were dull and washed out; many times the colors would wash out to a black/gray shade. I do not have a projector screen to test it's ability but have found that any white flat wall will be perfect. Our darker shaded walls produced a dimmer image that was still very clear. The darker walls actually was much more pleasing visually when we wanted the home theater set up. The speaker can be set to a very loud decibel but it is not the same as your surround sound. Nonetheless, the sound is great. The menu options are very easy to access via the 'Menu' button on the projector itself. Here you can access tabs labeled: BASIC, WIRELESS LAN, SECURITY, MAIL, OTHERS, RESET and COMPLETE. Images can be stretched, rotated, pulled, dimmed, brightened, lengthened, shortened; you name it!

A little gem that I recently discovered is the ability to download an app to your phone and wirelessly project your images to the Epson device. Having company/family over and have a lot of images to show off of the little tykes? This device once initially set up can project all the images in a snap. Watch Grandparents, "ooh and ahhh".

My only issue to date are that the machine runs extremely hot from the very first 5 minutes. This makes me wary towards it's durability when it comes to the bulbs. Another personal issue is that even though it is labeled for HD widescreen multi-media projector; it isn't labeled for home theater purposes. IF the Home theater model is anything like this one then it should be an awesome device to own.

Highly recommend for business, schools and homes that have the need to project images, projects and occasionally movies to a larger scale. The color brightness and vividness will knock your socks off. Just be aware that it runs hot!

title: Smart Phone and X-box One love it...
text:
In our set up we are currently using a Linksys WRT AC1200 router and have cable provided through Time Warner. Currently based on our package access our internet speed caps at 200MB for downloads. We have many devices that use our wifi at the same time and many people streaming Netflix, our Direct TV boxes and X-box.

Our apartment in NY is about 60-65 feet in overall length and located on the second floor. Our router is located in the master bedroom which is on the other side of our living room where an Apple laptop, Samsung Note 3 and X-Box One were tested for distance.

Using the original antennas that came with the AC1200 router:
SPEED TEST
XBOX One: 2.8MB
Samsung Note 3: 18 MB
Apple Laptop: 185MB

Using High Gain Antennas:
SPEED TEST
XBOX One: 25.4MB
Samsung Note 3: 129 MB
Apple Laptop: 190 MB

As you can see from the above results we did not feel a difference with the laptop but a very marked positive with the smartphone and XBOX.

We further tested the antennas by going to the ground street level outside of our apartment. We found that we still had a great connection and speed levels. Replacing the antennas to the OEM we were only capable of achieving 1 bar of our wifi level indicators and the speed suffered.

Highly recommend these antennas because they make the Linksys line of routers even further capable in the right environment. If you struggle with slow speeds and consistent signal loss in a two story or larger home, then this would offer a consistent connection with improved speeds. The length of our single level apartment and many connected devices proved to be too much for the regular sized antennas. We are dticking with these and will recommend to others with the same issue.

title: Not a sound bar.  Overpriced.
text:
I wanted to love this sound bar... Never have I owned a Bose speaker system (except for the one that comes pre-wired in our vehicles), and I have always believed that you were paying for the name rather than quality. After using this bar for the last three weeks, I am saddened to report that my opinion has not changed.

There are three different inputs available on the sound bar- OPTICAL, CO AUX and AUX. We have the speaker connected to our 50 inch LG LED television in our bedroom. The living room already has a receiver and 7.1 speaker set-up. Unfortunately, the BOSE does not have an included subwoofer, nor does it come with mounting bracket. This is an unnecessary extra cost that one may need to take into consideration.

This speaker was exclusively designed to 'enhance' the dialogue. As much as you may want to call it a sound bar, it is just an amplifier. A very expensive amplifier. It comes with a remote that is pretty well thought out and can be used as an universal remote. There is also bluetooth connectivity, to stream music to this speaker from any bluetooth enabled device. It remembers the last eight connected devices. A big fail is that you need to manually disconnect each device before it will be able to stream from a different one. This was very cumbersome. Getting back to the enhanced dialogue function... it can only be activated from their included remote. We programmed our Direct tv remote to operate all the devices including this bar. It took a bit to program but the most upsetting thing was that you lose your on screen visual volume display from your television once the sound is pushed through the bar. I personally couldn't live without the visual acknowledgement when raising and lowering the volume.

Do not recommend this Bose as a conventional sound bar. Even when using it with the enhanced dialogue it only makes it a bit clearer. This can be easily remedied with your television's setting if you are having this issue. This Solo 5 system is not necessary unless your television speakers sound like utter garbage and even then I would recommend a cheaper sound bar with subwoofer included. You cannot activate the dialogue feature from your Direct tv or other universal remote. By the third trial week, I awoke and turned on my television as usual. There was not any sound. After a frustrating few minutes I decided to unplug the Bose and try again. The sound was still not emitting. I unplugged and left it for five minutes. After waiting, the sound was now live again. Not sure what happened, but that is the day that I disconnected the system.

There isn't a booklet that explains how to achieve this and after playing around for an hour with the keyboard attached to my laptop, I just handed it off so that it can be placed in our son's bedroom. I love the way the color schemes are so programmable down to the patterns, number of colors and even regions on the keyboard that will light up. It was dizzying and exciting all at the same time. Now my 11 year old was able to assign some functions to the macro keys and he LOVES them and the keyboard. As a former secretary, I love how the keys feel under my fingers. They are responsive, quick and so very tactile! As I mentioned before, the keyboard is heavy and for not moving around. It was designed to stay firmly in place while you are hardcore gaming without any slide. There is also an accessory wrist pad that attaches but has to be purchased separately. At this price point I do feel as if Dell should have included this accessory. There are also adjustable leg angles; three to choose from.

Highly recommend from a novice that is new to this higher end of keyboards that are tailored to gaming. One of these days I will have my son teach me how he was able to assign the functions that he wanted to execute to the programmable keys. Aesthetically this is a beautiful keyboard that surely lights up a room even when the room is bright. I am concerned for individuals that are affected by bright lights because it can become a bit overwhelming with certain patterns flashing while gaming. Would I recommend this keyboard to a hard-core gamer? Probably not, but I don't believe that the hardcore gamer is what they were attempting to reach. With the customized colors and flashing patterns, teens and consumers looking for that step up from the basic cheesy unresponsive keyboard. With the price there better be a 50 million durable cycle life for the keys. Dell needs to provide adequate directions for those that are new to these types of programmable keyboards.

The best description would be from when technology was attempting different/new things in the early 2000s with the ALL-in One smart remotes. You could literally assign your AC, lights and certain air machines to power on once you figured out the code for your appliance, and while really cool and the beginning of SMART in your home, it was cumbersome and not user-friendly. Relative/friends could not come over and use your awesome new remote because every button was assigned a feature. They would always ask for the basic cable or television remote. THAT IS THIS WATCH. Cool, different, claims to do much but is not user-friendly. The dial is so tiny... I shouldn't have to translate how many steps I have actually walked. If you are having an off day, you will surely mix up which button corresponds with which feature.

I also need to mention that it doesn't stay connected as we have become accustomed to with our other smart devices. I have had to constantly reset the watch and app so that they can continue to sinc. At the end of the day, I just hold my phone in my hand so that I do not miss any important calls while in stores. Do not recommend unless you go to their website and download a manual before purchase! title: Good-bye wires and clutter!
text:
[[VIDEOID:9681233f80f4af74f0d0ad442e7db5da]] Our most recent set up was 10 years old and cost a lot individually. The speakers were a 6.1 set from Klipsch, subwoofer Energy and Denon receiver. This was the living room set up and took A LOT of wiring. Over the decade, things were moved, disconnected/reconnected etc. Eventually we were bare bones with just the center and two front speakers connected because no one wanted to go reconnect near the ceiling. The receiver started acting out after Con Edison had that big transformer explosion (looked like alien invasion) in our neighborhood. We lost an XBOX one and the Denon receiver started going in and out. Before this decade old set up it was a Sony 5.1 system with subwoofer and receiver. We LOVED the Sony speakers sound and bass.

Fast forward to now... going back to the wiring! It was disgusting. I kid you not it looked like a networking room in a company with wires everywhere. We attempted to hide and even went through a portable fireplace firebox. This SONY 3.1 Dolby Atmos upscaler does not need that! One wire and you are set via bluetooth. Connecting took all of 5 minutes and we did not use the included instructional manual. Grateful that this company still provides these booklets rather than having you search online from the start. The facade of the soundbar will scroll whichever sound setting you are currently using. This is easily read from the couch which is about 7.5 feet away. While this isn't a true 7.2 system, with their technology, Sony claims that they will upscale sound via their Immersive AE (audio enhancement). They claim to emulate virtual surround speakers and a vertical surround engine. In other words, sound will not only be from the three front but also around you and from above you. Does it accomplish this? Well no, but not because it doesn't try. The cold hard truth is that there are not speakers all around, at your foot level and above you... so you will not be able to hear the jet in Top Gun going from the right to the left. The jet will go but more of a squiggly sound. If you aren't intently listening for these specific things, then the sound is AWESOME! It isn't tinny or punchy; it is immersive, surrounding and makes the hair on our bodies stand and quiver.

The remote is straight-forward and simple. I love that I can cycle through the different modes, Immersive AE, Cinema, Music, Standard, Night Mode, Dolby and DTS modes. Take the necessary 15-20 minutes to really play around with each of the functions so that you can understand when they should be activated/de-activated. A one size fits all approach does not work when it comes to viewing television, gaming or streaming films! The subwoofer is wireless and was connected to the bar right out of the box. We have only had one issue when the woofer went into stand-by and wouldn't power on... we turned off and reset to get it fired up.

I uploaded a 30 sec video of some Transformer film... while you may not be able to discern all the effects or the subwoofer thumping, it is important for readers to hear it's capabilities. The volume was set to 27 and subwoofer to 7 out of 12. The sound is all encompassing and makes you feel surrounded... it is a good attempt at a theater immersive experience at home and on a budget. Again, you experience will be affected positively or negative by your selection. Play with the settings and you will not be disappointed.

Highly recommend this middle of the road Sony 3.1 Soundbar for it's upscaling ability and the fact that it will play Dolby Atmos content. If you are down sizing or streamlining your home theater set up, I don't believe that you will be disappointed! We are officially not bringing back all the aforementioned equipment and sticking to the Sony Soundbar.

title: Doesn't capture from VCRs
text:
I've been looking for a way to convert family videos recorded on VHS and Hi-8 to a digital form. I've tried MPEG-2 capture and DV capture and haven't been happy with either result, so I had high hopes for the Hauppauge 1212 HD-PVR with its hardware H.264/AVC encoder.

Unfortunately, the HD-PVR is not useful for this purpose because the hardware locks up, hangs, or loses sync (resulting in a split screen effect that persists until the box is rebooted and the software reset) whenever there is a glitch in the video signal from the VCR. And unfortunately, there is such a glitch every time the camera was turned off and then back on again -- whenever recordings overlap, or there is a gap in the recording (tape taken out and later re-inserted). Also, pressing fast forward or rewind on the VCR to position the capture point while monitoring with the anemic software that's provided for capture/editing also causes the box to hang up. This makes it really hard to locate scenes on the tape: hit play, hit rewind, reboot the PVR, restart the software so you can monitor the input, press pause--whoops, another glitch, reboot the PVR, restart the software... you get my drift.

I contacted Hauppauge tech support and I was told that this is expected behavior -- the converter requires a stable video source and VCRs are anything but that. I considered getting a SIMA or ACE timebase corrector that performs full-frame time base correction, but those are not made anymore, go for a pretty penny on EBAY, and seem like overkill when the next generation of an encoder like this one might have TBC built in.

So, the HD-PVR is unfortunately useless for capturing from VHS, which as of this writing, the product description touts as a feature. And that's too bad, because the video I was able to capture between hangs was quite good. For that, and the ability to capture from component inputs (which works quite well, from what I understand, although I didn't try it), I'll still give it two stars. But zero stars for its VHS capture capability and mediocre software, which needs to be reinitialized whenever the box hangs.

<sigh> maybe the next version...

title: Regularly drops wireless connections
text:
I bought this router to replace an aging two-year old D-Link DGL-4300 "gamerlounge" wireless B/G router. Figured I'd make the jump to wireless N, and use the 5ghz band to link this router with a Linksys wireless bridge in my downstairs A/V cabinet that also contains a TIVO HD-XL, PS3, XBOX360, and Roku Soundbridge. Currently, except for the TIVO, each of those devices has its own wireless receiver.

Unfortunately, Linksys let me down. This router seems to turn off the wireless connection every 24-48 hours and the only way to get it turned back on is to log into the router's web browser and reboot it. Also, my wireless laptop cannot see any of the computers on my wired network -- not sure why this router is not bridging the connections. The DHCP list is flaky -- I'll reserve DHCP connections for various mac addresses, and the next time I check, the reserved IPs and mac addresses reappear in the list of items that can be reserved. The logging is worthless -- it collects minimal data, and no clue about why the wireless connections keep getting dropped; there are no diagnostics that are helpful. We have two iPhones in the house, and when this happens, they can't connect to this router but as soon as I reboot the router, the connection is available. It's really tedious to have to do that every day or two. As far as I can tell, there is no way to tell which network (2.4GHZ or 5GHZ or wired) that a given DHCP client is connected to, which is hugely annoying when you have an unrecognized device connected -- if it's connected wirelessly, I must have set it up, but it's still annoying to have no description of the device. (I look up the mac address online which at least tells me the manufacturer.) Finally, the UPNP configuration just doesn't work -- I have two programs that use UPNP to open a temporary hole in the firewall (a Windows Home Server and uTorrent), I have UPNP enabled in this router and neither program can successfully configure it.

With my wireless B/G laptop, I get download rates of 600-800 kbps and upload rates of 300kbps when I'm sitting downstairs directly below this router (this is using the speedtest at [...] . I got 3mbps with the B/G D-Link router -- still not stellar, but acceptable. Fortunately, the wired connections on this router are decent -- get 28mpbs down, and just under 2mbps up using Turbo RoadRunner. But I bought this to serve wireless connections.

There are just a lot of things wrong with this router. Also, some of the online help and the installation program's messages need some serious proof-reading, which always makes me wonder about the quality that goes into a product.

I did upgrade the firmware as soon as I got this, but the last update was from May (it's now the end of September, 2009 as I write this). According to the Linksys website, there is supposedly a v2 hardware version of this router; when I purchased at the start of September, I got a v1 and there was no version indication on the outside of the package. Also, check the LinkSys website -- many many complaints about dropped connections with this router. The advice Linksys is giving out is to turn off the 5ghz radio becasue overheating might be causing the problems -- effectively turning this into a much cheaper single-band router. No thanks.

Anyway, this is going back this weekend and I'm going to try out the latest D-Link product. The DGL-4300 "Gamerlounge" router was fantastic (the power supply finally died and the router's been flaky since then, so I think it was damaged when the power brick failed); I think I'll try the latest version of their product. It's just a shame that nobody makes a cadillac consumer-level product these days, but for [...], I expected better.

title: Great quality but picky
text:
I gave this three stars despite the fact that I finally wound up returning the card. I purchased this to capture old family video (VHS and Hi8), so I can't say how the HD capture functions work. I did not have any trouble installing the card or getting it to work with the provided capture software for 720x480 NTSC interlaced video capture onto a dedicated to video, nearly empty 4TB Hitachi hard drive and the video and audio quality was good.

I returned it because there were two big issues:

1) The audio would drift out of sync with the video despite the capture software reporting no dropped frames -- after 1/2 hour of capturing, the audio would precede the video by 5 seconds. I contacted Blackmagic support about this, and they told me that this indicates that the storage system isn't fast enough. The system test utility said the system was plenty fast enough for NTSC capture and even 720p capture (not so much at higher data rates). I countered by asking why it wasn't reporting dropped frames if this is the case, but didn't get a reply. I also asked about this in their forums without any replies.

2) The card doesn't appear to perform any time base correction, so there was lots of noise in the individual horizontal lines (edges wiggling back and forth on VHS capture). While I could fix that during the editing process, it seems to me that a card in this price range should be able to do that. In their defense, I suspect this card is more oriented towards capturing HD sources.

On the upside, the colors were better than my other capture device, which I am now successfully using -- a Canopus ADVC-300, which captures to DV using the more restricted DV color space. But the ADVC-300 performs line-based time-base correction so the overall captured video stream looked better (despite the DV intra-frame compression), and audio sync is rock-solid; dropped frames are extremely rare, and only between recordings when the VCR is trying to re-sync.

I also tried the Hauppauge Colossus capture card, but the software provided with that card made it pretty much unusable (you must install and use the included software, which constantly nags you to purchase the full version) and I also had audio sync problems with that card. I did download a full trial version of the capture/editing software but it didn't solve the audio sync problems and still crashed frequently. It also captures to a compressed h.264 stream which is convenient if you simply want to preserve your videos without much effort or editing, but the audio sync problems were a killer.

For reference, the machine is a 2008 vintage Dell 730x with an Intel Core-i7 920, 16GB of RAM, NVIDIA GeForce 285 video, an SSD boot drive, and the 4TB drive for captures. The hardware should be capable, but the Blackmagic forum does describe issues with the X58 chip set.

So, my advice: try this card if it fits your needs but be sure to buy from a vendor that accepts returns.

title: A decent first try, but too many glitches for me
text:
I *really* wanted to like this box -- been looking for a one-size-fits-all streaming box forever. I have a Boxee Box (fantastic until it was abandoned by the developers and D-Link), Western Digital WD-Live, Chromecast, TiVo HD-XL (which does Amazon and Netflix, both poorly) and Oppo BluRay Player with built-in apps (does a great job but has a terrible interface). None of these devices support Amazon Video except TiVo and it doesn't do Prime Video, so I figured I'd try the Amazon Fire TV to see if it might replace these devices.

The short answer is no -- there are just too many glitches, so it's going back within my 30 day trial period. The first issue is compatibility with my Marantz AV8801 -- I could not get the Amazon Fire TV to display full-screen using any of the available rear HDMI inputs. All content showed in a box in the middle of the TV screen and try as I might, I couldn't find any setting either in the Amazon Fire or in the Marantz to change that. Plugging in Chromecast or WD-Live to the same input worked just fine -- 1080i output to my admittedly old Sony RPTV and 2-year old Sony LCD TV using the Marantz' two HDMI outputs. Plug in the Amazon box and everything is fuzzily displayed in what looks like a 360p box floating in the middle of the screen.

In desperation, I tried the front panel HDMI input, and the Fire TV did work properly with that input. It's not any different than the rear inputs and the settings in the receiver were the same, but for some reason that worked and displayed a beautiful image. But that led to the next problem -- try as I might, I could not get the Amazon to output anything other than 2 channel Dolby Digital sound. It's supposed to have Dolby Digital Pro (whatever that is -- it is on the list of audio formats that my receiver supports, but I'd never heard of it) but I couldn't get it to output anything other than stereo. Using Netlix, I watched "Doctor Who" with both the Amazon FireTV and the Chromecast (same episode) and the Chromecast sound was much better.

I also have a Plex server, and the availability of the Plex app for the FireTV was another reason I wanted to try this device. That was a non-starter -- while the very first program I tried to play streamed properly (causing me to declare success), after that nothing worked. I'd start a program and it would sit and spin for a while and eventually declare the program unplayable (no problem on the Chromecast), and once that happened, then the FireTV wouldn't play anything at all (including Netflix or Amazon VOD) until I power-cycled the FireTV. And when it did work (which was maybe 1 out of 10 programs that I tried, with frequent power cycles), I just got the two-channel audio. It's been several months since the FireTV and Plex were released, so there has been plenty of time to work out the kinks.

So the Amazon FireTV is regretfully going back (and I need to figure out how I can get the $5 I paid for Plex back as well). I'm giving it three stars because it did play Amazon VOD well, has a good remote, never stuttered on playback (when it worked, that is), and has a truly speedy interface. It may work perfectly well for a lot of people with simpler setups -- that is, who will plug it straight into a TV and just want Amazon VOD and Netflix. I'm looking forwards to the inevitable v2, which will hopefully have all the kinks worked out. I hope it also supports DTS and lossless Dolby or DTS multichannel audio formats (like Boxee or the Oppo BluRay player do) -- that make that a no-brainer. But for now, color me disappointed.

text:
I originally bought this "Clipper Pro" bluetooth receiver in February of 2017 to use with my LG OLED TV that has built-in Bluetooth, for late-night TV watching. I'm happy to report that it works perfectly. While the receiver has the AptX-LL low-latency codec, the LG TV doesn't have this (as far as I know, and I've searched for the info). Still, there's still no annoying delay so maybe LG compensates in some other way. In any case, the sound quality is better than fine -- far better with my $40 Japanese-made earbuds than with some similarly-priced earbuds with built-in bluetooth that I tried and returned. The sound is not as good as my $300 Sony noise-cancelling bluetooth headphones that I use at work, but I prefer earbuds when laying down anyway. So a huge advantage is that you can use the headphones of your choice with this receiver.

I also have a Sony LCD TV, which inexplicably doesn't have built-in Bluetooth, I purchased [[ASIN:B01N5KKUR0 Avantree aptX LOW LATENCY Bluetooth 4.2 Transmitter for TV PC (3.5mm, RCA, Computer USB digital audio) 100ft Range, Dual Link Wireless Audio Adapter for Headphones - Priva III [24M Warranty]]] at the same time. It has no battery and needs to be plugged in, which is what I wanted. It also has a low-latency codec and works just fine with the receiver.

Full disclosure: this receiver did die after about 9 months -- it just stopped charging. I thought it was out of warranty so I replaced it with a "Saturn Pro" unit: [[ASIN:B00LAZ6RTW Avantree aptX LOW LATENCY Bluetooth Transmitter and Receiver 2-in-1, Wireless 3.5mm audio Adapter for Stereo Speakers, Headphones or TV - Saturn Pro]], which is less compact but has a longer battery life and doesn't need to be charged as often. That also works fine, and it can function as a transmitter but I don't use it that way. It's great that both receivers worked when plugged into the charger; that eliminates some battery-life anxiety.

In January, just before throwing the dead unit away, I noticed it has a 12-month warranty, not 90 days as I assumed. I contacted Avantree by email and they quickly sent me a replacement unit which works perfectly. I am continuing to use the Saturn Pro with the LG and am using the new Clipper Pro with my Sony TV.

Anyway, five stars because it works well, and also for the 1 year warranty and great vendors service.

title: Dang, this is a good tripod!
text:
I have a regular camera tripod that I don't particularly like -- it's big, clunky, doesn't have a ball head, and the mount is a pain to attach to my Nikon D-750 DSLR because it's a bit bigger than the base of the camera. I have some vacations ahead and wanted a tripod that I could put into my luggage without putting the bag over the airline limit, so I ordered this one.

I'm happy to say that this tripod exceeds my expectations in every way. The legs fold 180 degrees up over the head so it doesn't need to be disassembled (I honestly haven't seen that before, and was impressed). They snap solidly into position, and the legs use levers that lock the extensions into place instead of twists (I had a tripod that did that and it was annoying). The center post does use a nut but it was still easy to use and presumably makes it more compact. The mount is the best part -- again, I may have used the wrong tripod in the past, but this one uses a ball head can solidly hold my 4 pound camera at a multitude of angles. The mounting plate slides on and off and its a reasonable size (doesn't extend beyond the bottom of my camera like my annoying other tripod). There's also a bubble level in the back and this is the first tripod I've owned that's holds the camera up above my head and I'm 6'4".

I normally don't even bother using a tripod because the camera is fast enough for hand-held shots, but there are times when it's needed and this tripod is quick to set up and enjoyable to use. I'd also love to find a iPhone 13 Pro Max mount that would slide into the top of this tripod -- maybe NIANYISO will make one.

Overall, very pleased. Great tripod!

title: Nice 9-outlet USB powerstrip for desk
text:
I ordered this power strip for my motorized desk, which has a 1" solid bamboo top. It fit perfectly -- just the right size or the gap between monitor and phone on my desk -- and is rock-solid, once attached. The strip is made out of ABS plastic (feels really solid) and has a right-angle plug on the end of the cord, which is what I prefer.

I checked each 120V power outlet with a tester and they're correctly wired for polarity and ground, but I wouldn't expect anything less. I also used each of the four USB type a ports to charge my iPhone Pro Max for a bit and it did that fine as well, but I have no way to test the USB outlets for power delivery and there are no embossed symbols next to the ports. Two are orange and two are white -- not sure why, but the box claims two of the outlets are Qualcomm QuickCharge(TM)(R) enabled and I'm guessing it's the orange ones although that color coding normally means "sleep and charge ports" or "always on ports" on a laptop. Maybe the vendor will update the description to explain.

There's an Off/On/Reset switch on one end by the cord and surge protection is claimed as well. The 120V power outlets are a bit stiff, but I'd expect those to loosen up over time and at least dangling power bricks won't fall out (see photo of the back). They are not tamper-resistant, so don't stick a fork in the outlets.

Finally, the Amazon page claims the strip is ETL listed (it's like UL-approved) but there's no such indication on the box or flag on the cord and I couldn't find the vendor on the Qualcomm website as a licensee. So I have to knock a star off for that. It may be under a different name, but again, no indication on the box.

Still, nine well-spaced 120V outlets that can accept power adapters are pretty good in such a compact form factor -- not quite sure how they managed it but it works well for me.

title: Loud, doesn't move much air
text:
First, the good: the fan is well made, looks sturdy, and is USB powered, and even includes a USB extension cable. It's about 3" in size (7cm). I have several 5" (12cm) USB fans that I use to cool external USB disk drives -- these dramatically extend the life of these devices, and I also used one to cool a TiVo (notorious for overheating) and a cable modem (ditto).

The 5" fans are nice and quiet, even at their highest speed, and the ones I use have a 3 speed switch and a USB pass-through so they can be daisy chained. This fan is unfortunately much louder -- a consequence of being smaller, I'm sure -- and doesn't move nearly as much air as the 5" fan. I tried this fan on my TiVo across my office and the whine was distracting. So I'd recommend this only for cases where a 3" form factor is required and you're not near the equipment (maybe a closed cabinet). Certainly a speed control would help -- I found it doesn't take moving much air to keep a device much cooler than it would be without moving air. Or better, go with a 5" fan with a speed control and you can decide exactly how much air you need and how much noise you can tolerate.

title: Captures onto a USB stick -- great solution!
text:
I've been trying to capture family videos from the 1980s and 1990s into my computer. I have a Canopus ADVC-300 which captures to DV video at about 14GB/hour. I made a pass over all the videos using that and the .AVI files that produces are great for editing, but the colors look washed out because the DV video format doesn't handle the full range of colors that NTSC TV provides. So before tossing the tapes, I wanted to capture again.

I've been through several HDMI capture device and always ask myself, "how hard can it be". It turns out it's quite hard. They require that you use software like OBS Studio, which has a learning curve and some inscrutable options -- plus there's that USB 3 or HDMI cable snaking across the room to your computer.

This ClearClick device claims to improve on that by allowing video to be captured directly to a USB memory stick (more on that later). So I figured I'd give this a try as unattended capture of these family videos would be wonderful.

But first, I have to convert the VCR's S-Video or composite video output to HDMI. Since my A/V receiver (Denon 8500HA) can play VHS on my TV over HDMI, it's clearly capable of upconverting 480i or 240i or whatever VHS happens to be. It will upconvert all the way to 4k (or even 8k, except I don't have an 8k tv).

Once the ClearClick device arrived, I formatted a 32GB SanDisk USB 3 memory stick, plugged it into the device, connected it to my Denon receiver and the 1080p TV in my office and pressed play on the VCR. While I could see the video on the attached 1080p TV, I could not get this box to stop blinking red which appears to mean that it's not capturing.

By looking at the manual, I found that one reason is that the input signal might be HDCP copyright protected. These are family videos (VHS and VHS-C from those huge 1990s camcorders), so they're certainly not Macrovision-encoded and I doubt the Denon would sniff that out and HDCP encode the HDMI outputs. So I wrote to Denon's great support and learned that, lo and behold, all HDMI output is HDCP-protected, regardless of the source. D'oh!

But all is not lost. I then ordered a $10 composite to HDMI converter -- "Mini AV2HDMI" here to do the job that I was hoping the expensive Denon could do: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0B63PTYT3. I wasn't expecting great things but thought it might come in handy for trying out video capture solutions. Lo and behold, it worked perfectly with this capture device as soon as I connected it to the VCR and the ClearClick: I pushed play on the VCR, pushed the button on top of this device, watched the video on the connected 1080p TV and when it was done, I had files on the USB memory stick! The quality was far better than I expected: the AV2HDMI device must do the de-interlacing so the picture was a bit soft, but it also took care of occasional tearing at the bottom of the video (must do some time-base correction). Pretty amazing for a $10 device and I'll add that the colors were accurate, saturated, clear, and wonderful -- much better than DV video capture.

The ClearClick device upconverts the low-resolution VCR files to 1080p at 60 fps, which is overkill so I'm going to investigate how to reduce that when I get some more free time. Also, the audio is AAC LC with a variable bit rate of 62.5kb/s which is pretty low, although the captured stereo audio sounded fine in headphones. At this rate, the mp4 files consume about 220mb a minute. For comparison, 480p DV video is about 233mb/minute -- but it's only compressed in-frame, while this device puts out MPEG-4 (mp4) files with AAC LC audio, which are compressed across frames. DV video is easy to edit with non-linear non-destructive editors like Premiere Pro; MPEG-4 video, not so much but I have another editor, TMPGenc Smart Video Renderer, that can handle this kind of video and only re-encodes frames that are actually changed.

The AV2HDMI box can also produce 720P output and I may switch to that since they're VCR files. More experimentation is in order.

Finally, as I mentioned, one huge advantage of this device over the other two I already own is the ability to capture directly to a memory stick. I found that when capturing video on USB to my dekstop, I can't really use my computer while it's capturing because that results in dropped frames or lockups, plus I have a long USB cable snaking across my room. Being able to capture onto USB is such a huge feature that I don't know why other devices can't do it.

Regarding the FAT32 file format, the device also claims to support EXFAT which breaks the 32GB barrier. I did not try that because I happen to be using a 32GB Sandisk USB memory stick, which is the size limit for FAT32.

So far, I'm really really pleased with this capture box. It's not easy to get started -- you do have to be motivated, but for anyone who is game to do this, I can heartily recommend this ClearClick device over all of the others I've tried so far.

title: Great HDMI splitter -- best one I've tried
text:
I have a Denon 8K-capable A/V receiver in my office that has two HDMI outputs: one runs the 4K TV and surround system in my family room and the second is connected to a 1080p TV in my office. The Denon has a mirrored monitor 1 and monitor 2 output (zone 2 goes to the master bedroom) but when mirroring, it appears to downgrade to the least common denominator so when the office TV is on, the main TV only gets a 1080p signal and I lose HDR/Dolby Vision and surround sound in the family room so I'm always unplugging the office HDMI cable. This splitter solves that problem nicely and the Denon is no longer confused. The 4K output of the splitter is hooked up to a video capture device because I uses the Denon to digitize family videotapes -- it does a good job with upconverting the gawd-awful VCR signal to 720p or 1080p with decent deinterlacing. This splitter allows the capture device to work properly with the Denon's output -- for some reason, the capture device does not like the digital signal the Denon produces.

I'm still experimenting with what else this device will do, but it's done everything I asked it to so far without any trouble. The splitter is solidly built, and high quality with plenty of indicators telling me what it's doing (not always the case with these kinds of devices). Highly recommended!

title: Must have for traveling to Europe
text:
I'm going to be traveling to southern Europe soon and also joining a Mediterranean crusie and wanted to try a new kind of power adapter. The ones I have are the cubes that plug into a wall socket and they tend to get weighed down and fall out and then you find nothing charged overnight. This adapter has an honest-to-goodness cord, an EU plug, along with a stackable US and UK adapter which will make it perfect for a nightstand where it can charge 5 devices at once with room for additional power bricks if you have more devices than that, or, say a 120V/240V compatible laptop. Yay!

The only reason for 4 stars instead of 5 is the fake ground pin on the outlets. I'm not sure why this is even there because charging adapters, 120/240V laptop power supplies don't need a ground. Because having the ground implies that a ground is available might contribute to a shock hazard and someone might plug in an extension cord. I do plan to use this as a desktop powerstrip/charger when I return but the 3-prong outlets without a ground gives me pause when it's used as a power strip and someone plugs something like a vacuum cleaner into it that needs a ground.

But for traveling, this looks like just the ticket. Just don't plug in something that needs to be grounded.

title: Rugged ethernet switch that appears to be suitable for attics
text:
I have a single Cat-6 wire going into my top attic from my router, and five Cat-6 cables going from there to various wall drops on my second floor. I've been using consumer-grade switched (Linksys, NetGear) and I found that with the 120-130F heat during the summer, they typically only last a year or two. I would also like to mount a Power-over-Ethernet camera in the soffit over my driveway. This unit claims to handle temperatures up to 180F (which seems like a stretch) and provides POE, so it should fit the bill and the price is reasonable compared to other switches I looked at.

While the instructions are just a little cryptic regarding hard-wiring the power to the switch, I hooked it up and tested it on my workbench by connecting it to my existing switch -- it does what it says. When it gets consistently cooler and I get a free weekend, I'll climb into my attic and replace the switch that's up there. This switch is solid metal and I'm not expecting any problems, although the power supply looks like a typical laptop power supply and it's 48V so hopefully it's rated for those temperatures as well. I'll give it a shot and report back if it fails -- but I don't expect that to be the case.

title: Excellent upgrade for my x99 Alienware Area-51 Gen 2 Desktop
text:
The other day, my trusty Alienware Area-51 Gen 2, an Intel i7-5820k 3.3ghz 6 core CPU on an X99 chipset threw a memory fault. It turned out that the case just needed dusting and the memory re-seating but that reminded me that I'm still running 16GB of 2133mhz Dell memory from when I purchased the machine way back in May of 2016. Geez, that was over 6 years ago and it still runs like a bat out of hell. This was the first glitch I can remember.

I remember at the time that 32GB of DDR4 memory was very expensive and 16GB was plenty but I figured I'd look again. Lo and behold, it's come down near the $100 range! I first checked Micron's website because they have a compatibility checker, but they only offered memory rated CL19 and higher -- faster memory was "backordered". However, I found this Corsair memory on Amazon for about the same price as on the Micron website, rated at 3200mhz which is the top option in the Alienware BIOS, Intel XMP support, and claimed to be CL16, which is about as good as it gets right now. It arrived in 2 days (another plus), and I just installed it then booted into the BIOS. It detected 32GB but still at 2166mhz. I then turned on the XMP function, rebooted, and lo and behold, it chose 3200MHZ and the BIOS says 16 and a bunch of other numbers I can't see without rebooting.

I then held my breath and booted into Windows. Now, after a full day of using Visual Studio and Adobe Lightroom, the system is still rock-solid and, dare I say it, noticeably quicker than before (and it was no slouch). I don't know if that's because I doubled the amount of memory (likely), or the 3200mhz vs 2133mhz but me likey.. a lot! I was thinking that it was time to replace this machine but now I'm thinking that I can wait another year or two.

Posting this mostly so others looking for Alienware Area-51 Gen2 compatibility will know that this memory works as the Amazon memory checker was non-committal. It works... and works well.

I currently work at home, but we have some trips planned to visit some aging family and I will be taking along my laptop and putting in some hours at our destination to avoid using too much vacation time. A second monitor will be immensely helpful in this case, and it doesn't really take up much more room than the laptop itself. I expect it to be incredibly useful for that.

I do have the Apple A1438 Lightning to HDMI adapter, and I connected it to my iPhone 14 Pro Max using the vendor's instructions in the Q&A above. It doesn't work despite the fact that I powered both the adapter with a lightning cable and this monitor with a USB C power cable -- I tried both USB C port to make sure. The monitor would start up, say "no signal, entering power save mode". I tried Netflix, YouTubeTV, YouTube on the monitor. I was successful at playing YouTubeTV over a hotel TV over a VPN in Greece, so I know this Apple HDMI adapter works.

I do not see any mention of HDCP copy protection in the specs, and I suspect this is the problem -- copy-protected sources will simply not play on this monitor. Not a problem for the intended purpose: a second monitor for your laptop, but don't expect to enjoy movies during your downtime. If this turns out to be an incorrect analysis, I'll come back and put back the 5th star on the review.

As far as a wishlist, I do wish it had some smarts like AirPlay or ChromeCast so I could, for example, use it as an external monitor on my iPhone, which would not require HDCP. Also, the slot for the more reclined position is not deep enough, so it really won't stay put in that position, but the more vertical angle works well enough. Finally, I see there are screw holes in the back which look like they could attach to a stand or wall mount, but there are no instructions, VESA pattern (if it's VESA at all) or screw sizes in the documentation.

So a mixed bag. Four stars because it's fit for purpose, but it doesn't make any of the stretch goals.

title: Still problematic to install and use, and uses ony expensive Dymo labels
text:
This is the third Dymo Lablewriter I have owned. After a miserable experience with the first many moons ago (can't remember the number but it looked similar to this one), I pretty much switched to Brother label printers and now have three of those, plus one that prints on laminated tape -- all connected to my computer at tje same time, and it's trivial to switch between them.

But… then I then wanted to print 4x6 labels so I purchased a Dymo 450XL a few years ago, and had no end of trouble with that printer despite using nothing but genuine Dymo labels -- I have five rolls of 4x6 labels that I bought cheap when a nearby office was closing. I ultimately had to give up and trash that printer as it would disconnect from my computer without warning, would not work through a USB hub at all but insisted on being connected directly to the computer, often required a power cycle to get it to print, and when it did print, it would often not detect the end of a label, printing the first label and then spitting out 5 feet of additional blank labels before I could pull the plug and tediously wind the labels back in. Again, these were Dymo-branded 4x6 labels! That 450XL eventually went into the garbage -- I despised it so much I didn't even want to saddle a charity with it. To be able to print USPS postage labels through Ebay or PirateShip, I then bought a Brother QL-800 printer, along with a roll of 2-3/7" wide label tape after discovering that USPS now prints postage on 2-3/8" x 7" labels. This works perfectly: the Brother QL-800 has an automatic cutter which works like a dream -- and I've used 3rd-party 2-3/7 tape in that printer without any problems at all or warnings from the printer.

Now that a year has gone by since I trashed the Dymo 450XL, I was offered this 550 printer. While I was a little aghast at the price, since there's not much risk, I thought "why not give Dymo another chance". The Dymo embosser-type label maker I had as a kid holds fond memories and I can always use one more size of pre-loaded labels on my shelf. So I ordered this printer even though I was a little leery of the requirement that a new generation of "genuine Dymo labels" must be used and third-party labels will not work. I had recently read a very negative blog post by a trusted source who was migrating from the 450 to the 550 because Dymo did something that prevented his 450 from working properly. He that talks about the Dymo label requirement, as there is apparently some kind of RFID chip on the hub of each label roll -- the author has many older Dymo labels that are now useless, although Dymo did offer to swap them out (something that might be useful to readers of this review). I knew that my Dymo 4x6 labels will not fit in this printer to begin with, so that's fortunately not a factor; the Brother postage labels work fine for me but Brother doesn't do a great job with address labels, while Dymo used to do address correction and print USPS bar codes and the blog post implied that Dymo was restoring this feature to their software. That's the main reason I ordered this particular printer -- to get those capabilities back.

Now for the review. As you can see from the photos, the printer is packed well, and uses an inline power brick. It includes a USB 2.0 cable with a sticker that says "install software first". I did that -- I can only surmise that Windows 10/11 ships with some kind of compatible printer driver that wins if the official Dymo software is not installed when the USB cable is connected. Seems that's a problem that could be worked around as most other recent USB products I've purchased don't have this limitation. Dymo: just give Microsoft your latest driver, or work with them to solve this problem as this appears to cause a lot of grief. I did manage to install the software without trouble by following the instructions to the letter (I had uninstalled previous Dymo software a long time ago). I also connected the printer to a USB 3 hub, and they apparently have solved that particular problem as the software had no trouble finding the printer.

The first problem I had was when I was trying to register the printer on the Dymo website. The Dymo website insists that I enter a phone number, which I really don't want to give them, so I just entered a 555 prefix movie/TV number, which it found acceptable and is a number reserved for TV/movie use. Strike 1: no company should require a phone number at product registration time -- I was tempted to abandon the registration process right then and there but continued on. I then managed to fill out everything else but when I submitted, the "Language" field turned red and has an empty drop-down list. I can't submit the form without selecting a language, but I can't select a language because the list is empty. I then refreshed the form, started over, this time the field said "English" and I pressed "Submit". The screen flashes but there's no acknowledgment. I'll assume it worked, but no idea. Strike 2: Arrrrrgh! This doesn't bode well for Dymo's software skills.

Now that my printer may or may not be registered, I loaded the labels. The package included three rolls of labels but just one core to mount the labels on. This makes it a real nuisance to change labels, compared to Brother's "drop in" system, where labels always come on a form. I finally figured out how to do that, and tried to advance the labels. After a few tries of repeatedly threading the labels, I got it to feed, but even that was harder than it should have been.

So I figured I'd print an address. I entered my address onto a label and then looked for an option to add the USPS bar code. No joy. While the "fix US address" button did manage to fix my purposely mistyped street name and added the 9-digit zip code, it did this only if I clicked in the address first before clicking "fix US address". If the address did not have the focus, it would say "Address Updated" without actually making any changes to the address, which could be a problem if it's incorrect. The moral: click in the address first.

But most annoying: there does NOT seem to be an option to generate the USPS bar code, which is something that I'm sure my previous Dymo software was able to do. Strike 3.

And now I went to try to print the address label (without the barcode), and I noticed the bottom of the application says "DYMO LabelWriter 550 Disconnected". Sure enough, I try to print and nothing happens. It looks like the printer powered off while I was playing with the label program. The Dymo Connect program doesn't have an option to change or disable the timeout on the printer, nor does the print driver (this is where Brother has this function) and there is nothing in the instructions that mentions this. Strike 4. Is there a strike 4?

Finally, it looks like Dymo installed a windows service, "DYMO Connect PnP Service". Why does a label printer need to install a Windows service? The software should NOT run unless I'm actually running the software. One possibility is that other computers on the network can use the label printer, although I've seen nothing that makes me believe this is true and this doesn't apply to me anyway. I stopped and disabled the service and it appears that I can still print. But then: it printed most of the first label, reported an error with the power button flashing; when I pushed the power button it then finished printing the label, spat out two blank labels, and finally printed the label again. Strike 5.

D'oh!

I printed the label again and it worked this time. And now, after writing some more of this review, the printer has turned itself off again.

So far, I'm not impressed -- especially when the printer spat out two blank labels like my 450XL used to and these have to be expensive Dymo labels. Also, for the price, I'd expect a built-in paper cutter --something the much less expensive Brother QL-800 has. And it can use generic labels!

title: Good card reader for lightning iPad and iPhone
text:
I have both the official Apple SD card reader and USB 3 adapter. When we are on trips, every night, I transfer photos from my Nikon D750's SD cards to my iPad and let it upload them into iCloud -- that way, if I lose my camera or the SD card fails, I still have my photos. I ordered this so I'd have a spare and only have to carry one adapter.

Sure enough, it works with my iPad (didn't try it with my iPhone but the results should be identical). When you plug in either this adapter or the Apple adapter, nothing happens. You have to click on Files and then the button at the top left of the screen. A panel slides out that has the name of your card or USB memory stick. Click on that and you can see what's on the card/stick and you can copy it to your iPad or iPhone.

Another review mentioned not being able to import photos directly into the camera roll. That is possible: in Photos, click the top-left menu and you'll see Devices about half-way down. In my case, the card is named "D-750" and I can import even Nikon NEF raw photos into the camera roll.

I also use Lightroom on my iPad, although I prefer to copy to the Apple camera roll because I have more iCloud storage than Adobe Lightroom cloud storage. In Lightroom, click the three ... and select Import. You can look at the Lightroom storage, camera roll, or the attached device.

One nice thing is that this device can actually handle a USB 3 memory stick. When I connect the Apple adapter and plug in a USB 3 stick, the iPad says "This device requires too much power". However, the battery meter on my iPad (a 12.9" iPad Pro) goes down 1% every 1-2 minutes that a USB 3 stick is connected, and the memory stick does get warm. I'd suggest you copy the contents of the stick to the iPad or iPhone so you can disconnect it.

An alternative is to connect a lightning power cable to the lightning port on the adapter. I confirmed that my iPad charged while accessing the memory stick using this method.

I don't have a "TF" card (whatever that is), so I couldn't try that.

Really the only negative thing I can say is that the adapter doesn't feel quite as solid as the Apple SD adapter -- SD cards feel a little "rough" when going in and you do have to line it up perfectly straight to insert it, while the Apple adapter is silky-smooth and kind of guides the card in. Of course, Apple stuff is the Cadillac and while this might be a Chevy, it's more than good enough. And the ability to use USB 3 memory sticks is a big plus. Highly recommended!

title: Cheap but incredibly useful external hard drive converter
text:
Like many enthusiasts, I have a number of internal 2.5" hard drives -- in my case, small SSDs -- in a drawer. This case effectively replaces the SATA connection with a USB 3 connection, allowing me to use these drives.

I plugged one of the first SSDs I purchased -- an OCZ Trion 256GB model into the drive. After figuring out how to get it apart (the clamshell slides apart -- don't pry it), I used the included USB 3 A to USB-C cable, plugged it into the front of my computer and it was detected immediately. No drivers needed.

As a test, I copied a 5GB file from my C-drive SSD to this device over a USB 3 connection and the transfer rate initially zoomed to 120MB/sec (that's bytes, not bits) but then dropped and swayed between 50 and 80MB/sec. Not too shabby.

Why not 5 stars? The case is plastic. It includes some sticky felt pads with no instructions as to what these are four -- I'd imagine they are to stabilize a skinny drive in the case so it won't rattle around, but no way of knowing. But the bigger issue is heat. The shell is plastic without ventilation, and I'd expect a hard drive to get quite warm. The instructions say the drive will sleep after 10 minutes, and this might be to help protect the drive, but it really needs some kind of heat sink. This is not a problem for an SSD unless it's heavily used. And if you're archiving onto a hard drive, you might not run it long enough for overheating to be come a problem.

Finally, one warning before I go further: SSDs are NOT a good backup medium, as the cells lose their charges unless refreshed. If you back up, and put it on the shelf, don't expect your data to still be good after a year -- maybe a lot sooner.

For the price, though, it makes a bare SSD or maybe even a 2.5" hard drive that's sitting in a drawer at least a little useful.

title: had a better looking aesthetic design and (hopefully) would provide motion detection ...
text:
I had been looking for a security camera to replace the camera that my actual security camera provided to me simply because the motion detector on my security camera that they had provided did not seem to work very well. This camera promised a wider field of view, had a better looking aesthetic design and (hopefully) would provide motion detection that would actually work right when someone, or something, moved in the front of my house.

Setting up this camera, per the instructions provided (which are all pictures in lieu of words) appears to be very easy and quick and, had the process worked correctly, I'm sure would have been super easy. Well it wasn't quite that easy because I got just partially into the setup process before the entire process simply did not work for me.
To setup the camera you simply power it on by connecting the enclosed ac adapter (which has a smallish block, no need to worry about it taking up multiple slots on your power block), wait until it flashes orange, then, on your phone or tablet, download either the iOS or Android app from D-Link and start it up. It should find your camera, which mine did, right away. Then you are asked to input a short code which is provided both on the documentation for the quick install and on the camera itself. You are able to type in the code or have the camera simply snapshot it to log it in automatically.

In my case this is where it all went south. After inputting the code manually on my iPad it said that the camera was "pairing" and to wait a moment. I waited. And then I waited some more. And finally after several minutes it gave me an error that it was unable to pair. So I did this process again to no avail. I tried it a third time and this time I used the camera to take a picture of the code just to try something different. Unfortunately the result was the same. So I then switched up things and tried it on my iPhone 6 Plus. Same result. Tried again and again over the course of the next 30 minutes, all to the same error message. I then decided to go ahead and reset the camera. To do so there is a small hole on the bottom of the base in which you insert a pen and hold, the camera will then reset. I tried this and recycled the camera from power in a hard reset and still no luck.

Finally I decided to try to sign into the app using my login name and password before pairing the camera. I did this on my iPad. No change, still cannot pair the camera. I then tried logging into my account on my phone and then pairing the camera in the same manner. This worked. I have no real idea what, if anything I did. I can guess that signing into the account prior to pairing the camera assisted in some fashion but then that did not work on my iPad so I am not sure that to be the case. Honestly it just seemed as if I did it enough that eventually it worked.

This entire process took just over an hour of doing the same thing again and again and again and was fairly frustrating, I will not lie. One can only assume (hope) that this process was an exception to the norm and the actual pairing will work on the first try for most people and, if that is the case, then this camera should be very easy and simple to get it up and running.

Once I got the camera going the picture was amazing. It's also very wide, they call it 180 because that's the view that you get a full 180 degrees of view. You can also pinch zoom in to see better detail and it works really well. So the actual picture and field of view gets 5 stars.

Lastly, there is the issue of motion detection. After installing my 64gb memory card and formatting it, both of which were very easy thanks to the documentation on D-Link's site, I was ready to set the camera up in its permanent place of residence near my front door and see what, if anything, it detected and would it actually record those events in the manner in which I desired?

I'm happy to report that on this test it passed with flying colors. Any sort of motion in the front area triggers an alert to my iPad and iPhone and records a short clip of the event. The clip is also not "cut off" and by that I mean that in some cameras they get motion and start recording but they may miss some of the action because they don't backtrack to where the motion is when they record the clip.
This is not an issue with this camera. It will detect motion and the clip that is recorded does not start off AFTER the motion but actually a few second prior to it. Also, all clips recorded on to your memory care are all easily accessible for further review at any time. The older clips will be deleted as well once space becomes a premium and you will not have to do this manually (as is done on some cameras including the camera this one is replacing, this may not sound like a huge deal but trust me, it is!).

One thing of note as well, there are controls in the app to adjust the sensitivity for the motion detection. This is very important because as you may or may not know too sensitive of motion detection and you get a lot of false alerts and not sensitive enough you get no alerts. So because of this it is nice to have the ability to adjust this range. Also of note, the screen for motion detection control is sectioned off into blocks (so that you can highlight certain blocks and make them more sensitive while making other areas much less sensitive). This took a little tuning but once you get it right it makes the world of difference!

The software app provided by D-Link on iOS, works really well and is very simple to use. Again please note though that I have found no way to view your camera on a PC, right now all I have found is the app. There is only one issue with the app that I have found that is worthwhile to note and that is that when one does the live view of the camera and then zooms in that you are then unable to return to the home screen and are "stuck" in the live view. You can zoom in and out no problem but you cannot exit this screen. The only way out of it is to kill the app and restart it. I am hopeful that this is a bug in which D-Link is aware of and this will be fixed in a future update. Also, be aware there is no PC software for watching the camera from a PC, at least none that I could find. Everything software wise will be done from a phone or a tablet and not a PC.

All in all I'm very happy with this camera and plan to use it as my point of security for the front of my house going forward. The setup process was quite easy until the pairing incident and yes that was quite frustrating but once that was overcome everything else has worked quite well. I'd definitely recommend this camera to anyone looking for a very nice, quality camera with a beautiful design and a very, very wide field of view with a very nice resolution. I would also not hesitate to recommended this as a security solution as well, due to how it detects and records motion.

Check this camera out if you are in the market for a new camera!

title: ... a while but was unsure of what I would like to go with but ultimately when the opportunity came ...
text:
I had been looking to get into the speak-your-command speaker game for a while but was unsure of what I would like to go with but ultimately when the opportunity came to get the UE Blast with Alexa I jumped at the chance. While I had some experience with issuing commands to my Xbox I knew the experience of using Alexa was much better since I had set them up as gifts for relatives in the past. When I received the UE Blast it was nearly fully charged and had minimal packaging. It was ready to go out of the box but I did have to download and configure the app which was pretty easy. After linking it to my account on Amazon and establishing a bluetooth and wifi connection I was ready to test it out.

The speaker itself is quite similar in design to another speaker that my wife and I had been using for a couple of years now, that is the UE Boom. It's bigger and has better sound. I knew that our experience with the UE Boom had been a positive one, the speaker held a charge a long time, was easy to pair and had excellent sound so I held high hopes for the UE Blast. Once everything was configured the UE Blast was very easy to use by issuing Alexa commands. The toughest part is remembering the best way to address the commands, although it should be noted that Alexa doesn't require rote, specific type of commands (as the Xbox does) but through practice my wife and I have found out that it does respond to certain phrasings better than others. You also have to learn to add a slight pause after saying "Alexa" and not just start yelling out commands but that becomes second nature in practice.

I was highly disappointed to see that Alexa could not control Spotify and that Spotify would only work when using a Bluetooth command, similar in nature to the UE Boom. Spotify is my primary music source and I do not like that Amazon seems to want to steer you to their Amazon Prime Music direction. However, it should be noted that you do not have to be a subscriber to the Amazon music service to use Alexa on this device, but it will open up more music, including your own if you have a subscription to it.

I have used the speaker twice now in long sessions and the first session I got about 7 hours out of moderate listening levels which was, in my opinion, disappointing considering the speaker promises "up to 12 hours". We all know "up to" is the key there but still, roughly half of the promised amount is not what I'd consider a home run. The second time listening from a full charge we got roughly 9 hours and that is listening at moderate listening levels so that was a bit better. It honestly made me wonder if the first I was not at a complete charge. It should be noted here that the only way to know the charge level of the speaker is through the app and you will only know two levels of charge, full charge or partial charge and that is a sincere lack of information in my opinion that needs updated with a future fix for the app.

The quality of the sound of the speaker is very high for a large room and the speaker will fill the room with sound. Any larger than a large room though and the speaker will struggle but for most people volume or clarity of the music will not be any issue whatsoever. It was disappointing that I was unable to band my UE Blast to my UE Boom to create a stereo, or mirror, effect from one source. I worked on this for well over an hour before looking online and determining it simply is not possible.

So word to the wise, if you already own a UE product and are considering buying this to add on as a "stereo" effect or even just a multi-room, one source solution you will be out of luck. It remains to be seen if this will be fixed in a future update but I sincerely doubt that it will happen based upon my research.

Ultimately I do recommend this device, it's very clear, very loud, integrates Alexa commands perfectly and has decent battery life. Just be aware though that it won't control Spotify via Alexa, the battery life is not what is promised (but still good overall) and it will not pair with another UE device.
Another downside of course is the price. I am not completely sure this is a great value for most people but I will say if you have the money the device will not disappoint. For most people on a budget this would be a better value purchase on sale or at a discounted rate perhaps on Black Friday. There are certainly more reasonably priced devices that will do many of what this speaker offers. But if you want a great all-in-one solution, are aware of some of the limitations of the device and its app and are willing to pay the money you cannot beat the UE Blast.
