title: Not thrilled, but satisfied
text:
The Voyager 510 works like a charm. Connects easily and fairly quickly, I guess (my first cell phone and my first Bluetooth headset). Range is incredible, although I can't conceive any situation in which I'd need to go more than five feet away from my phone (it's usually in my pocket or on my desk). So far I've gotten great battery life. I like the blue LED.

A few downsides:

-Frequency range of the headset isn't fantastic. The sound quality of it is good, but not superb. This is more of a problem with Bluetooth than with the headset itself, though.

-Ergonomically questionable-- it fits very well once you get it on, but it's a little hard to adjust, especially when it's on your ear. It also feels very flimsy. I wouldn't mind having a little more weight so I could feel safe just putting it in my jeans pocket.

-Volume buttons and especially the power buttton are rather hard to fiddle with while it's on your ear.

title: Great multi-purpose lens
text:
This is the first lens I got for my Canon 20D. It's a great lens to start out with, as it covers a great range. 28 is pretty useful, but it's not something you can really use for actual wide-angle. Still useful for relatively close shots. 105 has proven incredibly useful for portraits, nature stuff, pretty much everything I've tried out so far. The versatility of this lens-- that it can be used close to the subject and far away-- is definitely one of its best features.

3.5/4.5 can be a bit blurry. I generally do pretty well, but I was taking some odd pictures today that didn't come out too well-- different objects at different places, which a higher f-stop would have totally solved. I think someone said in another review to go for around 8...

USM is absurdly fast. I can't get over it. (Having lived in point-and-shoot / Canon FD land before I got this camera...) Definitely don't settle for the cheaper version of this-- this lens is ergonomically and optically an excellent lens for $100 more than the cheap one. USM, great range.

title: Worth about... $8
text:
After the Apple Store told me it was "probably going to have to replace my entire screen for $1600" after my wi-fi antenna broke, I started shopping around for a cheap alternative. It's hard to argue with an $8 adapter, even if it doesn't work very well. I had some problems getting this set up because the install CD didn't work. I called 24-hour tech support and had to first negotiate some language or basic competency barriers with their tech support: "Hey, I can't use the CD to install the driver and I can't download it from the internet because my wi-fi card isn't working and therefore I can't download from the website because I have no wireless connection"-- and then they say, "Just download this driver from the internet over your wireless connection." I decided that my only option would be to use a *different* computer to download the driver and install that. Waste of time, there, but, again, eight bucks.

The wireless is fast enough, but it isn't terribly fast. The major problem is that it is horrifically unreliable-- the response time for connecting to a network and actually getting to a website, for example, is spotty and unpredictable-- it'll cut out for absolutely no reason and it frequently forgets networks or will forget a network password and then will suddenly remember. I'm not sure why this is happening. Have never heard back from their tech support. It has stopped working entirely at my house and it works at my office but is spotty-- would think it was an issue with the router but my phone and iPad work just fine.

But for $8, again, I can't *really* complain that much. On the plus side, this is a $1592 discount to replacing my entire computer-- and it DOES work, most of the time- so there's always... ALWAYS a silver lining.

title: Some advantages on the S7 and S6, but some technical-- and tech support- issues that need to be worked out
text:
I got this as a replacement for two S7 Edges that I had to return. I figured it'd make sense to try for a fancy new phone, seeing as it has been many moons since I've had an actual brand new phone. I was deciding between this and the OnePlus 5, but this came with a bunch of free stuff and I have had major issues with getting support for products that aren't sold or supported by my wireless carrier, plus the OnePlus had a couple of weird compatibility issues that I wasn't as much of fan of.

Pros and cons here:

+ Amazing camera-- performs great in low light, much faster than previous models, and some fun new features.
+ Fast processor. Fast fingerprint sensor and many more options for unlocking that I haven't tried yet.
+ Much faster startup than S7 Edge.
+ Excellent battery life. I can go through the whole day without worrying about running out of power, which is great, because now I have to buy all new freaking USB-C chargers, because capitalism.

- Bixby is truly horrendous-- would rather not have anything at all than a built-in personal assistant that is completely useless, doesn't understand basic speech, and can't really do anything. "Bixby, is there a hardware store around here?" "Let me see... do you want to call John Doe?" Made worse by the fact that Samsung has attempted to needlessly gamify the Bixby concept, so you get experience points when you talk to it.
- Samsung tells me that the voice-to-text that they use in the Samsung keyboard is the same as the Bixby voice recognition, which is effectively useless. It misses every other word and mistranslates most words. I had very few issues with my S6, S7, or BlackBerry Q10 before that.
- Fingerprint sensor is mildly frustrating on the back but you do get used to it.
- Lack of a home key is sometimes unreliable for full-screen applications.
- Some issues with unreliable full-screen/split-screen performance within specific software. I've had this issue only with YouTube and Google Maps, but it's frustrating.
- Battery, while taking a long time to get to 5%, will die almost immediately as soon as it hits, say, 3 or 4%. I know this is a question of software rather than hardware as far as how they display it, but my S6 and S7 were much more accurate in terms of how much life was actually left. It is the difference between having to run to a charger to ensure that your phone doesn't turn off in the middle of doing something and, well, keeping it on.
- Takes FOREVER to charge with the OEM charger-- a couple of hours to a full charge and no quick charging on the factory OEM charger. Sometimes won't charge at all with lower-ampacity chargers, which is an obnoxious design flaw of planned obsolescence slash idiocy.
- Some software issues that I didn't have on the S7 and S6 including with Netflix, some radio streaming apps, Facebook, and odds and ends with a couple of other things. I'm used to these things taking several months to get resolved.
- I've had some charging issues that no one, including Samsung, Amazon, or T-Mobile, will propose resolving other than to replace my device. This is the third replacement phone I've tried to get for my S6 Edge, whose battery life started to wane to the point of being totally unusable after a couple of years. It's extremely frustrating to deal with this.

I will revise my review in another couple of months-- will see how it goes.

title: Durable, waterproof, and pretty ergonomic-- very few complaints
text:
I wanted to wait until I had put this through the wringer before writing a review. It has survived several intensive trips, so now I am ready to tell all.

I spent a lot of time shopping around for a bag. I do a lot of traveling and I do a lot of photography, but I also enjoy the ability to stuff as much stuff as possible into my bag. I looked at bags by Peak, which I loved online but didn't love them as much in person because they had a weird clip and the fabric seemed kind of weird. I also looked at Lowepro. They were ugly but functional and got good reviews. I also looked at Vanguard but I opted against them because I couldn't tell how big their bags actually were, given that there was a huge range and some of them seemed outlandishly enormous, but they all look the same in photos. Finally, I looked at a bunch of Brand X ones on Amazon. I don't mess with the "straight-from-China" products most of the time because it's nearly impossible to get warranty or support issues settled, and Amazon has taken to giving me grief when I raise questions about warranty issues. But this one got good reviews and the price was right.

Ergonomics: The bag is fairly comfortable even with a heavy load, though it doesn't have the featherlight feel on your back that my Ortlieb Packman 2 does. It still has a bunch of great straps that allow you to tie down a tripod or attach whatever else you want, perhaps a jacket, sleeping bag, drone, I dunno. The straps feel quite durable. When the top is really full, it is impossible to close the strap, and I read this complaint in another review. My solution is to not pack it quite as full. You can't exactly go grocery shopping with this bag. There is an EXCELLENT feature that lets you unzip the rolltop section without unrolling it. This my Ortlieb does NOT have, and it is an amazing feature for things like a sunglasses case or a jacket that you need to quickly extract but don't want to unroll the top. The clip is pretty heavy-duty steel, and has a magnet.

Space: The camera case itself fits my 6D II with any lens on it. It does not, however, fit all of my lenses, and the divider isn't really that functional. That's fine, because it can fit what I need, and anything else I can fit in the top rolly part. Fully stocked, I can fit the camera, three lenses, a laptop, Kindle, small notebook, microphone, packable jacket, tripod, filters, batteries, and a water bottle. It *may not fit* under seats in commercial airliners when full, but only barely if it doesn't fit.

Water resistance: So far, so good-- survived a rainstorm in New Orleans and one in LA and a snowstorm in Michigan.

Complaints: The laptop sleeve *barely* fits my 2012 MacBook Pro, and it feels as though I have to squeeze it in when the rest of the bag is full. There is also a quirk with the top pack portion where when you put stuff in it, it can get smooshed down in between the compartments, so it's actually possible to lose stuff inside the bag. Plan ahead and this is far less likely to happen. The sort of tote strappies on the top velcro together and they're very nice, but I am unconvinced they will hold up terribly well over time. We will see!

title: Flawless setup, super reliable, until...
text:
We bought this to replace a single router that we were using for a large (5br) house where it's five of us with pretty heavy internet demands (work-from-home, gaming, streaming, as we millennials do). The single router was also not cutting it given the heavy masonry walls and the like, which seriously block signals in some spots. With this, we have the devices placed in a sort of zigzag on the first, second, and third floors. They are fast (400+Mbps), and the signals are generally way better than the built-in router in the C*mc*st modumb-- we can typically get signal in the front yard and about half of the back yard, through foot-thick brick walls and stuff.

The setup was super easy and everything was hummin', working flawlessly for about a year, at which time things decided to start going wrong. Basically we lose internet connectivity for a split second, but it happens on everyone's devices, whether phones, Macs, or PCs. The internet will drop out and then come right back. It's not an ISP issue because it's the wi-fi signal itself. The diagnostics do not show anything wrong. It doesn't make the internet unusable, but it does happen about an average of once per day per device, which is especially problematic when we're using things like VPN's that then drop and have to reconnect (logins, etc.).

Google is not able to be reached by phone, and when I wrote to the e-mail form they provide on their website, it got bounced back. Not really sure how a trillion dollar company can be that completely incompetent.

text:
I have now owned this lens for a while and have come back to upgrade my review but leave some drawbacks so other shoppers will be aware.

The good points of this lens, that made me keep it instead of return it, are the unusual qualities it has to go macro on the one end of the range, and zoom to a virtual wide angle at the other extreme. These two views broaden my ability as photographer in ways that none of my other lenses do. I hardly ever use the middle of this lens. I grab it for the big wide picture, or the super close up shot. Anything in the middle, I'd rather use my 50mm prime lens.

I really wanted a macro for close up flower photography, I maybe should have looked at a few other options. This does do macro but I could have gotten even more zoom with another lens choice. At least it lets me get close. I can put the lens as close as I want to the flower or object. It is great in autofocus or manual. It produces nice pictures as long as, and only if, there is a lot of light. Otherwise you'll get a big shadow from where the flash on your camera couldn't reach over the lens in it's way. I read about this but didn't think it would happen to me. Think again. You'll need to use your extra attaching flash or get more light. So basically I end up only doing macro photos outside or in bright light.

Reading the reviews got me excited for this lens. I started thinking I didn't really need a prime, or a dedicated macro lens, because here was this great lens that could offer other shots too. Everyone seemed to say it was so sharp and so great. Don't be too gullible. It's very slow. That means blurry pictures or no action shots or no twilight shots. If you already have a prime lens, fine. But don't cheat yourself thinking this thing can do it all.

Probably the reason I kept it, aside from the fun of the macro being alright, is the wide angle side. I use it more than I expected. Especially if I tilt the camera down, it creates almost an arc view that a true wide angle lens can produce. I like it so much that I plan to buy a dedicated wide angle prime lens next time I buy a lens.

If you are not looking to replace your kit lens with a better "everything" lens, this might be great for you. But if you really wish you had a macro and you feel you might get something extra here, it might be better to focus on your main priority.

Get a filter. I figured I'd order one later or pick it up at the shop. Local shop was a lot more. Now I have to order one. Should have just done it at the same time.

I do like the lens and I never use my kit lens anymore. But I would never in a million years trade my 50mm prime lens for this. I only like it since I have both (not to mention others).

title: great camera for a great price
text:
I ordered this backup camera and monitor for my 05 Silverado. Running the camera feed cable from the rear of the truck into the cab was a bit tricky, but any backup system would offer the same challenge. I have waited a couple months before reviewing this to be sure it would last. So far, everything is still working just fine. I like how the camera itself can swivel up or down for tuning to your personal needs. I pull a boat and this makes it very easy to back up right to the trailer. I simply angle the cam down so I have a clear close view of the hitch and can back up to the perfect spot every time.

Another cool feature is that there are 2 video inputs. One is dedicated to the rear camera and the other is an aux input. You can feed any other video source into the aux input and it will display all the time except when the vehicle is put into reverse. As soon as you take the vehicle out of reverse, the display automatically switches back to aux input. You have the flexibility of installing a second camera somewhere else on the vehicle to allow a view all the time except when in reverse.

The display will show the rear camera only when you are in reverse or rather when the rear backup lights power on the camera. In other words, anytime the camera is powered on, the display will show it. So I decided to run another switched 12v power feed to the camera that I can turn on whenever I want to from within the cab. Sometimes its nice to be able to see what's behind you without having to put it in reverse.

The only, and I mean the only, bad thing I can say about this unit is that the pedestal for the monitor is limited in its range of motion but probably ok for most installations. But the real problem is that the 3M tape used to mount the monitor to the dash (or where ever you chose) just doesn't hold up. When I finished my installation, everything looked great and no cables or wires were visible and the monitor was mounted to the face of the dash below the heater controls. When I returned to the truck about 2 hours later to leave, the monitor was hanging by the cable because the double sided tape just wasn't strong enough to stick. (And yes, I cleaned the dash thoroughly with alcohol before applying the adhesive tape) I eventually had to drill 2 small holes and screw it to the underside of my dash near the floor. Its still easy to see and has some range of motion, but I just hated drilling 2 tiny holes in my dash, even though they wouldn't be visible if I removed the monitor. At least I know now that I won't find my monitor hanging by the cable when I get into my truck.

The unit as a whole is working great and provides me that extra sense of security knowing I won't back over one of the kid's bikes or worse, a kid. Don't be discouraged by anyone who gives this item a bad review simple because they had difficulty installing it. Any system you buy will come with the same challenges. For vehicles that do not have factory backup cameras, I definitely recommend this system

title: Not what I expected
text: This was my first action cam purchase. I bought it to mount in a gimbal on my drone. The main reason I bought it, other than price, was the video out feature so I could use it for FPV. That's where the frustration began.  If you mount it right side up, the micro USB port for video out is inaccessible due to its location in the gimbal. So I had to mount it upside down to put the video out port away from the gimbal support. Then I had to go in the camera menu and rotate the picture 180deg. So far so good. Now, to get video out to the video transmitter, you must go in to the menu and turn on "Tv out ON".The problem with doing this is that once it's mounted in the gimbal, you can't access the menu because you can't see the screen. So that would mean disassembling the camera support and removing the camera to turn on video out before every flight. Another thing, when you turn " tv out" to ON, the only button that works is record (OK button), and there is no way to return to the menu after that. Your only option is to stop recording and power down the camera and turn it back on. Then if you want to turn "tv out" back on again, you have to remove it from the gimbal all over again. I was hoping the wifi app would allow me to turn "tv out" on from there so I wouldn't have to remove it from the gimbal, but it's not even an option from the wifi app. Also , there is no option to simply leave  "tv out " turned on all the time. So every time you power it up, you must remove it from the gimbal and go thru the menu to turn it back on. This camera would have been a good buy, except for this feature. I have a couple 808 cams and they feed video out all the time. I guess I assumed this would do the same. Lastly , when I loaded the wifi app, it wouldn't connect. Tried over and over. Finally removed the app and reloaded it again . I finally got it to connect. I was really disappointed that the app has so few menu options. It's basically just good for viewing what the camera is seeing. Overall, this is not an ideal action camera for drone use with a gimbal. Way too many obstacles to make this worth while.

title: Update -- Recent updates have made it much better
text:
It is close to being a good computer, but I think it needs one more generation to work the kinks out. First off, let me say that I am a professional software engineer and computer expert, so my experience likely isn't user error. So with that said, this is what I think. Any one of these items probably would not be enough to disqualify the laptop, but all combined, it is not an experience up to my expectations.
- When I first got the laptop about three weeks ago, it wouldn't recognize the wifi card. All I had done to that point is go through the Windows setup screens and set the timezone, my user name, etc. So literally 5 minutes into the experience. I had to go into the system properties, disable the wifi card, and then re-enable it. Very strange. It has worked fine since then but it was not a great start.
- A couple of times during system reboots for Windows updates, software installs, or whatever, there is a BIOS message saying the hard drive couldn't be found. It does proceed to boot up normally, but again -- no warm and fuzzies from the messages.
- The screen resolution is super high, which could be a good thing. Unlike MacBook Retinas, you can put the laptop into "native" resolution without third party utilities. Of course, on a screen of this size, using native resolution isn't very desirable unless you have terrific eyes. The reason I mention this is because instead of just changing the laptop to different resolutions, it seems to want you to leave it at native resolution and just adjust the text size percentage (to 130% instead of 100% or whatever). If you change actual screen resolutions, it gives a warning message and doesn't look so great. This may be a Windows 10 "feature" instead of an issue with the laptop. It's just a little weird and hard to find the right setting.
- The battery life is inconsistent. I have very few applications installed, have just a few open, and use it 100% for programming, so just text editors and browser open. I don't keep the screen at 100% brightness. Sometimes the battery will last for 7 or 8 hours, and other times it will last for just 4 or 5. Again -- not sure if Windows 10 or Dell issue, but I shouldn't have to spend time researching and trying to figure it out. It should just work.
- The touchpad is nice but inconsistent. Sometimes two finger scrolling works, sometimes it doesn't. Sometimes tapping on the touch pad works for clicking, other times I have to do a full press of the touch pad to register a click. Is it Windows or Dell? Not sure.
- The standby mode is horrible. This is the final straw for me deciding to return it. I should be able to close the lid and have it go to sleep. Then when I come back, it should wake up right where I left off with minimal battery drain. Preface this with the fact that I did ensure that my settings for closing the lid and power button are set correctly in the control panel. At first, the behavior was wildly inconsistent. I would shut the lid and sometimes it would sleep, sometimes it would appear that it had rebooted, and another time the battery was completely dead as if it never went to sleep. So I modified my own behavior to press the power button, watch it go to sleep, and then shut the lid. I could have lived with this inconvenience, but it didn't really help. I started to encounter these issues:
* When the computer comes back from sleep, all of my windows get stacked in the upper left of the desktop. I have to resize and drag them all back into place every time I wake it up. Annoying. I did Google this and it could be Windows 10. It might be resetting the resolution every time it wakes up, which moves the windows to the upper left.
* Standby is not instantaneous to come back on. It first spins on the Dell BIOS screen for several seconds. When it does come back, sometimes as many as 15 seconds later (this doesn't sound like a lot but it is if you are sitting there and expecting it to come back from standby), sometimes all of my windows will be gone as if it rebooted without telling me.
* The battery life is really bad in standby. I have a 4 year old Vaio Z this is supposed to be replacing, and it could go for days in standby. This computer sucks 50% a day. Today was the worst -- it's a Monday as I write this review. I had the laptop plugged in, asleep and fully charged on Saturday. I unplugged it and put it directly into my bag. I did not use it Sunday. This morning I went to turn it on and it's stone dead out of power and my charger is at home so it's a brick for the day.

So the bottom line is I own the old Vaio Z and a 15" Macbook Pro Retina (almost 3 years old). I don't want to compare too much to the Mac for fear of being labeled some kind of Mac fanboy. But the experience with this particular computer isn't even close to the Vaio -- even in its old age -- never mind the Mac. I will be keeping the Vaio for a while longer and waiting for something better to come along.

-- UPDATE Feb 2016 --
I updated the BIOS and the drivers. There were also some Windows 10 updates that came out. The laptop is working much better, including the standby battery life being mostly fixed, so I upped my rating to four stars and have decided to keep it. It's too bad these updates weren't available for launch.

-- UPDATE Aug 2016 --
The laptop overall is good, not great. It's definitely worlds better than when I bought it, but there is still funky behavior with the standby mode (it takes many seconds and shows the BIOS screen to come out of standby instead of just turning on). There have also been times when it seems to turn itself back on even with the lid closed inside of the sleeve/case, so it gets burning hot and the battery drains. I spent too long trying to research this one and turned off every possible setting it could be. This hasn't happened in a couple of months so maybe they have fixed it.

So overall a 4 star rating.

title: Excellent all around earbuds
text:
Received my AirPods Pro a couple of days ago and have been using them day and night since. I also have the new Bose 700's, which I've been using daily for a couple of months so I'll compare to them.

I commute each day on a noisy city bus. Sometimes there are people talking and sometimes there's nothing but the loud noises of the bus. The Bose headphones are not sweat or weatherproof, and so are not useful outside unless the skies are clear. With winter coming, the Bose also prevent wearing a winter hat, so I decided to buy the Air Pods for use in commuting and then use the Bose once I get to my desk at work.

I have never owned AirPods before. A friend at work has regular AirPods (not Pro), and the photo attached to my review shows the difference in size. These were easy to set up -- you just hold your unlocked iPhone a couple inches away from the AirPods in their charging case (with the case open). It's all seamless. They automatically showed up in my Macbook bluetooth menu once connected with the iPhone, so all I had to do was click "connect" in the bluetooth menu.

Interestingly, the play/pause squeeze of the stem doesn't seem to work for controlling the laptop -- maybe it only works for Apple Music, which I don't use so I didn't test. And the other thing different -- and worse -- than the Bose is that if I pause on the laptop and then play again on the phone, the AirPods are not automatically connected and the music came out of the phone directly. The Bose connects to two devices at once so it will play whichever one is playing sounds (which can be annoying if the phone is playing and the computer gives a notification sound or vice versa). But in order to play again on the phone, I had to go into the phone Bluetooth menu and reconnect (not re-pair, just reconnect). So my conclusion is you have to manually reconnect for device switching. You get a little alert sound when connected -- no voice, no battery status, no "connected to xxx" like the Bose does -- nothing else.

For music quality, the Bose quality is a fair amount better -- which would be expected since they are full size over the ear headphones. The AirPods Pro are still very good though, and unless you are an audiophile, you won't be disappointed.

Charging the AirPods case uses a standard iPhone/iPad lightning charger. It comes with a cable that will connect to a later model Macbook USB C port -- so USB C to lightning. If you want to use an outlet, you will need to have an existing lightning charger, which most of us have plenty of anyway. It's hard to tell when the case is completely charged. The orange light comes on but goes off after just a few seconds, instead of just staying on and changing to green once they're fully charged. The first night I got them, I charged them in the case overnight before using them. When I connected them, they said the AirPods were only 58% charged, so I'm not sure why they weren't 100% if left in there overnight.

There is a nice new longpress feature on the volume of the iPhone that appears when the AirPods are connected to the iPhone. You can control the volume (you can't control the volume right on the AirPods, which is a slight bummer but it's okay) and noise cancelling from this new interface.

There's no tapping on these AirPods -- you slightly squeeze the little stem. There is a soft click when it registers, almost like pressing a touch pad. It took a few seconds to figure out how to do it, but it's been fine since. A longer squeeze toggles between the noise cancellation modes. There's a slightly different sound for going into transparency mode and going into noise cancellation mode, but in a quiet room it's hard to tell which mode you're in, as opposed to the Bose, which literally tells you in a voice.

Transparency mode uses microphones to let in the sound around you, so that you can keep them in while still talking to people. This is how they differ from noise isolating earbuds, which block your ear from hearing anything but don't have active noise canceling. These have noise canceling I'll talk about in a minute. But there is also an "off" mode available only (that I've found) through the volume long press described above. These just put them in basic noise isolation mode -- I'm guessing similar to previous AirPods.

For noise cancellation, they are surprisingly very effective. More effective than I thought they would be. They are best at blocking out white noise -- bus engines, office sounds, fans, etc. They are good at voices if it's just people talking in a group at a normal volume. But when I walked through the busy office cafeteria at lunch time, they did not do as good of a job as the Bose at blocking out the loud talking and other uneven cafeteria noises. Interestingly, they do a great job at blocking one-off noises like a door slamming or someone dropping something. The Bose have a hard time with sounds like that for some reason. I would say they are 80-90% as effective as the full size over ear Bose overall, which is very impressive.

For comfort, obviously the Bose are better (and sound better) for hours of desk usage, and also given that the battery on the Bose is about 19 hours and these are about 4, the Bose will be what I use all day at my desk. But for moving around, walking the dogs, commuting, and portability, the AirPods are terrific and don't hurt at all or cause my ears to sweat like the Bose do after a while.

Would definitely recommend.

title: Good features and good value
text:
I use Powerbeats every day for walking the dog, listening to podcasts around the house, etc, so I am very familiar with them. Even though these headphones are 10x cheaper, I'm going to compare them so you can tell what you'll be missing between these and high end headphones in the same category.

First, these headphones didn't include extra ear bud sizes or a USB C charging cable, even though the description said they would. Maybe I got someone else's return. But that forced me to find a charging cable that worked, and unfortunately it revealed something I didn't like. I tried using a standard phone USB C wall charger, 20W or 30W. It would not charge these. Then, I tried a Macbook Air USB C charger and that would not work either. I remembered a flashlight I bought that only worked with a super low power charger, like plugged into the side of a computer or into a USB lamp or something. This worked with that. So it reduces the flexibility or using these.

The other thing that stuck out right away was how long they are. You can see in the photo these headphones compared to the powerbeats. And they have a wire that won't completely straighten out even after a few days. This is something that can be overlooked for the price.

The ear hooks are large and part that goes across your ear is bulbous and not super attractive, but if you are just wearing them around the house or on a dog walk who cares.

Pairing the headphones was easy, but it would not be easy to re-pair them with another device as you have to hold down the power button for longer than it takes to pair them to turn them off. It would be a pain to switch back and forth. So one device for these.

Mine came only with the small size ear tips, so the sound was tinny. I listened to some different songs on Spotify and switched back and forth with the Powerbeats to compare. Then I found some extra ear tips from other earphones and fortunately they fit on these, so I was able to fit them properly. Once I did that, I was very impressed with the sound. They sounded nearly as full as the Powerbeats, and for podcasts I could barely tell the difference.

These of course don't have all of the phone/text announcement functionality of the Powerbeats, but there is a lady's voice with a thick accent that reads incoming phone numbers to you on a call. Call quality is good with no complaints from anyone I talked to.

One thing I liked more than the Powerbeats is I could go forward or back 30 seconds in my podcasts by holding the volume up or down for a second rather than double clicking on the Powerbeats. Double clicking doesn't always work right and this was more reliable (although it is hard to tell at first which side of the controller has the volume/play buttons with your fingers without looking as 3 sides of the controller have texture on them)

I wish the wire was a little different and the way you turn them off and on was a little different (it's not easy to turn them off as you have to watch the tiny little light carefully) but overall for 1/10 the price of Powerbeats, these are a great bargain.

title: Great for the money but have limitations
text:
It almost goes without saying that earbuds this inexpensive would have limitations, but I will lay out what I found and you can decide if the tradeoffs are worth it.

- Pairing -- was mostly easy except it took a couple of tries as the instructions didn't work the way they said for me. It's also a little lame that the name of these are "Earbuds" in the bluetooth list. Would have been nice to get something more specific.
- Looks and fit -- the earbuds are not labeled L & R from what I could see and I looked several times, so you have to remember which one is left and right when you take them out of the case. Once in the correct ear, they fit well and stay in seemingly as well as Airpods do. They look good enough to wear around also. They have a little "o" on the stems that looks like the Oakley brand, but it's really just an outline of the microphone. I wore them for several long walks and kept them in my ears for an hour or two at a time and aside from not being to hear anything or anyone (see below), they were never uncomfortable.
- "Noise Cancelling" -- not sure if they are just talking about noise cancelling for the microphone, as the only noise cancellation these have is by blocking your ear so you can't hear people and things around you very well. There's no noise cancellation to turn on and off. I don't really like not being able to hear when I take my dogs for walks, so I didn't like this.
- Sound quality -- this is probably the best part of these. I played various genres of music and listened to some podcasts and all sounded pretty much as good as the expensive Beats Fit Pro I have.
- Controls -- This is another weak spot. You have to single, double, or even triple click the top of the stems to do things, and the triple click to change volume was very hard to make work regularly. I would end up skipping forward or skipping to the next song (double click) and pausing (single click) with my three clicks as my finger tended to stick to the stem during clicks. I also inadvertently made songs pause when routinely adjusting them in my ears as a click would register. The stem squeezing of Airpods is much better, but then again those have no volume control and these do if you can get it to work.
- Call quality -- I made several phone calls on these and people said I sounded fine and couldn't hear my environment. I could hear others fine as well, so this is a strong point.

Overall, I would recommend these if you don't care if outside noises get blocked out and you only need to play and pause, or occasionally skip forward or back. If you are on a tight budget, or, as someone else said, you want a backup set of earbuds, these would make a great choice.

title: Connected to Firecube and Xbox Series X
text:
This is a great monitor for the money. I looked at it a few months ago and didn't get it, but then when the price dropped $200 I went for it.

I wanted a monitor that supports HDMI 2.1 for all of the Xbox latest generation video compatibility, but also have an Amazon FireCube and wanted to switch back and forth to stream shows at my desk. This monitor works great with the Xbox, and after some tweaking, great with the FireCube as well.

-- Whatever you plug into HDMI 1 will be the default when you turn it on, no matter what it was on before, so you have to fiddle with the little joystick in back to change inputs quite a bit if you don't have your most frequently used device on HDMI 1. This is a pain.
-- There is no easy way that I can see to tell if it's on or off other than the screen being slightly lit. Sometimes it's hard to see that, and I have turned it off when it's already on before. A little LED light on the bottom of the bezel like most other monitors would have been nice.
-- When I first hooked up the FireCube, it would not run 4K and switched back to 1080p HD. It gave a message that the monitor does not support HDCP 2.2, which is apparently some type of copy protection. I did happen to have an HDMI audio extractor on hand so I could route audio out of my previous speaker-free monitor: "J-Tech Digital 4K 60HZ HDMI Audio Extractor Converter SPDIF". When I hooked up this device, I was able to get 4K UHD on the streaming services, and it looks as good as it gets.
-- There are so many settings within the menus and I have not messed around with them because I'm not sure what they all do. I have it mostly at the default settings and it still looks great, but I'm sure I can get it better if I take some time and figure out the settings.
-- Gaming on it is amazing. I've been playing the new Call of Duty and it looks terrific.
-- I like how I can output audio from the monitor's headphone jack to my desktop speakers and it will play the audio of the currently selected input. Coming from a sound-free monitor, it's a nice feature.
-- My previous monitor was 24" and with the thin bezel, this monitor is not much larger, so that's a plus.

Overall, I'd highly recommend this monitor, especially at this price point.

title: Definitely does what it is supposed to do
text:
TL;DR -- As you can see in the photo, this thing really works. All of those wires were previously either on my desk or hanging down randomly with me trying to avoid hitting them with my feet.

This under desk organizer will take some time to put together and get your wires on, but it is worth it. At first I assembled it with the little grabbers facing the wrong way, but fortunately I hadn't fully tightened all of the screws yet. I did need a good screwdriver to get the screws tightened, but once they were on there was no budging or wiggling at all of the parts. They feel very sturdy.

Then I cleared everything off of my desk and looked at it as a good opportunity to wipe down my desk, move it away from the wall, and clean the floor too. So this item is a good excuse to start fresh and clean.

The hardest part of the install was screwing the little vice things tight enough so they'd be super firm on the desk. I used an adjustable wrench for this, and due to the lack of a good angle, it took a few minutes as I could only turn them a quarter turn at a time. But it felt so tight that it could have been built into the desk.

I snaked my rather large power strip onto it, and then my ethernet switch. One by one, I then put the power cords, network cables, and excess wires from the HDMI cords onto it. One cool unexpected thing is that it comes with a lot of velcro cord wraps, so you can get just the length of wire you need, then roll up the rest with a cord wrap and stick it on the holder.

One time, I kind of forgot I was on a not completely stable surface and pressed hard on a power cord to plug it in. As I felt the under desk organizer start to bend, I cursed and thought all of my work would collapse. But it held fine and I braced the organizer with one hand and plugged in with the other.

Now I have an organized and clean desk. With how high it is on the back underside of the desk, there's no real way to accidentally knock the organizer around. It is sturdy enough to hold a lot of stuff, including my power strip, so the people who said it's flimsy either didn't really try it or didn't install it correctly. Although, I probably wouldn't put a powerstrip with battery backup in it as those might actually be too heavy.

I would highly recommend this item -- it's a great value.

title: Good, but unfortunately not great
text:
First, these sound great, as expected from the product write-up. They're not exaggerating.

There's an app you can download to adjust some things, and I tried configuring things via the app. The app connected perfectly with my already-paired earbuds, but there were a couple of things I don't know what they meant, including a hearing test with no indication as to how it modified any settings. It is nice that they made an app, though.

I also like how they have a button on the case for pairing, rather than just opening the case or other methods. It makes it so you can pair them to other devices. I have a couple pairs of earbuds I don't use anymore, but I'm not sure how to reset them or pair them with another device, so I can't give them to anyone either. These come with instructions on how to factory reset right in the manual.

I tested them with various genres of music, and they sound great, as mentioned above. I also tested them with podcasts, and they were crisp and clear.

During this testing, I noticed they weren't fitting tightly or very comfortably, and that's where things started to go down a bit.

I decided to try them for a couple of dog walks. I take fairly long walks at night and need reliable and comfortable earbuds. These felt like they were going to fall out -- they never did, but they felt like they were about to -- which was not ideal and made me nervous about losing one in the dark.

To add to this issue, there are touch controls on the top of each earbud, not buttons, on these. So every time I went to adjust them, I'd instead turn up the volume, turn down the volume, skip a track, or even put them into "game mode" somehow. I tried to adjust them by just moving the stalk, but it was hard to get them in place.

Airpods fit me fine, and with earbuds that have the adjustable tips, I take a standard medium size, so I like to think my ears aren't too strangely shaped.

So my final verdict is that if you are going to be using these just sitting at a desk or not moving around much, they are great and sound terrific. But they may not be the best choice for outdoor activities due to the touch controls and lack of ability to fine tune the fit.

title: Quickly becoming my favorites
text:
These headphones are so light and comfortable. And they sound great.

They come in nice high quality packaging, and although I'm not so sure Monster is the same premium brand it used to be, these are as good as much more expensive headphones.

They charge with a proprietary magnetic charger, which is not ideal since it's another wire to carry when traveling and to make sure you don't lose.

Once charged, they pair super easily once they power on the first time. They are super light, are easy to put on, and have an unusual bendy wire to connect the two ear pieces rather than a floppy wire like most one piece headphones.

They fit easily over my ears and required very little adjustment. I then played some music on my phone and the sound is so good. Unlike regular ear buds or in ear headphones, these don't actually go in your ear. They seem to just be tiny speakers and the wire just holds them in place about 1/4" from your ears. You can see in the photos I took that they are actually flat on the part near the ear, and there's no need for any type of different size tips or fitting.

Unfortunately, there is something not very good about them, and it's the tiny and awkward control buttons. There are two buttons with several things you can do with each. One button is for power off/on, volume up, play/pause, fast forward, and answering calls. The other is for volume down, rewind, and hang up. Various combinations of long press or single, double or even triple clicking the buttons do things.

The problem is the location and size of the buttons. I could only use my fingernail to press the main button when they were on, and the second button is on the curved part of the ear piece and is super hard to find while on the move, nevermind get enough leverage on it to press. I did get it so I could turn the volume up or play/pause when I wanted to, but skipping commercials in podcasts -- forget it. I had to pull my phone out of my pocket and control the player right on the phone.

As I said, the sound quality is really good for music or listening to podcasts, and the comfort level can't be beat, even wearing glasses. I wore them pretty much all day for a couple of days including on walks, to the grocery store, or just working at my desk. I like how I can hear the outside environment during use. I don't personally like earphones that block all noise by blocking your ear. At no point did my ear get sore or did anything dig in to my skin, like many other inexpensive headphones do after a while.

Despite the awkward controls, I still give these 5 stars and would highly recommend them.

title: Good USB C Docking station... But nothing amazing
text:
This is the fifth USB C docking station I have tried out and am reviewing. I've tried ones with ethernet, ones without. Ones meant for multiple monitors, and ones with a single HDMI. Some of them have 3 or 4 USB ports, some have 2. The point is, there are a lot of different combinations of ports and features on these docking stations.

What is similar, though, is the underlying functionality. All of them regardless of the price, have worked well as a power passthrough and have connected easily to two different Windows laptops I've used for testing -- a Dell Latitude 5500 series, and a Lenovo 13" laptop. I have not tested on Mac.

This particular unit has lots of different ports, and what seems to increase the price over others is the inclusion of two HDMI ports and a DisplayPort, instead of just one HDMI port on more inexpensive models from different brands. It also has two USB 2.0 ports and a USB 3.1 port and an extra USB C port, aside from the USB C power input port.

There is no indicator light on this hub for power, but there are the little blinking lights on the ethernet port. The lack of a power indicator light is a minor disappointment as that's a feature that appears on much cheaper models.

I tested most of the ports and they all work fine, with the exception of the Micro SD. The port has the nice "spring" feature where you push it in and it springs to click in, and the push again to pop out. But I had a hard time getting my card to click in, and then I got nervous when I could not get my card to push in to spring out. It took several tries for each, and I wouldn't trust it for a card I needed to put in and out a lot. While it was in, the data read fine though.

My laptop seems to have only a DP 1.2 USB C port, so I was only able to power a single 4K monitor at 4K resolution. Once I connected a second monitor, they both downscaled in resolution.

The bottom line for this is if you need all of the extra ports and have a DP 1.4 USB C on your laptop, then this would be a great docking station for you. But if you do not have 1.4, or do not need all of the ports, then much cheaper docking stations will do the exact same thing, take up less room on your desk, and save you some money in the process.

title: It's nice but not flawless
text:
I spent a few days testing this before writing a review. It seems like the "slim wallet" package is the card, along with a wallet with their logo on it. So you could always just buy the card and put it in your own wallet if you like the wallet you have.

The wallet they provide has a tight fitting pocket for the tracking card, which makes it hard to take the card in and out for charging. But I figured out how to press the button on the card through the wallet, so I don't have to take the card out often.

The credit card slots are too tight for my liking. It was hard to get my credit card out at a restaurant. I have a single card in each of the 6 slots -- I'm not doubling up cards. I'm hoping it loosens up over time, but so far, not ideal.

The card comes with a proprietary magnetic charger. One end is the magnet charging part, and the other is USB A, for use in any charger. The charger has a nice little green light on it, and the card charged up pretty quickly. The battery life of the card is good, with the app still showing a full charge a few days later.

Speaking of app, they make you download their app to pair with the card and track your card/wallet. I created an account pretty easily and pairing was easy too. They make you name your card but I'm not sure why and it didn't really explain. Maybe there's people with a lot of these cards. I just named it after my dog.

Once you get past that, you're kind of on your own to figure out how it works and what you are supposed to do. The instructions get you through the pairing process and provide a QR code for more info that didn't really lead to anything useful.

I figured out you can make the card beep from the app if you want to know where it is -- providing it's within bluetooth range of your phone. It's really loud, and works similarly to Find Your Phone functions for iPhones. My started beeping instantly each time I tested, and I had to acknowledge by pressing the button on the card (through the wallet as I couldn't get the card out easily) and then press the little pulsing alarm thing in the app. The app didn't seem to know that I had already cleared the alarm.

You can also double click the button on the card to beep your phone if you have your wallet but not your phone. That also beeped my Apple Watch, and I had to acknowledge it on both my watch and phone.

The app shows you a number of bars depending on how close your phone is to your wallet. At times, the wallet blocked bluetooth signals enough to keep all bars from turning on even when the wallet was directly next to the phone. It seems to take between 10-20 seconds for the bars to update. I experimented on the large floor in my office building and walked or ran away from the wallet. After 15 seconds or so, the number of bars would reduce. Then I would walk slowly toward the wallet and see if I could use the app as a "you're getting warmer" or "you're getting colder" tool. It updates too slow for that, and there's no indication of which direction the card is in, so the signal strength bars aren't as useful for finding your wallet.

In the app, it shows the "history" of your card, with various connection and disconnection times. But even when I was 35 miles away from home at the office, the history still showed my home address, so not sure that's so helpful.

There is also a map view, but that probably just uses the GPS from your phone. The product description mentions crowd-sourced location capabilities when the card is outside of bluetooth range, but there must not be enough people with the app near my home or office as when I went away from these places by even 1/2 mile and left my wallet behind, it did not update the location.

I would say this is a good device for finding your wallet within bluetooth range of your phone, but I'm not so sure it would help too much if your wallet gets stolen by someone or lost at some mall, unless you can go back and track it down with the help of the app before someone swipes it.

I'd also say you might be better off with just the card and getting a wallet of your choice. You'd still be able to use their app and all functionality.

title: Really good -- they check every box
text:
I've tested and reviewed no less than 10 different pairs of earbuds and headphones. Most of them are good at some things, but then have some issues that prevent them from becoming my every day favorites.

They have a rocker switch for volume up/down. They also have a separate clickable button for play/pause/answer call. I like this separate button. All controls are repeated on both earbuds, so you can use your left or right hand to control them. This proved to be helpful when I was walking the dogs.

When I put on a podcast, it sounded perfectly fine. The volume rocker switch doubles as fast-forward/rewind, making it easy to skip over podcast commercials, although it took some practice to figure out how long to hold the volume up button to fast forward without turning the volume up.

I have walked about 5 miles in these, including in a rain storm, and I am pleased at how I can still hear the outside environment. I was also happy that there was no discomfort or digging into my ears or skin after extended wear like some other units I've tested. I also wore them around the house even with nothing playing and at times I forgot I had them on.

Phone calls worked fine, and I asked people on the other end if they sounded okay. No complaints.

So far, there are only two minor things I wish were different. The first is there is no way to turn them on or off outside of the charging case. Sometimes I just want to wear them for a short time, take them off, turn them off, then turn them on and put them on an hour later. But I have to carry the case around for this.

Speaking of the case, there's no indicator on the outside of the case showing that they are charging or what the charge level is. It's on the inside of the case. I have other earbuds which show information on the outside of the case, which is helpful.

Overall, these are really good earbuds and a great value. They do pretty much everything much more expensive name brand earbuds do and sound just as good too. I highly recommend them.

title: Sound quality great. Controls are touchy.
text:
These earbuds look great, fit well, and sound really good. They sound just as good as the Beats Fit Pro and Airpods Pro I also own.

They come in very nice packaging that rivals Apple packaging in quality. There's a cool "tree" of extra ear tips that I hadn't seen before and a little branded USB C charging cord (no power brick) wrapped in a tiny velcro strip.

I like the matte gray color mine came in and they fit great right out of the box. I never felt like they were about to fall out.

The instruction guide isn't very comprehensive in any one language, with a few sentences and visuals in 14 different languages. Pairing took two tries for me, but I have probably 40 things paired to my old iPhone by now so it could just be my phone.

I couldn't tell from the photo before I got them and I was hoping that there is a button press action for controlling them, but unfortunately they are touch controls, meaning you tamper with your music accidentally every time you adjust them.

There are functions that you need to do on either the left or right earbud to do, making it a little tricky if one of your hands is full (like from carrying a bag or walking a dog). I like earbuds that have an actual press to avoid false clicks and where you can do things on either earbud.

I could not get double tapping to work regularly no matter how much I tried, which meant I could not get my podcast to skip commercials. I kept pausing and unpausing. There is also no volume control on the earbuds.

The active noise cancelling is more like active noise reduction. The earbuds themselves block out environment noise just by the fact that they block your ears. When you turn on noise cancellation by long pressing on the right earbud -- a touch action I was able to do -- a woman's sultry voice tells you that noise cancellation is now on. When you turn it off there's a beep. I tried it with different fans, TV noise, and traffic noise. Sometimes it was hard to tell if it was doing anything or not, but in a controlled environment I would guess it cuts down environmental noise by about 20%. So it's nothing like the Beats Fit Pro, Airpods Pro, or Bose 700's.

Because they block out so much on their own and have the extra noise cancellation boost, these would probably be good for a library, office or gym, or commuting on a bus or subway. I would not want to wear them on a bike, while jogging, or when you need to hear the environment around you.

Overall, if the controls were just a little bit more refined, these would definitely be 5 stars, but I think since these are priced like a premium product they should have controls better or equal to earbuds that cost half as much as these.

title: Touchy controls but good overall

Because of the longer loop, I had to take my glasses off to put them on, but then they took over the space where my glasses sit, so the glasses have to go on top of them.

The sound is good, but not amazing. They sound perfectly fine playing music or listening to podcasts. I did not hear any substantial difference.

The controls are performed by tapping on, or holding, the logo. Of course when you are wearing them you can't see where the logo is, and there's no tactile clue on the logo, so you have to get used to that. They also made it so to turn up the volume or skip forward is one side, and turn down the volume or skip back is the other, so that makes it a little tough if one of your hands is full from carrying a bag or walking dogs.

Single click modifies volume, and double click is play/pause. I was unable to consistently get it to do what I wanted, so if I started my double click not exactly on the logo, it would only register one click and change the volume. I ended up just using my phone to control things as it grew too frustrating.

They do seem well made, though, and the battery life is great. They are light on your head and comfortable for long stretches of time. I wore them once in a heavy rainstorm and they worked just as well as on a sunny day. They let through outside environmental noise which is good if you are active outside and need to hear your surroundings, but if you have a lot of external noise like busy traffic you won't be able to hear them much at all.

If you are okay working around the idiosyncrasies of the touch controls, then I'd recommend them.

title: Good UPS Backup - Compared to Similar APC BR1500MS
text:
I have a lots of expensive electronics that I've started hooking up to UPS systems to protect from power surges, brownouts, etc. that come along with the summertime with storm season and everyone running their air conditioners. I first purchased an APC BR1500MS which I'd say would be the APC equivalent of this CyberPower Unit both in specs/features and price. Been running this for a few weeks now and plenty satisfied...
No complaints on the APC, but there are some aspects of the CyberPower unit that I've found to be preferable.

Pros:
- The unit comes with the battery pre-installed. This was a big pro to me as it's a bit of a pain to have to connect a battery, and I've have them spark on me before when connecting APC units which is a little sketchy.
- This unit is plug and play. With the pre-installed battery all you need to do is plug in your equipment and plug it into the wall.
- Pure Sinewave is a big plus for me since I'm using this to back up a NAS server and sensitive electronics.
- Also the AVR is a nice feature, again, especially in the summer. I've had AVR kick on almost daily to keep my power supplied clean.
- Has 12 outlets (6 battery / 6 surge) as compared to APC which has 10 (5/5)
- The tillable color LCD is a really nice touch. Switching through the menu is very clear and informative and it's just nice to have a color LCD.
- It's Smart: I plugged the included USB cable from the unit into my NAS server and it instantly recognized the make/model, estimated backup time, etc. and was able to configure all kinds of settings such as automatic shutdown, all without needing to install any software, my system just picked up the unit as soon as it was plugged in. This surprised me.

Cons:
- Honestly I can't think of anything that I can say as a negative for this unit.

Overall, since purchasing, this has protected my server and other electronics from 5 quick power surges that normally would have caused an unwanted shutdown and potential damage. And the AVR seems to kick in when the air conditioner is running, and at certain times of day. The unit was super easy to install and comes with a good warranty and $500,000 Connected Equipment Guarantee as compared to APC's $250,000. I don't have $250k worth of electronics plugged into either unit, but it's nice to have the warranty and guarantee. Also, the fact that my server instantly recognized the UPS when plugging in the USB cable without installing any software was a really nice touch, and gives me an extra piece of mind that it will automatically power off if it senses that the battery is getting low.
Overall, though you do pay a little bit of a premium for the Pure Sinewave and I'd consider this a mid-tier to premium unit, I'm really satisfied, and it's worth every penny if it saves my expensive electronics from failing or potential damage from surges or just bad power that comes through the lines, especially in the summer.
Definitely recommend. If I had to choose the APC BR1500MS or this unit, I'd choose the Cyber Power, and would recommend for sure.

Unfortunately, I've been quite disappointed. I'll either be returning or putting it in the guest room. The unit will not play back HDR video and chokes when attempting to, even 1080p. To make matters even worse, it doesn't seem to handle HEVC media well in general. Meanwhile, my 10yr old Apple TV will play back 10-bit HDR files without issue, even though it technically doesn't support them.
The unit is fast/responsive enough, but again, no more so than my old Apple TV.
Also, closed captions don't work without going through hoops in the menus of the system/apps... and even then I've needed to turning them on directly from the TV for them to display! What a joke...
If it weren't for the fact that I only paid $29.99 for the unit (on flash sale) I'd be taking this up with Roku directly.
This unit may be fine for people that just want to use it to watch Netflix, but has been a real disappointment for me, and not living up to the features/capabilities claimed by it. I'll be going back to my trusty Apple TV for the meantime, and will stick with a new one when I truly need to upgrade. Maybe others have better luck, and I'm a bit of a "power user", but for me this has been a real nuisance and disappointment. At the end of the day I find you pretty much always get what you pay for... and this unit has been an overall disappointment.

title: Nice UltraWide For MacBook (USB-C with PD and hub)
text:
I recently changed jobs and decided to change from using a dual monitor setup to this UltraWide monitor, and overall I'm quite pleased with it. The panel in general has been good so far, and looks very nice paired with my MacBook, which was just plug and play with the included USB-C cable.

For the price point, this monitor has been great and has all the features I was looking for, specifically USB-C connectivity with Power Delivery (charges laptop up to 60W, which has been plenty for my M1 MacBook Pro as well as hub/data transfer, which is nice to be able to have one cable without needing a dock (though may not be enough to charge more power hungry laptops). It is quite sleek looking with the included base, and is VESA mount capable, which I'll likely take advantage of in the future. The screen itself is plenty bright, even with backlighting set at 50%, and is quite sleek and close to "borderless". Colors look natural and the resolution is sharp and looks great with MacOS. The built-in speakers are also fine, better than many other monitors I've used/owned, but not a substitute for external speakers for listening to music, at least for me. For general/office use they're fine.

My one "nit-pick" is that the screen has a factory installed matte film over it which I understand is to reduce glare and finger prints. In concept this is a nice idea, and it does make the monitor easy to clean. That said, when first opening/turning on i could see a few tiny bubbles/imperfections near the edges which made me think this was a removable plastic film... it's not. The bubbles/imperfections are hardly noticeable, only with close inspection of the borders when the screen is off. Very minor imprecation in this built-in film aside, I do see benefits in glare reduction and ease of cleaning. All that said, it would be nice if there were no imperfections at all... considering this was pre-installed at the factory and is not removable without damaging the screen.

Overall, I've found this to be a good monitor for the price point, and have been quite satisfied with it.

title: Integrated our TV perfectly into the Home Theater system! The discovery of the year!!
text: This cable works perfectly to integrate my new smart tv into my surround sound/home theater system. Quality was awesome and the price was very good. The braided cable is very classy looking in my wire bundles! I recommend it highly! Since I had never used the optical audio ports in my equipment before there were a few things I learned. 1) Take the protective caps off of the cable ends (I didn't make this mistake but other reviewers have mentioned it), 2) When you plug the cables into your equipment make sure you plug them in firmly until they snap or click into place.3) Don't kink the cable.  The optical "signal" inside the cable is actually a laser beam and I guess it is possible to block that light if the cable kinks. The greatest benefit I have enjoyed from this cable is that now all of my TV audio is routed through the surround sound system but I can choose to skip the surround sound and just listen to the tv audio if I wish. It just simplifies things a lot for my wife who gets a little tangled up when trying to watch the tv but hates trying to figure out which buttons and remotes to use. One thing about this cable, though... it looks like the ends are gold plated but they are just gold plastic (The knurled grips are very sturdy and do appear to be gold colored metal, though). The cables are great quality and the price was very good... just don't expect the ends to be gold plated metal... the cable is optical, not electrical so metal ends are not needed! I found a pretty good explanation of optical audio cables at the How to Geek website. Read this and you will learn more. howtogeek.com/241828/what-is-the-optical-audio-port-and-when-should-i-use-it/  Please click the button below if you found my review useful. Thanks!

The best way I can describe it is, you get pretty-much the same sound in the earbuds that you get through the phone's built-in speaker: all treble, hissing, blaring upper midrange, like a really badly encoded MP3 being played through really cheap laptop speakers. I'm not sure if this is a limitation of Bluetooth audio transmission or what, but it really doesn't matter...

As a result, to me this is useful only as a hands-free calling device... and who needs a lanyard with two earbuds and a control module hung around their neck when they could just use an on-the-ear bluetooth hands-free instead? title: A review focusing on streaming and network support
text:
First the basics: It sounds pretty good for the price, of course you will not want to be using this for audiophile music listening, but the audio remaster/simulated tube amp modes are fun to play around with. The pseudo-surround modes work really well for music and television/movies if you like that sort of thing as opposed to original stereo mixes. There are many options in any given mode (blu-ray, streaming app, etc) to control picture and sound settings and variables. The menus are simple and straightforward, but the remote is a bit awkward, as the button arrangement makes it too easy to accidentally hit the HOME button (throwing you out of what you were doing) instead of the up-arrow button, for example. Navigation is a bit laggy; it usually takes the system 2-4 seconds to respond on screen to a button press. I have not had any issues playing blu-ray discs, startup time and chapter/menu changes are reasonable.

As for streaming and networking: This unit supports what I consider to be the "worthwhile" streaming apps, Netflix, Hulu, Crunchyroll, Amazon, YouTube, etc etc; you will not get the 1000+ channels that are available on Roku, but in my experience (I owned one once) about 980 of those 1000 channels are useless. I wanted an affordable all-in-one unit that would stream, provide a sound system, and play DVD and Blu-ray so I wouldn't have 4 or 5 remotes to keep up with, and this unit satisfies that objective. Netflix for whatever reason is noticeably slower to load than it is on my PS3 or in the outdated VIERA that was built into my Panasonic TV, although once it does load, it streams smoothly. Everything I have streamed with this unit so far has worked flawlessly. The VIERA Connect marketplace is simple and you can arrange your app screen however you like; you also have lots of other connectivity options such as data discs, USB, SD cards, etc, and you can connect it to your home network.

It has DLNA support, although DLNA itself is not very useful and the Windows Media Server is fairly limited; I was able to play files via network share that I could not play through the Windows Media Server. You can also connect directly to a network share and play various video files from your PC. I have successfully played MP4 and MKV files (encoded with Handbrake using the AppleTV 3 defaults), but if you like subtitles (anime), this unit will fail you in that respect-- I have spent several hours trying to make videos that will display subtitles on this unit but so far the only solution is to "burn in" the subtitles by remuxing the video, which gives you ugly, jagged, blurry subtitles that are legible but very unpleasant to read. It also does not support chapter stops within MKV or MP4 files. It also will not play .ISO files, it looks like the Western Digital Live is the only unit that will, but it has had very troubling reviews in regards to stability and operation.

Before I bought this unit, I was using a laptop hooked up to my TV via HDMI for all of my streaming, but this was very awkward; almost all of my streaming is Netflix and Crunchyroll, and neither performed well through their websites versus through the apps on my wife's PS3. The website streams would freeze, stutter, time out, and in the case of Netflix, it was almost impossible to maintain a HD stream. By using the apps in the BTT190, I am no longer having to tolerate any of these issues, and I am able to do everything with a single remote (well, two if you count the DirecTV remote) versus having to fumble with a laptop, mouse, dragging browser windows from screen to screen, etc... so I am keeping the laptop only for mounting ISOs and playing them through Media Player Classic (since there is no better solution to playing ISOs at this time), and I am able to do everything else with the BTT190. Victory!

title: Works well but needlessly difficult to set up
text:
The stand itself is reasonably solid and sturdy, although the base will slip and slide on your desk unless you put something underneath, like rubber strips or feet. I would've liked more stability and security where the post attaches to the base, but the main issue I have with this stand is that it is needlessly difficult to adjust. The rings that go around the post would've been much easier to manage had they had a large knob that you can screw/unscrew to loosen the rings, but instead the rings use two recessed allen-bolts (one on each side of the post), making adjustments very tedious as both have to be tightened and loosened with an allen wrench just to move the display up or down.

The stand also uses a circular knob-clamp design (I'm sure there's a proper name for this) with 3 allen bolts spaced equidistant around the knob that attaches to the stand. To rotate or tilt the monitor, again you have to break out the allen wrench, which is a smaller one than the one used for other adjustments (so now you have 2 allen wrenches to keep up with). As always goes with this knob-and-ring clamp design, a quarter-turn of a bolt may be the difference between too tight and too loose.

Once you get it set up, it serves it's purpose, and hopefully you will only have to set it up once. Just be prepared to spend a lot more time making adjustments than you should.

text:

title: Detects flying insects but not cars moving - UPDATE 4/21/2020
text:
UPDATE 4/21/2020 : It has taken some time, but with the assistance of Ring technical support (who contacted me, I did not have to contact them), I have finally managed to get the cameras working in an acceptable manner, it just takes trial and error, and most importantly, *a good wifi signal*.

Motion detection technology itself still has room for improvement and I believe my initial expectations may have been a bit unrealistic. I did upgrade my router to a Netgear Nighthawk and that did noticeably improve my signal strength, which has resulted in more reliable and consistent recording; I strongly encourage you to test your wifi strength at the locations you have decided to mount the cameras, and if your reception is weak you should be prepared to either upgrade your router, add a mesh or repeater, or be willing to live with subpar performance from your camera.

Here are some things I discovered in the course of a few hours of tweaking various settings:
MOTION VERIFICATION - if you have this "On" you may end up with recordings that are "cut off at the beginning", for example rather than see a car pull into your driveway, driver get out, and walk to the house, you may only see the edge of the guy's shoulder move out of the picture and then a view of his car sitting there in the driveway. On the other hand, having this "Off" may cause trivial notifications, such as headlights passing by, insects flying in front of the camera, etc... I ended up with one camera having this turned off and the other two having it turned on to get the results I wanted.
MOTION SENSITIVITY - Don't let the dramatic THIS IS GOING TO RUIN YOUR BATTERY LIFE! warning scare you, I had to set the motion sensitivity to about 70% to get my Side camera to pick up motion near the edge of the range, my other cameras were fine at around 30%. One way to think of this is, if you want to capture motion out towards the edge of the range of the camera, like a back yard, you should turn up the sensitivity; if you are using your camera to cover a smaller area like a back porch, a lower sensitivity will be fine.

Be prepared for the batteries to not last "months", one of mine already needs to be recharged and the other two probably will by the end of May. But given the limits of current battery technology that's really not bad, I'm fine with it... just keep accessibility in mind when you mount these things because you will need to pull the batteries every 4-12 weeks and recharge them. I may pick up a spare battery.
******************************************************************************

I am very frustrated with these cameras so far. The only reason I haven't returned them (yet) is because there doesn't seem to be much of an alternative when it comes to battery powered cameras. I have spent way too much time tweaking the motion detection settings and the cameras are still doing stupid things like sending an alert when a tiny moth flies in front of the camera but doesn't detect when one of our kids gets into his car and pulls out of the driveway. If it's not going to detect someone getting into a car and driving off then so much for it being of any use as a security camera. I've relocated one of them once and the other one twice and it hasn't helped. I still get notifications and play back the video and see absolutely nothing happening, or they miss events that definitely should have been captured, I can see it being too sensitive or not sensitive enough, but how can it be wrong both ways?! It's like they are doing the exact opposite of what they are supposed to do, capturing what should be ignored and vice versa. And they're both doing it! On top of that, despite claims of battery life lasting for "weeks or months*, one camera is already down to 77% after being in use for only 6 days; the other is at 97%.

If I can't get better results from these things by near the end of my 30 days, I'm sending them back. I will update with the final verdict... but I've all but given up.
