title: 5-star concept, poor execution
text:
First, if you are reading this, congratulate yourself for being smart enough to just glance at 4k reviews with an average 4.5 star rating and click Add to Cart assuming that this is a 4.5 star product.
One of the most frustrating things about being a consumer these days is when you come across something that appears to be a great product, exactly what you are looking for, but when you get it you discover that it has been so poorly manufactured or constructed that you've either wasted your money, been bait-and-switched, or will have to put additional work into getting the product up to what it should've been to begin with. This is one of those cases.
As many others have pointed out, the huge failure here is that the snaps are too loose and will break free under the slightest force. I think the disparity in reviews is due to how people are using these things, if you're putting lightweight objects in these and are not interacting with them very often, it is an attractive product; but for the advertised use of storing records, it is a total failure as they simply cannot accommodate any movement without the sides coming unsnapped, potentially causing an avalanche of your records hitting the floor. The manufacturer needs to fix this, if they do they will have an excellent product on their hands. So close, but here they snatched defeat from the jaws of victory.
Rather than return the ones I bought, I'm going to see if i can make them useful by adding steel clips to the corners to prevent the snaps from breaking loose, if that doesn't work I think some small nut-bolt-washers through the top corners and painted black will do the trick. In the meantime, putting the lid on before lifting the box seems to keep the snaps from breaking free. But in its current state, there's no way I would trust this thing with my records.
UPDATE: Simply by adding a small binder clip to each corner where the snaps are, these boxes seem to be holding together well and not unsnapping like they were before. I still don't believe I would trust fully loading it with records and then trying to carry it around, but a partial load would probably be ok (put the lid on first) and these are otherwise useful for general storage. Still, the manufacturer needs to do something about those snaps.

title: The BEST wireless carplay adapter.
text:
I've tried a few wireless adapters and read reviews of many many more. This one is by far my favorite of the bunch. The first thing that drew me to it is the form factor. It just looks like a USB flash drive. I love that I can just plug it in and not have a big box sitting in my storage compartment. Its out of the way so i can make full use of that storage tray, and it matches the rest of my interior. As you can see in the first picture I uploaded, you can barely even tell its there. Now I can hop in my vehicle and leave my phone in my pocket and still get the full functionality of carplay. If I'm on a long trip and want to charge my phone I can just plug it into the additional charge port inside the center console and still utilize the wireless adapter. This means that unless the adapter quits working, I can basically just plug it and forget about it forever.

Speaking to the actual performance of the device, it is top notch. Sound quality does not seem to be any worse than any other bluetooth or wireless operation. My truck doesn't have the best sound system but it sounds great to me. It doesn't affect mic quality at all, people on the other end can hear my fine just as usual. There is a slight delay for playing/pausing music. Scrolling through your library is flawless, but once you select a track/album there is about a 2 second delay before the audio starts. The same goes when you skip a track or when you hit pause/play. Always about a 2 second delay. This delay is not present when the system just goes to the next track when one is finished, only if you manually play/pause something. This also does not seem to cut anything off, it just plays the audio 2 seconds later than you would normally hear it. I see this issue described with pretty much every carplay wireless device, however this one is much less prominent than the other adapters I have tried myself.

I have never experienced the "gps delay" others describe on a lot of other (more expensive) devices. I have used apple maps for navigation a few times through this device and it works just fine. It calls out the directions well before the turns so no issues.

The only other common issue with wireless carplay adapters is the time it takes to connect. My Honda Ridgeline has a very slow radio startup anyway, probably about 20-25 seconds before I can connect my phone even when wired. This is extended an extra 5-7 seconds with this device. I would estimate total time to connect at just over 30 seconds. Completely acceptable in my opinion, and compared to other wireless adapters.

This adapter also came with a couple dongles in case your car has a different kind of USB connector. I do not need these dongles but with them included it should be able to plug into pretty much any car with carplay.

I cannot recommend this device enough. Don't waste your money on the adapters 2-3 and even 5x more expensive than this one. This one is the best designed of them all and works as well as the best of them. The only reason I can see to pass on this device is if you specifically want the classic box form factor that connects with a cable. That may work better for some setups.

Easy 5 stars for this one.

title: Not a top tier record player, but a good value.
text:
I had to think quite hard about how I would score this overall, but the bottom line is you are getting a complete package that looks very nice and does work well (for the most part) for a very good price tag. I’ll go into detail below.

Looks: this thing is beautiful, it looks awesome on the table I set it up on. Looks vintage but not old. The player and the speakers match and both look fantastic.

Sound quality: Overall the sound quality is ok. Not great. The clarity is good, but the speakers are just way to small to produce any bass at all. I feel at lower volumes it sounds pretty good but the louder you go the more obvious the lack of bass becomes. I didn’t expect much at this price, but I’m telling you, there is virtually zero bass from these speakers. The plus here is you can likely just plug in any speakers you want, it just uses basic RCA connectors on the back.

Bluetooth feature: Excellent. Easy to connect, plays music from my phone just fine. As stated above, the included speakers are pretty poor overall so I don’t see myself using this for the Bluetooth much, if at all beyond just testing it.

Record playback: Ok so for the most part the record playback is awesome. Threw a few of my 40-50 year old vinyls on and they played and sounded great (as good as these speakers can do). Two small issues with the turntable. First, it does not spin completely flat, at first I thought one of my records was warped but its the turntable, when it turns you will notice your record moving up and down every so slightly. It’s almost unnoticeable unless you are at eye level with the record. This isn’t a huge issue as the arm moves up and down with it. Does not seem to affect the sound at all. The other issue is that it seems to be spinning a bit slow. It took me hours of listening to music to notice, but if you play a 5 minute song on your phone and on vinyl at the same time the song on the phone ends a couple seconds sooner. I’m not sure what a normally acceptable tolerance for RPM speed is on a turntable, for this kind of money this is probably more than acceptable. It really doesn’t change how the music sounds to any noticeable level but I thought it would mention it.

Again, I think at this price point this setup is decent. I’m not sure if you can get a complete package as nice as this one for less, or even the same money. If you want the best of the best, you’re gonna pay for it. If you just want a cheap setup to play old (or new) vinyls, this is a solid pick.

title: I was Sorely Disappointed with this Camera
text:
I will begin this review letting readers know that I am a current owner of a Canon G1X and I have owned both the S95 and Canon G12. After reading the information regarding this camera on the web, I felt that it would be an appropriate step forward for me to embrace a new iteration of the "G" series body and enjoy some technical advances (WiFi and NFC) that this unit brought to the table.

First and foremost, this unit insulted me right out of the box. Canon built a massive camera, stuffed it into a tiny package and then destroyed any usability by installing the most useless and flimsy "Grip" which no adult male could possibly use under normal circumstances. I have average size hands, and found it impossible to use this camera effectively without cradling it with both hands or mounting it on a tripod. To add injury to my insult, Canon offers to sell me the correct handgrip for the camera for an additional $30 plus shipping and tax. Something that should have been placed on the camera in the first place.

Overall, use of the camera is quite similar to its previous generation, albeit now the unit does offer enhanced communications through NFC and WiFi, but learning how to use these features proved to be difficult because the manual fails to properly explain in detail how to setup, and initiate the software used to enable the features.

Image quality is essentially the same as the G1X, and I did not expect any real improvement since the heat generated by constantly having the rear screen on all the time in this little body will certainly offset any gain made by software processing.

My bottom line advice to shoppers, get your hands on the unit prior to committing the 800+ dollars on this camera. I think that if I had the chance to hold the camera and take some test shots, I would have considered it more carefully.

title: Great camera. Easy installation if you don't use Static ...
text:
Great camera. Easy installation if you don't use Static IP. Otherwise, can be a bit tricky. I had a small narrow space to install the camera (recessed sidelight) so I couldn't pair it with the solar panel (sold separately) and instead used this device, https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B01MDR2LDK (OUTXE 10,000 mAh Power Bank). After one week, Camera and Charger are still at 100%. My thinking is, when the Power Bank depletes it will recharge via its built-in solar panel, and even if it takes a week to recharge, the camera battery won't take a week to discharge. I'll see long term how this works out, but after a week - it's working out.

UPDATE:
Charger mentioned previously kept the camera charged to 100% for two months before I needed to remove the Power Bank and bring it inside to charge it. Camera would occasionally get down to 75% charge then back to 100%. Still have the camera in place and it's 100% charge. The Power Bank I velcroed beneath it, so it was as simple as unplugging it from the camera and bringing it inside to wall charge. Charger was still at 25% but we've had some overcast days so I decided to bring the Power Bank inside to get the job done faster. Overall, nice setup and I don't need to remove the camera from the base - just the solar charging Power Bank itself which is stuck on the wall next to it with velcro - easy setup and much lower profile for tight spaces, and slimmer look than the large Ring Solar Panel, which I couldn't use due to space constraints.

UPDATE 2 (LOWERING rating to FOUR until software update fix, and that needs to happen soon):
After almost 1 year, I've only had to charge my Solar Power Bank twice. Long periods of overcast days eventually drained it. Though the Ring has not once lost a charge or been inside to charge. The system works. However, there was a recent Ring App Update and it is NOT good. Missing "Settings" option entirely, and crashes A LOT. Doesn't work for more than a hour or two without restarting the app and logging in again. Hope they get that fixed quickly because it could ruin an otherwise good product and good review.

UPDATE 3 (Back to 5 stars ):
What I assume was a software update a while back fixed the intermittent issues with the software frequently crashing, and now it seems rock solid as original. The charging setup I'm using is working out fantastic. On sunny days the Solar Power Bank recharges itself then trickle charges the Ring camera. I've not yet, not once, had to bring the Ring camera inside to charge. And, I've only had to bring the Solar Power Bank inside twice to charge, and it's been over a year! Also, to whom it may concern, the OUTXE Power Bank I purchased has apparently been updated to this unit, https://www.amazon.com/OUTXE-10000mAh-Flashlight-Waterproof-Portable/dp/B077SN8J8Q.

text:
Finally, I can replace my onboard sound card (Realtek). The onboard card was fine until I had to find new drivers after a reinstall, and couldn't find any compatible with Windows 10. Tried several and they were all unstable at best and caused random system freezes. I even tried a new Creative Labs sound card and had the exact same problem finding stable drivers with Windows 10. So, I uninstalled all those failed driver attempts manually with Autoruns (MS Sysinternals app) then when I had a clean stable system again, I did this...

Now that things were back to onboard sound disabled in BIOS and system stable with the default Windows sound driver, I thought I'd try this StarTech USB sound card, because I was out of options frankly and didn't want to buy a new system board (cpu, memory, etc), and I'm very glad I did. Install was as simple as plugging it into my Logitech G51 (5.1 Surround system) and I had sound again. Well, at least stereo sound from Left/Right. At this point, I didn't install the StarTech USB drivers that came with it figuring I'd run into the same issues with old drivers from circa 2008 running on Windows 10, so I went a totally different direction.

This is what works for me. Instead of the StarTech drivers I downloaded the "Dolby Access" App from the Windows Store (you can get it from Dolby.com too) and voila! I have Dolby Atmos sound playing on my 5.1 surround speakers! Sounds fantastic! You will have to turn on Spacial Sound and set it to "Dolby Atmos for Headphones" in the Sound Tray Icon (not quite intuitive). I think it's treating my Logitech 5.1 setup as if they are a set of headphones. Sound is very immersive. I liked it so much I purchased the "Dolby DTS Headphone:X" app as well. Since I can control the EQ through the Logitch G51 Console it works amazingly well for me.

title: Quite good...a beastly bass!
text: This is my first Harman/Kardon product (I frequently use headphones from their sister company AKG), and I was curious to compare it with the Bose speakers and the Onkyo mini hi-fi system, which I have at home. My impressions are generally positive - the speaker impresses first and foremost with its deep, resonant bass. It actually has such a bass that it nearly rivals the low frequencies of my 50-watt guitar amplifier! Beside the bass, the sound is generally decent, but not stellar - might be a close match to the Bose speakers, but is not as impressive as what Onkyo delivers. The overall clarity/mid-range and trebles leave something to be desired. Given that this is a mono speaker, the level of audio detail is actually quite good. At least to my ears, though, it doesn't seem sharp enough to be outstanding. I don't know how the stereo Onyx Studio 4 sounds, so I cannot tell if the Onyx Studio 5 is an upgrade or a downgrade. The volume is mighty and can fill out a large room easily. The bluetooth pairs easily and works very well. The material feels premium and solid as expected from a company with the reputation of Harman/Kardon. The speaker is portable, though leaning toward heavy - around 3 kg./ 6.5 pounds. It sits well on hard surfaces and even when pushed doesn't tilt. Overall, it is a good product, to be sure, and one that stands out chiefly through its beastly bass!  I am pleased with this purchase but expected somewhat richer/clearer overall sound.

title: A real improvement in sound quality!
text: I consider myself an early-stage audiophile :) - listening to music and playing music are hobbies of mine, and in the past year or so, I started getting quite picky about the quality of the audio streams/files I enjoy listening to daily. My experience with DACs is limited - I have a Shanling M1 at home that acts as a DAC and doubles as a portable Hi Res player, and in comparison to it, the DragonFly Black is a significant improvement. It works very well with my Android phone and streams flawlessly MQA files from Tidal and FLACs from my own collection. If you purchase the USB Audio Pro Player and the embedded Bit Perfect option for Android devices (about 12 bucks in total), you can stream MQA files at frequencies that exceed greatly the native support Android offers, and enjoy greater clarity and more ambient sound. If you have higher-end external headphones and/or speakers, then the experience becomes truly immersive! I am very pleased to have found this little device. title: Entry-level premium earphones? Hmm...maybe not!
text:
These earphones will probably please audio purists who dislike any sound accent. The Shure SE112 sound flat, quite flat. If you buy the memory foam tips that Shure makes (the L-size is so over-sized that most people would probably need an M or an S), there is a slight improvement in sound, but it still sounds flat. There is moderate bass, but the mids remain hollow and expressionless, and drums occasionally tend to sound tinny. Instrument separation is okay, but the sound signature is not what I imagine by buying entry-level premium headphones. I have AKG and KZ earphones at similar or lower price levels that have warmer/brighter, punchier, and richer sound (particularly the AKG). Playing with equalization helps a bit, and using a DragonFly Black DAC makes the sound acceptable, but simply not good enough for something that bears the Shure logo.

As other reviewers have pointed out - these earphones have an usual positioning and their thick cable is not very friendly in terms of staying behind one's ear. Once you use the Shure foam tips, sound isolation is great, though. I have a loud lawnmower that gets cut out effectively when using these earphones. I am puzzled, though, after reading so many positive reviews of these SE112s at professional/amateur audiophile web sites. In my opinion, they are middle-of-the-line in the sub-50$ segment and you can definitely do better. I am not an audio professional, but have been playing musical instruments as a hobby for over 20 years and have a trained ear. I certainly see myself using these earphones in noisy environments, but not with a DAC or when relaxing - their sound signature is not what I was looking for.

title: This barlow lens DOES NOT provide a 5x magnification!
text:
I have two other Barlow lenses (both made by Meade Technologies) that offer 3x and at 2x magnification respectively. The SVBONY 5x Barlow lens provides magnification that is a bit worse than that of the 3x Barlow lens by Meade. I would guess that the real magnification of the SVBONY 5x Barlow is actually only around 2.5x.

The image quality is acceptable. The lens, however, has noticeable chromatic aberration (color distortion) and when viewing Jupiter, for instance, you will see a small rainbow-colored globe. This is not supposed to happen and I highly doubt that it is a true 3-element apochromatic lens.

If you are new to astronomical observation and you are looking for an affordable Barlow lens, with which to extend the magnification of your scope, look elsewhere. This Barlow lens is very cheap but the quality is simply not good. Orion's Shorty 2x Barlow or Meade's 3x Barlow would be a good start. That being said, I cannot recommend the SVBONY 5x Barlow lens. title: A nice beginner-friendly scope!
text:
This Newtonian reflector telescope is very well made and very easy to use. If you have realistic expectations (it is not going to produce a stunning large image of Saturn, even at 200x magnification, which is its maximum useful magnification), they will be fulfilled by this model. You would likely need a few additional Barlow lenses (I would recommend the affordable and well made lenses by Meade, such as their 3x and 2x Barlow lenses--around 30$ per lens), but other than that, you will be able to view the night sky comfortably with this scope. It is great for observing the planets and their moons (mostly Jupiter's), the Moon, and even some deep sky objects like the Great Orion nebula. The provided eyepieces offer a 20x and a 40x magnification. With a 3x Barlow lens, you can make that a 60x and a 120x magnification, which would allow you to see the planets (their image will be still reasonably small, though, but if the Barlow lens is of good quality, it will be quite clear).

The only part that requires a bit of assembly is the EZ Finder II Reflex Sight. Make sure that you align it with the object that you see in your eyepiece when daylight is lower (maybe 30-40 minutes before twilight, so that you can see clearly the LED red dot). Aligning is reasonably easy (I had no prior experience doing so) and it works well.

Once you attach the EZ Finder II to the scope, you are good to go. You can put the scope on a small 3- or 4-legged stool, or on a table. You can also use a tripod that has a 1/4 screw (or a quick-release plate). The scope will weigh about 7 to 7.5 pounds with the Barlow lenses, so the tripod should be able to support that weight.

At this price, there is a lot that you can do with this Newtonian beginner's model, and it is very well made. This is my second telescope (until now I've been mostly using Celestron astronomical binoculars), and I am enjoying watching the starry skies with it!

I am something of an audiophile and the most obvious plus of these wireless earbuds is their sound quality: clear, well-defined, leaning slightly towards a warmer/darker signature that becomes more prominent with a pair of Comply foam tips. The earbuds come with a variety of silicone tips, but to unlock their full potential, you should replace the silicone tips with memory foam ones and the difference will be very obvious. I personally prefer using Comply Isolation T500 tips.

The earbuds pair very easily with a smart phone and the connection appears to be robust. That being said, adjusting them to fit your ears will likely stop playback and you will need to restart it. Tapping one of them once sometimes results in fast forwarding or rewinding, while in fact it is supposed to pause/play a song, but that may be just me not being accustomed to the controls.

The instruction booklet is translated a bit poorly in English, but is understandable. The battery life, as far as I can tell, is good. After listening to music for about an hour, the battery level showed 90%. Charging is very easy and the charging case is well made. The two electrode ends on each earbud are nested a bit inward, which is good because in this way they are protected better. I've had other wireless earbuds in the past that became useless because the electrode surfaces got damaged/scratched and would not charge. These earbuds appear better equipped to prevent this from happening.

Are these the best earbuds at this price level? Probably not. There are very competitive and impressive multi-driver wired earbuds at the 40-50 USD price level, such as the RevoNext QT2 or the Senfer DT6, but these Tozo T6 sound pretty good and would satisfy even more demanding audio consumers (like myself). So far, I haven't found an obvious con except the slightly messy controls. Where it matters the most - in the sound quality department - the Tozo T6 offer great value!

title: Delivers quality!
text:
I am an amateur musician and also an audiophile, and care a lot about the quality of the sound that comes out of the devices I am using, be they musical instruments, earphones, hi-fi stereo systems, Bluetooth speakers, or soundbars. I can definitely recommend this soundbar on the basis of its performance: the sound is well-defined, clear, and the subwoofer offers deep and resonant bass without excessive rumble or distortion. From the five sound modes, I find myself preferring "Game" probably a bit better than the others because it adds additional clarity, while boosting slightly the overall volume. But, if you are listening to a very bass-heavy music track, you might wish to switch to the "Smart" sound mode.

The soundbar offers three options to connect to the TV: 1) wirelessly; 2) through a HDMI cable, using the HDMI ARC port of the soundbar and the TV; 3) through an optical audio cable. The HDMI ARC connection is the best option in terms of sound quality and I recommend it (if your TV has a dedicated port for it). Keep in mind that if you accidentally plug out the charging adapter, etc., while the soundbar is working, it might lose the TV ARC (HDMI ARC) connection to the TV and may be unable automatically to re-detect it. The solution is to unplug all cables from the soundbar and the subwoofer (as well as the HDMI cable from the TV), plug out any charging adapters/cables from electrical outlets, and wait for about 8-10 minutes before reconnecting them. The soundbar will once again recognize the TV ARC (HDMI ARC) connection.

The subwoofer and the soundbar pair automatically on their own, so no additional setup is necessary. Overall, the change in terms of TV sound is significant. Put a Dolby 5.1 movie/trailer to watch or stream and you will be feeling as if you were in a multiplex movie theater.

Can the volume become loud? Yes - it can get pretty loud and easily fill a large room. When I stream music from apps like Tidal, I am keeping it around level 20 (out of 100) and it is loud enough to fill the whole living room.

Overall - this is a quality product that is priced well. It is a budget-friendly, mid-range offering by Samsung with a sound quality that feels closer to the premium tier. I have various systems/speakers at home by Bose, Onkyo, and Harman Kardon, and this soundbar comes close to them in terms of the clarity and attractiveness of its sound profile(s).

text:
The earphones have a clear, relatively neutral, and bright sound with just enough bass for those who do not mind a less prominent bass presentation. I personally prefer a stronger bass response (my favorite earphones are the more V-shaped RevoNext QT2 and the amazing Senfer DT6) and had to tweak a bit the sound, using the MSEB algorithmic software on my R3 Pro Saber DAP. This worked quite well and the T3 began sounding better and better.

If you are a basshead, this earphones will not appeal to you, no matter how much you tweak the bass response. And - you really need a quality audio stream to appreciate the detail and the clarity of the sound that the T3 provides. I stream from Qobuz and Tidal and the difference from playing MP3 files is very significant.

I have a large collection of chi-fi earphones and for quite a while was steering clear from the T2 hype, since I don't like very neutral sound or overly bright presentations. The T3, while still fairly bright, offers depth and clarity and just enough tweakable bass response to make the listening experience pleasant to my ears. Will they become my daily choice? Time will tell. They are not the most comfortable earphones to wear, so this may be a factor too.

title: A fun-sounding V-shaped presentation!
text:
This is a pleasant addition to my growing collection of ChiFi earphones and IEMs. I prefer a slightly V-shaped presentation to a completely neutral one, and in this regard, the TRN V80 delivers the goods! The sound is warm, with a well-expressed bass that will satisfy most bass-lovers. The sub-bass is very well extended, while the mids are relatively balanced. The highs are bright and forward, and could be a bit of an issue if you are treble sensitive.

At this price range and with this sound signature, the main competitor for the TRN V80 would be the RevoNext QT2, in my opinion. There are plenty of similarities in their sound presentation with the QT2 perhaps delivering a slightly better overall timbre (at least to my ears). The TRN V80 gives an energetic, vivid, and fun sound that those who generally prefer V-shaped presentations with plenty of bass and with forward and bright highs will enjoy.

In terms of comfort, these IEMs are surprisingly good, given that they are slightly heavy. The build quality looks great. The box with accessories, on the other hand, is quite plain and basic but I normally do not consider this a factor. I replaced the stock silicone tips with Comply Isolation 500 tips, and the stock cable with a 16-core NiceHCK silver-plated upgrade cable.

In conclusion, these are not the best-sounding IEMs at the ever-growing budget IEM ChiFi market, but they do a lot of things right, will please almost anyone who likes ample yet controlled bass and bright highs, and have a pretty good technical ability. Their soundstage is a bit narrower than on other similarly-priced models, but by no means too narrow. 4 stars.

title: Finally - a convincing KZ IEM!
text:
I own many Chi-Fi IEMs, among them a few by KZ (ZSN and ZS 10). The ZSN were fun V-shaped IEMs with a somewhat peculiar timbre and very bright highs, while the original ZS 10 was possibly the worst experiment in the IEM-making industry - muddy, lifeless, dark, and unnatural. Honestly, my expectations for the ZS 10 Pro were not high, even though the initial reviews were excellent. I finally decided to try them and was very pleasantly surprised - they have nothing in common with the original ZS 10!

I replaced the stock cable with a NiceHCK 16-core silver-plated upgrade cable and the silicone tips with a pair of Comply Isolation 500 memory foam tips. I tested the ZS 10 Pro on a R3 Pro Saber DAP, streaming hi-res files from Tidal, Qobuz, and also trying a few FLACs from my own collection. And I must admit that the ZS 10 Pro impressed me!

The sound is very clear and natural, the brightness is more controlled than on other KZ models I've tried, and the bass is very well expressed without overemphasis even through memory foam tips. Vocals sound natural and do not feel more recessed. Not all genres sound equally immersive, though - the ZS 10 Pro shines with pop/electronic, but has less brilliance with metal/hard rock. The curve seems to be halfway between V-shaped and neutral, which is a plus for me because I don't like completely neutral signatures (and steer clear of brands like Shure, even though I own a pair of their earphones and very rarely use them).

The comfort is average, better than on the KZ 10 and about the same as the ZSN. The stock cable is not good at all and since the IEMs sound so good out of the box, you should consider replacing the cable with an upgrade 8- or 16-core audio cable.

There are a number of other very competitive offerings with a similar signature and a similar price tag that you can buy on Amazon - RevoNext QT2, TRN V80, Blon BL-03, etc. The KZ ZS 10 Pro has a more controlled treble that all those and a slightly more clear nod toward balancing the sound (the others are firmly V-shaped, fun-sounding IEMs). It compares favorably also to slightly more expensive and more balanced IEMs like the Tin HiFi T3. It adds better bass presence and controls more the treble in comparison to the T3, and has a similar clarity of sound.

In conclusion - finally, there is a great-sounding offering from KZ!

title: For a single dynamic driver IEM - this one is excellent!
text:
I was pleasantly surprised by how well-tuned these BL-03 IEMs are. Given the single dynamic driver, I was quite skeptical that they could stand their ground when compared with the likes of the QT2, ZS 10 Pro, or the T3. They actually can and come close! They can't resolve as much detail as the ZS 10 Pro, nor can they sound as clear as the T3, but their sound is very musical and pleasant nonetheless - slightly V-shaped with elevated bass and treble, but also with alive and well-defined mids. They certainly make it very hard for any other single-driver earphone in the sub-40$ range to compete with them.

I read complaints that their odd teardrop/UFO-like shape may be uncomfortable. They fit quite well in my ears, using a pair of Comply Isolation 500 tips. My only gripe is that the 2-pin connection on each IEM is a bit strange and standard upgrade 2-pin cables get in with some difficulty (I need to push hard to make the pins go all the way).

I certainly enjoy the sound of the BL-03 and I am glad I bought them; they make a nice addition to my growing Chi-Fi IEM collection. Most audio enthusiasts will be pleased with these budget-friendly IEMs, despite their humble boxing and single dynamic driver per IEM. Are they the best-sounding out of the box IEMs under 50? They are certainly in the Top 10, in my opinion, contesting with the likes of the Senfer DT6, RevoNext QT2, TRN V80, Tin HiFi T2, and the KZ ZS 10 Pro. To my ears, the ZS 10 Pro hold an edge, given their higher detail resolution and slightly more balanced presentation with more controlled treble. The BL-03, however, can really challenge the multi-driver DT6, QT2, and V80! Well done, BLON!

title: A decent budget desktop PC that needs RAM upgrade
text:
I bought this Acer tower to use as a home office desktop and it seems to be doing a good job. The i3 10th generation quad core processor is reasonably capable and, according to cpubenchmark.net, has a pass mark score of 8918, which puts it well above the average CPU. The 8 GB RAM is not enough, though, and I ordered another 8 GB module to upgrade the RAM to 16 GB. The exact RAM module that this Acer came with is this: https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00XLXWD5S/.
You can upgrade the RAM to 32 GB, but to do so, you will need to order two 16 GB modules. There are two RAM slots that can each take up to 16 GB.

This desktop came with Windows 10 Home (version 1909), which I upgraded to 20H2. It also included a 30-day trial of Norton Security, which I replaced with Bitdefender. Make sure that you use Norton's removal tool if you wish to uninstall the program because otherwise it could mess things (has done it before and so have other AV products - the most notorious, in my opinion, being McAfee).

Other impressions: the PC is really quiet unless installing Windows updates, at which point every now and then the fan makes a high-pitched noise. It is quick and responsive and does average office tasks + video streaming, etc. quite well. The Wi-fi 6 is good and doesn't drop the signal. One unusual thing (I believe someone else mentioned this too) is that Windows initially did many driver updates, mostly related to the Realtek audio system. The Samsung SSD makes a difference and multitasking is quick. I am not a gamer, although I sometimes play games from Steam. Given the Intel HD 630 graphics onboard, which are midrange at best, you won't be able to play any demanding games.

Overall - at this price point, this desktop offers really good value. The two cons are the need to upgrade the RAM - the 8 GB module on board works fine out of the box but during installations, etc. at times the RAM usage exceeds 80%. The other con is the keyboard - not too comfortable and very basic, lacking backlit keys, etc. The wired mouse, on the other hand, is quite comfortable to use.

title: Great picture quality and vivid colors, but poor sound and no Ambient Mode
text:
We just bought this new budget-friendly Samsung LED 4K UHD TV from one of our local outlet stores (the model is the same as the one Amazon sells and the price is also identical). We used a wall mount to place the TV on the wall in our kitchen. The TV is very thin (about 1' altogether and the top bezel is only about half an inch or so). If you plan mounting the TV on a wall, it uses a standard VESA 200 x 200 mm. wall mount and you need 4 M8 x 1.25 screws - Samsung says to use 11-13 mm. ones but I only could find 16mm. ones in our local hardware store, which, after putting a thin washer on each screw to make the screws slightly shorter, worked perfectly.

Compatibility with external devices appears to be very good - we use Roku on all our Samsung TVs and putting a Roku 4K streaming stick was very easy. The TV was very fast to update its software and we could enjoy streaming a 4K UHD HDR movie in no time!

But - be warned, the sound on this TV is probably the worst I heard from a Samsung TV. It is hollow and even somewhat muddy. We were able to pair easily through Bluetooth the TV with a mini Hi-Fi system and, thankfully, there is no lag between the sound and the picture. But, if you plan to use the TV without an external speaker or a soundbar - its own sound is very subpar!

All in all, the picture is extremely good - vivid, bright colors and excellent 4K detail. The remote, on the other hand, is very thin and this may not necessarily be a plus. Since we bought from Amazon last fall a TU-8000 model for one of our bedrooms, it came with Ambient Mode. The AU-8000, however, has no Ambient Mode, contrary to what some websites list about this model. So, if you want the TV to blend with your room décor - this model won't do.

Also - you'll probably want to opt out of the annoying ads when you do the initial setup of the TV, so do not accept the "Interest-Based Advertisement Service".

The price is quite good at the time of writing this (just before Black Friday), so the TV definitely delivers where it matters most - in terms of picture and functionality. Its sound quality is a big minus, though, and you'll definitely want to pair it to an external speaker.

title: An improvement over Roku!
text:
We've been using Roku on our home TVs for the past 6-7 years and we've tried virtually all types - the Roku 4K streaming sticks, the Premiere +, and the Roku Ultra. The Apple TV 4K is an improvement over all of them, offering smoother streaming experience that is perceptible both in terms of 4K HDR and HD content.

Roku is probably a bit easier to navigate, as some of the buttons on the Apple TV remote are strangely placed, but our Samsung TV remote actually doubles as another remote, and if you have iOS devices, they can easily become remotes too.

The Apple TV console itself is a heavier than the Roku consoles. During streaming and gaming, it gets warm, but so does Roku. It was reasonably easy to set up. The Samsung TV did not recognize it right away, but after fiddling with its settings (manual input), it did. If you have an iOS device, you can very quickly transfer account and wi-fi info to the console, and also use the iOS device to type in passwords, etc.

The only con at this point is the free space. After the initial setup, you will likely only have somewhere between 19 and 21 GB left, so if you want to download games from the Apple Arcade - there won't be much space to do so. Pairing an Xbox controller was relatively easy (but I had to unpair it first from another iOS device). Games look good and there is no lag (the A12 Bionic chip is good enough to handle even the more demanding types). 32 GB (29.5 GB really), however, is too little (if you care about games) and will quickly fill up.

All in all, this is a capable streaming console that is a step up over Roku and certainly a step up over Chromecast (one of our TVs has Chromecast). It is much pricier than both, which is another con, but seems worth the additional investment.

title: Works well after some tuning. Had to change some settings to make the 5Ghz network visible.
text:
Our Netgear C6250 was growing old (6+ years) and we decided to replace it with a Motorola MG8702 (Wi-Fi 5 + Docsis 3.1) modem/router combo. We have Spectrum (the Ultra plan@500 Mbps) and the specs of the MG8702 looked quite good.

Our impressions are mostly positive (we bought ours from a local BestBuy store, though the price here on Amazon, at the time of writing this, is a bit lower). The most important issue is this: by default, the router was set NOT to transmit the 2.4Ghz and 5Ghz separately, but it was tramsitting instead only the 2.4 Ghz network (even though both the 2.4 and 5GHz indicator lights were lit). To make the 5Ghz network visible, I had to log in the router settings (by going to 192.168.0.1) and then I had to disable the "band steering" option. Band steering uses by default a single SSID name and password for both bands. Once it was disabled, the two bands were separated (the router briefly interrupted the connection and then restored it), and this made the 5Ghz network visible to devices in our house.

The wireless speeds are reasonably good. When close to the router, we get about 450-460 Mbps on our mobile devices and about 150-200 Mbps in more remote rooms (our house is about 2800 square feet). Our Ring cameras also work well with the 2.4GHz network. We hope that this modem/router combo will last and the Docsis 3.1 standard will guarantee more stability. The router is apparently capable of supporting at least 40 separate devices.

Lastly: this model is approved by most major cable internet providers for speeds of up to 1 Gb and works well with Spectrum (activation was quick - we had an online chat session with a Spectrum agent and after providing the MAC address of the router, it was activated in less than 5 minutes).

In terms of how it looks and feels: it is quite light but also quite tall, and will not fit easily on TV stands that do not have plenty of space between the shelves. Overall - it is good, but by no means jaw-dropping. Our older Netgear router was able to supply about 80% of the bandwidth that this newer Motorola model provides. We can only hope that it will turn out to be durable and stable (like the Netgear was).

5 stars for the device, minus 2 stars due to the self-serving money grab Linksys-Cisco tech support. The RE-1000 is a truly amazing device. But, not without an occasional problem As some reviews mentioned it may drop or disconnect the signal. I have had mine for 9 months and it stopped working. I tried re-installing via the CD and directions but my computer/router would not recognize the extender/device. So I researched the Internet and tried some other recommended fixes to no avail. I called Linksys-Cisco tech support, and just as another reviewer mentioned, as soon as they realized I was outside the 90 day warranty, they immediately tried to sell me the $29.99 "talk to a technician" service or the $39.99 for 6 month service!!! Why would I pay $30-40 for an extender that cost me $80? Then tech support tried telling me I needed a new router and extender and if I BUY NOW - I get 10% discount, but only if I buy now! Wow - what a deal---NOT!! WHAT A MONEY GRAB! Linksys-Cisco YOU OUGHT TO BE ASHAMED OF YOUR SELFS!!! And in this economy too!

The FIX:

What they would not tell me without picking my pocket for at least $30 minimum is if you locate the tiny hole on the extender and depress it with a pen for 8 seconds - the extender will reset itself and allow the computer/router to locate the extender and connect!!!

It's now working fine and I did not have to pay $30-40 or buy a new router as they suggested. So, the message is: buyer beware and if you are beyond the 90 days, don't be fooled into spending needless money for what may be a simple fix!!

And when I do get ready to buy another router or extender -- it WILL NOT be a Linksys-Cisco! Fool me once, shame on you, fool me twice, shame on me.

title: I like it, but with some reservations
text:
First of all, I got my G1 for $380.00 from Amazon's Warehouse Deals, in brand new condition, so I cannot complain too much. A mini-DSLR-like camera for $70 less than the price I paid for my LX3 compact a little over a year ago. But while I like the camera a lot, there are a few things I don't like about it.

The fully articulating LCD screen is fantastic. I simply cannot go back to a camera without one, and will probably buy the Canon 60D if I ever decide to get a DSLR.

G1 Pros:

Good build quality overall

Articulating Screen

Nice electronic view finder

Great manual focusing function (manual focus assist allows you to easily choose the point of focus and magnify it by 10x so it is easy to get focus spot-on)

compact size

Sharp kit lens (14-45)

interchangeble lenses

G1 cons:

The histogram does not function in manual mode...this is really a pain at times. How this was allowed on the final G1 product is beyond me; it may be a small camera, but it still was designed to appeal to serious photographers...and manual mode with no active histogram, what the hell? (the histogram does however function in review mode, and it functions fully in Aperture priority and shutter priority)

Auto bracketing is poorly implemented, at least for HDR. You have choices of 3 or 5 shots too tightly spaced, or you can choose 7 shots that only range from -2 to +2. So you either don't get the full dynamic range that you need, or you get 7 shots which eats up memory and wastes time...and it still might not give you the full range that you need. For general shooting, it might be fine, but for HDR it is very inefficient.

High isos not too good. I think iso 800 is as high as you would want to go.

The rubber around the evf tears out easily and is difficult to put back into place.

No video...this really isn't a big deal for me, but it would be nice to have video capability for the rare occasion that I might want it. (the G2 has video, but the lens is apparently not quite as good quality as the lens that comes with the G1)

Photos appear brighter on the LCD than they do when transferred to the computer (dialing down the color and brightness of the LCD helped with this)

Summary:

I like the size of the G1 and I love the fully articulating screen. For me it strikes a good balance between DSLR performance and compact size. I usually carry my cameras in a bag anyway, and the G1 fits easily into many small bags...even with an extra lens and accessories, it is not much of a burden.

UPDATE: 2-25-2011 The G1 is really growing on me and it just feels right to me now. No, it is not the smallest, no it doesn't have THE best image quality, and it can be challenging in low light, but it strikes a really nice balance for me. I only want, and can only afford one camera right now, and the G1 really hits the sweet spot. Once accustomed to it, it handles really well, and just takes some great pics.

The build is beautiful, it just oozes quality. It is like a little brick in my hands, and I mean that in a positive way; it is very substantially built. I owned the Fujifilm X20 briefly, but for about half the price, I like the X10 better.

The X10 doesn't have the multi-exposure feature (it does have some limited bracketing, but no creative laying of one exposure over the other) and there is no information in the viewfinder, and there is supposedly a slight improvement in image quality in the X20 that I won't be pixel-peeping for anyway. I actually miss the multi-exposure the most.

Fuji has a list of something like 51 improvements that were made to the X20 over the X10. To my mind, only a few of them were significant, many others were addressed in firmware updates, and others were just new advertising hype, about old things that were already present in the X10.

title: Nice alarm, with a few limits.  Not bad for the price.
text:
I really wanted to enjoy this alarm clock, but there are a few detracting issues that caused a good amount of stress and concern overall.

Pros include that it does the thing where it brightens over time before the alarm goes off. Really nice feature, and the illumination on it is really good. It can get super bright, enough to light up a room (to the point of being almost painful to look at when set to max). Most of the functions can be switched on and off via Alexa or the custom app from the manufacturer, but it does require allowing access to a third part "plugin", and wifi access to the device. It can auto-set the time from the device you use to set it up, or from network, or manually via buttons (with a limitation).

Cons include that only way to get this on the network is via an app, which you must install to access the online functionality. Also, two of the four alarms are settable via the buttons on the device; while alarms 3 and 4 are ONLY settable via the custom app provided by the manufacturer. (No, you can not set the times for any of them via Alexa; only toggle the alarm on and off.) Speaking of the buttons, there's plenty of them, and all are very small and circled around the edge. They're all about 1/4" square, and white with slight indents for the icons (which are impossible to see, feel or differentiate without the manual present). The snooze button is twice the size of the normal ones, and centered at the top, but it's awkward to hit and still rather tiny (about 1" by 1/4"). To shut off the alarm via button (any alarm) you can hit the "alarm 1" button, which is the 5th button up on the left... easy to hit, right? Alarm 1 button also shuts off all alarms, not just alarm 1. The alarm sound options are one of 7 canned sounds (including silence, in case you just want the light effect), and the radio. Finally, while the listing says one can schedule the alarm by day of week, that function appears to not work at all. I've tried several variations of which days to set alarms, and found that the alarm always goes off that the set time every day. The app (and Alexa) can do simple IFTT things to turn alarms on/off automatically, but that's kind of a pain to setup, and relies on there servers working for free forever (good luck with that). I asked for help on the function via the app, and the app later said I had a reply, but there was no way to check on the reply. I did not get an e-mail (checked spam filters, etc). Also, you need an e-mail account to "activate" the app via a verification code...

One of the harder parts of this is that the manual is often confusing, and it's not clear how to do the thing you want to do with the buttons, the app, or connecting to Alexa. Like many of the Alexa enabled devices out there, this requires a plugin app, which means you have to grant permission to the manufacturer to access the system, and the network you're on. It also means that if (when) the manufacturer decides to turn off that server, your service for that device goes away as well. While many of the settings on this CAN be programmed via the buttons, it's much harder to do, and effectively eliminates the use of alarms 3 and 4, which (due to not having any buttons to access) are not programmable nor can be toggled on/off other than via the app/service.

Overall, a nice product. But the dependency on an external server, and lacking clear ways to program some of the features via buttons on the device is a real let down. They could have easily come up with a combo to program all 4 alarms with the 15-ish buttons on the device, but didn't. You can set all kinds of random things via buttons (one is dedicated to the color it lights up with...), but not alarms 3 and 4, which one would think is kind of central to an alarm clock.

title: Great monitor for the price
text:
I picked up two of these for a work from home system. I prefer to run my monitors in vertical mode to make reading documents easier, and wanted displays that would work in that orientation. These did not disappoint. The default stand is a sturdy metal base and pole, very simple to attach. The mount is a simple VESA click-in (with 100mm holes optional). The stand can rotate to portrait or reverse portrait mode, and the monitors run well in that orientation. The fonts are crisp, and because of the extra display size and slightly lower resolution, they're easy to read. The display is bright, the OSD menu is rather simple to use once you get the hang of using the little joystick (and realize you can press it down as a click action), and the functions all make sense.

Cons:
The speakers on these are pretty much useless. At 100% they're barely audible, and project out from the bottom of the screen in horizontal mode. They're on and at 70% by default, even when nothing is plugged in. If you use a display only interface (VGA/DPort), and there's no audio plugged in, the monitor will buzz or humm occasionally. You can mute it in the menu, but honestly it should default to mute if there's no audio plugged in.

On one of the two monitors I got, the bottom right corner has a slight darker/bluish tint to it, almost like something is pressing on the screen lightly. It's a super minor defect, so I'm ignoring it for now, and hoping it's not a sign of something more going wrong with it.

As another review noted, the panel doesn't reach the edge of the display, leaving about 1/4" around the top/sides, despite the bezel being super thin. It's better then the last monitor pair I had, which had 1/2" bezel all around, but it's still there. Not unexpected, thanks to the review here, but still disappointing.

There is also a significant color delta between the two monitors, depending on it you use VGA, DPort or HDMI for input. If you change input type, you effectively have to re-color-balance the display again. Not the worst, and they give you three "modes" to save color settings into (probably just for this), but still annoying.

title: Delivered what they promised, reasonable deal.
text:
This was a refurb, as stated, and was in reasonable shape for what it is. The system was clean of junkware, has a legit version of Win10 installed, and all the hardware they said was in it, was. The SSD was relatively low runtime, per diagnostics. The case had a few dings and scratches, but that's expected of a refurb. It came with a beefy power cable, a new-ish keyboard, and an optical mouse still in it's sealed bag.

So why am I dinging it a star? Because they were kind of sloppy on the refurb side.

Hardware: It has a new-to-it power supply. I know because it doesn't match the model, lacks the header to hold the front fan shroud in place, and wasn't screwed in, at all. Sliding about half an inch when pushed. Happily it was packed in 15 yards of bubble wrap, so no damage. Despite having replaced the supply (1/4 of the size of the case), the internals had a good amount of dust. How you leave that in, I have no idea, but they did. title: Awesome radios, with nice features if you're tech-ish.
text:
These radios are great. They have plenty of channels and several nice features that allow for limited privacy even in a shared spectrum area.

With a cable (yes, buy one, you'll want it) and support software (from dealer, very responsive) you can set several options. Those include battery save/scan cycle intervals, voice announce, and several per channel options, including a custom DCS and/or voice scrambling (garble). Mind you, scrambling on these has limits. This isn't encryption as much as it is re-ordering sample chunks (~10ms intervals?). This introduces a slight propagation delay, but does make conversations harder to hear. If one talks slowly though, you can still make out 80% of it. Better than nothing though.

Hardware wise they're built very solid, have a great range, and good battery life. The charger is well built, and can hold/charge a battery with or without a radio attached (so can charge a spare alone). The only down-side I found is that the VOX feature on these is... limited. Even at the highest level, the mic sometimes has problems hearing/maintaining enough to use it reliably vs the PTT button. It may work better with a headset, but with the built-in mic, it's not very functional. Overall, that was the only negative I could find, and for the price, and all the other features it has, it's a great buy for the money.

UPDATE July 22: After a month or so, these radios have continued to impress. There are a few nice features not noted (voice alert for low battery, for example), and scanning both open and DCS coded channels. Used on a 12 acre area with a large ravine, and all parties could hear clearly. That includes at far ends and in the ravine, where even cell signals and other radio tends to fall or and/or vanish. Very impressed with the clarity and strength overall. Battery life tends to be significant as well, with standby time in the 2-day range.

For what I use it for, it's running under 2% most of the time, and showing no difficulty handling multiple streams to several devices from Prime and/or a local server. title: Interesting cheap 2.5Ghz Wifi module
text:
I currently have a desktop system that I wanted to put on a rolling stand to enable easier movement around the house. I thought this little add on would be perfect for the job. While it could do the job, it's painfully slow at doing so.

The Pros:
* Installs on Windows 10 on it's own (doesn't need the driver CD)
* Finds and connects with 2.5Ghz based systems (up to 801.11n)
* Provides reasonable connectivity with the wifi point.
* Chipset provides AP capabilities in some OSes.
* Has a reasonable range, slightly better than other USB dongles tried.

The Cons:
* Slow speed. Best I saw was closer to 50Mbps, averaging 30Mbps.
* Custom software on the CD doesn't actually work in Windows 10.
* AP based software fails to work in Windows 10.
* Antenna neither detaches, nor rotates, only bending up to 90°.

To be clear, I attempted initially by simply plugging the USB dongle in, allowing Windows to select it's own drivers. I did have it check, once online, to find any updates. After a poor speed performance, I decided to try installing the drivers/software on the CD. The CD software has custom drivers and a resident app, providing profiles and settings for optional features. Unfortunately, it would appear that the software is not fully linked in with the current version Windows 10, failing to establish a wifi connection. Even after a reboot, I needed to use the windows connection assistant to setup the connection.

I tested by saturating the connection by copying a 2G file from a wired system, with both devices using SSD drives. With a direct line, I got well over 900Mbps, and on an older laptop with integrated 801.11n card I saw a peek of 64Mbps, averaging about 60Mbps. Even with the current drivers and software, the best I was able to get from this device was a peek of 45Mbps (or about 4.5MBps), averaging 31Mbps, which is under 1/4 of the speed advertised.

The antenna not rotating, and only bending up to 90° in one direction is also problematic. This means there are only three possible antenna positions: bend at 90° as shown in the package, bending at 45° upward, or straight out as pictured with driver CD. It can not be rotated or removed, and if the hinge is examined, one can see it's simply a wire routed in a plastic shell.

title: Nice cable, but not true USB-C 2.0, only USB 2.0
text:
First: This is for a USB-C to USB-C "2.0" cable.

The first thing that struck me when I got this was the thinness of the cord. True USB-C cables are thicker out of necessity, in order to have the number of wires at the proper thickness to handle the current and data rates they use. On closer inspection of the text, I noted that while this claims to be a "2.0" cable, it gives the max speed of 480 Mbits/s, which is actually USB 2.0 spec. This means it is likely a USB 2.0 cable (not USB-C 2.0), that happens to have USB-C ends.

Since USB 2.0 spec can only handle up to 5v and 500ma, I do not believe it will handle a true 60W load. Given the size of the wire, it would be unsafe, as it would require lines thicker than what could possibly be inside this cable housing.

Data transfer tests and charging test bear this out. It caps out at around USB 2 speeds for data, and can not deliver true fast-charge current using a fast-charger module. It can do normal USB slow charging over time, and does transfer data (slowly). I suspect if I open this cable it would only have 4 wires internally, and enough circuitry (diodes mainly) to handle the plug orientation stuff to allow current and data flow. Looking edge-on into the cable, only a handful of pins are even present (6-ish of the 24 possible), which is another indicator of it's design.

For the misleading advertisement, and a clearly a false claim (60W), I ding it twice. If you want something to connect two USB-C devices with low power and slower data rates, this is a cheap alternative to a more expensive cord. If you want fast charging, or full data rates, this is not the cord you're looking for.

text:
I have several remote devices that combine to make a reasonable multi-media center. The goal for this remote was to remove the 5 separate remotes needed now to control things and merge them into one. This seemed to fit the bill, and eventually did, with a caveat or two.

To start with, I got the 8 device version of this, not the 6 device one. The style is nice, and the buttons are reasonably sized in most cases. It takes two AA batteries (not included) and comes with a paper list of thousands of codes to use based on brand and device type. The coloring for the backlighting is a nice light blue, which remains on for several seconds after the device is used. Programming is described above in the add, which is important, because there is NO DOCUMENTATION on how to enter programming mode that ships with the device.

On the up-side, the list of codes and supported devices is quite comprehensive, and I was (eventually) able to find the proper code for each device I wanted to program. The device selection buttons on the top are labeled (TV, DVD, BluRay, etc), but there's no need to program them to match the device type you're using. If you wanted to control 4 separate TVs, for example, you could program each of the 4 across the top to be TVs. The code numbers are not specific to the button type.

One ding I have against this is the lack of a feature it lists a code for, but does not actually support. The paper listing shows an entry for X10 controls under home automation (a very old powerline based system using RF predating Zigbee and such). While it lists three items for X10, the one that I cared about does not in fact work. This is probably a left-over from a previous model which had the required RF chip (which this model lacks).

The other major ding is the lack of an auto-search feature for codes by manufacturer. This device does NOT have the feature. So if you have an RCA sound system, for example, you have to manually enter and test each ID until you find one that works (powers on device). Then you have to validate the buttons you care about work. In some cases, several codes will power a device on/off, but the buttons are not all aligned to work properly. This makes discovering the code very difficult. In the case of the RCA entry, there are well over 20 possible codes. I really wish groups that made devices like this had a way to lookup the code given a manufacturer and model number.

Overall this is a great device for controlling multiple parts of an entertainment system for your home in one slightly complex remote instead of several simpler ones. If you're looking for one that supports an odd-ball manufacturer, this is likely your best bet outside of a programable one (which is more expensive and way more complex to setup).

title: Nice stand with poor quality control
text:
The stand arrives in a rather nice canvas carrying case, along with three large plastic spring-loaded clips. The case is split into three parts, the two side parts hold the stands, and the center holds the pole segments for the 10' pole.

The stands are a little odd until you figure them out. There are telescoping poles with twist-tightened screws that allow for various heights. The feet are connected at two places; at the top where the pipe goes through, and via a bar at the mid-point to a second base to which the bar is attached. As the pole base approaches the leg base, the legs form a tripod of various width, and the bar height is changed by up to a foot. That base is stored all the way down, so that the pole-base is lower than the feet. When in use, the pole-base can be pulled nearly to the top of the foot-base. This is likely why some people think the base is not able to reach full height, as it's not obvious that the leg bars can in fact fully invert, giving the center polls more height.

The cross bar is rather light, and comes in 4 segments. Two segments have a slotted hole to mount over the screw top of the tripod stands. Three of the segments have small connector bits that fit within the pole and are riveted on one side. These compress and snap into holes on the other side of a given pole. You can use two, three, or all four poles, though with all four there is a slight bowing just from the weight of the pole, yet alone anything hanging from it.

Unfortunately, the riveting done is not very well quality checked. As a result, one of the poles in my set has the rivets rotated nearly 20 degrees from where the matching holes are in the other end, where there others line up properly. This means either the prongs won't go through the holes, or if they do the pole has a 20 degree twist, making the whole stand unstable. The only fix is to drill holes to match and line up with the off-center riveted pole so it can line up properly (which is difficult and messy to do with thin rounded metal that you don't want to dent in any way).

Overall to get the proper height, one must have the legs fully extended, which makes the stand a little wobbly. If you can handle it being a few inches under the max height, it's far more stable, assuming your bars all line up.

I'll also note that the upper pole is just wide enough to not be able to handle most standard clip-rings, which are often used to hold light curtains and such. They simply don't fit over the top pole due to the width.

Overall, this is a reasonable kit for the price, but the quality control is rather low. That it comes with no instructions (something one really needs for the legs), and lacks quality control enough to have a reliable kit, I can't really recommend this for most setups.

title: Nice colorful connectors
text:
One of many tasks I do on occasion is running network wires from one place to another. That often involves making a small batch of normal cables, or cutting a specifically long run after properly routing it around. That often involves putting heads on these cables, and/or jackets to help identify them in a patch closet on occasion.

I saw these and though they would be great for several tasks, and could fix two issues at once. One is that they
would really stand out from the normal clear connectors and common rubber color jackets. The other is that I rather despise rubber jackets often used in networking. They tend get in the way more from disconnecting when you want to than they protect a cable from accidental disconnects.

These connectors and jackets are all quite colorful, and of course the jacket that ships with them are matching (and made of the same material). The head allows the wires to pass through, which makes lining things up and validating before the crimp much easier with the right tool. And the jackets click and lock on to the head when slid up, making it a near seamless unit.

These jackets have a small guard,, which is about as flexible as the clip itself and a little larger. It's also made in such a way that it almost becomes a useful lever to push the clip when you want to, rather than a hinderance to ever releasing.

The only problem I have with them is the toughness of the jacket plastic. The guard and tension reliever are almost as rigid as the connector itself, being made of effectively the same plastic. I've had at least two of the tensioners break on me already after only a few wiggles from use with a laptop, leaving a sharp pokey bit on the line. Being harder plastic, they're not quite as easy as the softer rubber jackets to peel off of the line when they fail and start drifting around.

title: Nice board, Also works with ESP8266 with proper libraries
text:
[[VIDEOID:aeff8f298a4d8cd55e4201c205fa6345]] I saw this and thought it could be useful with a few project ideas I had on the table. As I tinker with more ESP architectures that just UNO R3s, I was hopeful the hardware would prove to be compatible with other systems. One thing I did NOT expect was the size. Note that this thing is large, 12" by 6" roughly, and the LEDs are large SMD mounted, in bright red.

Hardware:
The hardware itself is pretty well designed and laid out. There's a rather simple set of pins that make an SPI bus to pipe in data. There's a cable connector on each side of the device, which should (per documentation) allow you to string several of these together, either horizontally or vertically (per arrows on the back of the device). There are convenient screw posts in the plastic, and the plastic itself on the bottom edge has hole for a mounting plate. The entire panel has an indent to allow some type of fill (think caulk) to bind them together nearly seamlessly. And the back of the board is somewhat protected by the harnessing of the plastic frame.

For power, this thing is a bit of a beast. You CAN run it off just driver current from a device, but it's rather dim if you do. There's a power connector on the back for a 5V supply, that then amplifies to a rather bright display. The downside to the power adapter is it sticks out from the back at a 90° angle (pictured), where all the other cables could optionally lie flat. Future designs with this mounted parallel to the board would make this far better for most applications.

The software for this... Is a mess. On their site, you need to figure out that this product ID is E908 to get their zip file, which has outdated libraries for the Uno board timer and an ancient version of the DMD board driver. The demo relies on a timer only on the Uno, and is not compatible to other devices. If you instead just grab the DMD2 library in the library manager (which their documentation tells you to do, but then never uses), you can simply run it with that directly.

Because of the way the display works, you must refresh it often. On the Uno an internal interrupt timer is used for this, which not all boards have in abundance. The display itself has no memory, so you need to get back to powering the LED before it goes out after a refresh cycle.

========= ESP 8266 info ===========
You may have noted that in the video posted I used an ESP8266 on a generic NodeMCU. Since this board only has a couple timers available, the DMD2 library winds up having to use timer0, which is also used to aid in running Wifi. You can only have one or the other active at the same time, but you can switch quickly between them (though you may drop packets). The proper pinout for an ESP8266 is : A->D0, B->D6, R->D7, OE ->D3, CLK->D5, SCLK->D8. For the code, remove all timer references (DMD2 does it internally) and change the board declaration to the SPI variant, specifying the GPIO for the off pins as such:
SPIDMD dmd(D_WIDE, D_HIGH, 0, 16,12,15); // GPIO for OE,A,B,SCLK respectively.

Power drain and watchdog: I did note that in some setups the system would at times catch and reset via watchdog. I suspect that was due to the power source dipping and causing a brown out. If you're going to drive the board at high intensity, I suggest having at least a 2A supply. Possibly more if you're going to start chaining them together to make a real marquee or such.

Overall, this is a pretty cool pre-built panel. If you enjoy tinkering with hardware, and can do the basics of wiring up a device, then this is a simple way to get a lot of visual bang for your buck. At the current price, it's a pretty good deal for something of this size and quality.

title: Solid serial dongle with full 9-pin support
text:
I've seen lots of sub-par serial connectors on the market, so when I saw this one for a low price I was somewhat sceptic. No reason to be. Not only is this a solid little converter, but it has lots of features that many dongles in it's price range don't come close to matching.

Software wise, this auto-detects and installs it's drivers in Windows 10 and Ubuntu (18.06) on it's own. The driver is detectable by anything that can see a COM port, and the typical mechanism for using CTS/DTR and the like work wonderfully over USB. I was able to flash a rather picky ESP8266 module with this with no issue.

I'll note that the hardware is also quite solid, and well encased. The pins are labeled on the board, with the extended pin set, as well as a separate 5V out, which is a true 5v, even when VCC is set to a lower voltage via jumper. This is great for supplying 5V to a module that then wants to use a TTL level that differs for communication. So a 5V module using 3.3V serial can all be powered off this one dongle, assuming it stays under the required amperage.

I'll also note that the cable that comes with it is very much made for this device. One side is a 6x1 female pin header, with six split female 1x1 headers on the other side. Yes, you can use random other header cables if you like, but that it comes with it's own is nice.

The only improvement I would suggest is that the cable that ships with it be keyed and/or shift colors to match low-voltage standards. (eg. VCCis red, GND is black, etc) Simple enough to do with a pin and a few seconds, but it would be better if it was setup that way by default. And given that's the worst I can say about it? Awesome product.

title: Cheap, too cheap to bother returning, otherwise I would.
text:
I have at least two other devices like this that I've used for most of the past 2 or 3 years to convert some nice wired gaming headsets into bluetooth headsets for use online. I love them, but after a few years, battery life is shortening, so I'm looking for new options (as that model is no longer made). I thought this was a reasonable option, but it's really not.

Pros: Small form factor, pairs with most bluetooth sources, comes with converter.

Cons: TONS. Battery life is quite short (under 3 hours). In stereo mode the sound is nice, but there's upwards of a 2 SECOND DELAY, making it worthless for anything but listening to music. In headset mode, there's no delay, but it sounds like the audio is playing through a wet cloth. This isn't just mono, so the mic can use the other channel for return bandwidth. It's also cropped on both the high and low end, making it sound muffled and dull. So those are your choices: Reasonable but delayed stereo audio, or muffled mono with no delay and a mic (on device).

I'll note that I tested this with at least 3 devices, including a phone, a laptop with BT3, and a desktop with BT5. All three had the same issues. None of these issues are present on my other BT receivers with the same sources; all others provide reasonable audio in mono/headset mode with no delays. So it's not the transmitters or drivers doing this, it's this junky hardware.

TL;DR: Unless you're using this JUST for listening to podcasts or music, skip this one. If it were more expensive, I'd bother with returning it. But it's frankly just more hassle that it's worth at this price.

title: Good choice for tapping into or splicing low voltage wiring.
text:
I purchased these to do work on a low-voltage electrical system in my golf cart. The existing lines for various lights run the length of the vehicle, and adding additional side reflectors was looking like a bit of a nightmare until I saw these. This pack has two sets of connectors, one for splicing pairs of wires together, and another for tapping into an existing wire to fork off another pair. I used mainly the latter, but did use one of the pair splicers to move/extend the line for one of the upper rail lights.

The connectors work rather well with 20 gauge wire. One set I had was 16 gauge, which worked only if I stripped the insulation first (but that's not their fault, it's rated for 18 to 22). For proper gauges, simply place the wire in the clamp system and press down until the wires are gripped in the tongs. They automatically slice through the shielding and connect with the wire inside. When using the tap style connectors, pay attention to which line goes to which, or you may wind up inverting your polarities! The path is easy to see thanks to the clear plastic. The grips can be pulled open again with a small screw driver if needed, but will leave the wires with a split in the insulation if you do. You'll probably never want or need to do so, but it's nice to know the option is there.

The only thing of note is that if you're not using 18 gauge wire (and maybe even if you are) these make no attempt at waterproofing the connection. If you're using these in an exposed system, or in an area with mild exposure (like under a golf cart), you probably want to have something to help with that, like hot glue, epoxy, or shrink wrap. Given the solid connection and ease of use, these definitely make simple fixes and add-ons easier.

The output is quite smooth and doesn't fluctuate much even if the input voltage does. It continues working cleanly well down into the 30v ranges. I will note that the 10A limit is rather hard edged. You don't want to go past it for long, so a 10A fast blow fuse is your best friend. I've got this running several 12V based items, including a few small display items and LED lighting (markers, headlights, glow lights, etc). This would likely be fine for a small radio as well, so long as the speakers aren't going much above about half the rated wattage.

The package is water proof, so long as you use proper connectors on the line endings. The whole case is a heat sink. If you're using it close to the 10A limit, it will get pretty warm. If you plan on doing that, best to bond it to the frame if you can, either via U-bolt or thermal epoxy, depending on your comfort level. For stand-alone use, it may be worth using a small 12v fan to cool it for heavier loads.
