title: Old and New, Best of Both worlds
text:
I have several IP cams that I've used for ages in my home setup. My main requirements for an IP cam to stay in my home is the ability to be totally local-controlled, and to be able to capture motion and have the video eventually wind up on my local system without a monthly service fees. You've be AMAZED at how few IP cameras pass that simple test.

This camera is a BLEND of the best of both worlds. It has a reasonable set of apps that allows for simple configuration and setup (Win/iOS/Android/Mac), as well a micro-web interface. The apps have options that allow for remote view (if desired) and to initiate device recording/pictures. It ALSO has the old-standard IPCAM micro-web server, complete with all the settings to enable the old-school functionality (like FTP push, 264/265 codec configs, etc). This means it can do BOTH the standard local control things AND shiny new "people detection" and remote view if you prefer it. You literally can't go wrong with this one.

The app/software is rather nice and has a good UI experience. I tried out the Android app, the Windows app, and the IPCAM web interface. The ONLY negative I had in this was getting it going initially. To configure it via Wifi (AP mode), you MUST use one of the apps. You can still config it via local web using a network cord though, so that's nice. Once the app connects, it can do most of the settings, though not all of them. Most notably, the app can only set alarm window 1 (where the web interface can do 4 regions, if you use ActiveX/IE/Edge).

The web setup is similar to the old IPCAM setup, just slightly updated. The main view still has the option to download the ActiveX component for use with IE (RIP). It's an updated version to what I had installed, and yes, you can still access it that way with the IETab extension for Chrome. But gone are the choices for push style on the front page, because the monitor page detects your browser version and provides the proper pusher automatically. Chrome/FF get HTML5 push (with audio!), IE/Edge get ActiveX, all else get a JS looper on frame capture.

Feature wise, this camera offers both motion/zone detection, and "Human tracking", which does image analysis to find what looks like a human outline in the image. This alarms can be ORed or ANDed which is SUPER nice if you want to capture any motion, with or without people. It also offers options for the camera lights, and how to operate them. You can do the normal on/off/auto, but included is another option of "smart lighting". The camera has both IR and white LED. Smart lighting runs IR until it detects motion, and then throw the white led on to get better images (and scare the crap out of the random ally cat as it traverses your porch a night...)

I will note that the motion zone setup menu item is still hidden from non-IE browsers in the web interface, and still needs the old ActiveX plugin when run in IE mode. You can set the boxes via URL though if you know the right commands, so it's less critical. The "masking" feature has gone missing, so you can't mask out areas to avoid reflections or what not. Probably less of an issue on PTZ cameras vs fixed, so not a huge loss.

Other differences from the older IPCAM interface include:
You have a choice of H.264 or H.265 compression profiles, and ratios, which is nice.
You do NOT have a choice of frame size. Stream1 is 1920x1080, Stream 2 is 640x352.
Audio capture DOES work, but is fixed at G711 8K 8-bit (and G726 was removed).
Input/Output volume is adjustable separately.
There is also an "audible alarm" and "lights on" option for motion detection.

If you have an older setup, where you're using standard bullet IP Cams (Zmodo, Wansview, IPCAM, or any of those older long-gone cameras)... This is the camera for you. If you want a snazzy new app based camera, with options of local device push notifications and remote-view, and cloud storage? This device is ALSO for you. And if you want to pick and choose what parts you want and don't want? This is a device you want to pick up.

Add the outdoor rating on top of all this, the good cable management, and the slide-on mount system, and this is a solid camera that should work for just about anyone. It has RTSP/RTMP support, ONVIF, several DDNS/Platform supports, and more. I'm likely to purchase another one or two of these, because products with this versatility are VERY hard to find these days. Finding this in a PTZ capable camera, with a reasonable sized sensor? This is the hotness. Get it while you can!

title: Great functionality, if you can get it setup and stable
text:
I picked this up to use as a bridge, to bring a wifi signal in from across a yard, to a small camper. Getting wifi inside the camper is difficult, being effectively a tin can. Putting this in one of the hood vents gave it coverage from the elements, while still having no metal between it and the distant router. sing the wizard, I then put it in bridge mode, connected to the house wifi as "input", and was able to then run a line to the PC from the jacks for reasonably stable network. It was delighted to see that it also worked as a repeater, meaning my phone could also connect to it via wifi and get back to the house internet as well.

This device can work in several modes, including being a traditional router, an AP device (for LAN parties?), and in a repeater/bridge mode. There's a wizard to set it up in each mode, which does most of the tinkering for you. You can go in and modify some settings as needed, but often changing things outside of the wizard makes it go unstable. Even just changing the remote network name and password, I found it easier to factory reset the device and run the setup wizard again.

Once you get it running in the proper mode, it works well. I will note that it's not designed for use with more than about a dozen devices. Around that point it starts to get a little jittery again. But if you're looking for a simple repeater, or a way to bridge from wifi back to a network line, this is likely going to be one of your cheaper and effective solutions.

My problems with the keyboard/mouse are 2 (two).
1) battery life: The manual states if they back lighting is 100% they keyboard will last for 15 hours. I believe max keyboard life with back light off is 2 weeks. So effectively I either have to charge it every night or turn off the back light. For the price of this device, I'd sure expect a decent battery!

2) No 'right click' button. The function button is large and takes up the place of the 'right click' and 'windows key' on a traditional keyboard. I can live without the windows button, as there is one on the left side of the space bar, but Logitech left out a helpful shortcut key by omitting the 'right click' key.

Overall the mouse is great with no issues, except battery life again.

If this combo were $50 i'd give it 4 or 5 stars. But for $150 Logitech is massively overcharging for what you get. Look elsewhere. I'm using this at work and charging it every night is possible but annoying. I won't be buying one to use at home though!

I'm debating returning this and just getting a standard old style dell keyboard for $20. My typing would improve and I'd save $100...

title: Exactly What I Needed
text:
I bought these radios to talk short range inside buildings. From being a licensed ham, I understood very well before buying these that the range would not be as described. That’s because the number given is with no obstructions. Basically if you went out in the desert you’d get a couple miles out of these radios. Don’t expect that in an area with mountains, trees, or being indoors. Especially with the tiny, non-detachable antenna. These radios program with my baofeng cable using chirp. I didn’t see this specific model on the list in chirp, but I don’t have the lastest version, and since many other brands make basically the same radio as this, I just selected the WLN KD-C1 from the list and it works. It gives an error on the first try but just upload/download the frequencies again and it will work. My baofeng UV-5R’s made a loud popping noise when using a speaker mic or earpiece every time a button was pressed and these radios are significantly better with speaker mics and earpieces. These radios are simple to use and that’s exactly what I wanted.

These are listed as license free, but they are 3 Watts and can transmit on the ham frequencies. Unless the law is only radios with a detachable antenna need a license, you should probably get a license. Although the signal doesn’t travel very far, I’d get a license anyway.

title: Almost perfect.
text:
For a medium sized camera this case is almost perfect. It has a hard shell front under the nylon covering to protect the lens area. For added protection it also has a padded back. Inside, the back area was smartly lined with a soft fleece to protect the camera's LCD screen. There is also a large pocket for your USB cable; however this pocket is too large and loose to hold extra SD cards--with any jostling they would likely slip out of the pocket into the case itself. That's a huge oversight, as there is no other place in the case to keep extra cards: this is the case's only flaw. The case of course comes with a strap that attaches to two exterior hooks, a belt loop strap down the back, and a solid zipper that keeps the case tightly closed.

In terms of size, this holds my Panasonic LX3 with a little room to spare, even with that camera's protruding lens. Smaller, pocket sized cameras with lenses that retract all the way into the body would probably be too small and bounce around inside. As designed, the case would likely be big enough for the likes of the Canon Powershot G11 (although that's just a guess), and of course smaller flash camcorders (as was intended).

In summary:

Pros:
Hard shell front, padded back.
Fleece lining at the back to protect camera LCD screens.
Good size without feeling too bulky.

Con:
No small pocket to securely hold SD or other memory cards--cards would likely slip out of the pocket into the case. (How did Case Logic miss this? A small SD card pocket seems like a logical inclusion for any digital camera case.)

title: Great headset for price
text:
For the price this is the best headset I've owned. I did really like my last one, a Jawbone Icon, but that one was over twice the price of this Jabra, and broke into three pieces after I dropped it on a wood floor. So this Jabra is my replacement. After over a week of use I'm happy to have it. The pros outweigh the cons. My list of each is below, with only one real con from my perspective.

Pros:
1. Easy setup: My iPhone didn't even require the headset's passcode, it just connected automatically.
2. Great Clarity: Jabra has always made good headsets and this is the clearest of the three or four Jabra devices I've owned.
3. Battery: After a few uses battery life seems strong, I got a whole week of occasional use and standby time before I had to recharge it. Heavy use would probably require daily charging.
4. Fit: The thin loop of wire that fits around the ear initially seemed far too loose, but it pivots in its fitting and therefore can be adjusted to fit snugly with a simple turn of the headset downward against your cheek. Additional rubber nubs for the inside of your ear and loops for the outside are included in the box (as is the charger, of course).

Con:
1. Voice Control (iPhone): Initially I was thrilled to notice that pressing the headset once activated my iPhone's Voice Control Feature. But then I realized that it almost never (only 1 out of 5 attempts) accurately recognized the actual voice command I was giving it. This was under reasonable usage conditions (driving at moderate speed, windows up, no music playing, etc.) This is unfortunate as I means I will still have to hold my iPhone directly up to my mouth to use the Voice Control feature.

Overall this is a great bluetooth headset for the price.

title: Very thin, very fast.
text:
This Freecom 500GB USB 3.0 HD is extremely thin, thinner than my iPhone 4S, just as tall and only a little wider. Easy to slip into a pocket. It's magnesium enclosure looks just like the casing on Apple's aluminum MacBooks, and looks good next to Apple's aluminum iMacs as well.

Equally impressive as its looks is its speed. For a small, external hard drive without its own power source (it draws power from the computer to which it is connected), this is a very speedy little drive. It has just one USB 3.0 port, but it is backwards compatible with USB 2.0. I do not have a USB 3.0 port on which to test this HD, but I ran two speed tests transferring a large file both to and from the drive using USB 2.0 ports on two different machines. title: A great idea with a significant design flaw.
text:
*First Impressions*
I really wanted to like this Monster iMotion Carplay device. It has a motion sensor that allows you to control your iPod/iPhone/iPad music playlists with simple hand gestures. The hand-motion based input accepts three simple hand gestures as commands: wave your hand to the right to skip ahead one track, wave it to the left to go back a track, and hold you hand still to either play or pause the music. A simple concept, however I've realized that it only works well under certain conditions. And the Monster iMotion seems to suffer from a significant design flaw which I discuss below.

First impressions were great. I plugged the AC and AUX connectors into my dash and connected my iPod Nano to the iMotion. I picked a playlist and started driving. I put my hand in front of the sensor and after a few tries (to figure out the speed my hand needed to wave to be accurately read by the sensor) I was playing, pausing, and moving forward and backward between the songs on my playlist. It was fun and easy and went well for a while.

On occasion the sensor seemed to interpret my attempts to forward to the next track as the play/pause command, but that may have been as much me getting used to making the correct gesture. Overall in the first 20 minutes of use sensor accuracy was good however and I was pleased with the device. Something I quickly realized is that the iMotion is fine if you are content to stick to one playlist but it does not allow you to navigate your iPod beyond whatever playlist/album/etc. you are currently listening to. To navigate between playlists/albums/etc. you still have to use the iPod interface as you normally would.

*Serious Design Flaw?*
After 20 minutes of using the iMotion device, however, I realized that it may well have a serious design flaw. At first I simply noticed that the songs were skipping ahead without any input from me. (Both my hands were on the steering wheel and the sensor was over a foot away from me.) Songs kept skipping forward, then stopped, then skipped forward again. This sequence happened repeatedly and I couldn't figure out why. Then I realized that a rapid succession of light and shadow passing over the face of the sensor was doing it. I was driving in the morning with direct sunlight streaming into my car. As I would make a turn, or drive where the sunlight passed through trees or something else that caused shadow and light to play across the face of the sensor, I noted that any series of shadows quickly passing over the sensor seemed to confuse it; the sensor interpreted these shadows as hand-gestures and started to skip forward through my playlist. It was annoying, and uncontrollable. Of course I realize that the work-around to this problem would simply be to turn the sensor away from the window or source of light/shadow, however that would also (at least in my case) mean turning the sensor away from the area where I could control it with my hand gestures, which of course defeats the purpose of using the iMotion device in the first place.

If the sensor is so easily confused by light and shadow, I simply don't see how this device, which exists to add convenience, will be useful to anyone who doesn't live under constant cloud cover or who perhaps drives mainly at night. I tried using it again later in the day, when the sun's light is higher and not so direct, and the sensor performed better but there were still a few occasions when some sort of light-shadow sequence caused it to start skipping songs forward again.

I don't like to post negative reviews but unfortunately this technical issue seems to be a real problem with the Monster iMotion. I won't be using it much as apparently I live in too sunny an area for the iMotion to function well for me.

I'm giving it three stars because it's a good looking device and a great idea, but it needs technological improvement to resolve the sensor issue. However it should work ok in for drivers in areas that aren't excessively sunny. (Could be a big seller in Seattle and Portland...)

In short:

Pros:
-Sound is very good as you would expect with Monster's gold plated 3.5mm AUX jack, etc.
-Compact unit has great Monster looks (Monster almost always designs attractive products)
-Clever AUX cable storage area helps keep AUX cord neat and tidy
-Flexible AC connector allows you to set sensor at many different angles
-Very convenient way to control your iPod playlist (provided you are content to stick to one playlist)

Cons:
-Major design flaw interprets light and shadows as hand gestures, causing unintended pausing/skipping/etc.
-Large Monster cable dongle was too big to work on my iPhone without removing the case
-No real need to use this with an iPhone 4S anyway, as Siri offers much more hands-free control via voice than the iMotion does with hand gestures
-Priced high for what limited functionality it offers

title: Great case but magnets are not well engineered
text:
After using this Belkin tri-fold cover for over two weeks I can only give this cover four stars. I really wanted to give it five, yet at times almost gave it three. It's built well and I love the feel--like a very tough, grippy suede. The cover shows the dirt but cleans off easily. The elastic strap that keeps the cover closed tightly works well--those of you who like Moleskine notebooks know exactly how this strap works. The inside material is very soft and seems unlikely to ever cause issues with the surface of your iPad. The various viewing angles achieved by folding the front cover are easy to position and hold steady.

However the biggest issue this Belkin iPad cover (at least my particular one) has is the magnets do not seem to line up well with the iPad itself. I have other iPad covers and when they close, the magnets in the cover turn the screen off immediately. With this Belkin cover the magnets do not always seem to line up as they should and once the cover is closed, half the time the magnets do not cause the iPad screen to shut off. This sometimes occurs even if I use the elastic strap to cinch the cover closed. This issue can be frustrating: I've noticed that my battery life goes down more quickly using this case than it does with other cases I own, as when I close the Belkin's cover I assume the iPad shuts off, but it hasn't and I come back a while later to find it still on. (Yes, I know there is a sound associated with the screen shutting off, but that sound does not play when the iPad is muted.)

Magnets in iPad cases are crucial, and need to work well. My experience with this Belkin case tells me that Belkin still needs to work this issue out. I considered giving the case only three stars due to the magnet issue, but everything else about the case--the look, feel, the grip--is great. So this case gets four stars, with reservations.

title: Small, fast, great color
text:
I have the day-glo/lime/traffic cone green Store'n'Go Flash Drive and it's a great color; great because it's such a garish green that you'll almost never fail to see it on your desk, no matter how much other junk is piled over this minuscule little thumb drive. It's nearly self-luminescent. It also has a nice rubberized casing which helps you hold it which really is a necessary feature, as this little drive is so small it would be hard to grip (or at least easy to slip) if it were smooth plastic or metal.

Data-transfer-wise it's average, hitting normal USB flash transfer speeds. I test it against a few other USB 2.0 flash drives (moving a 2GB file) and they all clocked in within a second of each other. So this Verbatim drive is on par with its competition.

If I have one criticism it's the feature described as the "Bonus key ring lanyard for mobile phones or key rings." If this flash drive cost more I would cry fowl here, "misleading advertising!" Because the "bonus keyring lanyard" is barely more than a piece of thin string (practically thread) with a tiny metal ring attached. I wouldn't trust this "lanyard" to not snap in a light breeze. But you are buying this for the 8GB, the color, the rubberized coating, etc. Not for the silly thread-lanyard.

So, if "small" and "cute" and "visible" describe your storage needs, this is the flash drive for you.

title: A great idea hobbled by lack of versatility
text:
You would think with a device like this you could project ANYTHING on your iPhone onto a wall. I was hoping to use this to project a few images and documents on the wall during a talk I recently gave. But alas, this hand-held projector ONLY lets you project photos and videos available in your iPhone/iPod's Photo app slideshow feature.

Very limiting. If that's all you want to do, this is an ok toy (but still pricey at $129). But if you want to project anything that is on your iPhone/iPod's screen, this is not the device for you.

Also, at relatively low lumens its output is pretty weak. Dark rooms are a must.

Finally, the new Apple dock connector (late 2012) will render this mini projector useless with new iPhones (i.e. iPhone 5) and iPods (late 2012) unless the adapter will work with this unit, but I have not tried it with the adapter.

I assume the manufacturer (General Imaging) will make a new unit that works with Apple's new connector. Hopefully they will also enable the new units to project anything on your iPhone's screen, not just what's in the Photo app. If they do not, this handheld personal projector will remain a one-trick pony.

text:

title: Fast setup, fast connection, just wish it had an inline plug
text:

Data speed seems great, but I did not do any speed tests. Seems far more rapid than my wifi for sure.

If I have one complaint with these and other powerline networking adapters is that they have no inline electrical plug. Given the size of these units, and the fact that like most people my outlets near my cable and broadband router require additional plugs for Blu-Ray players, game consoles, etc., I have no outlets to spare. These powerline adapters MUST be plugged directly into a wall outlet, they DO NOT work if plugged into a powerstrip. So you give up a crucial wall outlet by using these, which, because of their size, often mean sacrificing both outlets or resorting to adding additional powerstrips. A bit of a pain. So it would be great if these adapters had an additional three prong plug that you could then use to attach whatever device(s) were previously connected directly to the outlet.

If however you have an outlet to spare, these adapters work great for getting data to a far corner of your home at great speed.

title: Hands Down the Best Battery Pack for the Zombie Apocalypse*
text:
*As long as the Zombies don't take down the cell phone towers.

In case of Zombie Apocalypse, this is the USB battery pack you will want. Forget those namby-pamby sleek little battery packs with their cute colors and silly names. You won't last 10 seconds in an undead world with those. This one has "Hand Turbine Power," dang it. It's got a flipping' CRANK that you can turn and make power and charge your cell phones and other USB devices and I GUARANTEE you the Zombies won't see that coming. Sucker undeads.

I imagine two scenarios for this battery pack: Before Zombie Apocalypse (BZA) and After Zombie Apocalypse (AZA).

BZA: During BZA, this battery pack is kind of overkill. It's just a big heavy battery pack that you can charge via a conventional USB cable (included) when connected to your computer or home electrical outlet. The hand crank turbine thing is not needed, unless you want to impress your friends with demonstrations of your AZA readiness. Which leads us to...

AZA: Once AZA arrives, when you are on the run without access to the grid (because the grid was destroyed in your part of the world and you and your friends and possibly some suspected traitors in your midst but you just can't be sure are traveling together to some rumored part of the former USA that may still have power but you have to fight through hundreds of miles of undead territory first and you are pretty sure the chick you picked up in the last town has some latent form of the zombie disease but the leader of your group who is a total moron but is nevertheless unaccountably charismatic thinks this that girl is like totally hot even tough she's a bit of a b*&%^ and you just know there is gonna be trouble), you can HAND CRANK this Eton battery pack to generate power to charge your USB phones, iPads, etc.

Don't misunderstand. You WILL NOT be playing Angry Birds during the Zombie Apocalypse by generating electricity with this battery pack. Unless you are in a safe place and you find you have hours to spend cranking the handle of the "Turbine Power Generator" to charge your iPad. I know because it took me almost 5 minutes of cranking (at the suggested rate of two cranks per second) to get my iPad Mini from an 89% charge to 90%, at which point my fingers were a bit sore and not in any shape to fling electronic birds at snorting pigs. But I generated power, and that was A GOOD THING. At least it would be in the context of AZA. However I was in the context of my well-lit BZA kitchen, so it seemed like a bit of a waste of time, frankly.

So, let's sum up, shall we? So long as civilization doesn't go to hell in a hand basket (i.e. electrical grid destroyed, cell phone towers torn down for use as undead BBQ skewers which obviates the need to charge your iPhone, etc.), you probably won't have much use for this battery pack. But once we are AZA, boy will you be glad you have it. And if it all really does go to hell in a hand basket, this Eton battery pack has one awesome feature that ISN'T EVEN ADVERTISED. That is this: the Eton Rechargeable USB Battery Pack with Hand Turbine Power is HEAVY and SHAPED like a BRICK, and the "Hand Turbine" crank folds neatly into the battery pack's body, which all fits so nicely--and with perfect balance and heft--into the palm of your hand. Can you say "Hello Mr. Zombie, meet Mr. Battery Pack Brick?" (If not, practice until you can. You know what they say about preparing for the worst.)

Bottom Line: Until the Zombie Apocalypse occurs (BZA) I can't imagine you'll be inclined to get much use from this Eton battery pack with "Hand Turbine Power," as it is pretty heavy and not nearly as portable as those sleek little battery packs with their cute colors and silly names. But AZA, you will be soooo glad you have it.

Just be careful what you wish for.

(Readers, please note additional helpful information in the Comments that follow this review.)

title: A very nice case but does not seem to fit Retina iPad Mini
text:
The feel and look of this case are great. The canvas cover is even nicer than the photos make it appear. It grips well, the plastic is sturdy, the magnetic on/off feature in the cover works great. Even the elastic strap that holds it closed is well positioned. It was setting up to be my favorite case.

However I have a Mini with Retina display. When I put it in this case I noticed that my Mini did not quite click all the way into the plastic frame ("molded polycarbonate shell") of the case. It was almost all the way in, but never just quite. But it still held. So I was careful with it for a few days, and when my Mini never slipped out I figured it was going to work fine.

For the record, at the time of this review the Amazon website does not indicate that this case is Mini with Retina display compatible, but the Case Logic website does say this case is both Mini and Mini with Retina compatible. ("Whether working, reading or catching up with friends, these iPad® mini and iPad® mini with Retina display cases make it a snap.")

So, after about a week of use I noticed that the corners of the "molded polycarbonate shell" were cracking and chipping away. I never once dropped the case or did anything that might cause damage to it other than normal use, and that for only a short time. After looking closely it seemed to me that my Mini with Retina (which per Apple specs is 1mm thicker than the regular Mini) was putting additional stress on the corners of the shell. Now that it is chipped I am far less confident that it is capable of securely holding my Mini with Retina display and I am of course a little disappointed, because otherwise it's a great case.

title: Love Razer, Great Sound from these Headphones, but What's with the Green Cord?
text:
I'm a big fan of Razer products, have been for years, so I was pleased to see them enter the headphone market.

Razer is known for their quality gaming products. I have used a Razer Naga gaming mouse for four years with almost no issues, and it still works like new.

With these Adaro headphones Razer claims to have focused on three things: comfort, sound quality, and durability. They've been successful at all three, but I think they dropped the ball a bit on style (more below), which could affect durability and does somewhat affect ease of use. Let's take those each in turn:

Comfort: I've been listening to them for the past month for around two hours a day, and they've never felt uncomfortable, nor have they slipped off or bothered me in any way. Once they are on I cease to notice them and just enjoy the music.

Sound: The sound is wonderful for this price range. These headphones probably won't wholly satisfy audiophiles, but I have found nothing to complain about. They have a nice mid-range and highs, and the bass is great too but without being overly engineered, as bass is with such competing headphones as Beats by Dr Dre. Razer clearly wants these headphones to be enjoyed while both listening to music and playing games, and so they have been tuned appropriately, and for $100 I can't think of a better available option for those purposes.

Durability (as well as Style and Build Quality): First, the good: he style is classic and clean. Mostly black with the cool Razer logo on the earpieces. The build quality is great, they seem solid and well built which both contribute to the style and comfort. Ear cups and headband are soft enough without being squishy. In short the Adaros don't feel cheap and don't look cheap. But what I don't like is the neon-green plastic cord that runs from the left earpiece to your audio device. However I readily acknowledge that this is a subjective complaint and so I chose not to give Razer fewer stars. I still think this is a five-star product, but I do hope Razer considers the following:

Dear Razer,

Why the floppy, garish neon green cord on these Adaro headphones? The cord may not be of low quality, but it gives the appearance of low quality. It's rubbery and feels like it could kink permanently. It holds too much tension and won't lay flat. (Exercising with these is a pain--don't take them to the gym.) In fact, I've noticed that Beats headphones use a similarly unwieldy cord. But Razer, you are Razer! Be Razer, don't try to be Beats! Finally, while black and green have always been your primary logo colors, the bright neon green of the cord makes me think of cheap plastic Chinese toys. Couldn't you have worked in the green in a somewhat less overpowering way?

Why, Razer? Why this silly green cord? Did Engineering lose a bet with Marketing? Look at the cord on your awesome Naga mouse--you know, the braided fabric one? The one that lasts forever and lays flat, doesn't flop around like a fish out of water? I know you know which one I mean. Heck, you used it on the Adaro, but alas only inside the headband itself. I can see it tucked up in there. THAT'S the cord I want running out of the left earpiece down to the 3.5mm AUX jack and into my iPod. Make it green if you must, but give me that perfectly engineered braided cable your other great products are known for. That would make it a true Razer headset.

That's what I want, Razer. But still, you get five stars for the Adaro. Just please consider being more like yourselves on Adaro 2.0.

title: Good for limiting volume, not too expensive if kids break them
text:
When our kids use their iPads in the car they need headphones. My criteria for kid headphones are:
1) Parents need to be able to limit the volume so kids don't damage their hearing
2) The headphones need to fit--i.e. not slip off every two minutes
3) Not too expensive: kids break things all the time, headphones included

These headphones do the job...but it's definitely a minimum wage job.

The volume maxes out at 85db, which while high is still lower than what a number of adult headphones (Beats, etc.) can reach.

Fit is fine. A little loose on the head of our smallest, but the foam ear pads are somewhat grippy-- they stayed on and that's what counts.

For $15 you can't expect too much more. If they last a year under normal kid abuse--being dropped on concrete, stepped on, stuffed in and out of backpacks, etc.--I'll be happy. If they last more than that, then good for them.

Sound is ok--distortion creeps in as the volume goes up. I wouldn't use it myself to enjoy my own music, but that was not why I got these. Kids can hear music and voices on their movies/games, and that's all that matters.

I agree with another reviewer that the Left and Right indicators are small are hard to see (they are on the inside of the band), but I don't think my kids care either way and having the phones on the wrong ears does not seem to affect the fit.

So, for the price these make a good set of kids headphones. They are cheap and cheaply made--don't expect them to last forever.

title: Does not work with all cases, but still a well-built Belkin product, so be aware of the incompatibilities before you buy
text:
I have a lot of Belkin products and generally find them to be well made and well designed. This dual lightning dock however falls short of what I have come to expect from Belkin.

First, it is very well built charger for Apple devices with lightning pin sockets. Of that there is no doubt. However the design has some shortcomings. First, it is far too long than necessary to accommodate only two devices. At over 6 inches, I would expect a product this size to accommodate at least four devices. This really doesn't save much space, as nice and well built as it is.

The reason for its length is that it integrates two manual dials that allow you to adjust the height of the lightning pins, so you can raise or lower them to best fit your device. That's all fine and good, but it turns out that the lightning pins themselves are housed in a nearly 1-inch wide base/shoulder that itself is not adjustable. What this means in practical terms is that if you have a case on your iPad or iPhone that that does not leave at least a half-inch space on either side of your lightning pin socket (on the bottom), the pins on this Belkin charge stand won't be able to make it past your case and into your device.

So, for example, I use two nice cases for my iPhone 6, from Urban Armor Gear and Speck. I can't charge my iPhone in this Belkin charger when either of these cases are on my phone. That's a hassle, as I don't want to take the case off every night to charge my phone, especially when I can use the Apple charging cable (and other OEM lightning cables I have from Amazon and, surprisingly, Belkin) just fine.

Similarly with my iPad, I have some cases that work, and some that don't. It seems that the more protective the case, the less likely it is to work with this charger, but it all comes down to the amount of space the case leaves on either side of the lightning pin socket.

To be fair, Belkin does note, in small print on the side of the box, "For best results, remove case to dock." But again, this is a hassle, when there are so many other ways to charge your iPhone/iPad without always removing the case.

So, bottom line, this Belkin charger will ONLY work if your case's opening around the lightning pin socket is wide enough. I try to protect my Apple devices so I use good cases, and very few of them work with this Belkin charger. As it is, I can't recommend this case for general use, but if you keep your devices "naked" or use minimalist cases, or simply don't mind removing your case(s) each time you charge your device(s), this charger may be fine for you. That said, it's an expensive charging station for what I consider to be rather limited day-to-day functionality.

title: Best iPad Air 2 case I've found so far for Protection, Weight and Design [Updated with Customer Service Resolution]
text:
I've come to really appreciate UAG cases over the past few years. Initially their cases seemed merely to look tough, but not be quite as tough as they looked. Recently however UAG has earned a lot of credibility for the toughness of their cases (meeting military specs, etc.), without losing their cool designs. In short, they look tough AND are tough, but without the overkill on weight and bulkiness that you get with something like an Otterbox.

WEIGHT
For example, this Rogue Folio case for my iPad Air 2 looks tough, is tough, but is also surprisingly thin and light. Measured on my kitchen scale it weighs in at 315g, whereas my iPad Air 2 itself weighs 441g. So for the protection it offers, the case really doesn't add significant weight, and I can read with it for hours quite comfortably.

PROTECTION
The corners of the case hold my iPad securely, I've never once felt like it might slip out. The cover closes and stays closed with the magnetic tab, and the inside of the front flap is very soft, so it won't scratch the iPad's screen. The rubber lip of the case (that rises above the screen) is also high enough that on the odd chance you drop the iPad screen-side down with the front cover open, your screen should be pretty well protected. The inside of the case is honeycombed, which I assume adds strength while reducing weight. You don't see this anyway once the iPad is installed. Also the "frog skin" on the exterior is nice and grippy, so it doesn't slide easily and is easy to hold.

COVER and VIEWING ANGLES
The front cover is attached to the back by means of a folding "hinge" that allows the case to provide the multiple viewing angles. As a result, if not held properly the front cover will swing down quite a bit (the "hinges" are not at the side of the case, but rather in the middle of the back), and some reviewers have found this to be an annoyance. However the front cover can easily be folded back 180 degrees and held there while reading, and it lays flat, so for me this is not a problem. Given the other features of the case, and the great design, the extra play in the hinges of the cover is something that doesn't bother me at all.

CONCLUSION
I looked around at all the available iPad Air 2 cases, and my criteria were: 1) offers good protection, 2) is lightweight, and 3) has a cool design. This Rogue Folio ticks all the boxes, so I am happy. The red color does take the occasional smudge, but seems to clean up pretty well.

UPDATE: After 8 months, one corner of the case started to come apart from normal use, peeling back about two inches. No major drops or anything particularly abusive to the case. Just everyday use. I emailed UAG Support, attached a photo, and in less than 15 minutes they had arranged for a replacement. Thanks UAG. That's customer service.

Sound:
I agree with other reviewers who found these to be tuned for bass. It's absolutely the case. The bass (for this price point) is solid, and the best sonic feature of these headphones. I found the mids to be quite muddy, and the highs as well. If you want to experience this, play Capital Cities "Safe and Sound" through the Grinds. Right after the 2 minute mark there is a nice bass drop, and it sounds great. But over the next 20 seconds, as the song rises back to the mids and highs, the clarity is lost and you find yourself wishing for more tunes in the low range.

Also, the ear pads are not cupped, so they sit on the surface of your ears rather than surrounding them. This allows more ambient noise in.

So, if you want a stylish, well-made and reasonably priced set of cans, and you LOVE music that is bass heavy, these are a good purchase. But if you play a lot of rock and classical, I'd suggest looking for something tuned more neutrally.

These ELAC B5 have replaced my Pioneers.

Build quality is very good. Black vinyl has a nice silky feel. Grills appear to be plastic with a cloth cover, and look almost better without the cover. Binding posts are gold plated and easy to spin.

Sounds is, for bookshelves, wonderful. I was more than happy with my Pioneers, but these B5s in another league, and for only about $100 more. The bass reflex is really the most impressive part. If you don't have a subwoofer, in a small room you might not even notice as the bass is remarkable for most music. Mids are fine and highs seem really open--Diana Krall was a treat on these things.

I placed mine about two feet from the wall, which seems to work great. They even perform quite well driven by my old Luxman receiver (circa 1990, a mere 30 wpc, I think), which says a lot for these relatively inefficient speakers (85db).

In short, I am pleasantly surprised. They will not replace the speakers of my main two channel system (Magnepan MMGs), but for casual listening and streaming music, they are fantastic. At $229 they seem to be a steal (one early review said Jones was providing "$20,000 sound for around $200", although of course that's hyperbolic), and for a little more (around $270) one can step up to the B6s, which also seem like a great deal.

Although I’ve never used a case with my previous Apple laptops, the new Macbook is so light it makes me nervous—I can see myself knocking it off a table just by sneezing or something. I’ve been using UAG cases almost exclusively for my iPhones and iPads, and they have been great (a few problems, but UAG customer service sent me a replacement right away), so I decided to try this Macbook case as well.

Fit: It snaps on fairly easily. Only the front bottom lip, near the trackpad, gave me any trouble. But that’s ok—I’d rather the case fit too tight rather than too loose. There is sufficient space at the USB-C port and AUX jack for most peripherals. When fully closed, the case actually takes some effort to open, but I realized that by gently pulling out the two “teeth” at the front corners, then pulling up, the case opens more easily.

Color: The Ash grey looks awesome with the Space Grey Macbook. It’s more transparent than it looks in the UAG photos, but not clear like the Ice color, which would seem to be the better choice for the Gold and Silver Macbooks.

Grip: There is a nice, large frog skin grip at the back hinge, and another smaller one at the front (with the UAG logo). The frog skin grip at the back hinge, while flexible, still can lift up the entire case when the laptop is opened on a table or desk, and needs to be manually tucked out of the way. Perhaps this will change over time, as the grip gets used more and folds the way I want it.

Venting: The new Macbook has no fan, using the aluminum body to disperse the heat. The UAG case is well vented on the bottom, which allows the heat to pass through (and also keeps the case light).

Protection: I haven’t dropped my Macbook and don’t want to, but if I do, based on the feel of this case and my other UAG products (which have saved my iPhones and iPads many times) I feel confident it will protect my laptop.

Bottom line: most cases take away from the aesthetics of Apple’s beautiful products. But UAG cases (most of them) have cool, rugged designs that provide great protection. The same goes for this Macbook case. Though I prefer not to use a laptop case (the new Macbook is too pretty on its own), when I need one, this is the only case I’ll consider for the above reasons. It looks tough—cool tough, not ugly tough—and does the job.

title: Big sound in a small package that's clean, compact, and efficient
text:
Pros:
Small and compact
Big sound
Easy to set up and connect

Cons:
Sound is noticeably neutral—lacks character (note—this may not be a negative to some listeners)

Style and Power:
It’s a beautiful little box, burnished grey metal, black plastic, and silver dials. It’s very sharp looking, and takes up remarkably little space. It will sit either horizontally or vertically as needed. And even though it puts out 55 watts at 8 ohms (in my configuration), it doesn’t get excessively hot. (It’ll do 105 W at 4 ohms, and 70 at 6.) More than enough power, at least for a two channel bookshelf system. You can also connect a subwoofer.

Sound:
Sound is big and even. I connected the MusicCast to a pair of Andrew Jones ELAC B5 Debut bookshelf speakers. They are great speakers, and responded well to the MusicCast. In comparing the MusicCast to the other receivers I used, the MusicCast is what I would describe as technically precise—it seems to present the music neutrally, without adding much of its own character. In contrast, I had my ELACs hooked up to an old 1980s Luxman, and newer Peachtree Nova 125SE. Both add something unique to their sound: the lower powered Luxman remains remarkably warm despite its age, and the Peachtree pumps out the rich, full, powerful sound that they’ve become known for. The MusicCast, by contrast, provides big sound from a small package, but it’s somewhat flat, as if it’s trying not to offend. It does the job, and does it well, but it’s voice is still fairly generic. This is not in itself bad. Neutral sound is a fine thing, as long as that’s how you like your music. In short, the Yamaha MusicCast sounds a lot like it looks: clean, compact, and efficient.

Connectivity:
You can feed music in by Wifi and Bluetooth, or direct (optical, USB, 3.5mm and ethernet). If you don’t want to use Wifi and Bluetooth, a switch at the back allows you to shut them off. Speaker wires can be attached the usual ways, by screwing the exposed wire down or with banana plugs.

The App:
You need the app (in my case, downloaded from the App Store to my iPad) to set up the MusicCast. (See photos attached to this review.) I connected the app to my iTunes library via AirPlay. AirPlay is built into the music cast, so once I downloaded the app and it found the MusicCast, my iMac and iPad immediately recognized the device. If I have one complaint, it’s that the app is a bit clunky—getting to the Equalizer requires dropping through a few levels of Settings (see photo). You’d think that would be accessible within one click or swipe at the most. After all, there are no physical dials for these adjustments on the front of the unit itself. Perhaps a software update could add these things somewhere in the main interface of the app. On the other hand, if you use audio software such as Amarra, you can make the adjustments on your computer which would then feed to the MusicCast.

Conclusion:
I like it. A lot. It serves its purpose in our living room, and does it well. If connectivity is what you're after, it delivers. With AirPlay and Spotify built in, and multiple input options, the MusicCast is about as versatile as amplifiers come, and in a nice package that’s easy on the eyes and doesn’t crowd its neighbors on your shelf. However, if you want a little more from your music, a little more character, it may disappoint. That said, Yamaha knows sound, and for what the MusicCast was designed to do, I can’t really find any technical fault. My minor complaints are merely a matter of subjective preference. So I still give it five stars.

title: Amazingly easy setup, great picture, but in-app controls are a little weak
text:
Pros:

Small footprint, 360 degree horizontal panning, with limited vertical panning
High quality picture
Extra long power cord
Can record with mini SD card (not included)

Cons:
Panning is slow
Settings menu a bit hard to follow, in-app controls a little slow

Summary:
I was impressed with how easy setup was. I thought I would have to go online and setup an account, but instead I only had to download the Exviz app onto my iPhone. That let me setup an account with only an email address or mobile number. Then, a quick scan of the QR code on the base of the camera, and I was up and running. The app detected and used the WiFi network my phone was on. So, up and running in just a few minutes. And the extra long power cord made it easy to position the camera in just the right spot.

Then you can use the app on your phone to view the camera's image, pan horizontally 360 degrees, and up and down to a limited degree. Panning is a little slow, and the camera can not spin constantly in one direction--that is, it will pan right until the camera hits reaches the back of the unit, then you will have to pan left. You can go all the way around again to the back, but then it will stop and you'll need to pan back to the right...you can't just keep going. Not a big deal, but the unit pans slowly so it takes some patience.

You can set it to auto-follow movement, which is a nice feature, but setting that up in the app itself took some time. The settings menu is not the most intuitive--you'd expect it would be, given how easy it was to set up the camera itself. And you can also set it to send you messages when movement is detected, as well as set the sensitivity level for detecting movement. All in all, it's a feature-rich camera at a great price. The Nest camera is easier to use, but it's $200 and doesn't have a panning option. So, Ezviz is a pretty good deal.

My one complaint is the swipe-to-pan feature in the app. Because the camera pans so slowly, and the app itself is sensitive, it makes you feel like you need to swipe faster than it can pan, causing a sort of tactile disconnect. Not a big deal, but it feels awkward. I got used to it though.

Bottom line, I like this--I can monitor much of my house with its 360 viewing angle, though slowly. Add in the recording option, and it offers a lot of value for the price.

title: Much better than WiFi on my home network.
text:

Tripled my download speeds vs. WiFi

Cons:
None (so far)

Summary:
I first bought a set of TP link power line adapters about six years ago. At the time they worked, but the setup was a little cumbersome (pushing buttons simultaneously on both units, etc.). And the speeds were slower, the cost higher, and the units had only a single ethernet port. My how times have changed.

These new TP Link AV 1000 power line adapters are amazing. No setup issues at all. I plugged one in to the wall and my router, went across the house to my office, plugged the other one in. The green light came on, and I attached ethernet cables to both my desktop and laptop. The entire process took less than two minutes.

For the purposes of this review I ran multiple unscientific speed tests (using SpeedTest.net) to compare the power line speed to my WiFi. These were the averages:
WiFi: Ping 22ms, Download 12.17Mbps, Upload 4.37Mbps.
Powerline: Ping 21ms, Download 45.83Mbps, Upload 4.90Mbps.

Obviously, the Ping and Upload times were pretty similar, with a slight advantage to the TP Link. But the download speeds are where the TP Link power line adapters really shine. In the range of 3 to 4 times as fast as WiFi, at least for me. YMMV.

So far, no connection issues (drops, etc.). All working perfectly smoothly. No video streaming hiccups, and gaming response (FPS, etc.) is fast and butter smooth.

I'm sold. Love these things, and love that I don't have to worry as much about WiFi interference, etc.

Summary:
I have two other EZVIZ cameras and love them. Setup is easy (especially once you download the EZVIZ app). Other reviews have noted wifi connection issues, but I haven't had a problem at all. My network and app immediately recognized the Mini O camera once the QR code was scanned: I went from unopened box to network-enabled camera in about two minutes.

Images on my phone were crystal clear. Datestamp was accurate, and overall I was very pleased.

Connecting to Amazon Alexa/Echo was easy with the Alexa app (through the "Skills" feature.) Per EZVIZ:
(1) Select the “Enable Skill” button in the Alexa APP to link your EZVIZ account and discover your device.
(2) Select a suitable name for your camera in the EZVIZ APP.
(3) Discover your camera in the Alexa APP.

HOWEVER, I checked the camera when we were out after dark. It was in a closed room without light, although there was a bit of ambient light from the street. Nevertheless, the image was completely black. I checked again when we got home, tried different rooms, etc. Still black.

In short, the "Night Vision" claim with this camera is spurious. My other EZVIZ (a EZVIZ Mini 360 Plus) works great in the dark. But this Mini O does not. If there is some ambient light, it works well. But this is not a "Night Vision" camera--it is a low-light camera. Unless I have a defective unit, EZVIZ should be more clear on this matter. They say you can monitor a sleeping baby, for example, but if that child's room doesn't have a small source of light, from say a nightlight or hallway, the camera won't send back an image.

For that reason I can only give it three stars.

These headphones also come with a 1/4" adapter, so you can plug the 3.5mm jack into a pre-amp. I used these with a Peachtree DAC (awesome!) and they sounded great. But ANYTHING sounds great through a Peachtree. The headphones also come with a nice carrying bag.

Bottom line: if you like Blue's quality and aesthetic, you will love these headphones. I prefer a mouse for the simpler user interface. Drag and drop doesn't require me to click my left hand (I'm right handed). The small touchpad really makes this unbearable. The touchpad on a Netbook really serves a couple purposes. These are clicking webpage buttons and placing a cursor to location. The Netbook is a light use item; really used for internet surfing, e-mail, and lighter text editing. I use my touchpad for when I will only need to do simple thing. Other than that I tend to use the Nano and turn off the touchpad. I tend to move the cursor when I'm doing a lot of typing accidentally with the close quarters of the keyboard and touchpad area.

title: Easy to install, and works brilliantly
text:
The device does exactly as advertised, even better.

I have a Rega P5 and the directions from the website where you download the instructions state that Rega Turntables might not work with the included sliding base.

The P5 has the 3 point base and there are no issues. I can't speak for the old design for Rega as it had a threaded column under the pivot. But now that Rega has outfitted all new designs with the 3 point base this shouldn't be an issue with newer models.

Anyway the sliding base allow adjustments on positioning where the arm is picked up, so this make it much easier to set and adjust. Different records have different lead outs so, this adjustment is necessary after the initial set up.

Aside from the sliding base there are 2 other adjustment.

The first one sets how trigger reacts to pressure. This will allow adjustment for lighter arms by setting it to a hair trigger reaction.

The second adjusts the spring action on the lift. This allows you to lessen the spring for lighter arms and increases the spring pressure for heavier arms. You don't want to throw your arm up too fast.

Again easy to install, download the instructions and read. After reading the instructions, following them takes about 15 minutes to install. Just take your time before you locate the lifter. Make sure you are perpendicular the arm and are clear of any obstructions that would prevent appropriate adjustments afterward. You don't have to be perfect, the slider base will allow you be a little sloppy.

Regarding more recent reviews stating this is made out of cheap plastic and it isn't worth $5 much less $50. This is all subjective. I have this device on a $1200 Deck with a $600 cartridge. My Rega does not have an Auto-lift and I doubt any complaining to them will ever change their mind to add this feature. It just isn't going to happen. I've added pictures to me, it looks fine. My Deck has a black plinth with a silver tonearm. And I think it matches just fine. Mind you, any device you place on your plinth with affect the sound characteristics of your Turntable. So the lighter the better and the materials used to fabricate this device seem appropriate. If it were heavy it would it would definitely add mass to plinth. Personally I haven't noticed any changes after adding it probably because of the materials. Now, if you are putting this on a $200 deck, I could understand people complaining about the price. But to me, retipping my cartridge costs $400 and I can't use my deck until somebody by hand replaces the cantilever using a microscope. So, this little device delays the inevitable retipping process. If you are using a $200 deck, you have other options like buying a used deck that has either auto-lift or return.

If you don't like the looks of this device, there an an alternative made by Espressimo. It's made of brass and is double the cost of the Q Up. I bought my Q UP in March of 2013 and it still works flawlessly in May 2017. If you think this is too cheap looking, buy the brass one. But, Black and Silver is perfectly suited to my eyes as I don't own any audio gear that brass or gold. There is another alternative called the newer Little Fwend that was released in 2015. The Little Fwend is much nicer looking and cost $250. I've seen arguments that somebody should make tonearm lifter with better materials. Well, they are there. Espressimo has been making their lift for over 20 years. The Q Up is newer and much more affordable. If I had a $10K deck, maybe I would be more willing to buy a Little Fwend. For the cost of $50, the Q Up is quite reasonable. There are alternatives and one is twice the price, the other is five times the price. So if you want better materials and aesthetics, it will cost you. Contrary to those that think that somebody could make a cheaper tonearm lift, it isn't happening. The audiophile market usually sells expensive things. While this thing isn't exactly cheap, it is half the price of what was previously available in the Espressimo. And apparently if you use better materials and make it look less utilitarian, rather and making making it less costly as others reviews have asserted, the price jump is 500% that of Q Up. After 4 years of owning mine, it is still rated 5 Stars. I see now Q Up has deal if buy 2 of them at a reduced price. I wish they had that deal when I purchased mine. My other Rega, a P3 has Alphason tonearm lift that has been out of production for many years. The Alphason works with small magnets, one clipped on the tonearm and another on the plinth mounted bracket. The Alphason works, but no where near as well as the Q Up. I periodically have to adjust the Aphason because the clip moved when I released it from the bracket. I have never adjusted the Q Up after I first set it up over 4 years ago. This thing is rock solid. I would definitely have bought the double pack. For now I'll stick with the Alphason, but, TBH, I'll probably get annoyed with it and get a Q Up as I've recently started using the P3 a bit more after having set it in my remodeled office.

title: Best fit for SLR Magic 50mm/F1.1 Full Frame Sony E-Mount.
text:
This is a review fore the 253 Pouch with stated dimension of 2.5" dia. x 3" L. I really like these pouches for a couple of reasons. They work great because you don't have to deal with zippers and they don't take up a lot of room. You can a leave the Pouch on when you throw it on your camera bag because it doesn't add much added space over the dimensions of your lens. After you swap lens, they crush down and can be placed into your bag into pretty much any available space you have left.

I use it on an SLR Magic 50mm/F1.1 FE Lens for Sony Cameras. The dimension of that lens are 2.6" diameter and 3.5" Length including the backing cap. Both of these dimensions are larger than stated by OP/TECH USA. But it still fits. This is because the material is stretchy and the collar on the pouch cap is fairly long. The 253 has collar about 1.25 inches. So even though the lens actually sticks out over the lip of the bottom portion of the pouch the long collar allows you plenty of length to overlap the top and bottom by at least a 1/4". I state at least, because I like to keep the original lens cap at the bottom of the pouch as a spare, so there would be another 1/8" if I just left that cap at home. Mind you, this lens is at the upper end of what this lens will fit. Also, the 50mm/F1.1 has a simple 1/2" screw on ring for a lens hood. The hood is included in my dimensions, so reversible petal style lens wouldn't have worked. Without the spare lens cap and the hood removed, the lens actually fits perfectly. So I really like that the flexible design allows me to accommodate the accessories if I want to bring them along. I did buy a more traditional zippered pouch for this lens, but it ended up being over bulky to the point where I couldn't put it back into my bag after the lens swap, so I would just leave it at home. I like bring the pouch in the bag because it provides some organization during the lens swap. I'm mentioned, I like to have an extra lens cap, so I know exactly where to find it if I need it. Also, I have a place to put lens backing cap along with a spare body cap after the lens swap, so it's there when I do my next swap. For this lens, you can also insert the lens with the back to the top allowing you to leave the pouch on the lens during the swap. This might be a small thing, but it frees up your hands for a quicker swap allowing you to put the pouch into your bag last. So I just shove the backing cap along with the body cap back into the pouch and crush it and cram it into any available space I can find. This is extremely helpful when I've just swapped from a long telephoto zoom lens that is now taking up twice as much space as the 50mm lens. Pictures included show lens with and without the spare cap and lens hood.

If I could have one thing fixed on this pouch, I would ask OP/TECH a bit more silk screening. We've all seen athletic T-Shirts that have an oval of silk screening. That oval allows you write a name in the oval to allow the managers who do the laundry to sort out who they should return the shirt to after they've been laundered. Well, a similar silk screened oval would allow you to write the focal length to help identify it without pulling the lens out. This is particularly helpful if you are placing the lens with the front of the lens at the bottom of the pouch. If you have 2 lenses from the same manufacturer, you can have a couple of lenses have the exact same dimension because the lens bodies are shared and only the internal optics are different. I have Sigma 19mm and 30mm that like this. If I had Pouches for these lenses, I would have to pull out the lens to actually know if I had the lens the desired focal length.

title: Confirmed works Sony A6000 with TLL and HSS in Wireless
text:
Ok, the directions aren't really clear. There is English instructions, but they aren't written step by step. They are written in the object-description style, meaning there is a picture with a labeled object and it states what it does. Mind you this is not a factory kit, this is two separate products thrown in a box with some extras. So this is more or less why you don't have good instructions. There is no cross reference on how to use the products together since objects aren't on transmitter aren't mentioned in the flash instruction or vice versa.

But this is what you do to make it work wireless. Put the transmitter on the camera. Turn on the transmitter. (The other switch on the side doesn't turn on the auto focus assist, which is fine since the A6000 on-board one still works.) Set the Group and Channel. Set the Group to either TTL or Manual. Turn on the camera after the X1Ts receiver is turned on. Turn off "e-Front Curtain Shut" (A6000 Gear Menu 4). Turn on Wireless (WL) Flash mode (A6000 Camera Menu 2). Just a hint, you might want to set up either a camera memory setting or at least add Flash Mode to your Fn Menu so you don't have to find these settings later. [Edited Correction: you don't need to set the camera on WL, it works in all modes except Rear Curtain sync in HSS (should work below 1/250). Rear Curtain doesn't work simply because HSS is a series of bursts and there is no way to get this trail. Sorry about the confusion. My directions work, but the WL setting is not needed and is a bit misleading because it suggests other modes don't work. They do, fill flash mode works fine. The WL mode on the camera is apparently for optical sync and is ignored because this is a radio system.]

Turn on the TT685s Flash and press the button marked with the "z" a few times until it changes the display and buttons turn orange turn on slave mode. Then press the button 2 more times and the display will alternate from green to orange again. The first orange is optical slave and the second one is 2.4GHz slave. This is what you want. Now match the Group and Channel you selected in the X1Ts. Press the Test button on the X1Ts transmitter and the flash should fire. At this point you should see the Flash Mode change to match your settings on the X1Ts. You will either see TTL or M and whatever power settings you have on X1Ts. You can adjust any flash power settings from the X1ts and the Flash should change to match this setting.

There is nothing else to do to get to High Speed Synch (HSS) other than increasing the shutter speed past 1/250. Turning off the Front Curtain Shutter that you changed in the Camera menus should prevent issues with the Flash synchronization issues with the highest shutter speeds. At this point you should probably test it at 1/4000 of a second (max on A6000) to make sure you don't have any banding issues. If you see banding, double check the Front Curtain Shutter setting.

Ok, why the 5 star rating? Well Sony offers an optical solution where you have to buy the HVL-F20M flash as the master and another "good" HVL-FxxM Flash to work as a slave. The cost of this solution only slightly higher than the HVL-F20M flash and the Sony solution is Optical while this Godox combo is 2.4 GHz radio. With Sony, you have to change the Slave setting by actually using that flashes controls since only a optical signal is tranmitted with HVL-F20M and you don't get HSS much less TTL. Or you could use the $300 HVL-32M to work as a controller to actually get what you want, so you are looking at $600 just to get similar functionality. But to be honest your slave would actually be more equivalent to the $450 HLV-60M. So the current Sony solution is actually $300 for the head unit and $450 for the Slave for total of $750 for a HSS/TTL system.

What else is there? Well you can't bounce the flash on a Sony. The Flash has to be angled straight ahead at 90 degrees. This is true for either being on the Hotshoe or triggered wireless. The Godox doesn't care, it will fire without regard to the angling of the flash. Mind you Sony has promised a wireless commander head unit. But even if it cost $100, you will still be required to spend at lest $550. This set costs less than $200. There is a Pixel King solution, but, this will required your spend at least the cost of this combo for a kit with a transmitter and receiver. The Pixel King does not include a flash nor the $20 adapter that you will need to use it because it uses the old Minolta/Sony hotshoe, much less the flash.

So 5 stars because it just works and is at a very acceptable price point. The only downside is the hot shoe which is all plastic rather than having a proper metal plate. But, even if it breaks, you can cheaply replace either unit and still be way ahead in cost. And if you are replacing the Flash, now you have a dedicated 2nd Slave. I would just super glue the broken foot onto the include foot piece and use it on a tripod.

title: Exceptional lens for stills, maybe not so much for video.
text:
With the more recent price drop of this lens, I really love what this lens can do. It's sharp and the color rendering is amazing.

This lens isn't quiet at all. It makes noise, so I can't recommend this for video at all. It isn't loud, but I can see this being an issue if you have a microphone placed close to the lens. For that matter, changing the aperture also makes noise. That being said, I actually like that the motor is the way it is. It does focus by wire, but, you get a tactile feel when manual focus is active. I also own the 30mm f2.8 Sigma. It's quiet and it doesn't have any feedback manually focusing other than what you see through the viewfinder. This lens does. You feel the motor. With the Sigma, I really don't get any sense that any fine focusing I am attempting is actually doing anything. Using Direct Manual Focusing (DMF) with Focus Assist "on" this lens is brilliant. I back button focus, so I press and hold the AEL to activate it and it locks focus fast. If I rotate the focus ring, it zooms into the frame for detailed focus. I get what I want in focus then lock the focus by releasing the AEL button. Focus peaking still works zoomed in. Yes you can use eye tracking to get focus, but DMF is a bit more flexible if you also shoot landscapes or things that don't have eyes. Manual focus is actually quite good with this lens. You get that tactile feedback with the motor vibration and some added resistance to ring.There is no lag during manual focus. It feels perfect and you can actually see the focus moving about with focus assist and peaking. I prefer this over relying on the Camera AI to do this for me.

Is this as fast as the Sigma? Maybe a hair slower with good lighting because of the difference in motors. But as long as you have firmware 2.0 on the lens, it doesn't hunt. This firmware should be on all new lenses and allows both contrast and phase detection. The lens just doesn't hunt. The Sigma f2.8 only has contrast detection, and will hunt a bit, in less than great lighting. The Touit finds focus focus and locks. Yes, I think using DMF is a good choice as I don't think it focuses perfectly. But, using DMF with this lens is smooth as can be. You do add a second or two if you rotate the focus ring, but you are assured what you want is definitely in focus. If you are reading reviews about this lens written just after it was released, please note that firmware 1.0 did have focusing problems because it only allowed contrast detection. This was more of an issue with the cameras. Older NEX cameras did not have phase detections. Zeiss added the functionality after it was added to the camera sensors. Just know that this lens does actually locks focus fast, well at least it does on my A6000. I have to state, that using DMF is basically you hunting the same way the Sigma is hunting. So, overall you aren't saving anytime if you choose to manual focus. But you do get exactly what you in focus which is important if you are shooting at f1.8 with a shallow DoF. You can also chose not to manually focus and get a quick shot off if you need to. I personally find it annoying when a lens locks you out of taking a shot while it's hunting.

Is it as sharp as the Sigma? Well, the Sigma is a pretty sharp lens. While I don't think the lens is corner to corner sharp wide open, it is still very sharp until it get to the extreme corners. But stopping down to 2.8, it is at least as sharp to my eyes as the Sigma 2.8. What is outstanding is the color rendering. The Sigma just doesn't pop like the Touit. Sigma 2.8 isn't even close to the colors of the Touit. The 2.8 is less than half the cost of the Touit. So what do get if isn't any sharper than the Sigma? Better colors and over a stop of light faster lens.

I don't have the 35 Sony, so I can't comment on it. I'm sure it's good. It isn't supposed to be as sharp as either the Zeiss or the Sigma. But it does have OSS and a similar 1.8 aperture. So, this is probably the lens to get for video.

This lens is quite a bit heavier than the Sigma. But the Sigma is also very light. The Touit feels quite balanced on the A6000, more so than the Sigma. If you want something small and extremely light, the Sigma might be better for you. But, the added weight of the better optics is worth it to me. I wouldn't call either of the lenses heavy at all. But if you a taking selfies, the Sigma might be better choice since you aren't supporting the lens with your left hand.

I will state that I actually hate the lens hood. It is ridiculously large. The Sigma has a very small one. With the Sigma being a very short length, it's barrel is about half the length of the Touit, it actually give you some length to hold the lens. But the Touit's lens hood is as long as the Sigma lens, by itself. So the Zeiss with the hood attached protrudes about 3 times as far from the front of the camera than the Sigma 2.8. The filter thread is 52mm, so I'm going to get a knock off one of those Fuji rangefinder lens hoods. I think you need a lens hood because the front element is convex and protrudes outward, so stray light could enter from the sides. But come on, really? The front lens element is recessed inside of the barrel so you don't really need it for keep it from getting scratched like you would on a fisheye lens. Besides that, the Zeiss hood is made of thin plastic. It is just asking to be crushed by me knocking it into something.

title: It's small, under powered with a wonky on-off switch. Forget this thing and get a Godox.
text:
I bought one of these a few years ago when I first bought my A6000. It was the only only thing available at the time that was affordable, meaning below $200. That is not the case anymore. It works, but today, even at a discounted price, it's too expensive. If it were $50, it might be a good deal, but at $130, it's a terrible deal. For that price you buy a Godox TT-685S. The TT-865S offers all the feature you could ever want on hot-shoe mount flash. It has TTL, HSS, 2.4MHz radio for both slave and master and a lot longer throw of light. The HLVF20M is barely better than the tiny built-in flash on the A6000. It might throw 5 feet past it. The other thing about flash is the unique way you turn it on. To turn it on you straighten out the mount from the body. Sony did not put a normal thumb switch. This is bad because if you store this little flash it prone to turn on in your camera bag by something inadvertently bumping into the mount. It's a terrible design.

The one thing nice about this flash is that it's small. If you need a small flash, they don't get much smaller than this thing. Still, it doesn't offer much improvement over the built-in flash of the A6000. It can act as trigger for firing optically slaved off camera flashes. But if you need something same, Godox now offers TT-350S which is small, but offers all the same features as the TT-865S with a slightly shorter throw of light. The TT-350S is a lot cheaper than the HLVF20M. For newbies or times when you don't have time to manually adjust the power settings on the flash, TT350S has TTL. TTL allow the camera to calculate the flash power need for your shots based on your camera settings of aperture, ISO, and shutter speed. This isn't somethiing HLVF20M will do.It's completely manual. For the price of this flash you could get the TT350S with an X1T-S trigger for off camera flash. This flash is really not worth buying. If you are looking at Godox, make sure you buy the ones with an "S" as the suffix. The "S" means it has the proprietary Sony Multi-Interface Hot Shoe.

title: Great little tripod for travel, pics on family occasions, or a hobbist using a light-weight camera!
text:
I'm calling this an in-between tripod. It's a step up from the basic, consumer tripods that are typically too short and unstable. However, this tripod doesn't fit into a professional grade, either. But keep in mind that at this price, it provides a lot of value, especially for the traveling photo bug or even someone who needs to shoot a relative’s wedding (as long as the camera is lightweight - see below).

First, I was surprised at how lightweight it is. And yet, the legs and mount are relatively sturdy. The legs extend and collapse smoothly and lock securely at the desired height. The mount is a basic tilt and pan (up/down and right/left). The mount's locking knobs work well and keep the camera where you want it. (Note for video work, this is not a fluid head and doesn’t provide for smooth panning and tilt video shots – but at this price, it’s not reasonable to expect it.)

The legs will spread beyond the default "stop-lock" simply by pulling on the small tabs at the top of each leg. This feature can be useful if shooting on sloped or irregular ground, but keep in mind that you'll need to restore the default lock by pushing the tabs back to the original position. Otherwise, there's nothing to keep the tripod from spreading out beyond what's needed - and creating a possible "camera crash."

The mount has a "quick-release" feature, allowing fast camera removal for taking a shot on the fly, then replacing the camera on the tripod. There's also a spring-loaded mount for a cell phone that provides a firm grip that appears very secure.

There's a practical weight limit that is inherent in all tripods. This unit is ideal for cell phones, compact digital cameras, and Go-Pro-type cameras. A larger, DSLR-type camera can be mounted on this, but I would be concerned about tip-overs and accidental "bumps" becoming a catastrophic crash to the ground. Certainly, if you keep the legs short, you should be fine, but be aware of the top-heavy risk of using a DSLR on the top of a fully-extended, lightweight tripod.

Overall, this is a great little tripod for taking pics while traveling, on family occasions, or for the hobbist using a smaller, lighter-weight camera. It's well made, comes with a fabric carrying "sack," and for the price, is a great value!

Most of these DOA reviews are just people thinking the cables are universal like a hdmi or Ethernet cable. I returned 2 units before learning that. Then I replaced all of what I considered the ‘important’ cables. Surely I could leave the old sata power cable in place. Wrong!! Blew out a SSD and a couple of fans.

title: Blink rules!! Best Value for Home Monitoring!
text:
