Anyway, blink is awesome! Easy to install and I had a complete monitoring system setup in less than 15 minutes! I don't think you can find a better value for home monitoring system with no subscription fees.

Few observations

- comes with everything you need. It has a double sided tape or a screw. It comes with batteries too.
- Easy setup with your iphone or android. You just have to create an account and follow the prompts. You don't have to read the manual. The manual the comes with it is 1 page anyway which tells you to follow the prompt on the setup.
- view is a little fish-eyed but it covers more ground
- Resolution is pretty good - HD
- Motion sensor can be a bit sensitive but can be adjusted
- Does not have night vision. It does have "illumination" where it has an LED that lights up when its dark similar to a flash on your phone. You have to set it though - its off by default probably to save battery.
- The iOS app is much more stable than the android app. The android app keeps on crashing. Other than that, I love this device.
- You can arm/disarm the system. So arm it when you leave to turn on motion detection and disarm when you are home.

I think the software/app will only get better over time.

So with a new drive the raid is working again, however I would like to make sure everyone is aware of how slow this box is on USB 2 or 3. title: Good watch, good battery life, passive tracking functions are very poor. Active functions are good.
text:
Nice big face, easy to read. I can charge it once a day while I am in the shower and it keeps it charged enough that I can wear it normally. I got this for SPO2 monitoring. When I'm sitting up it seems to match the finger monitor

For the bad... Passive monitoring. The 245 is very poor at accuracy for sleep monitoring (a big factor in sleep monitoring is what you have configured for your sleep/wake times). My prior Fitbit was much better at sleep analysis. The 245 is very poor at passive heart rate monitoring, auto identification of activities has failed to identify any activity on it's own. Just for an idea of what to expect. My heart rate can be 160+bpm when I'm cycling, if the 245 had not been told I'm riding the bike it will register around 90-110bpm. So if you actually do something like climbing a bunch of stairs during your day, you cannot look back at the data and expect to see a real heart rate.

Active monitoring, so if you remember to tell the watch you are working out the heart rate monitor becomes much more accurate. GPS is very good for a watch during exercise. Unfortunately the SPo2 monitor is almost useless during activity, as you have to be very still for ~10 seconds for it to take a measurement.

I bought this to be a bridge between a passive monitor (like a fitbit) and a backup activity monitor (while you are performing a structured exercise event). It looks good, but is really only good at the Active monitoring. That is probably the trade off for battery life...

I can only hope the next version of the Apple watch has SPo2 and better battery life, because I've basically just bought a pretty watch.

title: High pitch whistling sound when using ANC and Transparency Mode
text:
I would love to love these ear buds, they are the only ones that will fit in my ears and stay there when I am working out and doing other things. With that said, there are so many issues I am having with these that I am going send these ones back and see if I am still having the same issue with the next pair.

1. I am hearing a very high pitch whistling sound when using ANC and Transparency Mode. The sound is coming from the right ear bud and will NOT go away unless I turn both ANC/Transparency mode completely off. This is NOT why I wanted to buy these ear buds. I could have just bought the regular AirPods if I didn't want those features. The issue gets louder in the right earbud when I am moving my head around. There was an extremely high pitch whistle in my ear as I was doing some work and had both my hands full. it hurt my ear and I removed the headphones completely. I have taken it to the Apple Store and they ran tests and said nothing was wrong. I think this is going to become an issue for Apple again just like the first gen AirPod pro issues with transparency mode and failing tests.

2. Bluetooth connection to my iPhone goes in and out. this is an issue with the bluetooth connection and how it's registering with the phone. I have set everything up properly (it's pretty simple), ran the trouble shooting steps (at the Apple Store) removed the device and reconnected it, reset all wireless connection in my phone and removed all bluetooth devices off of my phone and restored them. this did NOT fix the issue.

3.I am also having issues with the AirPods not moving from one device to another. there are times I am doing something on my phone or listening to something while working on my MacBook Pro. My computer sees that the AirPods are near and when I ask it to move to my computer because I want to watch/listen to something on my computer, they won't move over.

4. there is an issue with the volume, it won't get loud at all in any mode, I have gone into the settings to try to change it, but I'm not able to get it any louder and since I can't use the ANC, I hear everything around me and the volume won't go any higher.

I am NOT sure what is going on. I bought the first AirPod pros and they still work great (except for the transparency mode is completely out in the right ear ironically it's the same earbud every time that gives me issues). I am going to send these back and see if I can have them replaced since there seems to be multiple issues that are out of my control and the Apple Store also can't find it. I wish someone were able to hear what is going on especially the right ear piece to figure out what they issue really is.

It automatically found out my IP address and worked as soon as I plugged it in and turned it on. I did enter the DNS server address manually. I am using this router with a Netgear MA401 802.11b Wireless PC Card because it has better reviews then the Linksys wireless card.

I am in a split level 2000 sq foot house. My router is upstairs in a front bedroom. I have an excellent signal downstairs and in my back yard a fair signal. But, I noticed no degradation in surfing with a "fair" signal. There is a refrigerator in direct line where I get the fair signal and is probably the culprit. So, if you have a small, medium sized home you will most likely have great performance. The "fair" signal in the back yard doesn't seem to make any difference so this setup might even work good in a larger house. Just make sure you set up the WEP encripted security so your neighbors don't use your Internet access. That is easy too to set up!!! The only downside was my laptop battery died and I have to buy a new one. :-]

title: Not the "Perfect Lens", but close
text:
I waited 6 weeks for mine to arrive and used it almost immediately at an airshow featuring the Blue Angels. I took about 3 gigibytes of pictures at that show. I used the lens with a D50 in sports mode to capture the fast moving planes. It was a great day with not a cloud in the sky. When I later looked at the pictures I was dismayed to see significant light fall off or vignetting on the shots taken at 200mm with the lens wide open at f5.6.

This light fall off is the most significant problem I have noticed with this lens. I contacted Nikon and they said it was normal. Since the lens is made for the smaller DX sensor the diameter of the lens is smaller. This causes mechanical shadowing at long zoom lengths with the lens at the wide open settings of f5.6 until about f11. All lenses have light fall off, to some degree, at the edges. When you use a regular lens made for 35mm with the smaller digital DX sensors the fall off is outside the sensor and not seen. The light fall off was especially noticable with the blue/uniform background. If the background was "busy" the falloff would be less noticable.

Vignetting/light fall off is also usually seen on the wide side of zooms like this. I have not seen any with this lens. I do use a Hoya Pro 1/2 thickness filter so that a shadow is not made when shooting wide angles of 18mm - 28mm or so. I saw a technical review of this lens that noted it had significant outer distortion on pictures taken at 18mm but I have not seen that.

Pros

-Light weight for range
-Large range
-Vibration Reduction
-Sharp, crisp pictures with vibrant colors
-Fast Focus with manual focus adjustment ring for fine tuning

Cons

-Light fall off at long telephoto settings and large f stops
-Vibration Reduction helps with handheld shots but does not stop subject motion in low light, you still need a fast lens for that
-High price and limited availability
-Might get light fall off at wide angles unless expensive 1/2
width filter is used
-Lens Creep (but most telephotos have this to some extent)

I have since used the lens to shoot the Special Olympics. The outside track and field photos are excellent. Inside shots where hit and miss with subject movement in low light being the biggest culprit (was shooting no flash at 1600 iso).

For about the same money you can get a Nikon or Sigma 2.8 lens that covers approx. 80-200mm. I have read several opinions that you will still have fewer bad pictures with the VR of this lens and I believe that is true. It is not a perfect lens, but it takes great pictures once you know its limitations.

One tip - If you get this lens, when you use it on a tripod turn VR off, it will actually cause your photos to be blurry.

UPDATE-Fall 2008 I have stopped using this lens and am instead using the [[ASIN:B001DYC0CS Tamron 18-270mm f/3.5-6.3 Di II VC LD Aspherical IF Macro Lens for Nikon DSLR Cameras]] which has "Vibration Control" and a wider range going all the way out to 270mm. It focuses almost as fast and has a wider diameter hence the vignetting of the Nikon is gone. One last thing is that it has much less lens creep and even a lock at 18mm.

title: Never Worry About Getting Lost Again
text:
After lots of research I chose this as my first Auto GPS. I have used it for the past 3 months around Atlanta, a medium trip to Alabama, and on a 850 mile trip to South NJ. I would buy it again.

Pros
-great windshield mount (holds well yet easy to take off)
-fast calculations
-easy to use
-clear audio
-precise location (I have used earlier Magellan hand held marine models that were sometimes off by what seemed dozens of yards)
-enormous database of attractions, banks, restaurants, etc.

Cons
-you may make an incorrect turn at complex intersections just because of the limited amount of time you have to chose the street the GPS has you taking
-loss of signal around tall buildings (normal)
-no real time traffic or construction info
-no one button addition of locations to your favorite list

The funny thing is that we have taken a 4 hour (each leg) trip twice and have been given different directions for all 4 legs ...although they all took about the same amount of time. You would expect you would be taking the same route each time. I don't mean minor variations either. We went to North Central Alabama from Atlanta via Birmingham (Central) AL and the return directions went through Rome (North), GA.

I have it set to the British Lady voice, I like the accent.

I have not updated the maps or software because I have read several accounts of doing so freezes up the unit. It works so don't fix it. :-)

UPDATE 8/2012 Still going strong. But I decided to buy a [[ASIN:B003ZX8B2S Garmin nüvi 1450LMT 5-Inch Portable GPS Navigator with Lifetime Map & Traffic Updates]] for my wife because it has both free lifetime traffic and maps. I never connected my C330 to the computer because I read of so many reviews on here of that breaking it. Plus maps are so expensive compared to buying a new unit, its what I did with the 1450. So when I got the 1450, I connected it and went to the Garmin website and installed the free new map. It was so easy I decided to throw caution to the wind and connected the c330 and GUESS WHAT? The FIRST time you connect your Garmin and register it, apparently any model, you have a month to DL the latest map... FREE!!! Those maps are $50-75. So I jumped on that. DL the map updater but just like many said, it crashed on the computer and the Garmin said it was missing the system software and the map updater would no longer see the c330 attached, so I thought I had trashed it. A quick web search came up my having to download another updater, for the software, off the Garmin site called the WebUpdater. Although it was for XP SP 3, it worked on Windows 7 and I reinstalled the latest operating software. Then I went back and reran the Garmin Map Updater. Due to the size, and this happened with the 1450 too, you have to choose the section of the country you want loaded. I guess no cross country jaunts with a Garmin without somehow dl the other have of the country at the Mississippi. Anyway, If anyone still has their Garmin c330 and haven't connected it to their computer, find the cord and do, you can DL the latest map for free! And it won't trash the unit.

title: My Best "Cans"!
text:
When you first wonder what you are missing by listening to you music with those ear buds that came with your iPod, you can find yourself on a rewarding (and expensive)journey. I knew that the iPod earbuds were seriously lacking, many songs had muddled bass and highs.

My journey to find the perfect headphones started with the [[ASIN:B000BNZGKU Audio-Technica Airtight Dynamic Monitor Stereo Headphones]], an improvement over my iPod buds but very uncomfortable. My next leap was the [[ASIN:B000E9VKUQ Audio Technica ATH-A700 Closed-Back Dynamic Headphones With Double Air Damping]] and they are really a wonderful headset. The are a closed headset, and I wanted to hear an open one so I got the much touted for rock listening, [[ASIN:B0006DPMVS Grado SR80 Headphones]] which for awhile became my favorites. I am using all these cans with my Toshiba laptop and iTunes, mostly high vbr mp3s. For my iPod I am using both the [[ASIN:B000089GN3 Sennheiser PX 100 Collapsible Headphones]] and [[ASIN:B001B484D4 Yuin Pk2 Earphones]] both of which blow iBuds out of the water.

But once you start down this path, you seem to always want more. I had read many reviews on headfi.org and one had stated that the HFI-780 had good bass and were probably the best cans under $350, a pretty bold statement. I decided to take the plunge and they now are my favorites. I use them with my [[ASIN:B000RN3EN0 Toshiba Satellite X205-S9349 17-inch Laptop (Intel Core 2 Duo Processor T7100, 2 GB RAM, 240 GB Hard DRive, HD SuperMulti DVD Drive, Vista Premium)]], [[ASIN:B0002ICGDY Audio Advantage Micro USB Sound Card]], and a portable headphone amp (Little Micro Dot +) and this setup has the most full, crip sound I have yet to hear from any source. The lows are more defined and substantial then the Grados. The surround gives music more of a feeling that the music is being played live all around you, and you can pick out where instruments are being played.

When you upgrade to a headphone this good, there are some things you need to realize. First, there is a break-in period. Some like to use "pink noise" over a period of time. But no matter what you do, your headphones will sound different over time, usually for the better. You may also need to experiment with your setup. I initially was just playing out of the laptop jack, using the on board sound card. The Ultrasone's did not sound good with that setup, bass was not well defined, there was a hiss in the background and the music was not full. Using the Turtle Audio to process the sound removes the processing from the EM interference within the laptop that can cause distortion. The amp added fullness, I have the computer's volume to the max and adjust it with the amp's volume switch. Next, higher end headphones can amplify bad music sources. mp3s can have a whooshing noise in the background because mp3's are a compromise between file size and quality, so try and use higher vbr mp3's. And once you really hear what you are missing in your music, you know that these headphones really are worth the cost.

EDIT: For those that do not like the pleather pads, the velour pads for the [[ASIN:B0002V9EA4 Beyerdynamic DT 250 - Headphones ( ear-cup )]] which can be found online will fit it nicely. There is a metal band under the plastic cover on top that can be bent for those complaining of a too snug a fit.

EDIT 4/2011 Just under 2 years and they are still going strong. Clarity, strong base, large sound stage, these cans just seem to sound better and better. Amazon carries the [[ASIN:B0016MF7W2 Beyerdynamic EDT 200 Velour Padded Earcushions for DT250, DT280, Sony MDR7506 and V6 Headphones (Pair)]] now and they are cheaper then anywhere else since they are Prime eligible. title: See Ya Linksys
text:
I bought this to replace a long line of Linksys routers. Cisco/Linksys routers seem to last up to 3 years before errors start to show up. This last time I was replacing their new, Star Trek looking [[ASIN:B0014J07R2 Cisco-Linksys WRT54G2 Wireless-G Broadband Router]] that was less then 2 years old. In all fairness, this last router maybe wasn't going bad. I was having issues with my DSL service, probably related to the phone line in my house. But when it was suggested to buy a new router, by the ISP, I did not want to go with Linksys. I have been using them for a decade and they did seem to go belly up within 3 years. The geek at the ISP suggested Buffalo. Price seemed right and lots of good reviews. Now its a little different to set up then a Linksys, obviously, the IP address is different. But anyone who can set up a router manually will have no problems. I don't know about increased range. I am sitting downstairs, almost underneath it and have 4/5 bars on my [[ASIN:B002PY7OHQ Dell Inspiron Mini 10 10.1-Inch Obsidian Black Netbook with Integrated TV Tuner - Up to 6 Hours 20 Minutes of Battery Life (Windows 7 Starter)]]. I know I can't pick it up 4 houses down at the bus stop. But that may be due to the channel it is on. Anyway, throughput speed, at least at higher speeds seems to be higher on the Buffalo by 1-2mb/sec compared to the Linksys. I was getting 13mb/sec vs 12 on the Linksys. The only time I had an issue was after I flashed the bios. I thought I broke it. I tried several times to both manually and automatically connect to my cable modem without success. I also reset it a couple of times. Finally, I got it to connect. So, the moral of the story is, if its not broken, don't fix it. About the only thing I liked better with the Linksys was the cool software they had were you can see your network on a map and check the status of everything. I have a large network, 5 laptops, a wireless printer, 2 PS3s, and 3 Dish receivers (one wireless). The Buffalo is doing fine handling all that data.

IMPORTANT: It seems to ship with the firewall OFF. It can do stealth mode, which is its High setting and most recommended by security experts. I think they are wrong to do this, Linksys and Belkin don't.

UPDATE: After flashing to the newest firmware it has an intermittent problem with dropping packets (6-10%) and high jitter (stability of ping)of around 100ms (should be 1-3ms on a stable line). It happened every couple of days and would last for a about an hour or so. Recycling the power did not fix it. I confirmed this by testing directly connected to the cable modem when this was happening and it went away. I don't know if flashing did it or not, especially since its intermittent. Since switching back to my old Linksys router I have had no issues. Shame. Anyway. Contacted support and they want me to send in all the info which I will do sometime soon, to get a RTA. Anyway, you might want to not flash to the latest bios if yours is working fine.

text: I get this call from Comcast. Do you want to upgrade to a faster speed? Well, my speed was fine and I didn't want to pay for something faster. Then they said, oh, its the same price. Well then, what was the catch? I had to upgrade to a DOCSIS 3.0 modem. After lots of research this Motorola stuck out as reliable at a decent price. I talked them into just changing it over and when they did, I got about 10 more mbs then I was getting, blazing fast. To get the full speed effect over my wireless network I needed to upgrade to a N router. G wireless tops out in the 22-24mbs range. Its fast and easy to set up. It has features galore. It has great range. It is reliable. Its everything I need in a router. Between the last Linksys and this NetGear I did try a [[ASIN:B000AOKTJ8 Buffalo Technology Wireless-G High Power Router and Access Point with High Gain Antenna WHR-HP-G54]] that died shortly after I got it. The N band is great because I have high speed cable and in the mid 20mbps you hit the limit for G protocol. So to take advantage of the high bandwidth I needed an N router. title: First Impressions
text:
This isn't my first GPS, its about my 4th. The first 2 were handheld Magellans I used for boating. Our first car GPS was a [[ASIN:B0007LJHVA Garmin StreetPilot c330 3.5-Inch Portable GPS Navigator]]. That was an easy and dependable unit although the first time we used it, it took us on one wild ride that included going through college parking lots. It was like someone was reading a map as we went and saying, wait, go this way, afterward realizing it was a parking lot, not a public road. Anyway, the lifetime maps and traffic were selling points along with the mostly positive reviews here. Getting it out, connecting it to the computer to get the newest map was a breeze with my Windows 7 laptop with the supplied mini USB cord. I even decided to surprise my wife and downloaded some of the free car icons and decided, what the heck, and got the Darth Vader voice. haha. She currently is in Alabama, the same destination the old c330 took on us on a weird route the first time. Guess what? The 1450 did the same thing according to my wife. And it seems to have a malfunction in that Darth will say, "turn in a half mile" and will come on a few moments later and say, "turn in a mile" for the same turn. I called tech support about this, and they were backed up for 15-20 minutes. So I emailed them. That takes up to 3 business days. So for that kind of support, I have to knock the rating down a star. When I find out what the problem is, I will edit this review.

The good thing was, it was so easy to update the map on the 1450, I decided to connect my c330 and update the operating software. I had never updated the map on it because there are several reviews I read that said doing that trashes the unit. It works, the maps are old, but even if I didn't trash the unit, they are $50-75, it almost makes more sense buying a unit like this one. So I connected my c330 and find that when you register your GPS, you GET A FREE MAP UPDATE! You have a month to get your new update! So for all of those with old, unregistared Garmins, get your mini USB out and get your free map. Did I trash the unit? Well, I did run into a problem where I had to install the operating software again by downloading from the Garmin website software called the WebUpdater. But after I did that, the map updater worked. Ah, free is good.
item_title: Garmin nüvi 1450LMT 5-Inch Portable GPS Navigator with Lifetime Map and Traffic Updates (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

title: Do Yourself A Favor
text:
And pick one of these up if you own a laptop. I am kicking myself for not getting one for my year old laptop back when I first got it. My previous laptop I had used a Turtle Beach Micro Advantage which they don't make anymore and isn't Windows 7 compatible. I have some good headphones, the old version of the [[ASIN:B000G3LCQC Grado Prestige Series SR80i Stereo Headphone]], [[ASIN:B000E9VKUQ Audio Technica ATH-A700 Headphones]] and [[ASIN:B00101XVH2 Ultrasone HFI-780 S-Logic Surround Sound Professional Headphones]]. My HP Pavillion dv7 has Beats Audio but its really just average, more of a marketing ploy. So after looking around it was between the [[ASIN:B0036VO4X4 Turtle Beach Audio Advantage Micro II USB Analog & Digital Audio Adapter]] with is the new version of my old card, and the FiiO E10. The glowing reviews here and around he web led me to the E10. And the difference is noticeable immediately. Plug it in, it installs the drivers automatically and there is no mistaking the increase in sound quality. Everything has more punch. The midrange is now easier to hear and the bass is nice, tight and noticeable. The case is small and well built. It can handle headphones up to 300 ohm according to the FiiO website. Just take note that there is a counterfeit problem with FiiO devices and not all the sellers on Amazon are approved by them. Research on FiiO's website can help with IDing who to buy from and who to avoid. They may be selling a genuine product, but they aren't an authorized dealer.

Make sure you update your computer's profile for this device to output 2 Channel, 24bit 96000HZ to get the full effect of this device. To do this in Windows 7, after you install it, click on the Volume symbol. Once you do that, click on the device symbol for the E10, it will say it is a SPDIF Interface properties on the box. Change Sample Rates on Supported Formats Tab to 96.0 kHz and on the Advanced tab choose the output at 2 Channel, 24bit 96000HZ.

title: Spectacular!
text:
This is one stunning TV. Its my first plasma but my 6th HDTV of which most were LCD and one a RP CRT HDTV. It has the best picture of all of them and is simply riveting when a good HD source is played on it. I am currently using it with a [[ASIN:B005CLPP84 Roku 2 XS 1080p Streaming Player]], a PS3 and a Dish VIP 611 HD receiver. The picture on all inputs is just fantastic. I also have tried my laptop with it too.

The smart tv aspect is very fast and has a good selection of apps. I have yet to have it slow down or hesitate when choosing programming.

For the picture settings I am using the THX Bright Room Cinema during the day and THX Cinema at night. They both look so good, I haven't tried any other settings than those.

The sound is the weakest link. Its more the fullness than the clarity that is lacking. Even with new flat technology sub woofer built in, you aren't going to get much bass. For me, the unusual configuration of the room I am in made me decide to go with a TOS link from the TV's audio out to a [[ASIN:B00007JO2V C2G / Cables to Go 28733 Digital To Analog Audio ConverterDAC Black]] to a [[ASIN:B001MPWMDA Fiio E3 Headphone Amp]] for amplification to a [[ASIN:B00001P4XH Koss VC20 Volume Control]] to my [[ASIN:B00101XVH2 Ultrasone HFI-780 S-Logic Surround Sound Professional Headphones]] modified with [[ASIN:B0016MF7W2 Beyerdynamic EDT 250 Velour Padded Earcushions for DT250, DT280, Sony MDR7506 and V6 Headphones (Pair)]] for simulated surround sound and late night listening. BTW, no buzzing sound as some have reported with plasma TVs (seems to be mostly a Samsung issue looking at reviews)

I had ordered this from Amazon but initially looked like they would be late (got a last minute call it would be late a few hours vs days as initially thought) and cancelled and ordered locally. The Amazon install is hit or miss and the local install WILL put TVs on stands and where you want it so another reason to order locally.

Just remember there is a 200 hour burn in for plasma to help not get any retained images. I have been zooming in and have enjoyed movies and football and have no artifacts along with avoiding playing video games. Burned in images will eventually go away and there is a 15 minute wipe program to help the process along.

I bought this over the ST because of the THX settings and extra HDMI port. We may add an XBOX 360 for ESPN3 content. The pictures between this model and the ones above and below it are very similar and the higher model VT has been named by some publications and websites as the best looking HDTV of 2012.

title: Works Very Well
text: I live west of Atlanta, about 15 miles from downtown. This area is hilly and with trees. A few years ago I had a professional installer put an antenna on my house and he had to come back later and put a booster on it to help a few weaker channels. We have one room with no antenna or sat box and that is where we put the Leaf. Its on the second floor, but in the opposite side of the house from where the antennas are located in Atlanta so I wasn't too optimistic. My outside antenna gets around 65 channels. Sounds like a lot but many are parked and some are religious, etc.. The outside antenna gets all the major carriers. The inside antenna, surprisingly gets about 2 dozen channels. It gets the Fox, ABC, and UPN affiliates along with Peachtree which is what TBS is now called. It also gets some religious channels. So I was pleasantly surprised because I thought its location on the opposite side of the house would be an issue. I had tried one other indoor antenna and couldn't get anything so I recommend it if you are "cutting the cord" and don't want an outdoor antenna.

title: Hit Or Miss And A Little Expensive
text:
I can only give this four stars because it doesn't work perfectly. It's also been noted that it's not a full 1080 P device. It actually gives slightly lower resolution than full 1080p it is 1080x900p. It costs so much because it actually has a small computer device in it, with RAM because the lightning port is only a serial port. However the resolution may be increased with future iOS updates. The problems that I have are number one the picture doesn't totally fill the screen with every app and number two it's not DRM compliant so not all media will go to the television. This Hulu app seemed to work the best but some like NFL game rewind don't work at all, you get sound with no picture on both screens. By the way I'm using this with an iPad 4 with the latest version of iOS 7.

When it's working right, the screen of the iPad has a message that it's playing on TV. When it's not working right, the image mirrors on both TV and the iPad. The picture on the TV will be letterboxed and in the shape of the actual iPad. A pleasant surprise was the ability, by using the chrome app, to reach speed2.com and watch races, displayed in the correct 16:9 ratio. Both the Max go and HBO go programs worked well while Netflix and Crackle had problems. I tried a couple different titles on Netflix and one did not work right,where it was mirrored on the iPad on the TV, but another movie worked fine and the iPad On TV message and the TV displayed the picture properly. The Amazon app didnt work at all, seemed to be related to lack of DRM. DRM stands for digital rights media and it's a requirement for hdmi cabling so that movies cannot be copied to computers. Amazon may not have the rights to stream movies to a secondary device. The Chrome browser app also did not work right, it was mirrored on the iPad and the TV. I did not try Safari maybe it works correctly. However I did watch a short video on the Chrome app browser and it worked correctly. Another short video however did not. So it seems to be hit or miss.

Pros

-when it works it's great
-you can still charge your device while using it

Con

-price
-not all apps fill screen
-not all apps work at all with it, no DRM
-reports of lag
-not full/raw 1080p, which can lead to compression artifacts

title: Heat Kills
text:
Heat kills computers. And I have a [[ASIN:B004FN0T9U HP Pavilion dv7-4280us 17.3-Inch Entertainment Notebook PC (Silver)]], a brand with a bad reliability reputation because of heat issues. So when for the first time since I bought it new in late 2011 it shut down from overheating I started looking at cooling pads. After pouring over the reviews, I decided on this one. And for the day I used it, with an HDMI cable attached to my TV watching HD movies, no overheating. But using a program called Speedfan, core temps were still around 105C which is hot. But what helped drop my temps down drastically was spraying [[ASIN:B0007LBON4 Falcon Dust-Off XL, Disposable 10 oz. Can DPSXL 2-Pack-Camera]] into the vents below and on the sides as well as the keyboard. Now, with the Targas Chill Pad, I run in the 80sC max. So if you are having new heat issues with an older laptop, it might be a good idea to try blowing out the dust, as much as you can, and see if after you still have issues.

Pros

For me, being flat and not tilted since I use it on a desk a few feet from me along with a wireless keyboard
Very quiet
Quality construction, the fans are rated for double the hours of fans usually used in this type product
Light indicates its on, you'll need it since its so quiet
3 speeds plus the option of using two USB plug ins to increase power

Cons

On all the time, even when the computer is on standby/sleep
Uses two USB ports but I got around this by buying an inexpensive [[ASIN:B003M0NURK AmazonBasics USB 2.0 4-Port Ultra Mini Hub]]
White light is bright, brighter than the power light on my computer
You may not need this for an older laptop with new overheating issues, blowing out the vents my be all that's needed

text:

title: You Have To Love This Because It Works
text:
After messing around with two of the cheap Asian manufactured antennas with rotors (neither of which actually rotated right of the box) I finally coughed up a bit more change and bought this one from Winegard. I should have done this is the first place. In less than an hour I had removed the cheap Chinese junk antennae and replaced it with this one from Winegard.

I googled something like "correct direction to point antennae for maximum reception of San Francisco HDTV stations." I found a web page that had all the stations in my area listed and the direction in degrees around 360 from North to which to point the antennae for maximum reception. I then downloaded a free compass app for my Windows phone, and put as much of the antennae together before taking it up to the roof. Once mounted on the pole with the mounting hardware and tightened just enough to allow me to move the direction of the antennae, I fired up the compass app, and found my heading (324 degrees). I rotated the antennae by hand to that approximate direction, adjusted it a couple of times and then tightened it down all the way.

My HDTV (and probably yours) requires me to do a channel search after installing a new antennae or rotating an existing one. It's the way these sets find signals and add them to your list of available channels. I've got all the national network channels, including three flavors of PBS (nine total channels), have clean reception of CBS, FOX, NBC, ABC and a host of other stations I never knew existed before--61 channels in all.

Winegard has been making antennae of all varieties since I was a kid (a very long time ago) and they are known for excellent design, quality and for working well. This company knows how to build a great antenna so if you're looking for one to replace your cable provider with an outdoor antenna and streaming video from the net (like Amazon's Prime) this unit makes a great choice.

OTHER STUFF TO CONSIDER:
--I don't have a direct line of sight to Sutro Tower, where all the major networks and other stations have their antennae and that still did not keep this antenna from working.
--If you're a long way away from the TV station transmitters you may need to add a preamplifier unit to the installation. You'll know you need one if after installing your Winegard reception is still not great. You can find them here at Amazon.
--If you live in an area that doesn't have one huge tower all the stations antennae mounted on it like Sutro here in San Francisco, you may also need a reliable rotor to turn the unit. Again you can find a great one made by Radio Shack and sold on Amazon.
--Plan on another $50 for a heavy gauge 5 ft. pole, and an additional $50 for each additional 5 ft section. Even factoring in a preamp, a rotor and some lengths of pole, you're still going to come out way ahead of your cable bills.
--The higher you go, the more sturdy a mounting you'll need so there may be some costs for guy wire, screw eyelets, roof sealing compound for around the hole the screw eyelets make in the roof.
--This antenna does not come with any 72 Ohm coax so you'll need enough to run from the antenna to the set. This also means some crimping tools for the end hardware.

THAT WAS THE WORST CASE SCENARIO:
--Reality is the further you live away from the broadcast stations and if the stations transmitters are not at a central location, the more stuff you'll need to consider before buying this or any antenna.
--You'll likely end up needing the antenna, a 5 ft. pole, some coax and connectors, a piece of free compass software for your phone, or an old compass (remember those). If you figure a total budget of not more than $150, and factor in about 90 minutes of your time to assemble, install, and adjust direction you're likely to have enough left over for some good beer.

FINALLY:
All the essential hardware needed to mount the antenna to the pole and connect it to coax is included with the antenna. I had no missing parts.

For the money, this is a great value.

title: Adequate Product Needs Instructions--Still A Good Deal
text:
Good quality material-sufficient thickness to make a good screen protector and be reasonably easy to apply. The end result looks very good.

Pros:
-Comes with lint removal cloth
-Easy to use, rigid squeegee to push out bubbles
-Several pieces of tape to remove lint and dust particles from the underside of film while applying THIS IS A BIG DEAL and it's the first I've seen with this addition...

Cons:
NO INSTRUCTIONS INCLUDED so if you haven't applied one of these before you'll be lost and need to search on-line for how-to
Protective film only on ONE side. This is an issue because the squeegee applies pressure to the upper surface of the protector and can, if pressed with enough pressure mar the finish of the protector's surface.

QUICK HOW TO APPLY INSTRUCTIONS:

WHAT YOU'LL NEED:
a) One wide piece of baking parchment paper (18 inches) cut to a length of about 24 inches OR two pieces of standard width waxed paper cut to 24 inches long.
b) Some spray cleaner for eye glasses is nice but you can window cleaner IF you don't use too much (really just a spritz on a paper towel will do.
c) All the pieces from this kit laid out on the work surface (see step 1, below)

APPLYING THE SCREEN PROTECTOR (DON'T TOUCH THE STICKY SURFACE WITH YOUR FINGERS)
1) Do this on a dust free (or relatively so) surface. That means don't do it on top of your table cloth. Do it on a table top or counter top.
2) Wipe the table or counter top with a slightly damp cloth to remove dust particles then dry it with a piece of heavy paper towel.
3) Spread out a piece of wide baking parchment paper or two overlapping pieces of waxed paper (this is your work surface)
4) Take another paper towel and spritz it VERY LIGHTLY (half a spray or less) and wipe the iPad's screen and case. Get rid of all the smudges, dust and finger prints and be sure the screen is as dry as possible--completely dry is best.
5) Using the same paper towel, wipe the top of the screen protector sheet lightly and make sure it's dry. Do the same to the side that you will peel back before adhering the protector to the iPad's screen. This gets rid of stray dust particles and a bit of the static that builds up on the screen protector sheet.
6) Lay the iPad screen facing up onto the parchment or waxed paper surface and wipe the screen gently and completely with the dust removal cloth from the package. Be sure to get rid of any dust you can see (there's some you cannot see--more on that later)
7) Pick up the protector sheet and grab the tab with the number 1 printed on it.
8) Gently pull back about half an inch to one inch of this protective covering to reveal the adhesive side that will be placed against the iPad's screen.
9) Place this uncovered section on the iPad's screen at the correct end (remember--the camera hole and home button hole do go an specific ends so do this correctly.
10) At this time there may be some bubbles between the sheet and iPad screen. Gently push them out with the squeegee. It's easier to do this when you catch them near the edge that is just beginning to adhere. You can always pull the protector up a bit to get rid of bubbles.
11) PATIENTLY AND SLOWLY keep pulling the protective sheet back and off of the stick side of the protector sheet, laying the protector down a little at a time and using the squeegee to push out bubbles as you go.

THE TOUGH PART---
THERE ARE ALWAYS SOME MICROSCOPIC DUST PARTICLES THAT FIND THEIR WAY BETWEEN THE SCREEN AND THE PROTECTOR SHEET. THIS IS WHEN YOU USE THE DUST REMOVAL TAPE STRIPS.

A DUST PARTICLE CAN LOOK LIKE A BUBBLE. THIS IS BECAUSE THE PARTICLE IS 3 DIMENSIONAL AND AIR DOES SURROUND IT. YOU CANNOT SQUEEGEE THEM OUT.

THESE PARTICLES STICK TO THE UNDERSIDE OF THE PROTECTOR SHEET NOT TO THE iPad SCREEN.

DO STEP 12 BELOW IF YOU HAVE DUST PARTICLES.

12) Get a piece of the dust removal tape-pull it off the sheet it ships on. Hold it with the stick side up. LIFT the screen protector sheet just high enough to get the piece of tape under the protector sheet until you think you're in the correct spot. Stick the end of the tape strip to the underside of the protector and then pull it away. This should remove the dust particle IF you carefully noted the location of the dust particle. This part takes a while and can be frustrating. I learned to live with two or three because some just won't go away. IF A DUST PARTICLE will not come off with the supplied tape, try some scotch tape or a short piece of clear packaging tape-the adhesive is a bit stronger and can pull particles off that the tape strip included in the package will not. Fold over one end so you don't stick it completely onto the sheet as doing so will force you to use another protector.

13) Keep removing the protective sheet, laying the sticky side down onto the iPad's screen, using the squeegee to push out bubbles and the tape to remove microscopic (almost dust particles).
14) Finally the entire protective sheet will lay flat on the iPad's screen. Use the squeegee to push out any remaining bubbles.
15) Use the dust removal cloth from the kit to buff out any smudging caused by over zealous use of the squeegee.

Final note: The whole process takes at least 30 minutes and can take up to 45 to do carefully and properly to produce a result that is bubble free and has as few dust particles between the protector and screen. Take your time, be patient. Have a stiff drink AFTER your done.

title: Not A Complete Solution Until You Buy All The Supporting Apps
text:
Pogoplug (this and other models) are an inexpensive way to have some capabilities of more expensive Network Attached Storage (NAS) devices. The most significant difference is a Pogoplug does not come with a hard drive installed. You have to supply your own hard drive as the backup drive. Mostly, I don't recommend this device, or the other offerings in the product line. The Pogoplug is just the beginning of what it will cost to get a complete backup solution with remote access and cloud storage. It's a solution sold piece-by-piece and, in the end, for the same outlay you can buy systems with better functionality and more builtin features.

If all you want is a way to backup files from multiple computers running different Op Systems (e.g. Windows and Mac OS X) to a local backup system, the Pogoplug will do that. If, however, you want to access your files when you're away from home or the office where the Pogoplug is installed, you'll need to buy their app for that from the Pogoplug website.

If you want your files also backed up to cloud storage, you have to buy that as well from the Pogoplug website. They sell 1TB storage, although it's advertised as 'unlimited' cloud storage. In my opinion their cloud storage is expensive. Consider also it takes a very long time to upload 1TB of content and, should you decide to discontinue the service, it takes a lot longer to download that same 1TB.

The best way to think of a Pogoplug is that its like candy dispensing machine. You buy a Pogoplug (the machine) and get one piece of candy free as a promotional item. You purchase more candy one piece at a time. They sell a lot of candy and It's not cheap.

There are some things I like about this item and more I do not. For example, unless you're a big customer, tech support is only available by email. It takes a couple days for a question to turn around and for that and other reasons I don't like email support. Then, too, in order to get all the features I want is an expensive proposition, since the real meaty features cost extra. While Pogoplug Backup (the app that comes with the device) works on both PCs and Macs, it has an annoying glitch on the Mac platform. Whenever a computer restarts (often with all the software updates and service packs) Pogoplug software restarts as well. On the PC, this does not trigger a full backup of already backed up files. On the Mac it does. Essentially, the Pogoplug Backup app for Mac doesn't seem to keep track of what' been backed up so you get to work on a slowed down Mac while Pogoplug needlessly does a full backup. Further, while Pogoplug Backup updates files that have been altered, it does not have versioning.

The most frustrating thing about Pogoplug is that your files are stored on the device locally, on your local network. You'd think it possible to connect directly to the attached drive to access shared files. Not so! Access to files stored on your own drive, located in your own home or office are only available to you from other computers when logged into my.pogoplug.com through their interface. Think how you'll enjoy this when your internet connection is down or their site is down or a myriad other things get fouled up!

title: Easy To Setup Using WPS--Surprisingly Good
text:
This review is for the TP-link AC750 Dual Band WiFi Range Extender

I am using this on a network that has a Mac Mini, a couple of iPhones and an iPad. None of these devices could print to both printers; it was one or the other and not both on every single Apple product. After trying everything I could think of, I bought this extender and tried to set it up using the Quick Setup instructions. Anyone EVER had the experience of those Quick Setups working? I haven't and I've been using this stuff for decades. After Quick Setup failed to do anything other than connect to my router and open my network up to anyone that could get signal, I tried a different approach.

The EASIEST WAY TO SET THIS UP is to use the WPS button on your router and on the device. Press the WPS button on the router, then, press the WPS button on the extender. After a minute or so, the router and extender are paired/connected and the result is a secure connection to the router (uses the router's password--you do have a password don't you) with a much stronger signal in what were dead zones. Placement of the extender is sort of an experiment and moving it from plug to plug will show you the best location. Moving the extender after pairing does NOT foul up the connection.

I have two printers, a Samsung M2070W laser and an Epson Eco Tank inkjet. Both have wireless capability and can use WPS setup. To setup other WPS capable devices, just press the WPS button on the ROUTER and then the WPS button on the next device you want to connect. The connection to the router goes through the connected extender with no problem and does not interfere with the router/extender pairing. Do each device one at a time.

This was the solution I needed and now all wireless devices work together. It's a neat solution to solving signal strength and connectivity that can be an enormous hassle when using multiple devices from different makers.

title: Need A PhD in Tech To Install
text:
This review is for the TP-LInk Mesh WiFi M5 system.
—————
Amended April 28, 2020
Now that I’ve been using this for a couple weeks, I am returning to add these units HAVE NOT cured the dead spots that needed more signal strength. Yes, the WiFi signal is present in those areas of my home. However, the signal strength has not improved over what my centrally located router produced on its own. Essentially for my roughly $125, I got a couple stylish WiFi access points. What I DID NOT GET is the improved coverage promoted in the description.
—————
This IS NOT a plug it in and it works system. You need to know at minimum:
—Your current router’s IP address, the user ID for it, and the password. If you haven’t changed them from the default, you have no business installing a network anything, because you put EVERYTHING on your system at high risk for hacking. Why? The problem is that the default user ID and password are the SAME FOR ALL routers of the same brand (every brand router has a published default user id and password).
—You need to know which of several comm protocols your ISP uses.
—You need to know that IF YOU SWAP OUT YOUR ROUTER for one of the units, the others WILL NOT WORK to extend your WiFi network. For that you need to set these up as extenders, with the first being connected to your existing router.
—To set up a network of WiFi extenders, you need to know how to turn your existing router’s WiFi transmission off. Only then can you use these as extenders, satellites, or whatever you know them as.
—You are highly likely to have to update the firmware on each M5 device.
—You should set aside about two to three hours to set up a network of multiple devices.
—If you set these up as extenders, some of the default security features are switched off. You need to be sure these security features are enabled on your router instead.

I found this an unacceptably under-documented product that forces you to comb through the internet for proper setup tips. I loathe their little booklet that is “documentation” since it is a collection of single pages in multiple languages that direct you to the App Store or Google Play for the app that manages setup. That app is underpowered, has little relevant or helpful information.

I’ve been working with and installing systems from early (1990s) mainframes, Apple IIs, Macs, PCs of all flavors, and networks right up to now. Were it not for that experience, I might never have gotten this to work. Once installed, it works fine.

Recommendation: If your current router is older, you’re probably more likely to get better WiFi coverage by purchasing a newer, more current router. Try that first, and if you don't get the coverage you need, add a couple or three of these.

Filco makes the best keyboards I have ever used. They are expensive but they are exceptionally built and reliable. Most keyboards will last a couple years of hard use. Filco keyboards are build for decades.

Great product, can't give it enough praise.

title: Less is more.
text:
First off, I'm reviewing the Ninja Majestouch-2, Tenkeyless "Click Action", which entirely use Cherry MX Blues. This means they have an audible click and a tactile feel when they actuate at 60cN (about 61 grams or 2.1 ounces) of direct pressure. If you need to know more about the switches and how they work, do a quick search on whatever engine you prefer or buy some samples from WASD Keyboards and feel them out for yourself. Think a kit is somewhere like $15. Not bad to figure out which switches are for you, instead of dropping $80-160 on a quality mechanical keyboard only to find out you don't like the switches. Most gamers will like the "speed" and relatively quieter reds or blacks. I hate them, but the consensus is that they are "gaming switches". Brows are a middle ground of tactile--feel the bump as it actuates, but little sound unless you are bottoming out hard while typing. Blues tend to be the loudest of the easily found switch types, and have the tactile bump of browns. Greens are beefier actuation resistance switches with the bump and click of blues. Not going to go into clears, whites and the rest as I have little experience with them. I like the blues the most because the feedback seems to make me more aware of my typing and key actuation, so I tend to type faster and more accurately. When gaming, I know the key registered before I see the visual feedback due to the sound and feel. It's just my preference, though and everyone's varies. Reminds me more of the buckling spring switches from back in the day. One of the good points of mechanical keyboards--options for just about everyone.

I digress...to the review!

I borrowed my friend's Filco "Tactile" (MX Browns) Tenkeyless to see why he spent $150+ on a keyboard that had no features and not even a numpad. I was currently using a Logitech G19, which are pretty pricey but have an extremely long list of features. And an LCD screen. And millions of color options for backlighting. Filcos do not come standard with any of this. Not even dedicated media buttons or volume controls. They are just keyboards, and this model doesn't even have a numpad.

So why did I buy it? After a week I found that I was typing faster and more accurately, I had all but stopped using the numpad and had become faster using 8 fingers for numbers instead of 3 on the numpad, realized that without the numpad my mouse was more ergonomically aligned and my desk space was more efficient. I didn't miss a single one of the bells and whistles of my G19. Even the volume controls. I had quickly learned all the hotkeys and shortcuts for most of my programs/games that I would have to use without the extra buttons and features, and was faster it without them.

The biggest difference was when I went back to the old rubber-dome topped light-show that was formerly my favorite gaming toy. It felt cheap. It was $30 more than the filco, but it felt cheaper by far. It wasn't nearly as sturdy (Filco's feel like they could be used to break down a door, exceptionally solid and a little heavy). The Filco never budged while typing or resetting my hand position after grabbing paperwork. The G19 is made of plastic and it felt very flimsy after using the steel back-plated Filco. The G19's keys felt squishy and likely to fail. It felt huge, bulky, gimmicky and why did I need back-lights? I know where the keys are. When using the filco, I pretty much didn't look down at all. I just knew that everything is where it was supposed to be, and there was never a need to check my work. I only had 87 keys to keep track of--only regularly use 70 or so. I think the G19 has 136. I soon realized that I preferred the essentials. Though my typing did retain it's accuracy, I did lose some speed without the mechanical switches.

This was a few years ago. I finally ponied up and dropped some dough on the last keyboard I may actually need. Mechanical keyboard switches are rated up to 50 million keystrokes each. Rubber dome are 1-5 million keystrokes.

All in all, I'd say Filco's are expensive, but justifiably so. They are made to last, and sacrifice bells and whistles for reliability and ergonomics. I've had mine for 2 months. I gave my wife my flashy other keyboard. She prefers the soft-feel of the rubber domes and how quiet they are, but thinks the LCD screen and extra keys are silly. Now I'd say I agree with the latter.

If you know someone who has one, see if you can borrow it for a week. Try before you buy. But for me, this is the greatest keyboard made since the IBM Model M Keyboard. Which--if you're too young to have used or never had the pleasure--was a true pleasure to type on.

title: First one faulty. Second works just fine.
text:
The first one I received in the mail had the absolute worst mouse on a trackpad I've ever used. It's jittery, randomly right-clicks, gets stuck on some invisible force field, randomly selected while scrolling. It was just worthless. I tried on multiple devices with the unifying receiver and Bluetooth. Just terrible on everything. I own MANY Logitech products and I couldn't be more let down by such a piece of trash. Where is QC? Requesting a replacement, The new one works well enough. Not nearly as responsive as the DiNovo Edge (greatest HTPC Keeb ever made, REALLY wish they'd bring it back), but it also isn't over $200. The Edge didn't go out without a fight, but my toddler thoroughly smashed it while I was getting his breakfast. So I needed a replacement, and it looks like their best model right now for the category is this. First off, this is NOT as good as the Edge, but we'll let it stand on its own merit, not just a long-winded side by side.

Construction quality is so-so. It feels too plastic-slick. VERY light, which is great for carrying around, but terrible for it staying in place. Every time you hit a key or barely nudge it, the whole thing gets pushed around.

The keys are less than optimal, not concaved and therefore really weird to touch type on, which is what you need to do when looking across a room at a TV or projection screen. Also, it's a bit spongy on the feel, but this reduces the sound, which is positive when using for media. I'm typing on it right now, and it isn't too bad for accuracy, but absolutely not preferred for usage due to the shape of the keys. I'm a proficient touch typist and there are still moments I doubt if I'm aligned properly. Sure, there's the homing bumps on F and J, but the rest of my fingers could be slightly off center, so I find myself second-guessing. I think they went for looks over functionality on a lot of the features. I'm not expecting Signature Plastics keycaps or mechanical switches, but just a bit more attention to the part of the keyboard you actually interact with--the keys--might be a good idea.

The left-click mouse button on the top left corner is clever, but you'd think they'd have the right click close by...yet it is the primary function of the F5 key. Weird. I get that you still have the dedicated buttons next to the pad, but if you are standing or in some way--not resting the board on your lap--it makes it unwieldy.

The battery life, insofar, is spectacular. They did a great job there. I have a feeling it will be weeks before needing charging. I haven't found any hardware indicators, but as long as you don't forget to charge it a couple times a month you'll be fine.

Connectability works (being recognized when turned on). There really isn't a way to make "it does the job" sound like it's something amazing. Either it works or it has issues or just doesn't work at all. This is the first of the three.

Range. VERY good. Even on Bluetooth, I was able to use it 60+ feet, with 2-3 basic walls in between, not a hickup. Could probably go further. If one was using this to teach a class with a projection system and the PC it was connected to was at the back of a medium theatre or college classroom, I think it'd still work just fine.

The backlighting is pretty good, though I think they missed something with making the Functions pretty much invisible (just the alphas, modifiers and media keys light, not F1-F12, sleep/power and Bluetooth connect) as they are not backlit. Worse yet, they are a reddish brown, making them hard to see in even moderate lighting conditions. I touch type, but I don't have all the spacing memorized for the sleep button, blue tooth connecting and whatnot. Hitting the sleep button accidentally while watching a movie or with a presentation would kind of spoil the moment. Maybe have a button like that be off to the side or completely separate. Like the Edge...(again, so perfect).

The mouse touchpad on the new model I received was acceptable. It lags a tiny bit and isn't exactly precise, but it serves its functions. With gesture controls, it's pretty easy. The dedicated mouse buttons serve their function, but otherwise, they are pretty much unused with the ability to just tap on the pad or tap with two fingers for right-click. Dedicated (and lit) volume controls are nice. I like that they are separate and would be very hard to accidentally hit. The media keys are kind of "meh." Take them or leave them. As long as I can assign them to whatever I want, it's a non-issue. Seen one, seen them all.

Overall, this is an okay HTPC keyboard/mouse combo. Even with its shortcomings, I would find it average and worth what it costs. Not a great value, as I think it's pricing could be a little lower to make it punch up for its weight class, but it does the job.

3 solid stars. Would give it 3.5 if that was an option. 4 is reserved for something that goes a bit beyond the norm, while 5 is for best in class. I think some people think 5 should be for "if there's nothing wrong with it", but that means it's average, IMO. A solid C+ grade in this case. Like this.

title: The trick to scrolling is easy.
text:
Either you like TrackBall mice or you don't, but the one "downside" I've heard on the SlimBlade vs the TrackBall Expert is the scrolling ring on the Expert, vs the twisting motion on the SlimBlade. Here's the trick: don't twist the ball on the SlimBlade. Put your finger down on the chrome ring (which is more of a track, as it is hollowed out for this exact action) around the ball and move it like you do on the Expert. Your finger will contact at the perfect angle to twist the ball as if you were using the ring, without using your thumb or another finger and it will also make an almost tactile click while doing it. Since the ball has decent weight, it will hold momentum for long scrolls with a flick of the finger, but has the distance control for fine scrolling.

Besides that, it's a dream to use. I find myself being much more efficient, and my work space is much more organized while doing projects. If you like TrackBall mice, it's wonderful. If you prefer using a traditional drag about mouse that has you move your whole arm a foot back and forth a few thousand times a day, stick with that. I used to be that guy, but this has changed my mind.

title: My 3rd Powershot
text:
I got lucky with my very first digital camera; I bought the Canon Powershot A40 and haven't looked back. Now I'm upgrading for the 3rd time to the A75 (the A85 is just too much). Here's the amazing thing: with the last two PowerShots (A40 and A60), I took *over 5500* pictures and neither one coughed once. I sold the A40 6 months ago (after 4000 pics) and the current owner says it's still running like a champ. This line of digital cameras is the best thing going for the price. My Dad and brother both seem to insist on buying Nikon cameras. Then, every time we get together for the holidays, all I hear is "I wish my camera did that" or "Can I get a copy of your picture? It looks better." This camera sports features that even $400 cameras don't (I know, because I gave the other manufacturers an honest chance to get me to leave Canon this time, but they just couldn't offer anything comparable).

Now, I'm no dummy when it comes to photography. I've been an SLR user for many, many years (currently, I have a Canon EOS Rebel). Unfortunately, digital SLR's are still too expensive. I bought the Powershot because of the full manual mode (I do a lot of astrophotography and this is perfect for it). I have total control over the settings. Combined with a 52mm lens adapter, this camera satisfies 90% of my SLR cravings. The pictures are consistently crisp and well exposed. I rarely encounter a situation where the PowerShot isn't able to rock and roll. Battery life is stunning. I routinely get 500 pictures with the LCD on and maybe 30% flash (I have 2100 mAh NiMHs). Added features such as 600x480 movies, a really sharp panoramic mode (photos are "stitched" together on the computer), manual white-balancing option, histograms, manual focus, aperture/shutter priority modes and PictBridge printing are icing on the cake.

The one con I've found is that the Powershot line seems to perform a bit sluggishly in low-light conditions, often requiring a few seconds to get a decent reading.

This really is THE best camera in its class(IMO and that of many "professional" reviewers). If you search for a certain price or megapixel resolution and a Powershot "A" line is included in the results, buy it. You won't be sorry at all. If you buy one of the others, you'll honestly pay too much.

title: Negative reviews show lack of understanding...
text:
To begin with, if you're looking at this battery, you might have a D200. If so, you have no choice in the matter. Whether it's 1 star or 5, if you don't buy this battery you have a $1,700 paperweight (and yes, I'm the proud owner of a D200 in non-paperweight mode).

Second, the battery is not what's at fault here. The D200 is an energy monster. It sucks these poor little guys dry like a starved man at a all-you-can-eat. (This is the price of the incredible functionality offered by the D200. If you want longer bettery life, you'll have to give up MUCH of what makes the D200 the powerhouse it is.) The EL3e performs wonderfullly in the D70/50, providing slightly longer life than the recalled EL3a (the third contact on the EL3e is for the D200 only. The 70 & 50 both ignore it).

Bottom line: There is nothing wrong with this battery. If you have a D70 or D50, buy with the assurance it will take many, many shots on a single charge. If you have a D200, buy because you have to then realize that *you* determine how long the battery lives. A VR lens will cut an already "short" battery life even more. So, you can complain about the battery being the issue or the D200 being the issue. Only the latter is correct. If you want long battery life, go back to the D70.

Personal rant: The D200 is worth the reduced battery life in so many ways that I'm actually annoyed with those that complain about this. Sure, the battery could last longer, but why stop there? I'D like 20Mp, ISO speeds to 3200 with no noise at all, a 10-400mm VR lens tack sharp at all apertures with f/1.4 throughout. But you know what? Not gonna happen. The D200 provides FAR more capability than what you actually paid for (just ask D2X users), so stop whining about short battery life. There's no such thing as the perfect camera. The D200 comes so close, however, it's almost sacriligious to whine about it. By all means, let's teach Nikon a lesson! How dare they give us this camera at 2/3 of what they could *easily* sell it for and not give us 800 RAW's/charge? >:(

And FWIW, you most certainly CAN get 1800 JPG's from one charge, You just have to do it like Nikon did. Yes, their tests are unrealistic in that respect, but if you're so upset about it, return the camera and let someone who will appreciate it have their turn...

PS To "Dwarfbug" why did you give the *battery* 2 stars? These reviews are exactly that: reviews. Speak about the product in question. Don't just respond to someone's review and drop 2 stars with no explanation why. And also speak about something you know. There is no recall on the D200. There is a recall on the EN-EL3 which will not work in the D200 anyway. It is a D50/D70 battery and is replaced with either the EN-EL3a or the EN-EL3e (the "e" being a pretty sweet deal (some even resell them to D200 users a buy TWO 3rd party EN-EL3a's (Targus, etc))).

title: Excellent replacement for the 18-200mm VR
text:
I carried an 18-200VR for a year and half and, though I loved it, I was often dissappointed by what I perceived as a kind of softness. Reading reviews of this lens led me to try it as a substitute. I have yet to be disappointed. I perceive an almost twofold increase in overall image sharpness, often able to make out the individual hairs in pictures of my baby where the 18-200 would "muddy" them on occassion. The additional 16-18mm on the wide end comes in handy as well.

The lens itself is a bit smaller than the 18-200 and feels "better" on my D300, putting the center of gravity closer to the body (a personal preference, to be sure) and being a bit more compact. It is quite responsive, perhaps more so than the 18-200 because it has a shorter range to cover. It is also not subject to the lens creep that plagued the 18-200.

Though I bought the 18-200 well before the 16-85 was released, if I was doing it "today," I'd skip the 18-200 altogether and grab the 16-85 and save the difference for the 70-300mm. I'm not knocking the 18-200 which is the ultimate "walk around" lens (I can't even begin to count the number of times I took a shot at 18mm and then zoomed in 200mm the next minute), the loss of image quality wound up being the deal killer for me. Though I've sacrificed the 85-200 range with this lens, the added sharpness more than makes up for it and the 16-18 range means I change to my wide-angle a bit less frequently.

All-in-all, I feel like this lens may have been the best value in a "workhouse" lens for my purposes.

title: A triumph of form over function.
text:
OK, I'll begin by saying that the new Shuffle is, without doubt, one of the smallest, sexiest MP3 players I've ever seen. I love how it looks. It's... compelling. Of course, with this level of form, some functionality is lost. With the 3G Shuffle, it's the buttons (or lack thereof).

Apple decided to move the buttons off the controller and onto the headphone cord. There are two major flaws that I can see:

1. I can't use "any old" pair of headphones anymore. Sure, the music still plays, but if I can't pause, skip, turn the volume up/down, what's the point. I'm now tied into either Apple's headphones or third-party headphones with the controller. Gone are the days of a "headphone catastrophe" where the headphone cord gets pinched while traveling and I have to run out to a store and grab a pair of substitute $10 phones. I now have to either shell out $20-30 and/or find a local Apple store. Not good. (And let's not even talk about using it with my car stereo...)

2. The controls are... in a bad place. It's kind of hard to grab the controller without looking when it's bouncing around near my jaw while running. Today, it took me about 5-6s to actually get a hold of the darned thing and skip ahead. Later in the day, I grabbed it a bit quicker but then accidentally yanked the earbud out. This was obviously designed without testing it "in the field."

To both of the above, some comment: "wait until Apple releases an adapter with controls in a better position that allow you to use normal headphones." Of course, my reply is "I already spent $80 on this thing. You want me to spend MORE?"

In the end, this is one sweet of technology that just screams "impress your friends." Of course, you don't hear it whispering "and secretly dread using me anywhere but in your living room chair."

At least Apple's not discontinuing the 2G Shuffle...

title: Screw knob came off on first use
text:
The idea behind this clamp is brilliant. Unfortunately, the design misses on a key point: the knob used to tighten and loosen the clamp may be subjected to a lot of force. I clamped mine down pretty tight on a railing to be sure my camera was secure. When I came back to unclamp it, the knob simply twisted off. Upon closer inspection, the knob has threads in the center that screw onto the same threaded piece that holds the clamping foot pad. With very little force, it simply unscrewed itself since the foot had enough pressure to stay stationary. It took quite a bit of effort to get the the clamp off in the end because the knob would simply not stay on for me to unscrew. Perhaps there was some kind of glue and I just got a bad one. Not sure, but it has definitely rendered it useless for the moment. Perhaps some SuperGlue might work...

It is also worth nothing that this retailer has marked this up over twice what the MSRP is. Check B&H Photo or REI for a more reasonable price.

EDIT: After the discussion with Raleighphile, I'm putting a few stars back. The clamp really is a decent device, but I think the decision of not adding a thread locking agent to nut in the clamp is a potential design flaw. If you're dealing with a surface that is not slick, be sure to pay extra close attention to how hard you tighten it down. If you're cognizant of the limitations (or add threadlock like I did), it really is a decent little gadget to have, but loses two stars for forcing me to do what the manufacturer should have done.

title: Excellent surge protector, but *don't lose the remote*
text:
I'll begin with the positives, because when I hit the sole negative of this surge protector, it may be enough to completey skip the purchase.

First and foremost, the idea of two power "zones" is excellent. I have really enjoyed the ability to have a "TV Night" zone and then a "Movie/Game night" zone. That I can have a setup where I can choose to only power the TV, DVR, HTPC and so on without having to fire up the power bricks for the XBox, PS2, stereo receiver, etc is excellent. Instead of running power to every device, I can choose just to power half of them. While 3 or 4 zones would be even better, the mere fact that they even thought to give me the choice of two is excellent. (And just to be clear, you can have both zones on at once).

Second, the layout is intelligent. Though the strip is rather large, there are no outlets that are "too close." They're all evenly spaced out and have a kind of stair-step tier system, so that the top row is recessed a bit, keeping bricks from bumping into one another is they overhang a bit.

Third, the look of the strip is a nice black that blends in easily with an entertainment center. The plugs are all on the back, so from the front you don't see anything but the little power circle.

Finally (and this is the negative), there's the remote! I'll begin by saying that being able to turn the strip off an on from the couch is great. Since the remote uses RF and doesn't require line-of-sight you could also hide it in a way that you wouldn't have to worry about being able to get to a master switch. But therein lies the problem: there's no master switch. So if the remote slips between the sofa cushions, you can forget watching TV. As far as I've been able to determine, there is no physical switch on the strip. Lose the remote and you have to go buy a new strip. If the battery dies and you don't have a replacement, no TV for you! (And it's not even a AAA that runs the remote, but a CR2032 watch battery that is not often on hand). This proves to be a fatal flaw, as you become so paranoid about losing the remote, you don't take it to the sofa but instead leave it where you know it won't disappear, effectively defeating the purpose of a remote.

In the end, a genius designed everything on this strip but the ability to turn it on and off. Whoever said "hey, let's design it so that you can ONLY turn it on with a remote that's incredibly easy to lose" should be fired. Just imagine how likely you'd be to buy a TV that could only be turned on with a remote the size of a pack of cards. If you'd get that TV, get this strip. If you wouldn't take the chance on an easily-lost remote sending your TV to the curb, skip this...

EDIT: Please see Robbit's comment on the ability to unplug the power strip and plug it back in to get "always on" functionality.

title: Bass is a bit too strong, but otherwise quite nice
text:
To get straight to the point, the bass on this things is wayyyyyy powerful. To my ears, it's actually *too* powerful, sometimes overpowering the lyrics in bass-heavy songs (with today's uninspired lyrics, one does have to wonder if they're actually meant to be heard). I think it's important to know about this, since not everyone wants booming bass in their ear, but that's about the only thing I find as a serious "con."

The cord itself is pleasingly long. I'm 6'4" and, with the earbuds in, the end of the cord comes down to my knees. This is great for situations where you may have the player at your back (e.g. running) and need a longer cord. The flat cord is supposedly less prone to tangling and, while this has been true, it does seem to be harder to actually find the jack in all that cord. The jack itself is angled at almost 90º, which is great in some situations but not so much in others (personally, I like it, but I could see it being a problem for others). It's also worth noting that the sealed nature of the ear buds means taps on the cord transmit the sound to your ears. With the volume at a reasonable level, this isn't noticeable, but at low volumes, you'll hear it every time the cord bumps up against something.

The volume control is worth talking about. It is not actually the type that controls the device to which it's connected. Instead, it's an in-line potentiometer design that increases/reduces the volume *after* it leaves the device. That is to say that you'll never be able to increase the volume on the device from the headphones. If you set the volume at 50%, 50% is all you'll get at "max" volume on the headphones. This is actually a nice feature, imho, since you can set an upper limit and then have finer control through the headphones. On the other hand, the slider on the headphones isn't particularly precise, so the practice doesn't quite keep up with the theory. Still, it's nice to know you won't accidentally run the volume all the way up while running then blow your ears out next time because you forgot to to turn things down. The button used to pause/play/skip seems to work fine, though as an Apple person, the entire volume button assembly is a bit too large for my tastes. The microphone works well enough, but the fact that the cords themselves pass the sounds of "bumps" and "rubs" makes it less useful than I'd like.

In the end, I'm generally pleased with the headphones. Compared to the retail price of Apple Earpods, this seem to be reasonably priced for the increased bass response, longer cord, etc. That said, were it not for the extra-long cord, I might look elsewhere, if only because the bass is a bit too over-tuned for my tastes.

EDIT (9/2014): I'm rethinking my take on the bass. I have several sets of earpods/headphones and I've come to rely on these when I want nice bass. That's not to say I carry these all the time, but if I can tell a song has a nice bass line, I'll reach for these every time.

title: Some of other reviewers' issues explained?
text:
First, to get the basics out of the way, the AmazonBasics is what it says it is: an Apple-certified Usb-to-Lightning cable. It is capable of both charging and providing a data connection for syncing. The cable itself is a bit stiffer than Apple's cables and, from an admittedly perception-based standard, not built as well. That said, it "works as intended" with all of my devices (iPhones, iPad, iPods). Now, on to some of the points raised by other reviewers:
