There are plenty of inexpensive, smaller caps to be used, so why Amazon chose not to use them is beyond me. That said, I have not have the issues with getting the Lightning end to fit my various cases. I have no doubt that there are cases out there where it would not fit, but I'm willing to bet those were designed with Apple's cables in mind, rather than third-path options. It has not been an issue for me.

2. Regarding the incompatibility message, this comes from plugging the cord into unpowered or low-powered USB hubs/chargers. I immediately got an incompatibility error when I plugged my iPhone into my unpowered USB hub, but I also got the error *when using an Apple cable*; a clear indication that the "accessory" in question was the hub, not the cable. For those with an AmazonBasics Lightning cable, I would suggest testing with an Apple cable anytime you get an error message. I think you'll find the issue lies with the Usb port, not the cable itself.

In the end, I honestly can't recommend this cable. While I applaud Amazon's decision to get a third-party cable out there, the price difference is usually about 3-4 USD. For that difference, I'd much rather go with the smaller, better-constructed Apple cable. **THat said,** I would absolutely go for the shorter 4-inch cable Amazon sells. I can think of numerous situations where a short cable can be a benefit (e.g. traveling with a battery pack). I would consider the 4-inch cable to be 4 stars.

tl;dr: Cable works just like an apple cable, but at the cost of a bigger form factor and cheaper construction. Any errors are likely due to the USB port, not the cable (verify this using Apple cable). 3-foot cable is not worth the price savings, but 4-inch is.

title: Great sound and noise isolation, but the if the cord bumps anything, you'll hear it.
text:
This is really a quite nice headset. The ear pads are nice and cushiony and insulate you from outside noise quite well (though they're not well ventilated, so your ears can get a bit hot on a warm day). The head "strap" is also reasonably comfortable. The sound is excellent. Since there's not much outside interference, you can hear all the little things you'd otherwise miss from people chatting around you, etc. The bass is very "bass-y," with nice, deep booms, but not at the expense of the higher range. All in all, this headset delivers on sound quite well. In that respect, they're well worth it. So why 3 stars? The cord messes it all up.

I've not really been able to nail down the culprit yet, but the way the cord is connected to the headset results in pops and scratches anytime you bump or rub the cord along something. I don't mean the sound itself "pops" or "scratches" like a poor connection, but rather that the cord carries the vibration into the headset and you can tell you just hit something. It's sort of like when you tap on the outside of a headset and you can hear the "thump thump" of your finger, expect that with this headset, just shifting on the couch will carry that sound to the headset. It can get rather annoying, causing you to spend more time trying to get in a "still" position than actually enjoying the sound. I've tried it when gaming on a portable device, and I find I have to go through all sorts of cord positions before I can find one that won't carry the bumps and scratches from moving the device this way or that. In the end, it's annoying enough that I've just gone back to my old Razer Charcarias which has a cloth sheath that absorbs those vibrations (and which also has better construction for the ear pieces). In the end, I feel like Razer put some serious money into constructing the speakers, and then skimped on construction.

title: Does the job, but heat and intermittent remote connection dampen the experience
text:
I feel there are plenty of reviews here that cover the basics, so I'm going to focus on two drawbacks that take some of the fun out of the action cam. (But to be clear, I agree wholeheartedly with the positive comments here (as well as some of the more reasoned negatives)).

My first concern is the heat generated by the actioncam. It's nothing that would prove uncomfortable if you were wearing it on a headband, but when kept in the splash-proof enclosure, I am concerned about the possibility of overheating on hot Texas days. While I would love to mount this to my bike for one of my 30-mile rides, I'm loathe to do so because of how it gets in the poorly-ventilated case. On a 100ª day, I'm not convinced that the actioncam won't overheat, either shutting down to protect the components or, worse, damaging itself. "Don't carry it in the case" someone might reply. I'd agree, especially since the likelihood of it getting splashed on said hot day is slim. The problem with this, however, is that the lens is one of the most exposed things I've ever seen. There's no sort of flange to offer even minimal protection against rocks, bugs, crashes, etc. I've accidentally left fingerprints more often than I care to count just from brushing the lens (get a Nikon Lens Pen for this). As such, the case is pretty much required for any sort of activity. (The converse of all of this, however, is that the cam should function fairly well in cold weather).

My second primary complaint is the remote. While I should begin by saying it's one of the coolest things I've seen in a long time, the novelty quickly wears off when you're faced with what I consider to be an under-featured software set combined with intermittent connectivity issues. I used the cam on an 8-hour drive across Texas (I used the intervalometer to take one shot every 5s and then spliced them all into a time lapse video). Since the cam was pointed out the windshield (and because the LCD showing pictures taken is on the right*), I needed the remote to see if the cam was taking shots regularly. 3/4 of the time, the remote seemed to connect via Wi-Fi just fine, but at least 1/4 of the time, it simply would not, even after turning it off then on again. As far as I know, this wasn't an interference issue and I had updated all of the various firmwares. For whatever reason, the remote just wouldn't sync up. Perhaps this is easily fixed in a future software update, but for the moment, I don't feel I can rely on the remote (and the smartphone app is only so-so and not really worth using, imo). It's a brilliant idea, however, so I hope Sony gets those kinks worked out.

Despite the above negatives, I still give the actioncam 4 stars. As others have noted here, it really is a great little machine and has many well-thought-out functions. The negatives, while important to know about (which is why I've focused on them here) do not seriously detract from the overall experience. Does Sony have a GoPro killer on their hands? I have to say no. But if you buy a Sony rather than a GoPro, have you made a mistake? Not at all. I think what we (finally) have is a choice. Sony's managed to catch up, and I think we all benefit from this.

*The cam can actually be used upside down if you change a software setting, but in my case, it obscured my view of the road more than I wanted, so I kept it in the "upright" orientation.

EDIT: One final negative: the MicroSD card can be put in backwards! Sony, in their infinite, um, wisdom has included a flash card slot that's intended for two different formats. As a result, there are no physical guides to ensure you don't put a MicroSD in backwards. This is idiotic in my opinion, and has led to me putting it in wrong at least 3 times (there's no easily-seen guide to help put it in right that I've seen). Be sure to check by turning on the actioncam before you seal it all up. Don't assume that because the card fit, you put it in right.

title: Dell should have skipped this particular price war, and you should skip this particular Dell.
text:
I've spent a long time waffling on writing this review because I wanted to be sure I wasn't writing on initial impressions but on actual use. After two months, I feel comfortable rating this one star because... "I hate it." In fact, the only reason I feel comfortable giving one star is because Dell (thankfully) included the option to use this computer as an external monitor. Having taken the time to uninstall all of the "bloatware" that Dell includes and upgrading the internal hard drive to a Solid State Drive, I have still found little use for this as a computer. Whether it's a result of Windows 8.1 bogging down the system, or just an exceedingly weak hardware suite, this computer really isn't up to the task for just about anything.

Dell's first mistake was to include a dual-core Celeron processor alongside Windows 8. The other models in this line include beefier processors and, I'm sure, perform much better. Whether it's running an Adobe Flash applet in a browser, watching YouTube videos, multitasking between two office apps, or even checking e-mail, this Dell continually chokes whenever any sort of stress is put on the CPU. One would think that 4Gb of RAM would be sufficient, but this appears not to be the case. And given that there is only one slot for a RAM module, upgrading to 8Gb (at almost a third of the basic price of the computer) seems frivolous.

The form factor is admittedly fantastic. The monitor can be set at multiple angles and offers a pleasing aesthetic, provided you're willing to invest in right-angle USB adapter to keep cords from poking out of the right side of the monitor. The included keyboard and mouse, while basic, work well. The controls on the back are reasonably accessible, though you ave to memorize what each does and, if you're like me, will find the decision not to include volume buttons to be an annoyance.

As mentioned above, performance is dismal. Any sort of multitasking, even with an SSD, results in significant slowdowns. Background processes? You better kill all of them if you want any responsiveness. And don't expect to leave many applications open. You'll need to shut each one of them down to preserve what little responsiveness there is. Even using the surround setting for the included sound system is going to cost you, and the audio quality isn't even that impressive to begin with.

In the end, I've had to resort to simply using this as a nice, but expensive, external monitor. In that role, it performs well (though there's a glitch where the OSD stays on in the main computer sleeps the screen and you wake it back up).

All told, I would *strongly* urge those looking for a computer to stay away from this particular model and spend the extra money on the quad-core version. I really don't even think this is a suitable computer for children or those who just want a barebones computer, especially given the wide range of less expensive laptops on the market. Perhaps the only realistic option would be to uninstall Windows 8 and install Windows 7, which appears to put less stress on the system. Even then, it likely wouldn't be worth the cost of buying a windows 7 license.

Dell should have skipped this particular price war, and you should skip this particular Dell.

title: Who knew an iPhone could double as a garage door opener?
text:
Insofar as I was only given one of these to test, I can't comment on the entire range of uses of to which one could put this slick little device. What I CAN comment on, however, is that it makes an awesome remote garage door opener. As far as installation goes, I simply replaced the manual opener button on our wall with this device. And when I say "simply," I do mean it. Granted, I'm pretty tech-savvy, but at no point did I feel like the process would have been beyond the average user (though I would encourage owners of this to Google around for one of any number of useful guides that walk you through the process). The wiring was very straightforward and the mounting only took a couple of screws in the sheetrock (I used sinkers to be sure). One this was on (and I turn the power breaker back on (please turn the power breaker off before installing)), I set the WeMo up on our wireless network and then downloaded the iOS app. From there, it's been a very simply process of pulling up the app and controlling the garage door. I've even tested it when we were out-and-about and it's worked swimmingly.

One thing I do feel needs to be pointed out is that, as sold, this is not a device that will let you check to see whether you left your garage door ( or other device) up (or on). This is a "dumb" switch, so you won't be able to pull it up while you're at the restaurant to be sure you closed the garage door. To do that, you'll need to purchase an additional magnetic sensor that you mount near the door to provide feedback regarding the door's position. While this is not something I've gotten around to, it is definitely on the To-Do list. From what I've been able to read online, it's yet another straightforward process, though it does require running wires either through the attic or, if looks aren't important, along the ceiling using any number of attachment options (I'll likely just use a staple gun with rounded staples). Once you've done this (or so I've read), you'll have feedback concerning the state of the door and will then be able to check at the restaurant. In no way does this additional step detract from my "love" for this device, but I do feel like it's an important note for those looking to buy.

So, in short:
-Plan for 30-60 minutes for installation (depending on your familiarity with wiring)
-Be ready to buy an additional component if you want feedback concerning whatever device you've hooked it up to
-Don't expect there to be "thousands of uses" around the house, but for the uses it's designed for, be ready to have loads of fun. :)

From the standpoint of aesthetics, the pictures on the site do the lamp justice. title: The best solution to mounting an iPhone that I've ever seen
text:
Hands down, this is the best solution to using an iPhone as a cyclocomputer that I've ever seen. If you can get over the idea of destroying your $600 computer in a bike crash (I'm trying to!), this is perfect.

For beginners, Annex have developed a case that actually works for day-to-day phone usage. With the exception of the fact that the mounting receptacle on the back means the phone won't really lay flat on a table (it'll wobble a bit if you're not pressing in the center), it works great. it's slim, so it fits in a pocket well, but is made to take a hit (as far as I can tell, without actually having tested the case taking a hit). The lip around the screen could be a bit deeper, but it seems most cases are moving towards this "low profile" design and exposing the screen to more danger. The case feels good in the hands and isn't slippery or anything. The button coverings are responsive, as one would expect.

The mounting system itself is genius. You can look at the pictures to get a better idea, but you basically mount a small "knob" the the handlebar stem, put the case on it at a 45º angle, then turn upright. The case locks in with a satisfying click and really can't be budged without reaching below and pressing the blue collar down. The is no rattling or wobbling while riding, and the phone stays nice and steady when using the screen. The minimalist approach employed here is more secure than any of the options I've tried before, and at half the "bulk" of many of them.

Included with this is a brilliant weather cover. Made of a clear plastic, it fits over the Annex case like a sleeve, covering up all the various nooks and crannies to protect against sweat, rain, puddle splashes, etc. The camera is covered by this clear protective "jacket," but pictures still come out pretty well. You could definitely get a license plate if you needed, or a picture of something cool along the ride (though it takes some practice to learn how to remove the case with one hand while riding). The cover does keep you from being able to use any of the ports, so you'll want another option for music if you do that while riding.

The only real negative I can think of is that the case and protective cover and both *very* tight. Tighter than anything I've come across. This is good, because it means they're ultra-secure once in place, but it also means they can be something of a pain to put on and remove. For the case itself, this isn't much of an issue (like it said, it's great for day-to-day), but the protective cover, not so much. On the other hand, I'd rather have a tight weather cover to keeps rain, etc from seeping in than a loose one.

All in all, I absolutely recommend this kit. And at the listed price, it's even a bargain. Best thing I've ever seen. :)

PS You can also buy other mounting items that work with the case. I bought "Wall Mount Twin Pack" and stuck one on the console in my car. I can now quickly and easily mount my iPhone in my car. Such a brilliant system!

EDIT 4/28/2015: I have taken off a star because the rain cover has proved to be something of a liability. While it covers the phone well, it's just not tight enough to keep water, etc from slowly creeping up the sides. To be honest, I don't think there's anything they could do about it, but it does mean the cover is a false sense of security. A simply solution is to run some tape around the seam on the back, but that means you've planned ahead and have tape. The rain cover's still better than nothing, but not the amazing I originally thought.

title: Excellent for extreme conditions. Less convenient as day-to-day.
text:
First off, this is one heck of a case when it comes to protecting your phone from the elements. Assuming the case is put together correctly, I don't see that there's anyway for water, dust, etc to get at the phone. The screen self is unprotected (by design), but the gasket that fits around it does an excellent job of forming a waterproof seal (your screen can get water on it all day long and be fine. It's the various seams on the phone that are the trick). The TouchID cover works like a champ, and all of the other buttons are way to operate, with the exception of the mute button, which is *far* too stiff for my preferences (I have to use my thumbnail to flip it, which gives me pause about how long the rubber will last at that point, and whether I might be creating a situation were water would eventually get in).

A separate line is warranted for the sealed headphone extension jack. It is brilliant! It screws into the case and has an O-Ring that creates a waterproof seal. Since water can't really travel down the inside of the extension, you can easily listen to music, etc in a full-on rainstorm. Of course, your headphones might not "weather" (yuk yuk) things so well, but the phone itself will be safe. It's an excellent solution that works great (until you lose the extension (see below)).

In short, if you're out and about in extreme conditions, this is absolutely the case to have. I would trust this case just about anyway. It's in day-to-day use that I wouldn't want to use it.

Because of how well the case is designed for extreme conditions, you sacrifice quite a bit when conditions aren't so extreme. The port for charging is covered in such a manner that *only* Apple charge cables work. There's just enough room for them to slide in. All other 3rd-party cables I tested would *not* fit to charge. Also, the headphone jack is protected in such a way that only the thinnest jacks will fit, and even then, they can' be very hard to remove unless you pull on the cord (a no-no). In my experience, I could only get Apple headphones to fit, and there was barely enough of the plastic sheather sticking out to grab to remove them. The protection around the flash on the camera is such that you *will* get coloration on the flash from light bouncing off the colored covered. For the pink case, this means all of your photos will have a slight pink tint if you use the flash. It's not terrible, but something noticeable if you pay attention to color accuracy in photos. So basically the case is fine for day-to-day if you only have Apple chargers, use a Bluetooth headset, and don't take many pictures with a flash. Not exactly a normal day for me.

In the end, I decided to rate this case on how well it functions for extreme conditions. If I were to take this as a day-to-day case, I'd have to give it only 3 stars, but I the intended audience for this case are those who are really hard on their phones. If you're out mountain-biking, out in a heavy rainstorm, at the beach, skiing, etc, you'll love this case. If you're just out for a run or going grocery shopping, it'll get in the way (at least on the points I mentioned above. If you're just using it for apps, etc, it'll be fine).

title: Basically a simpler, easier-to-read "Kill-A-Watt"
text:
As the title suggests, this energy monitor works similarly to the "Kill-A-Watt" type of energy monitors. For those unfamiliar with energy monitors, the idea is fairly simple: you plug the monitor into a wall outlet and then plug whatever device you want to track into the monitor. Depending on the sophistication, you can track all sorts of metrics. And while the Kill-A-Watt offer far more monitoring options, Belkin's "Conserve Insight" gives the user convenience. Specifically, the readout of energy usage is not part of the wall plug assembly, so you don't have to get under your desk with a flashlight to see your usage.

Belkin keeps things fairly simple with the information it provides. You get either instantaneous or average (monthly or yearly) readouts of carbon footprint (you can set the conversion factor), cost (you have to enter the cost manually), or raw energy usage in kWh. Because the readout is attached with a fairly long cord, you're able to set it up somewhere that it's easier to read (e.g. your outlet is below a desk or behind furniture). That's it! Basically, plug it in, choose the readout you want, decide on instant or average and then let it do its business.

The device itself is well built. Though the wall plug is a bit large, in my experience, it did not obscure the second plug.

All told, I'm glad to have an easier-to-read alternative to my Kill-A-Watt (though I still love all the information my KAW can give me).

title: Excellent sound, fantastic size, but USB-C means yet another cable
text:
After using this BT speaker for a few months, I'm thoroughly impressed. The two most important things (to me)--sound and size--are spot on. Construction is solid and "ease of use" is exactly what I would expect. In short, aside from a rather steep price point, I would absolutely recommend this to friends.

My initial concern for the speaker was whether it could deliver "full" sound in such a small package. This became a non-issue the moment I plugged it in. While I have some speakers with much "punchier" bass (specifically, the UE Mini Boom), the Beoplay still delivers in this area. It does an excellent job of reproducing the "depth" that comes froma bass line, even if it falls short on the "thump." Mids and highs are reproduced quite well, with everything coming to together with nice balance. The app improves on this with "ToneTouch." I would suggest looking into the app on your particular store, but basically you have a slider that moves around on an x-y plane with this quadrant providing "warmth" or that quadrant providing "brightness." You can increase or decrease the size of the circle you slide around, so you can make the effects more pronounced. While I would prefer a traditional equalizer setup, I feel like this works fairly well, and it's definitely more accessible to someone who doesn't quite understand the frequency sliders. Ocverall, I would rate the sound experience a 9/10.

The size is the next best thing. I have BT speakers with smaller footprints, but they tend to either be thicker or have terrible sound. None are able to fit in a pocket AND sound great. The P2 does. Basically, if I can fit my flat hand into a pocket in a bag or my pants, the P2 will fit. The added leather cord is a nice touch for carrying around, but I took mine off since I didn't want to deal with it while carrying the speaker around in my bag. Weight is also a non-issue. This doesn't mean the P2 is light, but I doesn't weigh me down at all. The construction is also solid, but I can't speak to how well it handles abuse (I tend to take care of my electronics).

As far as cons are concerned, I really only have one, and I suspect it will depend on the individual: I do not like having to carry a USB-C to charge (though at ~10h of playtime, I can definitely make it through a day). I'm sure that at some point in the future, USB-C will be ubiquitous, but right now it's a 3rd cable I have to carry around. I did purchase a Micro-USB-to-USB-C adapter that helps, but it's still one more thing to keep up with. I've actually taken one star off because I don't see the need for USB-C for the sole pupose of charging a speaker. If B&O had just gone with Micro-USB, I'd have absolutely no complaints.

So, to recap, excellent sound, fantastic size, but marred by the choice of USB-C interface for charging.

title: I'd love to see this become a "thing."
text:
When I requested this item for review, I didn't exactly know what I was getting. A 'digital cause button' was about the extent of it. I knew it would be something I could wear and that it would allow me to displey static images or GIFs, but that was about it. I had no idea how cool the implementation would be. I expected a lower-res screen, but was pleasantly surprised to find that, at least to the naked eye, I can't see the pixels. I expected something somewhat sluggish, but can happily report that the button is nice and responsive, switching between my various images/GIFs quickly, and displaying even complex GIFs smoothly. I thought it would be heavy-ish, but it feels just right. I doubted the battery would last long, but have had no problem wearing it throughout the course of a day without needing to recharge (I doubt I could go morning to night on a single charge, especially when using a GIF, but anywhere from 5-8 hours has been common). I thought loading images would be some sort of tedious plug-it-into-my-computer process, but the mobile app makes things a snap.

Basically, the "BEAM button" pairs to your phone and you then either browse an impressive library of images and GIFs (some user-created, others obviously coming from commercial sources), pick what you like, and load it. While the loading process can be slow for complex GIFs (several minutes if it has a lot of frames), the onboard storage has enough space for more images/GIFs than I'm likely to use in a month. If you don't find what you like, you can load your own images/GIFs and, with a reasonably intuitive editor, get them ready for the button (color balance, crop, filters, add text, make a slideshow, etc). Once the image is loaded, just press the button on the right to get to the image you want.

I really hope the company behind this digital "cause button" manages to do well enough to eventually get the cost of entry down, because this thing is awesome and I'd love to see it catch on!

text:

The GOOD:
This is a really good first time budget surround sound speaker set, like if you are in college or have a small budget or have a computer you play video games on, or have a small room for Netflix and chill times, you can turn each speaker up or down individually, the blue tooth works pretty decent and connects, but this surround sound is nothing extraordinary

*This is not real 5.1 surround , the reason its called 5.1 is because it has 5 speakers and 1 sub lol! all it does is just split the channel left to right all the time when you plug it in

*It has outdated connections! you can can not use HDMI, YOU CAN NOT USE OPTICAL, (unless you get a adapter , GOOD LUCK FIGURING WHAT KIND) and you barely can use the red and white RCA cords , i have a hisense smart tv and the only way i was able to get this semi-surround sound to work was to plug the adapter they give you from the red and white rca's into the headphone port of my tv, good thing my tv has a dual out so i don't have to have surround sound on 24/7 but some tvs wont have that luxury :(

*The Back Speaker wire is not that long for a living room , its only long enough for a Bedroom unless you splice and extend it, but who wants to go through all that, and if you do splice it, the Blue LED's will not work

*The Remote is the most terrible layout ever! the volume button should be where the "Turn down sub button" is
trust me you will get mixed up every time you go to turn down this device only to see that you are turning down the sub instead of the volume

*it never actually shuts off, you will see 2 led lights blinking in the dark like a alarm clock that needs to be reset

THE UGLY

*The L.E.D. on the main sub woofer is a gimmick , it turns a few colors and thats it!

So in conclusion only get this if this is going to hold you over till you get a better surround system, it will do the job mediocrely for the time being , and the people who are praising this either never actually had a real surround sound 5.1 or they got one for free..

title: Solid drive enclosure, well engineered and easy to get up and running.
text:
I was supplied a sample product by Etekcity to review. I tested this product with a fully up to date patched Windows 7 professional install and a Windows 7 Home Premium laptop.

Overall, the drive enclosure seemed to be a solid unit when compared to other drive enclosures I have used in the past. Solid does equal heavy - but if you're looking for a metal enclosure this one is very nicely put together.

It was not significantly larger than a notebook sized drive - I measured about 5" long by 3.5" across so you do not end up lugging around a massive enclosure to hold your tiny drive. I found the drive insertion and release mechanism extremely intuitive. The drive enclosure opens on the side with the slide of a sturdy plastic release button. As the side opens up, there is a 'finger' inside the drive case the actually pushes the drive out. For me it pushed it out enough (and I have fat fingers) to grab hold of and pull out.

The drive came with both USB 3.0 and eSATA external cables - so you won't be hunting through your cable box looking for the right cable to get up and running. Both cables were of good quality (much better than I would have expected for a device of this price range -- they appeared to be better quality than the cable that came with my new Samsung External Blu-Ray writer, to give you an idea).

I reviewed this enclosure with two different drives, both of which were old laptop drives that I had around. One was a Seagate ST916031AS and the other was a Toshiba MK2546GSX drive. Both worked with no issues at all.

I do have two very minor cons to point out: I presume because the enclosure is metal, it comes with a thin, cut piece of plastic to attach to the bottom of the drive before you slide it in the enclosure. It is the consistency of a screen protector for a smartphone. I would rather have seen this protective plastic attached directly to the inside of the enclosure so I can more readily slide multiple drives in and out of it.

The other con I found was that the instructions that came with the enclosure left a little to be desired. All in all, this device doesn't really require much in way of an instruction manual. Although, there were no instructions on what to do with the plastic protector for the drive. Just slide your drive in, select USB or eSATA and plug it in your computer.

title: Worked great to fix low WiFi signal in my basement.
text:
I was provided a sample to review by Etekcity.

I put this little router in place to amplify the WiFi signal in my basement. All it needed was a place to plug it in. This seriously little router really delivered much better than I had anticipated. And I have been working in the computer networking field for over 15 years - so to impress me with a networking box is saying something.

Overview: First off - this is one very powerful little router with very nice features - including advanced features that I did not expect to see in a router in this price range or of this size. Also - this thing is incredibly small. To put it in perspective, there is barely enough room on the bottom of this router for a standard sized WAN and standard size LAN port. The power plug on the back is thicker than the rest of the router. It is seriously small.

Pros:

Setup - Setup is very easy to use.
Signal Strength - According to my WiFi Analyzer Android app (which is great) Signal strength was better than my Linksys full-sized WRT-400N router that was half as far away. At approximately 40 feet, I had a signal strength of -47db.
Size - I cannot stress enough how small this thing is, yet it doesn't seem to give up on features or signal strength.
Many Advanced Features - This router supports advanced features I just didn't expect to see - such as IGMP proxy (advanced support for multicast). This is something that many don't need, but shows how industrial strength this thing is.
Repeater Mode - repeater mode supports repeating of multiple WiFi signals. Probably not needed at most homes (unless you have guest mode setup on your WiFi), but a very powerful feature.
Scheduled WiFi - This little router has the ability to schedule the WiFi portion on and off. If you know you're not going to be using WiFi at 3:00AM, why leave it on for the hackers to use?
Includes all standard WiFi router features - like MAC Address control.

Cons:

I was unable to determine where to download updated firmware (something I always try to do first thing when receiving something new like this).
This router does support only 2.4Ghz only. Probably not a huge problem for most users.
Kind of a goofy Windows 8 tile-like interface.
Only a single LAN port (which is probably enough for either repeater mode or AP mode).
When the device reboots, it always attempts to take your browser back to the default IP address of the router, even if you've configured a static (like I did in my setup).
When configuring repeater mode, I did not see all of the WiFi networks that I would have expected to see on the 2nd and subsequent entries into the menu.

Other:

In repeater mode, the router allowed me to configure all of the AP's it heard to be repeated. However only one of the additional AP's showed up in my laptop to select or in WiFi Analyzer. This and a couple of the other bugs make me think there are some items that could be perfected. However, I was very impressed with this little router.

I got this air cooler after seeing rave reviews on YouTube, pcpartpicker and new egg. For the price, they said it couldn't be best and it competes with liquid cooling at less than half the price of most name brand liquid cooler setups.

At first glance this thing was very intimidating out of the box. However putting it together was not a big deal at all with the included manual. The standard fan it comes with seems to max out at around 1,395rpm on my rig. Not terrible. What's better is that even on max I can barely hear any noise from the fan.

I LOVE that this fan is so quiet.

While keeping it keeps my AMD8570 (AM3+) at around 19~24c. Under load it's around 40~45c which isn't bad. This is at stock speeds with no oc. While running renders for 3 hours with 8 cores running a flat 100% my temp still never broke 45c. I don't think there are many other jobs that would hold all 8 cores at a pure 100% like rendering can and will do.

My case is the nzxt phantom (older model), which houses this with lots of room.
My motherboard is the Crosshair Formula-Z AMD AM3 by ASUS. This board works WONDERFULLY with this cooler, there is ample space for the heatsink no matter which way you want to rotate it. On my configuration I have the fan facing the memory sockets which sucks air in from the front and blows it out the back. With this motherboard configuration all 4dimm slots are free.

If you're looking for a mobo that will fit this without blocking your ram, and you're using an AMD CPU if recommend the Crosshair Formula-Z. You'll be able to use all 4 slots of ram of any size.

If you're using Intel: the manual comes with instructions on how to use this cooler with Intel sockets as well as all the hardware you'll need.

For the price this is a great cooler!

I used them for Spotify to test out their bass capabilities: at first I thought they had no bass and was disappointed. Then i noticed I could hear a lot of outside noise so I decided to try out all the different sizes of eartips that they included. I found that the large ones worked for me. It created a tight seal and blocked all noise. Also: bass is booming now. If you find that the sound isn't as loud as it should: i highly recommend trying all the different sized eartips. It's worth the effort. I cannot stress how important it is to try all the sizes of both fins and tips. It is a pain, but VERY worth the effort and will change your experience with these (or any) buds. I typically use medium fins and tips, but these required a size higher.

Battery life is amazing. I charged them only once during about 10 hours of listening. As soon as I pop them out of the case, they're connected to my phone and ready to go. As I write this: I am using them on my Kindle to watch movies.

This is the main thing that I was worried about after reading so many wireless reviews: sound synch. With these it is no problem at all! There's no delay and no audio synch issues. These work perfectly. Netflix, YouTube, prime video, etc.

I am very happy with these!

I also tested the call quality: their voice was loud and clear (played in stereo) and they said they couldn't tell i was speaking from a wireless headset.

title: Excellent hardware. Firmware is buggy and weak.
text:
RT-N66U hardware performance is by far the best consumer wireless router I have ever seen. My house is a century old three stories brick house. I used to bridge three wireless access points to blank the entire house with wireless signal. After getting my RT-N66U and paired it with uBee DDM3513 modem in my basement, I am having full signal strength throughout every corner of my basement and rooms on 3 floors up. Now with just one RT-N66U, I have wireless internet speed of 26 mbps up / 4.5 mbps down in every single room in the house. Impressive performance!

Now the disappointment. I have to agree with the other reviewers here. The firmware needs a lot help.

1. With the last Firmware Version:3.0.0.3.112, I am not able to change DHCP range. Not able to reserve IP. I had to down grade to Firmware Version:3.0.0.3.108 to be able to do both.
2. Firewall configuration option is limited
3. I lost my security configurations after a reboot. My RT-N66U turned into a open WIFI spot.
4. No alerts can be sent via email.
5. Minor issues all over the interface. Over all UI (User Interface) is clumsy and not practical.
5. Automatic firmware upgrade did not work on mine. I had to download the file from ASUS web site.

It seems to me that ASUS UI is lost in between a fancy looking interface and a practical, functional configuration panel. As a network engineer and architect for over 16 years, I can see ASUS is trying to make its firmware UI user friendly for regular consumers and also sophisticated enough for pro-sumers to take advantage of what the an excellent piece of hardware can offer. They are just not quite there yet.

ASUS if you are reading this, put a team of network engineer, customer service, and developer together to rework the firmware. Just relying on programers are not enough. Otherwise it would have been a dream product.

If anyone has luck with 3rd party firmware working on RT-N66U, please let me know. I really like the hardware design. I wish the firmware were as good.

title: Decent wireless headphone for most people. But may not for the audiophiles
text:
Just for the reference, I am a Sennheiser user. I own all of their top end in earbuds, on the ears, and over the ears headphone. So I am the type who prefers the type of headphones that clearly produce the native sound from the source.

To me, Anker Soundcore Liverty 2 Pro produces clear High (even a little too much treble to my ear) and a perfect amount of low for the size (just right amount of warm base), but unfortunately the middle is clearly missing. If you are an audiophile, it will be obvious to you. However, since this phone can be tuned to your unique hearing profile (first of its kind, that's why I'm trying it), I found it actually do compensate some of its lacking of middle to the point most people might not even realize the missing middle frequency. So yes, setup and turn on your hearing profile.

Who is ASL2 Pro for?

Most people will find it of a very decent wireless headphone in its price range. Beautifully designed and quality built, very portable, and it is comfortable to wear (make sure to find yourself with the proper fitting, cause it also effect your sound quality).

For audiophiles, you may be bothered by the hissing at the high and the lacking of the middle, despite the overall sound quality can be tuned to quite decent level due to its unique software and hardware capability. Yes, the ambien noise when no music is playing.

I have no problem commute with it. Hopefully Anker will update its firmware to dampen some of the hissing at the high. No sure about the lack of the middle if there is no driver to physically produce it. But maybe they can digitally compensate somewhat.

Yes, I would recommend it for most people at around $100 price range.

title: Only 2k. Not for 4K or DCI 60p shooters
text:
I really like Osee T7. It’s almost the perfect one for me for travel. But…

PROS:

1) Light weight and solid built
2) cooler display surface, and good battery life. My Shinobi 5 display runs hot very quickly. A same Sony F750 battery on Osee T7 lasted almost 2x longer than on Atomos Shinobi 5”.
3) 3000 nits is the brightest screen available at 7 inch right now
4) easy to control joystick and the best navigation manu in my opinion
5) ARRI mount so the monitor locks tight

CONS:
1) limited 2K, and definitely NOT a 4K display. False advertising?
2) for FUJIFILM XT4 owner, the only two 4K source can be displayed in its 2K 30fps display mode are “Internal/external output: Film/Flog or Flog/Film”. Not 4k 60fps but 2k 30fps.
3) in the rest cases, the best possible display you get is 1080p @60fps
4) the color accuracy is a bit off. Can’t be used for judging your color. It won’t matter much if you record in Flog. Not sure I can calibrate it or not.
5) quite a bit lag. Try to wave your hand before your camera and the lags on this display is quite pronounced. Not for shooting sports or fast moving objects. This is another big minus for me.

SUMMARY

If you don’t need to pull focus on a display higher than 1080p 60fps, at this price range, this is the best 7 inch option in terms of its quality, weight and features. It’s a perfect consumer product, best suited for most YouTubers, for casual travel or small home production.

For 4k60p or DCI60p shooters, and more serious videographers who wants a 7 inch real 2K resolution monitor display with the original feed, the only choice now is probably the newly introduced Atmos Shinobi 7. It’s over 2x the cost, or the old Shogun at over 3x the cost.

I have to try my Shinobi 7 for its battery life and its weight to determine if I will keep Osee T7 as my travel monitor.

text:
I bought mine from Costco. And upgraded two of many from Eufy Cam 2 Pros. I own latest and prior Eufy locks, doorbells, sensors, HomeBase2s and a HomeBase 3.

PROs:
1) better video quality
2) solar charging reduces the trips up a ladder to charge the battery.
3) expandable storage space up to 16TB.
4) improved recordings accuracy for thing I would like it to record.
5) AI helps but still a work in progress.

CONs:
1) buggy software. Some configuration interface are not optimized for iPad. One example that happens in both iPhone and iPad: The new video recordings indication square doesn’t update until you click on it. So you won’t know if there is any new recordings. But after you have seen it all, it shows the number of unseen recordings you have just seen and won’t reset to zero until whenever it decides to reset.
2) the only backward compatibility HomeBase 3 has now, with an amy of Eufy products I have, is EufyCam 2 pro.
3) way worse wifi reception at the same spots where the 2 Pros were placed. The only variances in my settings are the Cameras. Is Solar panel the culprit? I don’t know.
4) The solar panel produces average 80 mAh a day. 300mAh is about 2% of total battery. One cam3 charges a bit more while the other less. Given it is not summer anymore. So changing battery will still be required, just less trips.
5) higher battery consumption, (to be expected for 4K video)

In summary, the design is on the right track. But will need a lot more updates to meet the expectations Eufy has set in its advertisement. The company do have tracking records of continuing updates its firmwares, but not fast enough for cam3 in my opinion. It is a half baked product in my view.

At the current price and product level, I would recommend to hold off. Or even better going with Cam 2 Pro at a discount if 2k is enough for you and you don’t mind up a ladder once a couple of times a year

title: Good product I bought used.
text:
I bought this opened box new, seems someone couldn't get it to work returned it like new just opened box. Their loss my gain as I found why it 's not working for a few people and got it to work after a little accidental fumbling around. Find the system requirements, (they fail to tell you what you need to operate this) many people without Blu-ray on their laptop probably don't have the system requirements to use this product properly so there are complaints it doesn't work for them. Before returning the product try to make sure your computer is on single monitor mode not clone mode (for hooking up to a tv or another screen). My system requirements fall short, so I was bummed to find this out the hard way, but then I got it to work and it recognized the Blu-ray player after switching from clone(dual) mode to single mode. This means it won't run to my TV when I play the disc, but I can access the Bluray movies on my laptop now. I didn't have enough memory space to load the whole disc in an image onto my laptop, so you need the space if you seek to legally copy your discs and that's what you bought it for. I personally just needed the extra storage these provide as data disc writers, the plus was the great Slideshow producer program that comes with the install disc, probably would cost as much as the player itself to buy such software production programs, so it was a good bargain all in all. It also surprisingly has a 3d feature but since I can't hook up to my 3d TV I have to wait till my next computer before I explore that mode. The blu-ray player will not stream through BINO (used to make and view 2d-3d from files) even when removing restrictions on the protected disk they still won't be recognized in this format of Windows. I was hoping it would but it was disappointing that you can't access the disc like you can data discs.
***UPDATE** It occurred to me that I didn't try single monitor view just on the TV instead of the laptop, when I did the blue-ray did play onto my TV, so this is no longer an issue.

title: Used camera sold as a New Camera
text:
The box had been opened. Items were missing from the box which are being replaced by Sony after my phone call. The camera was sold to
Me as a new item although it should have been sold to
Me as a used item.

The camera itself is well built and appears to be a winner. After several strolls around the menus, it is clear that the menus were not developed by anyone who is a photographer. The menus are logical although contrary to what one normally encounters. They make sense once you spend some " quality time " playing with the camera.

The camera is light weight and easy to carry and use. The controls on the rear of digital cameras have always been problematic for me. Typically, I accidentally hit these buttons while shooting and have to spend time disengaging the functions I have accidentally set off. Sony has averted this by allowing you the option of not assigning functions to the buttons and controls. Wow ! This is great.
Also, The SONY RX1 sees in the dark in comparison to other cameras. It is a low light shooter.

The Raw files are HUGE and and my poor MacBook Pro keeps freezing and choking. I have learned that the Mac buffers fill up quickly and I empty them inelegantly by restarting the computer.This works and the flow of image processing goes forward if I allow the computer to reboot after having processed a series of files.

I have a Fuji X100s APS-C camera which is a wonderful camera which does most of what the RX1 does. The image quality is very comparable to the RX1R in average shooting conditions. The RX1r and the X100s are of similar construction, handling, and Image Quality. However, if want to shoot decent images in near darkness with high ISOs, The Sony is the clear winner.

If you are an OCD personality, as I am, the Sony RX1R will make you smile.

Just be prepared for the headaches associated with dealing with such large image files. My processing programs, Adobe ACR , Iridient RAW Converter, etc. operate SLOWLY and require regular reboots.

title: A Nice LCD
text:
After three months with this TV, I am very happy with the purchase. The first thing readers should be aware of are the negatives, if none of them bother you, then I'd go right ahead and buy this.

Three Big Negatives using Headphone Jack
1) Headphone jack volume controlled by TV volume.
This annoys me because as soon as you unplug the headphones, the sound comes on. If you were listening to something loud, or just at night and trying to be very quiet, you'll get a loud awakening. What would be better would be constantly outputting a signal w/gain to the headphone jack, that could then be controlled by the volume control on my cordless headphones (all cordless headphones and lots of corded headphones have volume control)

2) Headphone jack shuts volume off when headphone plugged in
This really annoys me. My TV is over the fireplace mantle, and using the headphones is a chore because you can't keep them plugged in, else you don't get any sound from the TV speakers.

3) Headphone jack shuts optical output down as well
This could have been a fix to #2, but when the headphone is plugged in, you lose optical audio output. So if you have a nice A/V Receiver handling all the audio and plug in your headphones, you lose sound.

Now I know some of you will just say - don't use the LG headphone jack. Use the one on your nice A/V receiver. This would work for my cable and blu-Ray which are plugged directly into the A/V Receiver, but unfortunately Netflix and other LG apps built into this TV and that won't work.

Other negatives:
4) Black Level. While the picture is gorgeous, black level is not. It is a very dark gray.

5) Rear Facing Inputs. I mounted this initially using a Chief Super Slim mount. Because the rear ports are facing the rear and not up or down, even with 90 degree cable adapters, the cables wouldn't fit (I got this within .25" from the wall). I actually had to get a different mount which now isn't so sexy and close to the wall.

POSITIVES:
1) Price - sub $1,500 for a Netflix ready TV that is 55" and LED backlit.
2) Netflix works like a charm.
3) Picture - beautiful on everything but Star Wars, the Dark Knight, Star Trek and other dark TV shows/movies. LOST looks amazing!
4) Remote - I usually hate remotes that come with TV's, but this one is nicely laid out and was easy to use before I programmed my learning universal remote with the codes.

title: Too Much Trouble, then it Broke
text:
A quick background is necessary. Back in March of 2015 I ordered a Zoom Telephonics AC1900 from Amazon. For two and a half years I had no problems EVER with this modem. However, my music service would stop from time to time because TimeWarner/Spectrum uses extremely slow DNS servers. The Zoom did not have customizable DNS settings and is forced to use the DNS from the provider. So I upgraded to the Motorola MG7550. I changed the DNS setting to use Googles (8.8.8.8 and 8.8.4.4) and my music streaming service was perfect. YEAH!

About six months later the WiFi started acting up, and for the next three months I found myself unplugging and restarting the unit about once every two weeks. This would fix all the issues. I never had to do this once with the Zoom.

Then, about a month ago the problems started daily. I contacted Motorola and we changed everything from the channel, to a bunch of other settings. Nothing worked, but Motorola's warranty is useless. Send the unit in (at your cost), wait a few weeks (without WiFi or Internet access in your home) and if we find a problem we'll fix it.

After spending countless hours with the unit already, I'd had it. I knew that every time I shut is off it would work flawlessly for 2 - 6 hours, then WiFi would be a problem. All hard wired products worked perfectly (two Fire TV boxes and a desktop computer). So I decided to pick up a Google WiFi 3 pack (expensive, yes) and put this modem into bridge mode.

So far Google has worked flawlessly. Hopefully it will for years to come (it better at $249).

And now the modem just died. No power, it just shorted out. It's going to be replaced but like I said above, it will take weeks to get the replacement, so I just ordered a LinkSys replacement and will eBay the Motorola replacement when I get it.

title: Installation Hiccup - Support Awesome
text:
For some odd reason Google WiFi app couldn't setup these devices. Got the message to contact my ISP, but I knew that wasn't the problem, so I called support. An agent picked up quickly and by resetting the units twice (remove power) and restarting my router, everything ended up installing.

Here's what is great about Google WiFi routers:
1) By creating a mesh network, I don't need to have WiFi extenders around the house with different names. For example, I had a Hawking Wireless Range Extender hooked up to my previous Wife/Router. It had its own name, so when people went outside and lost connection they had to reconnect. Now this was an issue most people only had to do once because smart devices remember WiFi hotspots and automatically reconnect, but they also hold on as long as they have service and sometimes at they hold on when the WiFi signal is weak and then the Internet would get slow. Not a problem with Google's WiFi, each extender (I bought a 3 pack) is seen as part of the same WiFi hotspot. So there is no connecting to different hotspots.

2) Guest WiFi - most WiFi routers have guest access (Internet only but no access to any items inside your network). Google allows you to customize access from the guest to allow some access to some devices. While this isn't something I do, I could imagine a situation where you might want to allow access to a music device for guest to control, but not your robotic vacuum.

3) Great phone app. Being able to see what devices are using the network, without going onto a computer and logging into an ip address, is a huge step in the right direction.

Some bad things.
A) You shouldn't have to have an Android / iPhone to get a WiFi network running. A laptop plugged into the unit should bring up a web interface. For most people, no big deal, but I still know a lot of elderly people without smart phones who would love a mesh network WiFi setup in their home.

B) Expensive. When buying multiple, the secondary units should be in line with most wifi range extenders (around $30). However, each unit in the box was identical, so the router capabilities are build into each one.

C) Only one unit can be used for hardwiring products. This one bothered me the most and its why I took a star away in the rating. I have a secondary dwelling. There is a eight port hub in there that would have been perfect to plug into the secondary unit, but that's not possible. While I though ahead and have a conduit with Ethernet connected from the hub to a switch, I can definitely see the need of using one of these secondary units for hard wired connections.

Overall, they are great WiFi routers. I recommend them whole heartedly.

title: Even at this price, might not be worth it
text:
[UPDATE Aug. 19, 2002]
Lowered Rating to 2 stars from 3.

The transformer in this sub always makes noise when its on. When working WITHOUT music, there is this constant hum from the power supply inside the unit, and the sub vibrates slightly all the time, causing low volume distortion. Shutting off the sub doesn't solve the problem entirely because it is also sending a signal to the attached speakers via the RCA plugs. To verify I attached my powered speakers directly to my DAC and they became 100% silent. Very annoying.

[Original Review]
Price is a BIG reason [under $100] why this subwoofer is getting 3 stars and not 1 star. Lets get this out of the way from the beginning, this is a TERRIBLE subwoofer. Distortion is through the roof. Now I'm not trying to compare this to a $1,700 subwoofer that I own for my home theater, I have a $150 Yamaha NS-SW050BL in my house for TV and that is lightyears better than this sub. I needed a subwoofer for my work desktop.

So why give it 3 stars? Why even KEEP it - just send it back? Because this terrible sub serves specific functions I find useful. The most important is the Line Outs. I happen to be using a DAC with only two RCA line outs, no dedicated sub output, coupled with two desktop speakers that have ONLY two line RCA inputs. Therefore it is very simple to send two RCA cables to this subs line in's, and then send the high frequencies back out to the desktop powered speakers. Believe me if any cheap Yamaha/Polk/Klipsh subwoofer had RCA outs under $200 skip this crappy Rockwell and buy them.

Secondly, because I'm in an office setting, I need to keep the volume relatively low. There are 16 volume markers on this and I've got this set around '2'. '3' is the maximum level I would use this sub, thereafter the distortion becomes unbearable. I'm no golden eared listener, the distortion is THAT bad when you hit the '4th' volume marker.

Build quality is close to garbage. I put in my Amazon RCA cables and pulled them out and the red plastic insert popped out of the Rockwell. Doesn't effect the connection, but really?!

My desk doesn't have enough space to put on two Kali LP-8's, so I need a sub to help out the 4" woofers on my desktop monitors. The sub also acts as a footrest.

Conclusion: If your needs are low volume rumble AND you need RCA Line Outs, I recommend this subwoofer. Otherwise STAY AWAY!

title: Touchy, Touchy !!!
text:
Not a computer person but love what they can do. I bought this combo based on a recommendation, but I am not impressed with the speed compared to the equipment I returned. Speedtest is still showing same 88-90Mbps using 1 ethernet connected computer with Cat 6a cable just 10 feet away.

Is it faster? Maybe though it will probably only be appreciated by someone who is a heavy user to wifi, gaming, downloads and streams on a regular basis. But for everyone else, probably not too noticeable.

Purchase vs renting? Only time will tell if it last more than 2.75 years, so for now 4 stars. This is Day 1, if it lasts then 5 stars.

Construction is very lightweight and falls over very easy just bumping the table, make sure to keep in a low traffic location or protect it with something.

Be aware these devices are very touchy and only like being connected one way - Period. I received it today and it took me over 2 hours to get it working properly. So after calling Comcast twice and losing an hour between call centers in the Philippines and Chicago, it was a nightmare and the modem still did not work when connected to the bundled R7000 router.

Totally flustered I went and searched the internet and the answer is...

With everything (computer, modem, router) not connected via cable or wifi and turned off. Start with turning on the modem and wait 7-10 minutes for all the lights to be steady and not blinking. Then before turning on the router, connect the ethernet cable from the modem to the router. Then turn on the router and wait another 7-10 minutes. Now start your computer. Then connect the ethernet cable to the computer.

I had connected all the wiring and was turning everything on in the same order but it would not work, so I hope this helps some else.

title: Like it, hate it...
text:
I was going to do a video review on this, but couldn't fit in the time to shoot and edit everything. There's so much to be said about this kit. Some pros, some cons. Just need to get some more information on this.

First of all, the pictures for this kit is TERRIBLY deceiving. The carrying case is MUCH larger, all the stands have equal base spread, the muslin background looks like high quality, and it makes the hair light stand/boom look nice and long. You won't get what you are seeing in the picture.

This kit would BEST be suited for a studio or a semi-permanent installation. It is my professional opinion that this kit not be used for any kind of mobile use. I've shot commercials for a good 6-7 years with Lowel florescent lighting kits, which were made for the specific use of setting up, moving around, and tearing down quickly. This kit from ePhoto doesn't do this. I've tried my hardest to assemble the kit and pack it away in a fashion that would be quick and low-frustration, but it simply isn't able to do this. The soft boxes are not like an umbrella setup, where you simply slide a sleeve up and down a rod, and the box spreads open. Nope, it isn't that simple. The hair light (the one on the boom) kinda does this, but the box doesn't securely stay open. Once in a while, even when I thought I had opened the box and locked it open, it would still collapse unexpectedly. A note about the softboxes too, the power cables are WAY too short. When the stands are fully extended, the power cords go halfway up the stands. You MUST get extensions for them. Nasty con for the lights indeed.

The two other lights (key and fill) have a weird rod and notch assembly. You have 4 rods. You take one rod, and connect it to one corner of the diffusion side of the box. Then the other side slips into a notch on the fixture itself. After putting all four rods in place, it will form the soft box. It's NOT a quick setup! It takes me at best 4-5 minutes of setup, and that's JUST one soft box assembly. After setting up all the stands and boxes, that's a solid 20 minutes lighting assembly. That simply can't happen on a shoot, especially if you want to project any sense of professional work. It's got to be no more than a 2 minute setup. And I do not recommend moving them around. There isn't a very confident sense of stability with these. Yes, if you're careful, you could easily and safely move them around, but honestly I wouldn't move these while still put together.

It's also my suggestion to get a much better set of Muslin backdrops. The picture shown here are very deceiving. When the stands are fully extended upwards, there is NO way those muslin sheets lay on the floor like they do in the pictures. The sheets are SO thin and delicate that you can easily tear them. This IS a result in terrible workmanship. There are loose threads and all kinds of bad sewing on each sheet it's not even worth it.

Also, the bulbs sounded very promising, however I wouldn't suggest them either. They flicker very nastily, and I had them plugged into clean power too, so it wasn't the electricity I was using. Possibly getting CFL bulbs or some kind of LED bulbs would work much better then the supplied florescent bulbs.

The carrying bag for the lights is so-so. I cant understand the orientation of the zipper/handles when it's closed. When you set down the bag, the handles are on top, and the flap/lid/zipper is on the side. Why? A lot of weight is placed on the zipper, and I'm afraid that one day the zipper will inevitably tear open from all the weight pulling at it. Why not put the zipper on the top side of the bag?

All in all, for this price, it's an o.k. kit. No matter what, replace the Muslin cloth and the bulbs with something else. If you're just using it as studio lighting where it's more stationary, it's an okay kit. IF you want to move it around and be an on-location kit, you'll have to do some modifications to the kit to make it more secure. However, I still do not suggest this kit, as the setup time will still be longer then desirable.

I hope this review affects everyone's decisions positively.

title: Great product for common situations, but NOT good for extreme movie enthusiasts or live-sound applications...
text:
This is an amazing wireless solution for listening to audio without being tethered down to one space.

This is an excellent solution to the following scenarios:
-Audio only playing devices such as radios, media players, etc.
-TVs. Even though there is a very slight latency, lip sync isn't THAT noticeable, especially after a few moments. Your brain will actually interpret and adjust these slight timing issues, and you can definitely get by. However, for the extreme movie/tv enthusiasts out there, it may be bothering.

Here's where it is NOT a good solution...
I work for my local church as a Director of Tech., and we use personal return mixers made by Aviom. Our worship leader was using a wireless transmission system, so she could walk around freely instead of being tethered to her Aviom by a wire. However, it broke, and she needed a new setup.

However, her Shure wireless monitor system was going to cost us AT LEAST $600 to replace. I believe I could find a more responsible solution to this problem! I was wanting to try this Bluetooth tech as a means to do this at the fraction of the cost, but these particular Avantree devices are Bluetooth 2.1, and as such have around 100ms latency.

In MOST common usages, this 100ms latency isn't such a problem at all. But for people who need near-zero latency, this is NOT the product for you!

Again, like I said before, this is actually a fantastic pair of devices for common situations! Four stars all the way!

But for the super enthusiasts or the people like me who are using it for live-sound situations that leave very little room for latency issues, this will NOT WORK WELL for you.

I really hope this helps anyone with a question like this. Please rate this review so it get's to the top...I don't see this kind of specific discussion being talked about on forums or anywhere on the net, and I think it needs to be seen and understood.

title: this is what I would like to say
text:
I have 18 years of professional tv broadcast experience, and after over a month of using this product, this is what I would like to say.

I think this video recorder has some amazing potential. I REALLY liked the idea of a stand-alone video recorder that didn't need a separate computer to make recordings. Just one push of the record button, and it's doing it's job...that's it! No other hassles to worry about. This kind of device is MEANT to be simple to setup and use, and I appreciate that kind of feature.

Another feature that I liked was that you could record from HDMI, VGA, YPbPr, AV, Audio L/R, external Mic. I can see how this would be very attractive to MANY users across the board, from the consumer digitizing old home videos, hobbyists users, and even up to a prosumer professional user. For OUR use, I wanted to have a HDMI recorder to record from the HDMI output of our BlackMagic ATEM TV STUDIO video switcher. Our church's video production setup uses 2-3 video sources to switch around per Sunday for 40-50 minutes at a time, so we wanted a simple to use video recorder that would record that long with prosumer quality video bitrates so we could post to YouTube. We didn't need a high-end professional recorder, but one that would do the job, so I decided to try this one out.

But in the end, I could only give this product two stars, because of a few reasons. One GIANT reason that I had to give it a low reason is because there would always be a video glitch in the recordings that would cause the VIDEO to lag behind the audio a half a second. But this glitch happened 4-8 times within 40-50 minutes, so at the end of our recordings, the video and audio was out of sync by 6-8 seconds. This desync in a/v is entirely unacceptable, even if you're just a consumer. I can't imagine how this glitch would be okay in any recording. It was in the raw recordings too, and just no way to fix this glitch.

Another reason why I gave it a low rating is in the quality of the final video. In the unit's settings, you only have "low, medium, high" recording options, but what's the bitrate in which you are recording? I was told that the high quality option was around 10-14 mbps (variable bit rates too, and no option to switch it to constant bit-rate), but visually the raw recordings did not reflect this at all. The only way I can convey this is to go watch a GOOD, PROFESSIONALLY made YouTube video and set the playback quality to 1080p, but then compare it to the 480p setting. There's just no sharpness to it at all...very blocky, very fuzzy, and so the maximum recorded quality of the Cloner Box Pro would really only be useful to perhaps VHS digitizing...but still not really useful if you want lip-synced video!

The customer and tech support was very responsive to my emails, and even let me give them some suggestions and feedback to their device. They did their best to help me troubleshoot, and even wanted my raw video recordings sent to them for analysis, but in the end, they left it as "We will try to fix this in the future." Sadly, this final response left me no other choice but to return it, which they agreed that they will give me a refund.

I would rate the customer assistance and tech help 5-stars!

I just wish there was a product like this one! As far as my researching has come up, there is no other stand alone video recorder that will take all HDMI, VGA, YPbPr, AV, Audio L/R, external Mic video inputs, record and playback with a USB drive, HDMI loop-out, and user-friendly, really easy to use. I mean really...this thing would have been a gem to keep and use for our church video productions!

My final cons on this device is listed below:
-Fix the video/audio sync issues.
-Fix the final recording qualities.
-Offer H.264/H.265 instead of .mp4

title: Aweful. Terrible quality.
text:
Cons: There's plenty.
1) If you plan on recording more than an hour's worth at a time, this recorder will split up your video files in one hour segments, and you lose some frames between every split. You HAVE to use an editing program to join the two or more video files back together. Annoying.
2) The audio is super low quality, and low in volume. Even at the highest recording quality, the audio sounds terribly compressed and bad. You get a constant hissing/noise from even the best recording option.
3) Speaking of the highest recording quality, it's garbage too. There are too many codec glitches going on. Huge blocks of the footage will start to glitch for a split second or two.
4) You have no control at what frame rate you can record to. It's all 60fps.
5) The charging cable is very proprietary. You cannot just pickup a USB style AC adapter and use it.

Pros:
1) I do like the idea of a battery in it. It falls roughly to 66% after an hour or so, so it doesn't last long.
2) Removable SDHC card selection is nice.
3) The on-board screen is nice.
4) The build quality is actually sturdy, and feels nice in your hand.

FInal Thoughts:
1) Someone here on the customer reviews said it was "meant for a professional", which is absolutely NOT TRUE. If you want to see what is really "professional", go get an Atomos and see what is really designed for professional use. If you want to use this for paid work, I as a client would be upset at the quality of the final product. Even if you were just sending the recording straight to the customer, this isn't even suitable for a final deliverable codec. So don't expect to do any recordings and try to edit and color correct the footage.

Do yourself a favor, and save up for a Atomos which would give you 10x better quality.

title: Best phone I have ever owned.
text:
HTC hit it out of the park with this one. I've never been a fan of their phones in the past because of reliability issues and their sense software was pretty bad. This phone is incredible. Build is wonderful. No case for about 6 months and it doesn't have a scratch. Design is beautiful. Screen is gorgeous. Camera Is hit or miss. It takes some truly beautiful photos sometimes. Other times they are awful. I like the idea of the ultrapixel camera but the technology has a ways to go. I love the wide angle lenses. You can capture quite a bit in a shot. The camera software is the best I've used. Adds a lot of useful features without making it complicated. On the software side sense 5 is hands down the best version of Android available. I even prefer it to stock android that comes on nexus devices. Adds a ton of utility while keeping it simple and fast/smooth as anything. The snapdragon 600 inside is more than enough to handle anything you throw at it. By far one of the fastest phones I've used, with the exception of the nexus 5. I didn't mention the speakers. They are everything their reputation suggests. Highest quality audio I've ever heard out of a phone. Could be a smidge louder, but I really can't complain since they're already louder than about everything out there. Also the fact that they face forward makes SO MUCH SENSE. Battery life is good as long as power saver is on. It's just okay without it. I only have 2 complaints. 1 is the button setup. It's awful. 2 capacitive keys doesn't make any sense. There are currently 4 actions bound to my home key. Tap, double tap, hold and swipe up. No logic in that. The other is the pre-installed AT&T garbage. There are like 15 apps that you can't uninstall. Most can be disabled but really? I wont use pay to use AT&T navigation over free Google maps. There are tons like that. And they add more with every update. I hate it. Not really a fault with the phone but the carrier.

To sum it up, I will be an HTC customer for a long time. If you're on the line, buy this phone. You won't regret it.

text:
The news is full of gibberish comparing the Kindle Fire to the Apple iPad. Why? These products are not designed to compete other than the fact that they are both essentially tablets. Amazon and Apple are targeting two different markets, and I believe that was Amazon's intent from the beginning. Every time a new tablet device is introduced it seems like the world has to compare it to the iPad whether it's designed as a competitive product or not, and that doesn't make sense. I own and use an iPad2 daily for business and personal purposes; the iPad has replaced the notebook computer I used to lug about in meetings, when traveling, etc. It's an excellent tool that I keep at hand all the time. It will perform most all of the same functions as the Kindle Fire as well as the functions I need for business purposes.

I purchased the Fire as a media device for use at home: my household uses it daily to read books, to listen to music, to watch video and to play games. It replaced an iPod Touch, actually. It's a very convenient way to browse the web, check email and so on. We use the internet heavily, and the Fire is an excellent portable household portal for our needs. The Fire compliments the iPad in my home by making these services available on an additional device, or becomes the primary portable device when I'm away from home with my iPad.

If I was pressed to find fault with the device, I would have to say that the power button on the bottom of the tablet is sometimes a bit difficult to find. Since ours is in a leather case, we don't have any issue with inadvertently turning it off like some have reported. I would also like a some more flexibility in organizing the apps/books/media on the main screen. For the initial release of a brand new product, I'd say it's pretty rock-solid compared to the other technologies I've reviewed in the past. I understand an update will be coming out within the next 2 weeks, and though I don't know what that will contain just yet, it does speak to Amazon's commitment to the product.

Some have complained about the ease with which apps and books are purchased using Amazon's store, making it possible for children to make unsupervised purchases. Personally, I have no problems with this and appreciate it... this device is a physical extension of Amazon's massive media marketplace and users know that before they purchase the Fire. Entering a complex password each time I make a purchase can be difficult, particularly when you're in a hurry or on the move. Only adults use the device in my household, and if children do get access, they do so only when they are supervised. Would I buy the Fire for a child to use? No, or not likely. In my opinion this is not a child's toy and parents who purchase them for their children should understand these and accept these risks up front. If Amazon were to implement a series of parental controls and other "child safety" features in order to appease this minority I would hope they would do so with a master control to either enable or disable the feature, as it seems unjust to punish the majority for the errors in judgement of the minority.

I would definitely recommend the Fire as an excellent alternative to other Reader devices. This device has a wealth of features that make it a wonderful personal media device. The strength of Amazon and the wealth of media they offer makes the device makes it a winner. Buyers who are looking at this device as a desktop/notebook replacement should rethink their strategy and look at other devices that are more appropriate. We're happy with our purchase decision and we look forward to the ongoing innovation Amazon continues to offer.

title: Easy to set up and install, high quality imaging day or night
text:
I ordered this camera to mount at the edge of my two-story deck so that I can see both under the deck and into the fields behind my home at any time. These areas are not easy to see either from above or below, and the camera gives me a way to easily look to see what's happening when I hear something moving about, day or night. I think it should also act as a deterrent for any would-be thieves.

Installing the camera is fairly straightforward. I set up the unit to attach to the network BEFORE mounting it, making the process so much easier.
