The included documentation does an excellent job of describing all of the different types of installation methods.

Pros:
- The camera is a PTZ camera, meaning that it's capable of panning, tilting and zooming the view and can be remotely controlled from another device or application.

- The recommended app works perfectly on my iPhone, but the camera does meet standards to work with multiple software applications. The camera is designed to be integrated into many security systems and can support recordings, motion detection, etc.

- The images from the camera are bright, very sharp and clear, whether in day or night mode. This aspect of the camera exceeded my expectations.

- For what it's worth, the camera also has a built-in microphone and speaker, enabling you to listen as well as see what's happening at any given time, and to verbally interact with the scene. The audio at the camera also exceeded my expectations.

Cons:

- The camera is designed to use 4 screws to mount to a flat surface, making for an easy installation. However, the base of each of the Wi-Fi antennas is attached to this base, and they extend deeper than the base of the unit. In other words, you can't successfully and completely tighten the base of the camera to a flat surface because the WiFi antennas stick out.

- The wiring and controls from the camera are three white cables that extend from the bottom of the mount. This cables include a port for power, an RJ-45 connection for an ethernet cable, and a reset button to perform a manual reset of the camera. By extending these from the base of the wall mount, it practically guarantees that the cables will block the view from the camera if you rotate the head to look behind the camera. In most installations that may not be a problem, but in my particular case, the camera is mounted so that I can see in the full 355 degrees that it supports. It's difficult to keep the cables out of the way.

- The Ethernet and Power cables to not provide adequate protection from water. If the Ethernet cable is actively in use for a wired installation, then the provided parts should provide a water-tight installation. But, if you're using the camera via Wi-Fi, there's no "cap" provided to seal the Ethernet connection. I had to fashion a seal using vinyl tape and the supplied connectors to make the connection waterproof. Likewise, the power plug does not truly seal when installed. I wrapped this connection with waterproof tape to protect the connection. The "reset button" does have a waterproof cap included.

For most of the user base, this would be a perfect outdoor PTZ camera. For my particular requirements, it's not perfect but it does work well after a bit of engineering. However, its virtually impossible to find such a capable, advanced function exterior camera at this price point. I still recommend the camera and would likely order it again based upon my experiences.

Other than the orientation of the power plug, I'm very happy with this surge suppressor and would definitely order it again. title: Capable scanner, software interface is clunky
text:
I work from home and manage a lot of documents, both for my office and for my homeowner's association. I frequently find myself with the need to scan a stack of documents for electronic filing purposes, and working with a clamshell scanner takes forever. When this device became available for review, I knew I had to give it a try.

First, this device is designed to be a space-saver... when not in use, it takes up a small amount of desktop real estate. All of the trays are designed to fold together to minimize the space required, and function to close up the orifices of the scanner to minimize environmental dust.

The scanner connects to your computer via a USB 2.0 interface. USB 2.0 is not the fastest method of connectivity available today, but it is adequate. I would expect most modern scanners to use USB 3.0. Power is provided to the unit via a brick power adapter. When not actively in use, the unit hibernates to a low power sleep mode.

While the documentation states that the document feeder will hold up to 50 sheets, I would say that's a bit high and have had better experience using a max of 20-30 pages. Scanning speed is driven by the quality and style of scan you choose... I like to maintain crisp, clean copies of documents, and I use the scanner at the 600 dpi setting, and scan in color. Also, the scanner is set up to scan both sides of the page simultaneously, which slows down the process. There is a software setting that eliminates the blank pages from the scan after the scan is complete.
Even at these settings, it will scan approximately 15 pages per minute. If I were to set it to single-sided, black and white at 200 dpi, the scanner's speed easily doubles.

The scanner is also shipped with TWAIN drivers, so if you have a software application that uses the TWAIN interface, you can natively scan documents into your app and bypass the clunky "eConnector" software provided with the scanner.

My biggest negative so far is the "eConnector" software. As another reviewer mentioned, most all scanners are basically created equal and it's the provided software that gives it a lot of its functionality. I've not tried all of the different features of this unit... and I doubt most users ever will. I just want to scan documents to a folder on my local system quickly, cleanly and effectively. With my other scanner, I can load the documents and press a single button on the scanner to activate and complete the scanning process. With this device, I click the button and it pulls up the software to the appropriate interface type. I have to click the mouse button at least 4 times to complete the scan. That's ridiculous. The software interface is a large, blue window that you can minimize or exit, but you can't resize it or relocate it on your screen. It's archaic and difficult to navigate.

Again, agreeing with another reviewer... if this scanner were priced between $100 and $200, I would be more apt to recommend it... but at over $300, I would agree that there are other solutions that would probably be of higher quality. I will continue to use it because I have it, but I would not buy this product.

My problem is that I have a newer home and the new electrical codes in the US require the ground lug to be at the top of the outlet. In other words, with a three-prong plug, the ground lug you typically see at the bottom of the plug is actually on top for safety reasons. If something metallic were to fall down across the plug, it would land on the static ground lug rather than shorting out the power lugs. This surge protector is oriented such that it only fits properly when the ground lug is in the lower position. So, if I plug it in to my outlet, the light is on top. That kind of works for me, but it's not what I had hoped for. My recommendation to the manufacturer it to make the orientation of the plug user selectable so that it works for either style of electrical installation.

Other than that obvious problem, the surge protector is well-made and appears to work great. The USB charging ports are a huge plus, and I use them regularly to charge a host of devices that have 5volt-1 amp charging requirements.

I'm giving the product 4 stars because all of it's other features and functionality are great. It's just not the right product for my needs.

title: Different take on a standard DTV antenna
text:
Digital TV Antennas are great for over-the-air viewing, but where do you put them so that they're out of the way? In the wrong location, they're useless, and can be subject to interference. Part of the appeal of this antenna was the ability to rest it on the top edge of the display. I do also like the concept of the TV backlight, and this seemed to be an easy way to add that functionality as well.

When used in combination with the antenna amplifier (which is a must in my location,) the antenna requires 2 power sources: one for the booster, and another for the light. These are independent, and the light is powered by a USB-A connector so that you can plug it into the USB port on a modern TV for power, which enables the power to alternate with the power to the TV. If you don't have a USB connector on the TV, you must use a separate USB power adapter (not provided) and use the inline switch to turn the light on and off. The power source for the amplifier is a plug adapter.

I personally wish that the amplifier power source was also a USB adapter... my power strip has a USB power source directly available, and it would be nice to use that rather than requiring one of the "large" sockets for oversized power adapters. The light output from this unit isn't as consistent as I've experienced with other solutions... in my case, it primarily lights the top and center area behind the TV rather than creating a consistent glow behind the unit. The antenna also has a built-in filter for Cellular interference, which IS a thing. In my area, due to the proximity of cell towers, I've added separate filters to other antennas to optimize signal. Finally, because the unit is designed to fit atop the TV, I was sincerely hoping that the antenna wouldn't require specific orientation to be receive a variety of channels. Sadly, that's not the case. While this one does do better than others I own, it's still not omnidirectional. With the top mount, it's not like you can re-orient the antenna separately from the TV, so the location of my TV ultimately determines what I can watch.

Again, this antenna still outperforms all of the others I own and I do like that it's relatively unobtrusive. I like the concept, but for my particular use and location, I don't know that I would buy it again. However, if you are more centrally located in a broadcast area, this may be a perfect solution.

It seems that the manufacturer has considered all but one important factor in the design of the power strip... the orientation of the plug. This is designed to fit a US plug with the 2 power spades at the top and the round static ground lug at the bottom. That's probably the most common orientation for a plug in homes, but electrical code dictates that the ground lug should be at the top, not the bottom... so if your plugs are oriented that way (and mine are,) the cord plugs in with the wire pointing upward from the plug rather than downward. Many manufacturers are now making the plug rotatable to select the proper orientation based upon the orientation of the plug.

All in all, I'm satisfied with the surge protector. For my particular application it fits well and looks good at the back corner of my desktop. title: A great beginner microscope for children to explore
text:
When I ordered this, I knew what to expect... I was ordering this for an 8-year-old to use to begin an exploration of the world around her. I didn't have the expectation that this would be a professional microscope or offer fabulous picture quality or off-the-charts magnification. I wanted something basic and easy to use that would spark her interest, not confound her. That being said, this device is perfect for my needs.

The microscope is both easy to set up and to use. The included instructions are brief and fairly thorough. I was able to set this up and have it charging within 5 minutes. The microscope does operate on a battery, which I didn't expect, and I don't know whether that's a plus or a minus. This means that you have to keep the device charged up in case you opt to use it, and your usage is limited to the run time of the battery. For an item like this, I'd actually prefer that it was plugged in all of the time. The microscope does not include a power adapter, just like most any other product on the market today. Simple 5-volt 1-amp USB-A adapters are plentiful... I have about 20 of them in a drawer. I also have a number of power outlets and power strips that offer built-in USB power. Since the power adapter is usually the first thing to fail in a product, I'm actually happy that it's USB-powered and that I can choose which adapter to use rather than being forced to use a particular adapter that I can't easily replace.

The quality of the image is good, but from what I've seen it's not 16MP. I would agree that the magnification is more like 50x, which for a microscope of this design is more than likely the max, especially around children. I've not worked with the App... but if it works, I can see it as an advantage as a way to easily share images that have been collected. It does have a pair of LED lights that are used to illuminate your target, and they are on gooseneck mounts so you can adjust them optimally to your need. Given that these are also powered by battery, I would like a way to control their power and/or dim their output.

Overall, I'm pleased with the product and have found it to be better than my expectations. This is a great learning tool for children. I can see that some adults could benefit from it as well for particular uses, like coin and stamp collecting. Based upon my experience so far, I would likely order this product again and I don't have a problem recommending it, as long as the buyer has reasonable expectations.

title: Solid, weighty keyboard with extremely sensitive keys
text:
I ordered this to use primarily as an alternative keyboard for my office notebook. I spend 8 - 10 hours per day at my desk, developing code and mining data from databases, so keyboarding really is my bread and butter. Finding a good, responsive and ergonomic keyboard is a must for me to be comfortable and successful. Likewise, I like a keyboard with a relatively light touch, as it saves wear and tear on my hands.

There are a number of things that stand out about this keyboard:

+ The base or upper platform of the keyboard is made of an alloy metal, and looks somewhat like a brushed stainless steel finish. It's weighty, and it doesn't scoot around on the work surface when you're typing.

+ The keyboard can be used as a rechargeable cordless keyboard, or you can connect it and use it as a corded keyboard. When corded, the backlight for the keys remains on by default, while in backlight it shuts off after a bit to conserve power.

+ As a rechargeable keyboard, the keyboard uses Bluetooth to connect with the system instead of relying on a dongle

+ With Bluetooth, it's possible to pair the keyboard with multiple systems.

+ They keyboard is designed to work with a Mac as well as a PC.

+ It has an extremely sensitive touch.

+ Software is available so that you can configure some of the keys and certain functions to operate according to your needs.

Things I'm not so happy with:

- The keyboard is EXTREMELY sensitive... as a touch typist, don't place your fingers on home row... instead hover over them. The slightest touch activates the key.

- The keyboard control software has to be downloaded from the company's site, but nowhere in the documentation is the name of the site listed! (Thank God for Google!)

- A programmable spin and click wheel is located in the upper left quadrant of the keyboard that can be used with a number of functions. HOWEVER... the placement of this knob is precisely where the Escape key should be located, and all of the function keys are shrunken somewhat and moved right to make room for this. After 35 years hitting Escape in the same location, I'm having a very hard time adjusting to this. I could live without the spin wheel much easier.

After using the keyboard for a couple of weeks, the jury is still out. I've still not become accustomed to the relocation of the Escape and Function keys. I still have problems where I breathe wrong and end up with extraneous characters appearing.

While the keyboard has a lot of good things going for it, based upon my experience to-date, I probably would not order it again. For my particular usage, it's just not the best choice. I do like its feel and weight, but I've spent more time using the backspace than I have the space bar. My recommendation to the potential buyer is to be well aware of the intended use and user of the keyboard before committing to a purchase.

Using the software, you can make multiple minute adjustments to the image to create exactly the light-level, sharpness and zoom level you want. You can also pan the image as necessary. When you achieve the perfect set of settings for your needs, you save this configuration. When you look at your Teams,
WebEx or Zoom camera options, you'll find this "virtual" camera listed for selection along with the default camera. You can create and save as many configurations as you like, based upon your environment or needs. As long as you have the Konnect software loaded, this works perfectly.

The downside is that you must have the Konnect software loaded to support these alternate virtual camera configurations. When the software is loaded, the camera is "on" or active. I've got in the habit of loading the software each morning when I start the system, then sliding the lens cover in place until I'm ready for a meeting.

By and large, I'm very satisfied with this camera. I love the results when using the software, but I wish that I didn't have to do so, or that there was a program "stub" I could run to perform most of this functionality automatically. So far, using the adjustments, this combination has provided the best visual I've found with my office computer. If more of the functionality were built into the driver or a background solution, I would likely be more apt to purchase this again in the future. Likewise, my recommendation hinges on this as well... many will find this solution too cumbersome and will only use the camera with the default setup, which makes it only slightly better than the many $30 versions in the marketplace.

Based upon my experience so far, I would definitely order this again if the need arose. It's a great combo and has exceeded my original expectations.

title: Electronic Whiteboard
text:
I ordered this specifically for use in our kitchen area for jotting down grocery lists, to-do items and the like. We actually have a large magnetic glass whiteboard, but it's not always easy to use when you're on walkabout trying to create lists. While this board is larger (a selling point for me,) it's extremely lightweight, the pen attaches at the upper right, and it works great.

The board is not backlit but relies on ambient lighting. I have a very bright space and the contrast between the green and black background is not nearly as crisp as is displayed in the photos in the ad. However, it's still quite legible.

I have no idea how much power this board uses, but it must be a very small amount as there's no switch to turn it on and off. There is a lock switch you use to enable the "clear" button on bottom front of the pad. I question that concept... if you have to unlock the screen to clear it, why not just clear it when you unlock it? The front-center has no other function that I'm aware of.

The only other "complaint" I have is that the pen has a rather blunt point. That's great for making large notes, but isn't ideal for smaller, cursive handwriting. I have another device like this that has a pen with a finer point, and it works well with this board.

As others have mentioned, when you place your palm on the board and apply too much pressure, it naturally results in an image. Since the "writing" is activated by pressure, that makes total sense. It's actually more resistant to palm pressure than I would expect.

What sets this product apart from other available products is the size of the writing area. The 15-inch diagonal writing space is just what we needed, and for that reason I would order this again. I deducted a star from the review because of the blunt pen. I truly wish manufacturers would consider making these in an even larger format to replace whiteboards in offices... I would buy one if it was available.

text:

What I can't get used to is the new ergonomic positioning of the keyboard. It's now thought that you should sit above the keyboard and have the keyboard tilt forward, which is supposed to be more natural. I can understand that, but I still can't get used to it. This keyboard has flip-out feel along the BACK edge to enhance the forward tilt. That will take getting used to.

The mouse is a comfortable fit in my hand, and I would love to rely on it, but I've found that its signal is not reliable. Every laser mouse I've used has worked great on my desktop without a pad, but this one skips and jumps constantly. I've tried using a pad, with no discernable difference. This is likely a flaw in the mouse I received for evaluation. I've tried resetting it, but with no luck. The keyboard does not have similar issues, so it has to be an issue with the mouse.

I'm giving the combo 4 stars - removing one star because of the mouse performance (I can only review what I receive for testing.) If the mouse worked as well as they keyboard, I would definitely give the combo 5 stars. This is a pricier combo, but I would consider ordering it again.

title: Fairly easy install, FM transmitter doesn't work well for me
text:
I drive a 2007 Toyota Prius; kind of old but TREMENDOUSLY reliable. While I can still integrate my iPhone to the car, that's about the limit of its functionality. I have the onboard Nav system, but that's DVD-based, and unless you purchase and physically install upgraded DVDs from time to time, your mapping info is out-of-date. The cost is exorbitant, and the drive is in a cage underneath the driver's seat and is not worth the effort to work with. Of course, I can use my iPhone 12 Pro MAX for Nav, and do so, but it's not the easiest to "navigate" or see. Adding this CarPlay device creates an easy to navigate, fully integrated solution between my car and my iPhone. I use it for music, calling, Nav, and messaging among other things. If I had passengers, I could use it to play video as well on long drives.

Installation is fairly straightforward... the biggest challenge for me was location. With the design of my dashboard, adhering a suction cup is impossible. The only solution was to attach it to the windshield. Because of cabling, it became apparent that the only suitable location would be resting on the dash centered between the driver and passenger. Because of my height, the display doesn't really impact my field of view. The power cord uses a standard cigarette lighter plug and also supports 2 additional USB devices (which is important for me.) While I don't like it, the power cord does work to rest next to the central console and is easy to keep out of the way.

The device gives you two options to connect to your car's audio: via a built-in FM Transmitter or using an AUX cable. I previously used an FM Transmitter with an Alexa Auto device, so I knew that option was viable. However, this CarPlay adapter only supports stations with a decimal of .0 or .5 (i.e. 101.0 or 101.5). In my area, I was using 103.7 which was clear and worked perfectly. With the CarPlay, I was unable to find any unoccupied space that didn't result in static. My car does have an AUX input, but several years ago I integrated an aftermarket SIRIUS receiver that "takes over" the AUX input in the system. While it's supposed to relinquish that when the SIRIUS is not in use, it doesn't work. The SIRIUS receiver is no longer in use, and ideally, I'd remove it from the car, but that means removing the entire dashboard to get to the cabling and I'm just not prepared to do that right now. So, for the interim, I picked up a smaller stereo computer speaker that uses an AUX connection for input and USB for power. It's lightweight and responsive, and I was able to mount it under the dash under the center console so it's not visible and is completely out of the way. The CarPlay is connected here, and for now, this works very well.

I won't discuss all of the settings and options available through the CarPlay device, but I'll say that it basically extends all automotive-oriented applications from the phone to the device and makes all easy to access. The device connected to the Bluetooth in my phone on the first try. Everything about this device (other than the FM Transmitter) works exactly as described and makes the integration of the phone and driving so much easier.

Would I order this again? Probably. I really counted on the FM Transmitter to work, but my temporary workaround seems reliable enough for now. Eventually I'll rework everything to make use of the car's AUX port. Or maybe I'll just wait until I get a new car in a couple of years? The device works fine for me for now. I honestly didn't realize how useful this could be else I would have jumped on the technology long ago. I wish there was more documentation as well... the documentation is sparse and leaves you to figure out some of the interactions by yourself. I would say that the functionality and usability is going to depend on a number of factors that are personal to the buyer, but for someone looking for a CarPlay solution, I think this is a good one.

text:
If you're like me, you have a zillion appliances or tools with cords, and managing those cords neatly is a problem. Wire twist ties are not a long-term solution. These Velcro cable ties are ideal, however.

Using these is simple: simply wrap the cable tie around the cord with the "soft" side facing outward. Insert the end of the tie through the loop and pull the tie tight around the cord, then smooth the loop-end of the tie around the cord to fasten the hook and loop closure. This ensures that the tie remains in position on the cord when the appliance is in use. When you're done, simply fold up the power cord and wrap the tie around it, fastening the end to the cable tie.

Would I order these again? Definitely, and in fact this is probably my third order for this type of product. I strongly recommend them to anyone who has to deal with cords, either for appliances they wish to organize, for cords that travel, etc. These ties are about 6-inches long, and while you can trim them with scissors to shorten them as necessary for smaller cords, they are too short to use with larger, heavier cords.

title: Easy install, easy setup
text:
I ordered this camera setup specifically to use as a security monitoring device for our pool area. We've had a number of late-night break-ins, so it's my hope that this device helps us to pinpoint the trespassers and pursue legal action.

The cameras are extremely easy to install and set up. Ours are located high up under a deck and provide coverage for the entire area, including the gate. We have the area very brightly lit, so night mode is not necessary.

Here are my issues:

- The cameras are battery powered and charge via a USB connection. The manufacturer claims the units should last a year on a single charge, but that's based upon approximately 20 activations per day/night. I expect that the units will receive a LOT more activations than that, so I already know my battery life will be significantly less.

- No suggestion is made for recharging the cameras after they're mounted. Since these are mounted outdoors and there aren't any power options nearby, I suspect I'll have to recharge them using a portable power bank.

If I ever have need for a dual display docking station, I may give it a try at that point. title: Easy to install and use to share dual monitors, keyboard, mouse and USB between 2 systems

This particular switch is very straightforward. You can connect 2 monitors via HDMI, as well as a wired keyboard/mouse or wireless version that uses a small USB-A transmitter. You then connect the two HDMI outputs from each computer to the switch, as well as a USB cable. The device is powered by the USB connection. It's true that you have to have extra cables on hand to make this work, but a pair of shorter HDMI cables and a pair of USB 2.0 cables are included. If you're combining two existing systems, you should have the 4 HDMI cables on hand, 2 per system, to plug into the switch, while using the provided cables between the switch and the monitors.

I have two 32-inch monitors that I use at 1920 x 1080 resolution, and they are as clear and are as responsive as if they were directly connected. The system still detects the monitors directly through the switch. The monitors have built-in sound, and I use one of them for computer audio via the HDMI connection. The audio portion passes through the switch with no problems. The switch also has two other USB 2.0 connectors you can use for other devices you need to share.

This device works perfectly for me. It's enabled me to take a pair of displays, and extra keyboard and mouse off of my desktop, for which I'm thankful. Everything works perfectly. I would definitely consider ordering this device again, and I have no reservations in recommending it to others.

The tablet comes with a range of accessories, including a mouse, keyboard, stylus, and case. The tablet uses Android 11, the latest version of the Android OS, so it should be compatible with newer apps for some time to come. The problem with most Android devices is that they're locked in to a particular version of Android, and once that becomes obsolete, you find that you can't use newer apps and have to buy a new device in order to upgrade the operating system.

The battery is a bit disappointing. I expected longer life based upon the specifications, but I've found that it sometimes has to be recharged more than once a day. Of course, my partner uses the device most all day, so maybe that should be expected.

Overall, I'm happy with the device. At this price point, I think it's the best I've tried. It still doesn't perform as I'd like, but to get that I'd likely have to shell out 3 to 4 times the price of this device for a high-end device. If your goal is to watch videos, play games and perform less-intensive applications, this is likely a good fit.

If the mouse runs down or is low on power, it connects to a cable with a USB-C connector that's at the front edge of the mouse. You can connect the mouse and it will continue to work while charging, and the cable is completely out of the way.

title: Great for everyday, not a powerhouse but quite capable
text:
If you're looking for a capable, solid everyday notebook to use for browsing, office tools and the like, this is a good choice. If you need significant computing power, or if you require high-end graphics for gaming, this is likely not your best choice.

The 15.6-inch display is relatively bright and clear. The notebook comes with Windows 11 S-Mode activated. If you want to use any software that's not part of the Microsoft Store or any browser other than Edge, you need to deactivate S-mode and use the system with Windows 11 Home. Making that change is a one-way street, however... once the system leaves S-mode, there's no option to return. My very first act with the notebook was to disable S-mode.

The system has 8 GB of RAM, which for basic needs is fine. I prefer to have more for some of the apps I used, but for casual use, this is fine. The 128GB M.2 SSD hard drive is responsive, but perhaps a bit small if you intend to store data locally. The drive can be replaced, but there's no option or space for an additional internal drive.

Battery performance is surprisingly good. I generally use the notebook more in the evenings and on weekends, but I find myself only charging once a week at most.

My biggest issue with the unit is the keyboard. When they say it's slimline, they mean it! The keys barely raise above the surface of the keyboard, so those who are used to mechanical keyboards with a more positive response will be challenged. That said, the keyboard does offer a numeric pad on the right, and although it's sub-sized compared with a normal keyboard, the fact that it's there is a positive for those of us who crunch a lot of numbers. By default, the "media" aspect of the function keys is activated. I jumped into the BIOS and changed the setting to enable the Function keys by default, as some of the apps I use rely heavily on function keys.

The mousepad is large and supports multi-touch. There are no physical left and right buttons... the lower left and right corners of the pad perform these functions. The display is not a touchscreen, so using the pad or adding a mouse are a must. Generally, the mousepad has functioned well for me but because I have larger hands, I still find my hand touching the touchpad errantly and causing the cursor to jump around.

Overall, I'm very positively pleased with this notebook and its performance. It's more than satisfactory for my intended purposes. For a student, or for someone with occasional needs, this is a great choice. As more and more apps move to the cloud, systems like this become more attractive. At this price point, I would order this again, and I have no problems recommending it to others. I've owned a number of Acer products, and so far, I've not been disappointed.

Naturally, since I finally have the system installed and ready to go, we've not yet had a weather alert. I assume I'll probably receive a test signal at some point. In our area we do have voice sirens that identify immediate emergencies, such as a tornado warning, but no indications for watch or other less threatening warnings. Having a device like this gives me a sense of additional security. Based upon my experience so far, I would order this again and have no reservation in recommending it to others.

title: Solid 8-port unmanaged switch
text:
I'm old school, and I much prefer wired networking to wireless when possible. It's far faster and more reliable, if less convenient. I have gigabit wired connections to most every room in my house. My televisions use streaming services that rely on wired connections, while other items like Smarthome switches, doorbells, cameras, etc. rely on wireless.

While it would be nice if every network connection was a "home run," or wired directly to a single, central switch sitting in front of the router, that's generally not possible in existing construction. For that reason you can use a switch like this to function as a "splitter" at the end of a home run to connect multiple wired devices to the network. For example, in my living room I have my smart television, a FireTV adapter and a WiFi access point all connected to a single unmanaged switch like this one. The same is true in my kitchen and my office.

This particular unmanaged switch works great. I used it to replace an old "dying" unmanaged switch in my office. Installation was simple... plug in all of the patch cables to the open ports and plug in the power. For most users, that's all you need to know. There's nothing strikingly different about this switch compared to other similar products except for the lightning protection that appears to be built in. I'm hugely in favor of that.

I would definitely order this again and have no problem in recommending it to others. It's an excellent product (so far) and hopefully it will continue to be so.

title: Using as an access point and it's working
text:
The TP-Link instructions for access point use are not so great. I had to play and play, but it works now. The actual setup steps are trivial, you just need to do them a certain way (for my home situation, anyway.) I have an existing wireless router and switch connected by wire to a cable modem that connects to the cable itself. The access point connection is by wire from any normal port on the back of the TP-Link to any normal port on your existing router. The pain is in getting the IP address onto the local network subnet (this is true for all routers and modems.) I searched for help in the internet and at, or near, the top hits were a good set of instructions from a user. Four stars because I don't feel in control of anything with the access point mode. But, I bought this as a cheap way to increase coverage to my yard. It works. The wired speed between this device and my router came in at 100Mbps full duplex "negotiated." It should be 1000Mbps or gig speed so I may look at my wiring and see if I can improve this. At the moment, I'm not concerned.

Hint: Set the TP-Link router IP address info in normal mode and only at the end of it all, switch to access point mode.

The card was inserted into a small reader that was then inserted into a 3.0 USB port brought normally to my PC front panel directly from the MB.

title: Excellent workmanship
text:
I bought these extension tubes for experimentation on my Canon DSLR cameras. I am very pleased with this purchase and the price is a bargain to say the least. You can't go wrong with this.

Construction is all metal, no plastic. Even Canon uses plastic on the mounts of some of its entry level lenses.
Build quality is very nice.
Fit to the Canon body (5D Mk2) and to the Canon lens mounts is very nice.

Tips on usage:

This product consists of 5 parts: 3 extension tubes, a camera body bayonet adapter and a lens bayonet mount adapter. You must use at least 3 parts together but the tubes can be stacked for additional combinations.

There are no optical parts. This is only meant to be a mechanical extension of your lens away from the camera focal plane in order to allow greater magnification of the image than the lens was designed for.

Image results will vary from lens to lens because the use of the extension tubes "cheats" on what the lens designer intended for the optical performance of the lens. Results will probably be better with a true macro lens. Some modern lenses might deliver terrible results. However, consider that plastic camera images are in vogue.

There are NO electrical connections between the camera body and lens with these adapters so the aperture must be used wide open on lenses which do not have a manual aperture ring (most modern DSLR lenses). Therefore, depth of field will be very limited. However, this is a great opportunity to experiment with focus stacking in Photoshop which works wonderfully on a static subject.

Exposure is semi manual too. On my Canon body I was able to use aperture priority and adjust the shutter speed to "match needle" for the exposure.

A sturdy tripod is virtually required but some interesting results might be achieved with hand holding at high ISO. If you have Photoshop, you must try focusing stacking. I know, I just repeated myself.

There are no instructions shipped with this product and none are really needed for most photographers. However, I did have a scare when I could not release the lens adapter from the lens. There is a small screw and I was trying to push it in to release. I discovered that the screw must be moved laterally, in the axis of the optics to release the lens.

Finally, this product must be used with care and patience because of the finely threaded components. When assembled the markings on the lens may not line up as normal but this does not alter performance.

So, go ahead and purchase this product and have fun experimenting with "super macro"

title: Very well made for the money
text:
If you're not hip to camera motion then you haven't been paying attention to Hollywood movies. Don't just get absorbed in the story. Watch the shots! A static landscape in a motion picture must have motion to be interesting and the way to impart that motion is to smoothly move the camera on a dolly or crane.

I almost spent $179. at the camera store for a skate dolly and I'm glad I found this unit instead. I figured for 30 some bucks I could always send it back if it was a piece of crap. To my pleasant surprise this product is very nicely made and is a great bargain. As another buyer suggested, the adjustment markings are of limited usefulness because there is no index reference but I can use the edge of the axel as a reference and that is pretty satisfactory. It can turn a circle with a radius as tight as about 5 inches (from mounting stud to subject) so it is well suited to tabletop product use. The wheel base is 4.5 inches. The skate wheels seem to be good quality ball bearing wheels and roll smoothly. The platform is made of metal, who-who!

I'm going to make a track for this skate with materials from Home Depot. I will use a 6" wide smooth board, about 6 feet long, and precisely attach quarter round molding the length of the board (curved side inwards) on each side to guide the wheels. I'll attach a 2 inch board perpendicular to the bottom to reduce flex. I have not tested this but I think it will work well. The board can then be set on whatever or even set diagonally and the skate rolled up the length of the board for a Hollywood motion shot.

title: I can't believe I spent $700 on a tripod
text: $700+ for a tripod is a s&%#t load of dough. Especially considering that I just spent $165 on a brand new Benro that is really nice. However, I was on assignment a couple weeks ago to shoot a parade and I needed to set up the Benro with an jib from indiSystems. Between the 2 sand bags hanging from a stone bag and the weight of the jib with counterbalance the Benro just could not handle it. One leg telescoped in despite the latch and the whole thing fell over. Fortunately for me, I had not yet attached my camera and there was no client standing by to look like a fool in front of. I shot the parade without the jib. Not until the next job did I realize that the middle leg clamp on the Benro had fractured (they replaced the part under warranty). Try shooting a job by jamming your broken tripod over a leather chair while shooting the chief of police. We must adapt. This episode convinced me that I needed to fess up and pay the bucks for an expensive tripod. However, the beefy Manfrotto metal tripod weighs in at 17 pounds. For and old fart such as myself, that is an awful lot of weight to carry around. The carbon fiber big Manfrotto weighs just 7 pounds and I must say, it is a lot easier to tote. I have used it yesterday on a location shoot with jib and all went well. It held the weight like a champ. Well, all went well except for crushing my thumb in the jib but that was just my fault. I was working alone on a job that required an assistant. We do what we must. The Manfrotto carbon fiber tripod has huge beefy legs but is feather weight for such a big tripod. Recommended. I'll just have to shoot a few more jobs to pay for it.

title: Love it, Love it, Love it!
text:
This QTVR head is a Chineese quasi knock-off of the $700. Manfrotto 303SPH QTVR Spherical Panoramic Pro Head. While the quality of the Manfrotto is undeniable, this unit is surprising well made and costs $500. LESS than the name brand. I am extermely happy with my purchase and pleasently surprised with the quality and functionality. Man, you'd have to making a ton of dough to justify the 303SPH and most photographers I know have to budget their gear purchases. So, this unit fills a long missing price point/utility factor for panorama shooters.

It appears to be made of steel with black paint. So, its's a little heavier than anodized aluminum and not quite as pretty, but quite sturdy. The bottom turntable has selectable click stops of 15 or 24 degrees or can rotate without click stops. The horizontal arm has click stops at 15 degrees. There are 2 circular bubble levels. It is flexible enough to be used with or without a battery grip.

The unit came with no instructions or website reference so I am docking it one star (would be a five star otherwise). A lot of though went into engineering this, even though the design is pretty much a copy. You'd think that they could afford an engineer to write instructions and a translator. However, most of the people buying his unit are pretty well versed on how these QTVR heads work.

One knob is unscrewed to unfold the unit from its transport configuration and replaced into another screw hole to secure it for use. When not in use, it fits into a small aluminum case with custom fitted foam padding. It takes some rehersal to go from case to ready-to-use but once you get it down you can reliably re-hit the nodal point with minimal fuss.

I am using it with a Canon 5D-2 and a Canon 6D. I use the Korean 8mm fisheye manual focus & aperture lens which is available for about $300. privte labeled with several different brand names. Despite that the lens is made for DX format it works fine with some image cropping on the full frame cameras. I use PTGui Pro which knows to ignore the image of the inside of the lens hood resulting from use on a full frame camera. So, I can get a full spherical pano (minus a little at top & bottom) with only 4 shots. Note, that it is possible to get an almost full spherical pano with this lens without the head reviewed here by just using a long trpod plate and pulling the camera back to get the entrance pupil of the lens over the tripod axis but NOT with the camera turned to portrait orientation. For serious pano work the camera must be in portrait orientation so that's why this QTVR head is indespensible even with a fisheye lens.

I graduate to this unit from a $70. Panosaurus which is made mostly out of wood. While it worked well for a super budget QTVR head, its most glaring deficiency is that it does not fold away for trasport and therefore would require a large case of its own, costing twice what the enclosed equipment is worth. So, the fact that this QTVR head folds to fit a small supplied case sealed the deal for me. I enthuisatically recommend ths unit! I just hope I can keep my competitive advantage and don't run across one of you shooters with this same QTVR head.

title: I was concerned about flicker but there is none.
text:
I looked at a number of flat panel LEDs and the reviews concerned me because flickering in the video file seems to be a common thread. Although it might not be visible to the human eye, the video clip is the proof. Recall, that the human eye cannot see the 60hz flicker of sodium and metal halide lamps that light our highways. The human eye cannot even see the flicker of 24 frames per second motion picture film. However, a flickering lamp can have an interference effect with the frame rate of the camera and produce zebra like lines that climb or descend the video image. I decided to purchase this based on the Yongnuo name, reasonable price and the nice appearance on the Amazon page.

I shot clips on a Canon 6D at 24 fps and 30 fps and at 10% lamp output, 50% and 100%. I saw no evidence of flickering (the moving zebras) in the footage, 6 clips altogether. That's great.

This unit is a 5 star for me. The exposure on the Canon 6D was ISO 200, 8 feet, 1/30 sec at f/6.3. Pretty respectable. The visual impression is that this lamp is very bright. I did a burn-in of 2+ hours at 100% power and the unit survived. The batteries were drained when I came back. I am using 3rd party Amazon purchased "Sony" 6900 mAh batteries. It takes two and does not come with batteries, so beware. This unit does have a cooling fan that is activated by internal sensor to keep the LEDs from overheating. When the fan comes on the sound can be picked up by a sensitive condenser microphone but I found it to be manageable by using a shotgun mic hung from a boom and processing noise removal in Audition CC. The power is adjustable from 1% to 100% by the same knob that turns the unit on. It is NOT supplied with AC power (an option) but I don't find that to be a problem because the unit burns for over an hour on batteries and it is so great not to have to bother with accessing power on location. These lamps are a dream on location because they pack into such a small package and set up so quickly. I was able to shoot an indoor interview with bright sun behind the subject. I used 2 of these lamps (yes, I bought a second one after testing the first) one as a key and another as a fill at 50% output. The bright sun coming in the window acted as the kicker light. My exposure was ISO 200, 1/30sec at f/16. The lamps provided just enough light to properly expose the faces and balance the background. Lamps about 3 to 4 feet from subject. Of course, the closer a lamp is to the subject, the softer the light renders on the subject and since there is no heat projected on the subject the closeness to the subject was not a problem.

The IR remote works well and allows remote control of the intensity 1% to 100%. Great to be able to turn the lamp off or adjust intensity when it is extended way up a light stand because is is on batter power, after all.

Because I did not have the right adapter with me to mount one of the lamps on my ⅝" stud light stand, I had to gaffer tape the lamp to the light stand. It held long enough to complete the shoot but came crashing down while breaking down the set. The Yongnuo unit survived the crash with minor scratches, a bent barn door and STILL WORKS. However, one of the batteries was smashed. This is proof enough to me that these lamps can survive some abuse.

Highly recommended. I held off writing this review until after I purchased the 2nd lamp and field tested them. Also, I wanted to get my hands on a 2nd one before they become scarce because these are so good.

So far for it being just 2 steps. I decided to unplug it and plug it in again. No difference. Next, I saw a small note that said "if the software doesn't load automatically, install it from the DVD". Well, the Dell XPS 13 doesn't have a DVD drive... First I tried to find the software on the Targus site but it wasn't there. Next, I used an iMac (yes!) to get the content from the DVD onto a USB memory stick. I then installed the software on the Dell and plugged the dock back in. No difference - still no drivers. It just never worked.

At this price, one would think it just works, and works well. Ignoring the rather cheap build quality (especially the power connection), it's clear that this docking station needs work to be truly "just working".

But after formatting (as NTFS) a drive in this enclosure on a PC with WIndows 7, it will allow you to open the disk once on a Mac and it will immediately bee seen as a 'read only' partition. Connecting it back to the PC, it's fine and is seen as a 'read/write' partition. Connect it back to the Mac, it's 'read only' again. Take the disk out of the enclosure and put it into a cheap USB 2.0 one, and it's all fine again on both systems.

title: What a boost!  But DSM continues to have its issues.
text:
I was the proud and happy owner of a DS411j for 2 years and had read a lot about the DS413. I did see the warning signs about a "blue blinking light of death" (BBLOD) but wasn't that worried about it given that in my experience, boot time is rather long on a NAS and one can't mistake it for a defect. Anyway, I performed a migration, which was very well described on the Synology site: update to the latest DSM, export your configuration settings, take you disks out, place them in the new unit in the same order, and go! After you install the DSM on the new unit, you restore your settings and voilà! Took me all of about 20 minutes; most of it was spent taking the disks out of their old brackets and putting them into the new ones.

What happened next? Well, after putting the new DSM on it and re-booting it, the DS413 came up and indeed there was a "BBLOD" for about 2 minutes. But then -as expected- the green lights started to blink and a minute or 2 later the 'beep' told me I was in business. My data was all there, and after restoring my setting, it was as if I had my DS411j back...with some MAJOR differences.

1. the DS413 is lightning fast compared to the DS411j. It's really night and day.
2. the DSM management UI is much more responsive.
3. the DSM413 is even more quiet than the DS411j.
4. the DSM413 looks like a modern piece of hardware. The DS411j looks like a 1-st generation iPod :)
5. the applications/services on the DSM413 are super fast. They are the same ones as on the DS411j, but they work better - especially the media-related services.

Now, am I entirely happy? With the hardware it's a resounding 'YES.' Not so with the DSM (version 4.1-2668):

1. the media indexing apps make no sense. Let's take the video station application. It wants to know the folder in which the videos are stored. I have a simple structure: /video contains folders that have the name of the movie and inside them the movie file (ripped DVDs to MKV using makemkv on the Mac) with the name of the movie and an cover art file (folder.jpg) How many movies does the app find? Zero...after a few hours of 'indexing' that is...
2. the complexity of some of the connectivity apps is staggering for non-network specialists. I am lucky in that I work for a firewall company and know a few things about ports, protocols, etc. but I see so many questions on the forums about it that I suspect many folks have given up. I'm sure that DSM can be much improved in that area.

>>> UPDATE 12/24/12: the movie station app ended up finding a large number of titles, but many were wrong, and unfortunately it can't play the vast majority of my MKV's... Since I have a Pivos AIOS as my steamer, it doesn't matter, but it does show that DSM is still a rather limited media platform.

>>> UPDATE 1/5/2013: the DS413 has been up and running for 2 weeks now and performs wonderfully. It now contains well over 1TB of DVD rips (my entire collection of DVD's is safe now) and I can stream them happily to my Pivos AIOS. I'm happy!

So for me, it's an awesome NAS with all the bells and whistles I need. I highly recommend it, even if you're somewhat network "challenged."

My final word of advice: wait for a few minutes before posting/flaming here saying the unit is faulty (or a piece of crap) because you saw a "BBLOD" and returning it. It takes a few minutes to boot, which I know seems old-fashioned, but that's how these things work.

title: I so wanted to like this wireless router.
text:
Oh, how I wished I would have liked this router...

I am a big fan of Synology. I have a great DS1515+/2xDX513 setup at home to store my many digital assets and I can't stop recommending it to everyone.

So when I received an email from them about a new version of the router software, I decide to check out the router itself, as I didn't know they had one. I love the DSM interface, so moving to a great wireless router with that same interface would have been perfect.

However...once I did the setup (easy!) and customized the settings to my liking (also easy!), it was time to walk around the house and check on reach, stability, and speed of the wireless capabilities. This is when the shock happened. I have an Xfinity 250Mbps plan. When holding my iPhone 6s or MacBook Pro next to the router, I got a measly 20-25Mbps throughput using Comcast's Speedtest. When walking away from the router for roughly 20 yards to a bedroom (I have a wood frame house), the throughput dropped to well below 20Mbps. Also, the signal strength at that point had dropped to the fifties/sixties depending how high I held the devices.

Now, you say, was there something wrong with my MacBook Pro? No. I hardwired it into the router and got to 250Mbps. Then, I unplugged it and it dropped back to 20-25Mbps.

I tried one more thing. I had initially 'collapsed' the two frequencies (2.4 and 5) into a single SSID and let the router figure out what was best. I went back to having separate SSIDs for the two frequencies. There was some variation between them in terms of speed, but I still got nowhere near the 250Mbps.

At that point, I gave up. I so wanted to like this router. And, even within 30 minutes of working on the interface, I so loved it. But in the end, no matter how good the management interface, I can't deal with wireless throughput that is at 10% of what it should be, or radio strength at 50% one room away.

title: Love it
text:
First things first: I work in network security. I'm not a layman when it comes to setting up a network. The Orbi system, however, doesn't require advanced skills to set up, configure, and maintain. Because I wanted to see how easy the mobile UI was, I set it up from the iPhone app. It just worked. Within 10 minutes after my modem rebooted I was up and running again with one base station and two satellites. Nothing to it.

Next, I wanted to tweak. That, I did in the web UI. Not because I wanted to, but because you have to. I set up my VPN and DDNS, forwarded port 5000 to my Synology system, enabled remote management, etc. If you have no idea what all that means, you can stop reading now, because you'll be more than fine. For the tweakers, my only gripe is that the web UI is slow and Spartan. It's slightly better than a CLI, but I have seen much better and faster UI from products with lot less capability. And, there are some very clunky things that require some "dirty" tricks to perform, such as determining what Orbi each of the clients connect to.

Finally, I wanted to measure and see if what Netgear claims is true in that it's not a WiFi extender but uses a dedicated channel to connect the base to the satellites. Well, their claims were true and I was able to get 250Mbps regardless of whether I was tethered or on WiFi or attached to the base or any of the two satellites. Nice!

As for the price, it's hard to determine what to compare it to. A $10 a month Comcast X1 Arris modem? A $100 Netgear WiFi router with 3 "ears?" A $400 Eero system? It's hard to tell, but if you need to tweak, "door" number 1 and 3 are closed. That leaves you lots and lots of choices for number 2, but I found that the speed and signal stability of the Orbi was just too good to ignore. Spread that premium out over 3 years and it's the price of a cup of Starbucks drink every week.

One thing that would be fabulous: a mobile app that can connect to the system like Eero. Sure, I can get to my full web UI, but Eero has shown that you can have a pretty UI and geekiness at the same time.

title: No revolution here...in fact, it’s the 90’s all over again.
text:
You would think that buying a Wi-Fi system in 2020 would give you a management UI that looks like ... not the 90’s. Sure you get a fancy but very limited mobile app, but to use any advanced feature, you need to use what must be the most primitive and slow UI I have seen. Now, if it all would work, you’d say “I’ll live with it” but that’s not even the case. Want to use non-standard DNS? forget about putting a secondary IPv6 address in. Want to update the firmware? It tells you there is no new version of it, when there really is. Oh wait, it tells you that there is no new version for the satellites, but that the service is not even available for the router. Need to commit changes? You go into “black hole mode” and need to refresh yourself. And the list goes on and on... Netgear, take a look at Synology RSM and see how great a management UI can be.
Then there is the Wi-Fi 6 “thing” and the promise that it’s blazingly fast. Well, my iPhone 11 Pro Max got the cold shoulder because it got automatically secluded to the 2.4Ghz band and nothing could get it unstuck. So not only didn’t it get the “Royal” 6 treatment, it got banned to a band that made it the slowest device on my network. Funnily enough, there is no way to see how fast the satellites are “talking” to the router (again, see how SRM does this) and after many tests I ran, I didn’t notice anything different in terms of speed or coverage from before as compared to my Synology RT2600ac router with 3 (sic) MR2200ac satellites.
And then there’s stability, or should I say lack of it. My Nest cameras were kicked off the network 6 times in the span of 16 hours (which is when I decommissioned the router) and no logs would tell me what just happened.

It’s too bad that my experience was so bad that I had to return it.

Finally, some packaging advice: bundles are great, but don’t confuse bundling and discounting. If you want to sell 1 router and 2 satellites for a good combined price, that’s OK. But what if someone wants to start with 1 and then expand? Why would you not allow that? oh wait...unless your OS doesn’t allow for more than 2 satellites (which you don’t state) or you want to force your customers’ hands early on. My advice: go a la carte and have promotional bundles.

title: Very easy to set up and use; very powerful, and plenty fast
text:
I have been an executive in the network security industry for 10+ years and was looking for a versatile switch for my home office that had both LACP capabilities for link aggregation to my Synology NAS as well as 10GbE ports (RJ45 and SFP+) in a small and silent form factor. After ample research, I came across the QNAP QSW-M408-4C by what can best be described as a coincidence and was immediately intrigued as it never came up in my searches and references. Fast-forward, I did my research on it and it seemed to have all the features I was looking for at a price that was similar to models from FS, Netgear, and Cisco, but at a much smaller size and with double 10GbE ports which is a huge plus.

When I received the QNAP switch, I hooked it up to my old 1Gb Netgear managed switch and accessed its web interface. That was easy because the QNAP switch is set up by default with DHCP turned on. From there, I set a new password, configured a static IP address, set up link aggregation (LAG) on 2 ports with LACP turned on, switched my Mac Pro (2019) from 1Gb RJ45 to 10Gb using a Sonnet 10GbE SFP+ card, and checked the firmware, which was up-to-date. Next, I shut it down, unplugged the Netgear switch, and replaced it with the QNAP switch by switching over all the cables. I turned on the QNAP and voilà, everything worked. It was that simple and took less than 5 minutes.

From there, I continued to configure a few more settings, such as IGMP, RSTP, QoS, and a media-streaming VLAN. All very easy thanks to the built-in setting guide on the right of the screen.

The switch has now been on for 48 hours with almost all ports occupied and without a single lost packet.

Is this the most feature-rich switch there is? No. IS it the cheapest? No. But is it the easiest to set up and use for the vast majority of consumers who are looking for 10GbE throughput and lots of ports? Absolutely. Out-of-the-box, it will do all that in an unmanaged way. But the management UI is trivial for most and offers easy ways to set up the vast majority of features one needs in a home office or small business setting.

I'm a big fan and highly recommend the QNAP QSW-M408-4C.

title: Very useful 10Gbps managed switch for (semi) professional use
text:
It's a good thing I understand networking well enough to design and implement it. This switch is an excellent addition to my home network because it provides eight 10Gbs ports that support fiber and RJ45 SFP+ transceivers and plenty of bandwidth. I use this switch in a room with a Synology NAS and three computers.

The initial setup was challenging because as soon as I put it on my network, it claimed 192.168.2.1 as its IP address, which happened to be the same address as my wireless router. That leaves you with two choices: you either work on configuring a new fixed IP address for the switch while it blocks network access for a while for everyone, or you use a separate computer that you connect directly to the switch to configure its IP address. Since it was easy to do the former, I changed it "live" and rebooted the switch, which is not a UI feature but means you have to unplug it. However, when it came back, it still was on the original IP address. You have to commit configuration changes via the menu, which could be more intuitive, but I found it out by exploring the manual on their website. So the second time, it was all good, and I could start configuring the network. As a side note: the manual on their website does not reflect the current UI version, but the operating instructions are essentially the same.

Two of the three computers use 10Gbps fiber links, and one uses a 10Gbps RJ45 link. That's plug-and-play easy.

The NAS is connected via two 1Gbps RJ45 interfaces using LACP link aggregation. That's more challenging to set up. The unit shipped with firmware that looked like LACP was enabled; it didn't. The UI said I successfully set up a group, but it didn't. I reached out to Mokerlink support, and within a few hours, they sent me a new firmware file that did the trick. From there, it took only a few steps to make LACP work.

This switch is not hard to use. Still, it may be too complicated for most as it does require a solid understanding of networking and exposes features that only (semi) professionals will understand.

I am a fan and recommend it.
